concepts.text: Electric Charge and Current

Electric charge Q is measured in coulombs (C); one coulomb is the charge of about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons, each electron carrying 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Electric current is the rate of flow of charge through a conductor, I = Q/t, and one ampere is a flow of one coulomb per second. Conventional current is taken to flow from the positive terminal to the negative terminal outside the source, opposite to the actual direction of electron flow.

concepts.plainText: I = Q / t   (1 A = 1 C/s)

concepts.text: Types of current:
items: Direct current (DC): flows in one direction only with a steady magnitude — batteries, solar cells, rectifier outputs.
Alternating current (AC): reverses direction periodically; the Nepal mains is a 230 V, 50 Hz sinusoid.
Current is measured with an ammeter connected in series with the load (very low resistance).

concepts.text: Voltage, Potential Difference and EMF

Voltage is the electrical 'pressure' that pushes charge round a circuit. It is the work done per unit charge, V = W/Q, so one volt equals one joule per coulomb. Potential difference (p.d.) is the voltage between two points of a circuit — for example the drop across a resistor — and it exists only while current flows through resistance. Electromotive force (EMF) is the voltage that a source (cell, generator) develops internally to drive charge; it equals the terminal voltage only at no load. A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the two points (very high resistance).

concepts.plainText: V = W / Q   (1 V = 1 J/C)

rows: Produced by a source: cell, battery, generator
Exists between any two points of a circuit
Effect of current flowing through a resistance
Equals the terminal voltage only at no load
Terminal p.d. on load: V = E − I r
Always greater than or equal to terminal p.d.
Sum of p.d.s round a loop equals the EMF (KVL)

concepts.text: Electric Power and Energy

Power is the rate of doing work or of converting electrical energy, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). For any element P = VI; combining this with Ohm's law gives P = I²R and P = V²/R for a resistor, where the power appears as heat (Joule heating). Larger units are the kilowatt (1 kW = 10³ W) and the megawatt (1 MW = 10⁶ W); motor outputs are still quoted in horsepower, 1 hp = 746 W (metric hp ≈ 735.5 W).

concepts.plainText: P = V × I = I² × R = V² / R

concepts.text: Energy is the total work done over a period of time, W = Pt. The SI unit is the joule (watt-second); the commercial unit is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), also called the Board of Trade unit or simply one 'unit' — the energy used by a 1 kW load running for 1 hour. 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Electricity bills are in kWh: a 2 kW heater run for 3 hours uses 2 × 3 = 6 kWh = 2.16 × 10⁷ J.

concepts.plainText: W = P × t = V × I × t = I² × R × t = (V² / R) × t

concepts.text: Ideal and Practical Sources
Source models used in circuit analysis:
items: Ideal voltage source: terminal voltage stays fixed whatever current is drawn; internal resistance R_int = 0.
Practical voltage source: an EMF E in series with a small internal resistance r; terminal voltage V = E − Ir falls as load current rises, and the short-circuit current is E/r.
Ideal current source: delivers a fixed current whatever the load voltage; internal resistance R_int = ∞ (in parallel).
Practical current source: an ideal current source in parallel with a large but finite resistance.
To 'kill' a source in superposition or Thevenin analysis, replace a voltage source by a short circuit and a current source by an open circuit.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Charge, Power and Energy

Current can be linked to the motion of the individual charge carriers. Suppose a conductor of area A contains n free electrons per cubic metre, each drifting with an average velocity v. In a time t every electron within a length vt of the wire, that is nAvt electrons, crosses a given section, carrying a charge nAvte. Dividing by t gives the current, I = nAev. For copper n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, so 2 A in a 2.5 mm² wire corresponds to a drift speed of only about 0.06 mm/s.

concepts.latex: I = n A e v_d, \qquad Q = It, \qquad N = \frac{Q}{e}
concepts.plainText: I = n A e v_d ; Q = I t ; number of electrons N = Q/e

concepts.text: The drift speed is tiny, yet a lamp lights the instant the switch is closed. This is because the conductor is already full of free electrons: closing the switch sets up the electric field along the whole circuit almost at the speed of light, and every electron everywhere starts drifting at once. Energy is carried by the field, not by electrons travelling from the source to the load.

When a practical source of EMF E and internal resistance r feeds a load R, the current is I = E/(R + r) and the terminal voltage is V = ER/(R + r). The source generates power EI, of which I²R reaches the load and I²r is wasted as heat inside the source. The fraction delivered, V/E = R/(R + r), is the efficiency of the source; it approaches 100% when R is much larger than r. When a battery is being charged, current is forced into its positive terminal and the charger must supply V = E + Ir.

concepts.plainText: I = E/(R + r); efficiency η = I²R/(EI) = V/E = R/(R + r)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - battery feeding a load
E = 12 V, r = 0.4 ohm, load R = 5.6 ohm
Step 1: I = E / (R + r) = 12 / 6.0 = 2 A
Step 2: terminal voltage V = E - I r = 12 - 2 x 0.4 = 11.2 V
Step 3: power generated = E I = 12 x 2 = 24 W
Step 4: power to load = I^2 R = 4 x 5.6 = 22.4 W; loss inside = I^2 r = 1.6 W
Step 5: efficiency = 22.4 / 24 = 93.3 %  (= R / (R + r) = 5.6 / 6)

Worked example 2 - heating water and the cost of energy
10 kg of water is heated from 15 C to 65 C by a 2 kW, 230 V heater, efficiency 90 %.
c(water) = 4200 J/(kg C), tariff Rs 10 per kWh
Step 1: heat needed = m c dT = 10 x 4200 x 50 = 2.1 MJ
Step 2: electrical input = 2.1 MJ / 0.9 = 2.333 MJ
Step 3: in kWh: 2.333e6 / 3.6e6 = 0.648 kWh
Step 4: time = energy / power = 2.333e6 / 2000 = 1167 s = 19.4 min
Step 5: cost = 0.648 x 10 = Rs 6.48; current = 2000 / 230 = 8.70 A

Circuit analysis uses the passive sign convention to decide whether an element absorbs or delivers power. If the current enters the terminal marked + and the product VI is positive, the element absorbs power (a resistor, or a battery being charged). If the current enters the − terminal, the element delivers power VI to the rest of the circuit, as a battery does when it discharges. In any complete circuit the power delivered by the sources equals the total power absorbed.

rows: Energy of one electron through 1 V

concepts.text: Common mistakes in power and energy problems:
items: Multiplying kW by minutes or seconds and calling the answer kWh; convert the time to hours first.
Using P = V²/R with a resistance found at a different voltage for a non-ohmic lamp; the resistance of a rated lamp is assumed constant only when the question says so.
Adding the ratings of lamps connected in series; for equal-voltage lamps in series the total power is less than that of either lamp alone.
Forgetting efficiency: output power = efficiency × input power, so the input (and the bill) is output ÷ efficiency.
Treating mAh as energy; mAh is charge, and energy in Wh = voltage × Ah.

concepts.text: When a lamp or heater is rated P watts at V volts, first find its resistance R = V²/P and then work at the actual voltage. At half the rated voltage a fixed resistance takes only one-quarter of the rated power.

formulas.plainText: I = Q / t
V = W / Q
P = VI = I²R = V²/R
W = P t = V I t
V = E − I r

notes.text: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J, and one 'unit' on an electricity bill is 1 kWh. Typical MCQs ask for the kWh-to-joule conversion or the cost of running an appliance: energy (kW × hours) × tariff per unit.
Watt is a unit of power, not energy. Watt-hour and kilowatt-hour are energy units, and a watt-second is a joule. 'Rate of energy' always means power.
Conventional current flows from + to − outside the source while electrons move the other way; all circuit analysis uses conventional current.

Ideal voltage source: R_int = 0. Ideal current source: R_int = ∞. A practical source approaches the ideal when its internal resistance is much smaller (voltage source) or much larger (current source) than the load.

concepts.text: Classification by Conductivity

Every material is classed as a conductor, a semiconductor or an insulator according to how easily it lets current flow. Conductors (metals) have a large number of free electrons — roughly one per atom, about 10²⁸ per m³ — so their resistivity is very low, 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω·m, and they allow easy flow of current. Insulators have almost no free electrons because their valence electrons are tightly bound; their resistivity is enormous, above about 10¹⁰ Ω·m, and they block the flow of current. Semiconductors such as silicon and germanium lie between the two (roughly 10⁻⁵ to 10⁶ Ω·m), and their conductivity can be controlled by doping, temperature and light.

rows: Rubber, glass, plastic, wood, mica, air

concepts.text: Energy-Band View

In the band theory of solids the electrons occupy a valence band and a higher conduction band separated by a forbidden gap E_g. In a conductor the two bands overlap (or the conduction band is partly filled), so electrons move freely under even a small electric field. In a semiconductor the gap is small — about 1.1 eV for silicon and 0.7 eV for germanium — so thermal energy at room temperature lifts some electrons across it and creates electron-hole pairs; more heat or doping increases the carrier count. In an insulator the gap exceeds about 3 eV (5.5 eV for diamond), and practically no electron can cross it at ordinary temperatures and voltages.
Common Conducting Materials

Silver is the best conductor of all but is too costly for general use, so it is reserved for contacts and plating. Copper is the standard wiring material because it combines low resistivity with ductility, strength and easy soldering. Aluminium has about 1.6 times the resistivity of copper but only 30% of its density, which makes it lighter and cheaper for a given resistance — the reason overhead transmission lines use aluminium conductors with a steel core (ACSR). Tungsten has a high resistivity and the highest melting point of any metal (about 3400 °C), which suits lamp filaments. Alloys such as nichrome, manganin and constantan have high resistivity and serve as heater elements and precision resistors. The conductivity order to remember is silver > copper > gold > aluminium.
Insulating Materials and Dielectric Strength

Insulators confine current to its intended path and protect people from shock: rubber, PVC and polyethylene sheath cables; porcelain and glass support overhead lines; mica separates heater elements and commutator segments; paper, transformer oil and varnish insulate windings; dry air and SF₆ gas insulate switchgear. Dielectric strength is the maximum electric field an insulator can withstand without breaking down, quoted in kV/mm (or V/m); when it is exceeded the material punctures and conducts, and the breakdown voltage of a sheet is V_b = E_b × thickness. A good insulator also needs very high resistivity, low dielectric loss, good mechanical strength and resistance to heat and moisture.
Effect of Temperature

Heating a metal makes its lattice ions vibrate more strongly and scatter the free electrons, so its resistivity rises — a positive temperature coefficient (α ≈ +0.004/°C for copper). Heating a semiconductor or an insulator instead frees more charge carriers across the band gap, so their resistivity falls sharply — a negative temperature coefficient. This is why an NTC thermistor is made from semiconductor material and why the insulation resistance of a cable drops on a hot day. Alloys such as manganin and constantan have almost zero coefficient, making them ideal for standard resistors and meter shunts; carbon also has a small negative coefficient.
Choosing a material:
items: Conductor: lowest resistivity and cost, ductility, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance — copper for general wiring, aluminium for overhead lines, silver plating for contacts.

High-resistance element: high resistivity, high melting point, low temperature coefficient, oxidation resistance — nichrome for heaters, manganin or constantan for precision resistors, tungsten for filaments.

Insulator: very high resistivity, high dielectric strength, low loss, thermal and mechanical robustness — PVC or rubber for cables, porcelain or glass for line insulators, mica for heaters and commutators, oil and paper for transformers.
Semiconductor: controllable conductivity — silicon for diodes, transistors, ICs and solar cells; germanium in early devices; gallium arsenide for high-frequency and optoelectronic devices.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Conductors and Insulators

A free electron in a metal is accelerated by the applied field and then scattered by vibrating lattice ions and by impurity atoms, so it gains only a small average drift velocity, typically a fraction of a millimetre per second. The conductivity follows as σ = neμ, where the mobility μ = eτ/m is set by the mean time τ between collisions. Heating the metal shortens τ, so its resistivity rises almost linearly with temperature. Impurity and alloying atoms shorten τ further; the lattice and impurity parts of resistivity simply add (Matthiessen's rule), which is why alloys have much higher resistivity and a much smaller temperature coefficient than the pure metals they are made from.

concepts.plainText: v_d = I / (n e A) ;  σ = n e² τ / m = n e μ

concepts.text: The value of the temperature coefficient depends on the reference temperature at which the resistance is measured. If α₀ is referred to 0 °C, the coefficient referred to t °C is α_t = α₀/(1 + α₀t), which is smaller: copper has α₀ ≈ 0.00427 per °C but α₂₀ ≈ 0.00393 per °C. When a resistance is known at t₁ and wanted at t₂, take the ratio of the two (1 + α₀t) factors instead of simply adding α₀(t₂ − t₁) to R₁; that shortcut is exact only when α is referred to t₁ itself.

Worked example 1 - copper wire resistance and its rise with temperature
Given: l = 500 m, A = 2.5 mm² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m², ρ = 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20 °C, α₂₀ = 0.00393 per °C
R₂₀ = ρl/A = (1.72 × 10⁻⁸ × 500)/(2.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 3.44 Ω
At 60 °C: R₆₀ = R₂₀[1 + α₂₀(60 − 20)] = 3.44 × (1 + 0.1572) = 3.98 Ω
Rise = 0.54 Ω, about 15.7 % for a 40 °C rise

Worked example 2 - aluminium instead of copper, same length and resistance
ρ_Cu = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, ρ_Al = 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m; density Cu = 8.9 g/cm³, Al = 2.7 g/cm³
Same R and l, so A is proportional to ρ: A_Al/A_Cu = 2.8/1.7 = 1.65
Mass is proportional to density × A: m_Al/m_Cu = 1.65 × 2.7/8.9 = 0.50
Result: the aluminium conductor weighs about half as much for the same resistance,
although its diameter is √1.65 = 1.28 times larger

Insulation resistance is measured radially, from the conductor out through the insulation to the sheath, so the current path is short and its area is very large, the opposite of conductor resistance. For a single-core cable of length l, conductor radius r₁ and insulation outer radius r₂, adding up thin cylindrical shells gives R_ins = (ρ/2πl) ln(r₂/r₁). A longer cable therefore has more leakage paths in parallel and a lower insulation resistance, whereas its conductor resistance is higher.

concepts.plainText: R_ins = (ρ / 2π l) × ln(r2 / r1)

rows: Cotton, silk, paper impregnated or in oil
Synthetic-resin enamels, cotton with phenolic resin
Mica, glass fibre, asbestos with organic binders
Mica, glass fibre with epoxy or alkyd binders
Mica, glass fibre with silicone resins

concepts.text: Common mistakes and special cases:
items: Leaving the area in mm² in R = ρl/A: 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², and forgetting this makes R a million times too small.
Adding α₀(t₂ − t₁) to R₁ when α is referred to 0 °C; use the ratio of the (1 + α₀t) factors instead.
Stretching a wire keeps its volume constant: if the length becomes k times, the area becomes 1/k and R becomes k² times.
Confusing dielectric strength (kV/mm, a material property) with breakdown voltage (kV, which also depends on thickness).
Carbon, electrolytes and semiconductors have negative temperature coefficients; a tungsten lamp's cold resistance is only about a tenth of its hot value, hence the switch-on surge.
Some metals and compounds become superconductors below a critical temperature and lose all resistance; mercury, at about 4.2 K, was the first found.
A pure semiconductor at 0 K has an empty conduction band and behaves as an insulator.

concepts.text: Insulation resistance falls as cable length increases (R_ins is proportional to 1/l), while conductor resistance rises with length (R is proportional to l). Insulation resistance also drops sharply when the insulation is hot or damp, so readings must be compared at the same temperature.

formulas.plainText: ρ = R A / l ;  σ = 1 / ρ
σ = n × e × μ
R_t = R₀(1 + α t)
E_b = V_b / d

notes.text: Conductivity order to memorise: silver > copper > gold > aluminium (> tungsten). Copper is used instead of silver because of cost; aluminium beats copper for overhead lines because of weight and cost, not conductivity.

Sign of the temperature coefficient: metals positive, semiconductors and insulators negative. A question saying 'resistance decreases on heating' points to a semiconductor, carbon or an electrolyte — never to a pure metal.
Dielectric strength (kV/mm) is a property of the insulating material; the breakdown voltage (kV) of a part also depends on its thickness: V_b = E_b × d.

Material-to-property pairs that recur in exams: manganin and constantan — near-zero temperature coefficient (standard resistors, shunts); nichrome — high resistivity plus high working temperature (heaters); tungsten — highest melting point (filaments); mica — heat-resistant insulator with very high dielectric strength.

concepts.text: Series and Parallel Combinations
Series Circuit

In a series circuit the elements are connected end to end so that there is only one path for the current. The same current flows through every element, the applied voltage divides among them in proportion to their resistances, and the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances — always larger than the largest single resistance. If one element fails open, the whole circuit is broken; this is why a string of series-wired decorative lamps all go out when one bulb fails.
Series rules:
items: Current: the same through all — I = I₁ = I₂ = I₃
Voltage: divides — V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃, each drop being IR
Resistance: adds — R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃; for n equal resistors R_total = nR
Power: adds — P = P₁ + P₂ + P₃; the largest resistance dissipates the most power (P = I²R)
Key point: if one component fails (opens), the entire circuit stops.

concepts.text: Parallel Circuit

In a parallel circuit all elements are connected between the same two nodes, so each has the same voltage across it and the total current divides among the branches — the smallest resistance carries the largest current. The reciprocal of the total resistance is the sum of the reciprocals (conductances add), so the equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest branch. If one branch fails the others keep working, which is why household appliances are wired in parallel across the 230 V supply and can be switched independently.
Parallel rules:
items: Voltage: the same across all — V = V₁ = V₂ = V₃
Current: divides — I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃, each branch current being V/R
Resistance: 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃, i.e. G_total = G₁ + G₂ + G₃
n equal resistors: R_total = R/n; two resistors: product over sum
Key point: if one component fails, the others still work.

concepts.text: For two resistors in parallel use the product-over-sum shortcut: Rp = R1R2 / (R1 + R2). It applies to two resistors at a time only — for three, combine two first and then repeat.
Voltage Divider, Current Divider and Reduction

Two resistors in series form a voltage divider: the supply voltage splits in the ratio of the resistances, V₁ = V × R₁/(R₁ + R₂). Two resistors in parallel form a current divider: the total current splits in the inverse ratio of the resistances, I₁ = I × R₂/(R₁ + R₂) — a branch current is proportional to the other branch's resistance, or equivalently to its own conductance. These two results give voltages and currents directly without first solving for the whole circuit.

concepts.latex: V_1 = V\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}, \qquad I_1 = I\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}

concepts.text: Series-parallel reduction method:
items: Identify groups that are purely series (same current, no junction between them) or purely parallel (connected between the same two nodes).
Replace each group by its equivalent: add series resistances; use product-over-sum or reciprocals for parallel ones.
Redraw the simplified circuit and repeat until a single resistance remains, then find the total current I = V/R_eq.
Work back outwards, using the divider rules to find each branch current and voltage drop.
Check: the drops along any series path add up to the supply voltage, and the branch currents at a node add up to the current entering it.

concepts.text: Cells in series and parallel (EMF E, internal resistance r each):
items: n cells in series: total EMF = nE, total internal resistance = nr — used to obtain a higher voltage.
n identical cells in parallel: EMF = E, internal resistance = r/n — used to obtain a larger current or capacity (Ah).
Never connect cells of different EMF in parallel: the higher one drives a circulating current through the lower.
Terminal voltage of any battery on load: V = E − Ir.

concepts.text: Worked example: a 6 Ω resistor is in parallel with a 3 Ω resistor, and the pair is in series with a 4 Ω resistor across a 12 V supply. Parallel pair: R_p = (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 2 Ω. Total: R_eq = 2 + 4 = 6 Ω, so I = 12/6 = 2 A. Voltage across the pair = 2 × 2 = 4 V and across the 4 Ω resistor = 2 × 4 = 8 V (check: 4 + 8 = 12 V). Branch currents: 4/6 = 0.67 A through the 6 Ω and 4/3 = 1.33 A through the 3 Ω (check: they add to 2 A, and the smaller resistor carries the larger current).
Going Deeper: Series-Parallel Networks

Both combination rules come straight from Kirchhoff's laws. In series the single current I flows through every resistor, so KVL gives V = IR₁ + IR₂ + … = I(R₁ + R₂ + …), and the bracket is the series total. In parallel the common voltage V drives V/R₁, V/R₂, … through the branches, and KCL gives I = V(1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …), so the conductances add. Each extra series resistor adds another drop, and each extra parallel branch adds another path, which is why a series total always exceeds its largest member and a parallel equivalent always lies below its smallest.

concepts.plainText: Three in parallel: Rp = R1 R2 R3 / (R1 R2 + R2 R3 + R3 R1)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - ladder network, reduce from the far end
30 V supply -> 5 Ω in series -> node A; 20 Ω from A to the return line;
also from A: 6 Ω in series with 14 Ω to the return line
Far branch: 6 + 14 = 20 Ω
At A: 20 Ω || 20 Ω = 10 Ω
Total: R_eq = 5 + 10 = 15 Ω, so I = 30/15 = 2 A
V_A = 2 × 10 = 20 V; current in the 20 Ω shunt = 20/20 = 1 A; far branch = 1 A
V(14 Ω) = 14 V and V(6 Ω) = 6 V (check: 6 + 14 = 20 V = V_A)

Worked example 2 - a voltage divider under load
Unloaded: 12 V across R1 = 4 kΩ (top) and R2 = 2 kΩ (bottom)
V_out = 12 × 2/(4 + 2) = 4 V
Load R_L = 2 kΩ across R2: R2 || R_L = 1 kΩ
V_out = 12 × 1/(4 + 1) = 2.4 V (a 40 % fall)
Load R_L = 200 kΩ: R2 || R_L = 1.980 kΩ, V_out = 12 × 1.980/5.980 = 3.97 V
Rule: keep R_L at least 10 times, preferably 100 times, the lower divider resistor

Worked example 3 - lamps of different rating in series (resistance taken as constant)
Two 230 V lamps, 60 W and 100 W, in series across 230 V
R60 = 230²/60 = 881.7 Ω; R100 = 230²/100 = 529 Ω
I = 230/(881.7 + 529) = 0.163 A
P60 = 0.163² × 881.7 = 23.4 W; P100 = 0.163² × 529 = 14.1 W
In series the 60 W lamp glows brighter (same I, higher R);
in parallel across 230 V the 100 W lamp is brighter (same V, lower R)

rows: Divides; smallest R takes the most
Conductances add; less than the smallest

concepts.text: When N identical cells are arranged in m parallel rows, each row having n cells in series (N = mn), the battery has EMF nE and internal resistance nr/m. The current in an external resistor R is nE/(R + nr/m), and for a fixed number of cells it is greatest when the arrangement makes the internal resistance equal to the external resistance, R = nr/m, which is the maximum power transfer condition in another form.

concepts.plainText: I = nE / (R + nr/m) ;  maximum when R = nr/m

concepts.text: Special cases shorten many problems. A resistor with a short circuit across it carries no current and can be deleted, and so can a resistor that leads only to an open end. In a balanced Wheatstone bridge (R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄) the two midpoints are at the same potential, so the element bridging them carries no current and may be removed or shorted without changing anything. A uniform wire of resistance R cut into n equal pieces that are then joined in parallel gives R/n².
Common mistakes:
items: Using product-over-sum on three resistors at once; it is valid for exactly two.
Swapping resistances in the current-divider rule: the current in R₁ is I × R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
Ignoring the load on a voltage divider: a load across the lower resistor always lowers the output.
Treating two resistors as series when a branch leaves the node between them; series requires the same current with no junction in between.
Assuming the higher-wattage lamp is always brighter: true in parallel, but in series the lower-wattage (higher-resistance) lamp dissipates more.
Forgetting internal resistance: n cells in series have nr, n identical cells in parallel have r/n.

concepts.text: For power questions, pick the formula that holds the common quantity fixed: in series the current is common, so use P = I²R and the largest resistor dissipates most; in parallel the voltage is common, so use P = V²/R and the smallest resistor dissipates most.

formulas.latex: R_s = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots + R_n \quad (n \text{ equal: } nR)
formulas.plainText: Rs = R1 + R2 + ... + Rn  (n equal: nR)
1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...  (n equal: R/n)
Rp = R1 R2 / (R1 + R2)

formulas.latex: E_s = nE,\; r_s = nr \qquad E_p = E,\; r_p = \frac{r}{n}
formulas.plainText: Series cells: E_s = nE, r_s = nr ;  parallel cells: E_p = E, r_p = r/n

notes.text: A parallel equivalent is always less than the smallest branch; a series total is always more than the largest member. Use this to strike out impossible options before calculating.
Product-over-sum works for TWO resistors only. For three or more, use reciprocals or apply the shortcut twice (combine a pair, then combine the result with the third).

Two equal resistors R in parallel give R/2, three give R/3, n give R/n. In series, n equal resistors give nR — so n equal resistors in series have n² times the resistance of the same resistors in parallel.

In a current divider the branch current is proportional to the OTHER branch's resistance: I₁ = I × R₂/(R₁ + R₂). Swapping the subscripts is the classic slip; check that the smaller resistor gets the larger current.

concepts.text: Star and Delta Networks

Three resistors joined at a common point form a star (Y or T) network; three resistors joined in a closed loop form a delta (Δ, mesh or π) network. Both are three-terminal networks. Some resistor arrangements, such as a bridge, contain no purely series or parallel groups, so ordinary reduction stalls; replacing a delta by an equivalent star (or vice versa) creates series-parallel paths and the reduction can continue. The two networks are equivalent when the resistance measured between every pair of corresponding terminals is the same, so the external circuit cannot tell them apart.
Delta to Star (Δ → Y)

Let the delta have R_AB between terminals A and B, R_BC between B and C, and R_CA between C and A, and write S = R_AB + R_BC + R_CA for the sum of the three. The star resistance connected to any terminal equals the product of the two delta resistances that meet at that terminal divided by the sum S of all three delta resistances.

concepts.plainText: R_A = R_AB·R_CA / S ;  R_B = R_AB·R_BC / S

concepts.latex: R_C = \frac{R_{BC} R_{CA}}{S}, \qquad S = R_{AB} + R_{BC} + R_{CA}
concepts.plainText: R_C = R_BC·R_CA / S ;  S = R_AB + R_BC + R_CA

concepts.text: Star to Delta (Y → Δ)

Let the star have R_A, R_B and R_C connected to terminals A, B and C. The delta resistance between two terminals equals the sum of the two star resistances connected to those terminals plus their product divided by the third star resistance. An equivalent compact form uses the sum of pairwise products P = R_AR_B + R_BR_C + R_CR_A: each delta resistance is P divided by the star resistance at the opposite terminal, R_AB = P/R_C.

concepts.plainText: R_AB = R_A + R_B + (R_A × R_B) / R_C

concepts.latex: R_{BC} = R_B + R_C + \frac{R_B R_C}{R_A}, \quad R_{CA} = R_C + R_A + \frac{R_C R_A}{R_B}
concepts.plainText: R_BC = R_B + R_C + (R_B × R_C) / R_A ;  R_CA = R_C + R_A + (R_C × R_A) / R_B

concepts.text: Balanced (Equal-Resistance) Case

When all three resistances are equal the formulas collapse to a single factor of 3: a delta of three resistances R_Δ becomes a star of three resistances R_Y = R_Δ/3, and a star of three R_Y becomes a delta of 3R_Y. Star resistances are therefore the smaller ones. This is exactly the case for balanced three-phase loads, and it explains why a delta-connected load draws three times the power of the same resistors connected in star on the same line voltage.

concepts.plainText: R_Y = R_Δ / 3 ;  R_Δ = 3 × R_Y

rows: Product of the two adjacent Δ resistances ÷ sum of all three
Sum of two Y resistances + their product ÷ the third

concepts.text: When to use the conversion:
items: Unbalanced bridge networks (a Wheatstone bridge off balance), where no two resistors are simply in series or in parallel.
Finding the resistance between two points of a lattice, a cube of resistors or another symmetrical mesh.
Converting a delta-connected three-phase load to an equivalent star for per-phase analysis, and vice versa.
Simplifying T and π attenuator or filter sections — the same formulas hold for impedances in AC circuits.

concepts.text: Worked example: convert a delta with R_AB = 6 Ω, R_BC = 12 Ω and R_CA = 18 Ω to a star. S = 6 + 12 + 18 = 36 Ω. R_A = (6 × 18)/36 = 3 Ω, R_B = (6 × 12)/36 = 2 Ω, R_C = (12 × 18)/36 = 6 Ω. Check by converting back: R_AB = 3 + 2 + (3 × 2)/6 = 6 Ω, as given. Note that every star value is smaller than the delta values it came from.
Going Deeper: Star-Delta Conversion

The formulas come from one idea: with any one terminal left open, the resistance between the other two must be the same for both networks. With C open, the star shows R_A and R_B in series, while the delta shows R_AB in parallel with the path R_BC + R_CA. Writing this for all three terminal pairs gives three equations; adding two of them and subtracting the third isolates each star resistance.

concepts.plainText: R_A + R_B = R_AB (R_BC + R_CA) / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA)

concepts.text: The Y→Δ formulas are easiest to remember in conductance form, where they look exactly like the Δ→Y resistance formulas: each delta conductance equals the product of the two star conductances at its ends divided by the sum of all three star conductances. This duality is also why balanced networks convert by the single factor 3 in both directions.

concepts.plainText: G_AB = G_A·G_B / (G_A + G_B + G_C), with G = 1/R

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - unbalanced bridge between A and B
A-C = 10 Ω, A-D = 20 Ω, C-D = 20 Ω, C-B = 12 Ω, D-B = 8 Ω
Balance test: 10/12 ≠ 20/8, so the C-D arm carries current
Convert delta ACD: S = 10 + 20 + 20 = 50 Ω
  Star arm at A = (10 × 20)/50 = 4 Ω
  Star arm at C = (10 × 20)/50 = 4 Ω
  Star arm at D = (20 × 20)/50 = 8 Ω
Path via C: 4 + 12 = 16 Ω   Path via D: 8 + 8 = 16 Ω
Parallel: 16 ∥ 16 = 8 Ω
R_AB = 4 + 8 = 12 Ω

Worked example 2 - star to delta with the compact form
Star: R_A = 3 Ω, R_B = 6 Ω, R_C = 9 Ω
P = R_A R_B + R_B R_C + R_C R_A = 18 + 54 + 27 = 99 Ω²
R_AB = P / R_C = 99/9 = 11 Ω
R_BC = P / R_A = 99/3 = 33 Ω
R_CA = P / R_B = 99/6 = 16.5 Ω
Check A-B (C open): 11 ∥ (33 + 16.5) = 544.5/60.5 = 9 Ω
Star gives R_A + R_B = 3 + 6 = 9 Ω  ✓

rows: A and B become one node
Only two resistors meet at C
R_AB open, R_BC = R_B, R_CA = R_A
C is the star point itself

concepts.text: Common mistakes to avoid:
items: Using the delta side opposite the terminal instead of the two sides that meet at it in Δ→Y.
Dividing by the star arm at one of the two terminals instead of the opposite one in Y→Δ.
Converting a delta whose resistors are not all joined to the same three nodes.
Applying R_Y = R_Δ/3 to capacitors: a capacitance triples, it does not divide by three.
Reporting a current through a resistor of the converted network as if it were a current in the original resistor.

concepts.text: Quick self-checks: every star arm must be smaller than both delta sides at its terminal, and R_A·R_BC = R_B·R_CA = R_C·R_AB after a Δ→Y conversion. Also, the terminal resistance with one terminal open must equal R_A + R_B for the star — test one pair before moving on.

Choose which triangle or star to convert so that the result produces series or parallel groups with the rest of the circuit. In a bridge, converting either end delta or the star at one of the middle nodes works; pick the one with the easiest numbers.

formulas.plainText: R_A = R_AB·R_CA / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA)
R_B = R_AB·R_BC / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA)
R_C = R_BC·R_CA / (R_AB + R_BC + R_CA)
R_AB = R_A + R_B + R_A·R_B / R_C

formulas.latex: R_{BC} = R_B + R_C + \frac{R_B R_C}{R_A}, \quad R_{CA} = R_C + R_A + \frac{R_C R_A}{R_B}
formulas.plainText: R_BC = R_B + R_C + R_B·R_C / R_A ;  R_CA = R_C + R_A + R_C·R_A / R_B
R_Y = R_Δ / 3 ;  R_Δ = 3 R_Y

notes.text: Δ → Y: 'product of the two adjacent over the sum of all three' — the star resistance at a terminal uses the two delta resistors touching that terminal. Y → Δ: 'sum of two plus their product over the third' — the delta resistor between two terminals uses the two star resistors at those terminals, divided by the one opposite.
Do not reverse the factor 3: star resistances are SMALLER (R_Δ/3) and delta resistances are LARGER (3R_Y). If your star values come out bigger than the delta values, the formula has been inverted.

The conversion preserves every terminal-to-terminal resistance, so external currents and voltages are unchanged — but the currents inside the original network are lost. Convert back if a question asks for a branch current of the original delta or star.
For Y → Δ the compact form R_AB = (R_AR_B + R_BR_C + R_CR_A)/R_C saves arithmetic: compute the sum of pairwise products once and divide by the opposite star resistance for each side.

concepts.text: How Circuits Are Classified

An electric circuit is a closed path through which current can flow, made of sources and elements joined by conductors. Circuits are classified in several independent ways: by the linearity of their elements, by whether their behaviour depends on the direction of current, by whether they can supply energy, by their size relative to the signal wavelength, by whether their parameters change with time, by the connection pattern and by the kind of supply. A single circuit belongs to one class in each pair — for example a resistor network fed by a battery is linear, bilateral, passive (apart from the source), lumped, time-invariant and DC.
Linear and Non-linear Circuits

A linear circuit contains only elements whose parameters (R, L, C) do not change with the applied voltage or current: the V-I graph is a straight line through the origin and the output is proportional to the input. Linear circuits satisfy homogeneity and additivity, so the superposition theorem, Thevenin's and Norton's theorems apply. A non-linear circuit contains elements whose parameters vary with V or I — diodes, transistors, iron-cored inductors near saturation, thermistors, arcs — giving a curved V-I graph; superposition does not hold and such circuits are analysed graphically, piecewise or numerically.
Bilateral and Unilateral Circuits

A bilateral element behaves identically for current in either direction — resistors, inductors and capacitors — so a network built from them, such as a passive filter or a transmission line, is bilateral. A unilateral element behaves differently for the two directions: a diode conducts one way and blocks the other; transistors, SCRs and vacuum tubes are also unilateral. A circuit containing any unilateral element is a unilateral circuit. The reciprocity theorem applies only to linear bilateral networks.
Active and Passive Circuits

Active elements can deliver energy to a circuit or amplify a signal: voltage and current sources (batteries, generators) and devices such as transistors and op-amps that need an external supply. Passive elements only absorb, store or dissipate energy — a resistor dissipates it as heat, an inductor stores it in a magnetic field and a capacitor in an electric field — and they can never provide power gain. A circuit with at least one energy source is an active circuit; one containing only R, L and C is passive. In the component classification used in electronics and in exam keys, semiconductor devices — diodes, transistors, ICs — are counted as active components and R, L, C as passive. Strictly, by the energy definition a diode cannot supply energy or amplify, so circuit theory treats it as a passive, non-linear, unilateral element; when an MCQ lists a diode beside R, L or C, the diode is the active one.

rows: Yes as a component (semiconductor); no gain by the energy definition

concepts.text: Lumped and Distributed Circuits

In a lumped circuit each element is treated as concentrated at a point and the connecting wires have zero impedance, so voltages and currents depend on time only. This is valid when the circuit is much smaller than the wavelength of the highest frequency present — at 50 Hz the wavelength is 6000 km, so all power and audio circuits are lumped. In a distributed circuit the resistance, inductance and capacitance are spread continuously along the length — a long transmission line, an antenna or a high-speed PCB trace — and voltages and currents vary with position as well as time, so per-unit-length parameters and wave equations are needed.
Time-invariant and Time-variant Circuits

A time-invariant circuit has element values that do not change with time, so a delayed input produces the same output, equally delayed — ordinary R, L, C networks with fixed values. A time-variant circuit has parameters that change with time: a potentiometer being turned, a switched-capacitor filter, a varactor whose capacitance follows a control voltage, or a modulator. Linear time-invariant (LTI) circuits are the ones to which phasor and Laplace analysis apply directly.
Open, Closed and Short Circuits; Connection and Supply
The three states a circuit path can be in:
items: Closed circuit: a complete path — current flows and the load works normally.
Open circuit: the path is broken (open switch, blown fuse, broken wire); R = ∞, I = 0, and the full source voltage appears across the gap.
Short circuit: a path of almost zero resistance bypasses the load; V ≈ 0 across it and the current is limited only by the source's internal resistance — dangerous, hence fuses and MCBs.
Series circuit: one path, same current everywhere. Parallel circuit: same voltage across every branch. Series-parallel circuit: a mixture, reduced step by step.

DC circuit: unidirectional steady current; in steady state only resistance matters (an inductor acts as a short, a capacitor as an open). AC circuit: alternating current (Nepal mains 230 V, 50 Hz); inductors and capacitors present reactance, so impedance, phase angle and power factor enter the analysis.

rows: Linear: R, L, C; superposition holds
Non-linear: diode, transistor; curved V-I graph
Bilateral: same both ways (R, L, C)
Active: contains a source, can amplify
Passive: only R, L, C; absorbs or stores

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Testing Circuit Types

To decide whether a circuit is linear, test its elements rather than its terminal graph. A practical source, an ideal source in series with a resistor, has the terminal line V = E − Ir, which does not pass through the origin, yet the circuit is still linear because every element obeys a proportional law. Superposition then applies to the independent sources: the response to all of them together is the sum of the responses to each one acting alone.

concepts.plainText: k(v1 + v2)² ≠ k·v1² + k·v2²  (square-law element fails additivity)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - a square-law element, I = 0.2 V²
3 V alone:  I = 0.2 × 9  = 1.8 A
2 V alone:  I = 0.2 × 4  = 0.8 A
Sum of separate responses = 2.6 A
Both together (5 V): I = 0.2 × 25 = 5 A  ≠ 2.6 A
Superposition fails: the element is non-linear
At 5 V: static R  = V/I = 5/5 = 1 Ω
        dynamic r = 1/(dI/dV) = 1/(0.4 × 5) = 0.5 Ω

Active and passive behaviour is decided with the passive sign convention: take the current as entering the element's positive terminal and compute p = v × i. A positive p means the element absorbs power at that instant; a negative p means it delivers power. A capacitor or inductor may deliver power for a while, but only energy it stored earlier, so its total absorbed energy never goes negative; an element whose total can go negative is active.

rows: Element absorbs power (acts as a load)
Element delivers power (acts as a source)
Total energy absorbed can be negative

concepts.plainText: θ = 360° × l/λ, λ = c/f  (electrical length)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2 - lumped or distributed? (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
(a) 300 km power line at 50 Hz
    λ = 3 × 10^8 / 50 = 6000 km
    θ = 360 × 300/6000 = 18°  -> long-line (distributed) model advisable
(b) 30 cm PCB trace carrying 100 MHz
    λ = 3 × 10^8 / 10^8 = 3 m
    θ = 360 × 0.3/3 = 36°  -> distributed (transmission-line) effects
(c) 2 m of house wiring at 50 Hz
    θ = 360 × 2/(6 × 10^6) ≈ 0.00012°  -> lumped
Common mistakes in classifying circuits:
items: Treating linear and bilateral as the same property: a thermistor is bilateral but non-linear.
Calling a circuit non-linear just because it contains an independent source; sources do not destroy linearity of the elements.
Deciding lumped or distributed from physical size alone: the test is size compared with wavelength, so it depends on frequency.
Confusing time-variant with non-linear: R(t) = 10 + 2t Ω is linear at each instant but changes with time.
Calling an inductor or capacitor active because it can release energy; it only returns what it stored.

rows: Any lumped circuit, linear or non-linear
Linear circuits (currents and voltages, not power)
Linear part of a circuit, seen from two terminals
Linear bilateral networks with a single source
Distributed circuits such as long lines

concepts.text: In DC steady state an inductor is a short and a capacitor an open, but only after the transient has died away. At the instant of switching the opposite is true: an uncharged capacitor behaves like a short and an inductor with no current behaves like an open.

For a classification MCQ, ask five quick questions in turn: Is there a source (active)? Are all elements proportional (linear)? Do any elements depend on direction (unilateral)? Is the circuit small compared with the wavelength (lumped)? Do any values change with time (time-variant)?

formulas.plainText: f(a·x1 + b·x2) = a·f(x1) + b·f(x2)  (linearity)
R = V / I (static) ;  r = dV / dI (dynamic)
Open circuit: R = ∞, I = 0 ;  Short circuit: R ≈ 0, V ≈ 0
l << λ = c / f  (lumped-circuit condition)
w(t) = ∫ v i dt ≥ 0  (passive element)

notes.text: Labels to memorise: R, L and C are linear, bilateral and passive; a diode is non-linear and unilateral; a transistor is non-linear, unilateral and active. Most 'types of circuit' MCQs test exactly these labels.

Diode ambiguity: exam keys classify semiconductor devices (diode, transistor, IC) as active components and R, L, C as passive. By the strict energy definition a diode is passive because it cannot amplify. In an MCQ, pick the resistor, inductor or capacitor as the passive element.
Superposition, Thevenin, Norton and reciprocity require linearity, and reciprocity additionally requires bilateral elements. KCL, KVL and the maximum power transfer condition hold for any circuit.
Open circuit: I = 0 and the whole source voltage appears across the break. Short circuit: V ≈ 0 across the short and the current is very large. Fuses and MCBs protect against shorts, not opens.

concepts.text: Statement

In a linear circuit containing more than one independent source, the response at any element (the voltage across it or the current through it) equals the algebraic sum of the responses produced by each independent source acting alone, with all other independent sources deactivated. Linearity means additivity (the response to a sum of inputs is the sum of the responses) and homogeneity (scaling the input scales the response). Resistors, inductors and capacitors are linear; diodes and transistors are not, so the theorem applies to linear circuits only.
Deactivating a Source

rows: Its voltage is forced to zero; any current may pass
Its current is forced to zero; any voltage may appear
Only the ideal part is switched off
Its value is set by circuit variables, not by an input

concepts.text: Procedure
Step by step:
items: 1. Select one independent source. Replace every other independent voltage source by a short circuit and every other independent current source by an open circuit. Leave dependent sources and all passive elements untouched.
2. Solve the resulting single-source circuit by series-parallel reduction, Ohm's law or the divider rules, and record the direction (or polarity) of the response.
3. Repeat for each remaining independent source.
4. Add the partial responses algebraically: contributions in the same direction add, contributions in opposite directions subtract.

concepts.text: Why Power Cannot Be Superposed

Power is a quadratic quantity (P = I²R = V²/R), so it is not a linear response. If two sources produce currents I₁ and I₂ in the same resistor, the true power is (I₁ + I₂)²R, which contains the cross term 2I₁I₂R that is absent from I₁²R + I₂²R. Always superpose currents or voltages first and compute power from the total.

concepts.plainText: (I1 + I2)² R ≠ I1² R + I2² R

concepts.text: Worked Example

A 12 V source with a 4 Ω series resistor is connected across a 6 Ω resistor. A 3 A current source is also connected directly across the 6 Ω resistor and pushes current through it in the same direction as the 12 V source does. Find the current in the 6 Ω resistor and the power it dissipates.
Solution by superposition:
items: 12 V source alone (open the current source): 4 Ω and 6 Ω are in series, so I' = 12/(4 + 6) = 1.2 A through the 6 Ω.

3 A source alone (short the voltage source): the 4 Ω now sits in parallel with the 6 Ω across the current source; by current division I'' = 3 × 4/(4 + 6) = 1.2 A through the 6 Ω, in the same direction.
Total current: I = 1.2 + 1.2 = 2.4 A.
Power: P = 2.4² × 6 = 34.56 W. Adding the partial powers (1.2² × 6 + 1.2² × 6 = 17.28 W) would give exactly half the true value; the missing cross term is 2 × 1.2 × 1.2 × 6 = 17.28 W.

concepts.text: The same method works for AC circuits with phasors, and it is the only elementary way to handle sources of different frequencies: solve for each frequency separately and add the time-domain responses.
Going Deeper: Superposition

Why superposition works: nodal or mesh analysis of a linear circuit gives a set of linear equations [G][V] = [I_s] whose right-hand side contains only the independent sources. The solution is [V] = [G]⁻¹[I_s], so every node voltage, and hence every branch current, is a weighted sum of the source values. Each weight is the response to that source alone with the others set to zero, which is exactly what superposition computes one source at a time.

concepts.latex: y = k_1 x_1 + k_2 x_2 + \cdots + k_n x_n
concepts.plainText: y = k1·x1 + k2·x2 + ... + kn·xn (response as weighted sum of independent sources)

concepts.text: The weights k are fixed by the passive elements and dependent sources only, so measuring the response twice with known source values lets you find them and predict the response for any other values. Dependent sources change the weights but do not add terms, which is why they stay in the circuit in every step.

Worked example 1: two voltage sources feeding one node
30 V behind 6 Ω and 12 V behind 3 Ω feed node T; T to ref 6 Ω.
30 V alone (12 V shorted): 3 ∥ 6 = 2 Ω
   V_T' = 30 × 2/(6 + 2) = 7.5 V  → I' in 6 Ω = 1.25 A
12 V alone (30 V shorted): 6 ∥ 6 = 3 Ω
   V_T'' = 12 × 3/(3 + 3) = 6 V   → I'' = 1 A
Total: V_T = 13.5 V, I = 2.25 A, P = 2.25² × 6 = 30.375 W
Nodal check: (5 + 4)/(1/6 + 1/3 + 1/6) = 9/0.6667 = 13.5 V  ✓
Wrong: I'²R + I''²R = 9.375 + 6 = 15.375 W

Worked example 2: dependent source kept active
20 V behind 5 Ω feeds node A; A to ref 10 Ω;
3 A independent source into A; dependent source draws 0.1·V_A out of A.
Node conductance with dependent source: 0.2 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.4 S
20 V alone: V' = (20/5)/0.4 = 10 V
3 A alone:  V'' = 3/0.4 = 7.5 V
V_A = 17.5 V
Check KCL: (20 − 17.5)/5 + 3 = 3.5 A in;
           17.5/10 + 0.1 × 17.5 = 1.75 + 1.75 = 3.5 A out  ✓

rows: A phasor exists for one frequency only
Cross terms average to zero over a period
Circuit with a diode or lamp

concepts.text: Sources of different frequencies are a special case worth remembering. If a resistor carries a DC current I₀ and sinusoids of RMS values I₁, I₂ at other frequencies, the products of different frequencies average to zero, so the average power is (I₀² + I₁² + I₂²)R and the RMS current is the square root of the sum of squares. A series capacitor passes none of the DC part in steady state, and an inductor offers no opposition to it.

concepts.plainText: I_rms = √(I0² + I1² + I2² + ...) for components of different frequencies

concepts.text: Common mistakes:
items: Opening a voltage source or shorting a current source instead of the reverse.
Removing the internal resistance of a practical source together with its EMF.
Switching off dependent sources.
Losing track of direction: record the direction of every partial current before adding.
Adding partial powers, or adding RMS magnitudes of same-frequency phasors that are out of phase.

concepts.text: Superposition is quickest when you need the contribution of one particular source, or when each single-source circuit collapses to a simple divider. For the full solution of a many-source circuit, nodal analysis is usually shorter; use it to check your superposition answer.

formulas.plainText: I = I' + I'' + I''' + ... (one term per independent source)
P = (I' + I'')² R, not I'² R + I''² R
Current divider: I1 = I × R2 / (R1 + R2)

notes.text: Superposition works for voltage and current but NOT directly for power. Power is nonlinear (I²R): add the partial currents first, then square.
Deactivating a source means setting its value to zero: voltage source → 0 V (short), current source → 0 A (open). Never remove the internal resistance of a practical source; it stays in the circuit.
Dependent (controlled) sources are never switched off. Treat them as ordinary circuit elements in every partial solution; only independent sources are taken one at a time.

concepts.text: Statement

Any linear, bilateral two-terminal network containing sources and resistances can be replaced, as seen from those two terminals A-B, by a single voltage source V_th in series with a single resistance R_th. A load connected between A and B cannot tell the difference: it receives the same voltage and the same current from the equivalent as from the original network. The theorem is most useful when one element (the load) is changed repeatedly while the rest of the circuit stays fixed.
Thevenin Voltage V_th

V_th is the open-circuit voltage across terminals A-B: remove the load, keep every source active and find the voltage between A and B by any method (voltage division, nodal analysis, superposition). Because nothing is connected across the terminals, no current leaves them, which is why V_th is also written V_oc.
Thevenin Resistance R_th
Three ways to find R_th:
items: Kill the sources: remove the load, replace independent voltage sources by short circuits and independent current sources by open circuits, then compute the resistance seen looking into A-B.
Ratio method: R_th = V_oc/I_sc, where I_sc is the current through a short circuit placed across A-B. This is the method to use when dependent sources are present.
Test-source method: with the independent sources killed, apply a 1 V (or 1 A) test source at A-B and take R_th = V_test/I_test.

concepts.plainText: R_th = V_oc / I_sc

concepts.text: Procedure
Solving a load problem with Thevenin's theorem:
items: 1. Identify the load element, remove it and mark the terminals A-B.
2. Find V_th = V_oc across A-B with all sources active.
3. Find R_th by killing the sources (or from V_oc/I_sc).
4. Draw V_th in series with R_th and reconnect the load R_L.
5. Load current I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L); load voltage V_L = V_th × R_L/(R_th + R_L).

concepts.plainText: I_L = V_th / (R_th + R_L)

concepts.text: Worked Example
A 24 V source feeds a series string of 4 Ω and 12 Ω. A load R_L = 6 Ω is connected across the 12 Ω resistor. Find the load current using Thevenin's theorem.
Solution:
items: Remove R_L. By voltage division the open-circuit voltage across the 12 Ω is V_th = 24 × 12/(4 + 12) = 18 V.
Kill the source (replace it by a short). Looking into the terminals, the 4 Ω and 12 Ω are in parallel: R_th = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3 Ω.
Reconnect R_L: I_L = 18/(3 + 6) = 2 A and V_L = 2 × 6 = 12 V.
Check against the original circuit: 12 Ω in parallel with 6 Ω is 4 Ω, total current 24/(4 + 4) = 3 A, voltage across the parallel pair 3 × 4 = 12 V, so I_L = 12/6 = 2 A, the same answer.

concepts.text: Relation to Norton

Thevenin and Norton equivalents are source transformations of each other: I_N = V_th/R_th, R_N = R_th and V_th = I_N R_N. Both describe the same terminal behaviour; choose Thevenin when the load is in series with the source path and Norton when parallel branches dominate.
Going Deeper: Thevenin's Theorem

Why can a whole network be squeezed into just two numbers? For a linear network the relation between the terminal voltage V and the current I drawn from the terminals is a straight line. A straight line is fixed by two points: its intercept on the voltage axis (I = 0, the open-circuit voltage) and its intercept on the current axis (V = 0, the short-circuit current). A voltage source V_th in series with R_th has exactly the same straight line, so it is indistinguishable from the original network at those terminals.

concepts.plainText: V = V_th − R_th × I (terminal line of any linear two-terminal network)

concepts.text: The formal proof uses superposition. Drive the terminals with a test current source I and split the response into two parts: the voltage with all internal sources active and I = 0, which is V_oc, and the voltage due to I alone with the internal independent sources killed, which is −R_th I. Adding the two gives V = V_oc − R_th I. This is also why the theorem needs the network to be linear, while the load attached to the equivalent may be anything, even a diode.
Special cases worth recognising at a glance:
items: A resistor connected directly across an ideal voltage source does not affect V_th or R_th and can be deleted.
A resistor in series with an ideal current source does not affect V_th or R_th either; the source forces its current regardless.
A network with only resistors and dependent sources has V_th = 0; only R_th exists and it must be found with a test source.
A balanced Wheatstone bridge gives V_th = 0 across the detector terminals, so no detector current flows whatever its resistance.
An ideal current source on its own has no Thevenin equivalent (R_th would be infinite), just as an ideal voltage source has no Norton equivalent.

concepts.text:
Example 1: 12 V source with 3 Ω to node A, a 2 A source injecting into A,
6 Ω from A to B (source negative). Find the current in a 4 Ω load across A-B.
V_th (nodal at A, load removed): (12 − V)/3 + 2 = V/6
  4 − V/3 + 2 = V/6  ->  6 = V/2  ->  V_th = 12 V
R_th: short the 12 V source, open the 2 A source: 3 Ω || 6 Ω = 2 Ω
I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L) = 12/(2 + 4) = 2 A

Example 2 (dependent source): 18 V source in series with 6 Ω to node A;
a VCCS draws (1/3)·V_A amperes from A to B. Load R_L = 4 Ω.
V_oc: (18 − V)/6 = V/3  ->  3 = V/6 + V/3 = V/2  ->  V_oc = 6 V
I_sc: V_A = 0, so the VCCS carries 0 A; I_sc = 18/6 = 3 A
R_th = V_oc/I_sc = 6/3 = 2 Ω   (killing the VCCS would wrongly give 6 Ω)
I_L = 6/(2 + 4) = 1 A

Example 3 (from two load tests): a 3 Ω load draws 2 A, an 8 Ω load draws 1 A.
V_th = I(R_th + R_L) for both tests:
  2(R_th + 3) = 1(R_th + 8)  ->  2R_th + 6 = R_th + 8  ->  R_th = 2 Ω
  V_th = 2 × (2 + 3) = 10 V
Check: 10/(2 + 8) = 1 A

rows: Solve the network twice (open, then shorted)
Dependent sources, or I_sc is easy
Kill independent sources, apply 1 V or 1 A
Measure V and I for two different loads

concepts.text: The theorem carries straight over to sinusoidal steady state: V_th becomes a phasor open-circuit voltage and R_th becomes the complex impedance Z_th seen from the terminals, found with the same rules. The load current is then V_th/(Z_th + Z_L), computed with complex arithmetic; adding impedance magnitudes instead of complex values is a common error.
Common mistakes:
items: Leaving the load connected while finding V_th or R_th.
Killing a dependent source; dependent sources always stay in the circuit.
Shorting a current source (or opening a voltage source) when killing sources.
Assuming the power lost in R_th equals the power lost inside the original network; the equivalence holds only at the terminals.

concepts.text: For ladder networks, apply Thevenin step by step from the source end: convert the source and first shunt resistor to a Thevenin equivalent, add the next series resistor, repeat. Each step is a one-line divider calculation.

formulas.plainText: V_th = open-circuit voltage across A-B
R_th = V_oc / I_sc
I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L); V_L = V_th R_L/(R_th + R_L)

formulas.latex: V_{th} = V_s \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}, \qquad R_{th} = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
formulas.plainText: For a divider: V_th = V_s R2/(R1 + R2); R_th = R1 R2/(R1 + R2)

notes.text: To find R_th: kill all sources (short voltage sources, open current sources) and find the resistance seen from the terminals. Remove the load first; it is never part of R_th.
Never kill a dependent source. When one is present, find R_th from V_oc/I_sc or with a test source; killing only the independent sources and 'looking in' gives the wrong answer.
A resistor connected directly across an ideal voltage source has no effect on V_th or R_th (it is shorted when the source is killed and does not change the source voltage), so it can be ignored.

concepts.text: Statement

Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced, as seen from its terminals A-B, by an equivalent circuit consisting of a single current source I_N in parallel with a single resistance R_N. Norton's theorem is the dual of Thevenin's: where Thevenin uses a voltage source with a series resistance, Norton uses a current source with a parallel resistance. Both equivalents give identical terminal behaviour for every possible load.
Norton Current I_N

I_N is the short-circuit current: replace the load by a short circuit (a zero-resistance wire) between A and B and calculate the current flowing through that short with all sources active. It is also written I_sc. Any element that ends up in parallel with the short carries no current and can be ignored in this step.
Norton Resistance R_N

R_N is exactly the Thevenin resistance: deactivate all independent sources (voltage sources → short circuit, current sources → open circuit), remove the load and find the resistance seen from A-B. Equivalently R_N = V_oc/I_sc, which must be used when dependent sources are present.

concepts.plainText: I_N = short-circuit current; R_N = R_th

concepts.text: Using the Equivalent
With a load R_L across the Norton equivalent, I_N divides between R_N and R_L:
items: Load current I_L = I_N × R_N/(R_N + R_L) (current-divider rule).
Load voltage V_L = I_L R_L = I_N × R_N R_L/(R_N + R_L).
A short-circuit load (R_L = 0) takes the whole I_N; an open-circuit load (R_L = ∞) develops V_oc = I_N R_N.

concepts.plainText: I_L = I_N × R_N / (R_N + R_L)

concepts.text: Thevenin-Norton Conversion

Converting one form to the other is a source transformation: V_th = I_N R_N and I_N = V_th/R_th, with the same resistance in both. The current-source arrow points toward the terminal that is positive in the Thevenin form. Because R_N = R_th, having either equivalent gives the other with one multiplication or division.
Worked Example

A 20 V source with a 5 Ω series resistor is connected to terminals A-B, across which a 20 Ω resistor is permanently connected as part of the network. A load R_L = 4 Ω is then attached to A-B. Find the load current using Norton's theorem.
Solution:
items: I_N: short A-B. The short bypasses the 20 Ω resistor, so I_sc = 20/5 = 4 A.
R_N: kill the source (short it) and look into A-B: 5 Ω in parallel with 20 Ω gives (5 × 20)/(5 + 20) = 4 Ω.
Norton equivalent: 4 A in parallel with 4 Ω. With R_L = 4 Ω: I_L = 4 × 4/(4 + 4) = 2 A and V_L = 2 × 4 = 8 V.
Cross-check via Thevenin: V_th = I_N R_N = 16 V (also 20 × 20/(5 + 20) = 16 V by voltage division), so I_L = 16/(4 + 4) = 2 A.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Norton's Theorem

Norton's theorem follows directly from Thevenin's. Rearranging the terminal line V = V_th − R_th I for the current gives I = V_th/R_th − V/R_th, which is exactly the equation of a current source I_N = V_th/R_th feeding the terminals with a resistance R_N = R_th connected in parallel. The two equivalents are therefore the same straight line on the V-I plane, read once from the voltage axis and once from the current axis.

concepts.plainText: I = I_N − V/R_N (terminal line in Norton form)

concepts.text: The Norton form is the natural choice when branches meet in parallel. Parallel Norton sources simply add their currents and their conductances, which is the basis of nodal analysis and Millman's theorem. It is also the standard model for devices that behave like current sources, such as the collector of a BJT or the drain of a MOSFET in saturation, modelled as a controlled current source in parallel with an output resistance r_o.

concepts.plainText: Parallel Norton sources: I_N = sum of I_k; 1/R_N = sum of 1/R_k

concepts.text:
Example 1: 36 V source with 6 Ω to node X, 12 Ω from X to B, 4 Ω from X to A.
I_N: short A-B. 4 || 12 = 3 Ω, total 6 + 3 = 9 Ω, source current 36/9 = 4 A
  current divider into the short: I_N = 4 × 12/(12 + 4) = 3 A
R_N: short the source: (6 || 12) + 4 = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω
Check: V_oc = 36 × 12/18 = 24 V = I_N R_N = 3 × 8 V
Load 8 Ω: I_L = 3 × 8/(8 + 8) = 1.5 A

Example 2: branch 1 = 10 V in series with 2 Ω, branch 2 = 3 A source || 4 Ω,
both across A-B and both driving current towards A. Load 4 Ω.
Branch 1 in Norton form: 10/2 = 5 A || 2 Ω
Combine: I_N = 5 + 3 = 8 A,  R_N = 2 || 4 = 1.333 Ω
I_L = 8 × 1.333/(1.333 + 4) = 2 A,  V_L = 2 × 4 = 8 V

Example 3 (dependent source): 12 V source, 4 Ω carrying i_x into node A,
a CCCS draws 0.5·i_x from A to B.
Open circuit: i_x = 0.5 i_x  ->  i_x = 0, so V_oc = 12 V
Short circuit: i_x = 12/4 = 3 A, CCCS takes 1.5 A, I_N = 3 − 1.5 = 1.5 A
R_N = V_oc/I_N = 12/1.5 = 8 Ω   (killing the CCCS would wrongly give 4 Ω)

In AC circuits the Norton current is the phasor short-circuit current and R_N becomes the complex impedance Z_N = Z_th; the conversion I_N = V_th/Z_th needs complex division, so both magnitude and angle change. The load current is then I_N Z_N/(Z_N + Z_L).
Special cases and common mistakes:
items: An ideal current source in series with a resistor is still just that ideal current source; the resistor affects neither I_N nor R_N.
Any resistor connected directly across A-B carries no current when A-B is shorted, but it does appear in R_N.
Dependent sources stay active when finding both I_N and R_N.
The direction of I_N matters: combining two Norton sources that drive opposite ways means subtracting their currents.

concepts.text: The Thevenin and Norton equivalents dissipate different internal power for the same load, so neither can be used to find the efficiency or losses of the original network; they are valid only for what happens at the terminals and in the load.

formulas.plainText: I_N = I_sc = V_th / R_th
R_N = R_th = V_oc / I_sc
V_th = I_N × R_N

formulas.latex: I_L = I_N \frac{R_N}{R_N + R_L}, \qquad V_L = I_L R_L
formulas.plainText: I_L = I_N R_N/(R_N + R_L); V_L = I_L R_L

notes.text: Norton and Thevenin share the same resistance; only the source changes. Given one equivalent, the other is one step away: I_N = V_th/R_th or V_th = I_N R_N.

Series versus parallel is the whole point. A current source in series with a resistor, or a voltage source in parallel with one, is never a valid Norton or Thevenin form; such a resistor does not affect the terminals at all.
When finding I_sc, any resistor connected directly across the shorted terminals carries zero current and drops out of the calculation; it reappears when you find R_N.

concepts.text: Statement

A source, or any linear network reduced to its Thevenin equivalent V_th and R_th, delivers maximum power to a resistive load when the load resistance equals the Thevenin (source) resistance: R_L = R_th. The theorem applies to a fixed source and an adjustable load. If instead the load is fixed and the source resistance can be chosen, load power is maximised by making the source resistance as small as possible.
Derivation Outline
Starting from the Thevenin equivalent with load R_L:
items: Load current I = V_th/(R_th + R_L), so load power P_L = I²R_L = V_th² R_L/(R_th + R_L)².
Set dP_L/dR_L = 0: (R_th + R_L)² − 2R_L(R_th + R_L) = 0, which gives R_L = R_th.
Substituting R_L = R_th gives P_max = V_th²/(4R_th). In Norton form, with V_th = I_N R_N, P_max = I_N² R_N/4.

concepts.plainText: Pmax = Vth² / (4 Rth)
Pmax = I_N² R_N / 4

concepts.text: Efficiency at Maximum Power

At R_L = R_th the same current flows through R_th and R_L, so as much power is lost inside the source as is delivered to the load: efficiency η = R_L/(R_th + R_L) = 50 %. Power systems therefore never operate at matched load; they keep R_th much smaller than R_L so that efficiency approaches 100 %. Communication, audio and antenna circuits accept the 50 % efficiency because extracting the largest possible signal power matters more than wasting a little source power.

concepts.plainText: η = R_L / (R_th + R_L) = 1/2 (50 %) when R_L = R_th

concepts.text: AC Circuits

For an AC source with Thevenin impedance Z_th = R_th + jX_th, maximum power is delivered to a load equal to the complex conjugate, Z_L = Z_th* = R_th − jX_th: the reactances cancel and the resistances match. If the load must be purely resistive, the best choice is R_L = |Z_th| = √(R_th² + X_th²). If only the magnitude of a fixed-angle load can be varied, choose |Z_L| = |Z_th|.

concepts.plainText: Z_L = conjugate of Z_th = R_th − jX_th

concepts.text: Applications
Impedance matching, where signal power counts more than efficiency:
items: Audio systems: matching an amplifier output to a loudspeaker, often through an output transformer.
Communication circuits: matching a transmitter or receiver to its antenna and transmission line.
Matching transformers, which make a load look like R_th to the source (turns ratio √(R_th/R_L)).
Solar photovoltaic systems: maximum-power-point tracking keeps the panel at its optimum load.

concepts.text: Worked Example

A source of 20 V with internal resistance 5 Ω feeds a variable load. For maximum power choose R_L = 5 Ω: I = 20/(5 + 5) = 2 A and P_max = 20²/(4 × 5) = 20 W; the source resistance also dissipates 2² × 5 = 20 W, so the efficiency is 50 %. With R_L = 15 Ω instead, I = 1 A, P_L = 15 W and efficiency = 15/20 = 75 %: less power to the load, but a higher fraction of the total.
Going Deeper: Maximum Power Transfer

The load power has a peak because two effects pull in opposite directions. A small load resistance draws a large current but develops almost no voltage, while a large load resistance develops nearly the full V_th but draws almost no current. Writing x = R_L/R_th turns the load-power equation into a single universal curve, P_L/P_max = 4x/(1 + x)², which is the same for every source. The curve is flat near its peak, so a moderate mismatch costs surprisingly little power.

concepts.plainText: P_L / Pmax = 4x / (1 + x)², where x = R_L / R_th

concepts.text: The table shows a useful pairing rule: two loads R1 and R2 with R1 × R2 = R_th² receive exactly the same power, one below and one above the peak (0.5 and 2, or 0.25 and 4, in the table). To find the loads that receive a chosen fraction k of P_max, set 4x/(1 + x)² = k and solve the quadratic k x² + (2k − 4) x + k = 0; its two roots are always reciprocals of each other. Efficiency, on the other hand, keeps rising with R_L, so a designer who wants both reasonable power and good efficiency chooses R_L a few times larger than R_th.

Example 1: 48 V source, 8 Ω in series, 24 Ω across the output,
then 4 Ω in series to terminals a-b. Find R_L and P_max.
V_th = 48 × 24/(8 + 24) = 36 V   (open-circuit voltage of the divider)
R_th = (8 ∥ 24) + 4 = 6 + 4 = 10 Ω   (source replaced by a short)
Choose R_L = R_th = 10 Ω
I = V_th/(2R_th) = 36/20 = 1.8 A
P_max = V_th²/(4R_th) = 1296/40 = 32.4 W
Check: I²R_L = 1.8² × 10 = 32.4 W

Example 2: 120 V rms, 50 Hz source with Z_th = 8 + j6 Ω.
(a) Conjugate load: Z_L = 8 − j6 Ω, i.e. 8 Ω with a capacitor of X_C = 6 Ω
    C = 1/(2π × 50 × 6) = 530.5 µF
    Total Z = 16 Ω (reactances cancel), I = 120/16 = 7.5 A
    P = V²/(4R_th) = 14400/32 = 450 W
(b) Purely resistive load: R_L = |Z_th| = √(8² + 6²) = 10 Ω
    |Z_total| = |18 + j6| = 18.97 Ω, I = 120/18.97 = 6.325 A
    P = I²R_L = 40 × 10 = 400 W   (less than the 450 W of case a)
Common mistakes in maximum power problems:
items: Using V_th²/R_th or V_th²/(2R_th) instead of V_th²/(4R_th); these give four and two times the true answer.
Matching the load to the source EMF's own internal resistance while ignoring other resistors in the network; always find R_th at the load terminals.
Setting dependent sources to zero when finding R_th; only independent sources are removed.
Taking Z_L = Z_th instead of its conjugate in AC problems; the reactances must cancel, not add.
Applying R_L = R_th when the load is fixed and the source resistance is the variable; then R_s should be as small as possible.
Mixing peak and rms values: with a peak amplitude V_m the matched power is V_m²/(8R_th).

concepts.text: Special cases are handled with the same idea. When a network contains dependent sources, R_th is found from the ratio V_oc/I_sc or by applying a test source with the independent sources removed, and the maximum power follows directly from the two terminal measurements. When a fixed resistor sits in series with the variable load, it is simply absorbed into the source side, so the variable part must equal R_th plus that fixed resistance. For a sinusoidal source, the conjugate-matched power is V_th²/(4R_th) with rms values, and the reactance of the source never dissipates power.

concepts.plainText: Pmax = V_oc × I_sc / 4, with R_th = V_oc / I_sc

concepts.text: Before computing, ask two questions: which element is variable (load or source), and is the load allowed to have reactance? A variable resistive load on a DC network gives R_L = R_th; a fully adjustable AC load gives Z_th*; a resistive AC load gives |Z_th|; a variable source resistance gives R_s = 0.

formulas.plainText: Condition: R_L = R_th
Pmax = Vth² / (4 Rth) = I_N² R_N / 4
P_L = Vth² R_L / (Rth + R_L)²
η = R_L / (R_th + R_L), × 100 for percent
AC: Z_L = complex conjugate of Z_th

notes.text: Whenever V_th and R_th are given and the maximum load power is asked, the answer is V_th²/4R_th. Remember the 4 (not 2): half the voltage appears across the load, and half the total power reaches it.
Maximum power transfer and maximum efficiency are different goals. At matched load efficiency is only 50 %; as R_L → ∞ efficiency → 100 % but the load power → 0.
Conjugate matching in AC means equal resistance and equal-but-opposite reactance. A common exam variant: 'source 4 + j3 Ω, purely resistive load' has the answer R_L = |Z_th| = 5 Ω, not 4 Ω.

concepts.text: Reactance

In AC circuits, inductors and capacitors oppose current with frequency-dependent reactance instead of fixed resistance. Reactance is measured in ohms, but unlike resistance it stores energy during one part of the cycle and returns it during the next, so it dissipates no average power.

concepts.latex: X_L = 2\pi f L, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}
concepts.plainText: XL = 2 pi f L; XC = 1/(2 pi f C)

concepts.text: Behaviour with frequency:
items: X_L rises with frequency: an inductor blocks high frequencies and passes DC (X_L = 0 at f = 0).
X_C falls with frequency: a capacitor blocks DC and low frequencies (X_C = ∞ at f = 0).
In a pure inductor, current LAGS voltage by 90°.
In a pure capacitor, current LEADS voltage by 90° (mnemonic CIVIL: in C, I leads V; V leads I in L).

concepts.text: Series R-L Circuit

The same current I flows through R and L. V_R = IR is in phase with I, while V_L = IX_L leads I by 90°. Adding them as phasors gives the supply voltage V = I√(R² + X_L²), so Z = √(R² + X_L²) and the current lags the voltage by φ = tan⁻¹(X_L/R), somewhere between 0° (pure R) and 90° (pure L). The power factor cos φ = R/Z is lagging. Phasor diagram in words: draw I along the reference axis; V_R lies along I, V_L points straight up, and their resultant V sits at angle φ above I. (Many books write the phase angle as θ instead of φ.)
Series R-C Circuit

Now V_C = IX_C lags I by 90°. The impedance is Z = √(R² + X_C²), the current leads the voltage by φ = tan⁻¹(X_C/R), and the power factor cos φ = R/Z is leading. Phasor diagram: V_R along I, V_C pointing straight down, and the resultant V below I at angle φ.
Series RLC Impedance
Impedance combines resistance and net reactance as a phasor. V_L and V_C are 180° apart, so only the difference X_L − X_C matters. Its magnitude and phase angle are:

concepts.plainText: Z = sqrt(R² + (XL − XC)²); tan(phi) = (XL − XC)/R

concepts.text: Transient Response to DC Switching

When a DC source is switched onto an R-L or R-C circuit the current or voltage does not jump; it follows an exponential curve governed by the time constant τ. R-L circuit: τ = L/R and the current rises as i = (V/R)(1 − e^(−t/τ)). R-C circuit: τ = RC; the capacitor voltage rises as v_C = V(1 − e^(−t/τ)) while the charging current decays as (V/R)e^(−t/τ). In one time constant a rising quantity reaches 63.2 % of its final value (a decaying one falls to 36.8 %), and after 5τ the transient is complete for practical purposes (99.3 %).

concepts.plainText: τ(RL) = L/R; τ(RC) = RC

concepts.text: Going Deeper: R-L, R-C and R-L-C Circuits

Complex (j) notation turns phasor diagrams into ordinary algebra. A resistor has impedance R, an inductor +jX_L and a capacitor −jX_C, so a series circuit has Z = R + j(X_L − X_C). The magnitude |Z| gives the current from I = V/|Z|, and the angle φ = tan⁻¹((X_L − X_C)/R) tells you whether the current lags (positive φ) or leads (negative φ). Multiplying every side of the impedance triangle by I gives the voltage triangle V_R, V_X and V, which is why voltmeter readings in a series circuit never add arithmetically.

concepts.plainText: Z = R + j(XL − XC) = |Z| at angle φ; I = V / |Z|

concepts.text: In a parallel circuit the voltage is common and the branch currents add as phasors. The resistor current I_R = V/R is in phase with V, the inductor current I_L = V/X_L lags by 90° and the capacitor current I_C = V/X_C leads by 90°, so I_L and I_C partly cancel. The total current is √(I_R² + (I_C − I_L)²) and the combined impedance is V divided by that current, always smaller than the smallest branch opposition in an R-L or R-C pair.

concepts.latex: I = \sqrt{I_R^2 + (I_C - I_L)^2}, \qquad Z_{R\parallel X} = \frac{R X}{\sqrt{R^2 + X^2}}
concepts.plainText: I = √(I_R² + (I_C − I_L)²); R in parallel with X: Z = RX / √(R² + X²)

rows: Raising f in an R-L pair

concepts.text: The transient results come from one first-order equation. For an R-L circuit, KVL gives V = Ri + L di/dt, whose solution rising from zero is i = (V/R)(1 − e^(−Rt/L)); the R-C case is identical with v_C in place of i and RC in place of L/R. Two continuity rules fix the starting point: capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot jump. So at t = 0+ an uncharged capacitor acts as a short circuit and an inductor carrying no initial current as an open circuit, while in DC steady state the capacitor is open and the inductor is a short. The time to reach any voltage v on a rising curve follows by taking logarithms.

concepts.plainText: t = τ ln(V / (V − v)); time to 50 % = 0.693 τ

concepts.text:
Example 1: series R = 15 Ω, L = 0.2 H, C = 80 µF on 230 V, 50 Hz
X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.2 = 62.83 Ω
X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × 80×10⁻⁶) = 39.79 Ω
Net X = 62.83 − 39.79 = 23.04 Ω (inductive)
|Z| = √(15² + 23.04²) = 27.50 Ω
I = 230/27.50 = 8.37 A, lagging by φ = tan⁻¹(23.04/15) = 56.9°
Power factor = cos φ = 15/27.50 = 0.546 lagging
V_R = 125.5 V, V_L = 525.6 V, V_C = 332.8 V
Note V_L = 526 V exceeds the 230 V supply; check √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²) = 230 V

Example 2: R = 47 kΩ, C = 22 µF (uncharged) switched onto 12 V DC
τ = RC = 47×10³ × 22×10⁻⁶ = 1.034 s
Initial current i(0+) = V/R = 12/47 kΩ = 0.255 mA (capacitor acts as a short)
At t = 1 s: v_C = 12(1 − e^(−1/1.034)) = 7.44 V
Time to reach 9 V: t = τ ln(12/(12 − 9)) = 1.034 × ln 4 = 1.43 s
Practically fully charged after 5τ = 5.2 s
Common mistakes and how to avoid them:
items: Adding V_R + V_L + V_C, or R + X, arithmetically; use the square root of squares because they are 90° apart.
Forgetting to convert mH to H and µF to F before using 2πfL or 1/(2πfC).
Assuming X_L > X_C always means lagging current; that is true in series, but in parallel the larger current flows in the smaller reactance, so X_L > X_C makes a parallel circuit capacitive.
Using τ = R/L or τ = RL for an R-L circuit; the correct time constant is L/R.
Treating a capacitor as an open circuit at the switching instant; it is a short at t = 0+ and an open circuit only in DC steady state.

concepts.text: For any series circuit question, write X_L, X_C, net X, |Z|, I and φ in that order before looking at the options. Most wrong options come from skipping the net-reactance step or from adding R and X directly.

formulas.plainText: XL = 2 pi f L
XC = 1/(2 pi f C)
Z = sqrt(R² + (XL − XC)²)
tan φ = (XL − XC)/R; power factor cos φ = R/Z
τ = L/R for R-L; τ = RC for R-C

notes.text: Check units before computing: f in Hz, L in henries, C in farads. Convert mH and µF first; unit slips are the number one cause of wrong options that LOOK right.
Impedances add as phasors, not arithmetically: R and X are at right angles, hence the square root of squares. Z = R + X_L is never correct.

One time constant: 63.2 % of the final value reached on a rising curve, 36.8 % left on a falling one. Five time constants: steady state (99.3 %). Both R-L and R-C use the same 63.2 % rule; only τ differs.
