concepts.text: Resonance Condition

Resonance occurs in a circuit containing both L and C at the frequency where the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal, X_L = X_C. Because X_L rises and X_C falls with frequency, there is exactly one such frequency, the resonant frequency f_r. Setting 2πf_rL = 1/(2πf_rC) gives f_r = 1/(2π√LC), which depends only on L and C and not on R.

concepts.plainText: fr = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC))

concepts.text: Series Resonance
A series RLC circuit resonates at the frequency where X_L = X_C. The reactances cancel, impedance drops to R (minimum), and current is maximum and in phase with the voltage.
At series resonance:
items: Z = R (minimum), I = V/R (maximum), phase angle 0°.
Power factor = 1 (unity); the circuit looks purely resistive.
Voltage across L and across C can each exceed the supply (Q times larger): voltage magnification.
Called an acceptor circuit because it accepts (passes) the resonant frequency and rejects others.
Below f_r the circuit is capacitive (current leads); above f_r it is inductive (current lags).

concepts.text: Quality Factor, Bandwidth and Half-Power Frequencies

The quality factor Q measures how sharp (selective) the resonance is: Q = X_L/R = X_C/R = (1/R)√(L/C), evaluated at f_r. It also equals the voltage magnification V_L/V = V_C/V at resonance. The bandwidth BW = f₂ − f₁ is the range between the two half-power (cut-off) frequencies at which the current falls to 1/√2 (70.7 %) of its maximum and the power to half; there Z = √2 R and the phase angle is ±45°. Since BW = f_r/Q = R/(2πL), a high Q means a narrow bandwidth.

concepts.plainText: Q = XL/R = (1/R) sqrt(L/C) = fr/BW
BW = f2 − f1 = fr/Q = R/(2 pi L)

concepts.text: Parallel Resonance

Parallel resonance is the dual: impedance is maximum (ideally infinite for lossless L and C), the line current is minimum and in phase with the supply, so it is a rejector circuit that blocks the resonant frequency. The branch currents in L and C are each Q times the line current (current magnification) and cancel each other. For a practical coil of resistance R in parallel with C, the impedance at resonance is the dynamic impedance Z_r = L/(CR), purely resistive. Used in tuning circuits (radio, TV) and as the tank circuit of LC oscillators.

concepts.plainText: Dynamic impedance at parallel resonance: Zr = L/(CR)

rows: Rejector; band-stop filter, tank circuit of oscillators

concepts.text: Worked Example

A series circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 100 mH and C = 10 µF and is fed from 100 V. LC = 0.1 × 10 × 10⁻⁶ = 10⁻⁶, so f_r = 1/(2π × 10⁻³) = 159.2 Hz. At resonance I = 100/10 = 10 A; X_L = 2π × 159.2 × 0.1 = 100 Ω, so Q = 100/10 = 10 (also (1/10)√(0.1/10⁻⁵) = 10); V_L = V_C = 10 × 100 = 1000 V, ten times the supply; BW = f_r/Q = 15.9 Hz, so the half-power frequencies are roughly 151 Hz and 167 Hz.
Going Deeper: Resonance

The half-power frequencies come from setting the net reactance equal to R, so that |Z| = √2 R. For a series circuit this gives ωL − 1/(ωC) = ±R, a quadratic in ω whose two positive roots are ω₁ and ω₂. Subtracting the two equations shows ω₂ − ω₁ = R/L exactly, which is why BW = R/(2πL) holds for any Q. Multiplying them shows ω₁ω₂ = 1/(LC) = ω₀², so the resonant frequency is the geometric mean of f₁ and f₂, and the curve is only symmetric about f_r when Q is high (about 10 or more).

concepts.plainText: fr = √(f1 f2); Q = 2π × energy stored / energy lost per cycle

concepts.text: At resonance energy swings back and forth between the magnetic field of L and the electric field of C, and the total stored energy stays constant at ½ L I_m² = ½ C V_Cm². The source only has to replace the energy burnt in R, which is I²R per second. The ratio of stored energy to energy lost per cycle, multiplied by 2π, is the general definition of Q; for a series circuit it reduces to ω₀L/R, and it also equals the ratio of the reactive power in L (or C) to the active power in R.

A practical tank circuit is a coil (L in series with its resistance R) in parallel with C. Making the admittance purely real gives a resonant frequency slightly below the ideal value, and resonance exists only if R < √(L/C). At that frequency the impedance is L/(CR) = Q²R, where Q = ω₀L/R is the coil Q. For the ideal three-branch parallel RLC circuit the roles of R are reversed: Q = R√(C/L) and BW = 1/(2πRC), so a larger parallel resistance gives a sharper response.

concepts.plainText: Coil in parallel with C: fr = (1/2π)√(1/(LC) − R²/L²)

rows: Lower coil Q, lower Z_r, wider BW
Current in L and C branches

concepts.text:
Example 2: coil L = 500 µH, R = 25 Ω, in parallel with C = 500 pF, V = 10 V
Ideal f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π × 5 × 10⁻⁷) = 318.3 kHz
R²/L² = 2.5 × 10⁹, tiny beside 1/(LC) = 4 × 10¹², so f_r ≈ 318.2 kHz
Q = ω0 L / R = (2 × 10⁶ × 5 × 10⁻⁴)/25 = 40
Z_r = L/(CR) = 5 × 10⁻⁴/(5 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 25) = 40 kΩ (= Q²R)
Line current = 10 V / 40 kΩ = 0.25 mA
Capacitor current ≈ V ω0 C = 10 × 2 × 10⁶ × 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 10 mA = Q × 0.25 mA
Common mistakes:
items: Using BW = R/L and calling it hertz: R/L is the bandwidth in rad/s; divide by 2π for Hz.
Taking f_r as the arithmetic mean of f₁ and f₂; it is the geometric mean, and the difference matters when Q is low.
Applying the series formulas Q = (1/R)√(L/C) and BW = R/(2πL) to a three-branch parallel circuit, where Q = R√(C/L).
Forgetting that a parallel circuit is inductive below f_r and capacitive above it, the reverse of a series circuit.
Using rms current in ½ L I² when the peak stored energy is asked for.

concepts.text: Quick checks: at f_r, X_L = X_C = √(L/C); Q (series) = √(L/C)/R; BW = f_r/Q. If an answer for f_r changes when only R changes (series circuit), a formula has been misapplied.

formulas.plainText: fr = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC))
Q = XL/R = (1/R) sqrt(L/C) = fr/BW
BW = f2 − f1 = R/(2 pi L)

formulas.latex: V_L = V_C = Q V \quad \text{(series, at } f_r)
formulas.plainText: At series resonance: V_L = V_C = Q × V
Parallel resonance dynamic impedance: Zr = L/(CR)

notes.text: Series resonance: minimum Z, maximum I. Parallel resonance: maximum Z, minimum I. Swapping these is the most common trap.
f_r depends only on L and C. Changing R alters Q, the bandwidth and the peak current, but never the resonant frequency of a series circuit.
At the half-power frequencies the current is 0.707 I_max, not 0.5 I_max: power is halved because it goes as I². The impedance there is √2 R.

concepts.text: Instantaneous Power

With v = V_m sin ωt and i = I_m sin(ωt − φ), the instantaneous power is p = vi = VI cos φ − VI cos(2ωt − φ), where V and I are rms values. It pulsates at twice the supply frequency about the constant term VI cos φ, which is the average (active) power actually converted into heat, light or mechanical work. The oscillating part averages to zero over a cycle and represents energy shuttling back and forth between the source and the magnetic or electric fields of L and C.
The Power Triangle

In AC circuits three powers coexist: active power P (watts) does real work, reactive power Q (VAR) oscillates in and out of fields, and apparent power S (VA) is the phasor total. Drawn as a right-angled triangle, P is the base, Q the vertical side and S the hypotenuse; the angle between S and P is the phase angle φ between voltage and current.

concepts.latex: P = VI\cos\phi,\quad Q = VI\sin\phi,\quad S = VI = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}
concepts.plainText: P = VI cos phi; Q = VI sin phi; S = VI = sqrt(P² + Q²)

concepts.text: The three powers:
items: Real (active) power P = VI cos φ, unit watt (W): the actual power consumed; read by a wattmeter; P = I²R.
Reactive power Q = VI sin φ, unit volt-ampere reactive (VAR): oscillates between source and load and does no net work; Q = I²X.
Apparent power S = VI, unit volt-ampere (VA): the total power the source must supply; transformers and alternators are rated in kVA.
Power triangle: S² = P² + Q², so S = √(P² + Q²); also P = S cos φ and Q = S sin φ.

concepts.text: Power Factor

Power factor pf = cos φ = P/S = R/Z is the fraction of the apparent power that does real work, where φ is the angle between voltage and current. In practical units pf = kW/kVA. It ranges from 0 to 1 and is described as lagging or leading according to whether the current lags or leads the voltage.
Power factor cos φ:
items: Unity for a pure resistance; zero for a pure L or a pure C.
Lagging for inductive loads (motors, transformers, fluorescent-lamp chokes); leading for capacitive loads (capacitor banks, synchronous condensers).
Low power factor means larger current for the same real power; capacitor banks are added in parallel to improve it.

concepts.text: Why a low power factor is bad:
items: For fixed P and V the current is I = P/(V cos φ): a lower pf means a larger current.
Conductors, switchgear, transformers and alternators must be rated for more kVA to deliver the same kW.
Higher I²R copper losses and a larger voltage drop in lines, so poorer voltage regulation.
Utilities charge a penalty when the consumer's pf falls below about 0.8 to 0.9.

concepts.text: Power-Factor Correction

A capacitor connected in parallel with an inductive load supplies leading reactive power Q_C that cancels part of the lagging Q of the load; P is unchanged, so S and the line current fall and φ shrinks. To raise the power factor from cos φ₁ to cos φ₂ the capacitor must supply Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂) VAR, and its capacitance follows from Q_C = V²/X_C = 2πfCV².

concepts.plainText: Q_C = P (tan φ1 − tan φ2); C = Q_C / (2 pi f V²)

concepts.text: Worked Example

A 230 V, 50 Hz single-phase motor draws 10 A at 0.7 power factor lagging. S = 230 × 10 = 2300 VA; P = 2300 × 0.7 = 1610 W; Q = √(2300² − 1610²) = 1643 VAR lagging. To raise the pf to 0.95: tan φ₁ = 1.020 and tan φ₂ = 0.329, so Q_C = 1610 × (1.020 − 0.329) = 1113 VAR and C = 1113/(2π × 50 × 230²) = 67 µF. The new apparent power is S = 1610/0.95 = 1695 VA and the line current falls from 10 A to 1695/230 = 7.4 A while the motor still receives 1610 W.
Going Deeper: Power in AC Circuits

Multiplying v = √2 V sin ωt by i = √2 I sin(ωt − φ) and using 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B) gives the expression below. The first term is constant; the second oscillates at 2ω and averages to zero over a cycle, so the average power is VI cos φ. Whenever φ is not zero, p goes negative for part of each cycle, which is the moment the inductor or capacitor hands stored energy back to the source.

concepts.plainText: p(t) = VI cos φ − VI cos(2ωt − φ)

concepts.text: Complex power combines all three powers in one phasor: S = V I*, where I* is the conjugate of the current phasor. Its real part is P and its imaginary part is Q, with Q positive for an inductive load and negative for a capacitive one. The conjugate is essential; multiplying V by I directly gives the wrong angle. In terms of the load elements, P = I²R = V_R²/R and Q = I²X = V_X²/X.

concepts.latex: S = V I^{*} = P + jQ, \qquad |S| = VI
concepts.plainText: S = V × conj(I) = P + jQ; |S| = VI

concepts.text: When several loads share a supply, complex power is conserved: the total P is the sum of the individual P values and the total Q is the algebraic sum of the Q values, with capacitive VAR counted as negative. The individual kVA figures do not simply add unless all loads have the same power factor. This is the basis of every power-factor correction calculation: the capacitor adds negative Q while leaving P untouched.

concepts.plainText: Line loss ratio = (cos φ1 / cos φ2)², for the same P and V

concepts.text:
Example 1: 230 V supply; heater 2 kW (pf 1) + motor 3 kW at 0.75 lagging
Motor: tan φ = tan(cos⁻¹ 0.75) = 0.882, Q = 3 × 0.882 = 2.65 kVAR
Total P = 2 + 3 = 5 kW
Total Q = 0 + 2.65 = 2.65 kVAR (lagging)
S = √(5² + 2.65²) = 5.66 kVA (not 2 + 4 = 6 kVA)
Overall pf = 5/5.66 = 0.884 lagging
Line current = 5660/230 = 24.6 A

Example 2: 40 kW, 400 V, 50 Hz single-phase load, pf 0.7 -> 0.95 lagging
tan φ1 = tan(cos⁻¹ 0.7) = 1.020, tan φ2 = tan(cos⁻¹ 0.95) = 0.329
Q_C = 40 × (1.020 − 0.329) = 27.7 kVAR
C = Q_C/(2πfV²) = 27 660/(2π × 50 × 400²) = 550 µF
Current before = 40 000/(400 × 0.7) = 142.9 A
Current after = 40 000/(400 × 0.95) = 105.3 A
Active power stays 40 kW; only Q and S change
Common mistakes:
items: Taking V × I as the power in watts; it is the apparent power in VA unless the pf is 1.
Adding kVA values of different loads arithmetically instead of adding P and Q separately.
Using peak values in VI cos φ: with V_m and I_m the average power is (V_m I_m/2) cos φ.
Forgetting that a capacitor's VAR output is 2πfCV², so it falls with the square of the voltage.
Over-sizing the correction bank so the net Q goes negative and the pf becomes leading.

concepts.text: Keep these tan φ values ready for correction problems: pf 0.9 -> 0.484, 0.866 -> 0.577, 0.8 -> 0.75, 0.707 -> 1.0, 0.6 -> 1.333. Then Q = P tan φ and Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂) take seconds.

formulas.plainText: P = V I cos φ, watts
Q = V I sin φ, volt-amperes reactive
S = V I = sqrt(P² + Q²), volt-amperes
pf = cos phi = P/S = R/Z
Capacitor VAR for pf correction: Q_C = P (tan φ1 − tan φ2)

notes.text: Given P and S, power factor is simply P/S. Given R and Z, it is R/Z. Both forms appear in board exams.
Reactive power is not 'lost' (its average is zero), but the extra current it demands causes real I²R losses and voltage drops in the supply lines. That is why utilities penalise a low power factor.

Sign convention: inductive Q is positive (absorbed, lagging pf) and capacitive Q is negative (supplied, leading pf). A capacitor 'generates' the reactive power that an inductor 'consumes', which is the whole basis of pf correction.

concepts.text: Principle: Electromagnetic Induction

All AC generators work on Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction: whenever the magnetic flux linking a coil changes, an EMF is induced in the coil equal to the rate of change of flux linkage NΦ. Lenz's law supplies the sign: the induced EMF acts so as to oppose the change producing it, which is the minus sign in the equation. The flux linkage can be changed by moving a coil through a stationary field or by moving the field past a stationary coil; both arrangements are used in practice.

concepts.plainText: e = −N dΦ/dt

concepts.text: For a straight conductor of length l moving at velocity v through a uniform field B, the induced EMF is e = Blv when the motion is perpendicular to the field, and e = Blv sin θ when the velocity makes an angle θ with the field lines. The direction of the induced current is given by Fleming's right-hand rule: hold the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand mutually perpendicular; with the thumb along the motion of the conductor and the forefinger along the field (N to S), the middle finger points along the induced current.

concepts.plainText: e = B l v sin θ

concepts.text: EMF of a Coil Rotating in a Uniform Field

Let a coil of N turns, each of area A, rotate at constant angular velocity ω in a uniform field B, starting with its plane perpendicular to the field, where the flux linked is maximum, Φm = BA. After time t the coil has turned through θ = ωt and the flux linked is Φ = BA cos ωt. Differentiating and applying Faraday's law gives e = NBAω sin ωt = Em sin ωt: the EMF is sinusoidal, with peak Em = NBAω = 2πfNBA. The EMF is zero where the flux linkage is maximum (coil plane perpendicular to B) and maximum where the flux linkage is zero (coil plane parallel to B), because there the coil sides cut the field lines fastest.

concepts.plainText: Φ = B A cos(ωt)
e = −N dΦ/dt = N B A ω sin(ωt) = Em sin(ωt)

concepts.text: What follows from the derivation:
items: The generated voltage and the current it drives have the general AC form v(t) = Vm sin(ωt + φ) and i(t) = Im sin(ωt + φ).
Vm and Im are the peak values, ω = 2πf rad/s is the angular frequency and φ is the phase angle.
Em = NBAω is proportional to the turns, flux density, coil area and speed; raising the speed raises both Em and f.
EMF and flux linkage are 90° apart: e is zero when Φ is maximum and maximum when Φ is zero.
Instantaneous EMF e = Em sin θ, where θ is the angle turned from the position of maximum flux linkage.

concepts.text: Single-Loop Alternator
Main parts of an elementary alternator:
items: Field system: permanent magnets or DC-excited electromagnets (N and S poles) that set up a uniform magnetic field.
Armature: the coil or loop in which the EMF is induced, mounted on a shaft driven by a prime mover (turbine or engine).
Slip rings: two continuous metal rings fixed to the shaft, each permanently connected to one end of the coil.
Brushes: stationary carbon blocks pressing on the slip rings, carrying the alternating current to the external load.
Because each coil end stays on its own ring, the load current reverses with the coil EMF, so the output is alternating.

concepts.text: In a 2-pole machine one complete revolution of the coil produces exactly one cycle of EMF: the load current flows one way while a coil side passes the N pole and the other way while it passes the S pole. In a machine with P poles each coil side passes P/2 pairs of poles per revolution, giving P/2 cycles, so the frequency is f = PN/120 with N the speed in revolutions per minute. Practical alternators are built inside out: the DC-excited field rotates and the armature winding is stationary, so the high-voltage, high-current output needs no sliding contacts and only the small field current passes through slip rings.

concepts.plainText: f = P N / 120  (P = number of poles, N in rpm)

rows: Very high (up to tens of kV)

concepts.text: Worked example: a 2-pole alternator is driven at 3000 rpm; its coil has 100 turns, each of area 0.02 m², in a uniform field of 0.5 T. Frequency f = PN/120 = 2 × 3000/120 = 50 Hz, so ω = 2π × 50 = 314 rad/s (equal to the mechanical speed 3000 × 2π/60 = 314 rad/s, as expected for 2 poles). Peak EMF Em = NBAω = 100 × 0.5 × 0.02 × 314 = 314 V and the RMS output is 314/√2 = 222 V. When the coil has turned 30° from the position of maximum flux linkage, e = 314 sin 30° = 157 V.
Going Deeper: The Generated EMF

The rotating-coil result can also be obtained by the cutting-of-flux method. Let each coil side have active length l and move in a circle of radius b/2, where b is the coil breadth, so its peripheral speed is v = ωb/2. At angle θ from the position of maximum flux linkage, only the velocity component perpendicular to the field, v sin θ, cuts flux, so each side generates Blv sin θ. The two sides of a turn add, giving 2Blv sin θ = Blbω sin θ = BAω sin θ per turn, exactly the result of the flux-linkage method.

concepts.latex: e = 2NBlv\sin\theta = NBA\omega\sin\theta,\qquad v = \frac{\omega b}{2},\; A = lb
concepts.plainText: e = 2 N B l v sin θ = N B A ω sin θ, with v = ωb/2 and A = l b

concepts.text: Since BA is the maximum flux Φm linked by one turn, the peak EMF can be written Em = NΦmω = 2πfNΦm. Dividing by √2 gives the RMS value, E = 4.44 f N Φm, the same EMF equation later used for transformers. It shows directly that at a fixed frequency the generated voltage is set by the turns and the flux, which in a real alternator is controlled through the DC field current.

concepts.plainText: E(rms) = 2π f N Φm / √2 = 4.44 f N Φm

concepts.text: In a machine with P poles, a coil side passes a N–S pole pair, and so completes one electrical cycle (360 electrical degrees), each time the rotor turns 720/P mechanical degrees. Electrical angle is therefore P/2 times mechanical angle, and the electrical angular frequency is P/2 times the mechanical angular speed. Putting the mechanical speed as N rpm gives f = (P/2)(N/60) = PN/120.

concepts.plainText: θe = (P/2) θm,  ωe = (P/2) ωm

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: 4-pole alternator, 1500 rpm, coil of 120 turns, Φm = 8 mWb
Frequency:      f = PN/120 = 4 × 1500/120 = 50 Hz
Peak EMF:       Em = 2πfNΦm = 2π × 50 × 120 × 0.008 = 301.6 V
RMS EMF:        E = Em/√2 = 213.3 V   (4.44 × 50 × 120 × 0.008 = 213.1 V)
Rotor turns 30° mechanical from the maximum-flux position:
                θe = (4/2) × 30° = 60° electrical
                e = 301.6 sin 60° = 261.2 V

Worked example 2 (cutting-of-flux method): 2-pole field, B = 0.8 T
Coil: 50 turns, length l = 0.4 m, breadth b = 0.2 m, speed 1500 rpm
ω = 2π × 1500/60 = 157.08 rad/s, f = 2 × 1500/120 = 25 Hz
Side speed:     v = ω × b/2 = 157.08 × 0.1 = 15.71 m/s
Per side peak:  Blv = 0.8 × 0.4 × 15.71 = 5.03 V
Per turn:       2 × 5.03 = 10.05 V
Coil peak:      Em = 50 × 10.05 = 502.7 V
Check:          NBAω = 50 × 0.8 × 0.08 × 157.08 = 502.7 V
Common mistakes in generation problems:
items: Putting the speed in rpm straight into Em = NBAω; convert first with ω = 2πN/60.
Leaving the coil area in cm²; 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m².
Using only one coil side in the cutting method; both sides of a turn contribute Blv.
Confusing poles with pole pairs: f = PN/120 uses the number of poles P, while f = p × n uses pole pairs p and speed n in rev/s.
Measuring θ from the wrong position: e = Em sin θ holds with θ taken from the plane of maximum flux linkage, not from the plane parallel to the field.
Treating the peak value as the RMS value when the question asks for the voltmeter reading.

concepts.text: At constant field, EMF and frequency are both proportional to speed: running an alternator 20% slow lowers both f and E by 20%. For a fixed 50 Hz, slow water turbines need many poles (24 poles at 250 rpm), while steam turbines use 2 or 4 poles at 3000 or 1500 rpm.

formulas.plainText: e = −N dΦ/dt
e = B l v sin θ
e = N B A ω sin(ωt) = Em sin(ωt)
Em = N B A ω = 2π f N B A

notes.text: f = PN/120 is a staple MCQ: 2 poles at 3000 rpm, 4 poles at 1500 rpm, 6 poles at 1000 rpm and 8 poles at 750 rpm all give 50 Hz. Rearranged, the synchronous speed is N = 120f/P.

The induced EMF is maximum when the flux linkage is zero (coil plane parallel to the field) and zero when the flux linkage is maximum (coil plane perpendicular to the field). Many candidates state the reverse; EMF depends on the rate of change of flux, not on the flux itself.

Slip rings deliver the coil EMF unchanged, so the output is AC; a commutator reverses the connections every half cycle, so the output is unidirectional. The EMF generated in the rotating coil is sinusoidal in both machines — only the collecting device differs.

Fleming's right-hand rule is for generators (direction of induced current); the left-hand rule is for motors (direction of force). In both, thumb = motion, forefinger = field, middle finger = current.

concepts.text: Peak, Average, and RMS Values

An alternating quantity changes continuously, so a single number is needed to state how large it is. Four are used: the peak (maximum) value, the peak-to-peak value, the average (mean) value and the root-mean-square (RMS) or effective value. Unless a question says otherwise, AC voltages and currents are always quoted as RMS values, and the sinusoidal factors below apply only to sine waves.
Peak value (Vm): the maximum value of the waveform amplitude, measured from zero; for a symmetrical wave the peak-to-peak value is 2Vm.
items: Vm = 1.414 × Vrms (sine wave)
Form factor = Vrms / Vavg = 1.11
Peak factor = Vm / Vrms = 1.414
Peak-to-peak value Vp-p = 2 Vm

concepts.text: Average Value

The average value is the arithmetic mean of the instantaneous values over a stated interval. For a symmetrical wave such as a sinusoid the positive and negative half cycles cancel, so the average over a full cycle is zero; the average is therefore taken over one half cycle. Integrating Vm sin θ from 0 to π and dividing by π gives Vavg = 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm. The average value is what a rectifier delivers as DC and what a moving-coil instrument responds to.

concepts.plainText: Vavg = (1/π) ∫₀^π Vm sin θ dθ = 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm

concepts.text: RMS (Effective) Value

The RMS value of an alternating current is the steady direct current that produces the same heat in the same resistance in the same time; it is also called the effective or virtual value. Because heating power is proportional to the square of the current, the RMS value is found by squaring the instantaneous values, taking the mean of the squares over a full cycle and then the square root. For i = Im sin θ the mean of sin²θ over a cycle is 1/2, giving Irms = Im/√2 = 0.707 Im. RMS values are used in every power calculation, P = Vrms Irms cos φ = Irms² R, and are what AC meters indicate.

concepts.plainText: Vrms = 0.707 Vm; Vavg = 0.637 Vm
Irms = √[(1/2π) ∫₀^2π Im² sin²θ dθ] = Im/√2

concepts.text: Form Factor and Peak Factor

Form factor = RMS value / average value describes the shape of the wave: 1.11 for a sine, 1.0 for a square wave and 1.155 for a triangular wave. Average-reading (rectifier) meters are scaled by 1.11 so that they read RMS for sinusoids. Peak (crest) factor = peak value / RMS value shows how far the peaks rise above the effective value: 1.414 for a sine, 1.0 for a square wave and 1.732 for a triangular wave; it matters for insulation stress and for the voltage ratings of capacitors and semiconductors.
Why Meters Read RMS

Moving-iron, electrodynamometer and thermal instruments respond to the square of the current, so they indicate true RMS for any waveform. Rectifier-type moving-coil meters and most low-cost digital multimeters measure the average of the rectified wave and multiply it by the sine form factor 1.11, so they read correctly only for sinusoidal quantities. Because heating, power and equipment ratings all depend on the RMS value, nameplate figures and the 230 V mains are always RMS.

Worked examples:
1. Nepal mains, 230 V RMS: Vm = 230 × √2 = 325 V, Vp-p = 650 V, and Vavg (half cycle) = 0.637 × 325 = 207 V, or 230/1.11 = 207 V.
2. A sinusoidal current of peak 10 A flows in 5 Ω: Irms = 7.07 A, Iavg = 6.37 A, and the power is Irms² R = 7.07² × 5 = 250 W, not Im² R = 500 W.
3. A square wave of amplitude 100 V: Vrms = Vavg = 100 V, so its form factor and peak factor are both 1.
Going Deeper: RMS, Average and Waveform Factors

The factor 1/√2 comes from the identity sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2. Over one full cycle the cos 2θ term averages to zero, so the mean of sin²θ is exactly 1/2 and the mean of v² is Vm²/2; its square root is Vm/√2. The result is the same for a cosine or for a sine with any phase angle, and it does not depend on frequency. For the average, the area under one half cycle of Vm sin θ is 2Vm, and dividing by the base π gives 2Vm/π.

concepts.plainText: Mean of sin²θ = (1/2π) ∫₀^2π sin²θ dθ = 1/2

concepts.text: When a waveform is the sum of a DC component and sinusoids of different frequencies, every cross-product term averages to zero over a common period. The heating effects therefore add: the square of the total RMS value equals the sum of the squares of the individual RMS values. RMS values of components at different frequencies never add arithmetically, and the full-cycle average of such a wave equals its DC component alone.

concepts.plainText: Vrms = √(V0² + V1rms² + V2rms² + …), V0 = DC component

concepts.text:
Example 1: v = 10 + 20 sin ωt V applied to a 10 Ω resistor
DC part: V0 = 10 V
AC part: RMS = 20/√2 = 14.14 V
Vrms = √(10² + 14.14²) = √(100 + 200) = 17.32 V
Full-cycle average = V0 = 10 V
P = Vrms²/R = 300/10 = 30 W
Check: DC alone gives 10 W, AC alone gives 20 W, total 30 W

Example 2: half-wave rectified sine, peak Vm = 100 V
Average: one hump has area 2Vm, the period is 2π
  Vavg = 2Vm/(2π) = Vm/π = 31.8 V
RMS: v² exists for only half the period
  mean of v² = (1/2)(Vm²/2) = Vm²/4, so Vrms = Vm/2 = 50 V
Form factor = 50/31.8 = 1.57
Peak factor = 100/50 = 2.0

concepts.plainText: Rectangular pulse train 0 to Vm with duty cycle D: Vavg = D Vm, Vrms = √D Vm

concepts.text:
Example 3: pulse train switching 0 V to 12 V, duty cycle D = 0.25
Vavg = D × Vm = 0.25 × 12 = 3 V
Vrms = √D × Vm = 0.5 × 12 = 6 V
Form factor = 6/3 = 2.0, peak factor = 12/6 = 2.0
A sine-calibrated average-reading meter would show 1.11 × 3 = 3.33 V
Common mistakes to avoid:
items: Using 0.707 and 0.637 for square, triangular, pulse or rectified waves; these factors belong to the pure sine only.
Adding RMS values of components of different frequencies arithmetically instead of as a root-sum-of-squares.
Using the peak value in P = I²R, which doubles the power of a sine wave.
Taking the full-cycle average of a half-wave rectified sine as 0.637 Vm; it is Vm/π = 0.318 Vm.
Forgetting that the peak-to-peak value is twice the peak value, i.e. 2√2 times the RMS value for a sine.

concepts.text: Sanity check: the RMS value is never smaller than the average of the magnitude, and the peak is never smaller than the RMS value, so form factor and peak factor are always at least 1. They equal 1 only when the magnitude is constant, as for DC or a square wave. A computed factor below 1 means a slip in the working.

formulas.plainText: Vrms = 0.707 Vm
Vavg = 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm
FF = Vrms/Vavg = 1.11
Peak factor = Vm/Vrms = √2 = 1.414
Vm = √2 Vrms = 1.414 Vrms

notes.text: Mains '230 V' is an RMS value. Its peak is 230 × 1.414 ≈ 325 V — a favourite one-mark question.
For non-sinusoidal waveforms the 0.707/0.637 factors do NOT apply; compute RMS and average from their definitions (for a square wave RMS = average = Vm).

The average of any symmetrical AC wave over a full cycle is zero. When a question asks for 'the average value' of a sinusoid it means the half-cycle average 0.637 Vm unless it explicitly says 'over a complete cycle'.
Power always uses RMS values: P = Irms² R = Vrms² / R. Substituting the peak value doubles the answer for a sine wave, because Im² = 2 Irms².

concepts.text: Three Phase System

A three-phase system has three sinusoidal EMFs of equal magnitude and frequency, displaced from one another by 120° (one third of a cycle). They are generated by three identical windings spaced 120° apart on the stator of an alternator and are labelled R, Y, B (red, yellow, blue) or L1, L2, L3. Phase sequence is the order in which the three voltages reach their positive maxima; RYB is the normal (positive) sequence, and interchanging any two lines reverses it and reverses the rotation of three-phase motors. In a balanced system the three voltages add to zero at every instant.

concepts.plainText: vR = Vm sin ωt, vY = Vm sin(ωt − 120°), vB = Vm sin(ωt − 240°) = Vm sin(ωt + 120°)

concepts.text: STAR (Y) CONNECTION:
items: Line voltage V_L = √3 × phase voltage V_ph; each line voltage leads its phase voltage by 30°.
Line current I_L = phase current I_ph.
Has a neutral wire: the common point of the three windings, giving a 3-phase 4-wire supply.
Two voltages are available: V_ph between any line and neutral, V_L between any two lines.

concepts.text: In a star connection one end of each winding (or load impedance) is joined to a common neutral point N and the other ends go to the three lines. Each line is in series with its winding, so I_L = I_ph. The voltage between two lines is the phasor difference of two phase voltages 120° apart, which has magnitude 2 V_ph cos 30° = √3 V_ph. In a balanced star system the three line currents sum to zero, so the neutral carries no current and a 3-wire supply is possible; the neutral is needed when single-phase loads make the system unbalanced.
DELTA (Δ) CONNECTION:
items: Line voltage V_L = phase voltage V_ph.
Line current I_L = √3 × phase current I_ph; each line current lags its phase current by 30°.
No neutral wire: only a 3-phase 3-wire supply is possible.
Used for motor windings, transformer windings and balanced three-phase loads.

concepts.text: In a delta connection the three windings are joined end to end in a closed loop and the lines are taken from the three junctions. Each winding is connected directly across two lines, so V_L = V_ph. Each line current is the phasor difference of the two phase currents meeting at that junction, 120° apart, hence I_L = √3 I_ph. Delta has no neutral and cannot supply single-phase loads at phase voltage, but the same impedance connected in delta draws three times the power it draws in star from the same lines.
Three Phase Power
THREE PHASE POWER (balanced load; φ is the angle between phase voltage and phase current):
items: Active power P = √3 × V_L × I_L × cos φ = 3 × V_ph × I_ph × cos φ, in watts (W).
Reactive power Q = √3 × V_L × I_L × sin φ = 3 × V_ph × I_ph × sin φ, in VAR.
Apparent power S = √3 × V_L × I_L = 3 × V_ph × I_ph = √(P² + Q²), in VA.
Power factor cos φ = P / S; the formulas are identical for star and delta connections.

concepts.plainText: P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ
Q = √3 V_L I_L sin φ;  S = √3 V_L I_L = √(P² + Q²)

concepts.text: A load is balanced when the three phase impedances are equal in magnitude and angle; the three currents are then equal and 120° apart, the neutral current is zero, and the total instantaneous power is constant at 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ instead of pulsating at twice the supply frequency as in a single-phase circuit. With an unbalanced load the three currents differ, the neutral (if present) carries their phasor sum, and the power in each phase must be calculated separately and added. Unequal loads on a 3-wire star system also shift the neutral point, giving unequal phase voltages.
Advantages of three phase over single phase:
items: Constant, non-pulsating power flow, so motors and generators run smoothly with less vibration.
Three-phase motors are self-starting (the windings produce a rotating magnetic field), simpler and smaller for the same output.
For the same power, voltage and line loss, three-phase 3-wire transmission needs only about 75 % of the conductor material of single-phase 2-wire.
Two voltages (400 V and 230 V) are available from one 4-wire supply, and rectified three-phase output has less ripple.

concepts.text: Power in a three-phase, three-wire circuit is measured by the two-wattmeter method: the current coil of each wattmeter is placed in one line and its pressure coil is connected between that line and the third line. The total power is P = W1 + W2 for any load, balanced or unbalanced. For a balanced load the readings also give the power factor from tan φ = √3 (W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2): the readings are equal at unity power factor, one reads zero at cos φ = 0.5, and below 0.5 one reading is negative and must be subtracted.

Worked example (Nepal supply): the three-phase distribution voltage is 400 V between lines, so the phase (line-to-neutral) voltage is 400/√3 = 231 V, the single-phase 230 V household supply. A balanced star load draws 20 A per line at power factor 0.8 lagging: S = √3 × 400 × 20 = 13.86 kVA, P = 13.86 × 0.8 = 11.08 kW and Q = 13.86 × 0.6 = 8.31 kVAR; each phase impedance is Z = 231/20 = 11.55 Ω. Reconnected in delta on the same 400 V lines, each impedance sees 400 V, so I_ph = 400/11.55 = 34.6 A, I_L = √3 × 34.6 = 60 A and P = √3 × 400 × 60 × 0.8 = 33.3 kW, three times the star value.
Going Deeper: Solving Three-Phase Circuits

Take V_R = V_ph∠0° and V_Y = V_ph∠−120°. The line voltage V_RY = V_R − V_Y is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by V_R and −V_Y, which are 60° apart, so its length is 2 V_ph cos 30° = √3 V_ph and it sits 30° ahead of V_R. The same construction applied to the two phase currents meeting at a delta junction gives I_L = √3 I_ph, with the line current 30° behind the phase current.

A balanced circuit is solved on a per-phase basis: find one phase voltage, divide by one phase impedance, and multiply the phase power by three. A delta load may first be replaced by its equivalent star, Z_Y = Z_Δ/3, and solved with V_ph = V_L/√3; both routes give the same line current and total power. The load angle φ is the angle of the phase impedance Z = R + jX, so cos φ = R/|Z| and P = 3 I_ph² R.

concepts.plainText: W1 = V_L I_L cos(30° − φ), W2 = V_L I_L cos(30° + φ) (balanced load, lagging pf)

concepts.text: Adding the two readings gives W1 + W2 = √3 V_L I_L cos φ, the total active power. Subtracting gives W1 − W2 = V_L I_L sin φ, so the total reactive power of a balanced load is Q = √3 (W1 − W2), and dividing the two results gives the familiar tan φ = √3 (W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2). The table shows how the ratio of the readings changes with the load power factor.

rows: W2 reads zero, W1 gives total power
Reverse a coil of W2 and subtract its reading
Readings equal and opposite, total power zero

concepts.text:
Example 2: two-wattmeter method, balanced load, W1 = 5 kW, W2 = 2 kW
P = W1 + W2 = 7 kW
tan φ = √3 (W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2) = √3 × 3/7 = 0.742
φ = 36.6°, power factor = cos 36.6° = 0.803 lagging
Q = √3 (W1 − W2) = √3 × 3 = 5.20 kVAR
Check: P tan φ = 7 × 0.742 = 5.20 kVAR

Example 3: unbalanced 4-wire star, resistive loads, RYB sequence
I_R = 10∠0° A = 10 + j0
I_Y = 20∠−120° A = −10 − j17.32
I_B = 30∠+120° A = −15 + j25.98
I_N = I_R + I_Y + I_B = −15 + j8.66
|I_N| = √(15² + 8.66²) = √(225 + 75) = 17.32 A
Note: the arithmetic sum 60 A or the difference 20 A are both wrong
Special cases worth remembering (balanced resistive loads, fixed supply):
items: Star load on a 3-wire supply with one phase open: the other two phases are in series across V_L and the total power falls to one half.
Delta load with one phase open: the remaining two phases still see V_L, so the total power falls to two thirds.
Star-delta starter: each winding gets V_L/√3 at starting, so line current and starting torque both fall to one third of their direct-on-line delta values.
An unbalanced 3-phase 4-wire load needs three wattmeters; two are enough for any 3-wire load (Blondel's theorem: one fewer than the number of wires).

concepts.text: Common slips: dividing the line voltage by a star phase impedance (use V_ph = V_L/√3), using √3 twice (√3 V_L I_L already contains it), taking φ as the 30° line-phase shift, ignoring the minus sign of a reversed wattmeter reading, and adding unbalanced line currents arithmetically to find the neutral current instead of as phasors.

formulas.plainText: Star: V_L = √3 V_ph, I_L = I_ph
Delta: V_L = V_ph, I_L = √3 I_ph
P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ
Q = √3 V_L I_L sin φ
S = √3 V_L I_L = √(P² + Q²)

notes.text: In Nepal the line voltage is 400 V and the phase voltage is 400/√3 ≈ 230 V. When a question says 'a 400 V three-phase supply', 400 V is the line voltage; a 'three-phase 230 V' figure is the phase voltage.

The √3 appears only once: P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ uses line values and P = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ uses phase values. Writing 3 V_L I_L cos φ or √3 V_ph I_ph cos φ is wrong; both correct forms give the same answer for star and for delta.
φ in the power formulas is the angle between phase voltage and phase current, i.e. the impedance angle of the load — never the 30° between line and phase quantities.

The same impedance draws three times the power and three times the line current in delta as in star from the same supply. Star-delta starters use this to cut the starting current of induction motors to one third.

concepts.text: Semiconductor Basics

Intrinsic: a pure semiconductor (e.g. pure Si or Ge) with equal numbers of free electrons and holes.
N-type: doped with a pentavalent impurity (e.g. phosphorus); the majority carriers are electrons.
P-type: doped with a trivalent impurity (e.g. boron); the majority carriers are holes.
Covalent Bonding, Energy Bands and Band Gap

Silicon and germanium are tetravalent: each atom shares its four valence electrons with four neighbours, forming a covalent crystal with no free carriers at absolute zero. At room temperature thermal energy breaks a few bonds, releasing a free electron and leaving a vacancy, or hole, that behaves as a positive carrier. Electrons and holes are generated in pairs, so in intrinsic material n = p = n_i, about 1.5 × 10^10 per cm³ for silicon at 300 K. When a free electron falls back into a hole the pair disappears; this is recombination.

In a solid the allowed electron energies form bands. The valence band holds the bonding electrons and the conduction band holds electrons that are free to move; the forbidden gap between them is the band gap E_g. In a conductor the two bands overlap, so electrons flow with no extra energy. In an insulator the gap is large (more than about 5 eV) and practically no electrons cross it. A semiconductor has a small gap, about 1.1 eV for silicon and 0.72 eV for germanium, so room-temperature thermal energy lifts a useful number of electrons into the conduction band.

rows: Very high, falls as temperature rises

concepts.text: Doping: N-type and P-type
Adding a controlled impurity, roughly one atom in a million, changes the conductivity by many orders of magnitude and makes the material extrinsic:
items: N-type: a pentavalent donor (phosphorus, arsenic or antimony) bonds with four neighbours and donates its fifth electron to the conduction band. Electrons are the majority carriers and holes the minority; each ionised donor is a fixed positive charge.

P-type: a trivalent acceptor (boron, aluminium, gallium or indium) has only three valence electrons, so one bond is incomplete. It accepts an electron from a neighbour, creating a hole. Holes are the majority carriers and electrons the minority; each ionised acceptor is a fixed negative charge.
Both types stay electrically neutral overall, because the fixed impurity ions exactly balance the free majority carriers.

concepts.text: Carrier Concentrations, Drift and Diffusion

In thermal equilibrium the product of the electron and hole concentrations is fixed for a given material and temperature, whatever the doping: this is the mass-action law. Adding donors raises n and lowers p by the same factor, so heavily doped material has very few minority carriers. For a typical silicon doping of 10^16 donors per cm³ the electron concentration is about 10^16 per cm³, while the hole concentration falls to about 2.25 × 10^4 per cm³.

concepts.plainText: n x p = ni^2   (mass-action law)

concepts.text: Two mechanisms move carriers. Drift is motion under an electric field: the drift velocity v_d = μE is proportional to the field through the mobility μ, and the conductivity is σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p). Diffusion is motion from a region of high carrier concentration to one of low concentration, with no field needed; it is the process that forms the depletion region of a pn junction. Electrons are more mobile than holes (in silicon roughly 1350 against 480 cm²/V·s), which is one reason n-channel devices are faster than p-channel ones.
Silicon versus Germanium and the Effect of Temperature

Silicon dominates because its larger band gap gives a leakage current about a thousand times smaller than germanium, it tolerates junction temperatures of 150 to 200 °C against 75 to 100 °C for germanium, it is abundant, and it grows a stable native oxide (SiO₂) that is essential for MOSFETs. Germanium offers higher carrier mobility and a lower forward drop of 0.3 V, so it survives in a few high-frequency and low-drop applications. In both materials raising the temperature generates more electron-hole pairs, so resistance falls: semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance, the opposite of metals.
Going Deeper: Carrier Statistics and Transport

The shortcut n ≈ N_D rests on two facts. At room temperature practically every donor and acceptor is ionised, and the crystal must stay electrically neutral, so the positive charges (holes plus ionised donors) equal the negative charges (electrons plus ionised acceptors): p + N_D = n + N_A. Combining this with the mass-action law gives a quadratic in n whose exact solution is shown below. When the net doping |N_D − N_A| is much larger than n_i, the square root collapses and n ≈ N_D − N_A, with p = n_i²/n.

concepts.plainText: n = (ND - NA)/2 + sqrt( ((ND - NA)/2)^2 + ni^2 ),  then p = ni^2 / n

concepts.text: A doped sample passes through three temperature regions. At very low temperature (freeze-out) the dopant electrons are not ionised and conductivity is tiny. Over a wide middle range, which includes room temperature, the dopants are fully ionised and the majority concentration stays close to the doping level: this is the extrinsic region where devices are designed to work. At high temperature n_i, which rises steeply as T^(3/2) e^(−E_g/2kT) and roughly doubles for every 10 °C near room temperature in silicon, overtakes the doping and the sample behaves as intrinsic material. The larger band gap of silicon pushes this limit far above that of germanium.

concepts.plainText: Jn = q n mu_n E + q Dn dn/dx;   D / mu = kT/q = VT (Einstein relation)

concepts.text: The total current of each carrier type is the sum of a drift term driven by the field and a diffusion term driven by the concentration gradient. For holes the diffusion term carries a minus sign, because holes diffusing towards +x are a positive current towards +x while dp/dx is negative. The Einstein relation links the two mechanisms: both are limited by the same collisions, so D = μV_T, about 35 cm²/s for electrons in silicon. Injected minority carriers diffuse an average distance L = √(Dτ) before recombining, where τ is the carrier lifetime.

Worked example 1: resistance of a p-type silicon bar
Given: N_A = 10^16 per cm³, mu_p = 480 cm²/V·s, q = 1.6e-19 C
       length 5 mm, cross-section 0.5 mm x 0.5 mm
sigma = q N_A mu_p = 1.6e-19 x 1e16 x 480 = 0.768 S/cm
rho   = 1 / 0.768 = 1.30 ohm·cm
L = 0.5 cm, A = 0.05 cm x 0.05 cm = 2.5e-3 cm²
R = rho L / A = 1.30 x 0.5 / 2.5e-3 = 260 ohm
Minority electrons: n = (1.5e10)² / 1e16 = 2.25e4 per cm³
(so ignoring electrons in sigma is fully justified)

Worked example 2: compensated silicon
Given: N_D = 5e16, N_A = 2e16 per cm³, n_i = 1.5e10, kT = 0.026 eV
Net doping N_D - N_A = 3e16 >> n_i, so the sample is n-type
n = 3e16 per cm³,  p = (1.5e10)² / 3e16 = 7.5e3 per cm³
E_F - E_i = kT ln(n / n_i) = 0.026 x ln(2e6) = 0.026 x 14.5 = 0.377 eV
sigma ~ q n mu_n = 1.6e-19 x 3e16 x 1350 = 6.5 S/cm
Note: all 7e16 ions scatter carriers, so the real mobility,
and hence sigma, is lower than this lightly-doped estimate.
Common mistakes in carrier calculations:
items: Writing p = n_i/N_D instead of p = n_i²/N_D; the mass-action law uses n_i squared.
Mixing centimetres and metres: with μ in cm²/V·s and concentrations per cm³, lengths must be in cm (1 µm = 10^-4 cm) and σ comes out in S/cm.
Using the donor density alone in compensated material; the majority concentration is the net doping |N_D − N_A|.
Using μ_n for p-type majority conduction; holes are about three times less mobile in silicon.
Adding the minority term to σ in doped material; it is many orders of magnitude smaller and can be dropped.

concepts.text: The mobilities in the table are for lightly doped material at 300 K. Mobility falls as temperature rises (more lattice scattering) and as doping rises (more impurity scattering), so heavily doped regions conduct less well than a simple q N μ estimate predicts.

Checklist for any concentration question: find the net doping, set the majority concentration equal to it, get the minority concentration from n_i² divided by the majority value, and use only the majority term in σ = q N μ. Confirm the product n·p equals n_i² before choosing an option.

formulas.plainText: n x p = ni^2
n ~ ND;   p ~ ni^2 / ND   (n-type)
sigma = q (n mu_n + p mu_p);   rho = 1 / sigma
vd = mu x E;   J = sigma x E   (drift)
ni is proportional to T^(3/2) e^(-Eg/(2kT))

notes.text: Pentavalent = donor = n-type = electrons majority; trivalent = acceptor = p-type = holes majority. Memorise the dopant lists: P, As, Sb for n-type and B, Al, Ga, In for p-type.
A doped semiconductor is still electrically neutral. Having electrons as majority carriers does not make n-type material negatively charged; the fixed positive donor ions balance them exactly.

Semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance: heating creates more electron-hole pairs, so resistance falls. Metals behave the opposite way, because heating only increases lattice scattering.
When a question gives n_i and a doping density, use n·p = n_i². For silicon with N_D = 10^16 per cm³, p = (1.5 × 10^10)² / 10^16 ≈ 2.25 × 10^4 per cm³.

concepts.text: The P-N Junction

A diode is formed by joining p-type and n-type semiconductor in a single crystal. Majority carriers diffuse across the junction and recombine, leaving a thin depletion region of fixed ionised atoms with no free carriers. The uncovered charge sets up an electric field, and the resulting built-in barrier potential (about 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium) stops further diffusion. The p side is the anode and the n side the cathode, marked by the band on the package.
Bias behaviour:
items: Forward bias (p to positive, n to negative): the barrier narrows, resistance is low and current flows freely once the applied voltage exceeds the knee voltage.
Reverse bias (p to negative, n to positive): the barrier widens, resistance is very high and only a tiny leakage (reverse saturation) current of minority carriers flows.
Excessive reverse voltage causes breakdown by the avalanche or Zener mechanism. This is destructive for a rectifier diode but is the normal working region of a Zener diode.

concepts.text: V-I Characteristic

The forward curve stays near zero until the knee (cut-in) voltage, about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium, then rises steeply and almost exponentially; the dynamic resistance r_d = nV_T/I_D is only a few ohms at milliampere currents. In reverse the current is the nearly constant saturation current I_S, of the order of nanoamperes for silicon and microamperes for germanium, until the breakdown voltage where it increases sharply. I_S roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature, and the forward drop falls by about 2 mV per °C.
Diode Current Equation
The ideal diode (Shockley) equation models current through the junction as a function of applied voltage. A single expression covers both forward and reverse bias:

concepts.plainText: ID = IS (e^(VD/(n VT)) - 1)

concepts.text: I_S is the reverse saturation current, V_T the thermal voltage (about 26 mV at room temperature), and n the ideality factor (1 to 2). For forward voltages above a few tenths of a volt the −1 is negligible and the current grows exponentially with V_D. For reverse voltages the exponential vanishes and I_D ≈ −I_S.
Diode Models

rows: Quick estimates, supply much larger than 0.7 V
Fixed drop of 0.7 V (Si) or 0.3 V (Ge)
Knee voltage in series with r_f (a few ohms)

concepts.text: Special Diodes

rows: AC to DC conversion, power supplies

concepts.text: An LED emits light when injected carriers recombine across a direct band gap (GaAs, GaP, GaN); its forward drop is 1.8 to 3.5 V depending on colour. A photodiode is reverse biased so that light-generated pairs in the depletion region produce a current proportional to illumination. A Schottky diode uses a metal-semiconductor junction with no minority-carrier storage, giving negligible reverse recovery time. A varactor exploits the fall of depletion-layer capacitance with increasing reverse voltage, and a tunnel diode is so heavily doped that quantum tunnelling gives a negative-resistance region in the forward characteristic.
Applications
Where diodes earn their keep in real circuits:
items: Rectification: a half-wave rectifier uses one diode; a full-wave rectifier uses a centre-tapped pair or a four-diode bridge, converting AC to pulsating DC.
Clipping and clamping: a diode with a reference voltage removes part of a waveform (clipper) or shifts its DC level (clamper).
Zener regulation: a Zener in reverse breakdown with a series resistor holds a nearly constant output voltage as the load or supply varies.
Freewheeling (flyback) diode: connected across an inductive load, it gives the stored energy a path when the switch opens and protects the switch from voltage spikes.
Signal work and protection: Schottky and fast diodes for demodulation, reverse-polarity protection and ESD clamping.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Diode Circuits and Calculations

Taking the logarithm of the forward Shockley equation gives V_D = nV_T ln(I_D/I_S). Two operating points of the same diode therefore differ in voltage by nV_T times the natural log of their current ratio, and I_S cancels out. With n = 1 and V_T = 26 mV a tenfold rise in current needs only about 60 mV more, and doubling the current needs about 18 mV. This is why the forward drop of a conducting silicon diode stays close to 0.6 to 0.8 V over several decades of current, which justifies the constant-voltage model.

concepts.plainText: V2 - V1 = n VT ln(I2/I1)   (about 60 mV per decade for n = 1)

concepts.text: Two kinds of resistance describe a diode. The static or DC resistance R_D = V_D/I_D is the ratio at one operating point and is tens to hundreds of ohms. The dynamic (AC) resistance r_d = nV_T/I_D is the slope of the curve at that point, is only a few ohms at milliampere currents, and is the one used for small signals superimposed on a DC bias. The operating point itself is where the diode curve meets the load line I_D = (V_S − V_D)/R drawn from V_S/R on the current axis to V_S on the voltage axis.

Worked example 1: diode current and resistances
Given: 5 V source, 1 kΩ series resistor, silicon diode (0.7 V), n = 1, V_T = 26 mV
Step 1  I_D = (5 − 0.7) / 1 kΩ = 4.3 mA
Step 2  Static resistance R_D = 0.7 V / 4.3 mA ≈ 163 Ω
Step 3  Dynamic resistance r_d = 26 mV / 4.3 mA ≈ 6.0 Ω
Step 4  Raising I_D to 43 mA would raise V_D by only 26 mV × ln 10 ≈ 60 mV

Given: 12 V rms secondary, 50 Hz, silicon bridge, load 100 mA, C = 1000 µF
Step 1  V_m = 12 × √2 = 16.97 V
Step 2  Two diodes conduct in series: V_m(out) = 16.97 − 1.4 = 15.57 V
Step 3  Without the capacitor: V_dc = 2 × 15.57 / π = 9.91 V
Step 4  Ripple frequency f_r = 2 × 50 = 100 Hz
Step 5  With the capacitor: V_r(pp) = 0.1 / (100 × 1000 µF) = 1.0 V
Step 6  V_dc ≈ 15.57 − 1.0/2 ≈ 15.1 V

A clipper removes the part of a waveform beyond a set level: a shunt diode in series with a battery V_B starts conducting when the output reaches V_B plus the diode drop, so the output is held there. A clamper uses a series capacitor and a shunt diode. On the first peak the capacitor charges to the peak voltage minus the diode drop, and afterwards it acts as a battery that shifts the whole waveform up or down without changing its peak-to-peak value. The RC time constant must be much longer than the signal period so the capacitor does not discharge between peaks.

Worked example 3: Zener regulator design and check
Given: V_in = 12 V, V_Z = 6 V, load 20 mA, desired I_Z = 10 mA
Step 1  I_R = I_Z + I_L = 10 + 20 = 30 mA
Step 2  R_S = (12 − 6) / 30 mA = 200 Ω
Step 3  Load removed: I_Z = 30 mA, P_Z = 6 V × 30 mA = 180 mW
Step 4  Choose a Zener rated well above 180 mW (e.g. 400 mW)
Common mistakes in diode problems:
items: Forgetting that a bridge has two diode drops in the conducting path while a centre-tapped rectifier has one.
Using the rms value where the peak is needed: V_m = √2 × V_rms.
Assuming a Zener regulates before checking that the open-circuit voltage across it exceeds V_Z.
Mixing up PIV: 2V_m for the centre-tapped circuit, V_m for the bridge and half-wave circuits.
Using the static resistance V_D/I_D in a small-signal problem, where the dynamic resistance nV_T/I_D is required.

concepts.text: When two diodes of different material are in parallel, the one with the lower knee voltage (germanium, 0.3 V) turns on first and clamps the voltage, so the silicon diode never reaches 0.7 V and carries no current.

formulas.plainText: ID = IS (e^(VD/nVT) - 1)
VT = kT/q ~ 26 mV at 300 K
ID ~ IS e^(VD/nVT)   for VD >> VT (forward)
rd = n VT / ID   (dynamic resistance)
IR = (Vin - VZ) / RS = IZ + IL   (Zener regulator)

notes.text: Remember the pair 0.7 V (Si) / 0.3 V (Ge). For circuit analysis with an ideal diode assume 0 V drop; with the practical model use the knee voltage.
A Zener diode regulates because the voltage across it stays nearly constant over a wide range of reverse current.
Reverse saturation current is a minority-carrier current: it depends strongly on temperature (roughly doubling every 10 °C) but hardly at all on the reverse voltage until breakdown.
The operating region of special diodes is a common MCQ: photodiode, varactor and Zener work in reverse bias (the Zener in breakdown); LED, Schottky and tunnel diodes work in forward bias.

concepts.text: Bipolar Junction Transistor

A BJT has three terminals — emitter, base, collector — and two pn junctions. It is a current-controlled device: a small base current controls a much larger collector current. Two types exist: npn, with a thin p-type base between n-type emitter and collector, and pnp, with an n-type base between p-type emitter and collector. On the symbol the arrow sits on the emitter and shows the direction of conventional current: it points outward for npn and inward for pnp.
Structure and doping of the three regions:
items: Emitter: heavily doped and moderately sized, so that it injects a large number of carriers into the base.
Base: very thin and lightly doped, so that almost all injected carriers cross it without recombining and only a small fraction leaves through the base terminal.
Collector: lightly doped and the largest region, so that it collects the carriers and dissipates most of the heat; its junction has the higher breakdown voltage.
Because of these asymmetries the emitter and collector cannot be interchanged in practice, even though both are the same material type.

concepts.text: Operation and Current Relations

For amplification the emitter-base junction is forward biased (about 0.7 V for silicon) and the collector-base junction is reverse biased. In an npn device the forward-biased emitter injects electrons into the base; because the base is thin and lightly doped, more than 95 % of them diffuse across and are swept into the collector by the reverse-biased junction. The few that recombine, together with holes injected back into the emitter, form the small base current. The collector current is therefore almost independent of collector voltage and is set by the base current, or equivalently by V_BE.

concepts.plainText: IE = IC + IB
beta = IC/IB;   alpha = IC/IE = beta/(beta + 1)

concepts.text: Alpha (α, the common-base current gain) is always slightly less than 1, typically 0.95 to 0.995. Beta (β or h_FE, the common-emitter current gain) is typically 50 to 300 and varies with temperature, collector current and from one device to another of the same type. Because I_E = I_B + I_C, the two gains are linked by β = α/(1 − α) and α = β/(1 + β).

Worked example: if α = 0.99 then β = 0.99/(1 − 0.99) = 99. With I_E = 10 mA the base current is I_B = I_E/(1 + β) = 10/100 = 0.1 mA and I_C = βI_B = 9.9 mA. Going the other way, β = 200 gives α = 200/201 ≈ 0.995.
Operating Regions

As an amplifier the transistor is biased in the middle of the active region, typically with V_CE ≈ V_CC/2, so that the output can swing both ways without distortion. As a switch it is driven hard between cut-off (both junctions reverse biased, I_C ≈ 0) and saturation (both junctions forward biased, V_CE ≈ 0.1 to 0.3 V). In saturation the collector current is limited by the external circuit rather than by βI_B, so the base is overdriven with I_B greater than I_C(sat)/β.

Leakage currents: I_CBO is the collector-base reverse current measured with the emitter open; it is the reverse saturation current of the collector junction and roughly doubles every 10 °C. I_CEO, the collector-emitter current with the base open, is much larger because the leakage acts as base current and is amplified: I_CEO = (1 + β)I_CBO. Including leakage, I_C = βI_B + I_CEO, and this temperature-dependent term is the cause of thermal runaway in a poorly stabilised bias circuit.
Configurations
Configurations, named after the terminal common to input and output:
items: Common Base: current gain α < 1, high voltage gain, no phase shift, very low input impedance; used in high-frequency amplifiers.
Common Emitter: high current gain β AND high voltage gain, 180 degree phase shift — the standard amplifier stage.
Common Collector (emitter follower): current gain γ = 1 + β, voltage gain about 1, high input and low output impedance — used as a buffer and for impedance matching.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: BJT Biasing and the Q-Point

The relation β = α/(1 − α) follows directly from I_E = I_C + I_B. Dividing by I_C gives 1/α = 1 + 1/β, which rearranges to both standard forms. Because α is so close to 1, a tiny change in α makes a large change in β: α = 0.99 gives β = 99, while α = 0.995 gives β = 199. Including the collector leakage, the complete collector current is I_C = βI_B + (1 + β)I_CBO, and it is this leakage term, doubling roughly every 10 °C, that a bias circuit must keep under control.

Biasing sets the DC operating point, or Q-point (I_CQ, V_CEQ), about which the signal swings. For a common-emitter stage with collector resistor R_C and emitter resistor R_E, every possible DC operating point lies on the DC load line V_CE = V_CC − I_C(R_C + R_E). Its end points are I_C(sat) = V_CC/(R_C + R_E) on the current axis and V_CE(off) = V_CC on the voltage axis. The Q-point is where this line crosses the output characteristic for the actual base current; placing it near the middle allows the largest undistorted swing.

concepts.plainText: VCE = VCC - IC (RC + RE)   (DC load line, IE ~ IC)

rows: Poor: I_C = βI_B changes in step with β; S = 1 + β
Good: a rise in I_C lowers V_C and so I_B
Best: I_C nearly independent of β when βR_E ≫ R_TH

concepts.plainText: VTH = VCC R2/(R1 + R2),  RTH = R1 || R2   (voltage-divider bias)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: fixed bias, check the region
Given: V_CC = 12 V, R_B = 470 kΩ, R_C = 2.2 kΩ, β = 100, V_BE = 0.7 V
Step 1  I_B = (12 − 0.7)/470 kΩ = 24.0 µA
Step 2  I_C = βI_B = 100 × 24.0 µA = 2.40 mA
Step 3  V_CE = 12 − 2.40 mA × 2.2 kΩ = 6.71 V
Step 4  V_CE > V_CE(sat) ≈ 0.2 V, so the transistor is active: Q = (2.40 mA, 6.71 V)
If β were 250: I_C would be 6.0 mA and V_CE = 12 − 13.2 < 0, impossible,
so the transistor saturates with I_C(sat) = (12 − 0.2)/2.2 kΩ ≈ 5.4 mA

Worked example 2: voltage-divider bias, exact and approximate
Given: V_CC = 18 V, R_1 = 82 kΩ, R_2 = 22 kΩ, R_E = 1.2 kΩ, β = 50, V_BE = 0.7 V
Step 1  V_TH = 18 × 22/104 = 3.81 V, R_TH = 82 × 22/104 = 17.3 kΩ
Step 2  Exact: I_B = (3.81 − 0.7)/(17.3 k + 51 × 1.2 k) = 39.6 µA
Step 3  I_C = 50 × 39.6 µA = 1.98 mA
Step 4  Approximate: V_E = 3.81 − 0.7 = 3.11 V, I_E = 3.11/1.2 k = 2.59 mA
Step 5  Check βR_E = 60 kΩ versus 10R_2 = 220 kΩ: condition fails,
        so the approximate method is not valid here; use the exact result

The stability factor S = ΔI_C/ΔI_CBO measures how much the collector current shifts when leakage rises with temperature. For fixed bias S = 1 + β, the worst case; the ideal value is 1. Adding R_E or feeding the base from the collector reduces S because any rise in I_C raises the emitter voltage, or lowers the collector voltage, and cuts the base drive. The voltage-divider circuit with a large R_E and a stiff divider (βR_E at least ten times R_2) gives S close to 1 and a Q-point almost independent of β.
Common mistakes in bias problems:
items: Forgetting the (β + 1) factor when referring R_E to the base circuit.
Calculating V_CE with I_C × R_C only, and leaving out the drop I_E × R_E.
Accepting a negative V_CE instead of recognising that the transistor has saturated.
Using the approximate voltage-divider method when βR_E is not at least 10R_2.
Treating the load-line saturation current as V_CC/R_C when an emitter resistor is present.

concepts.text: I_C = βI_B holds only in the active region. Always check the answer: if the calculated V_CE is below about 0.2 V, the transistor is saturated and the collector current is set by the external resistors, not by β.

For voltage-divider bias, first find V_B from the divider, then V_E = V_B − 0.7 V, I_E = V_E/R_E and finally V_CE = V_CC − I_C(R_C + R_E). This four-step route solves most Q-point problems in under a minute.

formulas.plainText: beta = alpha / (1 - alpha)
IC = beta x IB
alpha = beta / (1 + beta)
IE = (1 + beta) IB
ICEO = (1 + beta) ICBO

notes.text: Amplifier questions assume the ACTIVE region. Switching questions toggle between cut-off (OFF) and saturation (ON).

Beta is not a constant. It changes with temperature, collector current and between individual transistors of the same type, so good bias circuits (voltage-divider or emitter-stabilised) are designed to be insensitive to β.
The emitter arrow shows the direction of conventional current and always points from p to n: outward for npn (Not Pointing iN), inward for pnp.
Quick check: I_B/I_E = 1 − α = 1/(1 + β). A gain of β = 99 means exactly 1 % of the emitter current leaves through the base.

concepts.text: Field Effect Transistors

FETs (JFET, MOSFET) are voltage-controlled: the gate-source voltage controls the drain current, drawing virtually no gate current. MOSFETs dominate modern digital electronics. In a JFET the gate is a reverse-biased pn junction; in a MOSFET the gate is completely insulated from the channel by a thin layer of silicon dioxide, which is why it is also called an insulated-gate FET (IGFET). FETs are unipolar devices: current is carried by one type of carrier only, electrons in an n-channel device and holes in a p-channel device.
MOSFET Structure

An n-channel MOSFET is built on a p-type substrate, the body. Two heavily doped n+ regions form the source and drain, and between them the gate, a metal or polysilicon electrode, sits on a SiO₂ layer only a few nanometres thick. The four terminals are gate (G), source (S), drain (D) and body (B); in discrete devices the body is tied internally to the source, which also creates a body diode between drain and source. A p-channel MOSFET is the complement: p+ source and drain in an n-type substrate, operated with negative gate and drain voltages relative to the source.
Enhancement and Depletion Types
The two MOSFET families and how they differ at V_GS = 0:
items: Enhancement mode (normally OFF): no channel exists at V_GS = 0. A gate voltage above the threshold V_T attracts electrons under the oxide and creates (enhances) an inversion channel. The symbol shows a broken channel line, with the body arrow pointing inward for n-channel and outward for p-channel.

Depletion mode (normally ON): a channel is built in during manufacture, so drain current flows at V_GS = 0. A negative V_GS (n-channel) depletes the channel and reduces the current; a positive V_GS enhances it. The symbol shows a solid, continuous channel line.
Enhancement n-channel devices are by far the most common in digital ICs and power switching, because a normally-off switch is safer and easier to drive.

concepts.text: Threshold Voltage, Regions and Characteristics

The threshold voltage V_T (also written V_th or V_GS(th)) is the minimum gate-source voltage needed to form the channel, typically 0.5 to 2 V in small-signal ICs and 2 to 4 V in power devices. The excess V_GS − V_T is called the overdrive voltage. Which region the device is in depends on how V_DS compares with this overdrive.

rows: V_GS > V_T and V_DS < V_GS − V_T
Rises with V_DS, roughly linear at small V_DS
V_GS > V_T and V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T
I_D = k(V_GS − V_T)², independent of V_DS

concepts.plainText: ID = k (VGS - VT)^2   with k = (1/2) mu_n Cox (W/L)   (saturation)
ID = k [2 (VGS - VT) VDS - VDS^2]   (ohmic region)

concepts.text: The drain (output) characteristic plots I_D against V_DS for several values of V_GS: each curve rises steeply in the ohmic region and then flattens into saturation, with a higher curve for each higher V_GS. The transfer characteristic plots I_D against V_GS at constant V_DS: it is zero below V_T and then rises as a parabola. Its slope is the transconductance g_m = 2k(V_GS − V_T) = 2I_D/(V_GS − V_T), the gain parameter of a MOSFET amplifier. The very high input impedance (10^12 Ω or more) means the gate draws essentially only leakage current, so the DC input power is negligible.
Handling, Comparison and Uses

The gate oxide is so thin that a static discharge of a few tens of volts can puncture it permanently. MOSFETs are therefore shipped with the leads shorted or in conductive foam, handled at grounded workstations, and many ICs include protective diodes on every input. A gate must never be left floating in a circuit, because any stray charge can turn the device partly on.

rows: Low noise, stable (I_D falls as temperature rises)

concepts.text: Applications:
items: Switching: a near-ideal switch with very low on-resistance and negligible gate drive power in the steady state.
Digital ICs: CMOS logic, microprocessors, SRAM and flash memory (a floating-gate MOSFET stores each bit).
Power electronics: switch-mode power supplies, motor drives and inverters switching at tens to hundreds of kHz.
Analog circuits: high-input-impedance amplifiers, current mirrors and analog switches.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: MOSFET Analysis and Biasing

The square law comes from the charge in the channel. Once V_GS exceeds V_T, the inversion charge per unit area at a point x along the channel is C_ox(V_GS − V_T − v(x)), where v(x) is the local channel voltage that rises from 0 at the source to V_DS at the drain. The drift current is this charge times the electron velocity μ_n E, and integrating from source to drain gives the ohmic-region equation. When V_DS reaches V_GS − V_T the charge at the drain end falls to zero (pinch-off); beyond that point the extra voltage drops across the short pinched region and the current stays at its peak value, which is the saturation equation.

concepts.plainText: ID = mu_n Cox (W/L) [ (VGS - VT) VDS - VDS^2 / 2 ]   (same as k[2 Vov VDS - VDS^2] with k = mu_n Cox W / 2L)

concepts.text: Two second-order effects matter in practice. Channel-length modulation: in saturation the pinch-off point moves slightly towards the source as V_DS rises, so the effective channel shortens and I_D creeps up with V_DS; this is modelled by the factor (1 + λV_DS) and gives the finite output resistance r_o = 1/(λI_D). Body effect: if the source is above the body potential, the extra reverse bias widens the depletion layer under the gate and raises V_T, which is why stacked transistors in an IC have slightly higher thresholds.

concepts.plainText: ID = k (VGS - VT)^2 (1 + lambda VDS);   ro = 1 / (lambda ID)

concepts.text: JFETs and depletion MOSFETs obey the Shockley equation instead of the enhancement square law. Here I_DSS is the drain current at V_GS = 0 and V_P (the pinch-off voltage, negative for n-channel) is the gate voltage at which the channel is fully depleted. A depletion MOSFET can also be driven with positive V_GS, where the same equation predicts I_D above I_DSS; a JFET cannot, because its gate junction would become forward biased.

concepts.plainText: ID = IDSS (1 - VGS/VP)^2;   gm = (2 IDSS / |VP|)(1 - VGS/VP)

R_G from drain to gate, so V_GS = V_DS
V_GS = V_DD − I_D R_D, device always saturated

Worked example 1: divider plus source resistor (E-MOSFET)
Given: V_G = 6 V, R_S = 1 kΩ, V_T = 2 V, k = 1 mA/V²
Loop:   V_GS = V_G − I_D R_S = 6 − I_D   (I_D in mA)
Device: I_D = (V_GS − 2)²
Let x = V_GS − 2:  2 + x = 6 − x²  ->  x² + x − 4 = 0
x = (−1 + √17)/2 = 1.56 V   (other root −2.56 V gives V_GS < V_T, reject)
I_D = x² = 2.44 mA,  V_GS = 3.56 V
Check: V_DS must be at least V_GS − V_T = 1.56 V for saturation

Worked example 2: common-source gain with r_o
Given: I_D = 1 mA, V_GS − V_T = 1 V, λ = 0.02 V⁻¹, R_D = 10 kΩ
g_m = 2 I_D/(V_GS − V_T) = 2 × 1/1 = 2 mA/V

R_D ∥ r_o = (10 × 50)/(10 + 50) = 8.33 kΩ
A_v = −g_m (R_D ∥ r_o) = −2 × 8.33 = −16.7
Ignoring r_o would give −20, a 20 % overestimate
Common mistakes in MOSFET problems:
items: Squaring a negative overdrive: if V_GS < V_T the device is off and I_D = 0, not k(V_GS − V_T)².
Using the saturation equation without checking V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T; if the check fails, redo the problem with the ohmic equation.
Keeping the wrong root of the bias quadratic: reject any root that makes V_GS < V_T (enhancement) or V_GS beyond V_P (JFET or depletion).
Mixing k conventions: some books write I_D = (k'/2)(W/L)(V_GS − V_T)², so k in the form used here already contains the factor one half.
Forgetting that for a p-channel device V_GS, V_DS and V_T are all negative; work with magnitudes and then give the current direction (source to drain).

concepts.text: Every biasing problem follows the same three steps: write the loop equation for V_GS, substitute the device equation, then solve and check the region. Two roots always appear in a quadratic bias problem and exactly one of them is physical.

notes.text: BJT is current-controlled; FET is voltage-controlled. Examiners regularly test exactly this contrast.

Enhancement = normally OFF, channel created by V_GS (broken line in the symbol). Depletion = normally ON, channel depleted by V_GS (solid line). Questions often simply ask which type conducts at V_GS = 0.

The saturation region of a MOSFET is its amplifying (constant-current) region, the opposite of the BJT, where saturation means fully ON. In MOSFET language the fully-on switch state is the ohmic (triode) region.
Doubling the overdrive V_GS − V_T quadruples I_D in saturation because of the square law. Always check the region first: if V_DS < V_GS − V_T, use the ohmic equation instead.

concepts.text: Complementary MOS

CMOS technology builds every logic gate from complementary enhancement MOSFETs: n-channel devices in a pull-down network connected to ground and p-channel devices in a pull-up network connected to V_DD. The two networks are logical duals, so for any valid input combination exactly one of them conducts. Because it uses both n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs, CMOS combines very low power consumption with high noise immunity, and it is the dominant technology for microprocessors, memories and digital ICs.
The CMOS Inverter

The inverter has one nMOS (source to ground) and one pMOS (source to V_DD) with their gates joined as the input and their drains joined as the output. With the input LOW (0 V) the nMOS is off and the pMOS is on, so the output is pulled up to V_DD. With the input HIGH (V_DD) the nMOS is on and the pMOS is off, so the output is pulled down to 0 V. In either steady state one transistor is off, so no DC path exists between V_DD and ground and the output swings the full rail-to-rail range.

rows: In transition; brief supply current spike

concepts.text: Power Dissipation

Static power is almost zero because in steady state only sub-threshold and junction leakage flows, of the order of nanowatts per gate. Power is consumed while switching: charging the load capacitance C to V_DD and discharging it to ground dissipates C·V_DD² per cycle, so the dynamic power is P = C·V_DD²·f. A short-circuit component is added during the moment both transistors conduct. Dynamic power therefore grows with clock frequency and with the square of the supply voltage, which is why supply voltages have fallen from 5 V to about 1 V in modern processors.

concepts.plainText: P_dyn = C x VDD^2 x f

concepts.text: Noise Margins, Fan-out and Speed
What makes CMOS robust and fast, and its one weakness:
items: Noise margins: the inverter switches sharply near V_DD/2 and the logic levels sit close to the rails, so NM_H = V_OH − V_IH and NM_L = V_IL − V_OL are each roughly 30 % of V_DD, about 1.5 V at a 5 V supply against 0.4 V for TTL. This is the source of the high noise immunity of CMOS.
Input impedance and fan-out: every input is an insulated gate, so one output can drive 50 or more inputs; the limit is the added capacitance, which slows the edges, not DC loading.
Speed-power trade-off: propagation delay is roughly proportional to C·V_DD/I_D, so raising V_DD speeds the gate up but increases power as V_DD². The power-delay product is the usual figure of merit.

Latch-up: parasitic pnp and npn transistors in the substrate can form a thyristor-like path from V_DD to ground if an input or output is driven beyond the supply rails. Guard rings and clamp diodes prevent it, and unused inputs must never be left floating.

concepts.text: CMOS versus TTL

rows: About 10 nW static, rises with frequency
About 8 to 10 ns (74HC); 4000 series much slower
High (margins about 30 % of V_DD, about 1.5 V at 5 V)

concepts.text: Logic Families and Applications
CMOS logic families and where CMOS is used:
items: 4000 series: the original CMOS family with a 3 to 15 V supply; very low power but slow (tens of nanoseconds) and with weak output drive.
74HC and 74HCT: high-speed CMOS with TTL-comparable speed; 74HCT has TTL-compatible input levels for mixed systems. 74AC, 74LVC and lower-voltage families followed.
Memory: an SRAM cell is a six-transistor CMOS latch, DRAM uses one MOSFET and one capacitor per bit, and flash uses floating-gate MOSFETs.
Microprocessors, microcontrollers, FPGAs and image sensors are all fabricated in CMOS, because only its near-zero static power allows billions of transistors on one chip.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: CMOS Inverter and Gate Design

The voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) of the inverter can be traced by sweeping the input from 0 to V_DD and noting the region of each transistor. The output stays at V_DD until the nMOS turns on, falls steeply through the middle where both transistors are saturated and the gain is highest, and settles at 0 V once the pMOS turns off. The steepness of this middle section is what places V_IL and V_IH close to each other and gives CMOS its wide noise margins.

The switching threshold V_M is the input voltage at which V_out = V_in. Equating the two saturation currents, k_n(V_M − V_tn)² = k_p(V_DD − V_M − |V_tp|)², gives the formula below. With matched devices (k_n = k_p, V_tn = |V_tp|) V_M = V_DD/2; a stronger nMOS pulls V_M lower and a stronger pMOS pushes it higher. Because μ_n is about 2 to 3 times μ_p, the pMOS is normally made that much wider to centre V_M.

concepts.plainText: VM = (Vtn + r (VDD - |Vtp|)) / (1 + r),  r = sqrt(kp / kn)

concepts.text: The C·V²·f law follows from energy accounting. Charging the load from 0 to V_DD draws charge Q = C·V_DD from the supply, so the supply delivers Q·V_DD = C·V_DD² of energy. Half of it, ½C·V_DD², ends up stored on the capacitor and the other half is lost as heat in the pMOS; on the falling edge the stored half is dissipated in the nMOS. One complete charge-discharge cycle therefore dissipates C·V_DD², independent of the transistor resistances. In a real chip only a fraction α of the nodes switch each clock cycle, and leakage adds a static term.

Worked example 1: power of a processor core
Given: 10^6 gates, C = 10 fF each, α = 0.1, V_DD = 1.2 V, f = 1 GHz, I_leak = 100 mA
P_dyn  = α N C V_DD² f
       = 0.1 × 10^6 × 10×10^-15 × 1.44 × 10^9 = 1.44 W
P_stat = V_DD × I_leak = 1.2 × 0.1 = 0.12 W
P_total = 1.44 + 0.12 = 1.56 W
Dropping V_DD to 1.0 V: P_dyn = 1.44 × (1.0/1.2)² = 1.0 W

A static CMOS gate always has an nMOS pull-down network and a dual pMOS pull-up network with one transistor pair per input. Series nMOS implement AND inside the inversion, parallel nMOS implement OR, and the pull-up network swaps every series connection for a parallel one and vice versa. Transistors in series add their on-resistances, so series stacks must be widened: each of n series devices needs about n times the width of a single device for the same drive. This is why NAND (series nMOS, fast electrons) is preferred to NOR (series pMOS, slow holes).

Worked example 2: worst-case delay of a 2-input NOR
Given: each pMOS R_on = 2 kΩ, each nMOS R_on = 1 kΩ, C_L = 50 fF
Pull-up: two pMOS in series -> R = 4 kΩ
t_pLH = 0.69 × 4×10^3 × 50×10^-15 = 138 ps
