Common mistakes with CMOS questions:
items: Treating static power as the main loss: in active logic dynamic power C·V²·f dominates, while leakage matters mostly in idle or very dense chips.
Forgetting that power scales with V_DD squared: halving V_DD alone cuts dynamic power to one quarter, not one half.
Swapping the NAND and NOR structures: NAND = series nMOS and parallel pMOS; NOR = parallel nMOS and series pMOS.
Mixing up the noise-margin formulas: NM_H = V_OH − V_IH and NM_L = V_IL − V_OL, always output level minus input threshold on the same side.
Assuming CMOS fan-out is limited by DC current: it is limited by load capacitance and the resulting slower edges.

concepts.text: A standard TTL output guarantees only V_OH = 2.7 V, below the 3.15 V V_IH of a 74HC input at 4.5 V, so the HIGH noise margin is negative. Use a 74HCT part (TTL-compatible input thresholds) or a pull-up resistor when TTL drives CMOS.

formulas.plainText: P_dyn = C VDD^2 f
P_total = VDD I_leak + alpha C VDD^2 f   (alpha = activity factor)

formulas.latex: NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH}, \qquad NM_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL}
formulas.plainText: NM_H = VOH - VIH;   NM_L = VIL - VOL
tp ~ C VDD / ID   (propagation delay)

notes.text: CMOS = both nMOS and pMOS in every gate. Its two headline advantages are very low power and high noise immunity; static power is nearly zero and dynamic power is P = C·V²·f.
Never leave a CMOS input floating: it can drift to mid-supply, turn both transistors partly on and waste power, oscillate or trigger latch-up. Tie unused inputs to V_DD or ground.
Halving V_DD cuts dynamic power to one quarter, which is why IC supply voltages have fallen steadily, but it also slows the gate because the overdrive V_GS − V_T shrinks.
In the CMOS inverter the pMOS is the pull-up and the nMOS is the pull-down. In steady state exactly one of them is on; both conduct only momentarily during a transition.

concepts.text: Why Two Kinds of Model

A BJT is a non-linear device: its collector current depends exponentially on the base-emitter voltage. Solving an amplifier exactly with that law is impractical, so the analysis is split in two. The DC (large-signal) analysis uses a simple non-linear model to locate the quiescent operating point (Q-point: I_CQ, V_CEQ). The AC (small-signal) analysis then replaces the transistor by a linear circuit whose element values depend on the Q-point, and uses it to find gain, input resistance and output resistance. The total voltage or current at any node is the DC value plus the small AC value superimposed on it.
Large-Signal (DC) Models

The complete large-signal description is the Ebers-Moll model: two ideal diodes (base-emitter and base-collector) placed back to back, each shunted by a dependent current source that carries a fraction (alpha) of the other diode's current. It is valid in all four regions (active, saturation, cut-off and reverse-active) and is what circuit simulators use. In the forward-active region it reduces to I_C = I_S exp(V_BE / V_T), with I_S of the order of 10^-14 A and V_T = 26 mV at room temperature.
For hand calculation the exponential is replaced by piecewise-linear models, one per region:
items: Forward-active: the base-emitter junction is a 0.7 V battery (silicon), the collector is a current source I_C = beta I_B, and I_E = I_C + I_B = (beta + 1) I_B. This is the amplifier model.

Saturation: both junctions forward biased; V_BE is about 0.7 to 0.8 V and V_CE(sat) is about 0.2 V. The collector current is set by the external circuit and is less than beta I_B, so the transistor behaves as a closed switch.
Cut-off: both junctions reverse biased (V_BE below about 0.5 V); all currents are essentially zero and the transistor is an open switch.
Test for saturation: assume active operation, compute I_C = beta I_B, and check V_CE. If V_CE comes out below about 0.2 V (or negative), the assumption is wrong and the transistor is saturated.

concepts.latex: I_C = I_S e^{V_{BE}/V_T}, \qquad I_C = \beta I_B, \qquad I_E = I_C + I_B
concepts.plainText: I_C = I_S·e^(V_BE/V_T);  I_C = β·I_B;  I_E = I_C + I_B

concepts.text: The DC load line joins the two limits of the collector circuit V_CE = V_CC - I_C R_C: the cut-off point (I_C = 0, V_CE = V_CC) and the saturation point (V_CE = 0, I_C = V_CC / R_C). The bias network chooses where on this line the transistor rests; that intersection is the Q-point. For the largest undistorted swing the Q-point is placed near the middle of the load line (V_CEQ about V_CC / 2). The input signal then moves the operating point up and down the line about Q, and the small-signal models describe that movement.
Small-Signal (AC) Models

A signal is small when the AC part of v_BE is only a few millivolts, much less than V_T. The exponential curve is then indistinguishable from its tangent at the Q-point, so the transistor can be replaced by linear resistors and a controlled source. Three equivalent forms are in common use: the r_e model, the hybrid-pi model and the h-parameter model. They give the same answers; they differ only in which quantity is chosen as the control variable and in how the parameters are obtained.
The r_e model (Boylestad) uses the dynamic emitter resistance as its single key parameter:
items: r_e = V_T / I_E = 26 mV / I_E (in mA, giving ohms). At I_E = 1 mA, r_e = 26 ohm.
Looking into the base, the input resistance is beta r_e (more exactly (beta + 1) r_e), because base current is 1/beta of the emitter current.
Common-emitter voltage gain with a bypassed emitter: A_v = -R_C / r_e. With an unbypassed emitter resistor R_E it drops to about -R_C / (r_e + R_E).
Common-base gain is +R_C / r_e; the emitter follower has gain slightly less than 1 and output resistance about r_e.

concepts.text: The hybrid-pi model (Sedra-Smith) uses the base-emitter voltage as the control variable and a transconductance g_m:
items: g_m = I_C / V_T: the slope of the I_C versus V_BE curve at the Q-point; 1 mA gives 38.5 mA/V.
r_pi = beta / g_m = V_T / I_B: the resistance seen between base and emitter; it equals (beta + 1) r_e, approximately beta r_e.
r_o = V_A / I_C: the output resistance from collector to emitter caused by the Early effect (V_A about 50 to 150 V); often ignored when R_C is much smaller than r_o.

The controlled source is g_m v_pi (equivalently beta i_b), so the CE gain is A_v = -g_m (R_C parallel r_o). For high-frequency work the junction capacitances C_pi and C_mu are added to the same model.

concepts.text: The h-parameter model treats the transistor as a two-port network described by measured hybrid parameters. For the common-emitter connection the equations are v_be = h_ie i_b + h_re v_ce and i_c = h_fe i_b + h_oe v_ce. Each parameter is measured with either the output shorted or the input open, which is why data sheets can quote them directly. In simplified analysis h_re and h_oe are usually neglected, leaving only h_ie (input resistance) and h_fe (current gain), which then correspond exactly to r_pi and beta of the hybrid-pi model.

concepts.text: Worked Example

A silicon BJT with beta = 100 is biased at I_C = 1 mA and drives a collector resistor R_C = 5 kΩ with the emitter bypassed. Transconductance g_m = I_C / V_T = 1 mA / 26 mV = 38.5 mA/V. Input resistance r_pi = beta / g_m = 100 / 0.0385 = 2.6 kΩ. In r_e terms, I_E is about 1.01 mA so r_e is about 26 ohm and beta r_e is again about 2.6 kΩ. The voltage gain is A_v = -g_m R_C = -0.0385 x 5000 = -192, and the r_e model gives the same figure: -R_C / r_e = -5000 / 26 = -192. If the data sheet instead quoted h_ie = 2.6 kΩ and h_fe = 100, the h-parameter gain -h_fe R_C / h_ie would also be -192.
Going Deeper: Deriving and Applying the BJT Models

The transconductance comes straight from the exponential law. Differentiating I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T) with respect to V_BE gives I_S e^(V_BE/V_T) / V_T, which is simply I_C / V_T. The same law shows that V_BE rises by V_T ln 10, about 60 mV, for every tenfold increase in collector current, and by V_T ln 2, about 18 mV, when the current doubles. Expanding e^(v_be/V_T) as 1 + v_be/V_T + ... shows why the linear model needs v_be much smaller than V_T: at 5 mV the neglected square term is already about 10 % of the linear term.

concepts.plainText: g_m = di_C/dv_BE = I_C / V_T;  ΔV_BE = V_T·ln(I_C2 / I_C1)

concepts.text: In the Ebers-Moll equations each junction current follows the diode law, I_F = I_ES (e^(V_BE/V_T) − 1) for the emitter diode and I_R = I_CS (e^(V_BC/V_T) − 1) for the collector diode. The terminal currents are I_C = α_F I_F − I_R and I_E = I_F − α_R I_R. Reciprocity requires α_F I_ES = α_R I_CS = I_S. Because the collector is large and lightly doped, α_R is small (roughly 0.1 to 0.5), so the reverse-active current gain β_R = α_R / (1 − α_R) is usually below 1; this is why a transistor with collector and emitter swapped is a poor amplifier.

rows: V_BE ≈ 0.8 V, V_CE(sat) ≈ 0.2 V, I_C < β I_B
Roles swapped; β_R well below β_F

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - is the transistor saturated?
Given: V_BB = 3.3 V, R_B = 10 kΩ, V_CC = 5 V, R_C = 1 kΩ, β = 80
Assume active: I_B = (3.3 − 0.7) / 10 kΩ = 0.26 mA
  I_C = β I_B = 80 × 0.26 mA = 20.8 mA
  V_CE = 5 − 20.8 mA × 1 kΩ = −15.8 V  -> impossible
So the BJT is saturated: V_CE = 0.2 V
  I_C(sat) = (5 − 0.2) / 1 kΩ = 4.8 mA
  Forced beta = I_C / I_B = 4.8 / 0.26 = 18.5 (less than 80)
  Minimum base current for saturation = 4.8 mA / 80 = 60 µA
Converting between the model families (common-emitter h-parameters on the left):
items: h_fe = β and h_ie = r_π, so g_m = h_fe / h_ie; for example h_fe = 100 and h_ie = 2.5 kΩ give g_m = 40 mA/V, which at V_T = 25 mV means I_C = 1 mA.
h_oe = 1 / r_o, so a data-sheet h_oe of 20 µS corresponds to r_o = 50 kΩ in the hybrid-π model.
Common-base values follow from the CE ones: h_ib = h_ie / (1 + h_fe), which is r_e, and h_fb = −h_fe / (1 + h_fe), which is −α.
h_re and h_fe are dimensionless, h_ie is in ohms and h_oe is in siemens; that mix of units is why they are called hybrid parameters.

concepts.latex: A_i = \frac{h_{fe}}{1 + h_{oe} R_L}, \quad Z_i = h_{ie} - h_{re} A_i R_L
concepts.plainText: A_i = h_fe / (1 + h_oe·R_L);  Z_i = h_ie − h_re·A_i·R_L = h_ie − h_re·h_fe·R_L / (1 + h_oe·R_L)

concepts.text: Writing the CE gain as A_v = −g_m R_C = −I_C R_C / V_T shows that the gain equals the DC voltage dropped across R_C divided by V_T: a 5 V drop gives about −200 at V_T = 25 mV, whatever the individual values of I_C and R_C. The largest gain a single transistor can give, with only its own r_o as load, is the intrinsic gain g_m r_o = V_A / V_T, a few thousand. At high frequencies the hybrid-π model adds C_π between base and emitter and C_µ between base and collector, and the transition frequency where the short-circuit current gain falls to 1 is f_T = g_m / (2π (C_π + C_µ)).

Frequent slips in model questions: using r_e = 26 mV / I_E with I_E in amperes and quoting the answer in ohms without the factor 1000; taking g_m = I_B / V_T instead of I_C / V_T; forgetting R_L in parallel with R_C in the AC load; using −R_C / r_e when R_E is not bypassed; and trusting I_C = β I_B without first checking that V_CE is above V_CE(sat).

formulas.latex: I_C = \beta I_B, \qquad V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_C R_C
formulas.plainText: I_C = β·I_B;  V_CE = V_CC − I_C·R_C (DC load line)
r_e = V_T / I_E = 26 mV / I_E
g_m = I_C / V_T;  r_π = β / g_m;  r_o = V_A / I_C
A_v(CE) = −g_m·R_C = −R_C / r_e

formulas.latex: v_{be} = h_{ie} i_b + h_{re} v_{ce}, \qquad i_c = h_{fe} i_b + h_{oe} v_{ce}
formulas.plainText: v_be = h_ie·i_b + h_re·v_ce;  i_c = h_fe·i_b + h_oe·v_ce

notes.text: Two numbers unlock most model MCQs: V_T = 26 mV at room temperature and V_BE = 0.7 V. From them, r_e = 26 mV / I_E, g_m = I_C / 26 mV, and r_π = β / g_m. Check the units: I_E in mA gives r_e in ohms; I_C in mA gives g_m in mA/V.

Do not mix the two analyses. In the AC model every DC source is a short circuit (V_CC to ground) and coupling or bypass capacitors are shorts; in the DC model every capacitor is an open circuit. Using R_C in a DC calculation but forgetting that the AC collector load is R_C in parallel with R_L is a common slip.

The letters in h-parameters spell their meaning: i = input, r = reverse, f = forward, o = output, and the second subscript (e, b or c) names the common terminal. h_fe is simply the AC beta and h_ie the AC input resistance; h_re and h_oe are small enough to drop in most exam problems.

concepts.text: Oscillator as an Amplifier with Positive Feedback

An oscillator is an amplifier that supplies its own input. A fraction β of the output voltage is returned to the input through a feedback network in phase with the original signal (positive feedback), so once a signal exists it is regenerated on every trip around the loop. No external AC input is needed: the circuit converts DC power from the supply into a periodic AC output whose frequency is fixed by the feedback network.
Block diagram in words:
items: Amplifier of gain A (a transistor, FET or op-amp stage) that supplies energy and, if it is an inverting stage, 180° of phase shift.
Frequency-selective feedback network of transfer ratio β (RC ladder, LC tank or quartz crystal) that returns part of the output to the input and fixes the frequency.
Summing point where the feedback signal βV_o is added to the (zero) external input; the closed-loop gain A/(1 − Aβ) becomes infinite when Aβ = 1, which means a finite output exists with no input.

concepts.plainText: Af = A / (1 − Aβ)  → infinite when Aβ = 1

concepts.text: Barkhausen Criterion

For sustained oscillation at a single frequency the signal fed back must be exactly equal to the signal that produced it, in both magnitude and phase. This gives the two Barkhausen conditions: the magnitude of the loop gain must be unity, |Aβ| = 1, and the total phase shift around the loop must be 0° or 360° (an integer multiple of 2π). If the amplifier inverts (180°), the feedback network must supply the remaining 180°; if the amplifier is non-inverting (0°), the network must supply 0° at the oscillation frequency.

concepts.plainText: |Aβ| = 1 and ∠Aβ = 0°, 360°, ... (2πn radians)

concepts.text: Start-up, Amplitude Stabilisation and Damping

No external signal starts the oscillator: it starts from thermal noise and the switch-on transient, which contain components at every frequency. Only the component for which the loop phase shift is 0° is reinforced. To make it grow, the loop gain is designed slightly greater than unity, typically |Aβ| ≈ 1.05 to 1.1. As the amplitude rises, amplifier saturation or a deliberate non-linear element (thermistor, lamp, diodes or an automatic gain control loop) reduces the gain until |Aβ| settles at exactly 1 and the amplitude becomes constant.

rows: Growing: amplitude builds up until limited
Start-up condition; if uncontrolled, clipped and distorted wave

concepts.text: An LC tank that is set ringing and then left alone produces damped oscillations: energy is lost in the coil resistance every cycle, so the amplitude decays exponentially at the natural frequency. An oscillator produces undamped (sustained) oscillations by replacing the lost energy every cycle from the DC supply through the amplifier; the feedback network merely times when that energy is delivered.
Classification of Oscillators
Oscillators are classified three ways:
items: By waveform: sinusoidal (harmonic) oscillators using RC, LC or crystal networks, and relaxation (non-sinusoidal) oscillators such as multivibrators, 555 timers and UJT circuits.
By frequency-determining element: RC oscillators (phase-shift, Wien bridge), LC oscillators (Hartley, Colpitts, Clapp, tuned-collector, Armstrong) and crystal oscillators (Pierce, Miller).

By frequency range: audio frequency (about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, RC types), radio frequency (tens of kHz to hundreds of MHz, LC and crystal types) and VHF/UHF (LC with very small components or overtone crystals).
By mechanism: feedback oscillators that satisfy the Barkhausen criterion, and negative-resistance oscillators (tunnel diode, UJT, Gunn diode) that cancel the losses of a tank directly.

concepts.text: Frequency Stability and the Tank Circuit

Frequency stability is the ability of an oscillator to hold its frequency over time. It is degraded by temperature changes (which alter L, C, R and transistor parameters), supply-voltage variations, load changes (which alter the effective Q and phase), ageing of components and mechanical vibration. Stability improves with a high-Q frequency-determining network, because a high Q makes the phase change steeply with frequency, so only a tiny frequency shift is needed to restore the 0° loop phase when something drifts: crystal (Q of 10^4 to 10^6) is far better than LC (Q about 100), which is better than RC. Other measures are a regulated supply, temperature-compensating capacitors, buffer stages to isolate the load and light coupling between the tank and the amplifier.

A parallel L-C circuit is called a tank because it stores energy, exchanging it between the electric field of the capacitor and the magnetic field of the inductor once every half cycle. At the resonant frequency f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal, the tank impedance is maximum and purely resistive, and the circulating current is Q times the supply current. Placed in the collector or drain circuit, the tank selects f_0 and rejects the harmonics, which is why LC oscillators give a clean sine wave.
Going Deeper: Loop Gain, Start-up and Stability

The closed-loop gain of a positive-feedback amplifier follows from one line of algebra. The amplifier input is the external signal plus the returned fraction, V_i = V_s + βV_o, and the output is V_o = A·V_i. Eliminating V_i gives V_o/V_s = A/(1 − Aβ). As Aβ climbs towards 1 the denominator shrinks and the gain soars: with Aβ = 0.9 the gain is 10A, with Aβ = 0.99 it is 100A, and at Aβ = 1 a finite output needs no input at all. That is the precise meaning of "an oscillator is an amplifier that supplies its own input".

A useful way to picture start-up is to follow one frequency component of the noise around the loop. Each trip multiplies its amplitude by the loop gain |Aβ|, so after n trips the amplitude is V_0·|Aβ|^n. With |Aβ| a few percent above 1 the growth is geometric but slow, which is why an oscillator takes many cycles to reach full output; with |Aβ| below 1 the same law describes an exponential decay. Treating one trip as one cycle of the oscillation gives a quick estimate of the start-up or decay time.

concepts.plainText: Vn = V0·|Aβ|^n, so n = ln(Vn/V0) / ln|Aβ|

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: start-up time
Given: f = 1 kHz, |Aβ| = 1.05 at small amplitude,
       noise component V0 = 1 µV, target amplitude 1 V
Assume the amplitude is multiplied by |Aβ| once per cycle.
n = ln(1 V / 1 µV) / ln(1.05) = ln(10^6) / ln(1.05)
  = 13.816 / 0.04879 = 283.2  ->  about 284 cycles
Time = n / f = 284 / 1000 Hz ≈ 0.28 s
Limiting in the amplifier then pulls |Aβ| back to exactly 1.

Why does a high Q give good frequency stability? Near resonance the phase angle of a tuned circuit changes as tan φ ≈ 2Q·Δf/f_0. Suppose a transistor capacitance drifts and adds a small unwanted phase Δφ to the loop. The oscillator can only restore a 0° total by moving to a frequency where the tank supplies −Δφ, so the fractional frequency error is roughly Δφ/(2Q). The larger Q is, the smaller the frequency shift needed to absorb the same phase error.

concepts.plainText: Δf/f0 ≈ tan(Δφ)/(2Q) ≈ Δφ/(2Q), with Δφ in radians

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: phase drift versus Q
A stray phase error of Δφ = 2° appears in the loop.
Δφ = 2 × π/180 = 0.03491 rad
LC tank, Q = 100:
  Δf/f0 = 0.03491 / (2 × 100) = 1.75 × 10^-4 = 175 ppm
Quartz crystal, Q = 10^5:
  Δf/f0 = 0.03491 / (2 × 10^5) = 1.75 × 10^-7 = 0.175 ppm
Same phase error, 1000 times smaller drift with the crystal.

Worked example 3: temperature drift
Given: 5 MHz LC oscillator, temperature coefficient
       +20 ppm/°C, temperature rises by 25 °C
Δf = f × (TC) × ΔT = 5 × 10^6 × 20 × 10^-6 × 25
   = 2500 Hz = 2.5 kHz (frequency increases)
New frequency = 5.0025 MHz
Fractional change = 20 ppm/°C × 25 °C = 500 ppm = 0.05 %

concepts.text: Common mistakes when answering oscillator questions:
items: Using the negative-feedback formula A/(1 + Aβ) for an oscillator; positive feedback gives A/(1 − Aβ).
Adding stage gains in decibels but multiplying them as plain ratios inconsistently; two stages of gain 20 give 400, not 40.
Converting decibels to a voltage ratio with 10^(dB/10) instead of 10^(dB/20).
Forgetting to convert degrees to radians before dividing a phase error by 2Q.
Thinking a very large loop gain gives a bigger clean sine wave; it gives a clipped, distorted output.

concepts.text: Heavy loading of the tank or feedback network lowers the effective Q and the loop gain. If |Aβ| falls below 1 the oscillator stops, which is why a buffer stage is placed between the oscillator and a changing load.

formulas.plainText: |Aβ| = 1 and total phase shift = 0° or 360°
Af = A / (1 − Aβ)  (gain with positive feedback)
|Aβ| slightly > 1 to start; |Aβ| = 1 in steady state
f0 = 1 / (2π√(LC))  (tank circuit)
Q = ω0·L / r = (1/r)·√(L/C)  (r = coil resistance)

notes.text: Read the wording: loop gain slightly greater than one refers to start-up (oscillations build up); exactly one is the steady-state Barkhausen condition; less than one means the oscillations die out (damped).

A 180° shift from the amplifier alone is not enough; the feedback network must add the other 180° so the total is 360° (equivalent to 0°). A total of 180° is negative feedback and gives no oscillation.

The Barkhausen criterion is necessary but not sufficient: it must be met at only one frequency, otherwise the circuit may oscillate at several frequencies or give a distorted waveform. It is also strictly a small-signal steady-state condition; real oscillators run with Aβ slightly above 1 and rely on non-linearity to limit the amplitude.
Frequency stability ranking to remember: crystal (best, a few ppm) > LC (good, about 0.1 to 1%) > RC (moderate, a few percent). Higher Q of the frequency-determining network means better stability.

concepts.text: Why RC Networks at Audio Frequencies

At audio frequencies (roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and in practice up to about 1 MHz) the inductors needed for an LC tank would be large, heavy and lossy. RC networks are cheap and small, and their phase shift changes with frequency, so they can fix the frequency at which the Barkhausen phase condition is met. Because an RC network has no resonance, RC oscillators depend on the amplifier to hold the gain precisely and have poorer frequency stability than LC or crystal types.
RC Phase-Shift Oscillator

The circuit uses an inverting amplifier (common-emitter transistor, FET or inverting op-amp) that contributes 180° of phase shift, with three cascaded RC sections in the feedback path. At the oscillation frequency each section shifts the phase by 60°, giving 180° from the network and 360° in total. For identical R and C in all three sections the network output is only 1/29 of its input at that frequency, so the amplifier gain must be at least 29 for the loop gain to reach unity.

concepts.plainText: network attenuation β = 1/29, so amplifier gain A ≥ 29

concepts.text: Features of the phase-shift oscillator:
items: Simple and inexpensive; gives a good sine wave at a fixed audio frequency.
Frequency is changed by varying all three capacitors (or resistors) together, which is inconvenient, so it is normally used at one fixed frequency.
Loading of the network by the amplifier input and variation of transistor parameters make the frequency and amplitude less precise than in the Wien bridge circuit.
With an op-amp the inverting gain R_f/R must be at least 29; in practice it is set a little higher and amplifier saturation limits the amplitude.

concepts.text: Wien Bridge Oscillator

The Wien bridge oscillator uses a non-inverting amplifier (0° shift) with two feedback paths. The positive-feedback path is a lead-lag network: a series R-C arm (lead) followed by a parallel R-C arm (lag). At exactly one frequency, f = 1/(2πRC) for equal R and C, the phase shift of the network is 0° and its attenuation is 1/3. The negative-feedback path (R_f and R_1) sets the amplifier gain to exactly 3, so R_f = 2R_1 for an op-amp, making the loop gain unity.

Amplitude stabilisation: because the gain must be exactly 3, practical circuits make R_f or R_1 a non-linear element. A tungsten lamp or positive-temperature-coefficient thermistor in the R_1 position increases its resistance as the output grows, lowering the gain; alternatively, two back-to-back diodes (or Zener diodes) across part of R_f conduct at large amplitude and reduce the gain, or a FET used as a voltage-controlled resistor in an AGC loop does the same. The result is a very pure sine wave with total harmonic distortion well below 1%.
Features of the Wien bridge oscillator:
items: Lowest distortion of the common RC oscillators; the standard audio test oscillator (about 5 Hz to 1 MHz).
Frequency is easily varied over a wide range with a dual (ganged) variable capacitor or potentiometer.
Good amplitude stability because the gain is set by negative feedback, not by transistor parameters.
Uses both positive feedback (lead-lag network) and negative feedback (R_f, R_1 divider); the bridge is balanced at the oscillation frequency.

concepts.text: Comparison
Worked Example

A Wien bridge oscillator uses R = 10 kΩ and C = 0.01 µF in both arms of the lead-lag network, with R_1 = 10 kΩ in the negative-feedback divider. Frequency: f = 1/(2π × 10^4 × 10^-8) = 1/(6.283 × 10^-4) ≈ 1.59 kHz. The gain must be 3, so R_f = 2R_1 = 20 kΩ. If the same R and C were used in a three-section phase-shift oscillator, the frequency would be 1.59 kHz/√6 ≈ 650 Hz and the amplifier would need a gain of at least 29.
Going Deeper: Deriving and Designing RC Oscillators

The numbers 1/(2πRC√6) and 29 come from analysing the three-section high-pass ladder (series C, shunt R) with ordinary circuit laws. Writing α = 1/(ωRC) and solving the ladder from the output back to the input gives the transfer ratio below. Oscillation needs the network output to be exactly 180° from its input, which means the ratio must be a negative real number, so its imaginary part must vanish: 6α − α³ = 0, giving α² = 6 and ω = 1/(RC√6). Substituting α² = 6 into the real part gives 1 − 30 = −29, so the network returns −1/29 of its input and the amplifier must supply a gain of at least 29.

concepts.plainText: β = 1 / (1 − 5α² − j(6α − α³)), where α = 1/(ωRC)

concepts.text: Two variations are worth knowing. If the sections are low-pass (series R, shunt C) the same algebra holds with α replaced by ωRC, so the frequency becomes √6/(2πRC) while the attenuation is still 1/29. If each section is isolated by a buffer, the sections no longer load one another: each simply gives 60°, which happens when ωRC = 1/√3, and each attenuates by cos 60° = 0.5, so the network passes 1/8 and a gain of only 8 is needed. The loading between sections is what makes the unbuffered ladder so lossy.

concepts.plainText: β(Wien) = 1 / (3 + j(ωRC − 1/(ωRC)))

concepts.text: For the Wien lead-lag network with equal parts, the imaginary term vanishes only when ωRC = 1, which gives f = 1/(2πRC) and β = 1/3. Below this frequency the network leads, above it the network lags, and at every other frequency |β| is less than 1/3, which is what makes the network frequency-selective. With unequal arms (series R_s, C_s; parallel R_p, C_p) the network still has 0° at f = 1/(2π√(R_sC_sR_pC_p)), but its attenuation becomes 1/(1 + R_s/R_p + C_p/C_s), so the amplifier gain must rise to match.

Worked example 1: op-amp phase-shift oscillator for 800 Hz
Choose C = 10 nF in each section.
R = 1/(2π f C √6) = 1/(2π × 800 × 10^-8 × 2.449)
  = 8.12 kΩ  ->  nearest standard value 8.2 kΩ
Actual f = 1/(2π × 8200 × 10^-8 × 2.449) ≈ 792 Hz
The inverting amplifier's input resistor is the third R (8.2 kΩ,
returned to the virtual earth), so gain = R_f/R ≥ 29:
R_f ≥ 29 × 8.2 kΩ = 237.8 kΩ  ->  use about 250 kΩ for start-up

Worked example 2: Wien network with unequal capacitors
R_s = R_p = 10 kΩ, C_s = 10 nF, C_p = 20 nF
f = 1/(2π √(R_s C_s R_p C_p))
  = 1/(2π √(10^4 × 10^-8 × 10^4 × 2×10^-8))
  = 1/(2π × 1.414 × 10^-4) ≈ 1.125 kHz
Attenuation = 1/(1 + R_s/R_p + C_p/C_s) = 1/(1 + 1 + 2) = 1/4
Required gain A = 4 = 1 + R_f/R_1  ->  R_f = 3 R_1

The twin-T oscillator uses a notch network made of two T sections in parallel: one T has two series resistors R with a shunt capacitor 2C, the other has two series capacitors C with a shunt resistor R/2. At f = 1/(2πRC) the two paths cancel and the output of the network is zero. Placed in the negative-feedback path of an amplifier, the twin-T removes negative feedback only at the notch frequency, so a modest positive feedback path makes the loop gain exceed unity there and nowhere else, giving a sharply selective audio oscillator.

rows: 3 buffered high-pass RC sections (series C), 60° each

concepts.text: Common mistakes in RC oscillator calculations:
items: Putting √6 in the Wien bridge formula, or leaving it out of the phase-shift formula.
Writing the Wien condition as R_f = 3R_1; the gain is 1 + R_f/R_1 = 3, so R_f = 2R_1.
Using 6 instead of √6, which makes the phase-shift frequency 2.45 times too low.
Forgetting that frequency varies as 1/(RC): doubling both R and C divides f by four.
For a FET or transistor stage, ignoring r_d or R_C loading, which raises the gain actually needed.

concepts.text: Quick checks: with the same R and C, a Wien bridge runs √6 ≈ 2.45 times faster than a phase-shift oscillator. The gain numbers 3 and 29 are independent of the R and C values, so they can be used without any calculation.

formulas.plainText: f = 1 / (2π·R·C·√6)  (phase-shift oscillator)
Amin = 29 (β = 1/29)  (phase-shift oscillator)
each RC section shifts 60°; three sections give 180°
f = 1 / (2π·R·C)  (Wien bridge)
A = 1 + Rf/R1 = 3, so Rf = 2·R1  (Wien bridge)

notes.text: √6 belongs to the phase-shift oscillator and so does the gain of 29; the Wien bridge has no √6 and needs a gain of 3. Do not swap them.
The lead-lag network of the Wien bridge gives 0° phase shift at f_0, so it must drive a non-inverting amplifier. Connected to an inverting amplifier the circuit will not oscillate at f_0.

The formula f = 1/(2πRC√6) assumes the RC network is not loaded by the amplifier. For the transistor version the textbook result becomes f = 1/(2πRC√(6 + 4R_C/R)) and the required current gain rises above 29.
Frequency scales inversely with RC in both circuits: doubling C halves f. Numerical questions use convenient values, e.g. R = 10 kΩ and C = 0.01 µF give 1.59 kHz (Wien) or 650 Hz (phase-shift).

concepts.text: The Tuned (Tank) Circuit Principle

An LC oscillator uses a parallel L-C tank as its frequency-determining network. The tank resonates at f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)), where its impedance is maximum and purely resistive, so an amplifier loaded by the tank has maximum gain and no extra phase shift only at f_0. The tank rings between cycles, storing energy alternately in C and L; the transistor delivers a short pulse of current once per cycle to replace the energy lost in the coil resistance. Because the high Q of the tank filters out harmonics the output is a clean sine wave, and because inductors of a few µH and capacitors of a few pF are practical, LC oscillators cover roughly 100 kHz to several hundred MHz.

Tuned-collector oscillator: the simplest transistor LC oscillator places the tank in the collector circuit of a common-emitter stage. A secondary winding coupled to the tank coil (a transformer) returns part of the collector signal to the base, and the winding sense is chosen so that the transformer supplies the 180° needed to complement the inversion of the amplifier. With the tank in the base circuit instead it is called a tuned-base oscillator. The Armstrong oscillator is the same idea with a small separate tickler coil providing the feedback.
Hartley Oscillator

The Hartley oscillator uses a tapped inductor (or two series inductors L_1 and L_2) with a single capacitor C across the whole coil. The tap is held at a fixed AC potential (ground or emitter), so the voltages at the two ends of the coil are 180° out of phase: one end is driven by the collector and the other feeds the base, providing the phase reversal. The feedback fraction is approximately the ratio of the two coil sections, so the amplifier gain must be at least the inverse of that ratio. The frequency is set by C and the total inductance L_T = L_1 + L_2 + 2M, where M is the mutual inductance between the sections (M = 0 for separate, uncoupled coils). The frequency is easily varied with a single variable capacitor, which made the Hartley popular in early radio receivers.
Colpitts Oscillator

The Colpitts oscillator is the electrical dual of the Hartley: a single inductor L in parallel with two series capacitors C_1 and C_2 whose junction is at AC ground. The capacitive voltage divider provides the 180° reversal, and because series capacitors carry the same current the voltage across each is inversely proportional to its capacitance, so the feedback fraction equals the ratio of the two capacitances. The frequency is set by L and the series combination C_T = C_1C_2/(C_1 + C_2), which is smaller than either capacitor. Capacitors are cheaper and more stable than tapped coils and there is no coupling between coil sections, so the Colpitts is the most widely used RF oscillator and has better frequency stability than the Hartley; it is also the basis of the Pierce crystal oscillator, in which the crystal replaces the inductor.
Clapp Oscillator

The Clapp oscillator is a Colpitts with a third capacitor C_3 in series with the inductor. C_3 is made much smaller than C_1 and C_2, so it dominates the series combination and fixes the frequency: f ≈ 1/(2π√(LC_3)). The junction capacitances of the transistor appear across the large C_1 and C_2, so their variation with temperature and voltage hardly affects the frequency. The Clapp therefore has better frequency stability than the Colpitts and is tuned simply by varying C_3; it is the preferred LC oscillator where stability matters, for example as a variable-frequency oscillator in receivers.
Comparison

rows: L-C tank plus coupled feedback coil
Easy tuning with variable C; coil coupling affects frequency
Most popular RF oscillator; better stability than Hartley
Colpitts plus small C_3 in series with L
Best stability of the three; transistor capacitances swamped

concepts.text: Worked Example

A Colpitts oscillator has L = 50 µH, C_1 = 200 pF and C_2 = 300 pF. C_T = (200 × 300)/(200 + 300) = 120 pF. f = 1/(2π√(50 × 10^-6 × 120 × 10^-12)) = 1/(2π√(6 × 10^-15)) = 1/(2π × 7.75 × 10^-8) ≈ 2.05 MHz. A Hartley oscillator with L_1 = 20 µH, L_2 = 30 µH, M = 0 and C = 120 pF has L_T = 50 µH and oscillates at the same 2.05 MHz, illustrating that the two circuits are duals.
Going Deeper: Designing LC Oscillators

The tank formula comes from the condition that the reactances cancel: at resonance ωL = 1/(ωC), so ω² = 1/(LC) and f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)). A real coil has a series resistance r, and the tank then looks like a pure resistance R_D (the dynamic resistance) only at f_0. R_D is large, typically tens to hundreds of kilohms, so the collector load and hence the amplifier gain peak sharply at f_0. The sharpness is measured by Q; a higher Q means a larger R_D, a purer sine wave and less frequency drift when transistor parameters change.

Gain condition for the Colpitts: the two tank capacitors are in series, so they carry the same circulating current and the voltage across each is proportional to its reactance. The output (collector) voltage appears across the output-side capacitor and the feedback (base) voltage across the input-side capacitor, so β = X_C(in)/X_C(out) = C_out/C_in. Barkhausen requires Aβ ≥ 1, giving A ≥ C_in/C_out. The Hartley is the dual: β ≈ (L_in + M)/(L_out + M), which reduces to L_in/L_out for uncoupled coils. In practice the start-up gain is made two or three times the minimum; the amplitude then grows until transistor non-linearity and bias shift pull the average gain back to exactly 1/β.

concepts.plainText: Colpitts: β = C_out/C_in, A ≥ C_in/C_out;  mutual inductance M = k·√(L1·L2)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - Hartley with coupled coils
Given: L_out = 40 µH, L_in = 10 µH, coupling k = 0.5 (aiding), C = 100 pF
M   = k·√(L_out·L_in) = 0.5 × √(40 × 10) = 10 µH
L_T = 40 + 10 + 2 × 10 = 70 µH
f   = 1/(2π√(70e-6 × 100e-12)) = 1/(2π × 8.37e-8) ≈ 1.90 MHz
β   = (L_in + M)/(L_out + M) = (10 + 10)/(40 + 10) = 0.4
A_min = 1/β = 2.5  (design for about 5 to 7 for reliable start-up)

Worked example 2 - why the Clapp is more stable
Clapp: L = 50 µH, C_1 = C_2 = 1 nF, C_3 = 100 pF
1/C_T = 1/1000 + 1/1000 + 1/100 pF^-1  ->  C_T = 83.3 pF
f = 1/(2π√(50e-6 × 83.3e-12)) ≈ 2.466 MHz  (C_3 alone predicts 2.251 MHz)
A 10 pF transistor capacitance appears across C_2 (C_2 -> 1010 pF):
  new C_T = 83.4 pF, f falls by about 1.0 kHz (about -410 ppm)
Same 10 pF in a Colpitts with L = 50 µH, C_1 = C_2 = 1 nF (f ≈ 1.007 MHz):
  f falls by about 2.5 kHz (about -2480 ppm), six times worse
A smaller C_3 makes the Clapp even less sensitive.

rows: L and C_1 in series with C_2
Variable L or ganged C_1, C_2

concepts.text: Common mistakes in LC oscillator problems:
items: Adding C_1 and C_2 in a Colpitts; they are in series, so C_T is smaller than either capacitor.
Forgetting 2M in a Hartley with coupled coils, or adding M only once.
Dropping the 2π, which makes the answer 6.28 times too high.
Mixing units: 1 pF = 10^-12 F and 1 µH = 10^-6 H; a slip of 10^3 in C changes f by about 31.6 times.
Assuming f ∝ 1/C; in fact f ∝ 1/√C, so a 9:1 capacitor gives only a 3:1 tuning range.

concepts.text: Practical details: an RF choke in the collector (or drain) lead passes the DC supply current but blocks the RF signal, so the supply does not short the tank. Coupling capacitors block DC between stages but are large enough to be short circuits at f_0. At VHF the Colpitts is often built in common-base form, where the amplifier gives no inversion and the capacitive divider feeds the emitter in phase. FET versions work the same way; their high input resistance loads the tank less, so Q and stability are better.
For a Colpitts or Clapp numerical, first reduce the capacitors to one series C_T, then use f = 1/(2π√(L C_T)). For a gain question, remember the ratio flips: β = C_out/C_in but A_min = C_in/C_out.

formulas.plainText: f0 = 1 / (2π√(LC))  (tank circuit, tuned-collector)
f = 1 / (2π√((L1 + L2 + 2M)·C))  (Hartley)
f = 1 / (2π√(L·C1·C2/(C1 + C2)))  (Colpitts)
f ≈ 1 / (2π√(L·C3)) when C3 << C1, C2  (Clapp)

notes.text: Hartley: L_T = L_1 + L_2 + 2M, inductors in series add (plus the mutual term). Colpitts: C_T = C_1C_2/(C_1 + C_2), capacitors in series combine like parallel resistors. Using the wrong rule is the commonest numerical slip.
Two series capacitors give a smaller total capacitance than either alone, so a Colpitts oscillator runs at a higher frequency than 1/(2π√(LC_1)) or 1/(2π√(LC_2)) would suggest.
Hartley and Colpitts are duals: swap every L for a C and vice versa. Both need a tap (inductive or capacitive) at AC ground to provide the 180° phase reversal for a common-emitter amplifier.
Frequency stability ranking of LC oscillators: Clapp > Colpitts > Hartley > tuned-collector. If a question asks for the improved Colpitts or the most stable LC oscillator, the answer is Clapp.

concepts.text: Piezoelectric Effect

Certain crystals such as quartz, Rochelle salt, tourmaline and some ceramics are piezoelectric: a mechanical stress across the crystal produces a voltage between its faces, and conversely an applied voltage makes the crystal deform. Quartz is used for oscillators because it is mechanically strong, chemically stable and has a very small temperature coefficient. A thin slice cut at a precise angle (the AT-cut is common) with metal electrodes on its faces vibrates mechanically at a natural frequency fixed by its thickness; an AC voltage at that frequency sets up large vibrations, so electrically the slice behaves as an extremely sharp resonant circuit. Thinner slices give higher frequencies, from about 10 kHz to 20-30 MHz on the fundamental and up to about 200 MHz on overtones.
Electrical Equivalent Circuit

Between its terminals the crystal is modelled as a series branch L-C_s-R representing the mechanical vibration (L for the mass, C_s for the elastic compliance, R for frictional loss), in parallel with a mounting capacitance C_M (also written C_p) formed by the electrodes and holder. Typical values are L from a few millihenry (tens of MHz) to several hundred henry (low-frequency crystals), C_s of a few hundredths of a picofarad or less, R from a few ohms to a few kilohm and C_M of a few picofarads. The enormous L/C ratio is what gives the very high Q.

concepts.plainText: fs = 1 / (2π√(L·Cs))  (series resonance, impedance minimum ≈ R)
fp = 1/(2π√(L·Cs·CM/(Cs + CM))) = fs·√(1 + Cs/CM)  (parallel resonance)

concepts.text: Two resonances: at the series resonant frequency f_s the L-C_s branch alone resonates and the crystal impedance is minimum (approximately R). Slightly above it, at the parallel (anti-resonant) frequency f_p, the now inductive branch resonates with C_M and the impedance is maximum. Because C_s is much smaller than C_M, f_p exceeds f_s by only about 0.1 to 0.5 percent, a few hundred hertz to a few kilohertz at 1 MHz. Between f_s and f_p the crystal behaves as an inductor, and most crystal oscillators operate in this narrow band with the crystal replacing the coil of a Colpitts-type tank.
Q Factor and Frequency Stability

The quality factor Q = ω_sL/R of a quartz crystal is typically 10^4 to 10^6 (the syllabus quotes 10 000 to 100 000), compared with about 100 for a good LC tank and far less for an RC network. Such a high Q means the reactance and phase of the crystal change extremely steeply with frequency, so any drift in the transistor or supply is corrected by a minute frequency change. The result is frequency stability of the order of 1 to 100 parts per million (ppm) for a plain crystal: a 10 MHz crystal rated ±20 ppm stays within ±200 Hz. Temperature is the main remaining influence; an AT-cut crystal follows a cubic curve of a few ppm/°C away from its turnover temperature. A TCXO (temperature-compensated crystal oscillator) corrects this electronically to about ±1 ppm, and an OCXO (oven-controlled crystal oscillator) holds the crystal at a constant temperature for 0.01 ppm or better.
Crystal Oscillator Circuits
Common crystal oscillator circuits:
items: Pierce oscillator: a Colpitts circuit in which the crystal replaces the inductor, operating between f_s and f_p where it is inductive. Two capacitors to ground form the divider; with a CMOS inverter as the amplifier it is the standard microprocessor clock circuit.

Miller oscillator: the crystal is connected between the base (or gate) and ground, and an LC tank tuned slightly above the operating frequency sits in the collector (drain) circuit; feedback occurs through the internal collector-base (Miller) capacitance of the transistor.
Crystal-controlled Hartley or Colpitts: the crystal is placed in series with the feedback path so that feedback, and therefore oscillation, is possible only at f_s where its impedance is minimum.
Overtone operation: a crystal can be driven at its odd mechanical harmonics (3rd, 5th, 7th) using a tank that suppresses the fundamental, extending the range to about 200 MHz.

concepts.text: Applications and Limitations
Where crystal oscillators are used:
items: Clock generators for microprocessors, microcontrollers, digital watches (32.768 kHz) and computer buses.
Carrier and local-oscillator sources in radio transmitters and receivers, mobile phones and GPS receivers.
Frequency counters, signal generators and other laboratory reference standards.
Real-time clocks and communication systems where the timing of transmitter and receiver must not drift apart.

concepts.text: Limitations: the frequency is fixed by the physical dimensions of the crystal, so it cannot be tuned over a wide range. A variable capacitor in series or parallel (a trimmer, or a varactor in a VCXO) pulls the frequency by only a few hundred ppm, because the crystal is inductive only in the narrow band between f_s and f_p. Each frequency needs its own crystal, and the fundamental is limited to about 20-30 MHz because thinner slices become too fragile. Crystals also have a maximum drive level of a few milliwatts and can be damaged by mechanical shock.
Worked Example

A quartz crystal has L = 3 H, C_s = 0.05 pF, R = 500 Ω and C_M = 10 pF. Series resonance: f_s = 1/(2π√(3 × 0.05 × 10^-12)) = 1/(2π√(1.5 × 10^-13)) = 1/(2π × 3.873 × 10^-7) ≈ 411 kHz. Parallel resonance: f_p = f_s√(1 + C_s/C_M) = 411 kHz × √1.005 ≈ 412 kHz, only about 0.25 percent (1 kHz) higher. Q = ω_sL/R = (2π × 411 × 10^3 × 3)/500 ≈ 15 500, far above any LC circuit.
Going Deeper: Quartz Crystal Resonators

The closeness of f_s and f_p follows from the equivalent circuit. At f_p the motional branch is inductive and resonates with C_M, so its effective capacitance is C_s in series with C_M, which is only very slightly smaller than C_s itself. Writing f_p = f_s√(1 + C_s/C_M) and using √(1 + x) ≈ 1 + x/2 for small x gives the simple spacing formula below. Since C_s/C_M is typically 1/200 to 1/1000, the two resonances are only 0.05 to 0.25 percent apart.

concepts.plainText: fp − fs ≈ fs·Cs/(2·CM);  Q = (1/R)·√(L/Cs)

concepts.text: Reactance picture: below f_s the crystal is capacitive, at f_s it is a small resistance R, between f_s and f_p its reactance is inductive and rises steeply, at f_p the impedance is maximum, and above f_p it is capacitive again. A parallel-mode circuit such as the Pierce makes the crystal resonate with an external load capacitance C_L, so the actual frequency lies slightly above f_s. The crystal is therefore specified for a particular C_L, and changing C_L pulls the frequency: a smaller C_L raises it towards f_p and a larger C_L lowers it towards f_s.

concepts.plainText: CL = C1·C2/(C1 + C2) + Cstray  (Pierce load capacitance)
fL ≈ fs·(1 + Cs/(2(CM + CL)))  (load-resonant frequency)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - resonances and Q of a crystal
Given: L = 0.1 H, C_s = 0.05 pF, R = 100 Ω, C_M = 10 pF
f_s = 1/(2π√(0.1 × 0.05e-12)) = 1/(2π × 7.07e-8) ≈ 2.251 MHz
f_p = f_s√(1 + 0.05/10) = f_s × 1.0025 ≈ 2.256 MHz
f_p − f_s ≈ f_s·C_s/(2C_M) = 2.251e6 × 0.0025 ≈ 5.6 kHz
Q = ω_sL/R = 2π × 2.251e6 × 0.1/100 ≈ 14 100
Compare: a good LC tank has Q of about 100, so the crystal is about 140 times sharper.

Worked example 2 - Pierce clock design
Crystal: 16 MHz, rated C_L = 20 pF, ±25 ppm; board stray about 4 pF
C_L = C/2 + C_stray  ->  C/2 = 20 − 4 = 16 pF  ->  C_1 = C_2 = 32 pF
Tolerance: Δf = 16e6 × 25e-6 = ±400 Hz
Pulling check (C_s = 0.015 pF, C_M = 5 pF):
  f_L − f_s ≈ 16e6 × 0.015/(2 × (5 + 20)) = 4.8 kHz  (300 ppm above f_s)
Wrong C_1, C_2 would shift f by tens of ppm, eating the tolerance budget.

Overtone and series-mode circuits: a crystal vibrates mechanically only at odd multiples of its fundamental thickness-shear mode, so a 20 MHz cut can be used near 60, 100 or 140 MHz. Because the fundamental always has the most loop gain, an overtone oscillator needs an LC tank tuned near the wanted overtone to kill gain at the fundamental. In a series-mode oscillator the crystal sits in the feedback path, where its minimum impedance at f_s lets feedback through only at that frequency. In the Miller oscillator the crystal is between gate and ground and the drain tank is tuned slightly above the crystal frequency so that it looks inductive; feedback is through the gate-drain capacitance.
Common mistakes with crystal questions:
items: Placing f_p below f_s; it is always slightly above.
Forgetting the square root in f_p = f_s√(1 + C_s/C_M), which doubles the spacing.
Assuming overtones can be even harmonics; only odd overtones exist.
Treating ppm as percent: 1 ppm = 10^-6 = 0.0001 percent.
Adding the two Pierce capacitors; they are in series across the crystal, plus stray.

concepts.text: The watch crystal frequency 32.768 kHz equals 2^15 Hz, so a chain of 15 divide-by-2 flip-flops gives exactly 1 Hz. A ppm error translates directly into time error: 1 ppm is about 0.0864 s per day.

formulas.plainText: fs = 1 / (2π√(L·Cs))  (series resonance)
fp = fs·√(1 + Cs/CM), slightly above fs  (parallel resonance)
Δf = f0 × ppm / 10^6  (e.g. 10 MHz at ±20 ppm → ±200 Hz)

notes.text: Q of a quartz crystal: 10^4 to 10^6 (syllabus value 10 000 to 100 000). If asked for the reason for the high frequency stability of a crystal oscillator, answer: the very high Q of the piezoelectric quartz crystal.

f_p is slightly higher than f_s, not lower, and the two lie very close together (within about 0.1 to 0.5 percent). The crystal is inductive only between them; outside this band it is capacitive and a Pierce or Colpitts type circuit will not oscillate.
The crystal does not generate a signal by itself; it is only the frequency-determining element. The transistor or logic gate still provides the gain and the Barkhausen conditions still apply.
Crystal oscillators are essentially fixed-frequency devices. A wide tuning range is a property of LC and RC oscillators, never of the crystal oscillator.

concepts.text: Relaxation Oscillators: Non-Sinusoidal Generation

A relaxation oscillator has no resonant network. A capacitor charges through a resistor towards a supply voltage until a switching device (transistor pair, comparator, UJT or timer IC) reaches a threshold and abruptly changes state, discharging or reversing the capacitor; the cycle then repeats. The output at the switch is a square or pulse wave and the voltage on the capacitor is an exponential ramp, approximately triangular or sawtooth. The frequency is set by the RC time constant and the switching thresholds, so it is easy to vary over a wide range, but the stability is only moderate (typically 1 percent or worse).
Multivibrators
Two cross-coupled switching stages give three types:
items: Astable (free-running): neither state is stable; the circuit switches continuously with no trigger and produces a square wave. In the transistor version two common-emitter stages are cross-coupled through C_1 and C_2 with base resistors R_1 and R_2; each half-period is 0.69RC, so T = 0.69(R_1C_1 + R_2C_2).

Monostable (one-shot): one stable state; a trigger pulse switches it to the quasi-stable state for a fixed time T set by RC, after which it returns by itself. Used for pulse stretching, debouncing and fixed delays.

Bistable (flip-flop): both states are stable; it changes state only on a trigger and stays there, storing one bit. It has no timing capacitor, and because two triggers give one output cycle it also acts as a divide-by-two frequency divider.

concepts.text: The 555 Timer

The 555 is an 8-pin IC containing two comparators with thresholds at 2/3 V_CC and 1/3 V_CC (set by an internal resistive divider), an RS flip-flop, a discharge transistor and an output stage. In the astable mode the timing capacitor C charges from 1/3 V_CC to 2/3 V_CC through R_A + R_B and discharges back to 1/3 V_CC through R_B only, via the discharge pin 7. The output (pin 3) is high while C charges and low while it discharges, so the high time is always longer than the low time: t_H = 0.693(R_A + R_B)C and t_L = 0.693R_BC. The duty cycle therefore lies between 50 and 100 percent unless a diode is placed across R_B.

concepts.plainText: f = 1.44 / ((RA + 2RB)·C);  duty cycle D = (RA + RB)/(RA + 2RB)

concepts.text: In the monostable mode R_B is omitted, the trigger (pin 2) is pulled below 1/3 V_CC and the output goes high while C charges from 0 to 2/3 V_CC through R: the pulse width is T = 1.1RC regardless of the trigger length. The 555 operates from 4.5 to 16 V at up to about 500 kHz. Because the thresholds are fixed fractions of V_CC, the timing depends only on the external R and C and is almost independent of supply voltage, with a typical initial accuracy of about 1 percent and temperature drift of the order of 50 to 150 ppm/°C.
Schmitt Trigger and Hysteresis

A Schmitt trigger is a comparator with positive feedback, so it has two different switching thresholds: the output changes state when the input rises above the upper trip point V_UT and changes back only when the input falls below the lower trip point V_LT. The difference V_H = V_UT − V_LT is the hysteresis. It converts slow or noisy waveforms (sine, triangle) into clean square waves and prevents chatter near the threshold. With an inverting op-amp Schmitt trigger whose non-inverting input is fed from the output divider (R_1 from the output, R_2 to ground), β = R_2/(R_1 + R_2), V_UT = +βV_sat, V_LT = −βV_sat and V_H = 2βV_sat. Adding an RC network from output to the inverting input turns it into a simple square-wave relaxation oscillator.
Triangle, Sawtooth and Function Generators

Square to triangle: feeding a square wave into an op-amp integrator (R in series with the inverting input, C in the feedback path) gives a linear ramp downwards during the positive half-cycle and upwards during the negative half-cycle, that is a triangular wave of peak-to-peak amplitude V_sq T/(2RC), where T is the period of the square wave. Closing the loop, so that the integrator output drives a Schmitt trigger whose square output drives the integrator, gives the classic function-generator core that produces square and triangular waves simultaneously, the frequency being set by the integrator RC and the trigger hysteresis.

Sawtooth with a UJT relaxation oscillator: a capacitor charges through R from the supply V_BB. When its voltage reaches the peak-point voltage V_P = ηV_BB + V_D the emitter to base-1 junction of the unijunction transistor turns on abruptly, the negative-resistance region discharges C rapidly through the small base-1 resistor R_B1 until the valley point is reached, and the cycle repeats. The capacitor voltage is a sawtooth and the narrow pulse across R_B1 is used to trigger SCRs. The frequency is f ≈ 1/(RC ln(1/(1 − η))), where η, the intrinsic stand-off ratio, lies between about 0.5 and 0.8; R must lie between limits set by the peak-point and valley-point currents for oscillation to occur.

concepts.plainText: f ≈ 1 / (R·C·ln(1/(1 − η)));  VP = η·VBB + VD

concepts.text: A function generator is a laboratory instrument that produces sine, square and triangular (and often sawtooth and pulse) waveforms of adjustable frequency, amplitude and DC offset from a single core oscillator. The classic analogue design uses the Schmitt-trigger and integrator loop for the square and triangular waves and shapes the triangle into a sine with a diode-resistor network; modern instruments synthesise the waveform digitally (DDS) with a crystal reference for accuracy.

rows: Integrator fed by a square wave
No timing capacitor; toggles on each trigger

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Timing Relaxation Oscillators

Every timing constant in this subtopic comes from one rule for a capacitor charging through a resistor towards a final voltage: the time to move from a start voltage to an end voltage is t = RC ln((V_final − V_start)/(V_final − V_end)). In the 555 astable the capacitor charges towards V_CC from 1/3 V_CC to 2/3 V_CC, so the ratio is (2/3)/(1/3) = 2 and t = RC ln 2 = 0.693RC; the discharge towards 0 from 2/3 to 1/3 V_CC also gives a ratio of 2. In the 555 monostable the capacitor starts from 0 V, the ratio is 1/(1/3) = 3 and t = RC ln 3 = 1.0986RC, which is rounded to 1.1RC. Because every voltage in the ratio is a fixed fraction of V_CC, the supply cancels out.

An op-amp astable is an inverting Schmitt trigger whose output charges C through R into the inverting input. The capacitor swings between +βV_sat and −βV_sat while charging towards ±V_sat, so each half-period is RC ln((1 + β)/(1 − β)). With R_1 = R_2 (β = 0.5) the period is 2RC ln 3 = 2.2RC, and choosing β ≈ 0.462 (R_2 ≈ 0.86R_1) makes the logarithm equal to 1, so T = 2RC. A non-inverting Schmitt trigger (input through R_1 to the non-inverting input, R_2 from the output back to the same node, inverting input grounded) has trip points ±(R_1/R_2)V_sat instead.

concepts.plainText: T = 2RC·ln((1 + β)/(1 − β)), β = R2/(R1 + R2)  (op-amp astable)

concepts.text: In the square-triangle function generator a non-inverting Schmitt trigger drives an integrator whose output is fed back to the trigger input. The integrator output ramps at V_sat/(RC) and reverses whenever it reaches a trip point, so the triangle peaks are ±(R_1/R_2)V_sat. Covering 2(R_1/R_2)V_sat in each half-period gives T/2 = 2(R_1/R_2)RC, that is f = R_2/(4R_1RC). The frequency is changed with R or C and the amplitude with the ratio R_1/R_2, so the two adjustments are independent.

Worked example 2: triangle-square generator, V_sat = ±12 V
Schmitt: R_1 = 10 kΩ (input), R_2 = 20 kΩ (feedback); integrator R = 10 kΩ, C = 0.01 µF
Triangle peak = (R_1/R_2) V_sat = (10/20) × 12 = 6 V  ->  12 V peak-to-peak
f = R_2 / (4 R_1 R C) = 20k / (4 × 10k × 10k × 0.01 µF)
  = 2 / (4 × 10^-4 s) = 5 kHz
Square output: ±12 V at 5 kHz, 50 % duty

In the UJT oscillator the capacitor charges towards V_BB and the UJT fires at V_P ≈ ηV_BB, so with V_D neglected the charging ratio is V_BB/(V_BB − ηV_BB) = 1/(1 − η), which is where ln(1/(1 − η)) comes from; η = 0.632 gives ln 2.72 = 1 and T ≈ RC. Oscillation needs R small enough to supply the peak-point current I_P at V_P and large enough that it cannot hold the valley current I_V, otherwise the UJT latches on: (V_BB − V_V)/I_V < R < (V_BB − V_P)/I_P. A ramp generator becomes truly linear when the capacitor is charged by a constant current I, because the slope is then I/C instead of an exponential.

Worked example 3: UJT oscillator, η = 0.6, V_BB = 12 V, V_D = 0.7 V
R = 47 kΩ, C = 0.1 µF, I_P = 5 µA, V_V = 1.5 V, I_V = 4 mA
V_P = ηV_BB + V_D = 7.2 + 0.7 = 7.9 V
f ≈ 1/(RC ln(1/(1 − η))) = 1/(4.7 ms × ln 2.5) = 1/(4.7 ms × 0.916) ≈ 232 Hz
R_max = (V_BB − V_P)/I_P = 4.1 V / 5 µA = 820 kΩ
R_min = (V_BB − V_V)/I_V = 10.5 V / 4 mA = 2.63 kΩ
47 kΩ lies between the limits, so the circuit oscillates
Common mistakes in waveform-generator problems:
items: Writing R_A + R_B instead of R_A + 2R_B in the 555 astable frequency: the capacitor discharges through R_B only, but the period contains both intervals.
Swapping the duty-cycle expression: the output is high while C charges, so D = (R_A + R_B)/(R_A + 2R_B), always above 50 % without a diode across R_B.
Using 0.693 for the 555 monostable: its capacitor starts from 0 V, so the constant is ln 3 ≈ 1.1.
Taking a single trip point as the hysteresis: V_H is the full difference V_UT − V_LT, which is 2βV_sat for a symmetrical Schmitt trigger.
Forcing pin 5 of a 555 changes both thresholds (to V_C and V_C/2) and therefore the timing; the 0.693 and 1.1 constants hold only when pin 5 is left at 2/3 V_CC.

concepts.text: For any RC timing question, write t = RC ln((V_final − V_start)/(V_final − V_end)) first; the 0.693, 1.1, 2.2 and ln(1/(1 − η)) constants all drop out of it, so you never need to memorise them separately.

formulas.plainText: f = 1.44 / ((RA + 2RB)·C)  (555 astable)
tH = 0.693·(RA + RB)·C,  tL = 0.693·RB·C  (555 astable)
D = tH / (tH + tL) = (RA + RB)/(RA + 2RB)  (duty cycle, always > 50%)
T = 1.1·R·C  (555 monostable pulse width)
T = 0.69·(R1·C1 + R2·C2) ≈ 1.38·RC  (BJT astable)
f ≈ 1 / (R·C·ln(1/(1 − η)))  (UJT relaxation oscillator)

notes.text: 555 constants to memorise: 0.693 (= ln 2) for each charge or discharge interval, 1.44 (= 1/0.693) in the astable frequency, 1.1 in the monostable pulse width. The astable frequency contains 2R_B because C discharges through R_B alone.

A basic 555 astable cannot give a duty cycle below 50 percent, because the capacitor charges through R_A + R_B but discharges through R_B only. A true 50 percent square wave needs a diode across R_B or a flip-flop after the output.
Bistable multivibrator = flip-flop = one-bit memory. It is the only multivibrator with no timing capacitor, and it divides the trigger frequency by two.

Match the word to the waveform: multivibrator or 555 gives square or rectangular; integrator gives triangle; UJT relaxation oscillator gives sawtooth; Schmitt trigger converts any input to a square wave (hysteresis).

concepts.text: Gain and Decibels

Voltage gain A_v is the ratio of output to input voltage, current gain A_i the ratio of output to input current, and power gain A_p the ratio of output to input signal power. Because P = VI, the power gain equals the product of the voltage and current gains. All three are dimensionless: a gain greater than 1 means amplification and a gain less than 1 means attenuation. A common-emitter stage has both voltage and current gain, an emitter follower has current gain only (A_v about 1), and a common-base stage has voltage gain only (A_i slightly below 1).

concepts.plainText: Av = Vo/Vi, Ai = Io/Ii, Ap = Po/Pi = Av × Ai

concepts.text: Gains are usually quoted in decibels (dB), a logarithmic unit that turns multiplication into addition and compresses very wide ranges. Power gain in dB is 10 log10(P_o/P_i). Because power is proportional to the square of voltage (P = V²/R), a voltage or current ratio is converted with 20 log10; strictly this equals the power gain only when the input and output resistances are equal, but the 20 log convention is applied to every voltage ratio regardless. A gain below 1 gives negative decibels (a loss). The point at which the gain has fallen by 3 dB is the half-power point: power is halved and voltage is 0.707 of its mid-band value.

Worked example. A two-stage amplifier has voltage gains of 20 and 50. The overall gain is 20 × 50 = 1000, that is 20 log10(1000) = 60 dB; the same answer comes from adding the stage gains, 20 log 20 = 26 dB and 20 log 50 = 34 dB. If that amplifier raises 10 mW of input power to 1 W, the power gain is 100, which is 10 log10(100) = 20 dB, not 40 dB.
Impedances and Bandwidth
Z_in is the impedance the amplifier presents to its source and Z_out is the Thevenin impedance it presents to the load. The ideal values depend on which quantity the amplifier must preserve:
items: Voltage amplifier: Z_in infinite (draws no current from the source, so no signal is lost across the source resistance) and Z_out zero (the full output voltage reaches any load). Practical designs aim for high Z_in and low Z_out, as in an emitter follower or an op-amp.
Current amplifier: Z_in zero (all of the source current enters) and Z_out infinite (the same current is delivered to any load).
Transconductance amplifier (voltage in, current out): Z_in infinite and Z_out infinite. Transresistance amplifier (current in, voltage out): both zero.
For maximum power transfer between stages, Z_out of one stage should equal Z_in of the next; transformer coupling is used when this matching matters, for example at a loudspeaker or antenna.

concepts.text: The frequency response is a plot of gain (usually in dB) against frequency on a logarithmic axis. For an RC-coupled amplifier it is flat over the mid-band, falls at low frequencies because coupling and bypass capacitors present increasing reactance, and falls at high frequencies because junction capacitances, stray wiring capacitance (multiplied by the Miller effect) and the finite transit time of carriers shunt the signal. The lower cut-off f_L and upper cut-off f_H are the frequencies at which the gain drops to 0.707 of the mid-band value (−3 dB, half power), and the bandwidth is their difference; a direct-coupled amplifier has f_L = 0, so its bandwidth simply equals f_H. For a given device the gain-bandwidth product is roughly constant, so more gain per stage means less bandwidth.

concepts.plainText: BW = fH − fL; |A| at cut-off = A_mid/√2 = 0.707 A_mid

concepts.text: Distortion and Efficiency
Any change in the shape of the signal other than a scale factor is distortion:
items: Amplitude (non-linear or harmonic) distortion: the transfer characteristic of the device is not a straight line, so a pure sine input produces new frequencies at 2f, 3f and so on. It is measured as total harmonic distortion (THD) and is worst for large signals and for a Q-point near saturation or cut-off.
Frequency distortion: different frequency components are amplified by different amounts because of reactive elements, so a complex waveform changes shape even though no new frequencies are created.
Phase (delay) distortion: the phase shift is not proportional to frequency, so components arrive with different delays; it matters for video and pulse signals but is inaudible in audio.

Intermodulation distortion: two input frequencies generate sum and difference products. Crossover distortion in class B stages is a special case of non-linear distortion and is treated in the next subtopics.

concepts.text: The conversion efficiency of a power amplifier is the AC signal power delivered to the load divided by the DC power taken from the supply, where P_dc equals the supply voltage times the average supply current. Whatever is not delivered to the load is dissipated as heat in the transistor (and in any collector resistor), so P_D = P_dc − P_ac. Efficiency is the property that separates the amplifier classes: a class A stage draws its full supply current even with no signal, while a class B stage draws current only while a signal is present.
Coupling Methods and Cascading

rows: Flat over the audio band; poor at low frequencies because of coupling-capacitor reactance
No matching; DC power is wasted in the collector resistor
Small-signal audio and voltage-amplifier stages; cheap and compact
Poor and non-flat; winding resonance and core losses limit the band
Excellent matching through the turns ratio; higher efficiency because no DC is dropped in the load
Power-amplifier outputs and tuned RF stages; bulky and costly
Extends down to DC (f_L = 0); no reactive components
No matching; the bias of one stage affects the next and drifts with temperature

concepts.text: When stages are cascaded the overall gain is the product of the individual gains (each measured with the next stage connected as its load), so gains in decibels simply add. Bandwidth shrinks as stages are added because every stage contributes its own roll-off; for n identical stages the overall upper cut-off is f_H √(2^(1/n) − 1). Noise generated in the first stage is amplified by every following stage, so the input stage must be the low-noise one; later stages contribute little to the output noise.
Going Deeper: Small-Signal Amplifier Configurations

Small-signal analysis replaces the transistor by a linear model valid for small swings about the Q-point. For a BJT the simplest is the r_e model: the base-emitter junction looks like a resistance r_e = V_T/I_E seen from the emitter (about 25 Ω at 1 mA with V_T = 25 mV), and β r_e seen from the base, while the collector acts as a current source of α i_e. A signal voltage v_b at the base therefore drives an emitter current v_b/(r_e + R_E), where R_E is any unbypassed emitter resistance, and nearly all of that current flows through the collector load. The CE voltage gain is simply the ratio of the total collector load resistance to the total emitter-circuit resistance, with a minus sign for the 180° phase inversion.

concepts.plainText: Av = −(RC || RL)/(re + RE), with re = VT/IE; Rin(base) = β(re + RE)

concepts.text: An FET is modelled by a transconductance g_m from gate voltage to drain current, with an open-circuit gate. The common-source gain is −g_m (R_D ∥ R_L), and the source follower (common drain) gives g_m R_S/(1 + g_m R_S), always below 1, with an output resistance of R_S ∥ 1/g_m. For a JFET, g_m = g_m0 (1 − V_GS/V_P) with g_m0 = 2 I_DSS/|V_P|; for a MOSFET in saturation g_m = 2 I_D/(V_GS − V_t). Because g_m of an FET at a few milliamperes is far lower than the 40 mA/V per milliampere of a BJT, FET stages give less voltage gain but offer a practically infinite input resistance.

rows: Set by the gate bias resistor, very high

VCC = 15 V, R1 = 56 k, R2 = 12 k, RC = 3.3 k, RE = 1 k (bypassed), RL = 10 k

Each coupling capacitor forms a high-pass section with the resistance it sees: the input capacitor with R_s + R_in, the output capacitor with R_C + R_L. The emitter bypass capacitor is usually the one that sets f_L, because the resistance it sees looking into the emitter is tiny, R_E ∥ (r_e + R_s'/β), so it needs a much larger capacitance for the same cut-off. At high frequencies the device capacitances take over. Miller's theorem shows that a capacitance C_μ (C_bc) bridging an inverting stage of gain −A behaves at the input like C_μ(1 + A), so a small feedback capacitance becomes the dominant input capacitance and sets f_H.

concepts.plainText: fL = 1/(2π(Rs + Rin)Cc); Miller input capacitance CM = Cμ(1 + |Av|); then fH = 1/(2π Rth Cin)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: cut-off frequencies of the stage in example 1
Input coupling C1 = 10 uF, source resistance Rs = 600 ohm
fL(C1) = 1/(2 pi (600 + 1333) x 10e-6) = 8.2 Hz
High end: C_pi = 15 pF, C_mu = 3 pF, gain from base = -(RC || RL)/re = -193
Miller: C_in = 15 + 3 x (1 + 193) = 597 pF
Thevenin resistance driving the base Rth = Rs || Rin = 600 || 1333 = 414 ohm
fH = 1/(2 pi x 414 x 597e-12) = 644 kHz
Without Miller multiplication (18 pF) fH would wrongly come out near 21 MHz

When stages are cascaded, each stage's gain must be found with the next stage's input resistance as its load, and the first stage's input resistance loads the source. A practical method treats every stage as a Thevenin source of open-circuit gain A_oc and output resistance R_o, then multiplies the voltage-divider losses R_in(next)/(R_o + R_in(next)) at each interface. Buffers (emitter or source followers) are placed where a high-impedance stage must drive a low-impedance load, and the cascode (CE followed by CB) removes the Miller multiplication because the CE stage then sees only the tiny r_e of the CB stage as its load.

Common slips: forgetting R_L in parallel with R_C; using β r_e instead of r_e in the gain formula; ignoring the bias resistors R1 ∥ R2 when finding the stage input resistance; using the open-circuit gain of a stage while it is loaded by the next stage; and multiplying C_μ by A instead of (1 + A) for the Miller capacitance.

Quick checks: CE gain ≈ R_C/r_e bypassed or R_C/R_E unbypassed; follower gain just under 1; CB input resistance ≈ r_e. For n identical stages the overall f_H is f_H √(2^(1/n) − 1) and the overall f_L is f_L/√(2^(1/n) − 1): 0.644 for two stages and 0.510 for three.

Ap(dB) = 10 log10(Po/Pi)
BW = fH − fL
η = P_ac / P_dc × 100 %; P_D = P_dc − P_ac

notes.text: Half-power point: −3 dB, power halves, voltage falls to 0.707 (1/√2). Questions often ask between which points bandwidth is measured: the answer is where gain falls to 70.7 % of its maximum.
Decibel gains of cascaded stages add; linear gains multiply. Never multiply decibels, and never add linear gains.
20 log(V_o/V_i) equals the power gain in dB only when the input and output resistances are equal; the exam nevertheless expects 20 log for any voltage ratio and 10 log for any power ratio.

Ideal voltage amplifier: Z_in infinite, Z_out zero. Ideal current amplifier: the reverse. Remember it as: a voltage amplifier wants no current drawn at its input, a current amplifier wants no voltage dropped there.

concepts.text: Load Line and Q-Point

The DC load line is drawn on the transistor's output characteristics between the point V_CE = V_CC (where I_C = 0) and the point I_C = V_CC/R_L (where V_CE = 0); every possible operating point for that supply and load lies on it. The bias network fixes the no-signal operating point, the Q-point (I_CQ, V_CEQ), and the input signal swings the instantaneous operating point along the line about Q. How far down the line the Q-point sits decides for what fraction of each input cycle the transistor carries current, its conduction angle, and that in turn defines the amplifier class.
Class A

The Q-point is placed at the centre of the load line, V_CEQ about V_CC/2 and I_CQ about V_CC/(2R_L), so the signal can swing equally towards saturation and cut-off without clipping. The transistor conducts for the full 360° of the cycle and the collector current is a complete sine wave riding on the steady I_CQ, so the output is the most faithful replica of the input. A single transistor is enough, with either a collector resistor (series-fed, RC coupled) or an output transformer as the load. The price is a constant supply current, and therefore heat, even when no signal is present.
Class B

The Q-point is at cut-off: I_CQ = 0 and V_CEQ = V_CC, so the transistor conducts only while the input drives it on, for 180° of each cycle, and its collector current is a series of half-sine pulses. Because one transistor reproduces only half the waveform, two are used in push-pull: one handles the positive half-cycle and the other the negative half, and the two halves are combined in an output transformer or, in a complementary-symmetry stage, at the joined emitters of an npn and a pnp transistor. Standby current is zero, but the hand-over between the two transistors produces crossover distortion.
Class AB

The Q-point is placed slightly above cut-off with a small quiescent current, typically a few milliamperes to a few tens of milliamperes. Each transistor then conducts for a little more than 180° (the conduction angle lies between 180° and 360°), so around the zero crossing both are on and the hand-over is smooth. The collector current of each device is a half-sine pulse with a short overlap into the other half-cycle. Class AB keeps most of the efficiency of class B while removing its crossover notch, which is why almost all audio power amplifiers use it.
Class C

The Q-point is below cut-off: the base is biased negative (for an npn device), so only the peaks of the input drive the transistor into conduction. The conduction angle is less than 180°, commonly 90° to 150°, and the collector current is a train of narrow pulses. A parallel LC tank tuned to the signal frequency serves as the load; each pulse tops up the circulating tank current and the tank rings at its resonant frequency, producing an almost pure sine wave across it (the flywheel effect). Class C therefore suits single-frequency or narrow-band RF power amplifiers and frequency multipliers (tune the tank to a harmonic), but never audio, where the load is broadband.
Class D (Switching Amplifier)

Class D abandons linear operation altogether: the output transistors, usually MOSFETs, are driven as switches that are either fully on (saturated, near zero voltage) or fully off (zero current), so they dissipate very little power in either state. The input signal is compared with a high-frequency triangle wave to produce a pulse-width-modulated (PWM) square wave whose average value follows the input; the switches reproduce this at full supply amplitude and a low-pass LC filter removes the switching frequency, leaving the amplified signal. Efficiencies above 90 % make class D the choice for portable, battery-powered and high-power audio.

concepts.text: Identifying the class from a description:
items: Transistor always conducting, output an undistorted replica, hot even at idle: class A.
Two transistors each handling one half-cycle, zero idle current, notch at the zero crossing: class B.
Two transistors with a small idle current so that both are on near the zero crossing: class AB.
Current in short pulses, tuned LC load, single frequency: class C.
Transistors switching fully on and off, PWM drive, output filter: class D.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Conduction Angle, Output Stages and Power

The conduction angle follows directly from the bias. If a transistor starts to conduct only when the input sine wave V_p sin ωt exceeds some threshold V_on (its V_BE of about 0.7 V, plus any reverse bias V_BB applied to the base), it conducts between the angles where V_p sin ωt = V_on. That interval is 180° − 2 arcsin(V_on/V_p), which is the same as 2 arccos(V_on/V_p). With V_on = 0 the angle is exactly 180° (ideal class B); with a reverse bias it is less than 180° (class C); and with a forward pre-bias the threshold becomes negative and the angle exceeds 180° (class AB).

concepts.plainText: θc = 2 arccos(V_on / V_p), V_on = input level at which conduction starts

concepts.text: The simplest output stage is a class A emitter follower biased by a constant current source I from the negative rail. Its output can rise to nearly +V_CC, but it can fall only to −I R_L, because at that point the whole bias current flows in the load and the transistor cuts off. Choosing I = V_CC/R_L gives a symmetrical swing of ±V_CC, and the efficiency is then η = (1/4)(V_m/IR_L)(V_m/V_CC), which peaks at 25 %. With no signal the follower still dissipates V_CC × I, so it runs hottest at idle.

In a complementary class B stage with supplies ±V_CC, each supply delivers half-sine current pulses of peak I_m = V_m/R_L, whose average is I_m/π. The total supply power is therefore 2V_CC V_m/(π R_L), while the load receives V_m²/(2R_L). Whatever is left is heat shared equally by the two transistors, and it is greatest not at full output but at V_m = 2V_CC/π.

concepts.latex: P_L = \frac{V_m^2}{2R_L}, \quad P_S = \frac{2V_{CC}V_m}{\pi R_L}, \quad P_D = P_S - P_L
concepts.plainText: PL = Vm²/(2RL); PS = 2 VCC Vm/(π RL); PD = PS − PL (class B, ±VCC)

Worked example 1: complementary class B, VCC = +/-18 V, RL = 8 ohm, Vm = 15 V
Im = 15/8 = 1.875 A
PL = 15^2/(2 x 8) = 14.06 W
PS = 2 x 18 x 1.875/pi = 21.49 W
eta = 14.06/21.49 = 65.4 %   (check: (pi/4)(15/18) = 65.4 %)
PD (both) = 21.49 - 14.06 = 7.42 W, i.e. 3.71 W per transistor

Negative swing limit = -I RL = -12 V, so a 10 V peak output is undistorted
