Crossover distortion is easy to quantify. In an unbiased complementary pair the output stays at zero while |v_in| is below V_BE(on), so the output peak is V_p − 0.7 V and each transistor conducts for 2 arccos(0.7/V_p). With a 1.4 V peak input that is only 120° per device, leaving a dead zone of 60° around every zero crossing. For class D the losses are of a different kind: a MOSFET with on-resistance R_on in series with the load wastes I²R_on while on, so conduction efficiency is R_L/(R_L + R_on), and every transition adds a switching loss that grows with the switching frequency.

Common slips: using V_m²/R_L instead of V_m²/(2R_L) for load power (peak versus rms); treating the class B supply current as I_m instead of 2I_m/π; assuming class B dissipation is greatest at full output; and forgetting that a class A stage dissipates most with no signal at all.

Two numbers to remember: class B efficiency is proportional to V_m (halve the swing, halve η), while class A efficiency is proportional to V_m² (halve the swing, quarter η). Each class B transistor must be rated for about 0.2 × the maximum output power.

formulas.plainText: IC = (VCC − VCE) / RL  (DC load line)
Class A Q-point: VCEQ ≈ VCC/2, ICQ ≈ VCC/(2 RL)
Class B push-pull supply current: Idc = 2 Im/π ≈ 0.637 Im
Class D: V_o(avg) = D × VCC, duty cycle D = t_on / T

notes.text: Class is decided only by where the Q-point sits on the load line (centre, at cut-off, just above it, or below it), not by the device or the coupling. When a question describes the Q-point, translate it into a class at once.

In class C the collector current is a pulse but the voltage across the tuned tank is a sine wave. A question about the output waveform of class C expects the sinusoidal tank voltage; a question about the collector current expects pulses.

Class D is not named for digital; it is simply the next letter after C. Its transistors are switches, so the idea of a conduction angle does not really apply, and the output filter, not the transistor, shapes the waveform.

concepts.text: Efficiency of Class A

In a series-fed (RC-coupled) class A stage the Q-point sits at the centre of the load line, so V_CEQ = V_CC/2 and the supply delivers a steady P_dc = V_CC × I_CQ whatever the signal. The largest undistorted output has peak voltage V_CC/2 and peak current I_CQ, giving an AC load power P_ac = (V_CC/2)(I_CQ)/2 = V_CC I_CQ/4, so the maximum efficiency is 25 % and at smaller signals it is lower still. With a transformer-coupled load there is no DC voltage drop across the load, so the collector can swing over the full V_CC (peak voltage V_CC, peak current I_CQ): P_ac = V_CC I_CQ/2 and the maximum efficiency doubles to 50 %.

concepts.plainText: η_A (series-fed) = (VCC·ICQ/4) / (VCC·ICQ) = 25 %
η_A (transformer coupled) = (VCC·ICQ/2) / (VCC·ICQ) = 50 %

concepts.text: Efficiency of Classes B, AB, C and D

In a class B push-pull stage each transistor draws half-sine pulses of peak I_m, whose average is I_m/π; the two together draw I_dc = 2I_m/π from the supply, so P_dc = 2V_CC I_m/π. The load receives P_ac = V_m I_m/2, where V_m is the peak output voltage. Dividing gives η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC), which reaches its maximum of π/4 = 78.5 % when the output swings the full supply voltage (V_m = V_CC) and falls in proportion to V_m at lower volume. Class AB lies between 50 % and 78.5 % because its small quiescent current adds to P_dc. Class C reaches about 90 % because current flows only while the collector voltage is near its minimum, and class D exceeds 90 % because a switch that is either fully on or fully off dissipates almost nothing.
Distortion, Linearity and Heat

Class A has the best linearity: the transistor never leaves the active region and never switches, so harmonic distortion is lowest. Class B adds crossover distortion where one transistor hands over to the other; class AB removes that notch and approaches class A quality. Class C is grossly non-linear (its current is a pulse) and is acceptable only because a tuned load discards the harmonics, while class D linearity depends on the accuracy of the PWM modulator and the quality of the output filter, and switching noise must be kept out of the load. Distortion is quantified as total harmonic distortion (THD).

Heat is the practical penalty of low efficiency. A class A stage dissipates its maximum power, P_D = V_CC I_CQ, with no signal at all, so its heat sink must handle the full quiescent loss and the transistor actually runs cooler when a signal is present. A class B stage dissipates nothing at idle; its worst case is not at full output but when the peak swing is 2V_CC/π, about 0.637 V_CC, where the two transistors together dissipate 2V_CC²/(π²R_L), roughly 40 % of the maximum output power (one fifth per transistor). In complexity and cost, class A is simplest (one transistor, but a large heat sink or an output transformer), class B and AB need two matched transistors plus a bias network, and class D needs a modulator, gate drivers and an LC filter yet gets away with the smallest heat sink.

concepts.plainText: Class B: P_D(max, both devices) = 2 VCC² / (π² RL) at Vm = 2 VCC/π

concepts.text: Push-Pull Operation and Crossover Distortion

In a push-pull stage two matched transistors are driven by signals of opposite phase, obtained from a centre-tapped input transformer or a phase splitter, or simply by using a complementary npn-pnp pair fed from the same point; each transistor supplies one half-cycle and the outputs combine in the load. Because the two devices are driven in antiphase, the even harmonics (2nd, 4th and so on) that each generates through its own non-linearity are equal and opposite and cancel in the output, while the fundamental and the odd harmonics add, so the dominant residual distortion is the 3rd harmonic. In a transformer-coupled version the DC components also cancel, so the core does not saturate, and supply ripple appearing in both halves is cancelled too. The result is more output power, higher efficiency and lower distortion than a single-ended stage built from the same devices.

Crossover distortion arises in a pure class B pair because each base-emitter junction needs about 0.7 V before it conducts. While the input lies between roughly −0.7 V and +0.7 V neither transistor is on, so the output stays at zero and the sine wave acquires a flat step at every zero crossing. The step is of fixed size, so the relative distortion is worst for small signals, and it is rich in odd harmonics that sound harsh. The cure is to bias each base to the edge of conduction (class AB) with a small forward voltage supplied by diodes or a V_BE multiplier; negative feedback around the stage reduces the residual further.

rows: Small-signal and preamplifier stages, low-power hi-fi, RF driver stages
Crossover distortion at the zero crossing
Push-pull power stages where idle power must be zero
Very low once biased just above cut-off
Audio power amplifiers, hi-fi, public address, op-amp output stages
Very high; usable only with a tuned load
RF transmitter power amplifiers, frequency multipliers
Low after LC filtering; some switching noise
Portable and battery audio, subwoofer and car amplifiers

concepts.text: Choosing a class:
items: Audio (hi-fi, public address): class AB. It removes crossover distortion at little cost in efficiency; class A only where the lowest possible distortion outweighs heat and power consumption.
RF at a single frequency (transmitters, frequency multipliers): class C with a tuned tank for maximum efficiency; class A or AB where a modulated RF signal must be amplified linearly.
Battery-powered and compact equipment: class D, because efficiency above 90 % means longer battery life and little heat sinking; class AB when the simplest low-noise design is preferred.
Small-signal voltage amplification anywhere: class A, because efficiency is irrelevant at milliwatt levels and linearity is paramount.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Comparing and Choosing Classes

Efficiency tells how much supply power reaches the load, but the number that fixes the size and cost of the output transistors is the figure of merit: the largest power a device must dissipate divided by the largest power the stage can deliver to the load. A transformer-coupled class A stage dissipates its whole quiescent input V_CC I_CQ with no signal, while its maximum load power is only half of that, so its figure of merit is 2: a 10 W class A amplifier needs a transistor able to dissipate 20 W. In a class B pair each transistor's worst-case dissipation is V_CC²/(π²R_L) against a maximum load power of V_CC²/(2R_L), a ratio of 2/π², about 0.2. The same transistor can therefore deliver roughly ten times more power in class B than in class A.

concepts.plainText: Figure of merit = P_D(max)/P_L(max): class A (transformer coupled) = 2; class B = 2/π² ≈ 0.2 per transistor

concepts.text: Maximum efficiency is quoted at full output, yet speech and music spend most of the time far below full output. In a transformer-coupled class A stage the supply power is constant, so efficiency is directly proportional to the output power: at one tenth of full power it is only 5 %. In class B the supply current follows the signal amplitude, so efficiency falls only with the square root of the output power and is still about 25 % at one tenth of full power. This is why class B and AB stages run cool at normal listening levels while a class A stage runs hot all the time.

Reducing the conduction angle raises the ideal efficiency because current then flows only while the voltage across the transistor is near its minimum. For an ideal stage whose output swings the full supply, the efficiency depends on the conduction angle θ (in radians) as shown below; it gives 50 % at 360° and 78.5 % at 180°, the class A and class B limits, then about 84 % at 150°, 90 % at 120° and 94 % at 90°, approaching 100 % as θ shrinks. The price is that the fundamental output power for a given peak current falls, so practical class C stages settle at 120° to 150°. Class D escapes this trade-off by switching: its losses come from the on-resistance of the switches (conduction loss), the finite rise and fall times (switching loss, proportional to switching frequency), gate drive and the output filter.

concepts.plainText: η = (θ − sin θ) / (4[sin(θ/2) − (θ/2)cos(θ/2)])  (ideal, full swing, θ = conduction angle in rad)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: 20 W into the load at full output
Class A (transformer, 50 %): P_dc = 20/0.5 = 40 W, taken all the time
  Transistor heat: 40 W at idle, 20 W at full output -> rating >= 40 W
Class B (78.5 %): P_dc = 20/0.785 = 25.5 W
  Heat at full output = 25.5 - 20 = 5.5 W (both devices)
  Worst case = 0.405 x 20 = 8.1 W total, about 4 W per transistor
Class D (90 %): P_dc = 20/0.9 = 22.2 W, heat = 2.2 W
Conclusion: A needs a 40 W device and a large heat sink;
  B needs two 4 W devices; D needs the smallest heat sink.

Worked example 2: battery life, 12 V 5 Ah battery (60 Wh usable)
Average output 10 W
Class AB at 60 %: P_in = 10/0.60 = 16.7 W -> 60/16.7 = 3.6 h
Class D at 90 %:  P_in = 10/0.90 = 11.1 W -> 60/11.1 = 5.4 h
Switching to class D gives 50 % more playing time
  and cuts the heat from 6.7 W to 1.1 W.
Common mistakes when comparing classes:
items: Quoting the maximum efficiency for a stage that is running below full output; efficiency must be scaled for the actual level.
Sizing a class A transistor for the output power; it must be rated for the full quiescent dissipation, twice the maximum output.
Assuming class B dissipation is greatest at full output; it peaks at about 40 % of maximum output power.
Choosing class C for any wideband signal such as audio or an amplitude-modulated signal that must be amplified linearly.
Treating class D as distortion-free; its linearity depends on the modulator, dead time and output filter, and its fast edges cause electromagnetic interference.

concepts.text: For a selection question, ask three things in order: is the signal wideband (rules out class C), is lowest distortion at low power the aim (class A), and is efficiency or battery life the priority (class D, otherwise class AB).

formulas.plainText: η_A(max) = 25 % (series-fed), 50 % (transformer coupled)
Class B: P_dc = 2 VCC Im/π; P_ac = Vm Im/2
P_D = P_dc − P_ac
P_D(max, class B pair) = 2 VCC² / (π² RL) at Vm = 2 VCC/π

notes.text: Three efficiency numbers to memorise: 25 % (class A, series-fed or resistive load), 50 % (class A, transformer coupled) and 78.5 % (class B, equal to π/4). If a question specifies a resistive or RC-coupled load, answer 25 %; an unqualified 'maximum efficiency of a class A amplifier' question usually expects 50 %, the transformer-coupled figure.
Class A runs hottest with no signal; class B dissipates most at about 64 % of full swing, not at maximum output. A heat-sink question for class A must use the quiescent power V_CC I_CQ.

Push-pull cancels even harmonics and DC in the transformer core, but it does not cancel odd harmonics and does not by itself remove crossover distortion, which is an odd-harmonic effect cured by class AB bias.
π/4 = 0.785. For class B at less than full swing, scale the efficiency: at half the maximum swing it is 78.5 % × 0.5 = 39.3 %.

concepts.text: From the Class B Dead Zone to Class AB

A complementary-symmetry class B stage places an npn transistor above a pnp transistor with their bases tied to the input and their emitters joined to the load. The npn device conducts only when the input exceeds about +0.7 V and the pnp only when it falls below about −0.7 V, so for inputs between those limits neither is on and the output stays at zero. This dead zone of roughly ±0.7 V (1.4 V wide) flattens the output at every zero crossing and is the origin of crossover distortion. Because the notch is a fixed 1.4 V, quiet passages suffer proportionally far more than loud ones, and the distortion consists of harsh odd harmonics.

Class AB removes the dead zone by holding the two bases about 2V_BE (1.2 V to 1.4 V) apart with a bias network, so that both transistors carry a small quiescent current I_Q with no signal. Each device now conducts for slightly more than 180°, both are on near the zero crossing, and the transfer characteristic becomes a smooth straight line. Typical I_Q is a few milliamperes in small stages and 20 mA to 100 mA in loudspeaker amplifiers, small compared with peak load currents of several amperes. The stage remains a push-pull emitter follower: voltage gain near unity, large current gain and low output impedance.
Biasing Methods

Resistor divider. The simplest network is a resistive divider from the positive to the negative supply with a small resistor between the two bases; the current through the chain drops about 1.4 V across that resistor. It is cheap and needs no matched parts, but the bias voltage is fixed while the transistors' V_BE falls by about 2 mV per °C as they warm up, so the quiescent current rises with temperature, producing more heat and a further rise. This method is therefore used only together with emitter resistors and at modest power levels.

Diode bias. Two diodes in series between the bases, fed by a constant current from resistors or current sources, provide a bias voltage of two diode drops that closely matches the two V_BE values of the output pair. If the diodes are mounted on the same heat sink as the output transistors, their forward voltage falls with temperature at nearly the same rate as V_BE, so the bias tracks the transistors and I_Q stays almost constant: this is thermal compensation. The quiescent current is set by the diode current and by the ratio of transistor to diode junction areas. Diode bias is compact and is the standard method inside integrated circuits and op-amp output stages, but the bias voltage cannot be trimmed.

V_BE multiplier. A small transistor with resistor R1 from collector to base and R2 from base to emitter is connected between the two output bases. The transistor adjusts its collector current until the voltage across R2 equals its own V_BE, so the divider forces the total voltage across the network to V_BE(1 + R1/R2). It behaves as an amplified diode whose voltage can be set to any multiple of V_BE, usually with a trimmer in R1 or R2 to adjust I_Q precisely, and it tracks temperature when its transistor is mounted on the heat sink. It is the preferred bias element in discrete high-quality audio amplifiers.

concepts.plainText: V_bias = V_BE (1 + R1/R2)

concepts.text: Quiescent Current, Efficiency and Thermal Runaway

Choosing I_Q is a trade-off. A larger I_Q gives a smoother hand-over and lower distortion at small signals, but the standby power 2V_CC I_Q (for ±V_CC supplies) is dissipated as heat even in silence, pulling the efficiency below the 78.5 % class B ideal towards class A values. Thermal runaway is the danger: at a fixed base voltage the collector current increases steeply as the junction warms, more current means more heat, and without correction the transistor destroys itself. Three measures prevent it:
Protection against thermal runaway:
items: Thermally coupled bias elements: the bias diodes or the V_BE-multiplier transistor are mounted on the output heat sink so the bias voltage falls (about 2 mV per °C per junction) as the output devices warm.

Emitter resistors R_E of 0.1 Ω to 1 Ω in series with each emitter: any rise in I_Q increases the drop across R_E and reduces the effective V_BE, which is negative feedback that limits the current; they also equalise current sharing between imperfectly matched transistors.
A heat sink large enough to keep the junction temperature well below its limit at the worst-case dissipation.

concepts.text: The Complementary-Symmetry Stage

The complementary-symmetry output stage uses an npn and a pnp transistor as a pair of emitter followers and needs neither an output transformer nor a phase splitter: the same input drives both bases and each conducts on the appropriate half-cycle. With a single supply the output rests at V_CC/2 and reaches the loudspeaker through a large coupling capacitor; with dual supplies the output rests at 0 V and the load is connected directly. The bias network sits between the two bases and is driven by a class A voltage-amplifier (driver) stage. Where matched pnp power transistors are unavailable, a quasi-complementary design uses two npn power devices driven by a complementary pair of smaller transistors.

rows: Voltage drop across a resistor between the bases
None; I_Q drifts upward as the devices warm
Cheapest; requires emitter resistors; low-power use
Good when the diodes sit on the output heat sink
Standard in ICs and op-amps; not adjustable
Good when the multiplier transistor sits on the heat sink
Adjustable with a trimmer; used in discrete hi-fi amplifiers

concepts.text: Worked Example: Setting the Quiescent Current

A complementary stage runs from ±20 V with two bias diodes of 0.70 V each between the bases, so V_bias = 1.40 V. At the quiescent point each output transistor needs V_BE = 0.65 V, leaving 1.40 − 1.30 = 0.10 V across the two 0.5 Ω emitter resistors, so I_Q = 0.10 V / 1.0 Ω = 100 mA and the standby dissipation is 2 × 20 V × 0.1 A = 4 W (2 W per transistor) before any signal is applied. Reducing I_Q to 20 mA, by running the diodes at a lower current or using slightly larger emitter resistors, cuts the standby loss to 0.8 W while still eliminating the dead zone. If the diodes are fed at 5 mA, the two feed resistors must drop 40 − 1.4 = 38.6 V between them, so each is about 38.6 V / (2 × 5 mA), roughly 3.9 kΩ.
Going Deeper: Setting and Holding the Quiescent Current

The V_BE multiplier result follows from two facts. The multiplier transistor adjusts its own collector current until the voltage across R2 (base to emitter) equals its V_BE, so the current in R2 is V_BE/R2. If the base current is small, the same current flows through R1, so the total voltage is V_BE/R2 × (R1 + R2) = V_BE(1 + R1/R2). Whatever part of the incoming bias current is not needed by the resistor chain simply flows through the transistor. Because the whole voltage is a multiple of one V_BE, its temperature coefficient is multiplied by the same factor: a network set to 2V_BE falls by about 4 mV/°C, exactly matching the two output junctions it must track.

concepts.plainText: dV_bias/dT = (1 + R1/R2) × dV_BE/dT  (≈ −2 mV/°C per V_BE)

concepts.text: Why is fixed bias so dangerous? Collector current depends exponentially on V_BE, I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T), so an extra 18 mV of base-emitter voltage doubles the current and about 60 mV multiplies it by ten (V_T = 26 mV). At a fixed bias voltage, a temperature rise of only 9 °C lowers the required V_BE by 18 mV, which is the same as applying 18 mV more drive, and the current doubles. Emitter resistors change the law: the quiescent current becomes (V_bias − 2V_BE)/(2R_E), which responds only linearly and gently to a change in V_BE, and good thermal tracking of V_bias removes most of the remaining drift.

concepts.plainText: I_C2/I_C1 = e^(ΔV_BE/V_T); doubling needs ΔV_BE = V_T ln 2 ≈ 18 mV (V_T = 26 mV)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: design a V_BE multiplier for I_Q = 80 mA
Given: R_E = 0.33 ohm each, V_BE(Q) = 0.62 V (outputs and multiplier)
V_bias = 2 V_BE(Q) + 2 I_Q R_E = 1.24 + 2(0.08)(0.33) = 1.293 V
R1/R2 = V_bias/V_BE - 1 = 1.293/0.62 - 1 = 1.085
Choose R2 = 680 ohm -> chain current = 0.62/680 = 0.91 mA
R1 = 1.085 x 680 = 738 ohm -> 680 ohm fixed + 100 ohm trimmer
If the driver supplies 6 mA, the multiplier transistor takes
  6 - 0.91 = 5.1 mA (base currents neglected)

Worked example 2: thermal drift, R_E = 0.33 ohm each
Cold: V_bias = 1.30 V, V_BE(Q) = 0.62 V
  I_Q = (1.30 - 1.24)/0.66 = 91 mA
Outputs warm by 15 C: each V_BE falls 2 x 15 = 30 mV to 0.59 V
Fixed resistor bias (no tracking):
  I_Q = (1.30 - 1.18)/0.66 = 182 mA  (doubled)
Multiplier on the heat sink (-4 mV/C): V_bias = 1.30 - 0.06 = 1.24 V
  I_Q = (1.24 - 1.18)/0.66 = 91 mA  (unchanged)
No R_E and fixed bias: current x e^(30/26) = 3.2 times

Very large I_Q, overheating, likely failure
Output pair cut off at idle; crossover distortion returns

Hot at idle, lower efficiency, risk of runaway
Multiplier not on the heat sink

concepts.text: Emitter resistors are a compromise. Larger R_E stabilises I_Q better and forces paralleled transistors to share current, but every ampere of load current drops I × R_E across them, which wastes power and reduces the available output swing, so values of 0.1 Ω to 0.5 Ω are usual. With Darlington or compound output devices the bias network must supply four junction drops instead of two, about 2.6 V, which is easy with a multiplier and needs four diodes otherwise. In integrated circuits the bias diodes are diode-connected transistors that form current mirrors with the output devices, so I_Q equals the bias current multiplied by the ratio of emitter areas.
Common mistakes in class AB bias calculations:
items: Writing V_bias = V_BE × R1/R2 and forgetting the 1 in (1 + R1/R2).
Using one R_E instead of 2R_E: the quiescent current flows through both emitter resistors in series between the two emitters.
Counting the standby power from one rail only; with ±V_CC supplies it is 2V_CC I_Q.
Treating the bias diodes as if they carried the load current; they carry only the bias current, which must exceed the peak base current of the output transistors.
Mounting the bias element on the circuit board; without thermal coupling there is no tracking.

concepts.text: When adjusting a trimmer in a V_BE multiplier, start from the low-bias end and increase slowly while watching I_Q. Arrange the trimmer so that a worn or open wiper lowers the bias rather than raising it, because an open R1 drives the quiescent current to destructive levels.

Two numbers carry most bias questions: −2 mV/°C for every junction and 18 mV (at V_T = 26 mV) to double the current. Together they show that a 9 °C rise with untracked, undegenerated bias doubles I_Q.

formulas.plainText: V_bias ≈ 2 V_BE ≈ 1.2 to 1.4 V
V_bias = V_BE (1 + R1/R2)  (V_BE multiplier)
I_Q = (V_bias − 2 V_BE(Q)) / (2 R_E)
P_standby = 2 VCC × I_Q  (±VCC supplies)
dV_BE/dT ≈ −2 mV/°C

notes.text: Diode bias works because a diode's forward drop matches a transistor's V_BE (about 0.7 V) and falls with temperature at the same rate (about −2 mV/°C). Both halves of that sentence are exam answers: matching and thermal compensation.

Bias diodes or the V_BE-multiplier transistor must be thermally coupled to the output transistors (mounted on the same heat sink). Electrically correct bias with no thermal coupling still allows thermal runaway.
Increasing the quiescent current lowers crossover distortion but raises standby dissipation and lowers efficiency; class AB is a compromise, and at very large I_Q it turns into class A.
V_BE multiplier: V_bias = V_BE(1 + R1/R2). With R1 = R2 it produces 2V_BE and replaces the two diodes; it is also called an amplified diode.

concepts.text: The Ideal Op-Amp

An operational amplifier is a direct-coupled, very high gain differential amplifier with two inputs (inverting, marked -, and non-inverting, marked +) and one output. Its open-loop output is V_o = A_OL (V+ - V-), where the open-loop gain A_OL is around 10^5 for a general-purpose device such as the 741. Because that gain is so large and so poorly controlled, the op-amp is almost always used with external resistors that feed part of the output back to the inverting input; the closed-loop gain then depends only on the resistor ratio.
Ideal characteristics:
items: Infinite open-loop gain, input impedance and bandwidth
Zero output impedance and zero input offset voltage
Infinite common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) and infinite slew rate
With negative feedback: no input current flows, and V+ = V- (virtual short)

concepts.text: The Two Golden Rules

Every linear op-amp circuit can be analysed with two rules that follow from the ideal characteristics when negative feedback is present. Rule 1: no current flows into either input terminal (infinite input impedance). Rule 2: the output does whatever is necessary to make the voltage difference between the inputs zero, so V- = V+ (virtual short). In the inverting amplifier the non-inverting input is grounded, so the inverting input sits at 0 V even though it is not physically connected to ground; this node is called a virtual ground. Applying KCL at that node solves the circuit in one or two lines.

The two classic amplifier configurations differ only in where the signal enters. In the inverting amplifier the input reaches the inverting terminal through R_in, feedback resistor R_f returns the output to the same node, and the non-inverting terminal is grounded; the input current V_in / R_in must flow through R_f, giving an inverted output. In the non-inverting amplifier the signal drives the + terminal directly, and a divider R_f and R_1 from the output to ground feeds a fraction R_1 / (R_f + R_1) back to the - terminal; the output is in phase with the input and the gain is never below 1.

concepts.plainText: Inverting: A = −Rf / Rin.   Non-inverting: A = 1 + Rf / R1

concepts.text: Other standard circuits: the voltage follower (non-inverting amplifier with R_f = 0 and R_1 removed, so the gain is exactly 1; it is used as a buffer because its input impedance is enormous and its output impedance tiny), the summing amplifier (several inputs each through its own resistor into the virtual ground, so the output is the weighted, inverted sum), the difference amplifier (one input on each terminal with matched resistor ratios, so the output is proportional to V_2 - V_1 and common-mode signals cancel), the integrator (capacitor in the feedback path), the differentiator (capacitor in the input path) and the comparator, which uses no feedback at all: the output saturates at +V_sat when V+ exceeds V- and at -V_sat otherwise.

concepts.plainText: Summing: Vo = −Rf·(V1/R1 + V2/R2 + V3/R3)
Difference amplifier (R1 on both inputs, R2 to output and ground): Vo = (R2/R1)·(V2 − V1)
Integrator: Vo = −(1/RC)·∫Vin dt.   Differentiator: Vo = −RC·dVin/dt

concepts.text: Practical Limits of a Real Op-Amp

rows: Closed-loop gain accurate only when A_OL ≫ 1 + R_f / R_1
Tiny input current; bias current ≈ 80 nA
Output can drive loads of a few kΩ
Common-mode signals are strongly but not fully rejected

concepts.text: The op-amp is powered from a dual supply, typically +15 V and -15 V, and its output cannot exceed the rails; a 741 saturates at about +/-13 V with +/-15 V supplies. If the computed output (gain times input) exceeds the saturation level, the actual output is clipped at +/-V_sat. Bandwidth is also finite: the gain-bandwidth product is constant, so a non-inverting gain of 100 leaves only 1 MHz / 100 = 10 kHz of bandwidth. For large amplitudes the slew rate sets a separate limit: a sinusoid of peak V_p is reproduced without slew distortion only up to f_max = SR / (2 pi V_p).
Worked Example

A 741 with +/-15 V supplies is connected as a non-inverting amplifier with R_f = 90 kΩ and R_1 = 10 kΩ. Gain = 1 + 90 / 10 = 10, so a 0.5 V input gives a 5 V output and the closed-loop bandwidth is 1 MHz / 10 = 100 kHz. If the input rises to 2 V the ideal output would be 20 V, but the amplifier saturates at about 13 V and the peaks are clipped. For a 10 V peak sinusoidal output the slew-rate limit is f_max = 0.5 V/µs / (2 pi x 10 V) = 7.96 kHz; above that frequency the output turns into a triangle even though the small-signal bandwidth is 100 kHz.
Going Deeper: Op-Amp Analysis and Real Limits

Both basic gain formulas come from one KCL equation at the inverting input. In the inverting amplifier that node is a virtual ground, so the input current V_in/R_in has nowhere to go except through R_f, and V_o = −I R_f gives A = −R_f/R_in. In the non-inverting amplifier the node sits at V_in, so the divider R_f, R_1 must satisfy V_o R_1/(R_1 + R_f) = V_in, which gives A = 1 + R_f/R_1. The quantity 1 + R_f/R_1 is called the noise gain: it is the gain seen by anything that appears between the op-amp inputs, and it sets the bandwidth and the output offset of BOTH configurations.

concepts.plainText: A_CL = A_OL / (1 + A_OL·β), with feedback fraction β = R1 / (R1 + Rf)

concepts.text: The feedback formula shows why the ideal results work: when the loop gain A_OL β is much larger than 1, A_CL tends to 1/β = 1 + R_f/R_1 and the poorly controlled A_OL drops out. With A_OL = 10^5 and a target gain of 100 the actual gain is 99.9, but an op-amp with A_OL = 1000 gives only 90.9. Because the open-loop gain of a compensated op-amp falls at 20 dB per decade above a few hertz, the product of closed-loop gain and bandwidth stays equal to the unity-gain frequency, the gain-bandwidth product (GBW). The gain to use in BW = GBW/gain is the noise gain, so an inverting amplifier with gain −10 has the same bandwidth as a non-inverting amplifier with gain 11.

Worked example 1: inverting amplifier, Rf = 100 kΩ, Rin = 10 kΩ
op-amp GBW = 1 MHz, input offset voltage Vos = 2 mV
Signal gain      A = −Rf/Rin = −100/10 = −10
Noise gain       1 + Rf/Rin = 1 + 10 = 11
Bandwidth        BW = GBW / noise gain = 1 MHz / 11 = 90.9 kHz
Output offset    Vos × noise gain = 2 mV × 11 = 22 mV
(Using 10 instead of 11 gives 100 kHz and 20 mV: a common slip.)

Worked example 2: slew rate vs bandwidth, SR = 0.5 V/µs, GBW = 1 MHz
Non-inverting gain 10, wanted output 8 V peak
Small-signal bandwidth = 1 MHz / 10 = 100 kHz
Full-power bandwidth  f = SR/(2π Vp) = 0.5e6/(2π × 8) = 9.95 kHz
So an 8 V peak sine is clean only up to about 10 kHz.
At 20 kHz the largest clean peak is SR/(2π f)
  = 0.5e6/(2π × 20 000) = 3.98 V

Worked example 3: integrator, R = 10 kΩ, C = 1 µF, Vsat = ±13 V
Input: constant +2 V applied at t = 0, capacitor initially uncharged
Capacitor current  I = Vin/R = 2/10 000 = 0.2 mA (constant)
Output slope       dVo/dt = −Vin/(RC) = −2/0.01 = −200 V/s
Time to saturate   t = 13/200 = 65 ms
After 65 ms the output sticks at −13 V until the input changes.

concepts.latex: CMRR_{dB} = 20\log_{10}\frac{A_d}{A_{cm}}, \qquad V_o = A_d v_d + A_{cm} v_{cm}
concepts.plainText: CMRR(dB) = 20·log10(Ad/Acm);  Vo = Ad·vd + Acm·vcm, vd = V1 − V2, vcm = (V1 + V2)/2

rows: R; square wave in gives triangle out
Falls as 1/(ωC); triangle in gives square out

concepts.text: A comparator runs open loop, so its output is always at one of the saturation levels and the golden rules do not apply. When the input is noisy and changes slowly, the output may chatter as the input crosses the reference several times. Adding positive feedback (a Schmitt trigger) gives two thresholds: for an inverting Schmitt trigger with R_2 from the output to the + input and R_1 from the + input to ground, the thresholds are ±V_sat R_1/(R_1 + R_2) and the hysteresis is twice that.
Common mistakes in op-amp problems:
items: Using R_f/R_in for the bandwidth or offset of an inverting amplifier; the noise gain 1 + R_f/R_in is what counts.
Forgetting the output clips at ±V_sat: gain × input is only the answer when it lies inside the rails.
Confusing peak and peak-to-peak in the slew-rate formula f = SR/(2π V_p); V_p is the peak.
Taking CMRR in dB as 10 log instead of 20 log; it is a voltage-gain ratio.
Applying the virtual short to a comparator or Schmitt trigger, which have no negative feedback.

concepts.text: For any mixed-input circuit, use superposition: find the output from the inverting input with the other grounded (gain −R_f/R_1), then from the non-inverting input with the first grounded (gain 1 + R_f/R_1 times any divider in front of it), and add.

formulas.plainText: Av(inverting) = −Rf / Rin
Av(non-inverting) = 1 + Rf / R1
Voltage follower: Av = 1, Vo = Vin
Summing amplifier: Vo = −Rf·(V1/R1 + V2/R2)
Integrator: Vo = −(1/RC)·∫Vin dt
f_max = SR / (2π·Vp);  closed-loop BW = GBW / A_CL

notes.text: Non-inverting gain is always at least 1. If a computed 'non-inverting' gain comes out below 1, re-read the question: it is probably inverting (gain −R_f / R_in), or the resistors have been swapped.

The golden rules hold only with negative feedback and an unsaturated output. A comparator has no feedback, so V+ and V− are not equal and the output simply sits at +V_sat or −V_sat; applying the virtual-short rule to it gives nonsense.

The virtual ground of the inverting amplifier means its input impedance is just R_in, whereas the non-inverting amplifier presents the op-amp's own very high input impedance. This is why the non-inverting form (or a follower) is preferred when the source is weak.

concepts.text: Power BJTs vs Small-Signal BJTs

rows: metal or tabbed TO-220, TO-3 for heat sinking

concepts.text: A power transistor is defined by its ratings and the limits that must never be exceeded:
items: Maximum collector current I_C(max) and maximum collector-emitter voltage V_CEO, both printed on the data sheet.
Maximum power dissipation P_D(max) at a stated case or ambient temperature, and maximum junction temperature T_J(max), 150 to 200 °C for silicon.
Safe operating area (SOA): the region of the I_C versus V_CE plane bounded by I_C(max), P_D(max), V_CEO and the second-breakdown line; the operating point (including transients) must stay inside it.

Second breakdown: at high V_CE the current crowds into local hot spots in the large junction, the hot spot draws still more current (negative temperature coefficient) and the device fails even though the average power is within rating. It is the main reason power BJTs are derated at high voltage.
Thermal runaway: I_C rises with temperature, which raises dissipation and temperature further; emitter resistors, thermal feedback in the bias circuit and adequate heat sinking prevent it.

Darlington pairs raise the effective β to several thousand at the price of about 1.4 V V_BE and a higher V_CE(sat); paralleling transistors shares current, but each needs a small emitter resistor so the one with the lowest V_BE does not hog all the current.

concepts.text: Power Dissipation and Junction Temperature

The heat generated in the collector-base junction, P_D roughly equal to V_CE I_C, must flow from the junction to the case, from the case to the heat sink (through mica washer and grease) and from the heat sink to the surrounding air. Each stage offers a thermal resistance in degrees Celsius per watt, analogous to an electrical resistance with temperature as voltage and power as current. The junction temperature is therefore T_J = T_A + P_D theta_JA, where theta_JA = theta_JC + theta_CS + theta_SA. Since the junction cannot exceed T_J(max), the allowable dissipation falls linearly as the ambient (or case) temperature rises; this straight line is the power derating curve on the data sheet.

concepts.plainText: T_J = T_A + P_D·θ_JA,  where θ_JA = θ_JC + θ_CS + θ_SA

concepts.text: A heat sink works by lowering theta_SA: a bare TO-220 has theta_JA of about 60 °C/W, while the same device bolted to a finned sink can reach 5 °C/W or less. For example, with T_J(max) = 150 °C, T_A = 40 °C and theta_JA = 5 °C/W the transistor may dissipate (150 - 40) / 5 = 22 W, but only about 1.8 W without the sink. Data sheets quote the rating at 25 °C case temperature, so the derating factor 1 / theta_JC (watts per degree) must be applied whenever the case runs hotter.
Transformer-Coupled Class A Stage

In the series-fed class A stage the collector resistor wastes half the supply voltage and half the power, which caps the efficiency at 25 %. Replacing R_C by the primary of an output transformer removes that loss: the winding has negligible DC resistance, so V_CEQ is essentially V_CC, and the AC load line is set by the reflected load R_L' = (N_1 / N_2)^2 R_L. The collector voltage can swing from near zero up to 2 V_CC (the transformer inductance adds the stored energy to the supply), so the maximum theoretical efficiency doubles to 50 %. The turns ratio also matches a low-impedance load such as an 8 ohm loudspeaker to the several hundred ohms the transistor prefers. Drawbacks are the transformer's size, cost, DC core magnetisation and poor low- and high-frequency response.
Transformer-Coupled Push-Pull Class B Stage

The classic push-pull stage uses two matched transistors of the same type (both NPN), a centre-tapped input (driver) transformer and a centre-tapped output transformer. The driver secondary delivers two equal signals in antiphase, so Q_1 conducts on the positive half-cycle and Q_2 on the negative half-cycle; each is biased at cut-off (class B), conducts for 180° and idles the rest of the time. Their half-sine collector currents flow through opposite halves of the output primary and are recombined magnetically into a full sine wave in the secondary. Because the two currents flow in opposite directions through the core, the DC components cancel (no core saturation) and all even harmonics cancel, leaving only the smaller odd harmonics. Each transistor sees a reflected load R_L' = (N_1 / N_2)^2 R_L, where N_1 is the turns on one half of the primary, and the ideal maximum efficiency is pi / 4 = 78.5 %.

With both transistors biased exactly at cut-off, neither conducts until the base drive exceeds about 0.7 V, so the output is flat for a short interval at every zero crossing; this crossover distortion is most audible at low volume. The cure is class AB biasing: a resistor pair or a pair of diodes between the centre tap of the input transformer and the emitters holds each base a little above the knee, so a small quiescent current flows and the two half-cycles overlap slightly. The diode version also tracks the transistors' V_BE with temperature and protects against thermal runaway. The efficiency falls only marginally below 78.5 %.

rows: Two of the same type (both NPN)
One NPN and one matched PNP
Not needed; both bases driven together
Turns ratio matches any load, e.g. 8 Ω
Load must suit the transistors directly
Even harmonics and DC in load
Cancel with symmetric devices; capacitor or split supply blocks DC
Older audio, some RF and valve stages
Nearly all modern audio power amplifiers

concepts.text: Worked Example

A push-pull class B stage runs from V_CC = 16 V and drives an 8 ohm loudspeaker through an output transformer with 4 : 1 turns from each half of the primary to the secondary. Reflected load: R_L' = (4)^2 x 8 = 128 ohm. Each transistor swings its collector almost the full 16 V, so the peak collector current is 16 / 128 = 125 mA. Maximum output power: P_o = V_CC^2 / (2 R_L') = 256 / 256 = 1 W. The supply delivers a full-wave-rectified current of average 2 I_peak / pi, so P_dc = 16 x 2 x 0.125 / pi = 1.27 W and the efficiency is 1 / 1.27 = 78.5 %, the class B ideal. Each transistor dissipates at most about 0.2 P_o(max) = 0.2 W (at 63.7 % of full drive), so small devices suffice; a 4 ohm speaker with the same transformer would halve R_L' to 64 ohm and double the required current.
Going Deeper: Thermal Design and Transformer Output Stages

Heat flow obeys the same law as current in a resistor chain: temperature difference = power × thermal resistance. The dissipated power P_D is the 'current', each interface (junction to case, case to sink, sink to air) is a series 'resistor' in °C/W, and the ambient temperature is the 'ground'. Any intermediate temperature follows the same way: the case is at T_C = T_J − P_D θ_JC and the sink at T_S = T_A + P_D θ_SA. When several transistors share one heat sink, the sink resistance carries the total power of all of them, while each junction-to-case path carries only its own device's power.

Worked example 1: choosing a heat sink
P_D = 25 W, T_J(max) = 150 °C, T_A = 40 °C
θ_JC = 1.2 °C/W, θ_CS = 0.4 °C/W (mica washer with grease)
Allowed total   θ_JA = (150 − 40)/25 = 4.4 °C/W
Sink needed     θ_SA = 4.4 − 1.2 − 0.4 = 2.8 °C/W or lower
Check: T_S = 40 + 25 × 2.8 = 110 °C
       T_C = 110 + 25 × 0.4 = 120 °C
       T_J = 120 + 25 × 1.2 = 150 °C  (exactly at the limit)

concepts.plainText: P_D(T_C) = P_D(25 °C) − (T_C − 25)/θ_JC; derating factor 1/θ_JC W/°C, with θ_JC = (T_J(max) − 25)/P_D(25 °C)

concepts.text: On a log-log plot the safe operating area is bounded by four lines: a horizontal I_C(max) line (bond wires and metallisation), a line of slope −1 for constant power P_D(max) = V_CE I_C, a steeper second-breakdown line at high V_CE, and a vertical V_CEO line. Short pulses widen the area because the junction does not have time to heat, so data sheets draw extra curves for 1 ms or 100 µs pulses. The SOA is specified at 25 °C case temperature and shrinks as the case gets hotter.

For the transformer-coupled class A stage the best Q-point puts the collector current at I_CQ = V_CC/R', so the AC load line through (V_CC, I_CQ) reaches the V_CE axis at 2 V_CC. With full swing the output power is (V_CC/√2)(I_CQ/√2) = V_CC I_CQ/2 = V_CC²/(2R') while the supply delivers V_CC I_CQ = V_CC²/R', giving the 50 % ceiling. The supply power is constant, so the transistor runs hottest with no signal, when it dissipates all of V_CC I_CQ. With a smaller swing between V_CE(min) and V_CE(max) the efficiency follows the formula below.

concepts.plainText: η = 50·[(V_CEmax − V_CEmin)/(V_CEmax + V_CEmin)]² %   (transformer-coupled class A)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: transformer-coupled class A, V_CC = 15 V
Load 8 Ω, turns ratio N1 : N2 = 3 : 1
Reflected load     R' = 3² × 8 = 72 Ω
Best Q-point       I_CQ = V_CC/R' = 15/72 = 0.208 A, V_CEQ ≈ 15 V
Supply power       P_dc = V_CC × I_CQ = 3.125 W (signal or not)
Max output         P_o = V_CC²/(2R') = 225/144 = 1.5625 W
Efficiency         1.5625/3.125 = 50 %
Worst dissipation  3.125 W, at zero signal

Even-harmonic cancellation in push-pull follows from symmetry. Transistor Q_2 produces the same current waveform as Q_1 but half a cycle later, and the transformer responds to the difference of the two primary currents. Shifting a harmonic of order k by half a cycle multiplies it by (−1)^k, so in the difference the odd harmonics (including the fundamental) double while the even harmonics and the DC components cancel. Any mismatch between the two transistors breaks this symmetry and lets second harmonic through. In class B each transistor's dissipation peaks at V_CC²/(π² R') when the collector swing is 2V_CC/π, about 64 % of full drive, not at maximum output.

Worked example 3: push-pull class B at partial drive
V_CC = 20 V, reflected load R' = 80 Ω per half-primary, swing Vp = 15 V
Peak current    I_p = 15/80 = 0.1875 A
Output power    P_o = Vp²/(2R') = 225/160 = 1.41 W
Supply power    P_dc = 2 V_CC I_p/π = 2 × 20 × 0.1875/π = 2.39 W
Efficiency      1.41/2.39 = 58.9 %  (= 78.5 % × 15/20)
Per transistor  (2.39 − 1.41)/2 = 0.49 W
Worst case      V_CC²/(π² R') = 400/(9.87 × 80) = 0.51 W each

Frequent slips: using the whole primary instead of one half for R' in push-pull; forgetting that the heat sink resistance carries the combined power when devices share a sink; taking a data-sheet P_D rated at 25 °C case temperature as if it applied at a hot ambient; and assuming the class A transistor runs hottest at full output, when it is hottest at zero signal.

formulas.plainText: T_J = T_A + P_D·θ_JA
P_D(max) = (T_J(max) − T_A) / θ_JA
R_L' = (N1/N2)²·R_L  (load reflected to the primary)
P_o(max) = V_CC² / (2·R_L');  P_dc = 2·V_CC·I_peak / π
η(class A, transformer) ≤ 50 %;  η(class B push-pull) ≤ π/4 = 78.5 %

notes.text: Reflected load questions are pure arithmetic: square the turns ratio (primary to secondary) and multiply by R_L. For a push-pull stage use the turns on one half of the primary. A 4 : 1 ratio turns 8 Ω into 128 Ω, a 3 : 1 ratio turns 4 Ω into 36 Ω.

Second breakdown is not thermal runaway. Thermal runaway is a slow rise of the whole device temperature through β and I_CBO; second breakdown is a local hot spot at high V_CE that can destroy the device in microseconds while the average power is still within the data-sheet limit. Only the SOA curve protects against it.

Push-pull operation cancels even harmonics because the two half-cycles are mirror images; it does nothing for odd harmonics or for crossover distortion, which is why a small class AB bias is still required in every practical push-pull stage.

concepts.text: Why a Tuned Load

Radio, television and other RF signals occupy a narrow band around a carrier, with many other stations close by in frequency. An RF or IF amplifier must therefore amplify one narrow band strongly and reject everything else, which a resistor-loaded stage cannot do. A tuned amplifier replaces the collector (or drain) resistor with a parallel LC circuit, the tank. Its impedance is very high and purely resistive at the resonant frequency but falls rapidly on either side, so the voltage gain, which is transconductance times load impedance, peaks sharply at f_0. The tank also absorbs the device and stray capacitances into C, which is why tuned stages work at frequencies where a broadband amplifier would have no gain at all.
Resonance, Q and bandwidth of the tank:
items: Quality factor of the coil: Q = omega_0 L / R = 1 / (omega_0 C R), where R is the coil's series resistance. Practical RF coils have Q of 50 to 200.
At resonance a parallel tank with a lossy coil behaves as a pure resistance called the dynamic impedance, Z_D = L / (C R) = Q omega_0 L. This is the load the transistor sees at f_0.
The 3 dB bandwidth is BW = f_2 - f_1 = f_0 / Q. Higher Q gives a narrower, more selective response.

Selectivity is the ability to reject adjacent frequencies; it is quantified by Q and by the skirt steepness, often expressed as the ratio of the 60 dB to the 6 dB bandwidth (shape factor, ideally close to 1).
Voltage gain at resonance: A_v(f_0) = -g_m Z_D for a CE stage with the tank as its only load; away from f_0 the gain drops with the tank impedance.

concepts.plainText: BW = f_0 / Q;   Z_D = L / (C·R) = Q·ω_0·L

concepts.text: Gain and bandwidth cannot both be raised at will. For a single-tuned CE stage A_v(f_0) = g_m Z_D and BW = 1 / (2 pi Z_D C), so the product A_v x BW = g_m / (2 pi C) is fixed by the transistor and the total tank capacitance. Raising Q (a better coil or a lighter load) raises the gain but narrows the band by the same factor; a wider band is bought only with lower gain or a larger g_m. This is why wide-band IF amplifiers use several stages and why the stray capacitance C must be minimised.
Single-Tuned, Double-Tuned and Stagger-Tuned Amplifiers

A single-tuned amplifier has one tank, usually in the collector, coupled to the next stage by a capacitor or by a transformer whose untuned secondary provides impedance matching. Its response is the familiar bell-shaped resonance curve: a sharp peak, but skirts that fall away only gently, so the rejection of a station one channel away is poor. Cascading n identical single-tuned stages sharpens the skirts but shrinks the overall bandwidth to BW_n = BW x sqrt(2^(1/n) - 1), about 0.64 BW for two stages.

A double-tuned amplifier uses a transformer whose primary and secondary are both tuned to f_0 and coupled with coefficient k. At critical coupling, k_c = 1 / sqrt(Q_1 Q_2), the response is maximally flat with a bandwidth about sqrt(2) times that of the single-tuned stage and much steeper skirts. Under-coupling gives a sharper, lower peak; over-coupling (k greater than k_c) produces a double-humped response with a dip at f_0 but a still wider passband, which is exploited in IF transformers. Double-tuned stages therefore give better selectivity and a flatter passband, at the cost of alignment complexity.

Stagger tuning obtains a wide, flat passband from single-tuned stages by tuning each stage to a slightly different frequency: for two stages, one at f_0 + delta and one at f_0 - delta, with delta chosen so that the overall response is maximally flat. The product of the individual bell curves is a flat-topped band whose width is about sqrt(2) times the single-stage bandwidth, with steeper skirts than a cascade of synchronously tuned stages. Television and radar IF strips (several MHz wide) use stagger tuning because it avoids the coupled transformers of double tuning.

rows: Flat top over the whole strip
≈ √2 f_0 / Q for two stages, wider for more

concepts.text: Class C Tuned Amplifiers

For RF power a tuned load allows class C operation: the transistor is biased well below cut-off (negative base bias or a self-bias RC clamp), so it conducts for less than 180° of each cycle, typically 60° to 120°, and its collector current is a train of narrow pulses. Each pulse gives the tank a kick, and the tank's stored energy (the flywheel effect) sustains a clean sinusoid at f_0 between pulses, filtering out the harmonics in the pulses. Because current flows only while V_CE is near its minimum, dissipation is tiny and the efficiency can reach 80 to 90 %. If the tank is tuned to 2 f_in or 3 f_in the stage becomes a frequency doubler or tripler, since the pulses are rich in harmonics. Class C is unsuitable for audio or any signal whose amplitude carries information, because the output is not linear in the input.
Applications of tuned amplifiers:
items: RF amplifier and mixer stages of AM, FM and TV receivers, tuned to the wanted station.

Intermediate-frequency (IF) amplifiers: 455 kHz in AM receivers, 10.7 MHz in FM receivers, and 38.9 MHz (video IF) in analogue TV; these fixed-frequency stages provide most of the receiver's gain and selectivity.
Class C RF power amplifiers and frequency multipliers in transmitters.
Oscillators, where the tank of a tuned amplifier sets the frequency of the feedback loop.
Wireless communication front ends (mobile, Wi-Fi) using on-chip LC or SAW resonators.

concepts.text: Worked Example

A single-tuned amplifier has L = 100 µH, C = 100 pF and a coil Q of 50. Resonant frequency: LC = 10^-4 x 10^-10 = 10^-14, sqrt(LC) = 10^-7, so f_0 = 1 / (2 pi x 10^-7) = 1.59 MHz, in the medium-wave band. Bandwidth: BW = f_0 / Q = 1.59 MHz / 50 = 31.8 kHz, so the half-power points are at about 1.574 MHz and 1.606 MHz. Coil reactance omega_0 L = 2 pi x 1.59 x 10^6 x 10^-4 = 1000 ohm, so the coil resistance is R = 1000 / 50 = 20 ohm and the dynamic impedance is Z_D = L / (C R) = 10^-4 / (10^-10 x 20) = 50 kΩ (equal to Q omega_0 L). With a transistor of g_m = 40 mA/V the gain at resonance is A_v = 0.04 x 50000 = 2000, about 66 dB. If the coil Q were doubled to 100, the gain would double to 4000 while the bandwidth halved to 15.9 kHz, illustrating the fixed gain-bandwidth product.
Going Deeper: Tuned Amplifiers

The Q that sets the bandwidth of a working stage is the loaded Q, not the coil Q quoted on its own. First turn the coil's series loss into an equivalent parallel resistance R_p = Q_u ω_0 L (valid for Q_u above about 10). The tank is then shunted by the transistor's output resistance r_o and by the input resistance of the next stage, so the total resistance across it is R_T = R_p ∥ r_o ∥ R_in. The loaded Q is Q_L = R_T / (ω_0 L) = ω_0 C R_T, which is always lower than Q_u, and the stage gain at resonance is g_m R_T.

concepts.latex: R_T = R_p \parallel r_o \parallel R_{in}, \quad Q_L = \frac{R_T}{\omega_0 L} = \omega_0 C R_T, \quad BW = \frac{1}{2\pi R_T C}
concepts.plainText: R_T = R_p ∥ r_o ∥ R_in;  Q_L = R_T/(ω_0 L) = ω_0 C R_T;  BW = f_0/Q_L = 1/(2π R_T C)

concepts.text: To keep the loading light, the collector or the next base is connected to a tap on the tank coil, or the tank drives the next stage through a step-down secondary. A resistance R connected across n of the N turns appears across the whole coil as R (N/n)², so a 1 kΩ base input on a tap at one tenth of the turns looks like 100 kΩ across the tank. Tapping lets the designer choose Q_L, and hence bandwidth, while still using a practical coil.

Worked example 1: loaded Q, bandwidth and gain of a 455 kHz IF stage
Given: L = 200 µH, coil Q_u = 120, r_o = 100 kΩ, next stage 10 kΩ on a 1:3 tap, g_m = 20 mS
ω_0 L = 2π × 455e3 × 200e-6 = 571.8 Ω;  C = 1/(ω_0² L) = 612 pF
R_p = Q_u ω_0 L = 120 × 571.8 = 68.6 kΩ
Reflected load = 10 kΩ × 3² = 90 kΩ
R_T = 68.6 k ∥ 100 k ∥ 90 k = 28.0 kΩ
Q_L = R_T / (ω_0 L) = 28 000 / 571.8 = 49.0
BW = f_0 / Q_L = 455 kHz / 49.0 = 9.28 kHz
A_v(f_0) = g_m R_T = 0.02 × 28 000 = 560 (about 55 dB)

Every CE or CS tuned stage has a feedback path through the collector-base capacitance C_bc (C_µ in the hybrid-π model). With a tuned circuit at both input and output, this path can supply enough in-phase feedback near f_0 to make the stage oscillate, exactly as in a tuned-input tuned-output oscillator; even when it does not oscillate, the Miller capacitance C_bc(1 + |A_v|) detunes and loads the input tank. Neutralisation cancels the unwanted feedback: a small capacitor C_N feeds back a current of equal size and opposite phase, taken from a point on the output coil or a separate winding whose voltage is in antiphase with the collector (Hazeltine and Rice circuits). Alternatively the feedback is avoided altogether by a cascode (CE driving CB) or a common-base stage.

concepts.plainText: C_N·V_N = C_bc·V_c  ⇒  C_N = C_bc·V_c/V_N = C_bc·N_1/N_2 (N_1 collector winding, N_2 neutralising winding)

rows: Overall BW if each stage is 10 kHz

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: image frequency and RF-stage image rejection
Given: AM receiver tuned to f_s = 600 kHz, IF = 455 kHz, LO above the signal, one RF tank with Q = 50
f_LO = 600 + 455 = 1055 kHz
Image f_si = f_s + 2 × IF = 600 + 910 = 1510 kHz
ρ = f_si/f_s − f_s/f_si = 2.517 − 0.397 = 2.119
Image rejection α = √(1 + Q²ρ²) = √(1 + (50 × 2.119)²) ≈ 106, about 40.5 dB

In a class C stage the conduction angle is set by the negative base bias. With a DC bias of −V_B and a drive of peak V_p, the transistor conducts while V_p cos ωt − V_B exceeds V_BE(on), so the half-angle satisfies cos(θ/2) = (V_B + V_BE(on)) / V_p. A smaller angle raises the efficiency towards 100 % but reduces the output power towards zero, so practical stages use about 90° to 150°. When the collector swings from nearly 0 to 2V_CC across the tank resistance R_T, the output power is P = V_pp² / (8 R_T); for V_CC = 12 V and R_T = 200 Ω this is 24² / 1600 = 0.36 W.

Common slips: using the unloaded coil Q in BW = f_0/Q (the loaded Q_L is always smaller, so the real band is wider); forgetting that transistor and stray capacitance add to the tank C and pull f_0 down; dividing the bandwidth by n for n cascaded stages instead of multiplying by √(2^(1/n) − 1); and quoting the image frequency as f_s + IF (that is the local oscillator) instead of f_s + 2 IF.

Two shortcuts save time: BW = 1/(2π R_T C) needs no f_0 at all, and the gain-bandwidth product g_m/(2πC) gives the largest single-stage gain for a required bandwidth. Double-tuned at critical coupling and a flat-staggered pair both give about √2 times the single-tuned bandwidth.

formulas.plainText: Z_D = L / (C·R) = Q·ω_0·L  (tank impedance at resonance)
A_v(f_0) = −g_m·Z_D;   A_v × BW = g_m / (2π·C)

notes.text: Numerical items almost always reduce to f_0 = 1 / (2π√LC) followed by BW = f_0 / Q. Use powers of ten: µH is 10⁻⁶ and pF is 10⁻¹²; if LC comes out as 10⁻¹⁴ the answer is 1.59 MHz, and if it is 10⁻¹² the answer is 159 kHz.

The formula Z_D = L / (C R) uses the series resistance of the coil, not a parallel resistor. A tank with a lossless coil shunted by R_p has Z_D = R_p and Q = R_p / (ω_0 L). Mixing the two definitions gives Q values that are inverted.

Double-tuned and stagger-tuned circuits are two routes to the same goal, a flat wide passband with steep skirts: double tuning couples two tanks in one stage, stagger tuning spreads single tanks across several stages. Both trade some peak gain for bandwidth and selectivity.

concepts.text: Ohm's Law

Ohm's Law states that the current flowing through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points, provided the temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. Equivalently, current is directly proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance, and the ratio V/I is a constant called the resistance R. Here V is voltage in volts, I is current in amperes and R is resistance in ohms; any one quantity can be found when the other two are known.

concepts.plainText: V = I × R

concepts.text: The three forms of the law:
items: V = I × R — voltage drop across a resistance R carrying current I
I = V / R — current drawn by a resistance R from a supply V
R = V / I — resistance found from a voltmeter and an ammeter reading
The V-I graph of an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin; with V on the vertical axis its slope equals R

concepts.text: Limitations: Ohm's law holds only for ohmic (linear) conductors kept at constant temperature, such as metals and carbon resistors. It fails for non-ohmic devices whose V-I curve is not a straight line — semiconductor diodes and transistors, thermistors, vacuum tubes, electrolytes and gas-discharge lamps. Even a metal filament lamp departs from it because its temperature, and hence its resistance, rises with the current. Unilateral elements such as diodes break the law in a second way: their resistance depends on the direction of the current.

rows: Metallic conductors, wire-wound and carbon resistors
Diodes, transistors, thermistors, arc and discharge lamps
V-I graph: straight line through the origin
V-I graph: curved, may differ for each direction
R constant at a fixed temperature
R changes with V, I or current direction

concepts.text: Resistance, Resistivity and Conductance

The resistance of a conductor depends on its material, length and cross-sectional area. It is directly proportional to the length l and inversely proportional to the area A; the constant of proportionality ρ (rho) is the resistivity or specific resistance of the material — numerically the resistance between opposite faces of a 1 m cube of it, so its unit is the ohm-metre (Ω·m).

concepts.plainText: R = ρ × l / A

concepts.text: Key facts:
items: Resistivity (ρ) is a material property, measured in ohm-metres; copper ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m.
Doubling the length doubles the resistance.
Doubling the cross-sectional area halves the resistance; doubling the diameter quarters it, because A ∝ d².
Stretching a wire to n times its length at constant volume shrinks A to A/n, so R rises n² times.
For metals, resistance increases with temperature (positive temperature coefficient).

concepts.text: Conductance G is the reciprocal of resistance and measures how easily current flows: G = 1/R = I/V, with SI unit the siemens (S), formerly called the mho. Conductivity σ (sigma) is the reciprocal of resistivity, σ = 1/ρ, measured in siemens per metre (S/m); for a conductor G = σA/l. Copper has σ ≈ 5.8 × 10⁷ S/m, one of the highest values of any metal. Conductances of parallel branches add directly, which makes G convenient for parallel circuits.
Effect of Temperature on Resistance

The resistance of a pure metal rises almost linearly with temperature because the vibrating lattice ions scatter the free electrons more strongly. If R₀ is the resistance at 0 °C and α₀ the temperature coefficient of resistance at 0 °C (in per °C), the resistance at t °C is R_t = R₀(1 + α₀t). Between any two temperatures t₁ and t₂ the resistances are related by R₂ = R₁[1 + α₁(t₂ − t₁)], where α₁ is the coefficient at t₁; the coefficient itself falls with temperature, α_t = α₀/(1 + α₀t). Copper has α₀ ≈ 0.00427/°C (0.00393/°C at 20 °C), so its resistance grows by roughly 0.4% per degree.

concepts.plainText: R_t = R₀ (1 + α₀ t)

concepts.text: Sign of the temperature coefficient:
items: Pure metals: positive — copper ≈ 0.004/°C, aluminium ≈ 0.004/°C, tungsten ≈ 0.0045/°C.
Alloys such as manganin, constantan and eureka: almost zero — used for standard resistors and meter shunts.
Semiconductors, insulators, carbon and electrolytes: negative — resistance falls as temperature rises (the thermistor principle).

concepts.text: Worked example: a copper field coil has a resistance of 50 Ω at 20 °C. Its resistance at 70 °C, taking α₂₀ = 0.00393/°C, is R₂ = 50 × [1 + 0.00393 × (70 − 20)] = 50 × 1.1965 ≈ 59.8 Ω. Connected to a 230 V supply the coil draws I = 230/59.8 ≈ 3.85 A when hot, compared with 230/50 = 4.6 A when cold — Ohm's law must be applied with the resistance at the actual operating temperature.
Going Deeper: Ohm's Law and Resistance

Ohm's law has a microscopic form that explains where resistance comes from. Inside a conductor an electric field E drives a current density J (current per unit area), and for an ohmic material the two are proportional, J = σE. For a uniform wire of length l and area A the field is E = V/l and the current is I = JA, so I = σAV/l. Rearranged this is V = I × l/(σA), which is exactly V = IR with R = ρl/A. Resistance is therefore just conductivity scaled by the wire's geometry.

concepts.plainText: J = I/A = σE, so R = l/(σA) = ρl/A

concepts.text: For a non-ohmic device the ratio V/I changes from point to point on its characteristic. The value of V/I at a chosen operating point is called the static or DC resistance, while the slope ΔV/ΔI of the curve at that point is the dynamic or AC resistance. For an ohmic resistor the two are equal and constant; for a forward-biased diode the dynamic resistance is much smaller than the static value.

rows: Stretched to n times length (same volume)
Cut into n equal parts joined in parallel
each part R/n, n in parallel
Same material and mass, length × n

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - resistance of a line at working temperature
Aluminium wire: l = 2 km, d = 3 mm, rho(20 C) = 2.8e-8 ohm-m, alpha20 = 0.0039 /C
Step 1: A = pi d^2 / 4 = pi x (3e-3)^2 / 4 = 7.069e-6 m^2
Step 2: R20 = rho l / A = 2.8e-8 x 2000 / 7.069e-6 = 7.92 ohm
Step 3: R50 = R20 [1 + alpha20 (50 - 20)] = 7.92 x 1.117 = 8.85 ohm
Step 4: current from a 24 V source at 50 C: I = 24 / 8.85 = 2.71 A
Check: forgetting the /4 in the area would give R 4 times too small.

Because the resistance of a pure metal falls almost linearly as it is cooled, the straight line extended backwards meets zero resistance at a temperature −T, where T = 1/α₀. For copper T ≈ 234.5 °C. The resistances at any two temperatures are then in the ratio of their distances from −T, which avoids having to convert α from one reference temperature to another.

concepts.plainText: R₂/R₁ = (T + t₂)/(T + t₁), T = 1/α₀ ≈ 234.5 for copper

concepts.text:
Worked example 2 - finding temperature from resistance
A copper coil measures 30 ohm at 15 C and 35 ohm after running. alpha0 = 0.00427 /C
Step 1: R0 = R15 / (1 + alpha0 x 15) = 30 / 1.06405 = 28.19 ohm
Step 2: Rt = R0 (1 + alpha0 t)  ->  t = (Rt/R0 - 1) / alpha0
Step 3: t = (35 / 28.19 - 1) / 0.00427 = 0.2414 / 0.00427 = 56.5 C
Cross-check with T = 1/alpha0 = 234.2: t2 = (35/30)(234.2 + 15) - 234.2 = 56.5 C
Temperature rise = 56.5 - 15 = 41.5 C

A series combination of a positive-coefficient conductor and a negative-coefficient one can be made almost temperature independent. The change in total resistance for a small temperature rise Δt is (R₁α₁ + R₂α₂)Δt, so it vanishes when R₁α₁ = −R₂α₂. For example, 2 Ω of copper (α ≈ 0.0043/°C) needs 2 × 0.0043/0.0005 = 17.2 Ω of carbon (α ≈ −0.0005/°C) in series.
Common mistakes in resistance problems:
items: Using the diameter in place of the radius in A = πr², which makes the area four times too large.
Leaving the area in mm² or cm² instead of converting to m² (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m²).
Applying α₀ to a resistance measured at 20 °C; use α₂₀, the two-temperature formula or first find R₀.
Treating resistivity as if it depended on the length or area of the sample; it depends only on the material and its temperature.
Assuming a stretched wire only gets longer; at constant volume its area falls too, so R rises as the square of the stretch.

concepts.text: For stretch, cut-and-parallel and same-mass questions, work with ratios rather than actual values: write R ∝ l/A, express the new l and A as multiples of the old, and the answer usually drops out as n or n².

formulas.plainText: V = I R
P = VI = I^2 R = V^2/R
R = ρ l / A
G = 1/R = σA/l ; σ = 1/ρ
R_t = R₀(1 + α₀ t)
R₂ = R₁[1 + α₁(t₂ − t₁)]

notes.text: Power questions usually hide Ohm's law inside: memorize all three forms P = VI, I²R and V²/R so you can pick the one matching the given quantities.
Ohm's law applies to ohmic (linear) devices only — not to diodes, thermistors, or filament lamps at varying temperature.
A 'short circuit' has R ≈ 0 (V ≈ 0 across it); an 'open circuit' has R = infinity (I = 0 through it).

Unit traps: resistivity is in Ω·m (not Ω/m), conductance in siemens (S), conductivity in S/m and the temperature coefficient α in per °C. When a question gives R at 0 °C use α₀ directly; when it gives R at 20 °C use α₂₀ (0.00393/°C for copper) or the two-temperature formula.

concepts.text: Kirchhoff's Laws

KCL: the algebraic sum of currents at any node is zero (charge conservation). KVL: the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero (energy conservation). Ohm's law alone cannot solve a circuit with several loops or several sources; Kirchhoff's two laws supply the extra equations, and every network theorem in this topic is ultimately derived from them.
Circuit vocabulary used in every theorem:
items: Node: a point where two or more elements are joined. A principal node (junction) joins three or more branches.
Branch: a single element, or several elements in series, between two nodes; one current per branch.
Loop: any closed path through the circuit that passes no node more than once.
Mesh: a loop that encloses no other loop, the 'window panes' of a planar circuit.
Independent equations: a circuit with n nodes and b branches yields n − 1 KCL equations and b − n + 1 KVL (mesh) equations.

concepts.text: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)

Statement: the sum of currents entering a node equals the sum of currents leaving it; algebraically ΣI = 0 at every node. Principle: conservation of charge, because charge cannot accumulate at a junction. Sign convention: count currents entering as positive and currents leaving as negative (or the reverse), but use one rule for the whole node. A current whose direction was guessed wrongly simply comes out negative in the solution.

concepts.plainText: ΣI_in = ΣI_out at every node

concepts.text: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)

Statement: the algebraic sum of all voltages (source EMFs and element drops) around any closed loop is zero, ΣV = 0. Principle: conservation of energy, since a charge carried once round a closed path returns to its starting potential. Sign convention: walk round the loop in one direction; passing through an element from − to + is a voltage rise and is taken positive, passing from + to − is a voltage drop and is taken negative. For a resistor the drop is IR in the direction of the current, so the loop equation is often written as sum of EMFs = sum of IR drops.

concepts.plainText: ΣV(loop) = 0, i.e. ΣE = ΣIR

concepts.text: Nodal and Mesh Analysis
Two systematic methods built directly on Kirchhoff's laws:
items: Nodal analysis (KCL): pick a reference node (0 V), label the other node voltages, write KCL at each non-reference principal node with branch currents expressed as (V_a − V_b)/R, and solve. Current sources enter directly; a voltage source between two nodes fixes their difference.

Mesh analysis (KVL): assign a clockwise current to each mesh, write KVL round every mesh (a resistor shared by two meshes carries the difference of their mesh currents) and solve the simultaneous equations. Voltage sources enter directly; a current source fixes the current of the mesh it lies in.
A branch current is a mesh current or the difference of two; an element voltage is a node voltage or the difference of two.
Choose the method with fewer unknowns: n − 1 node voltages versus b − n + 1 mesh currents.

concepts.text: Source Transformation

A practical voltage source V_s in series with R_s behaves, at its terminals, exactly like a current source I_s = V_s/R_s in parallel with the same R_s, and vice versa; a load cannot tell them apart. The arrow of the current source points toward the terminal that is positive in the voltage-source form. Repeated transformations can collapse a ladder network into a single loop. Ideal sources (R_s = 0 for a voltage source, R_s = ∞ for a current source) have no equivalent and cannot be transformed.
Network Theorems
The theorems examiners love:
items: Thevenin's: any linear two-terminal network reduces to one voltage source V_th in series with a resistance R_th.
Norton's: the same network as one current source I_N in parallel with R_N (R_N = R_th, I_N = V_th/R_th).
Superposition: the response equals the algebraic sum of the responses to each independent source acting alone (the others replaced by their internal resistance).
Maximum power transfer: the load receives maximum power when R_L = R_th; the maximum power is V_th²/4R_th.

rows: Algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero (charge conservation)
Algebraic sum of voltages round a closed loop is zero (energy conservation)
Response = algebraic sum of responses to each independent source acting alone
Linear circuit with several independent sources
Linear two-terminal network = V_th (open-circuit voltage) in series with R_th
One load varies; find its V or I quickly
Linear two-terminal network = I_N (short-circuit current) in parallel with R_N = R_th
Same as Thevenin; convenient with parallel branches
Load power is maximum when R_L = R_th; P_max = V_th²/(4R_th)
V_s in series with R ⇔ I_s = V_s/R in parallel with R

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Kirchhoff's Laws and Systematic Analysis

Why only n − 1 KCL equations? Every branch current leaves one node and enters another, so if the KCL equations of all n nodes are added, every current appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign and the sum is identically zero. One node equation is therefore always a combination of the others, and it is dropped by making that node the reference. In graph terms a tree joins all n nodes with n − 1 twigs; each of the remaining b − n + 1 links closes exactly one independent loop, which is why that many KVL equations are needed.

concepts.plainText: [G][V] = [I_s]: G_kk = sum of conductances at node k; G_kj = −(conductance between k and j)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: nodal analysis with two unknown nodes
Circuit: 20 V source behind 4 Ω feeds node A; A to ref 4 Ω;
A to B 2 Ω; B to ref 8 Ω; 3 A current source into B.
KCL at A: (20 − VA)/4 = VA/4 + (VA − VB)/2
          → 5 = VA(0.25 + 0.25 + 0.5) − 0.5 VB = VA − 0.5 VB
KCL at B: 3 + (VA − VB)/2 = VB/8
          → 3 = −0.5 VA + 0.625 VB
From the first: VA = 5 + 0.5 VB
Substitute: 3 = −2.5 − 0.25 VB + 0.625 VB → VB = 5.5/0.375 = 14.67 V
VA = 5 + 7.33 = 12.33 V
Check at A: (20 − 12.33)/4 = 1.92 A in; 12.33/4 + (12.33 − 14.67)/2
            = 3.08 − 1.17 = 1.92 A out  ✓

When a voltage source joins two non-reference nodes, its current cannot be written as (V_a − V_b)/R. Enclose both nodes in a supernode, write one KCL equation for the whole enclosure, and add the constraint V_a − V_b = V_s. The dual situation in mesh analysis is a current source shared by two meshes: its voltage is unknown, so KVL is written round the supermesh that bypasses it, with the constraint that the difference of the two mesh currents equals the source current.

Worked example 2: mesh analysis (both mesh currents clockwise)
Mesh 1: 30 V source, 3 Ω, shared 6 Ω.  Mesh 2: shared 6 Ω, 4 Ω, 2 Ω.
Mesh 1: 30 = 3 I1 + 6(I1 − I2) = 9 I1 − 6 I2
Mesh 2:  0 = 6(I2 − I1) + 4 I2 + 2 I2 = −6 I1 + 12 I2  → I1 = 2 I2
Substitute: 30 = 18 I2 − 6 I2 = 12 I2 → I2 = 2.5 A, I1 = 5 A
Shared 6 Ω carries I1 − I2 = 2.5 A (direction of I1), drop = 15 V
KVL check, mesh 2: 15 V = 2.5 × (4 + 2) = 15 V  ✓
Power check: source 30 × 5 = 150 W; resistors
  5²×3 + 2.5²×6 + 2.5²×4 + 2.5²×2 = 75 + 37.5 + 25 + 12.5 = 150 W  ✓

rows: Current source shared by two meshes (supermesh)

concepts.text: In AC circuits KCL and KVL hold at every instant, so they also hold for phasors, but not for RMS magnitudes. Two currents of 3 A and 4 A that are 90° apart combine to 5 A, not 7 A, and three equal voltages 120° apart add to zero. Add the phasors (or the instantaneous values) first and take the magnitude last.
Common mistakes in KCL/KVL problems:
items: Changing the sign convention half-way round a loop or node; fix one rule for rises and drops and keep it.
Writing only one mesh current for a shared resistor instead of the difference I₁ − I₂.
Treating a negative answer as an error; it only means the assumed direction was wrong.
Adding RMS magnitudes of AC currents at a node as if they were in phase.
Transforming an ideal source, or using the transformed model to find the power lost inside the source.

concepts.text: Before solving, count: n − 1 node equations versus b − n + 1 mesh equations, and pick the smaller set. After solving, do a power balance (total power delivered = total power absorbed); it catches most sign errors in seconds.

formulas.plainText: Sum of node currents = 0; sum of loop voltages = 0
ΣI_in = ΣI_out (KCL)
ΣE = ΣIR round any closed loop (KVL)
I_s = V_s / R_s, same R_s moved from series to parallel

notes.text: KCL goes with conservation of Charge, KVL with conservation of energy (Voltage). Examiners swap them deliberately; the C in KCL is the reminder.
In mesh analysis a resistor shared by two meshes carries the difference of the two mesh currents. Writing only one of them is the classic sign error that makes every later answer wrong.

Source transformation preserves everything seen at the terminals but not what happens inside the source: the power dissipated in R_s is different in the two forms, so transform only the part of the circuit you do not need to look inside.

concepts.text: Alternating Current versus Direct Current

Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only and, from a battery, has a constant magnitude. Alternating current (AC) reverses its direction periodically and its magnitude changes continuously with time, so its average over a complete cycle is zero. Power stations generate AC because a coil rotating at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field naturally produces a sinusoidal EMF, and this sine shape is preserved through transformers and linear circuits. The Nepal mains supply is single-phase 230 V, 50 Hz AC, taken from a 400 V three-phase distribution network.
Sinusoidal Quantities

An AC voltage v(t) = Vm sin(2πft) is described by its peak value Vm, its frequency f and its period T = 1/f. Writing ω = 2πf, the general form is v = Vm sin(ωt + φ), where φ is the phase angle at t = 0. The value of v at any chosen instant is the instantaneous value; Vm is the amplitude, the largest instantaneous value reached. Two derived values also matter for exams: the average and the RMS value, covered in the next subtopic.

concepts.latex: v = V_m\sin(\omega t + \phi),\qquad i = I_m\sin(\omega t + \phi_i)
concepts.plainText: v = Vm sin(ωt + φ),  i = Im sin(ωt + φi)

concepts.text: Terms in the equation:
items: Instantaneous value v or i: the value at a particular instant t; it swings between +Vm and −Vm.
Amplitude or peak value Vm, Im: the maximum instantaneous value.
Angular frequency ω = 2πf, in rad/s: the rate at which the angle ωt advances.
Phase angle φ, in degrees or radians: the shift of the wave from the reference at t = 0.
ωt is in radians; convert to degrees (multiply by 180/π) before adding a phase angle given in degrees.

concepts.text: Derived values (details in Peak, Average and RMS Values):
items: RMS (root mean square) value produces the same heating effect as an equal DC value.
Average value is taken over a half cycle (the full-cycle average of a sine is zero).
Form factor = RMS / Average = 1.11 for a sine wave.
Peak (crest) factor = Peak / RMS = 1.414 for a sine wave.

concepts.text: Cycle, Time Period and Frequency

One cycle is one complete positive and one complete negative half cycle, after which the waveform repeats; in angle it spans 360° or 2π radians. The time period T is the time taken for one cycle, in seconds. Frequency f is the number of cycles completed per second, in hertz (Hz), so f = 1/T. Angular frequency ω = 2π/T = 2πf, in rad/s, is the angle swept per second by the rotating phasor that generates the wave. For the 50 Hz supply, T = 1/50 = 20 ms and ω = 2π × 50 = 314.16 rad/s.

concepts.plainText: f = 1/T,  ω = 2πf = 2π/T

concepts.text: Phase Difference and Phasors

Two sinusoids of the same frequency generally do not pass through zero at the same instant; the angle between corresponding zero crossings (or peaks) is their phase difference. With v = Vm sin ωt as reference, a current i = Im sin(ωt − φ) reaches its peak later and is said to lag the voltage by φ, while i = Im sin(ωt + φ) peaks earlier and leads by φ. A time displacement Δt corresponds to a phase angle φ = ωΔt = 360° × Δt/T. Phase difference has meaning only between quantities of the same frequency.
Phase relationships:
items: In phase (φ = 0): both waves pass through zero and peak together, as voltage and current in a pure resistor.
Lagging: the current peaks after the voltage, as in an inductive circuit (90° for a pure inductor).
Leading: the current peaks before the voltage, as in a capacitive circuit (90° for a pure capacitor).
Quadrature: 90° apart. Antiphase: 180° apart, so one wave is the negative of the other.

concepts.text: A sinusoid of fixed frequency is completely specified by its magnitude and phase, so it can be represented by a phasor: an arrow whose length is the RMS (or peak) value and whose angle from the reference axis is the phase angle, imagined rotating anticlockwise at ω rad/s. The projection of the rotating arrow on the vertical axis traces out the sine wave.
