Sinusoids of the same frequency are added by adding their phasors like vectors, which replaces lengthy trigonometry; the angle between two phasors is their phase difference, and the phasor further anticlockwise leads.
Why AC is used for generation and transmission:
items: Alternators are simpler and cheaper than DC generators: no commutator, so very high voltages and large ratings are possible.
Transformers work only with AC, so the voltage is stepped up for transmission (less current, less I²R loss, thinner conductors) and stepped down for safe use.
AC induction motors are rugged, self-starting (three-phase) and need little maintenance.
AC is easy to interrupt because the current passes through zero twice every cycle.
AC is readily converted to DC by rectifiers wherever DC is needed (electronics, electroplating, battery charging).

rows: High voltage, low loss; reactance and skin effect present
No reactance; HVDC only for very long lines
Harder: the arc must be forced to zero

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Sinusoids and Phasor Algebra

Before two sinusoids can be compared, both must be written in the same function with a positive amplitude. A cosine is a sine advanced by 90°, so cos ωt = sin(ωt + 90°), and a negative amplitude is the same as a 180° shift, so −sin ωt = sin(ωt ± 180°). Only after this rewriting can the phase angles be subtracted to give the phase difference. For example, i = 5 cos(ωt − 30°) is really 5 sin(ωt + 60°), so it leads v = 10 sin(ωt + 20°) by 40°, not lags it by 50°.

concepts.plainText: cos ωt = sin(ωt + 90°),  −sin ωt = sin(ωt ± 180°)

concepts.text: The sum of two sinusoids of the same frequency is always another sinusoid of that frequency. Writing each as a phasor and resolving it into a horizontal component (A cos α) and a vertical component (A sin α), the components simply add. The resultant magnitude follows from Pythagoras, or directly from the cosine rule applied to the two phasors, and its angle θ from tan θ = (A sin α + B sin β)/(A cos α + B cos β), the ratio of the vertical to the horizontal sum. Subtraction is done by reversing the phasor to be subtracted (adding 180° to its angle) and then adding.

concepts.plainText: R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos(α − β))

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: add i1 = 10 sin ωt and i2 = 20 sin(ωt + 60°) A
Horizontal sum: 10 cos 0° + 20 cos 60° = 10 + 10 = 20
Vertical sum:   10 sin 0° + 20 sin 60° = 0 + 17.32 = 17.32
Magnitude:      R = √(20² + 17.32²) = √700 = 26.46 A
Angle:          θ = tan⁻¹(17.32/20) = 40.9°
Result:         i = 26.46 sin(ωt + 40.9°) A
Check with the cosine rule: √(100 + 400 + 2·10·20·cos 60°) = √700  (same)
Note: the arithmetic sum 30 A would be correct only if the currents were in phase.

Worked example 2: v = 200 sin(100πt) V, a 50 Hz wave
(a) Value at t = 4 ms: angle = 100π × 0.004 = 0.4π rad = 72°
    v = 200 sin 72° = 190.2 V
(b) First time v reaches +100 V: sin θ = 100/200 = 0.5, θ = π/6 rad
    t = θ/ω = (π/6)/(100π) = 1/600 s = 1.67 ms
(c) Next time v = +100 V (falling): θ = π − π/6 = 5π/6
    t = (5π/6)/(100π) = 1/120 s = 8.33 ms
Calculator in degree mode for (a) would wrongly give 200 sin(1.257°) = 4.4 V.

concepts.latex: r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2},\; \theta = \tan^{-1}(b/a),\; a = r\cos\theta,\; b = r\sin\theta
concepts.plainText: r = √(a² + b²), θ = tan⁻¹(b/a), a = r cos θ, b = r sin θ

concepts.text: Three special cases save time. In-phase phasors add arithmetically (R = A + B); antiphase phasors subtract (R = |A − B|, taking the angle of the larger); phasors in quadrature combine by Pythagoras (R = √(A² + B²)). The operator j rotates a phasor 90° anticlockwise without changing its length, j² = −1 is a 180° rotation, and dividing by j rotates it 90° clockwise. In polar form, multiplication multiplies magnitudes and adds angles, while division divides magnitudes and subtracts angles.
Common mistakes in sinusoid and phasor problems:
items: Adding peak magnitudes of phasors that are not in phase; magnitudes add only when the angles are equal.
Comparing a sine with a cosine, or a wave with a negative amplitude, without first converting both to positive-amplitude sines.
Evaluating sin(ωt) with the calculator in degree mode while ωt is in radians.
Using tan⁻¹(b/a) blindly when a is negative; the angle must be placed in the correct quadrant (add 180°).
Mixing RMS and peak lengths in one phasor diagram; use one convention for every phasor.
Quoting a phase difference between waves of different frequencies, which keeps changing with time.

concepts.text: For a sum like A sin ωt + B cos ωt, write the answer at once as √(A² + B²) sin(ωt + tan⁻¹(B/A)); for example 30 sin ωt + 40 cos ωt = 50 sin(ωt + 53.13°).

formulas.plainText: v = Vm sin(ωt + φ)
f = 1/T
ω = 2πf = 2π/T
φ = ω Δt = 360° × Δt/T

notes.text: For 50 Hz mains remember T = 20 ms and ω = 2π × 50 = 314.16 rad/s; both appear directly in one-mark questions. Doubling the frequency halves the period and doubles ω.

In v = Vm sin(ωt + φ) the product ωt is in radians. Either keep the calculator in radian mode or convert with 180/π before adding a phase angle given in degrees; mixing the two units is the most common error in instantaneous-value questions.
Lead and lag are relative statements: if the current lags the voltage by 30°, the voltage leads the current by 30°. A negative phase angle in the equation of a quantity means it lags the reference.
Phase difference is defined only between sinusoids of the same frequency. Given a time shift Δt, the phase shift is 360° × Δt/T, so a 5 ms shift at 50 Hz is 90°.

concepts.text: What This Topic Covers

Semiconductor devices are components whose conduction is set by doping and by the voltages applied to their junctions, not by a fixed resistance. Section 1.4 of the NEC syllabus builds up from the physics of silicon and germanium to the pn-junction diode, the bipolar junction transistor (BJT), the MOSFET and finally CMOS logic. Together these devices form the basis of rectifiers, regulators, amplifiers, switches and every digital integrated circuit.
Roadmap of the five subtopics:
items: Semiconductor Basics: intrinsic and extrinsic material, energy bands, doping, majority and minority carriers, silicon versus germanium.
Semiconductor Diode: pn-junction formation, forward and reverse bias, V-I characteristic, Shockley equation, special diodes and applications.
BJT: npn and pnp structure, alpha and beta, CB/CE/CC configurations, cut-off, active and saturation regions.
MOSFET: insulated gate, enhancement and depletion types, threshold voltage, square-law saturation current, comparison with JFET and BJT.
CMOS: complementary nMOS-pMOS pair, the inverter, near-zero static power, noise margins, CMOS versus TTL.

concepts.text: The Device Family Tree

Every device here is built from the same two ingredients, p-type and n-type silicon. One junction gives a diode, which conducts in one direction only. Two back-to-back junctions give a BJT, in which a small base current controls a much larger collector current. Replacing the base contact with an insulated gate gives the MOSFET, in which a gate voltage controls the channel current while drawing almost no gate current. Pairing an n-channel with a p-channel MOSFET gives CMOS, the structure used in almost every microprocessor and memory chip.
Key Terms to Know First
Terms you will meet in every subtopic of this section:
items: Majority and minority carriers: the dominant and the scarce charge carriers in a doped semiconductor (electrons and holes respectively in n-type, the reverse in p-type).
Depletion region and barrier potential: the carrier-free zone at a pn junction and its built-in voltage, about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium.
Forward and reverse bias: the polarity that narrows the depletion region and allows current, or widens it and blocks current.
Alpha and beta: the BJT current gains I_C/I_E (slightly below 1) and I_C/I_B (typically 50 to 300).
Threshold voltage V_T: the minimum gate-source voltage that creates a channel in an enhancement MOSFET.
Current-controlled versus voltage-controlled: BJT versus FET, the most frequently tested contrast in this topic.

concepts.text: How the Exam Tests This Area
Typical MCQ patterns:
items: Device identification: which diode regulates voltage, which one emits light, which device has an insulated gate, which one is unipolar.
Biasing conditions: which junctions are forward or reverse biased in each BJT region, and which MOSFET type conducts at V_GS = 0.
Alpha-beta arithmetic: convert between the two gains, or find I_B and I_C from a given I_E.
Contrasts: BJT versus MOSFET, MOSFET versus JFET, CMOS versus TTL, enhancement versus depletion mode.
Standard values: 0.7 V and 0.3 V drops, 26 mV thermal voltage, band gaps of 1.1 eV (Si) and 0.72 eV (Ge).

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Device Families, Ratings and Data Sheets
Semiconductor devices can be classified in several independent ways, and a question may use any of them:
items: By number of junctions or layers: one pn junction (diode), two junctions (BJT), three junctions in a pnpn stack (SCR or thyristor), no junction in the current path (the MOSFET channel, the Schottky metal-semiconductor contact).

By carriers: bipolar or minority-carrier devices (pn diode, BJT, SCR) rely on both electrons and holes; unipolar or majority-carrier devices (JFET, MOSFET, Schottky diode) use only one type, so they store almost no charge and switch faster.
By control: two-terminal devices have no control input; the BJT is current-controlled; JFETs, MOSFETs and IGBTs are voltage-controlled.
By power level: small-signal devices (milliwatts, used in amplifiers and logic) versus power devices (watts to kilowatts, used in converters and motor drives), which need heat sinks.

rows: V_BE falls, so current can run away
High g_m, low V_CE(sat) at small currents
Fast switching, easy drive, dense ICs

concepts.text: A data sheet has two distinct parts. The absolute maximum ratings are limits that must never be exceeded, even briefly; operating a device at them gives no safety margin. The electrical characteristics are measured values (minimum, typical, maximum) at stated test conditions, such as h_FE at a given I_C and V_CE. Power ratings are normally quoted at 25 °C, and above that temperature the permissible dissipation is derated linearly: P_D(T) = P_D(25 °C) − k(T − 25), where the derating factor k (in W/°C, often quoted in mW/°C) equals 1/θ_JA, so that P_D(25 °C) = (T_J(max) − 25)/θ_JA.

rows: V_RRM (peak inverse voltage), I_F(AV), I_FSM surge
V_F at rated current, I_R leakage, t_rr
V_Z at test current, dynamic resistance r_z
V_DS(max), V_GS(max) about ±20 V, I_D, P_D
R_DS(on), V_GS(th), gate charge Q_g, capacitances
V_F at rated I_F, luminous intensity, wavelength

concepts.plainText: TJ = TA + PD x (theta_JC + theta_CS + theta_SA)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: choosing a heat sink
Given: P_D = 15 W, T_J(max) = 150 °C, T_A = 45 °C
       theta_JC = 1.2 °C/W, theta_CS = 0.3 °C/W
Step 1: total theta allowed = (150 - 45) / 15 = 7.0 °C/W
Step 2: theta_SA <= 7.0 - 1.2 - 0.3 = 5.5 °C/W
Step 3: pick a 4.5 °C/W heat sink (below the limit)
Check : T_J = 45 + 15 x (1.2 + 0.3 + 4.5) = 45 + 90 = 135 °C
Result: 135 °C < 150 °C, so the design is safe

concepts.latex: P_{BJT} = V_{CE(sat)} I_C + V_{BE(sat)} I_B, \quad P_{MOS} = I_D^2 R_{DS(on)}
concepts.plainText: P_BJT = VCE(sat) x IC + VBE(sat) x IB;   P_MOS = ID^2 x RDS(on)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: BJT or MOSFET as a 10 A switch?
BJT   : V_CE(sat) = 0.4 V, forced beta = 10 -> I_B = 1 A, V_BE(sat) = 1.0 V
        P = 0.4 x 10 + 1.0 x 1 = 4 + 1 = 5 W
MOSFET: R_DS(on) = 0.015 ohm, gate current negligible
        P = 10^2 x 0.015 = 1.5 W
Break-even (collector loss only): I^2 x 0.015 = 0.4 x I
        I = 0.4 / 0.015 = 26.7 A
Below about 27 A the MOSFET has the lower conduction loss;
the MOSFET loss grows as I^2, the BJT loss roughly as I.
Common mistakes with ratings and device comparisons:
items: Using the 25 °C power rating at a higher ambient temperature without derating it first.
Adding only the heat-sink thermal resistance and forgetting θ_JC and θ_CS, which are always in series with it.
Assuming V_CEO equals V_CBO; with the base open the collector leakage is multiplied by β, so V_CEO is lower.
Designing for the typical h_FE; a robust bias circuit must work over the full minimum-to-maximum spread.
Treating a MOSFET as lossless when on; R_DS(on) roughly doubles between 25 °C and 150 °C.

concepts.text: A MOSFET gate oxide is only tens of nanometres thick and is destroyed if V_GS exceeds its rating (typically about ±20 V). Static charge from handling easily reaches thousands of volts, so MOSFETs and CMOS ICs are stored in conductive packaging and handled with earthing straps.

For thermal problems write one line: T_J = T_A + P × (sum of all thermal resistances in the path). For derating, subtract k × (T − 25) from the 25 °C rating. For switch losses, BJT loss is V_CE(sat) × I_C (plus base drive) and MOSFET loss is I² × R_DS(on).

formulas.plainText: beta = IC / IB;   alpha = IC / IE
alpha = beta / (1 + beta);   beta = alpha / (1 - alpha)
ID = IS (e^(VD/(n VT)) - 1)   (diode)
ID = k (VGS - VT)^2   (MOSFET in saturation)

notes.text: Learn the devices as a ladder: diode (one junction), BJT (two junctions, current-controlled), MOSFET (insulated gate, voltage-controlled), CMOS (a complementary MOSFET pair). Most overview questions only ask you to place a device correctly on this ladder.

Two different quantities share the symbol V_T. In the diode equation V_T is the thermal voltage, about 26 mV; for a MOSFET V_T is the threshold voltage, typically 0.5 V to 2 V. Read the context of the question before substituting numbers.
Standard values used throughout this topic: silicon forward drop 0.7 V, germanium 0.3 V, thermal voltage 26 mV at 300 K, silicon band gap 1.1 eV, germanium band gap 0.72 eV.

concepts.text: What a Signal Generator Does

A signal generator produces a periodic electrical waveform of controlled frequency, amplitude and shape without any input signal, drawing its energy from the DC supply. When the output is a sine wave the circuit is called an oscillator; when it is a square, triangular or sawtooth wave it is usually called a waveform generator, relaxation oscillator or multivibrator. Every one of them is an amplifier arranged so that part of its output is returned to the input in phase (positive feedback), so the circuit sustains its own signal and converts DC power into AC.
Roadmap of This Topic
The five subtopics that follow build up the subject in exam order:
items: Oscillator Basics: positive feedback, loop gain, the Barkhausen criterion, start-up, damping and frequency stability.
RC Oscillators: phase-shift and Wien bridge circuits for audio frequencies (about 1 Hz to 1 MHz).
LC Oscillators: tuned-collector, Hartley, Colpitts and Clapp circuits for radio frequencies (about 100 kHz to several hundred MHz).
Crystal Oscillator: quartz-controlled circuits with Q of 10^4 to 10^6 and frequency stability measured in parts per million.
Waveform Generators: multivibrators, the 555 timer, Schmitt trigger, integrator and UJT circuits for square, triangular and sawtooth outputs.

concepts.text: Classification at a Glance

rows: Radio transmitters and receivers, local oscillators
Below 1 Hz to a few MHz
Square, pulse, triangle, sawtooth; low to moderate stability
Timers, clock pulses, sweep and trigger circuits

concepts.text: Key Terms
Terms the whole section builds on:
items: Positive feedback: a fraction β of the output is returned to the input in phase with it, so the amplifier reinforces its own output.
Loop gain Aβ: the product of amplifier gain A and feedback fraction β; the signal returned after one trip round the loop is Aβ times the original.
Barkhausen criterion: |Aβ| = 1 and total loop phase shift 0° (or 360°) at exactly one frequency for sustained sinusoidal oscillation.
Frequency stability: how little the output frequency drifts with temperature, supply voltage, load and ageing; quoted in ppm (parts per million) or percent.
Tank circuit: a parallel L-C combination that stores energy and rings at f = 1/(2π√(LC)); it fixes the frequency of LC oscillators.
Relaxation oscillator: a circuit that charges a capacitor slowly and discharges it abruptly through a switching device, producing non-sinusoidal waveforms.

concepts.text: How the Exam Tests This Area
MCQs on signal generators usually follow one of these patterns:
items: Barkhausen criterion: the loop gain needed for sustained oscillation (unity) and the loop phase shift (0° or 360°).
Component identification: Hartley = two inductors + one capacitor, Colpitts = two capacitors + one inductor, phase-shift = three RC sections, crystal = quartz.
Frequency formulas: 1/(2πRC) for the Wien bridge, 1/(2πRC√6) for the phase-shift oscillator, 1/(2π√(LC)) for LC types, 1.44/((R_A + 2R_B)C) for the 555 astable.
Gain requirements: A ≥ 29 for the phase-shift oscillator and A = 3 (R_f = 2R_1) for the Wien bridge.
Ranking: which oscillator has the best frequency stability (crystal) and which family serves audio (RC) or radio (LC) frequencies.
Waveform type: sinusoidal (RC, LC, crystal) versus non-sinusoidal (multivibrators, 555 timer, UJT relaxation oscillator, Schmitt trigger).

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Function Generators, Synthesis and Specifications

A laboratory function generator is built around a loop of two blocks: an integrator and a comparator with hysteresis (Schmitt trigger). The comparator output is a square wave; integrating it gives a triangle whose peaks switch the comparator back, so both waveforms come out together. A diode break-point shaping network then rounds the triangle into a sine wave with a few tenths of a percent to about 1 % distortion. The charging current of the integrator is set by a control voltage, so the same instrument can be swept in frequency (a voltage-controlled generator), and the output stage adds amplitude control, a DC offset, a step attenuator and a 50 Ω output resistance.
Common kinds of signal generator and what distinguishes them:
items: Audio-frequency (AF) sine generator: low-distortion sine, typically a Wien-bridge oscillator, about 10 Hz to 100 kHz.
RF signal generator: an LC or synthesized oscillator with AM/FM modulation and a calibrated output attenuator reaching microvolt levels, for testing receivers.
Function generator: square, triangle and sine (plus ramp and pulse) from one integrator-comparator loop, with a sweep input.
Pulse generator: independent control of repetition rate, pulse width, delay, amplitude and rise/fall times, for digital and switching tests.
Sweep generator: frequency moves automatically between two limits, so a filter or amplifier response can be displayed directly on an oscilloscope.
Arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) and DDS synthesizer: samples stored in memory are played out through a DAC, giving any shape with crystal-referenced frequency.

rows: Transient response, slew rate, tilt and ringing
Linearity checks, sweep and PWM reference
Harmonics with nD = integer are missing

concepts.plainText: square wave of peak A: v = (4A/π)(sin ωt + (1/3) sin 3ωt + (1/5) sin 5ωt + ...)

concepts.text: Modern generators obtain their frequency by synthesis rather than from a free-running oscillator. In a phase-locked loop (PLL) synthesizer a voltage-controlled oscillator is divided by a programmable number N and its phase is compared with a crystal reference of frequency f_ref; the loop filter adjusts the VCO until the divided output equals f_ref, so f_out = N f_ref and the step size (channel spacing) is f_ref. In direct digital synthesis (DDS) an n-bit phase accumulator adds a tuning word M on every clock pulse; the accumulator value addresses a sine look-up table whose samples go to a DAC and a low-pass reconstruction filter. Both inherit the fractional (ppm) accuracy of their crystal reference.

concepts.plainText: DDS with an n-bit accumulator: f_out = M·f_clk / 2^n; resolution Δf = f_clk / 2^n (PLL: f_out = N·f_xtal / R)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - PLL synthesizer
Crystal 12.8 MHz, reference divider R = 512
  f_ref = 12.8 MHz / 512 = 25 kHz  (= channel spacing)
Wanted output 90 MHz: N = 90 MHz / 25 kHz = 3600
Crystal tolerance ±2.5 ppm is carried to the output:
  error = 90 MHz × 2.5 × 10^-6 = ±225 Hz
Next channel (N = 3601) = 90.025 MHz

Worked example 2 - DDS tuning word
Clock f_clk = 125 MHz, accumulator n = 28 bits
  Resolution = 125 MHz / 2^28 = 125e6 / 268 435 456 = 0.466 Hz
Wanted f_out = 10 kHz:
  M = f_out × 2^n / f_clk = 10e3 × 268 435 456 / 125e6 = 21 474.8 -> 21 475
  Actual f_out = 21 475 × 125e6 / 2^28 = 10 000.08 Hz
Highest usable output < f_clk / 2 = 62.5 MHz (Nyquist); about 40 % of f_clk in practice

rows: Span of output frequency and its error
1 µHz to 20 MHz; ±20 ppm with a crystal reference
10 % to 90 % transition of a square or pulse
A few ns to tens of ns; t_r ≈ 0.35 / bandwidth
Output level range and DC shift
Up to 10 V p-p into 50 Ω, ±5 V offset
Fraction of the period spent high

concepts.text: A generator with a 50 Ω output behaves as an EMF in series with 50 Ω. Into a matched 50 Ω load the voltage is half the open-circuit value; into a high-impedance load such as an oscilloscope input it is almost the full EMF. Many instruments display the amplitude assuming a 50 Ω load, so a setting of 1 V p-p reads about 2 V p-p on a high-impedance scope. Also remember that dBm is a power level referred to 1 mW, so converting it to volts needs the load resistance.

For synthesizer questions write the relation first: PLL step = f_ref and f_out = N f_ref; DDS step = f_clk / 2^n (n = accumulator bits) and f_out = M × step. For waveform questions remember odd harmonics at 1/n for a square wave, 1/n² for a triangle, and all harmonics for a sawtooth.

formulas.plainText: |Aβ| = 1 and total loop phase shift = 0° or 360° (Barkhausen)
f0 = 1 / (2π√(LC))  (LC tank: Hartley, Colpitts, Clapp)
f = 1/(2πRC) (Wien bridge);  f = 1/(2πRC√6) (RC phase-shift)
f = 1.44 / ((RA + 2RB)·C)  (555 astable)

notes.text: Memorise the pairing: Hartley has two L (a tapped coil), Colpitts has two C (Capacitors). Clapp is a Colpitts with one extra series capacitor.

Do not confuse the Q of a resonant circuit with loop gain. Q describes how sharply the tank or crystal selects its frequency (crystal Q is 10^4 to 10^6); loop gain Aβ must be exactly 1 for steady oscillation whatever the Q.

Sinusoidal (harmonic) oscillators are built around a frequency-selective network: RC, LC or crystal. Square, triangular and sawtooth generators are relaxation oscillators built around a switching threshold and an RC timing element, so they have no resonant frequency in the LC sense.

concepts.text: What an Amplifier Does

An amplifier is an electronic circuit that increases the amplitude of a signal (its voltage, current or power) while preserving its waveform. The extra output power is not created from the signal: an active device (BJT, MOSFET or op-amp) uses the small input signal to control how much power is drawn from the DC supply and delivered to the load. The ratio of output to input is the gain, and an amplifier is judged by its gain, bandwidth, input and output impedance, distortion and efficiency.
Roadmap of This Topic
The four subtopics that follow build on each other:
items: Amplifier Basics: gain and decibels, impedances, bandwidth, distortion, efficiency, coupling and cascading.
Classification of Output Stages: where the Q-point sits on the load line and the resulting classes A, B, AB, C and D.
Comparison of Amplifier Classes: efficiency derivations (25 %, 50 %, 78.5 %), distortion, heat, cost and applications.
Biasing Class AB Output Stage: removing crossover distortion with diode or V_BE-multiplier bias while keeping efficiency high.

concepts.text: How Amplifiers Are Classified
The same amplifier can be named in several ways, depending on the property being described:
items: By signal size: small-signal (voltage) amplifiers handle millivolt inputs in the linear region; large-signal (power) amplifiers drive loads such as loudspeakers and antennas, where efficiency and distortion matter most.
By frequency range: audio (20 Hz to 20 kHz), radio-frequency (tuned, narrow band), video or wideband (a few hertz to several megahertz) and DC amplifiers (respond down to 0 Hz).
By inter-stage coupling: RC (capacitor) coupled, transformer coupled or direct coupled.

By conduction angle, the part of the input cycle during which the output device carries current: class A (360°), class B (180°), class AB (between 180° and 360°), class C (less than 180°), and class D, in which the devices switch fully on and off.
By configuration of the active device: common-emitter, common-base and common-collector (emitter follower) for BJTs, or common-source, common-gate and common-drain for FETs.

rows: Lowest distortion; small-signal stages, hi-fi where heat is acceptable
Crossover distortion at zero crossing; push-pull power stages
Very low distortion with a small bias; most audio power amplifiers
Heavily distorted pulses restored by a tuned load; RF transmitters, frequency multipliers
Low distortion after LC filtering; portable and battery-powered audio

concepts.text: Key terms you must be able to define:
items: Gain: ratio of output to input quantity; in decibels, 20 log for voltage or current and 10 log for power.
Bandwidth: frequency range between the lower and upper cut-off frequencies, where gain stays within 3 dB (70.7 %) of its mid-band value.
Q-point (quiescent point): the DC operating point (I_CQ, V_CEQ) fixed by the bias network with no signal applied.
Load line: the straight line of possible (V_CE, I_C) pairs for a given supply and load; the signal moves the operating point along it.
Conduction angle: the number of degrees of each 360° input cycle during which the output transistor conducts.
Efficiency: AC signal power delivered to the load divided by DC power drawn from the supply.
Crossover distortion: the notch produced near zero output when neither transistor of a class B pair is conducting.
Push-pull: two devices driven in antiphase so that each handles one half-cycle; even harmonics cancel.

concepts.text: How the Exam Tests This Area

Exam MCQs on amplifiers are mostly one-line recall items: matching a conduction angle to a class, quoting the maximum efficiency of class A (25 % or 50 %) and class B (78.5 %), naming the class that suffers crossover distortion (B) and the one that cures it (AB), identifying the class used for audio power (AB) or for RF tuned stages (C), and describing class D as a switching amplifier. Numerical items convert gains to decibels or compute efficiency from P_ac and P_dc, so keep the dB rules and the efficiency numbers at your fingertips.
Going Deeper: Amplifier Models and Feedback

Any linear amplifier can be drawn as a two-port with an input resistance R_i, an output resistance R_o and a controlled source. Which source is used depends on the input and output quantities: a voltage amplifier has a voltage-controlled voltage source A_vo·v_i, a current amplifier a current-controlled current source A_is·i_i, a transconductance amplifier a voltage-controlled current source G_m·v_i, and a transresistance amplifier a current-controlled voltage source R_m·i_i. The four models are interchangeable for a given circuit (for example G_m = A_vo/R_o), but the one whose ideal impedances match the real circuit gives the simplest analysis.

With a real source and load, each port forms a voltage divider, so the gain actually obtained is smaller than the open-circuit gain. For a voltage amplifier fed from a source of resistance R_s and driving R_L, only R_i/(R_i + R_s) of the source voltage reaches the input and only R_L/(R_L + R_o) of the internal voltage reaches the load. In a cascade the next stage's R_i is the load of the previous one, so every interface costs a divider factor; this is why buffers (high R_i, low R_o) are placed between stages.

concepts.plainText: vo/vs = [Ri/(Ri + Rs)] · Avo · [RL/(RL + Ro)]

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: loaded voltage amplifier
v_s = 10 mV, R_s = 10 kΩ, R_i = 40 kΩ, A_vo = 100, R_o = 1 kΩ, R_L = 4 kΩ
v_i = 10 mV × 40/(40 + 10) = 8 mV
v_o = 100 × 8 mV × 4/(4 + 1) = 0.64 V
A_v = v_o/v_i = 80;  overall v_o/v_s = 64 = 20 log 64 = 36.1 dB
P_i = v_i²/R_i = (8 mV)²/40 kΩ = 1.6 nW
P_o = v_o²/R_L = (0.64 V)²/4 kΩ = 102.4 µW
A_p = 64 000 = 10 log 64 000 = 48.1 dB  (not 20 log 80, since R_i ≠ R_L)

Negative feedback returns a fraction β of the output and subtracts it from the input. If A is the gain without feedback, the closed-loop gain is A_f = A/(1 + Aβ); the quantity 1 + Aβ is the amount of feedback (desensitivity), often quoted in dB as 20 log(1 + Aβ). When Aβ >> 1 the gain approaches 1/β and depends only on the passive feedback network. The same factor that divides the gain also divides fractional gain changes, harmonic distortion and noise generated inside the loop, widens the bandwidth (f_H rises and f_L falls by 1 + Aβ, so the gain-bandwidth product stays constant) and multiplies or divides the input and output resistances. Positive feedback (Aβ subtracting from 1) raises the gain and is used deliberately only in oscillators and Schmitt triggers.

concepts.latex: A_f = \frac{A}{1 + A\beta},\quad \frac{dA_f}{A_f} = \frac{1}{1 + A\beta}\,\frac{dA}{A},\quad f_{Hf} = f_H(1 + A\beta)
concepts.plainText: Af = A/(1 + Aβ); dAf/Af = (dA/A)/(1 + Aβ); fHf = fH(1 + Aβ), fLf = fL/(1 + Aβ)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: voltage-series feedback
A = 1000, β = 0.019, R_i = 10 kΩ, R_o = 2 kΩ, f_H = 20 kHz
1 + Aβ = 1 + 19 = 20  (26 dB of feedback)
A_f = 1000/20 = 50
If A falls 20 % to 800: A_f = 800/(1 + 15.2) = 49.4, only 1.2 % lower
f_Hf = 20 kHz × 20 = 400 kHz  (gain × bandwidth: 1000 × 20k = 50 × 400k)
R_if = 10 kΩ × 20 = 200 kΩ,  R_of = 2 kΩ/20 = 100 Ω

Worked example 3: two-stage cascade with loading
R_s = 10 kΩ; stage 1: R_i1 = 50 kΩ, A_vo1 = 40, R_o1 = 4 kΩ
stage 2: R_i2 = 12 kΩ, A_vo2 = 25, R_o2 = 500 Ω; R_L = 2 kΩ
Input divider      50/(50 + 10)   = 0.833
Interstage divider 12/(12 + 4)    = 0.75
Output divider     2/(2 + 0.5)    = 0.8
v_o/v_s = 0.833 × 40 × 0.75 × 25 × 0.8 = 500  ->  54 dB
Unloaded product 40 × 25 = 1000 (60 dB): loading costs 6 dB

Common slips: multiplying open-circuit gains without the divider factors at each interface; using Aβ instead of 1 + Aβ for the amount of feedback; applying 20 log to a power ratio; and assuming feedback raises the input resistance in every case. Series mixing at the input raises R_i, shunt mixing lowers it; voltage sampling at the output lowers R_o, current sampling raises it.

formulas.plainText: Av(dB) = 20 log10(Vo / Vi)
Ap(dB) = 10 log10(Po / Pi)
η = P_ac(out) / P_dc(in) × 100 %

notes.text: Memorise the class table as a chant: A 360° 25/50 %, B 180° 78.5 %, AB in between, C under 180° for RF, D switching above 90 %. Most amplifier MCQs are answered from one of those rows.
Voltage and current gains use 20 log, power gain uses 10 log. A ratio of 100 is 40 dB as a voltage gain but only 20 dB as a power gain; mixing the two is the most common decibel mistake.

The class letters rank neither quality nor age. They describe only the bias condition of the output device, so a class C stage can be the right choice (RF) even though its collector current is a train of pulses.

concepts.text: Principle of Orthographic Projection

Orthographic projection represents a three-dimensional object by two or more two-dimensional views, each obtained by projectors drawn perpendicular to a plane of projection. The observer is imagined at infinity, so projectors are parallel and every view shows true dimensions of surfaces parallel to that plane. It is the standard method for manufacturing and construction drawings because sizes can be measured directly.
Principal planes of projection:
items: Vertical plane (VP): receives the front view (elevation), showing length and height.
Horizontal plane (HP): receives the top view (plan), showing length and width.
Profile plane (PP): perpendicular to both, receives the side view (end view), showing width and height.
The line of intersection of HP and VP is the reference line XY; after projection the HP is rotated to lie in the plane of the VP.

concepts.text: Quadrants and Angles of Projection

The HP and VP intersect to form four quadrants (dihedral angles). Placing the object in the first quadrant gives first-angle projection; placing it in the third quadrant gives third-angle projection. Second- and fourth-angle projections are not used because after rotating the HP the front and top views overlap on the same side of XY.

rows: On the right of front view
On the left of front view
India (BIS SP 46), Nepal, Europe (ISO method E)

concepts.text: The method of projection is indicated in the title block by a symbol showing the front view and left side view of a truncated cone. In the first-angle symbol the circles (end view) appear to the right of the trapezium; in the third-angle symbol they appear to the left.
Projection of Points and Lines
Points in first-angle projection:
items: A point h above HP and d in front of VP: front view is h above XY and top view is d below XY, both on one projector perpendicular to XY.
A point lying in the VP has its top view on XY; a point lying in the HP has its front view on XY.
In third-angle projection the top view lies above XY and the front view below XY.

concepts.text: Straight lines:
items: A line parallel to a plane shows its true length on that plane.
A line perpendicular to HP appears as a point in the top view and in true length in the front view.
A line inclined to both planes appears shortened in both views; its true length is found by rotation or an auxiliary plane.

concepts.plainText: True length = sqrt(top view length^2 + (difference of end heights above HP)^2)

concepts.text: Multi-View Drawing Practice
Choosing and drawing views:
items: Choose as front view the side that shows the most characteristic shape and the fewest hidden lines.
Use the minimum number of views that fully describe the object: a cylinder or sphere-like part may need only two, most parts need three.
Views must be aligned on common projectors: front and top share length, front and side share height, top and side share width.
Hidden features are shown with thin dashed lines; axes of holes and symmetry with thin chain lines.

concepts.text:
Layout on sheet (first-angle):
           [ FRONT VIEW ]   [ LEFT SIDE VIEW ]
  --------------------------------------  XY
           [ TOP VIEW   ]
Layout on sheet (third-angle):
           [ TOP VIEW   ]
           [ FRONT VIEW ]   [ RIGHT SIDE VIEW ]

formulas.plainText: True length = sqrt(top view length^2 + (h2 - h1)^2)
Top view length = TL cos(theta), front view length = TL cos(phi); theta, phi = inclinations to HP and VP

notes.text: Remember the first-angle rule: what you see from above is drawn below, and what you see from the left is drawn on the right.
Nepal follows Indian and ISO practice, so first-angle projection is the default on drawings and in examinations unless stated otherwise.
Second and fourth quadrants are not used for drawings because the front and top views overlap after the HP is rotated.

concepts.text: Pictorial Drawings

A pictorial drawing shows the length, width and height of an object in a single view, so it is easy to understand even for non-specialists. The main families are axonometric projection (isometric, dimetric, trimetric), oblique projection and perspective projection. Pictorial views support orthographic drawings in catalogues, assembly instructions, sketches and presentations, but they are rarely used alone for manufacture because many lengths and angles are distorted.
Isometric Axes and Isometric Scale

In isometric projection the object is tilted so that its three principal edges make equal angles with the plane of projection. The three isometric axes appear 120 degrees apart: one vertical and two at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Lines parallel to these axes are isometric lines and are all foreshortened in the same ratio; lines not parallel to the axes (non-isometric lines) cannot be measured directly and are located by their end points.

concepts.plainText: Isometric length / true length = cos45 / cos30 = sqrt(2/3) = 0.816

concepts.text:
Worked example: isometric projection of a 50 mm cube
Isometric length = 0.816 x 50 = 40.8 mm on each of the three axes
Isometric view (true lengths) would draw each edge 50 mm
Ratio view / projection = 1 / 0.816 = 1.225, i.e. view about 22.5% larger
Isometric scale construction: true scale at 45 degrees, isometric scale at 30 degrees,
verticals dropped from true divisions give isometric divisions
Isometric view versus isometric projection:
items: Isometric projection: drawn with the isometric scale, so all isometric lines are 0.816 of true length.
Isometric view (isometric drawing): drawn with true lengths along the axes; same shape, but about 22.5% larger.
The isometric view is more common in practice because it saves drawing an isometric scale.
Circles on isometric faces appear as ellipses, usually drawn by the four-centre method or the box (offset) method.

concepts.text: Oblique Projection

In oblique projection the front face is drawn parallel to the picture plane in true shape and size, and the receding edges are drawn at an angle, usually 30, 45 or 60 degrees. It is convenient for objects with circles or irregular outlines on one face, since those are drawn in true shape.
Perspective Projection

Perspective projection shows an object as the eye sees it from a finite station point: projectors converge to the eye, so parallel receding lines meet at vanishing points and distant parts appear smaller. One-point (parallel), two-point (angular) and three-point (oblique) perspectives are distinguished by the number of vanishing points. It gives the most realistic image and is used by architects and in presentations, but it is not used for measurement.
When to use each pictorial method:
items: Isometric: technical illustration, piping isometrics, assembly sketches where all three faces matter equally.
Oblique: objects with a characteristic front face containing circles or curves.
Perspective: architectural renderings and presentations where realism matters more than measurement.
Orthographic: manufacturing and construction drawings where exact dimensions are required.

formulas.plainText: Isometric length = 0.816 x true length
Isometric view / isometric projection = 1/0.816 = 1.225

notes.text: If a question says isometric projection, multiply true lengths by 0.816; if it says isometric view or isometric drawing, use true lengths.
Cavalier oblique uses full scale on the receding axis and cabinet oblique uses half scale.
Only isometric lines can be measured directly; locate non-isometric lines and curves by plotting their end points or offsets.

concepts.text: Purpose of Sectional Views

When an object has complicated interior details, ordinary views are cluttered with hidden lines that are hard to read. A sectional view imagines the object cut by a cutting plane, with the portion nearer the observer removed, so that the interior is shown with visible lines. The cut surface is hatched to distinguish solid material from empty space.
Cutting-plane and hatching conventions:
items: The cutting plane is shown in an adjacent view by a thin chain line, thick at the ends and at changes of direction, with arrows showing the direction of viewing and letters such as A-A.
Section lines (hatching) are thin continuous lines, usually at 45 degrees to the main outline or axis, evenly spaced (commonly 1 to 2 mm apart, more for large areas).
Adjacent parts in an assembly are hatched in opposite directions or with different spacing; the same part is hatched identically in all views.
Hidden lines are normally omitted in sectional views unless essential for clarity.
Thin sections such as gaskets and sheet metal may be shown entirely filled (solid black).

concepts.text: Types of Sections

rows: Plane passes completely through the object
One quarter removed; half shows interior, half exterior
Cutting plane stepped to pass through off-line features
Cross-section rotated 90 degrees in place on the view
Cross-section drawn outside the view, labelled
Small portion broken out by a freehand line
Features rotated into the cutting plane

concepts.text: In a half section of a symmetrical object, a centre line (not a thick line) separates the sectioned half from the unsectioned half, and hidden lines are omitted from the unsectioned half. An offset section is drawn as if the cutting plane were flat; the changes of direction are not shown as lines in the sectional view.
Items Not Sectioned

Certain parts are not hatched when the cutting plane passes along their length, because a section would give a false impression of their shape and add no information. They are shown in outside view even though the plane passes through them; they may be hatched when cut across their axis.
Items normally shown unsectioned when cut longitudinally:
items: Shafts, spindles, pins, keys and cotters.
Bolts, nuts, screws, studs, rivets and washers.
Ribs, webs, spokes of wheels and teeth of gears.
Balls and rollers of bearings.

concepts.text: True Shape of a Section

When a solid is cut by a plane inclined to the reference planes, the section appears foreshortened in the ordinary views. Its true shape is obtained on an auxiliary plane parallel to the cutting plane. For a vertical cylinder cut by a plane inclined at angle theta to HP, the true section is an ellipse whose minor axis equals the diameter and whose major axis is D / cos theta.

concepts.plainText: Major axis = D / cos(theta), minor axis = D (vertical cylinder, plane at theta to HP)

concepts.text:
Worked example: vertical cylinder D = 40 mm cut by a plane at 45 degrees to HP
Minor axis of true section = D = 40 mm
Major axis = 40 / cos 45 = 40 / 0.7071 = 56.6 mm
Top view of the section = circle of 40 mm (coincides with the cylinder plan)
General conventions in sectional drawing:
items: Show the cutting-plane line in the view where it appears as an edge, and label the section view (SECTION A-A).
Choose the cutting plane through axes of symmetry or centres of holes.
Hatching should never be parallel or perpendicular to the main outline of the part.

formulas.plainText: Major axis of section of a cylinder = D / cos(theta)
True length along the cutting plane = top-view length / cos(theta)

notes.text: A half section suits symmetrical parts; it removes one quarter of the object and shows both interior and exterior in one view.
Do not hatch shafts, bolts, keys, ribs or spokes when the cutting plane passes along their length.
Revolved sections are drawn on the view itself, while removed sections are drawn away from the view and labelled.

concepts.text: Discount Rate and MARR

The minimum attractive rate of return (MARR), also called the hurdle rate, is the lowest rate of return an organisation will accept on a new investment. It is used as the discount rate when computing present worth. A project is economically worth doing only if it earns at least the MARR, because otherwise the money could be put to a better use elsewhere.
Factors on which the MARR is based:
items: Cost of capital: the weighted average cost of debt (loan interest) and equity (shareholders' expected return).
Opportunity cost: the return on the best alternative investment forgone.
Project risk: riskier projects are assigned a higher MARR (risk premium).
Inflation expectations, availability of funds and management policy.

concepts.text: Simple and Discounted Payback Period

The simple payback period is the time needed for cumulative undiscounted net cash inflows to recover the initial investment. It ignores the time value of money and all cash flows after the payback point. The discounted payback period first discounts each year's cash flow at the MARR and then finds when the cumulative present worth becomes zero; it is always longer than the simple payback for a conventional project. Both are measures of liquidity and risk rather than of profitability.

Investment Rs 10,000; inflow Rs 4,000/yr for 4 years; MARR 10%
Year  Cash flow  PW at 10%  Cumulative PW
 0    -10,000    -10,000     -10,000
 1     +4,000     +3,636      -6,364
 2     +4,000     +3,306      -3,058
 3     +4,000     +3,005        -53
 4     +4,000     +2,732      +2,679
Simple payback     = 10,000 / 4,000 = 2.5 years
Discounted payback = 3 + 53 / 2,732 ≈ 3.02 years
NPV at 10%         = +Rs 2,679
Net Present Value (Present Worth)

Net present value (NPV), or present worth (PW), is the sum of all cash flows discounted to time 0 at the MARR. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the MARR and adds that much value in today's money. NPV is additive across projects, uses all cash flows and accounts for time value, which makes it the most reliable single criterion. Its drawback is that it needs a chosen discount rate and does not show the rate of return directly.

concepts.plainText: NPV = sum over t = 0..n of CF_t / (1 + i)^t

concepts.text: Internal Rate of Return

The internal rate of return (IRR) is the interest rate at which the NPV of a project's cash flows equals zero, i.e. the present worth of inflows equals the present worth of outflows. It is found by trial: compute NPV at two rates, one giving a positive and one a negative NPV, then interpolate linearly between them. In the table example NPV is +355 at 20% and −25 at 22%, so IRR ≈ 20 + 2 × 355/380 = 21.87% (exact 21.86%). A non-conventional cash flow with several sign changes may have more than one IRR.

concepts.plainText: IRR ≈ i1 + (i2 − i1) × NPV1 / (NPV1 − NPV2)

concepts.text: Benefit-Cost Ratio and Decision Rules

The benefit-cost (B/C) ratio is widely used for public-sector projects such as roads, irrigation and hydropower. It divides the present (or annual) worth of benefits to the public by the present (or annual) worth of costs to the sponsor. In the modified B/C ratio, O&M costs are subtracted from benefits in the numerator instead of being added to costs.

rows: Ignores time value and later cash flows

concepts.text: The NPV profile is a graph of NPV against discount rate. For a conventional project (outflow first, then inflows) it falls as the rate rises and crosses the horizontal axis at the IRR. For a single project NPV, IRR and B/C always give the same accept/reject decision, because NPV ≥ 0 at the MARR exactly when IRR ≥ MARR and B/C ≥ 1.

formulas.plainText: NPV = −P + sum over t = 1..n of CF_t / (1 + i)^t
IRR ≈ i1 + (i2 − i1) × NPV1 / (NPV1 − NPV2)
B/C = PW of benefits / PW of costs

notes.text: For IRR interpolation choose two trial rates close together, one with positive and one with negative NPV; the wider the bracket, the larger the interpolation error.
Ranking mutually exclusive projects by their individual IRRs can give the wrong choice; use NPV or incremental IRR instead (see Comparison of Alternatives).
Payback is popular because it is easy and signals how quickly capital is recovered, but it is a screening tool: a project with a short payback can still have a negative NPV.

concepts.text: Types of Alternatives

Engineering decisions usually involve choosing among alternatives that meet the same need, such as two pump models or two road alignments. Before comparing them, the analyst must know whether the alternatives are mutually exclusive or independent, whether they are revenue or cost (service) alternatives, and whether their lives are equal. Only the differences between alternatives matter; costs common to all can be ignored.

rows: Steel or concrete bridge at one site
Several unrelated projects within a budget
A valid alternative if not required

concepts.text: The do-nothing (null) alternative keeps the current situation and has zero incremental cash flow. It is chosen when no alternative earns the MARR. When a service must be provided (e.g. a legally required treatment plant), do-nothing is not available and the least-cost alternative is chosen.
Equal-Life Present Worth Comparison

When alternatives have equal lives, compute each one's present worth at the MARR over that life and select the one with the highest PW (for revenue alternatives) or lowest PW of costs (for cost alternatives). Costs can be entered as positive numbers when only costs are compared, as long as the convention is consistent.
Unequal Lives: LCM and Annual Worth
Two standard ways to compare alternatives with different lives:
items: Least common multiple (LCM) of lives: repeat each alternative's cash flows until all end together, then compare PW over that common study period (lives 4 and 6 years give 12 years).

Annual worth (AW): convert each alternative's cash flows to an equivalent uniform annual amount over its own life; because AW is the same for every repeated cycle, alternatives can be compared directly without the LCM.
Both methods assume repeatability: each alternative can be replaced by an identical one at the same costs.
When repeatability is unrealistic, a specified study period with estimated salvage values is used instead.

concepts.plainText: AW = −P(A/P, i, n) + S(A/F, i, n) − annual operating cost

concepts.text:
Unequal lives at MARR 10%, no salvage, equal O&M
Machine X: first cost Rs 10,000, life 3 yrs
  AW = 10,000 x (A/P,10%,3) = 10,000 x 0.40211 = Rs 4,021/yr
Machine Y: first cost Rs 15,000, life 6 yrs
  AW = 15,000 x (A/P,10%,6) = 15,000 x 0.22961 = Rs 3,444/yr
Select Y (lower equivalent annual cost)
LCM check: 6 years, X bought twice, same ranking
Incremental Analysis (IRR and B/C)

Choosing the alternative with the highest individual IRR or B/C can be wrong because a larger project may add more total value at a lower rate. Incremental analysis orders alternatives by first cost, then examines the extra (incremental) cash flow of the costlier one over the cheaper one. If the incremental IRR (ΔIRR) is at least the MARR, or the incremental B/C (ΔB/ΔC) is at least 1, the extra investment is justified and the costlier alternative becomes the defender; otherwise the cheaper one is kept.

MARR 10%, life 5 yrs (P/A,10%,5 = 3.7908)
          First cost  Annual benefit  NPV      IRR
A         10,000      3,000           +1,372   15.2%
B         15,000      4,200             +921   12.4%
B − A      5,000      1,200             −451    6.4%
ΔIRR 6.4% < MARR 10%: extra Rs 5,000 not justified -> choose A
Same answer as choosing the highest NPV
Capitalised Cost and Replacement Analysis

Capitalised cost is the present worth of a project assumed to last forever, such as a dam, canal or permanent road. Because P/A tends to 1/i as n becomes infinite, a perpetual annual cost A has present worth A/i. Replacement analysis compares an existing asset (defender) with a new one (challenger): the defender's first cost is its current market value, sunk costs such as its original price are ignored, and the comparison is usually made on equivalent annual worth.

concepts.plainText: Capitalised cost = initial cost + A / i

formulas.plainText: AW = PW × (A/P, i, n)
Capitalised cost = P0 + A / i
ΔNPV = NPV_B − NPV_A = PW of incremental cash flow (B − A)

notes.text: For unequal lives, annual worth is usually the quickest route in an MCQ: convert each first cost with A/P over its own life, add annual costs, subtract salvage × A/F, and compare.
Never compare present worths of alternatives with different lives directly over their own lives; this favours the shorter-lived option unfairly. Use the LCM or annual worth.
NPV, AW and incremental IRR or incremental B/C always pick the same alternative when applied correctly at the same MARR.

concepts.text: Purpose of Depreciation

Depreciation is the decrease in value of a physical asset with time and use, caused by wear and tear, deterioration, obsolescence or inadequacy. In accounting and taxation it is the systematic allocation of an asset's cost over its useful life. Depreciation is not a cash flow, but it is a tax-deductible expense, so it reduces taxable income and income tax and therefore affects after-tax cash flow.
Key terms used in depreciation calculations:
items: First cost (P): purchase price plus installation and commissioning costs.
Salvage value (S): estimated value at the end of useful life.
Useful life (n): period over which the asset is depreciated.
Book value (BV): first cost minus accumulated depreciation to date.
Market value: the price the asset would actually fetch, which may differ from book value.

concepts.text: Depreciation Methods

rows: d × BV at start of year

concepts.plainText: Straight line: D = (P − S)/n; BV_t = P − tD

concepts.text: In the sinking fund method, depreciation is treated as equal deposits A into a fund earning interest i, so that the fund equals P − S at the end of life. Depreciation in year t is the deposit plus the interest earned on the fund. For P = Rs 50,000, S = 0, n = 4 and i = 10%: A = 50,000 × 0.10/(1.1^4 − 1) = Rs 10,774 in year 1, and Rs 11,851 in year 2. Declining-balance methods never reach zero on their own; DDB is often switched to straight line in later years.
Depreciation under Nepal's Income Tax Act, 2058 (2002)

For tax purposes, Nepal's Income Tax Act, 2058 (2002) groups depreciable assets into pools (blocks) rather than depreciating each asset separately. Depreciation for each pool is computed by the declining-balance (written-down value) method on the pool's depreciation base, which is adjusted for additions and disposals during the year. The rates are prescribed in a schedule to the Act and, like other tax details, are subject to amendment by Finance Acts; the rates shown below are as per the Act's schedule and should be checked against the current law.

rows: Rate (as per Act, subject to amendment)
Buildings, structures and similar works of permanent nature
Computers, data-handling equipment, furniture, office equipment
Construction and earth-moving equipment and other assets not in other pools
Intangible assets (other than those in Pool D)

concepts.text: Taxation System in Nepal and After-Tax Cash Flow
Main taxes relevant to engineering projects in Nepal (rates set by the annual Finance Act, subject to amendment):
items: Income tax: direct tax on income of individuals and entities under the Income Tax Act, 2058 (2002); corporate rates vary by sector.
Value added tax (VAT): indirect tax on the value added at each stage of supply under the Value Added Tax Act, 2052 (1996); the standard rate is 13%, subject to amendment.
Customs duty: levied on imported (and some exported) goods under the Customs Act; significant for imported plant and equipment.
Excise duty: levied on specified goods produced or imported, such as alcohol, tobacco and vehicles.
Other levies include local taxes, registration fees and royalties (e.g. hydropower royalty).

concepts.plainText: After-tax cash flow = BTCF − tax rate × (BTCF − depreciation)

concepts.text: After-tax cash flow (ATCF) is the before-tax cash flow minus income tax, where tax is computed on taxable income = BTCF − depreciation. Example: BTCF Rs 1,00,000, depreciation Rs 20,000, tax rate 25%: taxable income 80,000, tax 20,000, ATCF 80,000. The tax saving from depreciation (t × D = Rs 5,000 here) is called the depreciation tax shield, and it is why faster depreciation improves a project's after-tax present worth.

formulas.plainText: D = (P − S) / n

formulas.latex: D_t = d \cdot BV_{t-1}, \qquad BV_t = P(1 - d)^{t}
formulas.plainText: Declining balance: D_t = d × BV_(t−1); BV_t = P(1 − d)^t
ATCF = BTCF − t(BTCF − D)

notes.text: For DDB questions the salvage value is not subtracted before applying the rate: D_t = (2/n) × book value at the start of year t, starting from the full first cost.

Tax rates, pool rates and thresholds in Nepal are revised through annual Finance Acts and amendments; quote them as 'as per the Act, subject to amendment' and rely on concepts (pooling, declining balance, tax types) in answers.
Depreciation itself is not a cash outflow; it matters in economic analysis only because it lowers taxable income and hence the tax paid.

concepts.text: Bar (Gantt) Charts and Milestone Charts

A bar chart, developed by Henry Gantt, lists activities on the vertical axis and shows each as a horizontal bar against a time scale; the bar length equals the activity duration. It is simple, easy to read and good for showing planned versus actual progress to site staff and clients. A milestone chart is a variation that marks key events (milestones), such as completion of foundation or commissioning, which have zero duration.
Limitations of bar charts that led to network methods:
items: Interdependencies between activities are not shown, so the effect of one delay on others cannot be seen.
The critical activities and the float of non-critical activities cannot be identified.
Not suitable for large, complex projects with hundreds of activities.
Uncertainty in durations cannot be represented, and updating after changes is laborious.

concepts.text: Network Diagrams: AOA and AON

A dummy activity in an AOA network is shown by a dashed arrow; it consumes no time and no resources. It is used to show a logical dependency that cannot otherwise be drawn and to give two parallel activities between the same events unique i-j numbers. Fulkerson's rule numbers the events: number the start event 1, delete its outgoing arrows, number the new initial events next, and repeat, so every arrow goes from a lower to a higher number.
Forward and Backward Pass

The forward pass starts at time 0 and computes the earliest start (ES) and earliest finish (EF) of each activity; where several activities merge, ES is the maximum of the predecessors' EF. The backward pass starts from the project duration at the end and computes latest finish (LF) and latest start (LS); where activities burst, LF is the minimum of the successors' LS.

concepts.latex: EF = ES + t,\quad LS = LF - t,\quad TF = LS - ES = LF - EF
concepts.plainText: EF = ES + t; LS = LF − t; Total float TF = LS − ES = LF − EF

concepts.text: Types of float (slack) of an activity i-j:
items: Total float: time an activity can be delayed without delaying the project; TF = LS − ES.
Free float: delay possible without delaying the earliest start of any successor; FF = ES(successor) − EF.
Independent float: delay possible without affecting predecessors or successors even when predecessors finish late and successors start early; IF = ES(j) − LF(i) − t, taken as zero if negative.
Always IF ≤ FF ≤ TF. Critical activities have zero total float.

concepts.text: Worked Network Example

Act  Pred  t | ES  EF | LS  LF | TF  FF
A    -     3 |  0   3 |  0   3 |  0   0
B    -     4 |  0   4 |  1   5 |  1   1
C    A     2 |  3   5 |  3   5 |  0   0
D    A     4 |  3   7 |  4   8 |  1   1
E    B,C   3 |  5   8 |  5   8 |  0   0
F    D,E   4 |  8  12 |  8  12 |  0   0
Project duration = 12; critical path A-C-E-F (3+2+3+4)

In the example, E cannot start until both B (EF 4) and C (EF 5) finish, so ES(E) = 5. Paths are A-D-F = 11, A-C-E-F = 12 and B-E-F = 11, so the longest path, and hence the critical path, is A-C-E-F with duration 12. B and D each have 1 day of total float.
Crashing and Time-Cost Trade-off

Crashing shortens the project by spending extra money (overtime, more crews, better equipment) on selected activities. Direct cost rises as duration is reduced, while indirect cost (overheads, supervision) falls; the optimum duration gives minimum total cost. Crash only critical activities, starting with the one having the lowest cost slope, and recheck the network after each step because new critical paths may appear.

concepts.plainText: Cost slope = (Crash cost − Normal cost) / (Normal time − Crash time)

formulas.latex: EF = ES + t,\quad LS = LF - t
formulas.plainText: EF = ES + t; LS = LF − t

formulas.latex: TF = LS - ES = LF - EF,\quad FF = ES_{succ} - EF
formulas.plainText: TF = LS − ES = LF − EF; FF = ES(successor) − EF
Cost slope = (Crash cost − Normal cost) / (Normal time − Crash time)

notes.text: The critical path is the longest path through the network; it fixes the shortest possible project duration. List all paths and add durations to check your forward pass.
At a merge take the MAXIMUM EF for ES in the forward pass; at a burst take the MINIMUM LS for LF in the backward pass. Mixing these up is the most common error.
Crashing a non-critical activity only adds cost without shortening the project. Crash the critical activity with the lowest cost slope first.

concepts.text: Why PERT

PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) was developed in 1958 for the US Navy's Polaris missile programme, where many activities were new and their durations uncertain. Instead of a single duration, each activity is given three time estimates, and the method yields both the expected project duration and the probability of finishing by a given date. It is event-oriented and probabilistic, whereas CPM is activity-oriented and deterministic.
The three time estimates for each activity:
items: Optimistic time (a or t_o): shortest time if everything goes exceptionally well.
Most likely time (m or t_m): the time needed under normal conditions; the mode of the distribution.
Pessimistic time (b or t_p): longest time if things go badly, excluding major catastrophes.

concepts.text: Beta Distribution, Expected Time and Variance

Activity duration is assumed to follow a beta distribution, which is bounded between a and b and can be skewed either way. From this assumption the expected (mean) time is a weighted average giving the most likely time four times the weight of the extremes, and the standard deviation is one-sixth of the range.

concepts.plainText: σ = (b − a)/6; variance σ² = ((b − a)/6)²

concepts.text: Path Variance and Probability of Completion

The expected project duration T_e is the sum of t_e along the critical path. By the central limit theorem, the project duration is taken as normally distributed, with variance equal to the SUM of the variances of the critical activities. Standard deviations are not added directly; take the square root of the summed variance.

concepts.plainText: σ_path = √(Σ σ_i²); Z = (T_s − T_e) / σ_path

concepts.text:
Critical path: A then B
Act   a   m   b |  t_e  sigma  variance
A     4  10  28 |  12     4      16
B     5  11  23 |  12     3       9
T_e = 12 + 12 = 24 weeks; variance = 25; sigma_path = 5
P(finish within T_s = 29 weeks):
Z = (29 - 24)/5 = 1.0 -> P = 0.8413 = 84.1%
P(finish within 24 weeks): Z = 0 -> 50%
Useful standard normal values (area to the left of Z):
items: Z = 0 gives 50%: a schedule equal to the expected time has only an even chance.
Z = 1.0 gives about 84.1%; Z = 1.5 about 93.3%; Z = 2.0 about 97.7%; Z = 3.0 about 99.9%.
Negative Z gives probabilities below 50%, e.g. Z = −1.0 gives about 15.9%.

concepts.text: CPM versus PERT

rows: Repetitive work with known durations, e.g. construction
New, R&D-type projects with uncertain durations

formulas.plainText: Z = (T_s − T_e) / √(Σ σ_i²)

notes.text: Add VARIANCES along the critical path, not standard deviations. Two activities with σ = 3 and σ = 4 give σ_path = 5, not 7.
If the scheduled time equals the expected time, the probability of completion is exactly 50 percent; it is a quick check on any PERT answer.
Individual activity times follow a beta distribution, but the project duration (sum of many activities) is treated as normal by the central limit theorem.

concepts.text: Resources in Scheduling

A CPM or PERT schedule assumes unlimited resources, but labour, equipment, materials and money are always limited in practice. If every activity starts at its earliest start, demand for a resource usually shows sharp peaks and valleys, causing idle crews on some days and shortages on others. Resource management adjusts the timing of activities so that demand is practical and economical.
Key terms:
items: Resource loading (aggregation): adding up, period by period, the resource requirement of all activities in a given schedule.
Resource histogram: bar chart of resource units required against time; the ideal shape is roughly rectangular (uniform).
Resource allocation: assigning available resources to activities, deciding priorities when demand exceeds supply.
Resource-days (man-days): resource units × duration; the total area under the histogram.

concepts.plainText: Average resource demand = Σ(resource rate × duration) / project duration T

concepts.text: Levelling versus Smoothing

rows: Any activity, including critical ones if needed
Reduce peaks and valleys in demand
Keep demand within the available limit

concepts.text: Terminology differs between books: some Indian texts use 'levelling' for the time-constrained case, while PMBOK uses levelling for the resource-constrained case in which the finish date may slip and smoothing when it may not. MCQs often turn on the key difference: smoothing never changes the project end date, whereas levelling can.
Using Float to Smooth Demand

Project duration 6 days (A is critical); B, C, D independent
Act  Dur  Workers  ES  TF
A     6     3       0   0
B     2     3       0   4
C     2     3       0   4
D     2     3       0   4
Early start:  days 1-2 = 3+3+3+3 = 12, days 3-6 = 3  (peak 12)
Shift C to days 3-4 and D to days 5-6 (within float)
Smoothed:     every day = 6 workers  (peak 6, duration still 6)

Total demand is 3×6 + 3×(3×2) = 36 worker-days in both schedules, so the average is 36/6 = 6 workers. Shifting non-critical activities within their float moved the peak from 12 down to the average without changing the finish date. The area under the histogram is unchanged by smoothing; only its shape changes.
Heuristics and Priority Rules
Practical rules used in levelling and allocation (e.g. Burgess method, serial scheduling):
items: Schedule critical activities first; move activities with the largest float before those with little float.
When resources conflict, give priority to the activity with the least total float or the earliest late start.
Burgess method: try alternative start times and choose the schedule with the minimum sum of squares of daily resource demand.
Recompute floats after each shift, because moving one activity can use up float of its successors.

concepts.plainText: Burgess method: minimise the sum over days of (daily resource demand)²

formulas.plainText: Average resource demand = Σ(r_i × t_i) / T
Burgess method: minimise Σ R_d²

notes.text: Smoothing = project end date fixed, move only within float. Levelling = resource limit fixed, project may take longer.
Shifting activities never changes the total resource-days (area of the histogram); it only redistributes demand over time.
Moving a non-critical activity beyond its total float delays the whole project; moving it beyond its free float delays its successors.

concepts.text: Monitoring, Evaluation and Control

Monitoring is the continuous, routine collection and analysis of information on progress, cost and quality during implementation, comparing actual performance with the plan. Evaluation is a periodic, systematic assessment of a project's relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability. Control is the action taken when monitoring shows a deviation: correcting the work, revising the plan or changing resources.

rows: Are we doing things right, as planned?
Are we doing the right things; did it work?

concepts.text: Types of evaluation by timing and purpose:
items: Ex-ante (appraisal): before implementation, to judge feasibility.
Formative (on-going or mid-term): during implementation, to improve the project while it runs.
Summative (terminal): at completion, to judge overall achievement of objectives.
Ex-post (impact): some years after completion, to assess long-term impact and sustainability.

concepts.text: The Control Cycle and Progress Reporting

Control cycle
1. Set the baseline (scope, schedule, budget, quality standards)
2. Measure actual performance (site records, timesheets, invoices)
3. Compare actual with planned; compute variances
4. Analyse causes of deviation and forecast the outcome
5. Take corrective action; update the plan
6. Report and repeat each reporting period

Progress is reported through periodic reports, updated bar charts and networks, milestone reports and cost reports. An S-curve plots cumulative cost or work against time; it is S-shaped because progress is slow at the start, fast in the middle and slow again near completion. Plotting the actual and earned curves against the planned S-curve shows at a glance whether the project is ahead or behind and over or under budget.
Earned Value Management
Earned value management (EVM) integrates scope, schedule and cost using three values at the status date:
items: Planned Value (PV, or BCWS): budgeted cost of the work scheduled to date.
Earned Value (EV, or BCWP): budgeted cost of the work actually performed; EV = percent complete × BAC.
Actual Cost (AC, or ACWP): actual cost incurred for the work performed.
Budget at Completion (BAC): the total approved budget.

concepts.latex: CV = EV - AC,\quad SV = EV - PV
concepts.plainText: Cost variance CV = EV − AC; Schedule variance SV = EV − PV
CPI = EV/AC; SPI = EV/PV; EAC = BAC/CPI

concepts.text:
BAC = Rs 100 lakh; at month 5: PV = 50, EV = 40, AC = 45 (Rs lakh)
CV  = 40 - 45 = -5    (over budget)
SV  = 40 - 50 = -10   (behind schedule)
CPI = 40/45 = 0.889   SPI = 40/50 = 0.80
EAC = 100/0.889 = 112.5 lakh
ETC = EAC - AC = 112.5 - 45 = 67.5 lakh
VAC = BAC - EAC = 100 - 112.5 = -12.5 lakh

Negative variances and indices below 1 are unfavourable: CPI < 1 means over budget and SPI < 1 means behind schedule. EAC = BAC/CPI assumes the current cost efficiency continues to completion; other forecasts exist, such as EAC = AC + (BAC − EV) when the overrun is expected to be a one-off.
Logical Framework (Logframe)

The logical framework is a 4 × 4 matrix widely used by governments and donors for planning, monitoring and evaluation. Its rows form the vertical logic from goal to purpose (outcome) to outputs to activities (with inputs). Its columns are the narrative summary, objectively verifiable indicators (OVIs), means of verification (MOVs) and important assumptions or risks.

formulas.latex: CV = EV - AC,\quad SV = EV - PV
formulas.plainText: CV = EV − AC; SV = EV − PV
CPI = EV/AC; SPI = EV/PV

formulas.latex: EAC = \dfrac{BAC}{CPI},\quad ETC = EAC - AC,\quad VAC = BAC - EAC
formulas.plainText: EAC = BAC/CPI; ETC = EAC − AC; VAC = BAC − EAC

notes.text: Every EVM formula starts with EV: CV = EV − AC, SV = EV − PV, CPI = EV/AC, SPI = EV/PV. Negative or below 1 means bad news.
Comparing actual cost with planned value alone (AC vs PV) is misleading; without EV you cannot tell whether spending reflects progress or overrun.
Monitoring is continuous and internal; evaluation is periodic and often independent. Formative evaluation improves a running project, summative judges it at the end.

concepts.text: Risk, Uncertainty and the Risk Process

A project risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on one or more project objectives such as scope, time, cost or quality. Negative risks are threats and positive risks are opportunities. In the classical distinction, risk is a situation where the possible outcomes and their probabilities can be known or estimated, while uncertainty is a situation where the probabilities cannot be assigned. Risk management aims to increase the probability and impact of opportunities and reduce those of threats.
The risk management process (following PMBOK):
items: Plan risk management: decide approach, roles, budget, categories and the probability and impact scales.
Identify risks: list risks and their causes and effects in a risk register.
Perform qualitative analysis: rank risks by probability and impact.
Perform quantitative analysis: numerically estimate the combined effect on cost and schedule.
Plan and implement responses, then monitor risks throughout the project.

concepts.text: Risk identification techniques:
items: Brainstorming and expert interviews with the project team and specialists.
Delphi technique: anonymous rounds of expert opinion until the views converge.
Checklists and historical records from similar past projects.
SWOT analysis, assumption and constraint analysis, and root-cause (cause-and-effect) diagrams.
Site investigation and document review of drawings, specifications and contracts.

concepts.text: Qualitative Analysis

Qualitative analysis prioritises risks quickly using ratings of probability and impact, often on a 1-5 scale or as very low to very high. Multiplying the two ratings gives a risk score, and the probability-impact matrix places each risk in a red (high), amber (medium) or green (low) zone. High-priority risks go forward to quantitative analysis and response planning, while low risks are placed on a watch list.
Quantitative Analysis

concepts.latex: EMV = \sum_{i} p_i \times V_i \quad (\text{threats negative, opportunities positive})
concepts.plainText: EMV = sum of (probability x value) over all outcomes

concepts.text: Quantitative techniques:
items: Expected monetary value (EMV): probability-weighted average of outcomes; the sum of threat EMVs is a basis for the contingency reserve.
Decision tree analysis: decision nodes (squares) and chance nodes (circles); EMV is computed from right to left (rolling back) and the branch with the best EMV is chosen.
Sensitivity analysis: vary one uncertain input at a time to see which has most effect on the outcome, displayed as a tornado diagram.
Monte Carlo simulation: sample activity durations or costs from their probability distributions thousands of times to obtain the probability distribution of total cost or completion date.

concepts.text:
Decision: bid for a hydropower tunnel contract (Rs lakh)
Option A - bid high-risk tunnel job
  Good geology  p = 0.6  profit  +50  -> 0.6 x 50  = +30
  Poor geology  p = 0.4  loss    -20  -> 0.4 x -20 = -8
  EMV(A) = 30 - 8 = +22
Option B - bid small road job, certain profit +20 -> EMV(B) = +20
Decision: choose A (EMV 22 > 20), a risk-neutral choice
Risk Responses, Register and Monitoring

rows: Change the plan to eliminate the threat
Exploit: make sure the opportunity happens
Shift impact to a third party (insurance, contract clause)
Share: give part to a partner best able to capture it
Acknowledge; keep contingency or do nothing
Accept: take it if it occurs
Refer to a higher authority outside the project

concepts.text: The risk register is the central document of risk management. For each risk it records an ID, description, cause, category, probability, impact, score, owner, response strategy, trigger conditions and current status. Risk monitoring tracks identified risks, watches triggers, identifies new and secondary risks, checks residual risk after responses and uses risk audits and reserve analysis to see whether the remaining contingency is adequate.

formulas.plainText: Risk exposure = probability x impact
EMV = sum of (probability x value)
Contingency reserve = sum of probability x impact over identified threats

notes.text: Insurance, performance bonds and fixed-price subcontracts are TRANSFER. Redesigning to remove the hazard is AVOID. Extra site investigation or a stronger design is MITIGATE. Keeping a contingency reserve is ACCEPT (active acceptance).
In decision trees, subtract losses and costs: a threat's value is negative. Roll back from the right, compute EMV at each chance node, then pick the best branch at each decision node.

Qualitative analysis (probability-impact matrix) ranks risks; quantitative analysis (EMV, decision trees, sensitivity, Monte Carlo) puts numbers on their combined effect. Quantitative work is usually done only for the high-priority risks.

concepts.text: Sources of Project Finance

Project financing is the arrangement of funds needed to plan, build and start operating a project. Funds come from owners (equity) or lenders (debt), supplemented by grants, bonds and other instruments. The mix chosen affects the cost of capital, the risk borne by each party and the financial viability of the project.

rows: No fixed return; dividends paid from profit; highest risk and highest expected return
Fixed interest and repayment schedule; interest is tax-deductible; lenders have priority claim
Raise large sums from many investors at a fixed coupon
From government or development partners, usually tied to conditions
Profits ploughed back; no issue cost

concepts.text: Internal vs external sources:
items: Internal: retained earnings, depreciation provisions and sale of surplus assets; cheap and without loss of control, but limited in amount.
External: new share issues, bank loans, debentures and bonds, supplier credit, leasing, grants and soft loans; larger in amount but involve issue costs, interest or dilution of control.

concepts.text: Project Finance vs Corporate Finance

rows: A special purpose vehicle (SPV) created for the project
Whole balance sheet of the company
Cash flows of the project alone

concepts.text: Private Participation Models
Common concession and partnership models:
items: BOT (Build-Operate-Transfer): private party builds and operates the facility for a concession period, recovering its investment from user charges or tariffs, then transfers it to the government.
BOOT (Build-Own-Operate-Transfer): as BOT but the private party also legally owns the facility during the concession, then transfers it.
BOO (Build-Own-Operate): private party builds, owns and operates permanently; no transfer to the government.
BOLT/BLT (Build-Lease-Transfer) and DBFO (Design-Build-Finance-Operate) are further variants.
PPP (Public-Private Partnership): the umbrella term for long-term contracts in which risks, responsibilities and rewards are shared between government and a private partner.

concepts.text: Capital Structure and Cost of Capital

The debt-equity ratio D/E measures financial leverage. Higher debt raises returns to equity when the project performs well because debt is usually cheaper and its interest is tax-deductible, but it also raises the fixed repayment burden and the risk of default. Lenders therefore require a minimum equity contribution. The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is the average rate the project must pay its financiers and is commonly used as the discount rate or MARR for appraisal.

concepts.latex: WACC = \frac{E}{V} R_e + \frac{D}{V} R_d (1 - T),\quad V = D + E
concepts.plainText: WACC = (E/V) Re + (D/V) Rd (1 - T), V = D + E

concepts.text:
Worked example (Rs crore)
Equity E = 40, cost of equity Re = 15%
Debt   D = 60, interest   Rd = 10%, tax rate T = 25%
V = 100 ; D/E = 60/40 = 1.5 (60:40)
After-tax cost of debt = 10% x (1 - 0.25) = 7.5%
WACC = 0.40 x 15% + 0.60 x 7.5% = 6.0% + 4.5% = 10.5%

In Nepal, public projects are financed mainly through the government budget (revenue and domestic borrowing), together with grants and concessional loans from development partners such as multilateral development banks and bilateral donors. Private participation is encouraged through PPP and concession arrangements under the Public-Private Partnership and Investment Act, 2075 (2019), and many hydropower projects are developed by private promoters under BOOT-type licences with power purchase agreements with the Nepal Electricity Authority. Details and limits are set by the prevailing laws and policies, subject to amendment.

formulas.plainText: WACC = (E/V) Re + (D/V) Rd (1 - T)
Debt-equity ratio = D / E
After-tax cost of debt = Rd (1 - T)
