concepts.text: Going Deeper: Serial Timing, 8251A Programming and On-board Buses

Why the 16x clock? The receiver's clock is not locked to the transmitter, so it must find the middle of every bit on its own. When it sees the 1-to-0 edge of the start bit it counts 8 clock pulses, checks that the line is still 0 (a short noise spike would have gone back to 1), and then samples every 16 pulses, which lands close to the centre of each following bit. The two clocks may differ slightly, and the error grows bit by bit until the next start bit resets it, so the last sample (the stop bit) must still fall inside its bit cell.

concepts.plainText: Maximum total clock mismatch = 0.5 bit / (frame bits - 0.5); for a 10-bit frame 0.5/9.5 = about 5.3 %, shared between both ends

concepts.text:

41H = 0100 0001 -> number of 1s = 2 -> even parity bit P = 0
Data sent LSB first: D0..D7 = 1 0 0 0 0 0 1 0
Line: idle 1 | start 0 | 1 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 | P 0 | stop 1 | idle 1
Frame length = 1 + 8 + 1 + 1 = 11 bits
At 9600 baud: frame time = 11 / 9600 = 1.146 ms

D3 D2 = 10 (7 bits)   D1 D0 = 11 (64x)
Mode word = 1111 1011 = FBH   (write to C/D = 1 first)
Command   = 0011 0111 = 37H   (TxEN, DTR, RxE, ER, RTS)
For 1200 baud: TxC = RxC = 64 x 1200 = 76.8 kHz
Frame = 1 + 7 + 1 + 2 = 11 bits -> 1200 / 11 = 109 characters/s

concepts.text: SPI is really two shift registers joined in a ring: on each SCLK edge the master shifts one bit out on MOSI while the slave shifts one bit out on MISO, so after eight clocks the two have swapped bytes. Clock polarity and phase (CPOL, CPHA) give four modes that master and slave must agree on. I²C instead shares two open-drain lines: the master sends START (SDA falls while SCL is high), an address byte made of the 7-bit address and a R/W bit (1 = read), and the addressed device pulls SDA low in the ninth clock as ACK. USB, by contrast, is host-polled: the host schedules every transfer, devices get a 7-bit address at enumeration, and data is NRZI coded with a 0 stuffed after six 1s.
Serial I/O on the 8085 through SID and SOD (no UART hardware):
items: SIM: accumulator D7 = SOD data, D6 = SDE (must be 1 for D7 to reach the pin); keep D3 (MSE) = 0 to leave interrupt masks unchanged.
RIM: the level on the SID pin is copied into accumulator bit D7; RAL or ANI 80H then isolates it.
A = C0H then SIM drives SOD high; A = 40H then SIM drives it low.
Each bit is held for one bit time by a delay loop: at 3 MHz and 1200 baud that is 833.3 µs, or 2500 T-states including the loop overhead.
The software must send the start bit, 8 data bits LSB first and the stop bit itself, so the CPU is busy for the whole character.

Common slips: counting a frame as 8 bits instead of start + data + parity + stop; sending or reading data MSB first; computing parity over the whole frame instead of the data bits only; forgetting the 16x or 64x factor when converting TxC to baud; treating baud and bit rate as equal for multi-level signals; and forgetting the R/W bit when forming an I²C address byte.

For any serial timing question write the frame first (e.g. 8E1 = 11 bits), then use characters/s = baud / frame bits and time = characters x frame bits / baud. For the 8251A, build the mode word right to left: factor (D1D0), length (D3D2), parity enable (D4), even/odd (D5), stop bits (D7D6).

Characters per second = baud / frame bits = 9600 / 10 = 960
Bit rate = baud x log2(M), M = number of signal levels; binary M = 2 -> bit rate = baud
Efficiency = data bits / frame bits x 100 %; 8N1 -> 8/10 = 80 %

notes.text: Throughput questions: count the frame first. 8N1 = 10 bits, 7E1 = 10 bits, 8E1 = 11 bits, 7E2 = 11 bits, then divide the baud rate by that count to get characters per second. Do not divide by 8.

RS-232 levels are inverted and bipolar: logic 1 (mark, idle) is -3 to -15 V and logic 0 (space, start bit) is +3 to +15 V. Do not confuse them with TTL levels, and remember baud rate equals bit rate only for two-level signalling.

Distance and noise immunity come from differential signalling: RS-422 and RS-485 send each bit as the difference between two wires, so common-mode noise cancels and 1200 m is reachable, while single-ended RS-232 is limited to about 15 m. RS-485 adds tri-state drivers so many nodes can share one pair (multidrop).

concepts.text: Why DMA?

In programmed I/O the CPU moves every byte itself (IN, then MOV or STA, then a loop test) and polls a status flag while waiting, so a fast device can consume the whole processor. Interrupt-driven I/O frees the CPU while it waits, but each byte still costs an interrupt response, register saving, the service routine and a return, typically tens of clock cycles per byte. For high-speed block devices (disk, network, video, ADC sample streams) the CPU itself becomes the bottleneck. Direct Memory Access (DMA) solves this by letting a dedicated DMA controller (DMAC) transfer data directly between an I/O device and memory over the system buses, with the CPU involved only at the start and end of a block.
DMA Transfer Sequence
A block transfer proceeds in these steps:
items: 1. The CPU programs the DMAC: starting memory address, byte count, direction (read or write), transfer mode, and enables the channel.
2. The peripheral asserts DREQ (DMA request) to its channel when it has data or space.
3. The DMAC asserts HOLD (HRQ) to the CPU to request the buses.
4. The CPU completes the current machine cycle, floats (tri-states) its address, data and control buses, and replies with HLDA (hold acknowledge).

5. The DMAC now drives the buses: it asserts DACK to the device, places the address, generates IOR + MEMW (device to memory) or MEMR + IOW (memory to device), increments the address register and decrements the count register for each byte.
6. When the count reaches terminal count (TC) the DMAC asserts EOP, drops HOLD, and the CPU regains the buses; the DMAC may raise an interrupt so software knows the block is complete.

concepts.text: On the 8085 the HOLD input and HLDA output pins implement this handshake directly. The 8086 has the same HOLD/HLDA pair in minimum mode, while in maximum mode the bus is requested through the bidirectional RQ/GT lines. The essential contrast with interrupts: an interrupt (INTR to INTA) makes the CPU run a service routine, whereas a DMA request (HOLD to HLDA) makes the CPU give up the buses and stay idle or run from its prefetch queue.
DMA Transfer Modes

rows: The whole block moves in one hold period
CPU stalled for the entire block; fastest for the device
One byte or word per HOLD, then the bus is returned and requested again
CPU slowed slightly; program progress interleaved
Transfers only in bus cycles the CPU is not using
No slowdown at all; slowest for the device; complex hardware
Where the CPU must never be stalled
Transfers continue while DREQ stays active, pause when it drops
CPU stalled only while the device keeps up

concepts.text: The Intel 8237 DMA Controller
Key features of the 8237A:
items: Four independent channels (DREQ0 to DREQ3, DACK0 to DACK3), expandable by cascading a second 8237 through one channel of the master.

Each channel has a 16-bit address register and a 16-bit word count register, so one transfer can cover up to 64 KB; a page register outside the chip supplies the upper address bits (A16 to A19) on 8086 systems.
Priority between channels is fixed (channel 0 highest, 3 lowest) or rotating, chosen in the command register.
Supports single, block and demand transfer modes plus cascade mode, in read (memory to I/O), write (I/O to memory) and verify operations, and memory-to-memory transfer using channels 0 and 1.
Auto-initialise reloads the base address and count after terminal count so a channel can repeat without CPU help; EOP signals terminal count or can be driven externally to abort.
Operates at 5 MHz in the 8237A-5 version, moving up to about 1.6 MB/s; the CPU programs it through 16 addressable registers selected by A0 to A3 while it is a bus slave.

Number of transfers minus one; terminal count when it passes through zero

concepts.text: Tri-stated Buses and Bus Mastership

A bus can have only one driver at a time. When the CPU acknowledges HOLD it puts its address lines, data lines and the control outputs (RD, WR, IO/M, ALE on the 8085) into the high-impedance (tri-state) condition, so they neither drive 0 nor 1 and the DMAC can take over as bus master. External address latches and bus buffers are also disabled during HLDA. Once the DMAC drops HOLD, the CPU re-enables its drivers and continues the instruction stream exactly where it left off, because no registers were altered; DMA is invisible to the running program apart from the lost bus time.
Comparison of I/O Techniques

Not involved; DREQ goes to the DMAC

concepts.text: Throughput Example

Suppose a 4 KB (4096-byte) block is to be moved from a disk controller into memory. With interrupt-driven I/O, if each byte costs about 20 us of CPU time (interrupt latency, register saving, the service routine and the return), the block occupies the CPU for 4096 x 20 us = 82 ms. With DMA in burst mode at one bus cycle of 500 ns per byte, the whole block takes 4096 x 0.5 us = 2.05 ms of bus time and no instruction execution at all; the CPU only sets up the channel (a few microseconds) and handles one completion interrupt. The DMA path is about 40 times faster here, and the ratio grows as the device gets faster.
Going Deeper: DMA Timing and Controller Programming

Bus grant is never instant. The 8085 checks HOLD once per machine cycle and gives up the bus only at the end of the cycle it is running, so the DMA latency is short, of the order of one machine cycle. HOLD is not an interrupt: DI, masks and SIM have no effect on it. After HLDA the CPU runs no bus cycles (the 8085 can only finish an internal operation already under way, and an 8086 can keep executing from its prefetch queue), and when HOLD drops it continues with no registers changed.

concepts.plainText: Fraction of bus time taken by cycle stealing = transfer rate (bytes/s) x time per stolen cycle

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: CPU load for a 20 000 byte/s device
Interrupt I/O, 25 us per byte:
  20 000 x 25 us  = 0.5 s per second  -> 50 % of the CPU
Cycle-stealing DMA, 1 us per stolen cycle:
  20 000 x 1 us   = 0.02 s per second -> 2 % of the bus
At 50 000 byte/s the interrupt method would need
  50 000 x 25 us  = 1.25 s per second -> impossible (> 100 %)
DMA at the same rate needs only 5 % of the bus.

; Worked example 2: 8237 at I/O 00H-0FH, channel 1
; 1000 bytes, I/O -> memory, from 2000H, single mode
      MVI A,00H
      OUT 0CH       ; clear byte pointer flip-flop
      OUT 02H       ; address low  = 00H
      MVI A,20H
      OUT 02H       ; address high = 20H
      MVI A,0E7H
      OUT 03H       ; count low  (999 = 03E7H)
      MVI A,03H
      OUT 03H       ; count high
      MVI A,45H
      OUT 0BH       ; mode: 01 0 0 01 01 = single, write, ch 1
      MVI A,01H
      OUT 0AH       ; clear mask bit of channel 1

Reading the example: the 16-bit registers are written through one 8-bit port, low byte first, and an internal flip-flop chooses the byte, which is why it is cleared first. The count is 1000 - 1 = 999 because terminal count occurs as the count passes from 0000H to FFFFH. The mode byte 45H is built as D7D6 = 01 (single), D5 = 0 (increment), D4 = 0 (no auto-init), D3D2 = 01 (write: I/O to memory) and D1D0 = 01 (channel 1). The block ends at 2000H + 999 = 23E7H.

concepts.text: Addresses above 64 KB. The 8237 produces only A0-A15, so on an 8086 system an external page register supplies A16-A19 for each channel. The page register does not change during a transfer: if a buffer starts at 2FF00H and is 512 bytes long, the 8237 address wraps from FFFFH to 0000H after 256 bytes and the remaining data goes to 20000H, not 30000H. Drivers therefore place DMA buffers so they never cross a 64 KB boundary.
Common mistakes in DMA questions:
items: Loading the count register with N instead of N - 1 (both 8237 and 8257).
Mixing up the direction: a DMA read is memory to I/O (MEMR + IOW), a DMA write is I/O to memory (IOR + MEMW).
Confusing HLDA (CPU to DMAC) with DACK (DMAC to device).
Assuming the CPU saves registers or runs a routine during DMA; it only floats its buses.
Counting one bus cycle per byte for memory-to-memory copies; each byte needs a read and a write.

concepts.text: For DMA calculations, first find the time per byte (clocks per byte x clock period), then multiply by the number of bytes, and add any stated set-up and completion time. For the CPU fraction lost to cycle stealing, multiply the byte rate by the stolen cycle time; for interrupt I/O multiply the byte rate by the ISR time.

formulas.plainText: Burst DMA transfer time = number of bytes N x bus cycle time (4096 x 0.5 us = 2.05 ms)
Interrupt-driven CPU time = N x time per interrupt service (4096 x 20 us = 82 ms)
8237: 16-bit count register -> up to 65536 (64 KB) transfers per channel program
Maximum DMA data rate = 1 / bus cycle time (500 ns -> 2 MB/s)

notes.text: Keep the two handshakes apart: INTR -> INTA is an interrupt (the CPU runs an ISR), HOLD -> HLDA is a DMA bus request (the CPU floats its buses). The DMAC raises HOLD; the CPU answers with HLDA; the device sees DACK.

DMA bypasses the CPU, not the buses. The data still travels over the address and data buses; what changes is that the DMAC, not the CPU, generates the addresses and control signals. Also remember the 8237 word count register is loaded with (count - 1) because terminal count occurs when it decrements past zero.

Cycle stealing is named from the CPU's viewpoint: the DMAC 'steals' single bus cycles between CPU cycles, so a program slows a little but never stops. Burst mode gives the device the highest rate but stalls the CPU for the whole block, and transparent mode never stalls the CPU because it uses only cycles the CPU would have left idle.

concepts.text: Interrupt Processing Sequence in the 8086
When an interrupt of type n is recognised, the 8086 performs these steps in hardware:
items: 1. Complete the instruction currently being executed (an interrupt is never taken in the middle of an instruction, except that string instructions with REP can be interrupted between repetitions).
2. Push the FLAGS register onto the stack (SP = SP − 2).
3. Clear IF and TF so that the ISR starts with INTR masked and single-stepping off.
4. Push CS, then push IP, so the full return address is saved (SP is now 6 lower than before).
5. Read the new IP from memory address 4n and the new CS from address 4n + 2 of the Interrupt Vector Table.
6. Execute the ISR at the new CS:IP.
7. The ISR ends with IRET, which pops IP, CS and FLAGS in that order, restoring IF and TF as they were and resuming the interrupted program.

concepts.text:
For an external INTR request an extra step precedes the sequence: the 8086 checks IF at the end of the instruction and, if it is set, runs two INTA bus cycles to obtain the type number from the interrupting device. For NMI the type is fixed at 2, and for INT n or an internal exception the type is known from the instruction or the condition, so no acknowledge cycle is needed.
The 8085 is simpler: it pushes only the 16-bit program counter, resets the interrupt-enable flip-flop, jumps to the vector address and returns with an ordinary RET. Flags and registers are not saved automatically, so the ISR must PUSH PSW and PUSH the register pairs it uses.
The 8086 Interrupt Vector Table

The Interrupt Vector Table (IVT) occupies the lowest 1 KB of memory, from 00000H to 003FFH. It holds 256 entries, one for each interrupt type 0 to 255, and every entry is a 4-byte far pointer to an ISR: the low word is the offset (IP) and the high word is the segment (CS). Because each entry is 4 bytes, the entry for type n starts at physical address 4 × n.

concepts.plainText: Vector address of type n = 4 × n

concepts.text: Worked example: INT 21H.
items: Type = 21H = 33 decimal, so the entry starts at 4 × 33 = 132 = 00084H.
Memory 00084H and 00085H hold the ISR offset (low byte first); 00086H and 00087H hold the ISR segment.
If the four bytes are 10 00 00 F0 (in address order), the ISR is at CS:IP = F000H:0010H, physical address F0000H + 0010H = F0010H.
Going the other way: a vector found at 00034H belongs to type 34H ÷ 4 = 0DH = 13.

concepts.text: The 8259 Programmable Interrupt Controller
The CPU only ranks its own few inputs; priority among many external devices is decided by the 8259A, a 28-pin controller that funnels their requests into the single INTR pin of the 8085/8086:
items: Eight interrupt request inputs IR0 to IR7, each edge- or level-triggered as programmed. One master with up to eight slaves on its IR inputs (linked by the CAS0-CAS2 cascade lines and the SP/EN pin) handles 64 interrupt sources.

Interrupt Request Register (IRR): one bit per input, set when a request arrives. Interrupt Mask Register (IMR): a 1 bit masks (ignores) the corresponding input. In-Service Register (ISR): the bit of the request currently being serviced, so lower-priority requests are held off until an EOI.
Priority resolver: chooses the highest-priority unmasked request in IRR, sets its ISR bit and raises INT to the CPU.

Type number generation: the upper five bits of the vector type come from ICW2 and the lower three bits are the IR level, so with ICW2 = 08H the inputs IR0-IR7 produce types 08H-0FH (the PC convention: IR0 = timer at type 8, IR1 = keyboard at type 9).

End of Interrupt (EOI): the ISR must tell the 8259 when it is done by writing OCW2 (20H is a non-specific EOI that clears the highest ISR bit); otherwise no equal- or lower-priority interrupt is ever passed on. Automatic EOI mode clears the bit on the second INTA instead.

rows: Edge/level trigger, single or cascade, whether ICW4 follows
Upper 5 bits of the interrupt type (T7-T3) for 8086 mode
Master: which IR lines have slaves; slave: its ID 0-7
8086/8085 mode, auto EOI, buffered mode, special fully nested mode
Read IRR or ISR, poll mode, special mask mode

concepts.text: 8259 with the 8086, the INTA handshake step by step:
items: A device pulls an IR input; the 8259 sets the IRR bit, resolves priority against the ISR and IMR, and asserts INT (wired to INTR of the 8086).

If IF = 1 the 8086 finishes the current instruction and issues the first INTA pulse: the 8259 freezes the request, sets the ISR bit for the winning input and clears its IRR bit. Nothing is placed on the bus yet.

On the second INTA pulse the 8259 drives the 8-bit type number onto D0-D7 (AD0-AD7). The 8086 multiplies it by 4, reads the vector and enters the ISR. In cascade mode the master uses CAS0-CAS2 to tell the responsible slave to supply the type.
The ISR services the device and writes an EOI to the 8259 before IRET, clearing the ISR bit so that equal- and lower-priority requests can be recognised again.

concepts.text: Interrupt priority schemes: several general techniques decide which of several simultaneous requests is served first.
items: Fixed priority: each line has a permanent rank (the 8259 default, called fully nested mode, gives IR0 the highest and IR7 the lowest priority). Simple, but a busy high-priority device can starve the others.
Rotating priority: after an input is served it becomes the lowest priority, so every device gets a fair turn (8259 automatic or specific rotation set through OCW2).

Polled (software) priority: on a single interrupt the CPU reads the status of each device in a fixed order; the order of polling is the priority. Cheap in hardware, slow in response. The 8259 supports a poll mode through OCW3 in which the CPU reads the highest pending request instead of using INTA.

Daisy chain (hardware): the INTA signal passes from device to device along a chain; the first device with a pending request blocks the acknowledge from travelling further and puts its vector on the bus, so the device closest to the CPU has the highest priority.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: IVT Arithmetic and Programming the 8259

Multiplying the type by 4 is the same as shifting it left two places, so the 8086 can form the IVT address with no arithmetic unit at all: type 60H (0110 0000) becomes 01 1000 0000 = 180H. Going backwards, the low two bits of any IVT entry address are always 00, so an address like 00086H is not the start of an entry but the third byte (address 4n + 2, the low byte of CS) of the type 21H entry. Remember that each entry is itself a far pointer, so after reading it the CPU still has to form CS × 16 + IP to reach the routine.

concepts.text: Rotation keeps a busy device from starving the others. In automatic rotation, the level that has just been served becomes the lowest, so after IR3 the order is IR4, IR5, IR6, IR7, IR0, IR1, IR2, IR3. The set-priority command does the same job on demand: it names the level that must become lowest, and the one after it becomes highest. Both are OCW2 commands and can be issued at any time after initialisation.
Common mistakes in IVT and 8259 questions:
items: Writing 4 × type in decimal and reading the result as hex: 4 × 08H is 32 = 20H, not 32H.
Swapping the halves of an IVT entry: the offset (IP) is at 4n, the segment (CS) at 4n + 2.
Using the bit-mask form for a slave ICW3: the master gets one bit per slave, a slave gets its 3-bit ID.
Reading 1 in the IMR as enabled: a 1 in OCW1 masks that input.
Counting 8 inputs per chip in a cascade: each slave uses up one master input, so the total is 8 + 7s.
Forgetting D4 = 1 in ICW1 or D3 = 1 in OCW3, which turns the byte into a different command.

concepts.text: ICW2 is not an address. It gives the upper five bits of the type number; the 8086 then multiplies the type by 4 to find the IVT entry. With ICW2 = 08H, IR1 is type 09H and its vector is at 00024H, not at 00009H or 00008H.

formulas.plainText: Vector address = 4 × type n
IP is read from address 4n, CS from address 4n + 2
Type = vector address ÷ 4
FLAGS + CS + IP = 6 bytes pushed per 8086 interrupt
Max IR lines = 8 × 8 = 64 with one master and eight slave 8259s
Type = ICW2 base (multiple of 8) + IR level

notes.text: Address questions are pure arithmetic: multiply the type by 4 (or shift left two bits). INT 21H → 21H × 4 = 84H, INT 10H → 40H, INT 80H → 200H. Given an address, divide by 4 to recover the type.

Order matters: the 8086 pushes FLAGS first, then CS, then IP; IRET pops IP, CS, FLAGS. In the IVT the low word (offset/IP) comes first and the high word (segment/CS) second, exactly like any far pointer.

IRR, ISR and IMR are the three 8259 registers MCQs confuse. IRR = requests waiting, ISR = request being served, IMR = requests deliberately ignored. IRR and ISR are read via OCW3; IMR is written via OCW1.
An 8259 ISR that forgets to send EOI still returns normally, but the ISR bit stays set and the controller will never again pass a request of that or lower priority to the CPU.

Hexadecimal traps: segment × 10H means shift left by one hex digit, not multiply by ten; a 20-bit physical address has five hex digits; INT 21H is type 33 decimal, so its vector is at 4 × 33 = 132 = 00084H.

Pairs that get swapped: NAND/NOR are universal (AND/OR are not); ring counter n states, Johnson 2n; TRAP is non-maskable in the 8085, NMI in the 8086; PUSH decrements SP, POP increments it; MUL widens (AL × r8 → AX), DIV narrows (AX ÷ r8 → AL, AH).

concepts.text: Positional Number Systems

Digital systems use base-2 (binary), base-8 (octal) and base-16 (hexadecimal) alongside decimal. In a positional system of base (radix) b, the digits run from 0 to b - 1 and each digit position carries a weight equal to b raised to the position index: positions left of the radix point have weights b^0, b^1, b^2, ... and positions to the right have weights b^-1, b^-2, ... The value of a number is the sum of digit x weight over all positions. Binary is the natural language of hardware because a bit maps directly onto a two-state device; octal and hexadecimal are shorthand for binary since 8 = 2^3 and 16 = 2^4.

concepts.plainText: N = sum over i of (d_i x b^i), i negative for fractional digits

concepts.text: Conversions
Rules for converting in either direction:
items: Any base to decimal: multiply each digit by its positional weight and add, for both the integer and the fractional part. (1101.101)2 = 8 + 4 + 1 + 0.5 + 0.125 = 13.625.
Decimal integer to base b: divide repeatedly by b and collect the remainders; the first remainder is the least significant digit, so read the answer from the last remainder upward.
Decimal fraction to base b: multiply repeatedly by b and collect the integer parts (0 or 1 for binary); read them from the first product downward. Some fractions (0.1 in binary) never terminate.
Binary to octal: group bits in threes outward from the radix point (pad with zeros); each group is one octal digit. Binary to hex: group in fours. Reverse the process for octal or hex to binary.
Octal to hex or hex to octal: go through binary; there is no direct digit-by-digit rule.

concepts.text:
Convert 45.625 (decimal) to binary, octal and hex

Integer part           Fraction part
45 / 2 = 22 rem 1  (LSB)  0.625 x 2 = 1.25 -> 1
22 / 2 = 11 rem 0         0.25  x 2 = 0.5  -> 0
11 / 2 =  5 rem 1         0.5   x 2 = 1.0  -> 1  (stop)
 5 / 2 =  2 rem 1
 2 / 2 =  1 rem 0
 1 / 2 =  0 rem 1  (MSB)

45.625 = 101101.101 (binary)
       = 101 101 . 101   = 55.5  (octal)
       = 0010 1101 . 1010 = 2D.A  (hex)
Binary Codes: BCD, Gray and ASCII

Binary-coded decimal (8421 BCD) encodes each decimal digit separately as its own 4-bit binary value, so 259 becomes 0010 0101 1001. Only the ten patterns 0000 to 1001 are legal; 1010 to 1111 never appear in valid BCD. BCD is convenient for displays and calculators but wasteful (12 bits for 259 against 9 bits in pure binary, 100000011) and slower for arithmetic: when a BCD digit sum exceeds 9 or produces a carry, 6 (0110) must be added to correct it.

Gray code (reflected binary code) is an unweighted code in which consecutive values differ in exactly one bit, so a mechanical or optical encoder can never produce a wild intermediate reading while changing position. To convert binary to Gray keep the MSB and XOR each pair of neighbouring binary bits; to convert Gray back to binary keep the MSB and XOR each Gray bit with the binary bit just produced. Gray code cannot be used for arithmetic, but it is the labelling that gives Karnaugh maps their adjacency.

ASCII is the 7-bit alphanumeric code (128 characters, extended to 8 bits in practice) used for text: the digits '0' to '9' are 30H to 39H, 'A' is 41H and 'a' is 61H, so upper and lower case differ only in bit 5. Note that 10 in BCD is 0001 0000, two digit groups, whereas 10 in pure binary is 1010.
Logic Levels

A digital signal is not a single exact voltage but one of two ranges. Logic 0 (LOW, FALSE) is a band near 0 V and logic 1 (HIGH, TRUE) is a band near the supply (+5 V for TTL, +5 V or +3.3 V for CMOS families); the region between the bands is undefined and a gate output should never rest there. In positive logic the higher voltage represents 1 and the lower represents 0; in negative logic the assignment is reversed, the higher voltage means 0. The same physical gate therefore performs different functions under the two conventions: a positive-logic AND gate is a negative-logic OR gate, and a positive-logic NAND is a negative-logic NOR. Positive logic is assumed unless stated otherwise.

Noise margin is the amount of noise voltage a signal can pick up between a driving output and the receiving input before the level is misread. Because CMOS output levels swing almost rail to rail and its input thresholds sit at roughly 30 % and 70 % of the supply, CMOS has a much wider noise margin than TTL, which is one reason it dominates modern design along with its near-zero static power.
Going Deeper: Conversions, Codes and Logic Levels

Why does repeated division work? Any integer can be written N = q x b + r with 0 <= r < b, and in base b the remainder r is exactly the last digit, while the quotient q holds all the other digits shifted one place right. Dividing q again peels off the next digit, so the remainders come out least significant first. For a fraction the reasoning is mirrored: multiplying by b shifts the radix point one place right, so the digit that crosses into the integer part is the next fractional digit, and the digits come out most significant first.

Worked example 1: 7B.3 H to decimal and to octal

Decimal: 7 x 16 + 11 x 1 + 3 x 16^-1
       = 112 + 11 + 0.1875 = 123.1875

Octal via binary:
7B.3 H = 0111 1011 . 0011
regroup in threes outward from the point:
  001 111 011 . 001 100   (pad with zeros at both ends)
=  1   7   3  .  1   4    = 173.14 (octal)
Check: 64 + 56 + 3 + 1/8 + 4/64 = 123.1875

concepts.plainText: bits needed for N = ceil(log2(N + 1)); hex digits = ceil(bits / 4), octal digits = ceil(bits / 3)

concepts.text: Unknown-radix questions are solved by writing both sides as polynomials in b and solving. For example (121)_b = 144 gives b^2 + 2b + 1 = 144, so (b + 1)^2 = 144 and b = 11. Always check that every digit in the question is smaller than the base you find; a result that makes a digit illegal must be rejected.

Look at the 2421 and excess-3 columns: the code for 9 - d is the bit-by-bit complement of the code for d (4 = 0111 and 5 = 1000 in excess-3). Such codes are called self-complementing, and they let a machine form the 9's complement of a decimal digit with plain inverters. 8421 BCD is not self-complementing, and excess-3 is also unweighted because its value cannot be found by adding fixed bit weights.
Parity and ASCII facts that are easy to get wrong:
items: Even parity makes the total number of 1s (data plus parity bit) even; odd parity makes it odd. The parity bit is the XOR of the data bits for even parity and its complement for odd parity.
One parity bit detects any odd number of flipped bits but misses any even number, and it can never say which bit is wrong.
A Hamming single-error-correcting code needs p check bits with 2^p >= m + p + 1, so 4 check bits protect 8 data bits.
ASCII '0' to '9' are 30 H to 39 H, so value = code AND 0F H; upper and lower case letters differ only in bit 5 (20 H).

concepts.text: The guaranteed noise margin of a family is the smaller of NM_H and NM_L, and it is only meaningful when the driver and receiver levels are compared. When one family drives another, use the driver's V_OH and V_OL with the receiver's V_IH and V_IL: TTL driving 74HC gives NM_H = 2.4 - 3.5 = -1.1 V, which means the connection does not work reliably without a pull-up resistor or an HCT part.

n bits give 2^n combinations; largest unsigned value = 2^n - 1
Binary to Gray: keep MSB, then g_i = b_(i+1) XOR b_i
Gray to binary: keep MSB, then b_i = b_(i+1) XOR g_i
