formulas.plainText: Noise margins: NM_H = V_OH(min) - V_IH(min); NM_L = V_IL(max) - V_OL(max)

notes.text: For quick hex-binary work memorise the sixteen 4-bit patterns 0 to F. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits and one octal digit is exactly 3 bits, so hex-binary-octal conversions are pure regrouping with no arithmetic.
BCD is not binary. 1010 to 1111 are invalid BCD digits, and (25)10 is 0010 0101 in BCD but 11001 in binary. Read the question carefully to see which code is asked for.
Positive logic (HIGH = 1) is assumed in every gate definition unless the question says otherwise. Under negative logic the same chip that acts as AND behaves as OR, and NAND behaves as NOR.

concepts.text: What This Section Covers

A combinational circuit is a network of logic gates whose outputs at any instant are fixed entirely by the present combination of inputs. It contains no memory elements and no feedback paths, so the same inputs always give the same outputs, and a circuit with n inputs and m outputs is completely described by a truth table of 2^n rows and m Boolean functions. Syllabus section 2.2 covers the standard MSI building blocks (multiplexer, demultiplexer, decoder, encoder), the arithmetic circuits (half and full adders and subtractors, parallel adders, adder/subtractors) and the arithmetic of unsigned and signed binary numbers, including 2's complement and overflow.
Combinational vs Sequential Logic

rows: Flip-flops or latches store a state

concepts.text: Design Procedure
Every combinational block in this section is designed by the same six steps:
items: 1. Specification: state in words what the circuit must do (e.g. add two bits and produce sum and carry).
2. Fix the number of inputs and outputs and give each a letter symbol.
3. Derive the truth table: 2^n rows, one column per output.
4. Simplify each output function with a K-map or Boolean algebra to a minimal SOP or POS form.
5. Draw the logic diagram; convert to NAND-only or NOR-only if the question demands it.
6. Verify against the truth table. Analysis is the reverse route: diagram, Boolean expression, truth table.

concepts.text: Roadmap of the Building Blocks
The subtopics that follow, in the order the exam syllabus lists them:
items: Multiplexer (MUX): 2^n data inputs, n select lines, 1 output. Data selector and universal function implementer.
Demultiplexer (DEMUX): 1 data input, n select lines, 2^n outputs. Data distributor; a decoder with enable used as data.
Decoder: n code inputs activate exactly one of 2^n outputs (minterm generator, address decoder, BCD-to-7-segment driver).
Encoder: 2^n input lines produce an n-bit code; a priority encoder resolves several simultaneously active inputs.
Adders and subtractors: half adder, full adder, ripple-carry and carry-lookahead adders, half and full subtractor, 4-bit adder/subtractor with mode control, BCD correction.
Signed arithmetic: sign-magnitude, 1's and 2's complement, ranges, overflow detection and sign extension.
Also combinational: magnitude comparator (A>B, A=B, A<B), code converters (binary to Gray, BCD to excess-3), parity generator/checker.

rows: Minterm generation, chip select, display driving

concepts.text: Key terms used throughout the section:
items: Minterm m_i: the AND term that is 1 for exactly one input combination; a decoder output is a minterm.
Enable (E or G): a control input that must be active before the block responds; often active-low on real ICs.
Active-low: the signal is asserted at logic 0, drawn with a bubble or an overbar.
Propagation delay: time from an input change to the output settling; in a ripple adder it adds up stage by stage.
MSI: medium-scale integration, the 74-series packages (74138, 74151, 74283) that implement these blocks.
Universal element: a block (MUX, decoder plus OR, NAND gate) from which any Boolean function can be built.

concepts.text: How MCQs Test This Section
Questions on combinational circuits fall into a few recognisable patterns:
items: Counting rules: how many select lines for a 2^n:1 MUX, how many outputs from an n-input decoder, how many smaller blocks to build a larger one.
Identify the block from a one-line description (data selector, data distributor, minterm generator, resolves multiple active inputs).
Write or recognise the output expression: MUX output, half adder carry, full adder sum, subtractor borrow.
Numeric arithmetic: 2's complement of a pattern, result and overflow of an 8-bit signed addition, unsigned range of n bits.
Classify a named circuit as combinational or sequential.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Combinational Circuits

Most design questions begin as a sentence, and the hard part is turning it into a truth table. Name every input and output and state what 1 means for each (door open = 1, belt fastened = 1), decide which input combinations can never occur so they become don't-cares, and write one output column per function. Words such as 'either ... or', 'both', 'at least two' and 'unless' map to OR, AND, a threshold function and an AND with a complemented input. Only after the table is complete should K-maps be drawn, one per output.
Worked Example: BCD to Excess-3 Converter

Inputs ABCD = BCD digit (A = MSB); outputs wxyz = digit + 3
Digit  ABCD  wxyz        Digit  ABCD  wxyz
  0    0000  0011          5    0101  1000
  4    0100  0111          9    1001  1100
Don't-cares: 1010 to 1111 (never applied)

K-map results (Xs used where they enlarge groups):
  w = A + BC + BD
  x = B'C + B'D + BC'D'
  y = CD + C'D'      (C XNOR D)
  z = D'
Gates: 1 inverter for z, 1 XNOR for y, AND-OR logic for w and x

Analysis runs the other way. Label the output of every gate (T1, T2 ...), write each label as a function of the signals feeding it, working from the inputs toward the output, then substitute and simplify. Finally build the truth table and describe the behaviour in words. Two quick checks help: a NAND-NAND pair of levels is an AND-OR circuit, and a NOR-NOR pair is an OR-AND circuit, so many exam diagrams can be read at a glance.

rows: Add 0011; z = D', y = CD + C'D'
P = XOR of all data bits
Error = XOR of all received bits
G = AB', E = A ⊙ B, L = A'B

concepts.text:
xi = AiBi + Ai'Bi'   (1 when bit i is equal)
(A=B) = x3 x2 x1 x0
(A>B) = A3B3' + x3A2B2' + x3x2A1B1' + x3x2x1A0B0'
(A<B) = A3'B3 + x3A2'B2 + x3x2A1'B1 + x3x2x1A0'B0

Trace: A = 0110, B = 0101
  bit 3: 0,0 -> x3 = 1     bit 2: 1,1 -> x2 = 1
  bit 1: 1,0 -> x3x2A1B1' = 1  => (A>B) = 1
  (A=B) = 0 because x1 = 0;  6 > 5 confirmed

A parity generator adds one bit so that the total number of 1s is even (even parity) or odd (odd parity); the even-parity bit is simply the XOR of the data bits and the odd-parity bit is its complement. At the receiver a checker XORs all bits, including the parity bit, and a 1 flags an error. Parity detects any odd number of bit errors but misses every even number, and it cannot say which bit is wrong. The same XOR tree also builds Gray-code converters, which is why XOR gates dominate this family of circuits.

concepts.latex: t_{pd} = \frac{t_{PHL} + t_{PLH}}{2}, \quad t_{path} = \sum_{\text{gates on path}} t_{pd,i}
concepts.plainText: tpd = (tPHL + tPLH)/2; path delay = sum of the delays of the gates on that path

concepts.text: A combinational output is valid only after the slowest input-to-output path, the critical path, has settled. For a two-level SOP with input inverters that is inverter + AND + OR. Wide functions should be built as balanced trees rather than chains: combining 8 signals with 2-input gates takes 7 gates either way, but a tree has log₂8 = 3 levels while a chain has 7. Paths of unequal length also create short glitches, which is harmless in a combinational block that is sampled later but dangerous if the output drives a clock or asynchronous reset.

Segment c of a BCD-to-7-segment decoder (A = MSB)
c is lit for 0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 (dark only for 2 = 0010)
c = Σm(0,1,3,4,5,6,7,8,9) + d(10-15)
Groups: B (rows 01 and 11), C' (columns 00 and 01), D (columns 01 and 11)
c = B + C' + D   -> 0 only when B = 0, C = 1, D = 0 (digits 2 and code 1010)

Frequent mistakes: in Gray-to-binary conversion XOR each Gray bit with the previous BINARY bit, not the previous Gray bit; decide whether the display is common-anode (active-low drive) or common-cathode (active-high) before writing segment equations; state the 6 don't-cares of a BCD circuit or the minimal answer comes out larger; and count every gate level, including input inverters, when finding the worst-case delay.

formulas.plainText: Yi = fi(x1, x2, ..., xn): each output is a function of the present inputs only
Truth table rows = 2^n for n inputs
Number of distinct Boolean functions of n variables = 2^(2^n)
MUX: 2^n inputs need n select lines; decoder: n inputs give 2^n outputs

notes.text: The one-word test for combinational versus sequential is memory. Anything containing a flip-flop, latch, register or counter is sequential; adders, MUXes, decoders, encoders and comparators are combinational.

Do not confuse the direction of the blocks: a decoder goes from n lines to 2^n lines, an encoder from 2^n lines to n, a MUX from many to one and a DEMUX from one to many. Swapping decoder and encoder is the most common mistake.

Real 74-series parts usually have active-low enables and often active-low outputs (74138 decoder, 7447 display driver). Textbook truth tables are drawn active-high, so check the polarity stated in a question before reading its table.

concepts.text: Sequential Circuits, Latches and Flip-Flops

A combinational circuit's outputs depend only on its present inputs; a sequential circuit's outputs depend on the present inputs and on the state stored in memory elements, so the same input can give different outputs at different times. The memory element is a bistable: a circuit with two stable states that stores one bit. A latch is level-sensitive: while its enable (or clock) input is active it is transparent and the output follows the inputs. A flip-flop is edge-triggered: it samples its inputs only at a clock transition (rising or falling edge) and holds the result until the next active edge. Clocked sequential circuits are called synchronous; circuits whose state changes whenever an input changes are asynchronous.
SR Latch (NOR and NAND)

The basic SR (set-reset) latch is two cross-coupled NOR gates with complementary outputs Q and Q-bar. Inputs are active-high: S = 1, R = 0 sets Q = 1; S = 0, R = 1 resets Q = 0; S = R = 0 holds the previous state. S = R = 1 is forbidden (invalid): both outputs are forced to 0, so they are no longer complementary, and if both inputs then return to 0 together the final state depends on which gate is faster (a race). The NAND version uses cross-coupled NAND gates with active-low inputs: S-bar = 0 sets, R-bar = 0 resets, S-bar = R-bar = 1 holds and S-bar = R-bar = 0 is the invalid combination (both outputs 1).
Gated SR, D Latch, D and JK and T Flip-Flops

A gated (clocked) SR latch adds an enable input EN: two AND gates (or NAND gates in the NAND form) pass S and R to the latch only while EN = 1, and the latch ignores its inputs while EN = 0. The invalid state can still be reached while EN = 1. Feeding one input D to S and its complement to R gives the D (data) latch: only S = 1, R = 0 or S = 0, R = 1 are possible, so the forbidden state is eliminated and Q follows D while EN = 1 (transparent latch). Replacing the enable by an edge detector gives the D flip-flop, whose output takes the value of D that was present at the active clock edge (Q+ = D) and is otherwise insensitive to D. Because the output reproduces the input one clock later it is also called a delay flip-flop.
JK and T flip-flops:
items: JK flip-flop: J acts like S and K like R, but the outputs are fed back to the input gates so that J = K = 1 is no longer invalid; instead the output toggles (Q+ = Q-bar). J = K = 0 holds, J = 1, K = 0 sets, J = 0, K = 1 resets. It is the most versatile flip-flop.

T (toggle) flip-flop: one input T. T = 1 toggles the output at every active edge, T = 0 holds it. It is a JK with J and K tied together (J = K = T). With T fixed at 1 the output changes once for every two clock edges, so its frequency is half the clock frequency (divide-by-two), the basic building block of binary counters.
D flip-flop from JK: connect J = D and K = D-bar.

concepts.text: Characteristic Tables and Equations

rows: Next state Q+ for each input combination
00 to Q, 01 to 0, 10 to 1, 11 to Q-bar

concepts.plainText: SR: Q+ = S + R'Q, with the constraint SR = 0
JK: Q+ = JQ' + K'Q
T: Q+ = T xor Q = TQ' + T'Q

concepts.text: Excitation Tables, Direct Inputs and Timing

The excitation table is the characteristic table read backwards: given the present state and the required next state, it lists the inputs that produce the transition (X = don't care). It is the tool for designing counters and for converting one flip-flop type into another. Two further groups of terms complete the flip-flop:
items: Asynchronous (direct) inputs: PRESET (PR-bar) forces Q = 1 and CLEAR (CLR-bar) forces Q = 0 immediately, independent of the clock and of the synchronous inputs. They are usually active-low, are used to initialise a circuit at power-up, and activating both at once is invalid.
Setup time t_su: the synchronous inputs must be stable for at least t_su before the active clock edge.
Hold time t_h: the inputs must remain stable for t_h after the edge. Violating setup or hold time can leave the output metastable.
Propagation delay t_pd (t_CLK-to-Q): the time from the active edge until the output settles; typically 10 to 25 ns for TTL, a few ns for CMOS.
Maximum clock frequency: the clock period must be at least t_pd + t_su plus the delay of any logic between flip-flops.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Latches and Flip-Flops

Why does a pair of cross-coupled NOR gates remember a bit? With S = R = 0 each NOR gate simply inverts the output of the other, so the circuit is a loop of two inverters. Such a loop is stable only with Q = 1, Q-bar = 0 or Q = 0, Q-bar = 1, and it stays in whichever state it was last pushed into. A 1 on S forces the Q-bar gate to 0, which in turn drives Q to 1; once the feedback has taken over, S can return to 0 and the state is kept. The NAND latch works the same way with the roles of 0 and 1 swapped, which is why its inputs are active-low.

Worked example 1: NOR SR latch, starting with Q = 0
Step  S R   Q  Q-bar   Action
 1    0 1   0   1      reset (already 0)
 2    0 0   0   1      hold
 3    1 0   1   0      set
 4    0 0   1   0      hold, the latch remembers the set
 5    1 1   0   0      forbidden: outputs no longer complementary
 6    0 0   ?   ?      both inputs released together: race

Step 6 shows the race condition. After S = R = 1 both outputs are 0; when both inputs drop to 0 at once, both gates see 0 on both inputs and both start switching to 1. The faster gate reaches 1 first and forces the other gate back to 0, so the final state is decided by tiny, uncontrollable differences in gate delay. In ideal, perfectly matched gates the outputs could even oscillate. This is why S = R = 1 is not merely unused but forbidden.

A characteristic equation is obtained from the characteristic table like any other Boolean function: treat the inputs and the present state Q as variables, write Q+ as the output column, and minimise with a K-map. Any input combination that is not allowed (S = R = 1 in the SR flip-flop) becomes a don't care, which is why the SR equation is shorter than a direct sum of its minterms.

Worked example 2: characteristic equation of the JK flip-flop
K-map of Q+ (rows Q, columns JK in Gray order 00 01 11 10)
          JK=00  01  11  10
  Q = 0     0    0   1   1     -> group of two: J Q-bar
  Q = 1     1    0   0   1     -> wrap-around pair: K-bar Q
Q+ = J Q-bar + K-bar Q
Check J = K = 1: Q+ = Q-bar + 0 = Q-bar (toggle)

concepts.plainText: Gated D latch: Q+ = EN D + EN' Q (transparent when EN = 1, hold when EN = 0)

concepts.text: Conversion between flip-flop types uses the excitation table of the flip-flop you have. For each row of the target flip-flop's characteristic table, read off the inputs that the available flip-flop needs for that Q to Q+ transition, then minimise each input with a K-map, using the X entries as don't cares. The example below builds a T flip-flop from an SR flip-flop, a conversion not listed in the main table.

Worked example 3: SR flip-flop converted to a T flip-flop
T Q | Q+ | S R  (from SR excitation table)
0 0 | 0  | 0 X
0 1 | 1  | X 0
1 0 | 1  | 1 0
1 1 | 0  | 0 1
S: 1 only at T = 1, Q = 0 (X at T = 0, Q = 1)  ->  S = T Q-bar
R: 1 only at T = 1, Q = 1 (X at T = 0, Q = 0)  ->  R = T Q
S and R are never 1 together, so the forbidden input is avoided.

rows: General purpose, counters with fewest gates

concepts.text: Common mistakes in flip-flop questions:
items: Using the NOR-latch table for a NAND latch: the NAND latch holds with both inputs at 1 and is invalid with both at 0.
Treating J = K = 1 as set instead of toggle when tracing a JK sequence.
Mixing up the characteristic table (inputs give next state) with the excitation table (transition gives inputs).
Forgetting that a D latch follows D for the whole enable time, so the stored value is D at the moment the enable goes inactive.
Writing the T characteristic as XNOR: Q+ = T xor Q, not T xnor Q.

concepts.text: For any conversion, remember two shortcuts: to make a D flip-flop act like X, drive D with X's characteristic equation; to make a T flip-flop act like X, drive T with Q xor (X's characteristic equation). Both follow directly from Q+ = D and Q+ = T xor Q.

formulas.plainText: D flip-flop: Q+ = D (output follows the data present at the clock edge)
SR: Q+ = S + R'Q (S and R never both 1)
JK: Q+ = JQ' + K'Q
T: Q+ = T xor Q
f_max = 1 / (t_pd + t_setup + t_logic)

notes.text: The invalid input pair depends on the gate type: NOR SR latch, S = R = 1 (both outputs 0); NAND SR latch, S-bar = R-bar = 0 (both outputs 1). The hold condition is the opposite pair in each case.

Learn the four characteristic equations and the JK excitation table by heart. A JK with J = K = 1 (or a T with T = 1) toggles and halves the clock frequency; that single fact underlies every counter question.

Latch = level-sensitive and transparent while enabled; flip-flop = edge-triggered, output changes only at the clock transition. MCQs often test this distinction and the fact that the D latch and D flip-flop have no invalid state.

concepts.text: What a Microprocessor Is

A microprocessor is a programmable, clock-driven, register-based semiconductor device that reads binary instructions from memory, processes data according to those instructions and delivers results to memory or output devices. It is the central processing unit (CPU) of a computer fabricated on a single chip. On its own it can do nothing: it needs external memory to hold the program and data, and I/O devices to communicate with the outside world. Intel's 8085 and 8086 are the two processors the NEC syllabus is built around.
Microprocessor vs microcontroller, and the basic job of every processor:
items: Microprocessor: only the CPU on the chip (8085, 8086, Pentium). Memory, timers and I/O ports are separate chips connected over the system bus; suited to general-purpose computers.
Microcontroller: CPU, ROM/RAM, timers and I/O ports integrated on one chip (8051, PIC, AVR); suited to embedded control where cost, size and power matter.
Whatever the family, the processor repeats one loop endlessly: fetch an instruction from memory, decode it, execute it, and store the result.

concepts.text: Buses and Timing
Three groups of lines connect the microprocessor to memory and I/O (the system bus):
items: Address bus: unidirectional, driven by the processor. With n lines it can select 2^n distinct locations: 16 lines (8085) reach 64 KB, 20 lines (8086) reach 1 MB.
Data bus: bidirectional; its width is the word size of the processor and fixes how many bits move per transfer (8 for 8085, 16 for 8086).
Control bus: individual signals that time and qualify transfers, e.g. RD, WR, IO/M, ALE, READY, interrupt request and acknowledge, HOLD/HLDA.

concepts.plainText: N = 2^n locations, where n = number of address lines

concepts.text: Timing is built from the clock. One T-state is one period of the processor clock. A machine cycle is the time taken for one complete bus operation (opcode fetch, memory read, memory write, I/O read, I/O write or interrupt acknowledge) and takes 3 to 6 T-states. An instruction cycle is the time to fetch and execute one whole instruction and consists of 1 to 5 machine cycles; on the 8085 this ranges from 4 T-states (MOV A, B) to 18 T-states (CALL). The first machine cycle of every instruction is always an opcode fetch.
Internal blocks common to all microprocessors:
items: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): performs add, subtract, AND, OR, XOR, compare, shift and rotate on data supplied by the registers; its result updates the flag register.
Register array: fast on-chip storage for operands, addresses and status (accumulator, general-purpose registers, program counter, stack pointer, flags).
Control unit: decodes the opcode and generates the timing and control signals that steer data over the internal bus and out to the system bus.

Clock: from a crystal; the 8085 internally halves its 6.144 MHz crystal to 3.072 MHz, so one T-state is about 325 ns. Speed is quoted as clock frequency or as MIPS = clock / (average clocks per instruction × 10^6).

rows: Von Neumann: one memory and one bus shared by program and data; simpler but the shared bus is a bottleneck
Harvard: separate program and data memories with separate buses; instruction and data fetch can overlap
RISC: few simple fixed-length instructions, one per clock, load/store only touches memory, many registers, hardwired control
CISC: many complex variable-length instructions, memory operands allowed, fewer registers, microprogrammed control

concepts.text: Roadmap of section 2.4, in the order the app presents it:
items: Intel 8085 architecture: registers, flags, pins, interrupts and instruction length.
Intel 8086 architecture: BIU/EU pipelining, segment and general registers, 9 flags, min/max mode, memory banks.
Segment:offset and physical address calculation: physical = segment × 10H + offset with worked examples.
Addressing modes of 8085 and 8086: how an instruction says where its operand is.
Instruction set and assembly language programming: instruction groups, directives, a worked program, stack and procedures.

concepts.text: MCQs on this section are mostly one-line factual recall (bus widths, memory capacity, register names, flag bits, vector addresses) plus short calculations: 2^n memory size, T-state duration from a clock frequency, and 8086 physical addresses. Learn the standard numbers exactly; distractors are usually the same numbers shifted by one power of two or one hex digit.
Going Deeper: Memory Sizing, Instruction Timing and Performance

Why do n address lines give exactly 2^n locations? Each line carries one bit, so the address is an n-bit binary number, and an n-bit number has 2^n distinct patterns from all zeros to all ones. The first address is therefore 0 and the last is 2^n − 1, which in hex is simply n/4 digits of F when n is a multiple of 4 (16 lines → FFFFH, 20 lines → FFFFFH). If each location holds a word wider than one byte, the capacity in bytes is the number of locations multiplied by the word width in bytes.

concepts.plainText: Capacity in bytes = 2^n × w/8 (w = bits per location); last address = 2^n − 1

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: memory sizing
Given: 20 address lines, each location 16 bits wide
Locations      = 2^20 = 1,048,576 = 1 M
Bytes/location = 16 / 8 = 2
Capacity       = 1 M x 2 = 2 MB
Address range  = 00000H to FFFFFH (2^20 - 1)
Reverse: lines needed for 256 KB bytes
256 KB = 2^8 x 2^10 = 2^18  ->  18 address lines

The fetch–decode–execute loop can be written as a short sequence of register transfers. The program counter drives the address bus, memory returns the opcode on the data bus into the instruction register, and the PC is incremented so it already points to the next byte. The decoder then decides how many more machine cycles are needed: none for a register-to-register operation, one or two memory reads to collect an operand or address, and a memory or I/O write if a result must leave the chip.

Instruction cycle as register transfers
FETCH:   address bus <- PC
         IR <- memory[PC]        (read strobe active)
         PC <- PC + 1
DECODE:  control unit examines IR, plans remaining cycles
OPERAND: (if needed) read further bytes, PC <- PC + 1 each
EXECUTE: ALU operates, flags updated
STORE:   (if needed) memory or I/O write of the result

concepts.plainText: CPU time = instruction count × CPI / f_clk; average CPI = sum of (fraction × CPI) over instruction classes

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: timing and performance
Clock 2 MHz  ->  T = 1 / 2 MHz = 0.5 us
Program: 20 instr x 4T + 10 x 7T + 5 x 10T
Total T-states = 80 + 70 + 50 = 200
Time = 200 x 0.5 us = 100 us
Mix: 50% CPI 1, 30% CPI 3, 20% CPI 2 at 900 MHz
CPI_avg = 0.5 + 0.9 + 0.4 = 1.8
MIPS = 900 / 1.8 = 500

rows: (f / clocks per bus cycle) × bytes per transfer

concepts.text: Special cases and common mistakes:
items: The 8085 clock generator divides the crystal by 2, so always halve the crystal frequency before computing T; the 8086 with an 8284 clock generator divides by 3.
4000H is the number of locations for 14 lines, not the last address; the last address is 3FFFH.
A wider data bus moves more bits per transfer but does not add any addressable locations.
Pipelining reduces the average time per instruction, not the time of a single instruction; the first instruction still needs all k stages.

concepts.text: When a memory is word-addressable, 2^n gives words, not bytes. Multiply by the word width in bytes before quoting KB or MB, and keep bits (Kbit) and bytes (KB) apart.

For timing problems write three lines every time: T = 1/f, total T-states = sum over instructions, time = total × T. For performance problems, find the average CPI first, then MIPS = f in MHz divided by CPI.

formulas.plainText: Memory capacity = 2^n × word size (n address lines)
T-state duration = 1 / f_clk
Instruction cycle = sum of its machine cycles (1 to 5 on the 8085)
MIPS = f_clk / (CPI × 10^6), CPI = average clocks per instruction

notes.text: Address lines fix memory size, data lines fix word size. 16 lines → 64 KB, 20 lines → 1 MB, 24 lines → 16 MB, 32 lines → 4 GB. Every extra address line doubles the capacity.

Do not confuse the three timing units: T-state (one clock period) < machine cycle (one bus operation, 3–6 T-states) < instruction cycle (1–5 machine cycles). The opcode fetch is always the first machine cycle.
The 8085 and 8086 are Von Neumann, CISC processors. RISC (ARM, MIPS) and Harvard (8051, DSPs) appear only as comparison points in this syllabus.

concepts.text: Memory Classification

A microprocessor system stores programs and data in memory that the CPU reaches through three buses: the unidirectional address bus (CPU to memory), the bidirectional data bus, and the control bus (RD, WR, IO/M and similar signals). Memory is classified first by where it sits: primary (main) memory is semiconductor memory addressed directly by the CPU, while secondary storage (disk, SSD) and tertiary storage (tape) hold bulk data and are reached through I/O operations. Primary memory divides into RAM, which is volatile read/write memory, and ROM, which is non-volatile and normally read-only during operation.
Classification tree:
items: Primary memory -> RAM (volatile): SRAM, DRAM.
Primary memory -> ROM (non-volatile): mask ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash.
Secondary storage: hard disk (HDD), solid-state drive (SSD), optical disc.
Tertiary storage: magnetic tape and other archival media.

rows: Erased by UV light through a quartz window; whole chip

concepts.text: Memory Hierarchy

No single memory is at once fast, large and cheap, so systems arrange several levels: registers -> cache (SRAM) -> main memory (DRAM) -> secondary storage (HDD/SSD) -> tertiary storage (tape). Moving down the hierarchy, each level is slower, larger and cheaper per bit. The hierarchy works because programs show locality of reference: recently used code and data (temporal locality) and their neighbours (spatial locality) are likely to be used again, so a small fast level in front of a large slow one captures most accesses.
Address Lines, Chip Capacity and Chip Count

With n address lines a device can address 2^n locations, and a chip's capacity is locations x width. An 8K x 8 chip (8 KB) has 8192 locations, so it needs 13 address lines A0 to A12 and 8 data lines; a 4K x 8 chip needs 12. To build a larger memory from smaller chips, divide: 64 KB / 8 KB = 8 chips. The chips share the data bus and the low-order address lines, and the remaining high-order lines (here A13, A14, A15, three lines for eight chips) are decoded to pick one chip at a time.

concepts.plainText: Chips = total memory / chip size = 64 KB / 8 KB = 8

concepts.text: Address Decoding and Chip Select

The CPU's address lines are split into two groups. Low-order lines go straight to the chip's address pins; high-order lines feed a decoder whose output drives the chip select (CS or CE) input, so that only one chip responds to a given address. A 74LS138 3-to-8 decoder is the standard part: three select inputs (A, B, C), three enable inputs (G1 active high, G2A and G2B active low, one of which is usually tied to IO/M so that only memory cycles enable it), and eight active-low outputs Y0 to Y7. In full (absolute) decoding every high-order line takes part, so each location has exactly one address. In partial (linear) decoding some lines are ignored to save hardware; the chip then appears at several address ranges (foldback or mirror images), which wastes address space.
Worked memory map: 64 KB on an 8085 from eight 8 KB chips.
items: A0 to A12 connect to every chip's address pins; D0 to D7 connect to every chip's data pins.
A13, A14, A15 drive the 74138 inputs A, B, C; IO/M (low for memory) enables the decoder.
Y0 (A15 A14 A13 = 000) selects chip 0: 0000H to 1FFFH.
Y4 (100): 8000H to 9FFFH; Y5 (101): A000H to BFFFH; Y6 (110): C000H to DFFFH.
Y7 (111) selects chip 7: E000H to FFFFH. Each range spans 2000H = 8192 bytes.

concepts.text: Memory-Mapped vs I/O-Mapped (Isolated) I/O

An I/O port must also be given an address. With memory-mapped I/O the port occupies a location in the memory map, so it is reached with a 16-bit address and any memory-reference instruction (on the 8085: MOV, LDA, STA, ADD M and so on) while IO/M is 0. With I/O-mapped (isolated) I/O the ports live in a separate address space reached only by IN and OUT: the 8085 uses an 8-bit port address (256 input and 256 output ports) with IO/M = 1, and the 8086 uses an 8-bit fixed address or a 16-bit address in DX (64 K ports). Memory-mapped I/O gives richer instructions but consumes memory addresses and needs more decoding; isolated I/O keeps the full 64 KB for memory and uses simpler decoding but only the accumulator can talk to a port.

rows: All memory instructions (MOV, LDA, STA, ADD M)
Any register, direct arithmetic on port

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Memory Organisation, Decoding and Timing

A chip described as m × n has m addressable locations, each n bits wide. It needs log2(m) address pins and n data pins, plus chip select, output enable and write enable. When the required word is wider than the chip, several chips are placed side by side to form one bank (row), all sharing the same address and chip-select lines; when more words are required, banks are stacked and a decoder chooses one bank at a time. The total chip count is simply the product of these two factors.

concepts.plainText: Chips = (M / m) × (W / n) for an M × W memory built from m × n chips; decoder select lines = log2(M / m)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: 32 KB (32K x 8) from 4K x 4 chips, placed at 0000H-7FFFH
Chips per bank = 8 / 4 = 2      Banks = 32K / 4K = 8      Total = 2 x 8 = 16 chips
Chip address pins: 4K = 2^12 -> A0-A11 go to every chip
Bank select: 8 banks -> 3 lines A12, A13, A14 into a 74138; enable only when A15 = 0
Bank 0: A14 A13 A12 = 000 -> 0000H-0FFFH
Bank 1: 001 -> 1000H-1FFFH   ...   Bank 7: 111 -> 7000H-7FFFH
Check: 8 banks x 1000H = 8000H bytes = 32 KB

Worked example 2: partial decoding of a 4K x 8 EPROM (A0-A11 on chip)
CS active when A15 = 0 and A14 = 1; A13 and A12 not connected
A15 A14 A13 A12   block
 0   1   0   0    4000H-4FFFH  (intended range)
 0   1   0   1    5000H-5FFFH  (image)
 0   1   1   0    6000H-6FFFH  (image)
 0   1   1   1    7000H-7FFFH  (image)
2 unused lines -> each byte answers at 2^2 = 4 addresses (1 intended + 3 images);
16 KB of address space used by a 4 KB chip

Wait states solve a speed mismatch. The processor allows a fixed time for memory to respond, set by the clock and its bus timing. If a chip is slower, external logic pulls READY low; the 8085 samples READY in T2 and inserts one wait state (Tw) of one clock period for each period READY stays low. The number of wait states is the shortfall divided by the clock period, always rounded up, because a fraction of a wait state is not possible.

concepts.plainText: Wait states = ceiling((memory access time − time allowed by CPU) / clock period)

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: wait states
Clock 5 MHz -> T = 1 / 5 MHz = 200 ns
Time allowed by CPU with no wait state: 460 ns (given)
Memory access time: 600 ns
Shortfall = 600 - 460 = 140 ns
N_w = ceil(140 / 200) = ceil(0.7) = 1 wait state
With 1 wait state the memory gets 460 + 200 = 660 ns >= 600 ns
Common mistakes in memory interfacing problems:
items: Mixing Kbit and KB: a 64 Kbit chip holds only 8 KB.
Forgetting the width factor: 1K × 4 chips need two per byte, so chip counts double.
Off-by-one on the end address: last = start + size − 1, e.g. 8000H + 1000H − 1 = 8FFFH.
Using the wrong number of chip lines: the decoded lines start just above the chip's highest address pin.
Counting images: k undecoded lines make each location answer at 2^k addresses, not k.

concepts.text: For an address range, write the decoded high-order bits, then fill the chip's own lines with all 0s for the start and all 1s for the end. For the reverse question, size = end − start + 1, and log2(size) gives the number of lines that go to the chip.

formulas.plainText: n address lines -> 2^n locations (16 lines -> 65536 = 64 KB, 20 lines -> 1 MB)
Address lines needed n = log2(locations); 8 KB = 2^13 -> 13 lines
Chip capacity in bits = locations x width; 4K x 8 = 32768 bits = 4 KB
Number of chips = total memory / chip size
8085 isolated I/O: 8-bit port address -> 256 ports (8086 with DX: 2^16 = 65536)

notes.text: 'How many address lines for 64 KB?' -> 16, because 2^16 = 65536. Work backwards with powers of two: 1 KB = 2^10 needs 10 lines, so add 1 line for every doubling (2 KB = 11, 4 KB = 12, 8 KB = 13, 16 KB = 14, 32 KB = 15, 64 KB = 16, 1 MB = 20).

Partial decoding does not make a chip bigger; it makes the same chip answer at several ranges (foldback). If a question says some address lines are 'not connected' or 'don't care', the chip's true size is fixed by the lines that reach its pins, and the mirror ranges are found by toggling the unused lines.

DRAM is denser and cheaper than SRAM because each cell is one transistor plus one capacitor, but the capacitor leaks, so a refresh cycle must rewrite every row every few milliseconds. SRAM keeps its data as long as power is present and needs no refresh, which is why cache uses SRAM and main memory uses DRAM.

concepts.text: What Is an Interrupt?

An interrupt is a signal, from hardware or from software, that temporarily suspends the program the CPU is executing so that an urgent task can be handled. The CPU finishes the current instruction, saves enough information to come back later, and transfers control to a special subroutine called the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) or interrupt handler. When the ISR finishes, the saved state is restored and the interrupted program continues exactly where it left off, unaware that anything happened.
Interrupts are the main way an I/O device tells the processor "I need attention now" without the processor having to keep checking. Examples are a key press, a timer tick, a completed serial byte, a power-failure warning, or a divide-by-zero error inside the CPU itself.

rows: CPU repeatedly reads the device status
Device asserts an interrupt line when ready
Wasted in a busy-wait loop while the device is idle
CPU runs other work; responds only when needed
Depends on how often the loop checks
Interrupt pins, priority logic, vector table
Needs ISRs, state saving, priority handling

concepts.text: Classification of Interrupts
Interrupts are grouped along several independent axes:
items: Hardware interrupts arrive on a physical pin of the processor from an external device (keyboard, timer, 8259 controller). Software interrupts are caused by executing an instruction such as INT n in 8086 or RST n in 8085; they are used as system calls (for example INT 21H for DOS services).

Maskable interrupts can be ignored (masked) by the program: 8085 RST 7.5/6.5/5.5 and INTR, 8086 INTR. Non-maskable interrupts cannot be disabled and are reserved for critical events such as power failure: 8085 TRAP, 8086 NMI.

Vectored interrupts jump to a fixed, predefined address (8085 TRAP and RST 7.5/6.5/5.5; every 8086 interrupt through its vector table). Non-vectored interrupts require the device to supply the address or an instruction code on the data bus (8085 INTR).
Internal interrupts (exceptions or traps) are generated by the CPU itself when an abnormal condition occurs during an instruction: divide-by-zero, overflow (INTO) or single-step mode in the 8086.

Edge-triggered inputs respond to a transition (8085 RST 7.5 latches a rising edge; 8086 NMI). Level-triggered inputs must be held active until the CPU samples them (8085 RST 6.5, RST 5.5, INTR; 8086 INTR).

concepts.text: 8085 Interrupts

rows: None: device supplies RST n or CALL

concepts.text: Controlling 8085 interrupts:
items: EI (Enable Interrupts) sets the interrupt-enable flip-flop; DI (Disable Interrupts) clears it. When any interrupt is accepted the 8085 automatically disables further interrupts, so an ISR must execute EI again before returning if nesting is wanted.

SIM (Set Interrupt Mask) writes the accumulator to the mask logic: bits 0, 1, 2 mask RST 5.5, 6.5, 7.5 (1 = masked); bit 3 (MSE) must be 1 for the mask bits to take effect; bit 4 resets the RST 7.5 latch. Bits 6 and 7 drive serial output SOD.
RIM (Read Interrupt Mask) loads the accumulator with the mask status, the pending status of RST 7.5/6.5/5.5, the interrupt-enable flag and the serial input SID.

INTR is acknowledged with INTA; the external logic must place an RST n (one byte) or CALL (three bytes) opcode on the data bus. The eight software RST n instructions vector to 8 × n: RST 0 → 0000H up to RST 7 → 0038H.
TRAP and the RST 7.5/6.5/5.5 inputs are vectored: their service routines begin at fixed locations only 8 bytes apart, so each location normally holds just a JMP to the real ISR.

concepts.plainText: RST n vectors to address 8 × n (RST 5 → 0028H, RST 7 → 0038H)

concepts.text: 8086 Interrupts
The 8086 has two interrupt pins and 256 possible interrupt types:
items: NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt): positive-edge-triggered, cannot be disabled, always type 2 (vector at 00008H). Used for memory parity error or power-failure warning.

INTR (Interrupt Request): level-triggered, maskable by the Interrupt Flag IF. When accepted, the 8086 runs two INTA (interrupt acknowledge) bus cycles and the interrupting device, usually an 8259 PIC, places the 8-bit type number on the data bus during the second cycle.
INT n: a 2-byte software interrupt instruction (opcode CDH followed by the type n); INT 3 has a special 1-byte opcode (CCH) for breakpoints. INTO interrupts (type 4) only if the Overflow flag is set.

Predefined internal types: 0 divide error (DIV/IDIV quotient too large or divisor zero), 1 single step (executed after every instruction while TF = 1), 2 NMI, 3 breakpoint, 4 overflow. Types 5 to 31 are reserved by Intel; types 32 to 255 are free for the user.

concepts.text: Structure of an Interrupt Service Routine

An ISR looks like a subroutine but is entered by hardware and must leave the machine exactly as it found it. The CPU saves the return address (and in the 8086 the flags) automatically; everything else that the ISR touches must be saved on the stack by the programmer. The typical order is: save registers, re-enable interrupts if nesting is allowed, service the device (read or write the data port, clear the request), send any end-of-interrupt command to the controller, restore registers, and return with IRET (8086) or EI followed by RET (8085).

KBD_ISR:  PUSH AX          ; save every register the ISR uses
          PUSH DX
          STI              ; allow higher-priority nesting (optional)
          MOV  DX, 0300H   ; data port of the device
          IN   AL, DX      ; read the byte, clears the request
          MOV  [BUF], AL   ; store it for the main program
          MOV  AL, 20H     ; non-specific EOI for the 8259
          OUT  20H, AL
          POP  DX          ; restore in reverse order
          POP  AX
          IRET             ; pops IP, CS and FLAGS
Enabling, Disabling, Nesting and Latency
Controlling and living with interrupts:
items: In the 8086 the Interrupt Flag IF controls INTR only: STI sets IF (enable), CLI clears IF (disable). NMI, software INT n and internal exceptions are never affected by IF. Accepting any interrupt clears IF and TF automatically, and IRET restores them from the saved flags.

Nested interrupts: if the ISR executes STI (8086) or EI (8085) early, a higher-priority request can interrupt the ISR itself. Each level pushes its own return information, so the stack must be large enough for the deepest nesting expected.

Interrupt latency is the delay between a request and the first ISR instruction: the CPU must complete the current instruction (worst case the longest one), push the return state and fetch the vector. Long instructions, CLI sections and higher-priority ISRs all add to it, so critical sections that disable interrupts must be kept short.
Because the 8085 saves only the program counter, an 8085 ISR must PUSH PSW to preserve the accumulator and flags; the 8086 saves FLAGS automatically but not the general registers.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: How the 8085 Decides to Accept an Interrupt

At the end of every instruction the 8085 checks its five inputs in priority order. TRAP is accepted whenever it is present, because it bypasses both the enable flip-flop and the masks. Each RST input is accepted only if three things are true together: the request is present (the pin level for RST 6.5 and 5.5, the internal latch for RST 7.5), its SIM mask bit is 0, and the interrupt-enable flip-flop is set. INTR has no mask bit, so it depends only on the pin and the enable flip-flop.

concepts.plainText: RST 6.5 is accepted only if IE = 1 AND M6.5 = 0 AND the RST 6.5 pin is high

rows: M7.5, M6.5, M5.5 as currently set

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: build a SIM byte and decode a RIM byte

Goal: unmask only RST 6.5 and discard any old RST 7.5 request
  SOD SDE -  R7.5 MSE M7.5 M6.5 M5.5
   0   0  0   1    1    1    0    1   = 0001 1101 = 1DH

RIM returns A = 3AH = 0011 1010
  SID=0  I7.5=0  I6.5=1  I5.5=1  IE=1  M7.5=0  M6.5=1  M5.5=0
  RST 6.5 is requested but masked, so it waits.
  RST 5.5 is requested, unmasked and IE = 1:
  it is accepted at the end of the current instruction (002CH).

ORG  0000H
        JMP  MAIN        ; reset starts execution at 0000H
        ORG  003CH
        JMP  ISR75       ; 3-byte JMP fits in 003CH-003FH
MAIN:   LXI  SP,2100H    ; stack must exist before EI
        MVI  A,0BH       ; MSE=1, unmask RST 7.5 only
        SIM
        EI
LOOP:   JMP  LOOP        ; main work goes here
ISR75:  PUSH PSW         ; CPU saved only PC: save A and flags
        IN   40H         ; read the device, removes its request
        STA  2050H       ; store the byte for the main program
        POP  PSW         ; restore A and flags
        EI               ; takes effect after RET
        RET

Why EI goes immediately before RET: the 8085 delays the enable by one instruction, so the RET always completes before a waiting request is accepted. If EI were placed earlier, a second request could enter the ISR again while it still had registers on the stack, and a steady stream of requests could make the stack grow without limit. Putting EI at the very start is correct only when nesting is actually wanted and the stack is large enough.

Worked example 2: latency and stack for RST 7.5 at 5 MHz

T = 1 / 5 MHz = 0.2 µs
Worst case: request arrives as an 18-T CALL starts
  finish CALL          18 T
  push PC, go to 003CH 12 T
  JMP ISR75 at 003CH   10 T
To the vector : (18 + 12) x 0.2 = 6 µs
To ISR75 itself: (18 + 12 + 10) x 0.2 = 8 µs

Stack (SP = 2100H, return address 0126H):
  20FFH <- 01H, 20FEH <- 26H, SP = 20FEH

concepts.plainText: Latency = number of T-states before the ISR starts / clock frequency

concepts.text: Common mistakes with 8085 interrupts:
items: Writing mask bits with MSE = 0: SIM then ignores D2-D0 and the masks stay as they were.
Reading a 1 in a mask bit as enabled: in both SIM and RIM a 1 means masked.
Expecting EI to unmask RST 7.5/6.5/5.5: EI only sets the global enable; masks come from SIM.
Forgetting that SDE (D6) must be 1 for D7 to reach the SOD pin.
Expecting a short pulse on RST 6.5 or RST 5.5 to be remembered: only RST 7.5 is latched.
Skipping PUSH PSW in an ISR: the 8085 saves only PC, so the interrupted program's A and flags would be corrupted.

concepts.text: For any SIM or RIM question, write the byte in binary first and label the eight bits (SIM: SOD SDE x R7.5 MSE M7.5 M6.5 M5.5; RIM: SID I7.5 I6.5 I5.5 IE M7.5 M6.5 M5.5). Most wrong options come from a missing MSE or SDE bit or from reading a mask bit backwards.

formulas.plainText: RST n vectors to address 8 × n
RST 7.5 → 003CH, TRAP → 0024H
8086 NMI is type 2, vector at 4 × 2 = 00008H
Latency = time to finish current instruction + save state + fetch vector

notes.text: Memorise the 8085 vector addresses as steps of 8 from TRAP: 0024H (TRAP), 002CH (RST 5.5), 0034H (RST 6.5), 003CH (RST 7.5). Priority order is the same as the address order: TRAP > RST 7.5 > RST 6.5 > RST 5.5 > INTR.
IF (STI/CLI) masks only INTR in the 8086. NMI, INT n and the internal exceptions are always accepted, and a question that says "CLI disables all interrupts" is wrong.

RST 7.5 is the only 8085 interrupt that is edge-triggered and latched: a short pulse is remembered until served or until SIM bit 4 clears it. RST 6.5 and 5.5 are level inputs and are lost if the device drops the line before the CPU samples it.
In the 8085, accepting any interrupt resets the interrupt-enable flip-flop. Forgetting EI before RET in an ISR is a classic bug: the first interrupt is served and every later one is ignored.

concepts.text: Operator Groups
C operators by category (unary operators take one operand, binary two, and ?: is the only ternary operator):
items: Arithmetic: + - * / % (modulus works on integers only; / on two integers truncates toward zero).
Relational: < > <= >= == != (the result is an int, 1 for true and 0 for false).
Logical: && || ! (operands are any scalar; result is 1 or 0; && and || short-circuit).
Bitwise: & | ^ ~ << >> (integer operands, operate on individual bits).
Assignment: = and the compound forms += -= *= /= %= &= |= ^= <<= >>= (a += b means a = a + (b)).
Increment/decrement: ++x (pre: change first, then use) vs x++ (post: use first, then change).
Conditional: cond ? a : b, an expression form of if/else that evaluates only one branch.
Comma: evaluates left to right and yields the rightmost value; sizeof: compile-time size in bytes; (type): explicit cast.
Others: & address-of, * dereference, [] subscript, () call, . and -> member access.

concepts.text: Pre vs Post Increment

int x = 5, y = 5;
int a = ++x;   /* x becomes 6 first, then a = 6 (pre-increment) */
int b = y++;   /* b gets 5, then y becomes 6 (post-increment)   */
printf("%d %d %d %d\n", a, x, b, y);   /* 6 6 5 6 */

int n = 10;
printf("%d\n", n++ * 2);   /* 20: old value used, n is now 11 */
printf("%d\n", ++n * 2);   /* 24: n becomes 12 first */
printf("%d\n", n);         /* 12 */

Pre-increment changes the variable and yields the new value; post-increment yields the old value and then changes the variable. As a statement on its own, i++; and ++i; do exactly the same thing. Both forms need a modifiable variable (an lvalue), so 5++ and (a + b)++ are compile errors. Modifying the same variable twice in one expression without a sequence point, such as i++ + ++i or a[i] = i++, is undefined behaviour: different compilers print different numbers, so 'undefined' is the only defensible answer.
Precedence and Associativity

rows: Right to left (comma: left to right)

concepts.text: Reading the table in practice:
items: Multiplicative before additive: 2 + 3 * 4 = 14, and 10 - 4 - 3 = 3 because - is left-associative ((10 - 4) - 3).
Unary minus binds tighter than *: -a * b is (-a) * b; sizeof x + 1 is (sizeof x) + 1.
Relational beats equality beats logical: a < b == c < d parses as (a < b) == (c < d); a || b && c is a || (b && c).
Bitwise & ^ | sit BELOW == and !=, so x & 1 == 0 parses as x & (1 == 0) = x & 0 = 0. Always write (x & 1) == 0.
Assignment is right-to-left: a = b = c = 5 assigns 5 to all three; x = y == z stores the comparison result in x.
The comma has the lowest precedence: x = 1, 2, 3; leaves x = 1, while x = (1, 2, 3); gives x = 3.
Parentheses override everything; when in doubt in an MCQ, rebuild the expression with brackets level by level.

concepts.text: Arithmetic Details, Promotion and Casting
Integer division and modulus:
items: 7 / 2 = 3 and 7 / 2.0 = 3.5: one floating operand makes the whole division floating.
C99 truncates toward zero: -7 / 2 = -3 (not -4), and the sign of a % b follows the dividend a: -7 % 2 = -1, 7 % -2 = 1, 5 % -3 = 2.
The identity (a / b) * b + a % b == a always holds; a % b == 0 tests divisibility.
% is not defined for float or double (compile error); use fmod() from math.h.
1 / 2 * 4 = 0 because 1 / 2 is evaluated first as 0; 1 / 2.0 * 4 = 2.0. Division by zero with integers is undefined behaviour (usually a crash).

concepts.text: Implicit conversion (usual arithmetic conversions) and casts:
items: Integer promotion: char and short operands are promoted to int before any arithmetic, so 'A' + 1 is an int.
In a mixed expression the 'smaller' type is converted to the larger: int -> unsigned -> long -> float -> double -> long double.
Mixing signed and unsigned converts the signed value: -1 < 1u is FALSE because -1 becomes 4294967295.
Assignment converts the right side to the type of the left: int i = 3.9; stores 3; float f = 1 / 3; stores 0.0 (integer division happened first).
A cast (type)expr converts explicitly: (float)a / b gives the fractional quotient, (int)3.9 gives 3 (truncation), (char)65 is 'A'.
sizeof(a + 1.5) is 8 because the expression has type double; sizeof never evaluates its operand, so sizeof(i++) leaves i unchanged.

concepts.text:
int a = 7, b = 2;
float f = a / b;                     /* 3.0: integer division happens FIRST */
float g = (float)a / b;              /* 3.5: cast before the division */
printf("%d %d\n", -7 / 2, -7 % 2);  /* -3 -1 */
printf("%d\n", 5 % -3);             /* 2: sign follows the dividend (5) */
printf("%d\n", -1 < 1u);            /* 0: -1 converts to unsigned */
printf("%d\n", 10 / 3 * 3.0 == 10); /* 0: 10/3 = 3, 3 * 3.0 = 9.0 */
printf("%d\n", (int)(3.7 + 0.5));   /* 4: cheap rounding trick */
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(a + 1.5));   /* 8: expression is a double */
Logical, Bitwise, Conditional and Comma
Short-circuit evaluation and bitwise facts:
items: && stops at the first false operand and || at the first true one, so if (p != NULL && *p > 0) never dereferences a NULL pointer.
Skipped operands are not evaluated, side effects included: x = 0; y = x && ++x; leaves x = 0 and y = 0.
Logical operators return exactly 0 or 1: !5 = 0, !0 = 1, !!7 = 1, 2 && 4 = 1, 0 || 3 = 1.
x << n multiplies by 2^n and x >> n divides by 2^n for non-negative x; x & 1 tests odd, x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x (basis of the XOR swap).
2 & 4 = 0 but 2 && 4 = 1; & is bitwise, && is logical: the single most common mix-up in output questions.
?: evaluates only the chosen branch: max = (a > b) ? a : b; it can be nested and chained like an else-if ladder.

concepts.text: sizeof is an operator, not a function, and its result is a size_t (print with %zu or cast to int). On a typical 32-bit-int system sizeof(int) is 4, sizeof(3.0) is 8, sizeof(3.0f) is 4, sizeof('A') is 4 in C but 1 in C++, and sizeof of an array is the whole array in bytes. Because sizeof is evaluated at compile time from the type alone, sizeof(i++) leaves i unchanged and sizeof(x)/sizeof(x[0]) counts array elements.
Going Deeper: Evaluating Expressions Step by Step

Precedence and associativity decide only how an expression is grouped, not the order in which its operands are computed. In a + b * c the multiplication is grouped first, but the compiler may fetch a, b and c in any order. Only four operators promise to finish their left operand first: &&, ||, ?: and the comma operator. Everywhere else, if a side effect (++, -- or an embedded assignment) changes a variable that another part of the same expression also reads or changes, as in i++ + i, the behaviour is undefined. A plain i = i + 1 is fine, because the store happens only after the right side has been computed.

rows: x if c is non-zero, otherwise y (never both)

concepts.plainText: q = a / b truncated toward zero (C99 onward), a % b = a - q*b; e.g. -9 / 4 = -2 and -9 % 4 = -9 - (-8) = -1

concepts.text:
Output:
1 2 0
2 3 1
2 2 3

Trace:
a++ gives 0 (a = 1): && is false at once, b stays 2, r = 0
a++ gives 1 (a = 2): || is true at once, c stays 3, r = 1
b > c is 2 > 3, false: only c-- runs, r = 3 and c = 2

Output:
1 2 1 5.5

Trace:
p: x & (4 != 0) = 1011 & 0001 = 1   [(x & 4) != 0 would be 0]
q: x >> (1 + 1) = 11 >> 2 = 2       [(x >> 1) + 1 would be 6]
big: -2 becomes 4294967294u (32-bit unsigned), which is > 1u, so 1
d: 11 / 2 = 5 in int, 11 % 2 * 0.5 = 0.5, total 5.5

rows: char promoted to int ('A' is 65 in ASCII)

concepts.latex: x \mid (1 \ll k),\quad x \,\&\, \sim(1 \ll k),\quad x \oplus (1 \ll k)
concepts.plainText: set bit k: x | (1 << k); clear bit k: x & ~(1 << k); toggle bit k: x ^ (1 << k); test bit k: (x >> k) & 1

concepts.text: Mistakes that produce wrong answers in output questions:
items: ^ is exclusive OR, not a power: 2 ^ 3 is 1; two to the power 3 needs pow(2, 3) or 1 << 3.
a < b < c means (a < b) < c, which compares 0 or 1 with c (recent Clang versions even refuse to compile it); write a < b && b < c.
x & 4 != 0 and 1 << n + 1 group the wrong way; bracket every bitwise and shift sub-expression.
An assignment inside a condition, if (x = 0), stores 0 and is always false; if (x = 5) is always true.
(double)(a / b) casts too late: the integer division has already thrown the fraction away.
Shifting by a negative count or by at least the width of the type (1 << 32 for a 32-bit int) is undefined, and so is left-shifting a negative value.

concepts.text: These have no defined output: i = i++;  a[i] = i++;  i++ + ++i;  printf("%d %d", i, i++);  INT_MAX + 1;  and integer division or % by zero. If one of them appears in an output question, the only correct choice is undefined behaviour (compiler dependent).

formulas.latex: x \ll n = x \times 2^{n},\qquad x \gg n = \lfloor x / 2^{n} \rfloor
formulas.plainText: x << n multiplies by 2^n; x >> n divides by 2^n (non-negative integers)
(a / b) * b + a % b == a; the sign of a % b follows the dividend a
~x == -x - 1 in two's complement (so ~0 = -1, ~5 = -6)
result = (condition) ? value_if_true : value_if_false;

notes.text: & is bitwise AND, && is logical AND. 2 & 4 == 0 but 2 && 4 == 1. Likewise | vs || and ~ vs !: ~0 is -1 while !0 is 1.
x & 1 == 0 parses as x & (1 == 0) because == binds tighter than &; the result is always 0. Parenthesise bitwise tests: (x & 1) == 0.

For i = 3, an expression such as i++ + ++i is undefined behaviour: if 'undefined / compiler dependent' is offered as an option, it is the correct one. Only trust output questions that modify each variable once between sequence points.

Mixed arithmetic follows the widest operand: int / int stays int (7 / 2 = 3), but one float or double operand makes the whole result floating (7 / 2.0 = 3.5). Casting after the division, (float)(7 / 2), is too late and gives 3.0.

concepts.text: Streams and the Two Kinds of I/O

All standard input and output in C goes through streams declared in stdio.h: stdin (keyboard, buffered until Enter), stdout (screen, line-buffered) and stderr (screen, unbuffered, for error messages). Formatted I/O uses a format string containing conversion specifiers to translate between text and typed values: printf and scanf on the console, fprintf/fscanf on files, sprintf/sscanf on strings. Unformatted I/O moves raw characters or whole lines with no conversion: getchar/putchar, gets/puts, fgets/fputs, and the non-standard getch/getche from conio.h.
printf and the Format Specifiers

rows: double (printf promotes float to double, so %f works for both; scanf needs %f for float and %lf for double)
pointer address / a literal percent sign

concepts.text: Flags, field width and precision go between % and the letter: %[flags][width][.precision][length]specifier.
items: %5d right-justifies in 5 columns ('   42'); %-5d left-justifies ('42   '); %05d pads with zeros ('00042'); %+d always shows the sign (+42).
%.2f rounds to two decimals (3.14159 -> 3.14); %8.3f uses width 8 and 3 decimals ('   3.142'); the default precision of %f is 6.
%.3s prints only the first 3 characters of a string; %10s right-aligns a string in 10 columns; %-10s left-aligns it.
%*d takes the width from the next argument: printf("%*d", 6, 42) prints 42 in 6 columns.
%e prints 3.141590e+00; %g uses the shorter of %e and %f and drops trailing zeros (3.14).
A width smaller than the value never truncates a number: %2d with 12345 still prints 12345.
printf returns the number of characters printed; scanf returns the number of items successfully converted (EOF on end of input).

concepts.text:
int n = 42; double pi = 3.14159; char s[] = "exam";
printf("[%d]\n", n);          /* [42]       */
printf("[%5d]\n", n);         /* [   42]    */
printf("[%-5d]\n", n);        /* [42   ]    */
printf("[%05d]\n", n);        /* [00042]    */
printf("[%.2f]\n", pi);       /* [3.14]     */
printf("[%8.3f]\n", pi);      /* [   3.142] */
printf("[%s|%.2s]\n", s, s);  /* [exam|ex]  */
printf("[%x %o %c]\n", 255, 8, 65);   /* [ff 10 A] */
printf("%d\n", printf("hi"));  /* prints hi2: printf returns 2 */
scanf: Reading Formatted Input
scanf rules that produce most of the bugs (and MCQs):
items: Every non-array argument must be an address: scanf("%d", &n). Forgetting & compiles (maybe with a warning) and crashes or corrupts memory at run time.
An array or string name is already an address, so scanf("%s", name) takes no &.
%s skips leading whitespace and stops at the next whitespace, so it cannot read 'New Delhi'; use %[^\n] or fgets for a whole line, and give a bound like %29s to avoid overflow.
%d, %f and %s skip leading whitespace, but %c reads ANY character including the newline left by a previous Enter; write " %c" (leading space) to skip whitespace first.
%f reads a float and %lf reads a double: unlike printf, mixing them here is a real bug because the wrong number of bytes is written.
scanf returns the count of items converted (2 for "%d %d" on success) or EOF; a non-numeric character stops %d and stays in the buffer, so later reads fail repeatedly.
Input is line-buffered: nothing reaches scanf until Enter is pressed, and the '\n' itself remains in the buffer after a number is read.

concepts.text:
int age, a, b; char grade; char name[30];
scanf("%d", &age);        /* user types 21<Enter>: '\n' stays in the buffer */
scanf("%c", &grade);      /* reads that leftover '\n', NOT the letter!       */
scanf(" %c", &grade);     /* leading space skips whitespace: works           */
scanf("%s", name);        /* no &: name is already an address; stops at space */
scanf("%29[^\n]", name);  /* reads a whole line, at most 29 characters       */
int items = scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);  /* 2 on success, 0/1 on bad input, EOF at end */
Unformatted I/O Functions

rows: Read / write one character on stdin / stdout; getchar returns an int (EOF = -1) and waits for Enter because stdin is buffered
Read a line into s with NO length check (buffer overflow; removed in C11) / write s followed by a newline
Safe line read of at most n-1 characters (keeps the '\n' if it fits) / write s with no extra newline
Read a key immediately without Enter; getch does not echo, getche echoes the key
Character I/O on any stream; getc(stdin) is the same as getchar()
Formatted output into / input from a character array instead of a stream

concepts.text:
char line[50];
int ch = getchar();                 /* waits for Enter; returns an int */
putchar(ch);                        /* echo it */
putchar('\n');
gets(line);                         /* UNSAFE: no bound; never use */
fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin);    /* safe; keeps the '\n' if it fits */
puts(line);                         /* adds its own '\n' */
fputs(line, stdout);                /* prints exactly line, no newline added */
Formatted vs unformatted at a glance:
items: Formatted: printf/scanf family; converts numbers of any type using specifiers; flexible but slower because the format string is parsed at run time.
Unformatted: getchar/putchar, gets/puts, fgets/fputs, getch/getche; raw characters and strings only, no conversion, faster.
puts("Hi") is equivalent to printf("Hi\n") and printf("%s\n", s); putchar('A') is equivalent to printf("%c", 'A').
getchar/scanf wait for Enter (buffered); getch/getche return at once (unbuffered) but are not part of standard C or gcc on Linux.
printf returns the number of characters written, scanf the number of items read, getchar the character as an int or EOF, gets/fgets a pointer or NULL.

concepts.text: Output buffering matters too. stdout is line-buffered when attached to a terminal, so a printf without \n may not appear until a newline is printed, fflush(stdout) is called, or the program ends. fflush(stdin) is undefined behaviour in standard C (it happens to work on some Windows compilers); the portable way to discard leftover input is a loop such as while ((c = getchar()) != '\n' && c != EOF);. stderr is unbuffered, so fprintf(stderr, "...") appears immediately, which is why error messages go there.

Going Deeper: Flags, %g, scanf Controls and String I/O

printf walks through its format string from left to right. Ordinary characters are copied unchanged, and each conversion consumes the next argument, which must have exactly the type the specifier expects; a mismatch (such as an int passed to %f) or a missing argument is undefined behaviour, while surplus arguments are evaluated and ignored. A conversion first produces its natural text and only then applies the width, so each field contributes max(width, natural length) characters. Adding these lengths and the ordinary characters gives printf's return value.

rows: Left-justify inside the field (pad on the right)
Pad numbers with leading zeros; ignored with -, and for integers when a precision is given
Always print a sign for signed conversions
Print a blank where a + would go; ignored if + is also present
Alternate form: 0 prefix for %o, 0x or 0X for %x/%X, keep the point for %f/%e and trailing zeros for %g

concepts.plainText: each field prints max(width, natural length) characters; printf returns the sum of the field lengths plus the literal characters

concepts.text: How %g chooses between fixed and exponential style (P = precision, default 6; X = the exponent the value would have in %e style):
items: If P > X >= -4, %g uses fixed style with P - 1 - X decimals; otherwise it uses e-style with P - 1 decimals.
Trailing zeros, and a decimal point left at the end, are then removed unless the # flag is given.
100000.0 has X = 5, so it prints 100000; 1000000.0 has X = 6, so it prints 1e+06.
0.0001234 has X = -4 and stays fixed (0.0001234); 0.00001234 has X = -5 and prints 1.234e-05.
%.3g keeps 3 significant digits: 1234.0 prints 1.23e+03 and 3.14159 prints 3.14.
%e and %g always print at least two exponent digits, as in e+05 or e-12.

concepts.text: scanf controls that go beyond the basic rules:
items: A width limits one conversion: with input 12345, "%2d%d" stores 12 and 345.
An asterisk suppresses assignment: %*d reads a number and discards it, and it is not counted in the return value.
%i reads integers the way C constants are written (010 is octal 8, 0x10 is hexadecimal 16), whereas %d always reads decimal.
A scanset reads characters from a set: %[a-z] takes lowercase letters only and %[^,] takes everything up to a comma; always add a width such as %19[^,].
Whitespace in the format matches any amount of whitespace, including none; any other character must match the input exactly, or scanf stops and returns the count so far.
%n stores the number of characters consumed so far into an int and is not counted in the return value.

        4 items stored, so k = 4

concepts.text: Keep getchar()'s result in an int. With char c, the loop while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) either never ends (if char is unsigned, c can never equal EOF) or stops early at a 0xFF byte (if char is signed). Also never pass user text as the format itself, as in printf(line): any % inside it is treated as a conversion, so write printf("%s", line).

fgets(s, n, stdin) reads at most n - 1 characters and appends '\0'
printf returns the number of characters written; scanf returns the number of items converted (or EOF)

notes.text: In scanf the length modifier matters: %f for float, %lf for double, %ld for long, %c for char. In printf a float is promoted to double, so %f prints both; %lf is merely tolerated there.
scanf("%d", n) without & passes the VALUE of n as an address: it compiles but crashes or corrupts memory. Only arrays and strings are passed without & because their name is already an address.
After scanf("%d", &n) the Enter key's '\n' is still in the input buffer, so a following getchar() or scanf("%c", &ch) reads the newline instead of waiting. Use " %c" or consume the newline first.
gets() cannot limit how many characters it stores, so any long line overflows the array; it was removed from C11. Use fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin) and remember it keeps the trailing '\n'.

concepts.text: Selection: if, if-else, Ladders and Nesting
Forms of the if statement:
items: Simple if: the statement (or block) runs only when the condition is non-zero; if (x) is the same as if (x != 0).
if-else: exactly one of the two branches runs.
Nested if: an if inside another; the dangling-else rule pairs an else with the NEAREST unmatched if, regardless of indentation.
else-if ladder: conditions are tested top to bottom, the first true branch runs and the rest are skipped; the final else is optional.
Braces are optional for a single statement, but a semicolon straight after if (...) makes an empty body, so the next statement always runs.
The conditional operator cond ? a : b is an expression form of if/else and can be used inside other expressions.

concepts.text: switch-case
Rules of switch:
items: The controlling expression must be of an integral type: int, char, short, long or enum. float, double, strings and arrays are not allowed.
Each case label must be a compile-time integer constant (case 1:, case 'a':, case MAX: with #define); no variables, no ranges like 1..5 and no duplicate labels.
Execution jumps to the matching case and then continues into the following cases until a break or the end of the switch: this is fall-through.
default is optional, may appear anywhere (usually last) and runs when no case matches; without default an unmatched value does nothing.
break leaves the switch; a continue inside a switch refers to the enclosing loop, not the switch.
Several labels may share one body (case 'a': case 'e': ...), which is intentional fall-through.
switch tests only equality against constants; an else-if ladder is needed for ranges and floating-point tests. switch is usually clearer and faster (jump table) for menus.

concepts.text: The Three Loops

rows: Menus and input validation that must run once

concepts.text:
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)        /* init; test; update */
    printf("%d ", i);              /* 0 1 2 3 4 */

int n = 0;
while (n < 3) { n++; }             /* body runs 3 times, n = 3 */

int m = 10;
do { m++; } while (m < 5);         /* runs ONCE although 10 < 5 is false: m = 11 */

for (;;) { break; }                /* all three parts are optional: infinite loop */
for (i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i++, j--) ;   /* comma operator in init and update */
for-loop mechanics:
items: The initialisation runs once; the condition is tested before every iteration (a false condition at the start means zero iterations); the update runs after the body, then the test repeats.
When the loop ends normally the counter holds the first value that failed the test: after for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) the value of i is 5.
C99 allows a declaration in the init part; that variable exists only inside the loop.
for (;;) and while (1) are the idiomatic infinite loops; a missing update (while (i < 10) with no i++) is an accidental one.
Nested loops: the inner loop runs to completion for every iteration of the outer one, so bodies execute n x m times.
Avoid float counters: for (f = 0; f != 1.0; f += 0.1) may never stop because 0.1 is not exact in binary.

concepts.text: Jump Statements: break, continue, goto
Transferring control:
items: break leaves the innermost enclosing loop or switch immediately, and only that level: a break in an inner loop does not stop the outer loop.
continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the update part of a for loop or to the condition of a while / do-while loop.
goto label; jumps unconditionally within the same function; its accepted use is escaping from deeply nested loops in one step.
return leaves the whole function from any depth of nesting; exit() from stdlib.h ends the program.
break and continue are legal only inside loops (break also inside switch); elsewhere they are compile errors.

concepts.text: Counting Iterations and Classic Bugs
How many times does the body run?
items: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times (i = 0..n-1); for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) also runs n times (i = 1..n) but with different values of i.
for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) runs n + 1 times: the classic off-by-one.
for (i = n; i > 0; i--) runs n times; for (i = 0; i < 10; i += 3) runs 4 times (0, 3, 6, 9).
for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) runs ceil(log2 n) times: n = 100 gives 7 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64).
while (n) { n /= 10; count++; } counts the digits of n; while (n > 0) with n = 0 runs zero times but do { } while (n > 0) runs once.
Nested for i < n and j < n gives n^2 body executions; i < n and j < i gives 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1) = n(n - 1)/2.

concepts.text: Bugs that MCQs are built around:
items: if (x = 5) assigns 5 and is always true; if (x = 0) is always false. The comparison is ==.
for (i = 0; i < 5; i++); with a stray semicolon has an empty body; the block that follows runs once with i = 5.
while (i < 10); with a semicolon is an infinite loop, as is any loop whose condition variable is never updated.
for (unsigned i = 5; i >= 0; i--) never ends because an unsigned value is always >= 0 (it wraps to 4294967295).
A missing break in a switch silently runs the following cases; a break inside an inner loop does not exit the outer loop.
A variable declared in the for header (C99) does not exist after the loop; using it there is a compile error.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Tracing Loops, switch Internals and Jumps

Every for loop can be rewritten as a while loop: for (init; cond; update) body behaves like init; while (cond) { body update; }. The only difference is continue, which still runs the update in the for form but would skip it in the while form. To predict output, trace the loop in a table with one column per variable plus the condition, add a row for every test, and stop at the first row whose condition is false. The values in that row are the values the program sees after the loop.

rows: for (i = a; i <= b; i += s), a <= b

concepts.plainText: for (i = n; i > 0; i /= 2) runs floor(log2 n) + 1 times (n = 50 gives 6)

Output:
1
10
101
1010

Trace (the inner loop runs j = 1..i and prints j % 2):
i = 1: j = 1          -> 1
i = 2: j = 1, 2       -> 1 0
i = 3: j = 1, 2, 3    -> 1 0 1
i = 4: j = 1, 2, 3, 4 -> 1 0 1 0
Inner iterations: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 = 4 x 5 / 2
switch details beyond the basic rules:
items: The integer promotions are applied to the controlling expression, so a char or short is compared as an int; labels may be constant expressions such as 'a' + 1 or 2 * 3.
Two labels that evaluate to the same value, such as case 4: and case 2 * 2:, are a compile error even though they are written differently.
Labels may be written in any order and default may sit anywhere; if default is not last and has no break, control falls into the case written after it.
Statements placed after the opening brace but before the first case label are never executed.
A break inside a switch leaves only the switch; a continue inside a switch that is inside a loop continues that loop.
Compilers often turn a dense set of case values into a jump table, which is why a switch can be faster than a long else-if ladder.

2 2

Trace:
i = 0: s[0] = 'l' -> default, c = 1; s[1] = 'o' is not '\0', repeat
i = 1: s[1] = 'o' -> vowel,   v = 1; s[2] = 'o', repeat
i = 2: s[2] = 'o' -> vowel,   v = 2; s[3] = 'p', repeat

The five stacked labels share one body, and break stops the fall into default.
More loop traps worth tracing carefully:
items: while (n--) tests the old value, so it runs n times and leaves n at -1; while (--n) tests the new value, runs n - 1 times (for n >= 1) and leaves n at 0.
A comma inside a condition, as in i < 3, j < 5, evaluates both tests but uses only the last one (j < 5).
In a while or do-while loop, a continue placed before the update skips that update, so the loop may never end; in a for loop the update still runs.
while (i++ < 3) increments i even on the failing test: starting from 0, the body runs 3 times and i ends at 4.
Changing the counter inside the body adds to the header's step: for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) { i++; } advances by 2 per pass and runs 5 times.
goto can jump backward to build a loop, but only within one function; it can never jump into another function.

For switch questions, mark the entry label first, then read straight down until a break or the closing brace, ignoring the other labels on the way.
