notes.text: if (x = 5) assigns and is always true. The comparison is x == 5. Writing the constant first, if (5 == x), turns the slip into a compile error.

do-while always executes at least once, even when the condition is false from the start, because the test comes after the body. MCQs often pair this with a while loop that runs zero times on the same data.
A semicolon right after for (...) or while (...) is a legal empty statement: for (i = 0; i < 3; i++); printf("%d", i); prints 3 exactly once, and while (x < 5); with no body loops forever.
break exits only the innermost loop or switch. To leave two nested loops at once use a flag variable, a return, or a goto to a label after the outer loop.

concepts.text: Why Functions and Their Three Parts

A function is a self-contained block of code that performs one task and can be called from anywhere in the program. Functions give modularity, reuse, easier testing and shorter programs. Library functions such as printf and sqrt come with the compiler; user-defined functions are written by the programmer. Every user-defined function involves three things: a declaration (prototype) that tells the compiler the name, return type and parameter types; a definition that contains the body; and one or more calls. If the definition appears after main, the prototype is mandatory in C99 because implicit int declarations were removed.
Anatomy of a function:
items: Return type: any type except an array; void means nothing is returned (a bare return; is optional). main returns int.
Parameter list: type and name for each parameter; void f(void) takes none. In C, f() means 'unspecified parameters' (C89 style), so write void explicitly.
Formal parameters appear in the definition; actual arguments appear in the call. Arguments are matched by position and converted to the parameter types.
return expr; sends back exactly one value, converted to the return type, and ends the function; a function may contain several return statements.
Functions cannot be defined inside other functions in C (no nesting), but any function may call any other, including itself.
A call to a function with no prototype in sight is an error in C99 and a warning in older compilers; prototypes for library functions live in the headers.

concepts.text: Call by Value and Call by Reference
Parameter passing in C:
items: Call by value is the only mechanism in C: the function receives a COPY of each argument, so changing a parameter never changes the caller's variable.
Call by reference is simulated by passing an address with & and receiving it in a pointer parameter; the function then modifies the original through *p.
Arrays are the apparent exception: an array name decays to the address of its first element, so a function can modify the caller's elements.
To return more than one value, pass pointers to the result variables or return a struct.
C++ adds true references (void f(int &r)), function overloading and default arguments; those belong to the C++ subtopics.

concepts.text: Scope, Lifetime and Storage Classes
Scope and storage rules inside functions:
items: Local (auto) variables and parameters exist only inside their function or block; they are created fresh on every call and destroyed on return, so their values are not retained.
Two functions may use the same local names without conflict; a local with the same name as a global shadows (hides) the global inside that block.
Global variables are declared outside all functions, are visible from the declaration to the end of the file, are zero-initialised and are shared by every function that uses them.
static local: initialised once (default 0), stored in the data segment and keeps its value between calls: the idiom for call counters.
extern declares a global defined in another file; register asks for a CPU register and forbids &; auto is the default for locals and is never written in practice.
In short: storage class decides where a variable lives (stack, register, data segment), how long it lives (block or whole run) and its default value (garbage or 0).

concepts.text: Recursion

Recursion is a function calling itself, directly or through another function. A correct recursive function has a base case that returns without a further call and a recursive case that moves the problem closer to the base case. Every call gets its own stack frame with its own parameters and locals; the frames pile up until the base case is reached and then unwind, each returning its result to its caller. Without a reachable base case the stack grows until the program crashes (stack overflow). Any recursion can be rewritten as iteration, but recursion is the natural fit for factorial, Fibonacci, GCD, power, Towers of Hanoi, binary search and tree traversal.

long fact(int n) {                        /* n! = n * (n-1)!, 0! = 1 */
    if (n <= 1) return 1;                 /* base case */
    return n * fact(n - 1);               /* fact(4) = 4*3*2*1 = 24 */
}
int fib(int n) {                          /* 0 1 1 2 3 5 8 13 ... */
    if (n < 2) return n;                  /* fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1 */
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);       /* two calls: O(2^n) time */
}
int gcd(int a, int b) {                   /* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) */
    return b == 0 ? a : gcd(b, a % b);    /* gcd(48,18)->(18,12)->(12,6)->(6,0) = 6 */
}
int power(int x, int n) { return n == 0 ? 1 : x * power(x, n - 1); }  /* x^n */

rows: Function calls itself; uses the call stack
Loop repeats inside one stack frame
One frame per active call: O(depth)
Shorter and natural for trees, divide and conquer
Longer for those problems, natural for counting
Stack overflow if deep or no base case
Infinite loop if the condition never fails

concepts.text: Counting calls is a common question: fact(n) makes n calls (depth n) and runs in O(n); the naive fib(n) makes about 2^n calls because each call spawns two, which is why fib(40) is visibly slow while a loop is instant. Finally, a function pointer stores the address of a function: int (*fp)(int, int) = add; then fp(2, 3) calls add, which is how callbacks such as the comparator of qsort work.
Going Deeper: Recursion, Call Counts and Function Pointers

A function call is a fixed sequence: the caller evaluates the arguments, the values are copied into the parameters of a new stack frame together with the return address, and control jumps to the function. When return runs, its value is handed back and the frame is discarded. In recursion every active call has its own frame, so the name n refers to a different variable in each call. Two numbers describe a recursion and must not be confused: the depth is the largest number of frames alive at one moment (it decides stack use), while the total number of calls is how many frames are ever created (it decides running time).

The Tower of Hanoi shows how a recurrence gives a closed form. To move n disks from A to C, move the top n - 1 disks to the spare peg B, move the largest disk to C, then move the n - 1 disks from B onto it. The move count therefore obeys T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + 1 with T(1) = 1, giving 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, ... Adding 1 to both sides gives T(n) + 1 = 2(T(n - 1) + 1), so T(n) + 1 doubles at every step and equals 2^n. The smallest disk moves on every other move, 2^(n - 1) times in all.

concepts.plainText: T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + 1 with T(1) = 1, so T(n) = 2^n - 1 (3 disks: 7 moves, 5 disks: 31, 10 disks: 1023)

hanoi(3,A,C,B)

  move disk 3     prints 3:AC            (1 move)
  hanoi(2,B,C,A)  prints 1:BA 2:BC 1:AC   (3 moves)
Total = 3 + 1 + 3 = 7 = 2^3 - 1 moves; disk 1 moves 4 = 2^2 times

Output: sd(4)=4 sd(47)=11 sd(472)=13

Winding (calls go down, nothing printed yet):

Unwinding (each frame finishes its own line):
  sd(4)   r = 4 + 0   = 4    printed first
  sd(47)  r = 7 + 4   = 11
  sd(472) r = 2 + 11  = 13   printed last
Statements after the recursive call run in reverse order of the calls.

concepts.text: Function pointers, lifetimes and common mistakes:
items: int (*fp)(int, int) = add; declares fp as a pointer to a function taking two ints and returning int; without the parentheses, int *fp(int, int); declares a function that returns int *.
A function name decays to its address, so fp = add and fp = &add are equivalent, and fp(2, 3) and (*fp)(2, 3) both call add.
An array of function pointers such as int (*op[3])(int, int) = {add, sub, mul}; replaces a switch with a table lookup: op[choice](a, b).
Passing a function pointer as a parameter creates a callback: qsort calls the programmer's int cmp(const void *, const void *) for every comparison.
Never return the address of an automatic local: its frame is gone after the return. Return the value, or the address of a static or malloc'ed object.
In C a static local must be initialised with a constant expression (static int n = 0; is fine, static int n = f(); is not), and the initialisation happens only once.
Changing a parameter never changes the caller's argument, and in recursion n-- inside one call does not alter n in the caller's frame; f(n--) even passes the old value and recurses forever.

concepts.text: To trace a recursive function, write one line per call with its argument, then unwind from the deepest call upward. Statements before the recursive call run in call order (on the way down); statements after it run in reverse order (on the way back). Count calls with a recurrence such as C(n) = 2C(n - 1) + 1 rather than by listing every call.

Call by value means swap(x, y) with plain int parameters leaves x and y unchanged; the answer to 'what is x after the call' is its original value. Only a version taking int * (called with &x, &y) swaps them.

Calling a function defined below main without a prototype is an error in C99 (implicit declaration). Prototypes end with a semicolon; definitions do not, and a semicolon after the definition's closing brace is harmless but a semicolon after the header line is an error.
A static local keeps its value between calls but is still invisible outside the function; a global keeps its value and is visible everywhere. Both are zero-initialised, unlike an ordinary local.

concepts.text: One-Dimensional Arrays

An array is a fixed-size collection of elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory and accessed by an index that runs from 0 to size - 1. The declaration type name[size]; needs a constant size in C89 (C99 also allows variable-length arrays). Local arrays without an initialiser contain garbage; = {0} sets every element to zero, a partial initialiser zero-fills the remaining elements, and int a[] = {1, 2, 3} infers the size from the list. C does no bounds checking: reading or writing a[5] in a 5-element array compiles and silently corrupts memory.

int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};    /* a[0] = 10 ... a[4] = 50 */
int b[5] = {1, 2};                  /* rest are 0: 1 2 0 0 0 */
int c[] = {7, 8, 9};                /* size inferred: 3 */
int n = sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]);   /* 20 / 4 = 5 elements */
a[5] = 99;                          /* out of bounds: NO check, undefined */
printf("%d %d\n", a[2], *(a + 2));  /* 30 30 */
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(c));         /* 12 */
printf("%d\n", a == &a[0]);         /* 1 */
Array facts:
items: Elements are contiguous, so &a[i] = base address + i * sizeof(type); for int a[5] at address 1000, &a[3] is 1012.
The array name is a constant pointer to the first element: a == &a[0] and a[i] == *(a + i), but a = b and a++ are errors.
sizeof(a) is the whole array in bytes (n * sizeof(type)) inside the scope where it is declared; sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) gives the element count.
Arrays cannot be assigned or compared with = and ==; copy with a loop or memcpy and compare element by element.
Static and global arrays are zero-initialised; local arrays are not.

concepts.text: Two-Dimensional and Multi-Dimensional Arrays

int m[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};   /* 2 rows, 3 columns */
int k[2][3] = {1, 2, 3, 4};             /* row-major fill: {1,2,3},{4,0,0} */
int r[][3] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};        /* only the FIRST size may be omitted */
printf("%d\n", m[1][2]);                /* 6 */
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(m));             /* 2 * 3 * 4 = 24 bytes */
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++)
        printf("%d ", m[i][j]);         /* 1 2 3 4 5 6 */
int cube[2][3][4];                      /* 3-D: 2*3*4 = 24 ints, cube[i][j][k] */
Row-major storage and addressing:
items: C stores a 2-D array row after row: m[0][0], m[0][1], m[0][2], m[1][0], ... so the last index varies fastest.
Address of m[i][j] = base + (i * cols + j) * sizeof(type); for int m[3][4] at 2000, &m[2][1] = 2000 + (2 * 4 + 1) * 4 = 2036.
m[i] is the i-th row, itself an array of cols elements, and decays to a pointer to m[i][0]; m[i][j] == *(*(m + i) + j).
A 3-D array a[d1][d2][d3] holds d1 * d2 * d3 elements and &a[i][j][k] = base + ((i * d2 + j) * d3 + k) * sizeof(type).
When a 2-D array is a parameter every dimension except the first must be given: void f(int a[][3], int rows).
Matrix addition, transpose and multiplication (an r1 x c1 times a c1 x c2 matrix gives r1 x c2) are the standard 2-D array programs.

concepts.text: Arrays and Functions

When an array is passed to a function its name decays to a pointer to the first element, so the function receives an address rather than a copy: changes made through the parameter are visible to the caller, which makes array passing behave like call by reference. Because only the address arrives, sizeof(arr) inside the function is the pointer size (4 or 8), and the element count must be passed as a separate argument. int arr[] and int *arr are interchangeable as parameter declarations. A function cannot return an array by value; it returns a pointer to a static or dynamically allocated array instead.
C-Strings

The row-major formula follows from counting. For an array with M rows and N columns, reaching m[i][j] means skipping i complete rows of N elements each and then j more elements in row i, so the element sits i × N + j places after the first one; multiplying by the element size w gives the byte offset. Column-major order, used by Fortran and MATLAB, stores whole columns one after another, so the count becomes j × M + i. Languages whose indices may start at another lower bound, such as Pascal's A[1..10], subtract the bounds first, while C indices always start at 0. Because the compiler needs N to evaluate the formula, every dimension except the first must appear in a parameter declaration.

concepts.plainText: Row-major: Loc(A[i][j]) = B + w * ((i - Lr) * N + (j - Lc)), where N = number of columns and Lr, Lc = lower bounds (0 in C)
Column-major: Loc(A[i][j]) = B + w * ((j - Lc) * M + (i - Lr)), where M = number of rows

concepts.text: Details of the <string.h> functions that questions like to test:
items: strncpy(d, s, n) copies at most n characters; if s is shorter it pads d with '\0' up to n, and if s has n or more characters it writes no terminator at all.
strcat(d, s) starts writing at the '\0' of d, so d must already hold a terminated string and have room for strlen(d) + strlen(s) + 1 bytes.
strcmp compares characters as unsigned char values and stops at the first difference or at the end; the standard guarantees only the sign of the result, not a value such as 1 or -1.
strchr(s, c) and strrchr(s, c) return a pointer into s (subtract s to get the index) or NULL; the terminating '\0' counts as part of the string, so strchr(s, '\0') points at the end.
strstr(s, t) returns a pointer to the first occurrence of t or NULL, and an empty t matches at once, so strstr(s, "") returns s.
strlen walks the whole string on every call, so for (i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++) can cost O(n²) steps; store the length in a variable first.
fgets keeps the newline the user typed, while scanf("%s") stops at the first space or newline and leaves the rest in the input buffer.

Inside a function that receives an array, sizeof(arr) is the size of a pointer (4 or 8), not of the array, so the element count must always be passed as a separate parameter.

concepts.text: Array Name as a Pointer

In almost every expression an array name is converted to a pointer to its first element: arr is the same as &arr[0]. Because of this, arr[i] is defined as *(arr + i), and by commutativity of + even i[arr] is legal. There are two exceptions where the name means the whole array: sizeof arr gives the total size in bytes, and &arr gives a pointer to the whole array (type int (*)[n]) whose + 1 skips the entire array. An array name is not a variable, so arr++ or arr = p is a compile error, whereas a pointer that holds the same address may be moved freely.

int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};
int *p = a;                              /* a decays to &a[0] */
printf("%d %d\n", a[2], *(a + 2));       /* 3 3 */
printf("%d\n", 2[a]);                    /* 3 : legal, same as a[2] */
printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof a, sizeof p); /* 16 and 4 (32-bit) or 8 (64-bit) */
p++;                                     /* fine: p is a variable */
/* a++;   ERROR: an array name is not modifiable */
printf("%d\n", *p);                      /* 2 */
printf("%d\n", *a + 1);                  /* 2 : (*a) + 1, not a[1] */

concepts.text: Traversing an array with a pointer:
items: for (p = a; p < a + n; p++) sum += *p; uses the one-past-the-end address a + n as a limit; that address may be formed and compared but never dereferenced.
Equivalent index form: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += *(a + i); the compiler generates the same code.
A string is a char array ending in '\0', so char *s = str; while (*s) s++; walks to the terminator and s - str is the length.
Reversing with two pointers: int *lo = a, *hi = a + n - 1; while (lo < hi) { swap(*lo, *hi); lo++; hi--; }

concepts.text: 2-D Arrays and Arrays of Pointers

A 2-D array int m[3][4] is an array of 3 arrays of 4 ints, stored row by row (row-major). The name m decays to a pointer to its first row, of type int (*)[4], so m + 1 skips a whole row of 4 × 4 = 16 bytes. m[i] is the i-th row (itself decaying to int *), so m[i][j] is *(*(m + i) + j), and because rows are contiguous it also equals *(&m[0][0] + i × 4 + j). An array of pointers, char *names[] = {"Ram", "Sita"}, is different: each element is a separate pointer that may point to strings of different lengths (a ragged array), and names[i][j] is the j-th character of the i-th string.

int m[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};
int (*row)[3] = m;                 /* pointer to an array of 3 ints */
printf("%d\n", *(*(m + 1) + 2));   /* 6 : m[1][2] */
printf("%d\n", **(m + 1));         /* 4 : m[1][0] */
printf("%d\n", *(&m[0][0] + 4));   /* 5 : linear index 1*3 + 1 */
printf("%d\n", row[1][0]);         /* 4 : row behaves like m */
char *names[] = {"Ram", "Sita"};   /* array of 2 char pointers */
printf("%c\n", names[1][0]);       /* S */
int *ptrs[3];                      /* array of 3 int pointers, NOT int (*)[3] */
Passing Pointers and Arrays to Functions

C passes every argument by value: the callee receives a copy and cannot alter the caller's variable. To let a function change a variable, pass its address and dereference inside the function; this simulates call by reference and is how scanf, swap and every "output parameter" work. An array argument is passed as a pointer to its first element, so a parameter written int a[] or int a[10] is really int *a: element changes made in the function are visible to the caller, but sizeof(a) inside the function is the pointer size, so the length must be passed separately.
Returning pointers from functions:
items: A function may return a pointer to static or global storage, to heap memory from malloc, or to memory the caller passed in (for example, strcpy returns its destination).
It must never return the address of a local automatic variable: char *f(void) { char s[10]; return s; } returns a dangling pointer because s is destroyed when f returns.
When the function returns a malloc block, the caller owns it and must call free.
A 2-D array parameter must give every dimension except the first: void f(int m[][4], int rows), equivalent to int (*m)[4].

concepts.text: Function Pointers and Strings

A function pointer stores the address of a function: int (*fp)(int, int) = add; (the & is optional) and is called as fp(2, 3) or (*fp)(2, 3). Its main use is the callback: a routine such as qsort receives a comparison function through a pointer, so one sorting algorithm serves every data type. An array of function pointers implements menu dispatch tables. Strings are handled entirely through char pointers: char *s = "abc" points to a read-only string literal, whereas char s[] = "abc" makes a writable copy; string functions like strlen and strcpy walk the pointer until the '\0' terminator.

The C standard defines the subscript operator through pointer arithmetic: E1[E2] means *((E1) + (E2)). An array name decays to a pointer to its first element in every expression except when it is the operand of sizeof or of unary &, so a[i], *(a + i), *(i + a) and even i[a] name the same element. Decay keeps the address but fixes the type, and the type decides how far + 1 moves. That is why a, &a[0] and &a all start at the same byte, yet a + 1 and &a + 1 land in different places.

The same rule separates int *f(int), a function returning int *, from int (*f)(int), a pointer to such a function.

concepts.text: Defining and Using Structures

A structure groups variables of different types under one name, forming a record such as a student with roll number, name and marks. struct tag { members }; defines a new type (allocating no memory), and struct tag v; declares a variable of it; the two can be combined in one statement. A variable is initialised with a brace list in member order, or with C99 designated initialisers such as {.roll = 2}, and members are accessed with the dot operator. A whole structure may be assigned to another of the same type (all members are copied, including arrays), passed to and returned from functions, but structures cannot be compared with ==; compare member by member.
Rules for structures:
items: The definition (struct Student { ... };) is a blueprint and occupies no memory; memory is allocated only when variables are declared.
Members may be of any type: scalars, arrays, pointers, other structures, even a pointer to the same structure type; a structure cannot contain itself by value.
Structure tags live in their own namespace, so struct point point; is legal though confusing. Without a tag the type is anonymous and can only be used in that one declaration.
Members are laid out in the order declared, at increasing addresses; the address of the structure equals the address of its first member.
s1 == s2 is a compile error; s1 = s2 copies all members, and array members are copied deep.

concepts.text: Nested Structures, typedef and sizeof

sizeof(struct) is at least the sum of its members, but it is often larger because the compiler inserts padding bytes so that each member starts at an address that is a multiple of its alignment (an int at a multiple of 4, a double at a multiple of 8 on most compilers) and the total size is rounded up to a multiple of the largest member alignment so that consecutive elements of an array of the structure stay aligned. The exact result is compiler-dependent, so a question that expects it must state the sizes. Ordering members from largest to smallest minimises padding, and #pragma pack(1) removes it at the cost of slower, unaligned access.

concepts.text: Unions

A union is declared with the same syntax as a structure, but all of its members share the same storage starting at the same address, so its size is that of the largest member (rounded up to alignment). Only the member written most recently holds a meaningful value; reading a different member reinterprets the same bytes. Unions save memory when only one of several alternatives is needed at a time, model variant records (usually paired with a tag field that says which member is live), give access to individual bytes of a value (endianness test) and describe hardware registers.

rows: Each member has its own location
All members hold values at the same time

concepts.text: Enumerations and Bit Fields

An enumeration defines named integer constants: enum Color { RED, GREEN = 5, BLUE }; gives RED = 0, GREEN = 5 and BLUE = 6, each value being one more than the previous unless assigned. Variables of an enum type are stored as int (sizeof is normally 4) and can be used wherever an int is expected, but they make code far more readable than #define constants. Bit fields are structure members declared with a width in bits, such as unsigned int flag : 1; several of them are packed into one int so that flags and small counters use minimal memory. A bit field cannot have its address taken with &, cannot be an array, and its width cannot exceed the size of its base type; the order of bits inside the word is implementation-defined.
The user-defined types of C at a glance:
items: struct: heterogeneous record; every member has its own storage.
union: same syntax as struct but members overlap; size = largest member.
enum: a set of named integer constants; the underlying type is int.
typedef: creates an alias for an existing type; it never creates a new type or allocates storage.
bit field: a struct or union member of fixed bit width, used to pack flags.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Layout Rules, Union Reads and Bit Fields

The compiler lays out a structure with two rules. Before each member it rounds the current offset up to the next multiple of that member's alignment, and after the last member it rounds the total up to a multiple of the largest alignment in the structure. The first rule lets the processor fetch every member in one aligned access; the second keeps every element of an array of the structure aligned, because element i starts at i × sizeof(struct). The first member is always at offset 0, so a structure and its first member have the same address.

concepts.latex: o_k = \left\lceil e_{k-1} / a_k \right\rceil a_k,\quad e_k = o_k + s_k
concepts.plainText: offset o_k of member k = end e_(k-1) of the previous member rounded up to a multiple of its alignment a_k; its end e_k = o_k + size s_k
sizeof(struct) = end e_n of the last member rounded up to a multiple of the largest member alignment A

A union holds one value at a time, so the safe rule is to read the member that was written last. Structures may be assigned and passed by value (all members copied, array members included), but they cannot be compared with == or printed with a single printf; handle member by member.

concepts.text: Array of Structures

An array whose elements are structures stores a table of records: struct Student s[50]; holds 50 students, and s[i].marks is one field of one record. It is initialised with nested braces, filled and printed with ordinary loops, and searched by comparing a member of each element. Sorting records is done by comparing one key member and swapping whole elements, because s[i] = s[j] copies every member at once. The array occupies 50 × sizeof(struct Student) bytes, padding included.
Pointers to Structures

A pointer to a structure, struct Student *p = &s[0], reaches members either as (*p).roll or with the arrow shorthand p->roll, which means exactly the same. The parentheses are essential in the first form because . and -> have the highest precedence (together with () and []), so *p.roll parses as *(p.roll) and is an error. Incrementing a structure pointer moves it by sizeof(struct), i.e. to the next record, so an array of structures is naturally walked with a pointer. A string member reached through p->name is still an array: it must be copied with strcpy, not assigned with =.

concepts.text: Passing Structures to Functions

A structure can be passed to a function by value: the whole record is copied onto the stack, so the callee works on a copy and the caller's data is safe, but copying a large record on every call is slow. Passing a pointer copies only an address (4 or 8 bytes), is fast, and lets the callee modify the original through ->; declare the parameter const struct T * when modification should be prevented. Individual members can also be passed like ordinary variables (f(s.marks)). A function may return a whole structure by value, which is the usual way to build and hand back a record.

concepts.text: Dynamic and Self-Referential Structures

Records can be created on the heap when the count is known only at run time: struct Student *list = malloc(n * sizeof(struct Student)); then list[i].roll and (list + i)->roll both address the i-th record, and free(list) releases the whole table. A self-referential structure contains a pointer to its own type: struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; }; is the node of a linked list, and a version with left and right pointers is a tree node. The structure cannot contain a struct Node by value (it would be infinitely large) but a pointer to one has a fixed size, so the chain can grow one malloc at a time.
Checklist when structures meet pointers:
items: Use -> after a pointer and . after a structure variable; (*p).m and p->m are interchangeable.
scanf needs & for scalar members (&s.roll) but not for array members (s.name), which are already addresses.
String members are arrays: copy with strcpy(p->name, "Ram"), never p->name = "Ram".
Allocate with sizeof(struct T) or sizeof *p, never a hand-added sum of member sizes, because padding is included in sizeof.

concepts.text: Opening and Closing Files

C reads and writes files through the <stdio.h> stream functions. FILE *fp = fopen("name", "mode"); opens a file and returns a pointer to a FILE object that records the buffer, the current position and error flags; it returns NULL when the file cannot be opened (missing file in read mode, no permission, bad path), so the result must always be checked. fclose(fp) flushes the buffer to disk and releases the FILE; it returns 0 on success and EOF on error. Because output is buffered, data written may not reach the disk until fclose or fflush(fp) is called. Three streams are open automatically: stdin, stdout and stderr.

concepts.text: EOF is a macro with value −1 returned by fgetc, getc, fscanf and others when the end of the file is reached or an error occurs; it is why the character functions return int rather than char. feof(fp) becomes true only after a read has already failed, so the loop while (!feof(fp)) { fscanf(...); process(); } processes the last item twice; the correct idiom tests the return value of the read call itself. ferror(fp) reports a hardware or logical error on the stream, clearerr(fp) resets both indicators, and perror(msg) prints a system message for the last failure.
Binary Files and Records

A text file stores numbers as sequences of digit characters of varying length, is human-readable and portable, and may translate the newline character on some systems. A binary file stores the exact memory image of the data: a structure written with fwrite always occupies sizeof(struct) bytes, so the n-th record (counting from 0) starts at byte n × sizeof(struct). This fixed-length layout is what makes random access possible; the cost is that binary files are unreadable in an editor and not portable across machines with different sizes or byte order. On Unix the b in the mode is ignored; on Windows it disables the \n to \r\n translation, which would corrupt binary data.
Sequential vs Random Access

Every open file has a position indicator that says where the next read or write happens. In sequential access the program starts at the beginning and each operation advances the indicator, so reaching the 100th record means reading the 99 before it; this suits text files with variable-length lines and log files. In random (direct) access the program moves the indicator anywhere with fseek(fp, offset, origin), where offset is a long byte count and origin is SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR or SEEK_END; the call returns 0 on success. ftell(fp) returns the current byte offset from the start as a long, and rewind(fp) is equivalent to fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_SET) plus clearing the error and EOF flags. In the "+" modes an fseek or rewind is also required when switching between reading and writing, and in a or a+ mode every write still goes to the end whatever fseek says.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: File I/O in Practice

Every FILE stream keeps a buffer, a position indicator and two status flags, end-of-file and error. Output functions first copy data into the buffer, which is written to the file when it fills, when fflush(fp) or fclose(fp) is called, or when main returns or exit() is called; a crash or abort() can lose buffered data. The position indicator counts bytes from the start of the file and advances with every successful read or write, which is why ftell reports data that may still be sitting in the buffer. Input functions set the end-of-file flag only when they try to read beyond the last byte, and set the error flag on a device or logical failure.

concepts.text: Common mistakes in file programs:
items: Not testing fopen for NULL and then passing the NULL pointer to fprintf or fgetc, which is undefined behaviour.
Storing fgetc's result in a char, or looping on while (!feof(fp)) instead of testing the value that each read returns.
Forgetting the b on Windows for binary data, so every byte 0x0A written by fwrite gains a 0x0D in front of it and all later record offsets shift.
Opening a file that must be kept with "w", which silently destroys its contents; use "a" or "r+" instead.
Calling fflush(stdin) to discard input: fflush is defined only for output streams.
Mixing up fread's size and count: fread(buf, 1, 40, fp) returns a byte count up to 40, while fread(buf, 40, 1, fp) returns only 0 or 1.

concepts.text: Besides reading and writing, <stdio.h> manages whole files: remove(name) deletes a file and rename(old, new) renames it, both returning 0 on success and nonzero on failure, while tmpfile() creates an anonymous temporary file in "wb+" mode that disappears when it is closed. When an operation fails, ferror(fp) tells a real error apart from end of file (feof), clearerr(fp) resets both flags, and perror("msg") prints msg followed by a description of the error recorded in errno. A robust program checks every fopen, compares every read's return value with what it expected, and checks the result of fclose for output files, because a full disk may be reported only when the buffer is flushed.

For output-prediction questions, track three things line by line: the file's current contents, the position indicator in bytes from 0, and the value each call returns. Remember that fread and fwrite count items, fprintf counts characters, fscanf counts assigned items, and every read moves the position forward by the bytes it consumed.

concepts.text: Class and Object

A class is a user-defined type that bundles data members (attributes, state) with the member functions (methods, behaviour) that operate on them. It is only a blueprint: declaring a class allocates no memory. An object is a variable of a class type, an instance created at run time; each object gets its own copy of the data members, while the member functions exist once and are shared. Defining a class ends with a semicolon after the closing brace, a frequent syntax slip.

rows: Can hold member functions, constructors, static members
Types with invariants and hidden state
Data only; no functions, no access control

concepts.text: Access Specifiers
How the labels behave inside a class body:
items: A label applies to every member that follows it until the next label; labels may appear in any order and may be repeated.
Members written before any label are private in a class and public in a struct.
Access control is checked per class, not per object: a member function may touch the private members of another object of the same class (needed for copy constructors and operator==).
Friends (friend functions and friend classes) are the only outsiders that bypass private and protected.
Access specifiers are a compile-time rule; they do not change the memory layout or add run-time cost.
Data hiding convention: data members private, the operations that keep them consistent public, helper functions private or protected.

{ return r1.area() + r2.area(); }                  // r2 is a COPY of the argument

Objects in expressions and function calls:
items: Use . for an object (or reference) and -> for a pointer; p->m is exactly (*p).m. Precedence: . and -> bind tighter than *, so *p.m means *(p.m).
An array of objects Type arr[n] constructs n objects with the default constructor; Type arr[2] = { Type(1), Type(2) } constructs each element with a parameterised constructor.

Passing an object by value copies it (copy constructor runs, changes inside are lost); pass by reference (Type &) to modify it, by const reference (const Type &) to read it cheaply, or by pointer (Type *).
A function can return an object by value; the result is a temporary copy. Member functions can also return *this by reference.
Objects of the same class can be assigned with = (member-wise copy) and copied at definition; other operators (==, +, <<) work only when overloaded.

concepts.text: Defining Member Functions Inside or Outside the Class
Inside vs outside definition:
items: Inside the class body: short and automatically treated as inline; usual for one-line getters and setters.

Outside the class body: the declaration (prototype) stays in the class and the definition uses ReturnType ClassName::function(params); this keeps headers readable and lets the code go into a .cpp file.
The scope resolution operator :: tells the compiler which class the function belongs to; without it the compiler sees an ordinary free function that cannot access the private members.
A const after the parameter list must appear in both the declaration and the outside definition.

concepts.text: Encapsulation, Data Hiding and Object Size
Why data members are private and how objects sit in memory:
items: Encapsulation binds data and the functions that use it into one unit; data hiding (private) prevents outside code from putting an object into an invalid state, so validation lives in one place (the setter) and the internal representation can change without breaking callers.
Getters (accessors) return a value and are declared const; setters (mutators) validate and then store. Not every member needs both.
sizeof(object) is the total of its non-static data members plus alignment padding; member functions, static members and access labels add nothing (a virtual function adds one vptr).
An empty class has sizeof 1, never 0, so that two distinct objects always have distinct addresses.
The same member function code serves every object; the object it works on is passed implicitly as the this pointer.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Objects in Memory and in Function Calls

Behind the call obj.f(x), the compiler runs the single shared copy of f and passes it the address of obj as a hidden argument (the this pointer), which is why member functions add nothing to sizeof and yet every call still sees its own object's data. Access labels are checked only by the compiler and per class: c.secret is refused in main(), but a member function may read the private data of any object of its own class. An object passed by value is a separate copy, an object passed by reference or through a pointer is the caller's object itself, and an object returned by value is a fresh copy handed back to the caller. The program below shows all three cases.

a.cash = 50
spend(a)     : w is a copy; the copy drops to 20, a.cash stays 50   -> 50
spendRef(a)  : w is another name for a, so a.cash becomes 20        -> 20
refill(a)    : a copy of a (20) grows to 120 and is returned into b;
               a itself is untouched                                -> 20 120
Output: 50 20 20 120

concepts.text: The size of an object that holds only data members follows two alignment rules. Each member starts at the next offset that is a multiple of its own alignment (on a typical 64-bit compiler char is 1, short 2, int 4, and double and pointers 8), so padding bytes may be inserted before it. The total is then rounded up to a multiple of the largest member alignment, so that every element of an array of objects is also correctly aligned. Static data members, member functions and access labels are not stored in the object at all.

concepts.text: Constructors

A constructor is a special member function that is called automatically whenever an object is created, to initialise its data members. It has exactly the same name as the class, has no return type (not even void), is normally public, can be overloaded, and cannot be virtual or called explicitly like an ordinary function. If a class declares no constructor at all, the compiler generates a public default constructor that does nothing for built-in members; the moment you write any constructor, that implicit default one disappears.

rows: Box a; Box arr[3]; new Box;
Box b(5); Box b = Box(5); new Box(5);
Box c = b; Box c(b); pass or return an object by value
Only when the class does not declare its own

concepts.text: Rules and details that MCQs test:
items: Constructor overloading: one class may have several constructors with different parameter lists; the argument list at object creation selects one.

Member initialiser list Box(int l) : len(l) { } initialises members before the body runs; it is the ONLY way to initialise const members, reference members and base-class or member objects without default constructors. Members are initialised in declaration order, not list order.
A constructor with default arguments, e.g. Box(int l = 0), also serves as the default constructor; keeping it together with Box() makes Box a; ambiguous.
A single-argument constructor doubles as an implicit conversion (Box b = 5;); prefix it with explicit to allow only Box b(5).
Constructors cannot be inherited, cannot be virtual, and cannot be const; they may call other functions and may be declared private (singleton pattern).
C++11 adds delegating constructors (Box() : Box(0) { }) and uniform initialisation with braces: Box b{5};.

concepts.text: Copy Constructor: Shallow vs Deep Copy
Copy semantics:
items: The copy constructor runs when an object is initialised from another of the same type, when an object is passed to a function by value, and when a function returns an object by value. Plain assignment a = b after both exist calls operator= instead.
Its parameter must be a reference (usually const Box &); taking it by value would need a copy, which needs the copy constructor, and so on forever.
The compiler-generated copy constructor performs a member-wise (shallow) copy: pointers are copied, not the memory they point to.

Shallow copy is fine for classes with only value members; classes that own heap memory, file handles or other resources need a user-written deep copy, a matching operator= and a destructor (rule of three).
Passing objects by const reference avoids the copy altogether and is the normal choice for large objects.

concepts.text: Destructors
A destructor releases whatever the object acquired (heap memory, files, locks) and is called automatically when the object's life ends:
items: Name: tilde plus class name, ~Box(). No parameters, no return type, hence exactly one per class; it cannot be overloaded.
Called when a local object goes out of scope, when delete is applied to a heap object, when a temporary dies, and at program end for static/global objects.
Objects are destroyed in the REVERSE order of their construction (last created, first destroyed); array elements likewise in reverse index order.
If the class does not declare one, the compiler supplies an empty destructor; a class that owns resources must write its own.
A destructor may be called explicitly (obj.~Box()) but this is almost always wrong; a base class destructor should be virtual when objects are deleted through base pointers (topic 3.5).
The destructor must never throw; C++11 makes destructors noexcept by default.

concepts.text: Dynamic Objects and Object Arrays: new / delete

Box *p = new Box(7);        // allocate + run Box(int); prints "param "
delete p;                   // run ~Box (prints "destroy7 ") + free memory
p = nullptr;                // avoid a dangling pointer

Box *arr = new Box[3];      // 3 objects; DEFAULT constructor x3
                            // (no way to pass arguments to each element pre-C++11)
arr[1] = Box(4);            // temporary Box(4) assigned into element 1
delete[] arr;               // destructors x3 in reverse (arr[2], arr[1], arr[0])

int *k = new int(5);        // built-in type: value-initialised to 5
int *m = new int[10]();     // ten ints zeroed by the ()
delete k; delete[] m;

concepts.text: Memory pitfalls with dynamic objects:
items: Memory leak: every new needs exactly one matching delete; losing the pointer (reassigning it, returning early, an exception) leaks the block until the process ends.

Mismatch: memory from new[] must be released with delete[], not delete, otherwise only the first element's destructor runs and the heap can be corrupted. Never mix malloc with delete or new with free.
Double delete and use after delete (dangling pointer) are undefined behaviour; set the pointer to nullptr after deleting, since delete nullptr is a safe no-op.
A class that stores a pointer obtained with new should release it in the destructor, which makes the object's lifetime manage the memory (RAII).
Local objects on the stack are cleaned up automatically; prefer them, and reach for new only when the object must outlive the scope or its size is decided at run time.

concepts.text: Worked Example: Order of Constructor and Destructor Calls
Going Deeper: Object Lifetime, Copies and Clean-up

Every object's life is bracketed by exactly one constructor call and, unless it is leaked, one destructor call. Where the object lives decides when its constructor runs: a local object at its definition, a global object before main() starts, a static local object the first time control passes its definition, a heap object at new, and a temporary where the expression creates it. Destruction mirrors this: locals die at the closing brace of their block, temporaries at the end of the full expression (the semicolon), heap objects only at delete, and static and global objects after main() returns, last constructed first destroyed. Inside one object, member objects are constructed in declaration order before the constructor body runs, and destroyed in the reverse order after the destructor body.

concepts.text: The copy constructor runs whenever a new object is initialised from an existing one: T b = a;, T b(a);, T b{a};, and passing an object to a function by value. Since C++17, initialising an object from a temporary of the same type builds it in place, so T x = T(5); and return T(5); call only T(int) and no copy constructor. Returning a named local object may also skip the copy (named return value optimisation), so textbook counts that include that copy can differ from what a real compiler prints. Assignment a = b; between two existing objects never calls a constructor; it calls operator=.

Buf b = a : the copy constructor gives b its own int (1)  -> "copy "
Buf c(9)  : c.p -> new int holding 9
c = a     : operator= copies the value 1 into c's int     -> "assign "
*a.p = 5  : only a's int changes; b and c still hold 1
Output: copy assign 511
With the compiler's shallow versions, all three p would hold one
address: the line would print 555 and the three destructors would then
delete one int three times, which is undefined behaviour.

concepts.text: Traps in constructor and destructor questions:
items: Members are initialised in the order they are declared in the class, whatever order the initialiser list uses; a member initialised from a later-declared member reads an uninitialised value.
A constructor whose parameters all have defaults, such as W(int x = 5), is also a default constructor, so declaring W() as well makes W w; ambiguous.
explicit on a one-argument constructor blocks T t = 5; and calls such as f(5) that need an implicit conversion, while T t(5); and T t = T(5); still compile.
T(4); on its own line creates and immediately destroys a temporary, so its constructor and destructor output appear together at that point.
A static local object is constructed only on the first call and destroyed after main() returns, not at the end of each call.
An object created with new whose pointer is lost is never destroyed, so its destructor output never appears; every new[] also needs delete[].

concepts.text: Never let two objects own the same heap block. If a class has a destructor that deletes a pointer member, the compiler's shallow copy constructor and assignment make two objects delete one block, which is undefined behaviour. Either write all three members (rule of three) or forbid copying with T(const T &) = delete;.

Objects (and array elements) are destroyed in the reverse order of their construction
Every new must be matched by exactly one delete, every new[] by exactly one delete[]

notes.text: Deleting an array obtained with new Box[3] using plain delete runs only one destructor and corrupts the heap; use delete[]. The reverse mistake, delete[] on a single object, is equally undefined.

Output-order questions: constructors run in the order objects are defined, destructors in the reverse order; a heap object's destructor runs at delete, not at scope exit; a block-local object dies at its closing brace. Writing the sequence C.. D.. as in the worked example gives the answer quickly.

As soon as you declare any constructor, the compiler stops providing the default one: class B { public: B(int); }; makes B x; and B arr[5]; compile errors. Add B() or give the parameter a default value.

concepts.text: Static Data Members
A static data member belongs to the class rather than to any object; there is exactly one copy no matter how many objects exist (or even if none exist):
items: Declared inside the class with the keyword static, but defined (and storage allocated) exactly once outside the class: int Counter::count = 0; (no static keyword in the definition). Omitting this definition gives an undefined reference link error.
Initialised once, before main() runs, to zero if no initialiser is given; it is not initialised by constructors.
Accessed with the class name Counter::count or through any object obj.count; the class form works even when no object exists.
Not counted in sizeof(object) because it lives in static storage, not inside objects.
Typical uses: counting live objects, shared configuration, constants; a static const int member may be initialised inside the class.

concepts.text: Static Member Functions
A static member function is also class-wide:
items: It is called as Class::f() (or via an object) and can run without any object.
It receives no this pointer, so it can access only static data members, other static functions and its own parameters; touching a non-static member directly is a compile error.
It cannot be declared const, virtual or volatile, because all three concern a particular object.
static appears only in the declaration inside the class, not in an outside definition.

rows: No; may use static members only

concepts.text: const Member Functions and const Objects
Rules for const:
items: Writing const after the parameter list, double get() const, promises the function will not modify any data member; the compiler makes this (the object) const inside it. The const is part of the signature and must appear in both declaration and outside definition.
A const object (const Temp t(36.6);) can call only const member functions; the constructor and destructor run normally on it because they run before / after it is const.
A non-const object may call both const and non-const functions; a function may be overloaded on const alone (one version for const objects, one for others).
mutable, in one line: a data member marked mutable may be modified even inside a const member function or on a const object, used for caches and counters that are not part of the logical state.
Getters should be const so that they work on const objects and const references passed to functions.

concepts.text: The this Pointer
What this is and where it is used:
items: this is an implicit pointer parameter available inside every non-static member function, holding the address of the object the function was called on. For obj.f(), this == &obj. Its type is Class* const (Class const* inside a const member function).
Every member reference v inside a member function is really this->v; you write this-> explicitly only to resolve a name clash with a parameter or local variable.
return *this; returns the current object by reference so that calls can be chained (a.add(2).dbl()) and is the normal way to write operator= and operator+=.
Comparing this == &other detects self-assignment or self-comparison, e.g. at the top of an assignment operator to skip freeing memory that is about to be reused.
this cannot be assigned to and is absent in static member functions and friend functions; it can be passed to other functions or stored, for example in a linked list node.

concepts.text: Friend Functions and Friend Classes
Friendship grants a non-member full access to private and protected members:
items: A friend function is declared inside the class with the keyword friend but is NOT a member: it is defined like an ordinary function (no Class:: prefix), has no this pointer, and is called without an object (dot(a, b), not a.dot(b)). It receives the objects it works on as arguments.
The friend declaration may be placed under any access label; access specifiers do not affect it.
One function can be a friend of several classes (useful for a function that reads two different classes); a member function of class A can be a friend of class B (friend void A::f();).
friend class Printer; makes every member function of Printer a friend of Vec. Friendship is granted by the class being accessed, never taken.
Friendship is not mutual (Vec is not a friend of Printer), not inherited (derived classes of Printer get nothing) and not transitive (a friend of a friend is not a friend).

Typical uses: operator overloading where the left operand is not the class (cout << v, 5 * v), and functions that need the internals of two classes. Use sparingly, since every friend widens the interface and weakens encapsulation.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Static, const, this and Friends

A class body only describes a type, and the same class definition is normally included into many source files, so the declaration static int count; inside it cannot reserve storage without creating one copy per file. The out-of-class definition int Counter::count = 0; written in exactly one .cpp file is where the single shared object is actually created, and the linker connects every use of Counter::count to it. Static data members have static storage duration: they exist before main() starts, are zero-initialised when no initialiser is written, and live until the program ends. Integral static const members and static constexpr members may be initialised inside the class, and C++17 also allows inline static int count = 0; which needs no separate definition.

concepts.text: The compiler implements a member call obj.f(a) by passing &obj as a hidden first argument named this. Inside a non-const member function this has type T*, and inside a const member function it has type const T*, which is exactly why a const function can neither assign to ordinary members nor call non-const member functions. A static member function is called without any object, so no hidden argument exists; that is also why a static function cannot be const, volatile or virtual, since all three describe the object behind this. A friend function is an ordinary non-member even when its body is written inside the class, so it has no this either and must name the object it uses, as in v.x.
Mistakes that cost marks in this topic:
items: Repeating static in the out-of-class definition (static int Counter::count = 0;) is a compile error; the keyword belongs only on the declaration inside the class.
Dropping const from the out-of-class definition of a const member function: int T::get() { ... } does not match the declaration int get() const; and does not compile.
Counting objects in the constructor and destructor but not in the copy constructor, so copies are destroyed without ever having been counted.
Returning the object by value (T f() { ...; return *this; }) when chaining is intended: every later call in the chain changes a temporary copy.
Defining a friend function with a class prefix (void T::show(...)): a friend is not a member, so the compiler looks for a member that does not exist.
Returning int& to a data member from a const member function: the member is const there, so only const int& or a copy may be returned.

A static local object is constructed only on the first call of its function, and a counting constructor is skipped whenever the compiler-generated copy constructor is used.

Put int Counter::count = 0; in exactly one .cpp file, never in a header that several files include: each inclusion creates another definition and the linker reports a multiple-definition error. In C++17 the alternative is to write inline static int count = 0; inside the class.

Static member functions have no this pointer, so they may access only static members; they also cannot be const or virtual. A const object may call only const member functions. Both facts appear as "which of the following is valid" MCQs.

Friendship in three words: not mutual, not inherited, not transitive. A friend function is not a member, so it is called like a free function f(obj) and defined without the Class:: prefix, yet it can read obj's private data.

concepts.text: Conversions Among Basic Types

C++ converts values between its built-in types automatically whenever an expression mixes types or a value is assigned to a variable of a different type; this is implicit conversion, also called coercion. The compiler follows fixed rules: in a mixed expression the smaller operand is promoted to the larger type so that no information is lost, while on assignment the value is converted to the type of the variable on the left even if that narrows it. An explicit conversion, or cast, is written by the programmer to force a particular conversion at a particular point.
Implicit conversion rules:
items: Integral promotion: bool, char and short are promoted to int before any arithmetic, so 'A' + 1 is the int 66, not a char.

Usual arithmetic conversions: if either operand is long double, double or float, the other is converted to that type; otherwise integer rank decides (int -> long -> long long), and unsigned wins over signed of the same rank.
Assignment conversion may narrow: int i = 3.9 stores 3 (truncation toward zero, not rounding), and char c = 300 keeps only the low 8 bits, which is 44.
Sub-expressions are evaluated before the assignment converts: double d = 7 / 2 gives 3.0 because 7 / 2 is already an integer division; write 7 / 2.0 to get 3.5.
Any arithmetic value converts to bool as non-zero = true; a pointer converts to bool as not-null.

concepts.text:
int i = 7;  double d = 2.0;  char ch = 'A';
cout << i / 2 << " " << i / d << "\n";    // 3 3.5  (int/int, then i promoted to double)
cout << ch + 1 << "\n";                   // 66     (char promoted to int)
int t = 3.99;                             // 3      (narrowing on assignment)
double a1 = (double)i / 2;                // 3.5    C-style cast
double a2 = double(i) / 2;                // 3.5    function-style cast
double a3 = static_cast<double>(i) / 2;   // 3.5    C++ cast, checked at compile time

concepts.text: Basic Type to Class Type: the Constructor

A constructor that can be called with a single argument is a converting constructor: the compiler uses it automatically whenever an object of the class is required but a value of the argument type is supplied. Distance d = 2.5f; then d = 4.0f; and passing 2.5f to a function that takes a Distance all create a temporary Distance from the float through that constructor. Writing explicit in front of the constructor switches off this implicit use; the constructor then works only in direct form such as Distance d(2.5f), Distance(2.5f) or static_cast<Distance>(2.5f).
Class Type to Basic Type: the Conversion Operator

The reverse direction cannot use a constructor, because the destination type (float or double) is not a class and has no constructors. Instead the class defines a conversion function, also called a casting operator or conversion operator: operator float() const. It is a member function with no parameters and no declared return type, since the name already says what it returns. The compiler calls it whenever a Distance appears where a float is expected: float m = d; or 2 * d; or an explicit cast such as (float)d or static_cast<float>(d).
Class to Class Conversion
Converting an object of one class into an object of another can be written in either class:
items: Constructor in the destination class taking the source object: Fahrenheit(const Celsius& c). The destination must reach the source data through its public getters or by being a friend.
Conversion function in the source class: operator Fahrenheit() const written inside Celsius, which builds and returns the destination object.

Choose one place. If the destination has a converting constructor taking const Celsius& and the source has operator Fahrenheit() const, both are equally good for f = c or Fahrenheit f = c and the compiler reports an ambiguity error. (If the conversion function is not const and the source object is not const, the compiler prefers the conversion function — relying on that is fragile, so define only one.)
Only one user-defined conversion is applied automatically in a chain: the compiler will not silently go int -> Celsius -> Fahrenheit.

rows: Constructor in destination, or conversion function in source (not both)

concepts.text: Ambiguity and pitfalls:
items: Two equally good conversions make a call ambiguous: with both Distance(int) and Distance(float) defined, Distance d = 2.5 (a double literal) is rejected because the compiler will not choose between them.
A conversion function should be const because it does not modify the object; C++11 also allows explicit operator bool() const to stop unwanted implicit use.
Implicit conversions hide work: comparing a Distance with 3 may silently construct a temporary object. Mark single-argument constructors explicit unless conversion is intended.
A conversion function cannot declare a return type and cannot take parameters, but it may be virtual and is inherited by derived classes.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Data Conversion

All the implicit rules follow one principle: in a mixed expression both operands are converted to a common type chosen from a fixed ranking, and only an assignment, a return statement, an argument pass or a cast may move a value to a narrower type. The integer ladder by rank is int, long, long long, and float, double and long double sit above every integer type. When a signed and an unsigned operand of the same rank meet, the signed one is converted to unsigned, so -1 becomes the largest unsigned value and -1 < 1u is false. Narrowing is accepted silently in an ordinary assignment, but C++11 brace initialisation such as int n{3.7}; rejects it at compile time.

rows: Yes, only zero or non-zero survives

concepts.text: Base and Derived Classes

Inheritance creates a new class (the derived class or subclass) from an existing one (the base class or superclass). The derived class receives all data members and member functions of the base and may add its own or redefine inherited ones; the relationship is is-a (a Circle is a Shape). The benefits are code reuse, a natural class hierarchy, and the ability to handle derived objects through base pointers, which is the basis of the polymorphism covered in the next subtopic. The syntax is class Derived : access-mode Base { ... }; where the access mode (public, protected or private) controls how the inherited members appear inside the derived class.
What a derived class does NOT inherit:
items: Constructors and the destructor: each class writes its own, and the derived constructor calls a base constructor (C++11 can import base constructors with using Base::Base).
The copy-assignment operator= of the base, and the friend functions and friend classes of the base.
Private members are physically inherited (they exist inside every derived object and count in sizeof) but cannot be accessed by name from the derived class.
A function redefined in the derived class hides all base overloads of that name; use Base::name() to reach the base version.

concepts.text: Access Modes

Public inheritance keeps the base interface public and models is-a; it is the only mode in which a Derived* converts implicitly to Base* outside the class. Protected inheritance turns base public members into protected ones, and private inheritance makes everything private, so a class derived further down can no longer see them. If no mode is written, class defaults to private inheritance and struct to public. A private base member is always out of reach by name; the derived class must go through the base's public or protected functions.
Types of Inheritance

rows: One base, one derived: A -> B
Two or more bases into one derived: A and B -> C
class C : public A, public B { };
A chain: A -> B -> C (B is derived from A and is the base of C)
class B : public A { }; class C : public B { };
One base, many derived: A -> B, A -> C, A -> D
class B : public A { }; class C : public A { };
Any combination of the above, e.g. multilevel plus multiple
Vehicle -> Car, then Car and Engine -> SportsCar
A -> B, A -> C, then B and C -> D: D reaches A by two paths
class B : virtual public A; class C : virtual public A; class D : public B, public C

concepts.text: Ambiguity and the virtual base class fix:
items: In the diamond, D receives one A sub-object through B and another through C, so d.x is ambiguous and A's constructor runs twice for one D.

Declaring the intermediate classes with a virtual base class, class B : virtual public A and class C : virtual public A, gives D a single shared A sub-object: d.x is unambiguous and A's constructor runs once, called by the most-derived class D.
The keyword virtual is written in B and C (the classes that share the base), not in D.

Same-name members in unrelated bases stay ambiguous even with virtual bases: if A and B both define show(), then c.show() on a C object must be written c.A::show() or c.B::show(), or C must redefine show().

The order in class C : public A, public B fixes the order of base construction and the layout of the base sub-objects; multiple inheritance of classes is specific to C++ (Java allows it only through interfaces).

concepts.text: Constructors and Destructors in Inheritance

Constructors are not inherited, but creating a derived object always constructs its base part first: the base constructor runs, then the derived class's own member objects are initialised, and finally the body of the derived constructor executes (top-down). Destructors run in exactly the reverse order: the derived destructor body first, then the base destructor (bottom-up), so each class cleans up only what it built. In a multilevel chain A -> B -> C, creating a C runs A's, B's, then C's constructor, and destroying it runs ~C, ~B, ~A. If the base has no default (no-argument) constructor, the derived constructor must pass arguments to it explicitly in its initialiser list.
Order rules to remember:
items: Single inheritance: Base constructor -> Derived constructor; Derived destructor -> Base destructor.
Multilevel: grandparent -> parent -> child for constructors, and the exact reverse for destructors.

Multiple inheritance: base constructors run in the order the bases are listed in the class header, not the order written in the initialiser list; virtual base classes are constructed before all others.
Member objects are constructed after the base classes and before the derived constructor body, in their declaration order, and destroyed in reverse.
Make the base destructor virtual when objects are deleted through base pointers; otherwise only the base destructor runs, which is undefined behaviour.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Construction Order, Access and Name Hiding

The complete construction rule has four steps, applied recursively to every sub-object. First the virtual base classes are built, depth-first and left to right, and only by the most-derived class; then the direct non-virtual bases in the order of the class header; then the data members in their order of declaration; and finally the constructor body runs. The member-initialiser list only supplies arguments and never changes this order. Destruction walks the same list backwards, so every part is destroyed while the parts it depends on still exist.

concepts.plainText: Constructor order: virtual bases V, direct bases B1..Bn in header order, members m1..mk in declaration order, then the body; destructors run in exactly the reverse order

When a D is created, the initialisers that B and C write for their virtual base A are skipped, and the initialiser list of D decides which A constructor runs; if D names none, the default constructor of A is used. Consequently, a virtual base without a default constructor forces every class further down the hierarchy to call it explicitly.

concepts.text: Stream Class Hierarchy

A stream is a sequence of bytes flowing between a program and a device; C++ wraps every device (keyboard, screen, file, string) in the same class family so the operators << and >> work everywhere. The base class ios holds the formatting flags (width, precision, fill, base) and the error-state bits. istream adds input (>>, get, getline, read) and ostream adds output (<<, put, write); iostream inherits from both by multiple inheritance. The buffering itself is done by a separate streambuf object owned by the stream. The header <iostream> declares four ready-made objects.
Unformatted I/O Functions

Unformatted functions transfer raw characters without interpreting them and without skipping whitespace, so they are the tools for reading a full line, a single keystroke or a block of bytes. The formatted operators >> and << instead convert between text and typed values, and >> skips leading whitespace and stops at the next whitespace, which is why cin >> name reads only one word. peek() returns the next character without removing it and putback(ch) pushes one back, both useful for look-ahead; the free function std::getline(cin, str) does for std::string what cin.getline() does for char arrays.

cout.write(line, 5);       // exactly 5 bytes, even past a '\0'

ios::fixed, ios::scientific (group ios::floatfield): decimal or exponent notation; neither set means general notation.
ios::showpoint: always print the decimal point and trailing zeros; ios::showpos: print + before positive numbers.

concepts.text: Manipulators

Manipulators are functions inserted into the stream with << (or >>) that change its state without a separate statement, so formatting can be written inline: cout << setw(8) << x. The parameter-less ones (endl, hex, fixed, left, ws) live in <iostream>; the parameterised ones (setw, setfill, setprecision, setiosflags, resetiosflags, setbase) need <iomanip>.

Only width is consumed by a single insertion and then reset to 0; fill, precision and every flag stay in force until changed. Precision means the total number of significant digits in the default (general) notation but the number of digits after the decimal point once fixed or scientific is set. A user-defined manipulator is just a function taking and returning ostream&, e.g. ostream& tab(ostream& o) { return o << '\t'; }, and is used exactly like endl: cout << tab; parameterised versions need a small helper class or the setiosflags-style templates.

#include <iomanip>
cout << setw(8) << 123 << '|' << 45 << '\n';               // "     123|45"  (width used once)
cout << left << setw(6) << "ab" << '|' << '\n';             // "ab    |"
cout << right << setfill('0') << setw(5) << 42 << '\n';     // "00042"
cout << setfill(' ') << fixed << setprecision(3) << 2.5 << '\n';   // "2.500"
cout << scientific << 1234.56 << '\n';                      // "1.235e+03"  (precision 3 sticky)
cout << hex << 255 << ' ' << oct << 8 << ' ' << dec << 255 << '\n'; // "ff 10 255"
cout.unsetf(ios::floatfield);
cout << showpoint << 5.0 << '\n';                           // "5.00"  (3 significant digits)
Going Deeper: How Streams Format and Read

Each insertion with << reads the stream's current state: the flags, the width, the precision and the fill character. The value is first converted to text using the flags and precision, then padded with the fill character to the width, and finally the width is reset to 0, while every other setting stays until it is changed. In general notation (neither fixed nor scientific) the precision P is the number of significant digits, and the library chooses between plain and exponent form from the decimal exponent X of the rounded value, exactly like printf with %g. Trailing zeros are then removed unless showpoint is set.

Whatever settings the function changes stay in force afterwards. A manipulator with an argument needs a small helper: for example a struct stars holding a count, plus an operator<< for stars that writes that many asterisks, so that cout << stars{3} reads just like setw(3).

Mixing cin >> with getline is the most common input bug: the newline left by >> makes the next getline return an empty string. Add cin.ignore(100, '\n') or cin >> ws before getline. Also remember that setw on input limits a char array read to n - 1 characters, while setw on output never truncates.

For a formatting question, trace the state left to right: note the flags, precision and fill that are in force, apply setw only to the very next item, and check which notation is active before rounding. Write the result inside brackets while working so that padding spaces are counted exactly.

concepts.text: File Stream Classes

File handling in C++ reuses the console stream hierarchy: the header <fstream> derives ifstream from istream (input files), ofstream from ostream (output files) and fstream from iostream (files opened for both). Each owns a filebuf that talks to the operating system. Because they are ordinary streams, everything that works with cin and cout — the operators >> and <<, get(), getline(), read(), write(), manipulators and formatting flags — works unchanged on a file.
Defining, Opening and Closing a File

A file is defined by declaring a stream object and opened by associating that object with a file name, either in the constructor or later with open(name, mode). Opening creates the file when writing and fails when a file to be read does not exist; failure sets the failbit, so the stream should be tested right after opening. close() flushes buffered output and releases the file; the destructor does the same automatically when the object goes out of scope, but closing explicitly frees the file handle early and makes the intention clear.

#include <fstream>
ofstream fout("out.txt");                     // 1) constructor opens (mode ios::out)
ifstream fin;
fin.open("in.txt", ios::in);                  // 2) open() later
fstream f("data.dat", ios::in | ios::out | ios::binary);   // modes combined with |
if (!fin) cerr << "cannot open in.txt\n";     // open failure sets failbit
fout << "hello " << 42 << '\n';               // same operators as cout
fout.close(); fin.close(); f.close();         // flush and release the file

Open for writing; creates the file; alone it truncates
Append: every write goes to the end of the file

ios::out on its own behaves as ios::out | ios::trunc: an existing file is emptied. Add ios::app, ios::ate or ios::in to keep the contents.
ios::app forces all writes to the end even after seekp(); ios::ate only sets the starting position and later seeks are honoured.
ios::in | ios::out with fstream fails if the file does not exist; add ios::trunc to create it.
Use ios::binary for read()/write() of structures on Windows, where text mode converts \n to \r\n and treats Ctrl-Z as end of file.

concepts.text: Checking Streams and Error Handling During I/O

Every stream carries a state made of three bits: eofbit (end of input reached), failbit (an operation could not do what was asked, e.g. reading a word into an int, or open() failed) and badbit (a serious error such as a lost device). While all are clear the stream is good. Once failbit or badbit is set all further operations are ignored until clear() resets the state, which is why a loop must test the stream itself rather than eof() alone. Testing the stream in a boolean context (if (!fin), while (fin >> x)) is the idiomatic check. Alternatively stream.exceptions(mask) selects which bits should throw std::ios::failure instead, to be caught with try { } catch (ios::failure &e) { }; eofbit is normally left out of the mask because it is set together with failbit at the end of every input file.

concepts.text: Sequential Text I/O
Binary I/O and Random Access

Sequential text I/O stores numbers as readable characters in variable-length records, so the n-th record cannot be located directly. Binary I/O copies the bytes of an object with write() and read(), and random access moves the file position pointers before the transfer:
items: write(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&obj), sizeof(obj)) and read(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&obj), sizeof(obj)) transfer whole records; the object must be plain data (no pointers, no std::string).
Input streams have a get pointer moved by seekg() and reported by tellg(); output streams have a put pointer moved by seekp() and reported by tellp(); fstream has both.
seekg(offset, origin) with origin ios::beg (start), ios::cur (current position, offset may be negative) or ios::end (end of file); seekg(n) alone means from the beginning.
Fixed-size records make random access arithmetic simple: record n starts at byte (n - 1) * sizeof(record) and the record count is the file size divided by sizeof(record).
Updating a record: seekp to its offset, write the new bytes; deleting usually means copying all other records to a new file.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: File Streams in Practice

The state bits change only when an input operation actually tries to read. eofbit is set when a read runs into the end of the file. In a file that ends with a newline this happens one attempt after the last item has been taken, not at the moment the last item is read. When an extraction with >> finds nothing but whitespace before the end, its sentry fails, failbit and eofbit are set and the target variable is left unchanged; getline() instead empties its string first. That is why a loop controlled by !in.eof() processes the last word or number twice (or an extra empty line with getline), while a loop controlled by the read itself, while (in >> x), stops at exactly the right moment.

Output: red,green,blue,blue,

pass 1  in >> w reads "red"            prints red,
pass 2  in >> w reads "green"          prints green,
pass 3  in >> w reads "blue" and stops before the final '\n';
        no read has failed yet, so eof() is still false: prints blue,
pass 4  in >> w skips '\n', meets end of file, sets eofbit + failbit,
        w keeps "blue": prints blue, a second time
now eof() is true and the loop ends
Fix:    while (in >> w) cout << w << ',';   prints red,green,blue,
