A combination that has no fopen equivalent, such as ios::in | ios::trunc or ios::app | ios::trunc, makes open() fail and sets failbit.

concepts.text: What the STL Is

The Standard Template Library is the part of the C++ standard library that provides generic data structures and algorithms as templates. It has three main components: containers (objects that store collections of elements), algorithms (functions such as sort or find that operate on ranges of elements) and iterators (pointer-like objects that connect the two by pointing at elements inside a container). Two supporting pieces complete the picture: function objects (functors, e.g. greater<int>) that customise what an algorithm does, and allocators that manage container memory behind the scenes. Because algorithms talk to containers only through iterators, any algorithm works with any container that offers the right kind of iterator.
Containers
Sequence containers keep elements in the order you insert them:
items: vector (<vector>): dynamic array in contiguous memory; O(1) index access and push_back at the end (amortised); insertion in the middle shifts elements; grows automatically.
deque (<deque>): double-ended queue; O(1) push/pop at both ends and indexed access; elements in several chunks, not one contiguous block.
list (<list>): doubly linked list; O(1) insert/erase anywhere given an iterator; no indexing with [] and no random access.
array (<array>, C++11): fixed-size array wrapper, size is a template argument (array<int, 5>); knows its size, supports iterators.
forward_list (<forward_list>, C++11): singly linked list; forward traversal only, smallest overhead.

concepts.text: Associative and unordered containers are keyed and searched, not indexed by position:
items: set / multiset (<set>): sorted unique keys / sorted keys with duplicates allowed; implemented as balanced binary search trees (red-black), so insert, erase and find are O(log n).
map / multimap (<map>): sorted key-value pairs; map keys unique, multimap allows repeated keys; map supports m[key] which inserts a default value if the key is absent.
unordered_set, unordered_multiset, unordered_map, unordered_multimap (C++11): hash tables; average O(1) lookup, no ordering of elements.
Iterating a set or map visits elements in ascending key order (by operator< or a supplied comparator); iterating an unordered container gives no guaranteed order.

concepts.text: Container adapters wrap another container to give a restricted interface (no iterators):
items: stack (<stack>): LIFO; push, pop, top, empty, size; built on deque by default.
queue (<queue>): FIFO; push at back, pop from front, front, back; built on deque by default.
priority_queue (<queue>): always pops the largest element (max-heap by default, a comparator such as greater<int> gives a min-heap); built on vector by default.

O(1) at both ends; O(n) in the middle

concepts.text: Iterators
An iterator behaves like a pointer to an element: *it reads the element, ++it moves on, and it != end() tests for the end. Five categories, each adding capability to the previous:
items: Input iterator: read forward once, single pass (e.g. istream_iterator).
Output iterator: write forward once, single pass (e.g. ostream_iterator, back_inserter).
Forward iterator: read/write, multi-pass, ++ only (forward_list, unordered containers).
Bidirectional iterator: adds -- (list, set, map, multiset, multimap).
Random-access iterator: adds it + n, it - n, it[n], comparison with < (vector, deque, array, plain pointers).

Every container provides begin() and end(); end() points one past the last element, so [begin, end) is a half-open range. Constant versions are cbegin()/cend(); reverse iterators rbegin()/rend() traverse backwards.

concepts.text: Common STL facts worth memorising: vector::size() is the number of elements while capacity() is the allocated space; v.at(i) throws out_of_range but v[i] does not check; erasing from a vector invalidates iterators at and after the erased position; algorithms never change the size of a container (remove only moves elements, so it is paired with erase). MCQs usually ask which container fits a description (dynamic array, LIFO, sorted unique keys, key-value pairs), which header an algorithm needs, and the output of short vector, map or sort programs.
Going Deeper: Using STL Containers Correctly

A vector keeps its size() elements inside one block that has room for capacity() elements. When push_back finds size() equal to capacity(), it allocates a larger block, moves every existing element across, constructs the new element there and frees the old block, which is why every iterator into the vector becomes invalid at that moment. Implementations grow the capacity geometrically (typically by a factor of 1.5 or 2) rather than by a fixed amount, so reallocations become rarer as the vector grows. reserve(n) allocates room for at least n elements without changing size(), and shrink_to_fit() asks the vector to give back unused space.

concepts.plainText: With doubling capacity, n push_backs copy at most 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^k = 2^(k+1) - 1 < 2n elements in total (where 2^k < n), so the average cost per push_back is constant (amortised O(1)).

Key-value tree, O(log n) find and insert
Look up by key when order does not matter
Always take the largest (or smallest) next
Binary heap: O(1) top, O(log n) push and pop

concepts.text: Mistakes that give wrong output or undefined behaviour:
items: Keeping an iterator, pointer or reference into a vector across push_back or insert: a reallocation leaves it dangling.
Erasing inside a loop with v.erase(it); ++it; instead of it = v.erase(it); the old iterator is invalid after erase.
Calling remove() and expecting the size to shrink: remove only shifts the kept elements and must be followed by erase.
Using m[key] just to test whether a key exists: it inserts a default value; use find() or count() instead.
Calling binary_search on an unsorted range, or std::sort on a list (use l.sort()).
Expecting an unordered_map or unordered_set to print in insertion or sorted order: its order is unspecified.
Reading v[i] with i >= v.size(): no check is made; use at() when a bounds check is wanted.

concepts.text: Output shortcuts: set and map print in ascending key order; set and map silently drop a repeated key while multiset and multimap keep it; stack pops in the reverse order of pushing, queue in the same order; priority_queue always pops the largest element first (the smallest with greater<T>). For vector questions track size() and the element list after every call; capacity() is only guaranteed to be at least size(), or at least n after reserve(n).

formulas.plainText: vector: v[i] is O(1); push_back is O(1) amortised (occasional reallocation)
set/map find, insert, erase are O(log n); unordered_set/map are O(1) on average
sort is O(n log n); binary_search on a sorted range is O(log n); find is O(n)
A range is half-open [begin, end): end points one past the last element, size = end - begin

notes.text: Match container to description: dynamic array = vector; double-ended = deque; linked list = list; unique sorted keys = set; key-value pairs = map; LIFO = stack; FIFO = queue; largest first = priority_queue. stack, queue and priority_queue are adapters and have no iterators.

map::operator[] inserts a default-valued element when the key is missing, so a lookup written as m["x"] silently grows the map. Use find() or count() to test for presence. Similarly v[i] never checks bounds; only v.at(i) throws out_of_range.

sort() needs random-access iterators, so it works on vector, deque and array but not on list (use list::sort()). accumulate lives in <numeric>, not <algorithm>, and accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0) truncates a double sum because the initial value 0 is an int.

concepts.text: Why Exceptions

In C, a function reports failure through a return value (-1, NULL, an errno code) that the caller must remember to test, and the test is easily forgotten or awkward when the function already returns a value (what does divide() return when b is 0?). Exception handling separates error detection from error handling: the function that detects the problem throws an exception object, execution leaves that function immediately, and control is transferred to the nearest enclosing handler that can deal with it, possibly many calls up the stack. Errors cannot be silently ignored, the normal code path stays clean, and constructors, which return nothing, get a way to report failure.
try, throw and catch
Mechanics of the three keywords:
items: try { ... } encloses the code that may fail; one or more catch blocks must follow it immediately.
throw expression; creates a copy of the value (any type: int, const char*, a class object) and starts the search for a handler; the rest of the try block is skipped.
catch (Type name) { ... } handles an exception whose type matches; after the handler finishes, execution continues after the last catch block, not back at the throw point.

Stack unwinding: as control leaves each function between the throw and the handler, local objects are destroyed (their destructors run) exactly as on a normal return; heap memory freed only in skipped code leaks.
If the try block completes without throwing, all its catch blocks are skipped.

concepts.text: Multiple Handlers, Matching Order, Rethrow
Several catch blocks may follow one try; they are tested in the order written and the first match wins:
items: Matching is by type: an int handler does not catch a double (no arithmetic conversions), but a handler for a base class catches a derived-class object, and a pointer/reference to base catches derived.

Therefore write derived-class handlers before base-class handlers; a catch (exception&) placed first would swallow every std exception and the later specific handlers would be unreachable (compilers warn).
Catch by reference (catch (const T &e)) to avoid copying and to keep the dynamic type; catching a derived object by base value slices it.
catch (...) catches every type; it must be last and it cannot access the exception object.
throw; (empty throw) inside a handler rethrows the current exception object unchanged to an outer try; throw e; would throw a copy of the static type instead.
A try block can be nested inside another try or inside a handler; an exception not handled by the inner block propagates to the outer one.

concepts.text: Exceptions with Arguments and Nested try

Throwing a class object is the normal style because the object can carry arguments describing the error (the bad value, a message, a code) through its constructor, and because a hierarchy of exception classes lets callers choose how specific to be. Nested try blocks let an inner handler do local clean-up and then rethrow to an outer handler that reports to the user; an inner try without a matching handler simply passes the exception outward, and a throw inside a catch block is itself handled by the enclosing try, never by a sibling catch of the same try.
Exception Specifications, Uncaught and Unexpected
How a function advertises what it may throw, and what happens when nothing catches an exception:
items: Dynamic exception specification (pre-C++11): void f() throw(int, char); promised only those types, and void f() throw(); promised none. Violating it called std::unexpected(), which by default called std::terminate(); set_unexpected() could install another handler. Deprecated in C++11, removed in C++17.

noexcept (C++11): void f() noexcept; declares that f does not throw; if it does anyway, std::terminate() is called at once with no unwinding. noexcept(expr) is also a compile-time operator that yields true if expr cannot throw.

Uncaught exception: if the handler search reaches main() without a match, std::terminate() is called, which by default calls abort(); no destructors of main's locals are guaranteed to run. set_terminate(handler) installs a custom terminate handler that must not return.
Exceptions thrown by destructors during unwinding (a second active exception) also lead to terminate(), so destructors should not throw.

rows: virtual what() returns a C-string message; catch (const exception &) catches all of the below
Errors detectable before running: invalid_argument, domain_error, length_error, out_of_range
Errors only detectable at run time: range_error, overflow_error, underflow_error
vector::at(i), string::at(i) or map::at(key) with a bad index or key
new fails to obtain memory (new never returns NULL in C++; use new(nothrow) for that)
Failed dynamic_cast to a reference; typeid on a null pointer

concepts.text: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation) is the idiom that makes exceptions safe: a resource such as heap memory, a file or a lock is owned by a local object whose constructor acquires it and whose destructor releases it. Because stack unwinding runs destructors of every local object between the throw and the handler, the resource is released automatically whether the function ends normally or by exception. This is why smart pointers, fstream and lock_guard are preferred to raw new/delete and fopen/fclose in C++ code that may throw.
Going Deeper: What Happens After throw

When a throw expression runs, its operand is copied (or moved) into a special exception object whose type is the static type of the expression, so throwing a Base& that refers to a Derived object throws a Base. The run-time system then searches outward for a handler: first the catch clauses of the innermost enclosing try block, then those of the try blocks in each calling function in turn. Before the chosen handler runs, every automatic object created since that try block was entered is destroyed in reverse order of construction, innermost function first; this is stack unwinding. The exception object itself lives until the last handler dealing with it exits without rethrowing.

Output: +a +b +c -c -b caught 42 end -a

line 11  a is constructed in main: +a
line 12  main calls middle(); on line 9 it constructs b: +b and calls inner()
line 8   inner() constructs c: +c, then throws 42
unwind   inner() is left early, c is destroyed: -c
unwind   middle() is left early, "never" is skipped, b is destroyed: -b
line 13  catch (int e) in main receives 42: caught 42
line 14  execution resumes after the handler: end
exit     main returns and a is destroyed last: -a

An object counts as constructed only when its constructor finishes. If a constructor throws, the destructor of that object is not called, but every base-class subobject and data member that was already fully constructed is destroyed in reverse order, and memory obtained by new for the object is freed automatically. Raw resources acquired inside the constructor body are not released, which is another reason to hold them in members such as vector or unique_ptr. Destructors are implicitly noexcept since C++11, so a throw that escapes a destructor calls std::terminate(), and when no handler exists at all it is implementation-defined whether any unwinding happens before terminate().

rows: No, a derived object is sliced
Changes to e are lost on throw;
Changes to e survive a throw; rethrow
Needs throw new T (or the address of a static object, never a local); the handler must delete a new object
Must be last; use throw; to pass it on

concepts.text:
Output:
FileError: missing
runtime_error: missing

how = 0  throw; rethrows the original FileError object
         the first handler, catch (FileError &), matches
how = 1  throw e; copies e, whose static type is runtime_error
         the copy is a plain runtime_error: the FileError part is sliced off
         catch (FileError &) is skipped, catch (runtime_error &) matches
what()   still returns "missing", stored in the runtime_error part

concepts.latex: \text{catch}(B\&) \text{ takes throw } D \iff D = B \text{ or } B \text{ public base of } D
concepts.plainText: A handler for B (by value or reference) accepts a thrown D only when D is B itself or B is an unambiguous public base class of D; no int/char/double conversions and no user-defined conversions are applied (pointer handlers also accept derived-to-base pointer conversions).

concepts.text: Mistakes that change the output or break the program:
items: Writing catch (Base &) before catch (Derived &): the derived handler can never run.
Catching class exceptions by value: the copy is sliced and a virtual what() reports the base version.
Rethrowing with throw e; instead of throw;: it throws a copy of the static type, not the original object.
Expecting catch (int) to take a char, a short or a double: exception matching applies no arithmetic conversions.
Expecting the statements after the throw, or later in the try block, to run once the handler finishes.
Releasing resources with delete or fclose after code that may throw: unwinding skips them, so use RAII objects.
Letting an exception escape a destructor or a noexcept function: std::terminate() is called.

concepts.text: Library code describes its behaviour under exceptions with three levels of guarantee. The basic guarantee promises no leaks and objects left in a valid but unspecified state; the strong guarantee promises that an operation either succeeds completely or has no effect at all, as vector::push_back does; the no-throw guarantee promises that the operation never throws, which is exactly what noexcept declares. This is why noexcept matters in practice: when a vector reallocates, it moves its elements only if the element type's move constructor is noexcept (or the type cannot be copied), otherwise it copies them so that push_back can keep its strong guarantee.

To trace an exception question: (1) print everything up to the throw; (2) skip the rest of the try block and of every function being left; (3) run the destructors of their local objects, newest first and innermost function first; (4) pick the first handler, in written order, whose type matches; (5) continue after that try-catch, or keep unwinding if the handler rethrows.

formulas.plainText: throw → stack unwinding (destructors run) → first catch whose type matches, tested in written order
uncaught exception → std::terminate() → abort() (program ends abnormally)
throw() of C++03 is replaced by noexcept in C++11; throwing from a noexcept function calls terminate()

notes.text: Order of handlers: most specific (derived) first, base class later, catch (...) last. Type matching is exact apart from derived-to-base and pointer conversions: throw 3.5 is not caught by catch (int), and throw 'a' is not caught by catch (int) either.

After a handler runs, execution continues after the whole try-catch construct, never at the statement following the throw. Any cout in the try block after the throwing call is skipped, which is the basis of most output-prediction questions on this topic.

throw; (empty) rethrows the current exception and is legal only inside a catch block; anywhere else it calls terminate(). throw e; from a handler throws a copy, which slices a derived object caught by base value.

Three ways a program reaches std::terminate(): an exception with no matching handler, an exception escaping a noexcept function, and a second exception thrown while unwinding (e.g. from a destructor). std::unexpected() belongs to the old throw(...) specifications and is legacy.

concepts.text: How to use this sheet

Programming MCQs turn on a few dozen facts: sizes and ranges, precedence, what a construct defaults to, and the exact rule a keyword enforces. This page lists them section by section with the smallest code that shows each rule. Cover a block, write the fact from memory, then check the subtopic for the reasoning.
1. C basics: tokens, types, operators, I/O, control flow, functions, arrays

concepts.plainText: Signed n-bit: −2^(n−1) … 2^(n−1)−1;  unsigned: 0 … 2^n − 1

concepts.text: Token and identifier rules:
items: C89 has 32 keywords; identifiers start with a letter or underscore, contain letters, digits, underscores, and are case-sensitive.
Constants: integer (10, 012 octal, 0xA hex, 10U, 10L), floating (3.14, 2e3, 3.0f), character ('A', '\n', '\0'), string ("text", stored with a terminating '\0').
main returns int; a program starts at main and ends when main returns or exit() is called.

concepts.text:
int a = 5;
printf("%d %d", a++, ++a);   /* order of evaluation is unspecified: never write this */
int b = 7 / 2;                  /* 3: integer division truncates toward zero */
int c = -7 % 3;                 /* -1: sign of % follows the dividend */
int d = (1, 2, 3);              /* 3: comma yields the last operand */
Control-flow rules that decide output questions:
items: switch works on an integral type (int, char, enum); without break, execution falls through into the following cases.
do-while runs its body at least once; while and for test first. for(;;) is an infinite loop.
break leaves the innermost loop or switch; continue jumps to the next iteration (in a for loop the increment still runs).
if (x = 5) assigns and is always true; = versus == is the classic trap.
A semicolon after for(...) or while(...) makes an empty loop body.

concepts.text: Functions and recursion:
items: Arguments are passed by value; to change the caller's variable pass its address and dereference (swap via pointers).
A prototype declares name, return type and parameter types before use; a definition supplies the body.
Every recursive function needs a base case; each call adds a stack frame, so deep recursion can overflow the stack.
static local variables keep their value between calls; automatic locals are re-created each call.

concepts.plainText: factorial(n) = n × factorial(n−1) with factorial(0) = 1; n + 1 calls in total

concepts.text: Arrays and strings:
items: int a[10] holds a[0] … a[9]; total size = n × sizeof(type); a 2-D array is stored row-major, address of a[i][j] = base + (i × cols + j) × sizeof(type).
An array name decays to a pointer to its first element: a ≡ &a[0], a[i] ≡ *(a + i); sizeof(a) is the whole array only in the declaring scope.
A C-string ends with '\0': strlen("EXAM") = 4 but sizeof("EXAM") = 5. strcmp returns 0 for equal strings; strcpy/strcat need enough room in the destination.
scanf("%s") stops at the first space; use fgets to read a line.

concepts.text: 2. Pointers, structures and files

concepts.plainText: p + i moves i elements, not i bytes; pointer difference is measured in elements

concepts.text:
int a[] = {10, 20, 30, 40};
int *p = a;               /* p -> a[0] */
printf("%d", *(p + 2));  /* 30 */
printf("%d", *p++);      /* 10, then p -> a[1]: postfix ++ binds tighter than * */
int *q = malloc(5 * sizeof *q);  /* check q != NULL; free(q) when done */
Pointer rules:
items: int *p declares a pointer; &x gives an address; *p reads or writes the pointee. NULL pointers must not be dereferenced.
const int *p: data read-only through p;  int *const p: the pointer itself is fixed.
malloc returns uninitialised memory, calloc zeroed memory; realloc resizes; every malloc needs one free. Using freed memory = dangling pointer.
Passing a pointer lets a function modify the caller's variable; passing an array always passes a pointer.

rows: one at a time, same address
read (must exist) / write (truncate or create) / append (create if missing)
read and write; w+ truncates, a+ appends
random access; ftell gives the position; rewind goes to the start

concepts.text: 3. C++ classes
Class rules:
items: class members are private by default, struct members public; protected is visible to derived classes.
A constructor has the class name, no return type, and runs when an object is created; a destructor is ~Name(), takes no arguments and runs when the object dies (reverse order of construction).
Copy constructor: Name(const Name &other) — the parameter must be a reference; Box b = a; and passing/returning by value invoke it.
new/delete for single objects, new[]/delete[] for arrays; mixing them is undefined behaviour.

static data member: one copy per class, defined outside the class; static member function has no this. const member function cannot modify members; only const functions can be called on const objects.
friend functions/classes access private members but are not members, are not inherited and friendship is not transitive.
Default arguments are supplied from the rightmost parameter; inline is a request; references must be initialised and cannot be reseated.

concepts.text: 4. OOP features
Inheritance and overloading facts:
items: Constructors run base first, then derived; destructors run derived first, then base. Base constructors get arguments through the initialiser list.
Multipath (diamond) inheritance duplicates the common base; declare it a virtual base class to keep one copy.
Operators that cannot be overloaded: ::  .  .*  ?:  sizeof. Overloading cannot change precedence, associativity or the number of operands.
operator++() is prefix, operator++(int) is postfix. Binary operators as members take one argument; as friends they take two.
Basic → class conversion uses a constructor; class → basic uses a conversion operator (operator double()); class → class uses either, in the destination constructor or the source conversion function.

concepts.text: 5. Virtual functions and streams
Run-time polymorphism:
items: A base-class pointer to a derived object calls the base version unless the function is virtual; virtual gives dynamic (late) binding through the vtable.
virtual void f() = 0; is a pure virtual function; a class with one is abstract and cannot be instantiated, though pointers and references to it are allowed.
Make the destructor virtual when deleting derived objects through base pointers. Constructors cannot be virtual; static and friend functions cannot be virtual.

rows: minimum field width for the next output only
significant digits, or decimals with fixed

items: ifstream reads, ofstream writes, fstream both; modes ios::in, ios::out, ios::app (append), ios::ate (start at end), ios::trunc, ios::binary, combined with |.
Check is_open()/fail(); eof() becomes true only after a read fails past the end.
seekg/tellg move and report the get pointer, seekp/tellp the put pointer, relative to ios::beg, ios::cur or ios::end.

concepts.text: 6. Templates and exceptions
Rules to remember:
items: A function template is instantiated per type at compile time; an exact non-template overload is preferred over a template.

STL = containers (vector, list, deque, set, map, stack, queue, priority_queue) + algorithms (sort, find, count, reverse, accumulate) + iterators (input, output, forward, bidirectional, random access).
vector gives O(1) random access and amortised O(1) push_back; list gives O(1) insert/erase anywhere but no random access; map keys are ordered and unique, multimap allows duplicates.
catch blocks are tried in order, so catch derived exceptions before base ones; catch (...) must be last; throw; rethrows the current exception.
noexcept (C++11) replaces the old throw() specification; an uncaught exception calls std::terminate.
Catch by reference to avoid slicing and copying; throw by value.

Most output and compile-error questions yield to the same four checks, applied in order. First fix the type of every operand: int or double, char promoted to int, array or pointer, base or derived. Next group the expression by precedence and associativity, then apply side effects one statement at a time, noting where a value is copied and where a pointer or reference reaches the original. Finally ask what is printed and in which format, and for C++ which constructor, destructor or override actually runs.

notes.text: Output-prediction questions almost always hinge on one of: integer division, % with a negative operand, a++ versus ++a, missing break in switch, a stray semicolon after a loop header, or an array name used as a pointer. Check those five before computing anything.

Defaults that flip between C and C++: class members are private but struct members are public; C passes everything by value while C++ adds references; new/delete pair with each other and never with malloc/free; catch (...) must come last.
Sizes are platform-dependent, so a well-set question states them; if it does not, assume char 1, int 4, float 4, double 8, and remember sizeof("text") counts the terminating null.

concepts.text: Structure of a C Program

A C program is a collection of functions, and execution always starts at main(). Lines beginning with # are preprocessor directives handled before compilation: #include pulls in a header file that declares library functions (stdio.h for printf/scanf, string.h, math.h, stdlib.h; conio.h is a non-standard Turbo C header), and #define creates symbolic constants. In C99 main returns int, and return 0 tells the operating system the program succeeded. Every statement ends with a semicolon, and braces { } group statements into a block.
C Tokens

A token is the smallest individual unit that the compiler recognises; the compiler breaks every line into tokens before it can understand it. C has six kinds of tokens: keywords, identifiers, constants, string literals, operators and special symbols (punctuators). Whitespace and comments separate tokens but are not tokens themselves.

rows: 32 reserved words in C89; all lowercase; cannot be used as names
Names of variables, functions, arrays, labels
Sequence of characters in double quotes, ends with '\0'
Delimit blocks, calls, subscripts and statements

concepts.text: Identifier rules (asked in almost every MCQ set on tokens):
items: Must start with a letter (A-Z, a-z) or an underscore; it cannot start with a digit, so 1variable is invalid but variable1 is fine.
May contain only letters, digits and underscores: no spaces, hyphens, $, @ or other symbols (first-name and total$ are invalid).
Case-sensitive: sum, Sum and SUM are three different identifiers.
Cannot be a keyword: int is illegal as a name, but Int and INT are legal (though poor style).
C89 guarantees only the first 31 characters of an internal name are significant (63 in C99); names starting with an underscore are reserved for the compiler and library, so avoid them.

concepts.text: The 32 keywords of ANSI C (C99 added inline, restrict, _Bool, _Complex and _Imaginary):
items: auto  break  case  char  const  continue  default  do
double  else  enum  extern  float  for  goto  if
int  long  register  return  short  signed  sizeof  static
struct  switch  typedef  union  unsigned  void  volatile  while

concepts.text: Constants, literals and escape sequences:
items: Integer literals: decimal 42, octal 052 (leading 0), hexadecimal 0x2A; suffix U, L, UL or LL selects unsigned/long types (42L).
Floating literals are double by default (3.14); 3.14f is a float; scientific form 2.5e3 means 2500.0.
Character constants such as 'A' have type int in C (value 65), so sizeof('A') is 4 in C but 1 in C++.
Escape sequences inside quotes: \n newline, \t tab, \\ backslash, \' and \" quotes, \0 null, \a bell, \b backspace, \r carriage return, \xhh hex code, \ooo octal code.
const int MAX = 100; is a typed read-only variable checked by the compiler; #define MAX 100 is a textual replacement done by the preprocessor with no type and no semicolon.
enum colour {RED, GREEN, BLUE}; creates named integer constants starting at 0 unless a value is assigned; later names continue from the previous value.

concepts.text: Variables, Scope and Storage Classes

A variable is a named memory location whose declaration fixes its type and name and may give it an initial value (int count = 10;). A variable declared inside a block is local to that block; one declared outside all functions is global and visible from that point to the end of the file. Local variables without an initialiser hold garbage, while globals and statics are automatically set to zero. The storage class of a variable decides where it is stored, its default value, its scope and its lifetime.

rows: Created on block entry, destroyed on exit; the default for locals
Same as auto; faster access; the & operator cannot be applied
Whole program run; a static local keeps its value between calls; a static global is hidden from other files
Whole program run; declares a global that is defined in another file (no storage allocated)

concepts.text: Fundamental Data Types

rows: -128 to 127 (unsigned char: 0 to 255); stores an ASCII code

concepts.text: Type modifiers and sizing rules:
items: signed and unsigned change the range, not the size; short and long change the size. short int, long int and unsigned int may be written short, long and unsigned.
The standard only guarantees sizeof(char) = 1 and sizeof(char) <= sizeof(short) <= sizeof(int) <= sizeof(long) <= sizeof(long long); the sizes above are the usual ones on 32-bit and 64-bit gcc/MSVC.
sizeof is a compile-time operator (not a function) that yields size_t; sizeof(int) = 4, sizeof(3.0) = 8, sizeof(3.0f) = 4, sizeof(long double) is compiler dependent (8, 12 or 16).
void means 'no value': a function that returns nothing, an empty parameter list, or a generic pointer void * that can hold any address.
Mixing types promotes the smaller operand (int + float gives float); a cast forces a conversion, so (int)3.9 is 3 (truncation, not rounding). Details are in Operators & Precedence.
C89 has no bool type; any non-zero value is true and 0 is false. C99 adds _Bool via stdbool.h (bool, true, false); C++ has a built-in 1-byte bool.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Tokens, Types and Storage

The ranges in the size table follow from counting bit patterns. An n-bit type has 2^n patterns, and an unsigned type uses all of them for 0 to 2^n - 1. A signed type in two's complement gives the top bit a weight of -2^(n-1), so it covers -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1. The range is lopsided by one because zero uses up one of the non-negative patterns.

concepts.plainText: An n-bit unsigned type stores x mod 2^n; e.g. (unsigned char)300 = 300 - 256 = 44

concepts.text: Only unsigned arithmetic is guaranteed to wrap round: 0u - 1 is UINT_MAX, and an unsigned char holding 255 becomes 0 when 1 is added and the result is stored back. Signed overflow such as INT_MAX + 1 is undefined behaviour, and storing an out-of-range value in a signed type (200 in a signed char) is implementation-defined. Wrap-around questions are only answerable for unsigned types.

concepts.text: Type qualifiers and typedef in practice:
items: const int *p (also written int const *p): the int is read-only through p, but p itself can be pointed elsewhere.
int *const p: p is fixed to one address, but the int it points to may change; const int *const p fixes both.
volatile tells the compiler the value can change behind its back (hardware registers, signal handlers), so every read and write must really happen; const volatile suits a read-only hardware port.
typedef is a compiler-level alias: after typedef char *STR; the declaration STR a, b; makes two pointers, whereas #define PSTR char * turns PSTR a, b; into char *a, b; and b is a plain char.
In C a const int variable is not a constant expression, so it cannot be a case label; an enumeration constant or a #define macro can. C++ relaxes this rule.

concepts.text: Common mistakes and special cases:
items: 08 and 09 are compile errors: a leading 0 means octal, and octal digits stop at 7.
An octal escape takes at most three digits, so \1234 is \123 followed by 4; a hex escape keeps reading hex digits, so \x41B is one value (0x41B) that does not fit in a char.
Whether plain char is signed or unsigned is implementation-defined; write signed char or unsigned char when the range matters.
sizeof(long) is 4 on 64-bit Windows but 8 on 64-bit Linux, so always fix the sizes before working out a sizeof answer.
A float keeps only about 7 significant digits, so a float and a double both set to 0.1 compare unequal; never test floating values with ==.

notes.text: char stores the ASCII code: 'A' is 65, '0' is 48 and 'a' is 97, so 'A' + 1 == 66 == 'B' and '7' - '0' == 7. Printing a char with %d shows the code, with %c shows the character.
Integer division truncates: 5 / 2 == 2, but 5 % 2 == 1. Use 5.0 / 2 for 2.5. The same truncation happens when a double is stored in an int: int x = 7.9; gives 7.
#define takes no semicolon and no = sign: #define MAX = 100; replaces MAX with '= 100;' and breaks every use. A const variable does take both, and unlike a #define it has a type and a scope.
Local (auto) variables start with garbage, global and static variables start with 0. An MCQ that prints an uninitialised local has no defined answer; one that prints an uninitialised global prints 0.

concepts.text: What a Pointer Is

A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. Two operators do all the work: & (address-of) yields the address of an object, and * (indirection or dereference) accesses the value stored at an address. A pointer is declared as type *name; the type tells the compiler what kind of object lives at that address, which decides how *p is interpreted and how far p + 1 moves. Reading or writing *p reads or writes the pointed-to variable itself, so a pointer is an alias for another object.

int x = 5;
int *p = &x;                 /* p holds the address of x */
*p = 10;                     /* writes through p: x is now 10 */
printf("%d\n", *p);          /* 10  - the VALUE at the address */
printf("%p\n", (void *)p);   /* the ADDRESS of x, e.g. 0x7ffd3a2c */
printf("%p\n", (void *)&p);  /* address of the pointer variable itself */
int *r = p;                  /* two pointers may hold the same address */
*r = 20;                     /* x is now 20; *p is also 20 */
Declaration and initialisation rules:
items: In int *p, q; the * binds to the name, so p is a pointer but q is a plain int. Write int *p, *q; for two pointers.
A pointer must be given a valid address (&var, another pointer, the result of malloc, or NULL) before it is dereferenced. A declared but never initialised pointer is a wild pointer holding garbage.

NULL (defined in <stdio.h>, <stdlib.h> and <stddef.h>) is a pointer value that points nowhere; it compares equal to 0. Dereferencing NULL crashes the program, so test if (p != NULL) or simply if (p) first.

The size of a pointer depends on the machine, not on what it points to: sizeof(char *) == sizeof(int *) == sizeof(double *), which is 4 bytes on a 32-bit system and 8 bytes on a 64-bit system. sizeof(*p), by contrast, is the size of the pointed-to type.
Pointer types are not interchangeable: assigning int * to double * without a cast is an error or at least a warning, because the two types dereference and advance differently.

concepts.text: Pointer Arithmetic

Arithmetic on a pointer is scaled by the size of the type it points to. p + 1 is the address of the next object of that type, i.e. the numeric address plus sizeof(*p) bytes, so for an int pointer p++ adds 4, for a double pointer it adds 8 and for a char pointer it adds 1. The operators ++, --, +=, -=, + and - with an integer are all defined this way. Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them (type ptrdiff_t from <stddef.h>), not the number of bytes, and relational comparison (<, >, ==) of pointers into the same array compares their positions.

concepts.text: Tricky forms of * with ++ (postfix ++ binds tighter than unary *, and unary operators group right to left):
items: *p++ is *(p++): yields the value p currently points to, then advances p to the next element.
*++p advances p first and then dereferences the new position.
(*p)++ increments the value stored at p; p itself does not move.
++*p is ++(*p): the same as (*p)++ except that the expression evaluates to the incremented value.
*p + 1 is (*p) + 1, an int, while *(p + 1) is the next element; the parentheses change the meaning completely.

concepts.text: void, const and Multi-level Pointers

A void * is a generic pointer that can hold the address of any object type; it cannot be dereferenced or used in arithmetic until it is cast to a concrete pointer type. malloc returns void *, which converts implicitly to any object pointer type in C (C++ requires an explicit cast). A pointer to a pointer, int **pp = &p, stores the address of a pointer: *pp is p and **pp is the int; it is used for dynamic 2-D arrays and to let a function change a caller's pointer. Read const declarations right to left: const int *p is a pointer to a constant int (the pointee cannot be changed through p, but p can be moved), int *const p is a constant pointer to int (p cannot be moved, but *p can be changed), and const int *const p fixes both.

int x = 7, y = 9;
int *p = &x;
int **pp = &p;              /* pointer to pointer */
printf("%d\n", **pp);       /* 7 */
*pp = &y;                   /* changes p itself: p now points to y */
const int *a = &x;          /* *a = 1 is an ERROR, but a = &y is fine */
int *const b = &x;          /* b = &y is an ERROR, but *b = 1 is fine */
const int *const c = &x;    /* neither the pointer nor the pointee may change */
void *v = &x;               /* generic pointer: holds any address */
printf("%d\n", *(int *)v);  /* cast before dereferencing: 7 */
Dynamic Memory in C

Automatic variables vanish when their block ends, and array sizes must be known at compile time in classic C. The <stdlib.h> heap functions remove both limits: malloc(n) allocates n uninitialised bytes, calloc(count, size) allocates count × size bytes set to zero, realloc(p, n) resizes a block to n bytes keeping its contents (it may move the block and return a new address), and free(p) returns the block to the system. The size is always written as count × sizeof(type) so the code stays correct when the type changes. Heap memory lives until free is called, so it can be returned from functions safely, but every malloc must be matched by exactly one free.

#include <stdlib.h>
int n = 5;
int *arr = (int *)malloc(n * sizeof(int));  /* cast is optional in C */
if (arr == NULL) { puts("out of memory"); return 1; } /* always check */
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) arr[i] = i * i;  /* use like an array */
arr = realloc(arr, 10 * sizeof(int));       /* grow to 10, old values kept */
int *z = calloc(10, sizeof(int));           /* 10 ints, all zero */
free(arr);  arr = NULL;                     /* release, then neutralise */
free(z);                                    /* never free the same block twice */
Pointer pitfalls that MCQs like to test:
items: Dangling pointer: points to memory that has been freed or to a local variable whose block has ended; dereferencing it is undefined behaviour.
Memory leak: heap memory that no pointer references any more (for example, p = malloc(..) twice without free), so it can never be freed while the program runs.
Wild pointer: declared but never initialised; it holds a random address.
NULL pointer: intentionally points nowhere; safe to test, never safe to dereference. free(NULL) is harmless.
Double free and using the old pointer after realloc moved the block are both undefined behaviour.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Pointer Arithmetic and Heap Memory

Pointer arithmetic can be scaled only because every pointer type carries the size of its target. For T *p, the expression p + i is computed as the address in p plus i × sizeof(T) bytes, and p[i] is simply *(p + i). Subtraction runs the same rule backwards: the byte gap between two pointers is divided by sizeof(T), so q − p counts elements, not bytes. These results are guaranteed only while both pointers stay inside one array or at the address just past its last element; forming any other address, even without dereferencing it, is undefined behaviour.

concepts.plainText: byte gap from p to q = (q − p) × sizeof(T), where q − p is counted in elements

concepts.text: C++ as an Extension of C

C++ was designed by Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Labs (1979 onward, first called "C with Classes") as a superset of C: almost every valid C program is also a valid C++ program. C++ keeps the C syntax, operators, control statements and pointers, and adds object-oriented features (classes, inheritance, polymorphism), stronger type checking, references, function overloading, default arguments, inline functions, namespaces, templates and exception handling. Input and output use the stream objects cin and cout from <iostream> instead of scanf/printf, though the C library still works.

rows: One function per name; no default arguments
C89: at block start only (C99 relaxed)
Anywhere before use, including for (int i = 0; ...)

concepts.text: Namespaces
A namespace is a named scope that keeps identifiers of different libraries from colliding; the whole C++ standard library lives in namespace std:
items: Three ways to reach a member: full qualification (std::cout), a using-declaration (using std::cout;) that brings in one name, or a using-directive (using namespace std;) that brings in every name of the namespace.
The scope resolution operator :: also reaches a global variable hidden by a local one (::x) and defines class members outside the class body (Class::f).
Namespaces can be nested (a::b::c) and reopened: several files may add members to the same namespace. A namespace definition is not followed by a semicolon.
An anonymous (unnamed) namespace gives its contents internal linkage, like static at file scope in C.
Names can be aliased: namespace io = std; or (C++11) typedef-like alias for long nested names.
using namespace std; in a header file pollutes every file that includes it; prefer qualified names or using-declarations in headers.

concepts.text: Function Overloading
Overloading lets several functions share one name as long as their parameter lists differ (compile-time / static polymorphism):
items: Signatures must differ in the number of parameters, the type of at least one parameter, or their order. A different return type alone is NOT enough: int f(int) and double f(int) is an error.
Parameters that differ only by a top-level const (f(int) vs f(const int)) or by typedef name are the same signature. f(int*) and f(const int*) do differ.

Overload resolution picks, for each argument, the best match in this order: exact match (including array-to-pointer decay) > promotion (char/short -> int, float -> double) > standard conversion (int -> double, double -> int, derived* -> base*) > user-defined conversion (constructor or conversion operator) > ellipsis (...).
If two candidates are equally good the call is ambiguous and fails to compile, e.g. f(int) and f(double) called with a long, or f(int, double) and f(double, int) called with (1, 1).
Default arguments and overloading interact: void f(int); void f(int, int = 0); makes f(5) ambiguous.

The compiler implements overloading by name mangling: each overload gets a unique internal name that encodes its parameter types, which is why C++ names differ from C names (extern "C" turns mangling off).

concepts.text: Inline Functions and Default Arguments
inline asks the compiler to replace each call with the function body, saving the call/return overhead for tiny, frequently called functions:
items: inline is only a request. The compiler may ignore it for recursive functions, functions containing loops or switch, large bodies, functions whose address is taken, or virtual functions.
Because the body must be visible at every call, inline functions are normally defined in header files; unlike ordinary functions, an inline definition may appear in several translation units.
Member functions defined inside the class body are implicitly inline.

Inline vs macro: an inline function is type-checked, evaluates each argument exactly once and obeys scope; a #define macro is textual substitution done by the preprocessor, so SQR(x+1) expands to x+1*x+1 and SQR(i++) increments twice.
Excessive inlining enlarges the executable (code bloat) and can hurt cache behaviour, so it is not automatically faster.

concepts.text:
inline int sqr(int x) { return x * x; }         // body inserted at call site
#define SQR(x) x * x                            // macro: no type check

int volume(int l, int b = 1, int h = 1);        // defaults in the PROTOTYPE only
int volume(int l, int b, int h) { return l * b * h; }  // not repeated here

int main() {
    int r1 = sqr(2 + 1);     // 9
    int r2 = SQR(2 + 1);     // 2 + 1 * 2 + 1 = 5  (macro trap)
    volume(2);               // 2 * 1 * 1 = 2
    volume(2, 3);            // 2 * 3 * 1 = 6
    volume(2, 3, 4);         // 24
    return 0;
}
Rules for default arguments:
items: Once a parameter has a default, every parameter to its right must also have one: int f(int a, int b = 2, int c) is an error; int f(int a, int b = 2, int c = 3) is valid.
Arguments are matched left to right, so the caller cannot skip a middle parameter: f(1, , 5) is illegal.
The default is written once, normally in the declaration (prototype or header). Writing it again in the definition is a redefinition error.
Defaults may be constants, global variables or function calls evaluated at each call; they may not use other parameters of the same function.
A function with n parameters of which k have defaults accepts between n - k and n arguments.
Defaults are a lighter alternative to writing several overloads that differ only in trailing parameters.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Overloading, Defaults, References and Namespaces

When a call names an overloaded function, the compiler works in three steps. First it collects the candidates: every function of that name visible at the call. Next it keeps the viable ones, whose parameter count fits the arguments (counting default arguments) and whose parameters can each accept the corresponding argument by some implicit conversion. Finally it ranks each argument's conversion as exact match, promotion or standard conversion; a function wins only if it is at least as good for every argument and strictly better for at least one, and if no function wins the call is ambiguous and does not compile.

char s[3] = "abc"; is legal C (the '\0' is dropped) but an error in C++, where the array must have room for the terminator.
C++ keywords such as new, delete, class, this, template and namespace are ordinary identifiers in C, so int new = 5; is valid only in C.

items: cout << x uses the insertion operator and cin >> x the extraction operator; each returns the stream itself, which is why calls can be chained: cout << a << b;
cin >> skips leading white space and stops at the next white space, so it reads one word; std::getline(std::cin, s) reads a whole line.
If the input cannot be converted (letters typed for an int), cin sets its failbit, the variable receives 0 (since C++11), and later reads do nothing until cin.clear() is called.
std::endl writes '\n' and flushes the buffer; '\n' alone only writes the newline, which is faster when many lines are printed.
A bool prints as 1 or 0 unless std::boolalpha is used, and a char prints as a character while the same value stored in an int prints as a number.

Also remember that ::x always means the global x, never a variable of an enclosing block.

notes.text: Two classic one-liners: functions cannot be overloaded on return type alone, and default arguments must be filled from the rightmost parameter leftward. Expect an MCQ that shows int f(int a = 1, int b) and asks whether it compiles (it does not).

Never return a reference (or pointer) to a local variable: the variable is destroyed when the function returns and the caller gets a dangling reference. Returning a reference to a parameter that was itself passed by reference, or to a static/global, is fine.

Macro versus inline output traps: with #define SQR(x) x * x, the expression SQR(a + b) becomes a + b * a + b, and 10 / SQR(2) becomes 10 / 2 * 2 = 10. Parenthesise every macro argument and the whole body, or simply use an inline function.

float -> double and char/short -> int are promotions and beat conversions. So with f(int) and f(double), calling f('a') picks f(int) and f(2.5f) picks f(double); calling f(3L) is ambiguous because long -> int and long -> double are both conversions.

concepts.text: Purpose and Syntax

Operator overloading lets the built-in operators (+, -, ==, <<, [] and so on) work on objects of user-defined classes, so that c1 + c2 reads as naturally for two Complex numbers as it does for two ints. It is a form of compile-time polymorphism: the compiler picks the overload from the operand types. An overloaded operator is an ordinary function whose name is the keyword operator followed by the operator symbol. The compiler rewrites a + b as a.operator+(b) when the function is a member of the class, or as operator+(a, b) when it is a non-member function.
Rules every overload must obey:
items: You cannot invent new operators (no ** for power) and cannot redefine operators for built-in types alone: at least one operand must be a class or enumeration type.
Precedence, associativity and the number of operands (arity) are fixed: an overloaded * still binds tighter than +, and a binary + always takes exactly two operands.
Meaning is not enforced: operator+ may subtract, but good practice keeps the natural meaning of the symbol.
Five operators can never be overloaded: :: (scope resolution), . (member access), .* (pointer-to-member), ?: (conditional) and sizeof; typeid and the C++ cast operators are also excluded.
The operators =, [], () and -> must be member functions; every other overloadable operator may be a member or a non-member.
Default arguments are not allowed for overloaded operators, except for operator().

concepts.text: Member vs Friend (Non-member) Functions
Choosing the form:
items: Member function: the left operand is the object itself (*this), so a unary operator takes no parameter and a binary operator takes one.

Non-member function: all operands are parameters, so unary takes one parameter and binary takes two. Declare it friend inside the class if it must touch private data; otherwise it uses public getters.

Use a non-member when the left operand is not an object of your class: 2.0 * c needs operator*(double, const Complex&), and cout << c needs operator<<(ostream&, const Complex&) because the left operand is the stream.
A member overload never converts its left operand through a constructor, but a non-member converts either operand, which is why symmetric operators such as + and == are often written as friends.

rows: 2 parameters: T operator+(const T&, const T&)

concepts.text: Unary Operators: -, ++ and --

The prefix and postfix forms use the same symbol, so C++ tells them apart with an unused int parameter: operator++() is prefix and operator++(int) is postfix, and the compiler passes 0 as the dummy argument. Prefix should return a reference to the updated object (*this) so that ++(++c) works, while postfix must copy the old value, increment the object and return the copy by value, which is why postfix is slightly slower for class types. As friends the signatures are Counter& operator++(Counter& c) for prefix and Counter operator++(Counter& c, int) for postfix.
Binary Operators and Stream Insertion

Arithmetic operators build and return a new object by value, while comparison operators (==, !=, <, >) return bool; a magnitude-based operator< for Complex would compare re*re + im*im. The insertion operator << cannot be a member of Complex because its left operand is an ostream, so it is written as a friend taking (ostream&, const Complex&) and returning ostream& so that cout << a << b chains left to right. Extraction >> takes (istream&, Complex&), a non-const reference, because it modifies the object being read into.
Assignment, Subscript and Function Call
Return types and chaining:
items: Copy assignment, compound assignment (+=) and prefix ++ return T& (that is, *this) so calls can chain: a = b = c is evaluated as a = (b = c).
Arithmetic and postfix operators return a fresh T by value; returning a reference to a local object is a dangling-reference bug.
operator[] returns a reference so the element can be assigned to; add a const overload returning a value or const reference for const objects.
operator() may take any number of parameters, which lets an object behave like a function (a function object or functor), widely used with STL algorithms.
The compiler-generated operator= does a shallow member-wise copy; a class that owns heap memory must overload = together with the copy constructor and destructor (the rule of three) to deep copy.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Operator Overloading

For an expression a @ b the compiler collects three kinds of candidates: member functions a.operator@(b) of the left operand's class, non-member functions operator@(a, b) (friends declared in the class are found through the operands' class), and the built-in operator; ordinary overload resolution then picks the best match. A member candidate exists only when the left operand already is an object of the class, because no conversion is ever applied to the object that becomes *this, whereas a non-member lets both operands be converted by a converting constructor. That is why, with a constructor M(int), a member operator+ accepts a + 3 but rejects 3 + a, while a friend operator+ accepts both; marking the constructor explicit switches this conversion off.

concepts.plainText: a = b = c is evaluated as a.operator=(b.operator=(c)), so the inner call must return the object (normally T&, that is *this); a void return breaks the chain

concepts.text:
Worked example 1 - output: 7 5 7
Ctr a(5);      a.n = 5
b = a++;       postfix: old = copy of a (5); a.n = 6; b is the copy -> b.n = 5
c = ++a;       prefix:  a.n = 7; returns a itself; c copies it     -> c.n = 7
print          a.n = 7, b.n = 5, c.n = 7
The dummy int only selects the postfix version; the compiler passes 0.

Worked example 2 - output: [17][12][3]
c = 10 + a     int on the left: only the friend fits, 10 -> M(10)
               operator+(M(10), a) = M(12)                        c = 12
(a += b)       a.operator+=(b): a = 2 + 3 = 5, returns a (M&)
      += c     a.operator+=(c): a = 5 + 12 = 17                   a = 17
cout << a << c << b
               = operator<<(operator<<(operator<<(cout, a), c), b)
               each call returns cout, so the output is [17][12][3]

Relational operators are normally built from two primitives: define == and <, then write a != b as !(a == b), a > b as b < a, a <= b as !(b < a) and a >= b as !(a < b). In C++17 the compiler generates none of these, so a class with only operator== cannot be compared with !=. A class that overloads operator() produces function objects (functors); unlike a plain function, a functor can keep state in its data members between calls, and each copy of it keeps its own state.
Frequent errors in overloaded operators:
items: Returning a reference to a local result from operator+ (T& operator+(...) { T r; ...; return r; }): r dies at the closing brace, leaving a dangling reference.
Taking the right operand by non-const reference (T operator+(T &o)): then a + (b + c) fails because the temporary b + c cannot bind to T&.
Writing operator<< as a member function: it then has to be used as obj << cout, never cout << obj.
Returning void from operator= or operator<<: a single use works, but a = b = c and cout << x << y no longer compile.
Returning T& from postfix ++: the old value exists only as a local copy, so postfix must return T by value.
Defining both a member and a non-member version with the same parameter types, which makes every call ambiguous.

concepts.text: To trace an overloaded-operator program, first rewrite each operator as the call it becomes (a + b as a.operator+(b) or operator+(a, b), c++ as c.operator++(0)), keep the normal precedence and associativity, and note for each call whether it returns a copy or a reference to *this. Then evaluate the calls exactly like ordinary function calls.

Overloading &&, || or the comma operator turns them into ordinary function calls: both operands are always evaluated, so short-circuit evaluation is lost (C++17 still evaluates the left operand first). Avoid overloading these three.

formulas.plainText: a + b is a.operator+(b) for a member, operator+(a, b) for a non-member
For an n-operand operator: a member takes n - 1 parameters, a friend takes n
Prefix: T& operator++()  |  Postfix: T operator++(int) - the int is a dummy
Cannot be overloaded: ::  .  .*  ?:  sizeof

notes.text: operator++(int): the int is only a marker that means postfix. Prefix returns T&, postfix returns T holding the old value. For Counter d = c++; d keeps the value before the increment and c is incremented.
Without the if (this != &o) check, a deep-copying operator= applied to a = a deletes the data first and then copies from freed memory. Also remember to return *this, or a = b = c will not compile.

cout << obj works only with a non-member (usually friend) operator<< that returns ostream&. A member version would have to be called as obj << cout, because the left operand of a member operator is always *this.
Overloading never changes precedence, associativity or arity: in c1 + c2 * c3 the * runs first whatever your overloads do, and you cannot write a one-operand binary +.

concepts.text: Polymorphism: One Interface, Many Forms

Polymorphism (Greek: "many forms") lets the same function call behave differently depending on the object it acts on. C++ offers two kinds. Compile-time (static) polymorphism is achieved with function overloading, operator overloading and templates: the compiler picks the function from the argument types while compiling. Run-time (dynamic) polymorphism is achieved with virtual functions called through a base-class pointer or reference: the function actually executed is chosen while the program runs, from the real type of the object being pointed to.

rows: Virtual functions called through base pointers or references
At compile time from the static type of the expression
At run time from the dynamic type of the object
Hidden vptr in the object plus a per-class vtable
One pointer per object and one indirection per call
Shape *s = new Circle; s->area() runs Circle::area

concepts.text: Pointers to Base and Static Binding

Under public inheritance a derived object is-a base object, so a base-class pointer or reference may point to a derived object without any cast (upcasting is implicit). The reverse needs an explicit cast. When a member function is not virtual, the compiler resolves p->show() from the declared type of p, so the base version runs even though p points to a derived object. This is static (early) binding, and it is the default in C++.
Virtual Functions and Dynamic Binding
A virtual function is a base-class member function declared with the keyword virtual; it tells the compiler to defer the choice of function to run time. Rules:
items: Declare it virtual in the base class only; once virtual, it stays virtual in every derived class even if the keyword is omitted there.

The derived version must have the same name, the same parameter list, the same const-ness and the same (or covariant) return type; a different parameter list creates an unrelated overload that hides the base function instead of overriding it.
C++11 override after the parameter list asks the compiler to verify that the function really overrides a base virtual; final forbids further overriding.
Dynamic binding happens only when the call goes through a pointer or reference to the base; calling through an object (b.f()) is always resolved statically by slicing.
A virtual function cannot be static (no this pointer) and cannot be a friend (friends are not members); a constructor cannot be virtual, but a destructor can and usually should be.
If the derived class does not override, the base version is inherited and used; the base implementation can be called explicitly as Base::f().
Default arguments are bound statically from the pointer type, so keep them identical in base and derived versions.

concepts.text: Mechanism in outline: for every class with at least one virtual function the compiler builds one virtual table (vtable), an array of function pointers holding the address of the most-derived override of each virtual function. Every object of such a class carries a hidden pointer (vptr) that the constructor sets to its class's vtable. A call p->area() becomes: read p->vptr, take the entry for area in that table, call it. The lookup is constant time but is one indirection slower than a direct call and adds one pointer (4 or 8 bytes) to each object.
Virtual Destructors

When a derived object is deleted through a base-class pointer, the destructor that runs is chosen exactly like any other member call. If the base destructor is not virtual, only ~Base runs, the derived part is never cleaned up and the behaviour is formally undefined. Declaring the base destructor virtual makes delete p look up the real destructor in the vtable, so ~Derived runs first and then ~Base, as usual. Rule of thumb: any class that has one virtual function, or is meant to be used polymorphically, must also have a virtual destructor.
Pure Virtual Functions and Abstract Classes
A pure virtual function is declared by appending = 0 to the virtual declaration. The class then becomes an abstract class:
items: An abstract class contains at least one pure virtual function and cannot be instantiated: Shape s; and new Shape are compile errors.
Pointers and references to an abstract class are allowed, and this is exactly how polymorphic code is written: Shape *p = new Circle(2).
A derived class must override every pure virtual function to become concrete; if it leaves any unoverridden it is itself abstract.
A pure virtual function may still have a body defined outside the class (Shape::area() { ... }); derived classes can call it as Shape::area(), but the class stays abstract.
An abstract class can have data members, constructors (called from derived constructors) and ordinary member functions.
A class whose members are all pure virtual functions plus a virtual destructor acts as an interface: it fixes what derived classes must provide without supplying any implementation.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: How a Virtual Call Is Resolved

Every expression that names an object has a static type, fixed by its declaration, and the object it refers to has a dynamic type, the class it was actually created as. For a call p->f() the compiler always uses the static type to find the name, check access and pick among overloads; only if the chosen function is virtual is the body finally taken from the dynamic type, through the vptr. The function that runs is the final overrider: the most-derived override on the path from the static class to the object's class. Three situations make even a virtual call run a base version when the object is really a Derived: calling through a base-class object instead of a pointer or reference, qualifying the name as Base::f(), and calling from inside a base constructor or destructor.

Output: Bg Df Bf Bf Dg

p->g()      g is non-virtual: Base::g runs, prints Bg
            inside it f() is this->f(), virtual: prints Df
p->Base::f() qualified name, no dispatch: prints Bf
b.f()       b is a sliced copy whose dynamic type is Base: Bf
d.g()       static type Der: Der::g hides Base::g, prints Dg

rows: Looked up through the vptr at run time
Bound from the static type of p
Object's dynamic type is its declared type
Derived part not built yet or already destroyed
Defaults are bound at compile time
Derived f with different parameters or const
Not an override; it only hides the name

concepts.text: Construction and destruction explain the constructor rule. A Robot is built base first: while Machine() runs, the vptr points to Machine's vtable, so name() gives the Machine version. Robot() then resets the vptr to Robot's table before its body runs. Destruction reverses the steps: ~Robot's body, then its members, then ~Machine, with the vptr switched back to Machine's table before ~Machine's body. A virtual destructor is what lets delete m start at ~Robot even though m is a Machine pointer.

Output: M:machine R:robot ~R ~Part ~M:machine

new Robot   Machine() runs first, vptr = Machine table: M:machine
            Robot() runs, vptr = Robot table:         R:robot
delete m    ~Machine is virtual, so ~Robot runs first:  ~R
            member arm is destroyed after the body:   ~Part
            ~Machine runs with vptr back on Machine:  ~M:machine

concepts.plainText: sizeof(obj) = ceil((d + p) / a) x a, where d = bytes of data members (assuming no padding is needed between them), p = vptr size, a = the largest alignment requirement among the members and the vptr. Implementation-dependent: this assumes the usual model of one vptr per object; on a typical 64-bit system (4-byte int, 8-byte vptr with 8-byte alignment) one int plus the vptr gives ceil(12/8) x 8 = 16 bytes

concepts.text: Checklist for a correct override, and what happens when a rule is broken:
items: Same name, parameter types and const or ref qualifiers as the base virtual function; any difference creates a new function that hides the base one.
Return type identical, or covariant: Base* or Base& in the base may become Derived* or Derived& in the override; any other change is a compile error.
Access may differ: a private override is still called through a public base pointer, because access is checked against the static type.
Mark every override with override so mismatches become compile errors, and use final to stop further overriding or further derivation.
A pure virtual destructor, virtual ~Shape() = 0;, still needs a definition such as Shape::~Shape() {}, because every derived destructor calls it.

concepts.text: Three frequent bugs: a derived function missing the const of the base version (it silently stops overriding), deleting a derived object through a base pointer whose destructor is not virtual (undefined behaviour), and storing derived objects by value in a base-class array or parameter (slicing). Pointers, references and override avoid all three.

For an output question, first note the static type of each pointer or reference and the class each object was created as. Then check three things: is the function virtual at that static level, is the call made through a pointer or reference, and is a constructor or destructor running at that moment. Only when all three favour dispatch does the derived version run.

formulas.plainText: virtual T f(...) = 0;  (pure virtual; class becomes abstract)
sizeof(object) = data members + sizeof(vptr) when the class has any virtual function
virtual call: p -> vptr -> vtable[i] -> f(), one indirection, O(1)

notes.text: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer whose destructor is not virtual is undefined behaviour and typically leaks the derived part. Any polymorphic base class needs virtual ~Base().

Output-prediction trap: with Base *p = &d, p->f() runs Derived::f only if f is virtual in Base; otherwise Base::f runs. A call through an object (Base b = d; b.f()) always runs Base::f because the derived part is sliced off.

Overloading = same name, different parameter list, resolved at compile time (compile-time polymorphism). Overriding = same signature, virtual, redefined in a derived class, resolved at run time. Redefining a non-virtual function in a derived class is hiding, not overriding.

Constructors, static member functions and friend functions can never be virtual; a virtual call made from inside a constructor uses the constructor's own class version because the derived part does not exist yet.

concepts.text: Why Generic Programming

Generic programming means writing an algorithm or a data structure once, in terms of a type that is filled in later, instead of copying the same code for int, double, string and so on. In C++ this is done with templates: a template is a blueprint from which the compiler generates (instantiates) a concrete function or class for each type actually used. The generated code is type-checked and as fast as hand-written code, unlike C macros (no type checking) or void* tricks (no safety). The Standard Template Library is built entirely on this idea.
Function Templates
Rules of function templates:
items: Syntax: template <typename T> (or template <class T>) immediately before the function; typename and class mean exactly the same thing here.
Template argument deduction: the compiler works out T from the argument types at the call; every use of T must deduce to the same type, otherwise the call is an error.
Explicit arguments: maxOf<double>(4, 6.5) forces T; required when T appears only in the return type or cannot be deduced.
Multiple parameters: template <typename T, typename U> lets each argument have its own type; parameters given explicitly are matched left to right, the rest are deduced.
Each distinct set of template arguments produces a separate copy of the function (an instantiation) at compile time; the template itself generates no code until used.

concepts.text: Overloading Function Templates

A function template can be overloaded with other templates and with ordinary (non-template) functions of the same name. Overload resolution then follows a fixed preference: an ordinary function that matches the arguments exactly is chosen over any template; otherwise the template that fits with no conversion is chosen; if two templates both fit, the more specialised one (for example T* over T) wins; a non-template that needs a conversion loses to a template that matches exactly, because deduction can always produce an exact match.
Class Templates
Points about class templates:
items: Syntax: template <class T> class Name { ... };  T can be used for data members, member function parameters and return types.
Instantiation is always explicit for classes: Stack<int> s; the compiler cannot deduce T from a constructor call in C++11 (that arrived only in C++17).
Member functions defined outside the class need the full header again: template <class T> void Stack<T>::push(T x) { ... }. The class name is Stack<T>, not Stack.
Because the compiler must see the template to instantiate it, template definitions normally live in the header file, not in a separate .cpp.
Non-type parameters (template <class T, int N>) accept constant expressions such as array sizes; default template arguments (int N = 10) work like default function arguments.
Stack<int> and Stack<double> are unrelated classes: they share no static members and cannot be assigned to each other.

concepts.text: Specialisation in outline: a template can be given a special version for one particular type when the general code would be wrong or slow for it, written as template <> class Stack<bool> { ... } (explicit specialisation) or template <class T> class Stack<T*> { ... } (partial specialisation, classes only). Function templates allow full specialisation only; in practice an ordinary overload is preferred. Specialisation is what lets STL containers store bool or pointers efficiently.

MCQs often test the exact spelling of template headers (template <typename T>, template <class T> Stack<T>::push), what T is deduced as for a given call, and which overload is picked when a template and a non-template both apply. Trace the argument types carefully: an int literal is int, 2.5 is double, 'a' is char and "text" is const char*.
Going Deeper: Deduction, Specialisation and Instantiation

Template argument deduction compares each function parameter type P with the type A of the matching argument and solves for the template parameters. For a by-value parameter T the argument first decays: an array becomes a pointer to its first element, a function becomes a function pointer, and top-level const is dropped, because the function works on a copy. For a reference parameter T& or const T& nothing decays, so T can become an array type such as int[5]. Deduction does not apply the ordinary implicit conversions such as int to double (only small adjustments such as adding const are allowed) and never looks at the return type, which is why maxOf(3, 4.5) fails and why a parameter used only in the return type must be written explicitly.

Output (8-byte double and pointer, ASCII):
8 32
4 A 3.5

byValue(d)       T = double*, the array decayed: sizeof = 8
byRef(d)         T = double[4], no decay: 4 x 8 = 32
as<int>(d[3])    R = int given, T = double deduced: 4.5 -> 4
as<char>(65)     R = char: 65 is 'A', printed as a character
as<double>(7)/2  R = double: 7.0 / 2 = 3.5, not integer division

An explicit specialisation such as template <> void f<char>(char) is not a new overload: it only supplies a different body for one instantiation of an existing primary template. Overload resolution therefore works in two steps. First the compiler compares the ordinary functions and the primary templates, with their deduced arguments, and picks the best; an ordinary function wins a tie with a template, and between two templates the more specialised one wins. Only if the winner is a primary template does the compiler check whether that particular instantiation has an explicit specialisation, and use its body if it has.

Output: spec-char ordinary primary primary primary

f('x')       f(int) needs a char -> int promotion; the template gives
             T = char exactly, so the template wins, and f<char>
             has an explicit specialisation: spec-char
f(7)         f(int) and f<int> are both exact: the ordinary one wins
f(7L)        only the template is exact (T = long): primary
f<>(7)       empty <> allows templates only: f<int>, not specialised
f<int>('x')  T fixed as int, 'x' converted to 120: primary

Each distinct, complete list of template arguments names a different specialisation: default arguments are filled in first, so Row<> and Row<int, 3> are the same class while Row<int, 4> is another one with its own static members. Only what is used gets instantiated: a member function of Stack<int> is compiled only if it is called, so a class template can hold a type that lacks an operator needed by an uncalled member. The declaration template class Stack<int>; (an explicit instantiation) forces every member to be generated in that file, which lets template code stay in a .cpp file for a fixed set of types. Because non-type arguments are compile-time constants, a class template can even recurse on them, with an explicit specialisation as the base case.

concepts.latex: F\langle N\rangle = N \cdot F\langle N-1\rangle,\quad F\langle 0\rangle = 1
concepts.plainText: F<N>::value = N x F<N-1>::value, with the explicit specialisation F<0>::value = 1 as the base case; e.g. F<4> = 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 x 1 = 24, computed entirely by the compiler

concepts.text: Common mistakes with templates:
items: Naming a dependent type without typename: inside template <class C>, C::const_iterator it; does not compile; write typename C::const_iterator it;.
Giving a class template parameter a default and a later parameter none: template <class T = int, class U> class P; is ill-formed.
Using a run-time variable as a non-type argument: int n = 8; Buf<n> b; fails, while const int k = 8; Buf<k> b; is fine.
An out-of-class member definition must match its declaration exactly, including const: template <class T> T Box<T>::get() const { return v; }.
An explicit specialisation must be declared before the first use that would implicitly instantiate the same template arguments; place it right after the primary template.
Expecting a function template specialisation to beat an ordinary overload: specialisations never take part in overload resolution, so an ordinary overload is usually the clearer choice.
