concepts.text: To predict which function a call runs: (1) deduce T for every candidate template from the argument types, allowing no conversions; (2) rank the ordinary functions and templates, letting an ordinary function win a tie and the more specialised template win between templates; (3) only then swap in an explicit specialisation if the winning template has one. For class templates, fill in default arguments before deciding whether two names are the same type. Under C++17, Box b(2.5); deduces Box<double> from the constructor argument.

formulas.plainText: instantiations = number of distinct <T> argument sets actually used (zero if never called)
Stack<T, N> data storage = N × sizeof(T) bytes (plus the int top)
Overload preference: non-template exact match > template exact match > non-template needing conversion

notes.text: When an ordinary function and a function template both match a call exactly, the ordinary function is chosen. The template only wins when the ordinary function would need a conversion (e.g. print('a') with print(int) and template print(T) calls the template with T = char).

maxOf(3, 4.5) with template <typename T> T maxOf(T, T) is a compile error, not a promotion: deduction gives T = int from the first argument and T = double from the second. Fix it with maxOf<double>(3, 4.5) or two type parameters.

Outside the class, a member of a class template is defined as template <class T> ReturnType ClassName<T>::member(...) { ... }. Forgetting the <T> after the class name, or the template <class T> header, is the classic syntax slip.

concepts.text: Control Memory and Control Words

In a microprogrammed control unit the control signals for each step of an instruction are not produced by wired logic but are stored as binary words. The set of control signals active in one clock period is a control word; a control word stored in memory is a microinstruction; a sequence of microinstructions that carries out one machine instruction is a microprogram (a routine); and the memory that holds all the routines is the control memory. Because the microprograms rarely change, control memory is usually a ROM; a writable control memory allows dynamic microprogramming, where microcode is loaded from disk at start-up.
The pieces of a microprogrammed control unit (Mano's organisation):
items: Control address register (CAR): holds the address of the microinstruction currently being read from control memory.
Control memory (ROM): holds the microprogram; each word is one microinstruction.
Control data register (pipeline register): holds the microinstruction just read, so that its control bits can drive the datapath while the next address is being formed.
Next-address generator (microprogram sequencer): computes the next value of CAR from the current microinstruction, external status bits and the instruction opcode.
Subroutine register (SBR): saves the return address when a microprogram subroutine is called.

concepts.text: Address Sequencing

Each machine instruction has its own routine in control memory, and all instructions share a fetch routine and an effective-address routine. Executing an instruction therefore means: run the fetch routine, run the address routine, then jump to the routine for this opcode, and at its end return to fetch. The sequencer must provide the address transitions that make this possible.
Four ways in which the next microinstruction address can be formed:
items: Incrementing CAR: the normal case, CAR ← CAR + 1, moving to the next word of the current routine.
Branching, unconditional or conditional: the address field of the microinstruction is loaded into CAR, either always or only when a selected status bit (indirect bit, sign, zero) is 1.
Mapping: after fetch, the opcode bits of the instruction are transformed into the starting address of that instruction's routine, either by a fixed bit pattern or through a small mapping ROM.

Subroutine call and return: CAR + 1 is saved in SBR and CAR is loaded with the subroutine address; at the end CAR ← SBR restores the return address. The effective-address computation is the usual shared subroutine.

concepts.text: Mano's Microinstruction Format

Mano's example computer has a 128 × 20 control memory. Each microinstruction has three microoperation fields F1, F2 and F3 of 3 bits each, a 2-bit condition field CD, a 2-bit branch field BR and a 7-bit address field AD: 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 7 = 20 bits. Up to three microoperations (one from each field, chosen so they do not conflict) execute in one clock; the CD and BR fields together tell the sequencer how to form the next address. Because the opcode is 4 bits, mapping places routine starting addresses at 0 xxxx 00, giving each instruction 4 consecutive words.

concepts.plainText: Microinstruction length = F1 + F2 + F3 + CD + BR + AD = 3+3+3+2+2+7 = 20 bits

rows: CAR ← AD if condition true, else CAR ← CAR + 1
SBR ← CAR + 1, CAR ← AD if condition true, else CAR + 1

concepts.text: The microoperation codes of the three F fields (000 is NOP in every field):
items: F1: 001 ADD (AC ← AC + DR), 010 CLRAC, 011 INCAC, 100 DRTAC (AC ← DR), 101 DRTAR (AR ← DR(0–10)), 110 PCTAR (AR ← PC), 111 WRITE (M[AR] ← DR).
F2: 001 SUB, 010 OR, 011 AND, 100 READ (DR ← M[AR]), 101 ACTDR (DR ← AC), 110 INCDR, 111 PCTDR (DR(0–10) ← PC).
F3: 001 XOR, 010 COM (AC ← AC'), 011 SHL, 100 SHR, 101 INCPC, 110 ARTPC (PC ← AR), 111 reserved.
A symbolic microinstruction is written as LABEL: MICROOPS CD BR AD, one per line; the assembler converts it to the 20-bit word.

concepts.text:
ORG 64                        ; fetch routine
FETCH: PCTAR      U JMP NEXT       ; AR <- PC
       READ, INCPC U JMP NEXT      ; DR <- M[AR], PC <- PC + 1
       DRTAR      U MAP            ; AR <- DR(0-10), jump to opcode routine
ORG 0                         ; ADD routine
ADD:   NOP        I CALL INDRCT    ; if I = 1 fetch effective address
       READ       U JMP NEXT       ; DR <- M[AR]
       ADD        U JMP FETCH      ; AC <- AC + DR, back to fetch
INDRCT: READ      U JMP NEXT       ; subroutine: DR <- M[AR]
       DRTAR      U RET            ; AR <- DR(0-10), return
Horizontal vs Vertical, and vs Hardwired

rows: One bit per control signal, little or no encoding
Fields heavily encoded; decoders regenerate signals
Usually one or a few per word

concepts.text: Microprogrammed control compared with hardwired control:
items: Advantages: systematic design, easy to modify or extend the instruction set, supports emulation of another machine, simpler to debug, and fewer random-logic errors in complex CISC control units.
Disadvantages: slower because every micro-step needs a control-memory access, the control memory costs chip area, and the hardware to support it (sequencer, mapping logic) is itself non-trivial.
Hardwired control wins on speed and is used in RISC designs; microprogrammed control historically dominated CISC machines such as the VAX and early x86.

concepts.text: Worked example: a control memory of 128 words of 20 bits. The number of words fixes the address width, 128 = 2^7, so CAR and the AD field are 7 bits. If the design grew to 1024 microinstructions, CAR would need 10 bits and every microinstruction would lengthen by 3 bits in its AD field. The word length, 20 bits here, is fixed by how many control fields are packed into one microinstruction, not by the size of the memory.
Going Deeper: Sizing, Sequencing and Timing Microprograms

A microinstruction is sized field by field. Signals that may be active together each need their own bit, as in a horizontal format. A group of k signals that are never active together, such as the sources that drive one bus, can share an encoded field of ceil(log2(k + 1)) bits, because one code must mean 'none of them'. A condition-select field that chooses among c status bits plus 'always true' needs ceil(log2(c + 1)) bits, the branch-type field needs enough bits to name each kind of address transition, and the next-address field needs log2 N bits for an N-word control memory.

concepts.plainText: w = h direct bits + sum over encoded groups of ceil(log2(ki + 1)) + ceil(log2(c + 1)) condition bits + b branch-type bits + log2 N address bits

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: sizing a microinstruction
Given: 2K-word control memory, 12 independent signals,
       groups of 6, 15 and 3 mutually exclusive micro-operations,
       10 status conditions plus 'always', 4 branch types
Direct field         : 12 bits
Group of 6  (+ none) : ceil(log2 7)  = 3 bits
Group of 15 (+ none) : ceil(log2 16) = 4 bits
Group of 3  (+ none) : ceil(log2 4)  = 2 bits
Condition select     : ceil(log2 11) = 4 bits
Branch type          : log2 4        = 2 bits
Next address         : log2 2048     = 11 bits
Word = 12 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 11 = 38 bits
Control memory = 2048 x 38 = 77,824 bits = 9.5 KiB
One bit per signal in the groups would give 12 + 24 + 4 + 2 + 11 = 53 bits

rows: How the next address is obtained
The tested condition picks one of two explicit addresses in the word
CAR + 1 normally; the AD field on a true branch; SBR on RET; the mapped opcode on MAP
One address field; needs an incrementer and a multiplexer
Control words fall through to CAR + 1; separate branch words carry the condition and address
Shortest word; each branch costs an extra microinstruction
Opcode mapping (fixed bits or mapping ROM)
The opcode forms the routine's start address after fetch
Fixed bits waste unused words; a ROM allows any placement

concepts.text: Mano's sequencer is a 4 × 1 multiplexer in front of CAR whose inputs are CAR + 1, the AD field, SBR and the mapped opcode address. A second 4 × 1 multiplexer, steered by CD, picks the status bit T (U, I, S or Z), and small input logic turns BR and T into the select lines. JMP and CALL take AD when T = 1 and CAR + 1 when T = 0, CALL also loads SBR with CAR + 1 but only when the branch is taken, and RET and MAP ignore T altogether. A CALL whose condition is false therefore behaves exactly like a step to the next word.

Worked example 2: EXCHANGE with I = 1 (opcode 0011 maps to 0 0011 00 = 12)
CAR  Microinstruction          Effect                 Next CAR
64   PCTAR U JMP NEXT          AR <- PC               65
65   READ, INCPC U JMP NEXT    DR <- M[AR], PC+1      66
66   DRTAR U MAP               AR <- DR(0-10)         12
12   NOP I CALL INDRCT         I = 1: SBR <- 13       67
67   READ U JMP NEXT           DR <- M[AR]            68
68   DRTAR U RET               AR <- DR(0-10)         13 (from SBR)
13   READ U JMP NEXT           DR <- M[AR]            14
14   ACTDR, DRTAC U JMP NEXT   AC and DR swap         15
15   WRITE U JMP FETCH         M[AR] <- DR            64
Total: 9 microinstructions (7 when I = 0)

Long microprograms often repeat the same control word many times. A two-level store keeps each distinct word once in a nanomemory and replaces every microinstruction with a short pointer to it. For example, 1024 microinstructions of 120 bits containing only 128 distinct words need 1024 × 120 = 122,880 bits in one level, but only 1024 × 7 + 128 × 120 = 7,168 + 15,360 = 22,528 bits in two levels, about 18% of the original. The price is a second memory access in every step, and the Motorola 68000 is a well-known processor that used such a microcode and nanocode pair.

concepts.latex: S_{2} = N \lceil \log_{2} U \rceil + U\,w \quad \text{versus} \quad S_{1} = N\,w
concepts.plainText: Two-level store S2 = N × ceil(log2 U) + U × w bits, versus one level S1 = N × w (N microinstructions, U distinct words of w bits)

concepts.text: Timing rules for microprogrammed control:
items: Instruction time = (fetch-routine words + effective-address words when used + execute words) × microinstruction cycle; weight any optional part by how often it runs.

Without a pipeline register the microinstruction cycle is control-memory access time plus datapath time; with one it is the larger of the two, because the next word is read while the current one executes.
A branch that tests a status bit produced by the current microinstruction cannot be overlapped in the same way and can cost an extra cycle.
A hardwired unit produces each step's signals within a few gate delays, so the same sequence of steps runs faster; microprogramming trades that speed for ease of change.

concepts.text: Common slips: forgetting the 'none' code when encoding a group (8 signals need 4 bits, not 3); sizing the address field from the word length instead of the number of words; counting the fetch routine only once for a whole program; treating micro-operations in different fields of one word as sequential (they all take effect at the same clock edge); and assuming that CALL loads SBR even when its condition is false.

For a sizing question, write one line per field with its bit count before adding them, and check every encoded field for a 'none' code and the condition field for an 'always' code. For a Mano trace, list the CAR values in order: fetch 64, 65, 66, then the mapped address 4 × opcode, with 67 and 68 inserted whenever I = 1 leads to the INDRCT subroutine.

formulas.plainText: CAR bits = log2(number of microinstructions); 128 words need 7 bits
Microinstruction length = sum of field widths = 20 bits in Mano's format
Control memory size = 2^n words × w bits per word (128 × 20 = 2560 bits)
Mapping: CAR = 0, four opcode bits, 00, giving 4 words per routine

notes.text: Learn the CD and BR tables as pairs: CD 00 U, 01 I, 10 S, 11 Z; BR 00 JMP, 01 CALL, 10 RET, 11 MAP. A frequent MCQ gives a 20-bit word and asks which field is which, or gives 128 × 20 and asks for the CAR width (7).
The number of words in control memory sets the address width; the word length sets how many control fields fit. 128 × 20 means 7-bit addresses and 20-bit words, not the other way round.

Only one microoperation per F field can be chosen per word, and the three chosen must not conflict (e.g. F1 = ADD and F2 = SUB both write AC). That is why the routine for one instruction usually needs several microinstructions.
A microprogram subroutine differs from a machine-language subroutine: the return address is kept in SBR, a single register, so nesting of microprogram calls is normally one level deep.

concepts.text: Instruction Fields and Address Formats

A machine instruction is a binary word divided into fields. The operation code (opcode) says what to do, a mode field says how to interpret the address part, and one or more operand or address fields say where the data is. Instructions may be fixed length (typical of RISC, one word each) or variable length (typical of CISC). How many address fields an instruction carries depends on the CPU organisation: a general-register machine allows two or three, a single-accumulator machine needs only one because the accumulator is implied, and a stack machine needs none for arithmetic because the operands are the top two stack entries. The standard way to compare formats is to code the same expression, X = (A + B) × (C + D), where A, B, C, D and X are memory locations. Three-address instructions give the shortest program but the longest instruction words; zero-address (stack) instructions are the shortest but need the most of them; one-address (accumulator) code needs a temporary memory location T.

; three-address (general register CPU)
ADD  R1, A, B        ; R1 <- M[A] + M[B]
ADD  R2, C, D        ; R2 <- M[C] + M[D]
MUL  X,  R1, R2      ; M[X] <- R1 * R2
; two-address (one operand is also the destination)
MOV  R1, A           ; R1 <- M[A]
ADD  R1, B           ; R1 <- R1 + M[B]
MOV  R2, C           ; R2 <- M[C]
ADD  R2, D           ; R2 <- R2 + M[D]
MUL  R1, R2          ; R1 <- R1 * R2
MOV  X,  R1          ; M[X] <- R1

; one-address (accumulator CPU)
LOAD  A              ; AC <- M[A]
ADD   B              ; AC <- AC + M[B]
STORE T              ; M[T] <- AC
LOAD  C              ; AC <- M[C]
ADD   D              ; AC <- AC + M[D]
MUL   T              ; AC <- AC * M[T]
STORE X              ; M[X] <- AC

; zero-address (stack CPU); PUSH and POP carry an address
PUSH A               ; TOS <- M[A]
PUSH B               ; TOS <- M[B]
ADD                  ; TOS <- (A + B)
PUSH C               ; TOS <- M[C]
PUSH D               ; TOS <- M[D]
ADD                  ; TOS <- (C + D)
MUL                  ; TOS <- (C + D) * (A + B)
POP  X               ; M[X] <- TOS
Addressing Modes

The addressing mode is the rule that turns the address field of an instruction into the effective address (EA), the actual location of the operand, or into the operand itself. Modes exist to shorten instructions, to support pointers, loops, arrays and relocatable code, and to give the programmer flexibility. Some modes need no memory reference for the operand (implied, immediate, register), some need one (direct, register indirect, relative, indexed, base), and indirect needs two.

rows: Operand fixed by the opcode itself
CMA (complement AC); all zero-address stack instructions
ADD R1, #5; no memory access; good for constants
Operand in the register named by the field
ADD R1, R2; fastest, short field
ADD R2, (R1); register holds a pointer
LDA 500; one memory access for the operand
LDA @500 or LDA (500); two memory accesses
BR +8; PC already advanced; position-independent branches
LDA 200(X); XR steps through an array
Base register holds start of segment; field is displacement; supports relocation
EA = register, then register ← register + 1 (or + word size)
LDA −(R1); walks a table backward; stack push

concepts.latex: EA_{rel} = PC + A,\quad EA_{idx} = XR + A,\quad EA_{ind} = M[A]
concepts.plainText: Relative EA = PC + A; indexed EA = XR + A; indirect EA = M[A]

concepts.text: Worked example: an instruction at address 400 with address field 500 has already advanced PC to 401 when the effective address is computed. Direct mode gives EA = 500; immediate mode gives the operand 500 itself; relative mode gives EA = 401 + 500 = 901; if XR = 100, indexed mode gives EA = 600; if M[500] = 800, indirect mode gives EA = 800. Numeric questions of this kind are common, so always ask whether PC has been incremented before the relative addition.
Data Transfer and Data Manipulation Instructions
Data transfer instructions move data without changing it:
items: Load (memory to register) and store (register to memory); move (register to register, or in some machines any to any); exchange (swap two registers or a register and a memory word).
Push and pop transfer a word between a register or memory and the top of the stack, adjusting the stack pointer.
Input and output move a word between a register and an I/O port; in memory-mapped I/O the ordinary load and store instructions do this.

The same load can appear with several addressing modes (LD ADR direct, LD @ADR indirect, LD R1 register, LD (R1) register indirect, LD #NBR immediate, LD $ADR relative, LD ADR(X) indexed), each a different opcode or mode bit pattern.

concepts.text: Data manipulation instructions compute on data and update the flags:
items: Arithmetic: increment, decrement, add, subtract, multiply, divide, add with carry, subtract with borrow, negate (2's complement); available for signed/unsigned integers and often floating point and BCD.

Logical and bit manipulation: clear, complement, AND (mask bits), OR (set bits), exclusive-OR (toggle bits), plus flag control such as clear carry, set carry, complement carry, enable and disable interrupt.
Shift: logical, arithmetic and circular (rotate) in both directions, one bit or n bits per instruction, with the carry flag optionally included in the rotation.

rows: SHL: 0 into LSB, MSB to carry
SHR: 0 into MSB, LSB to carry
SHLA: like SHL; overflow if sign changes
SHRA: sign bit copied into MSB
Signed multiply/divide by 2 with sign preserved
No bit lost; used in CRC and bit-field work
ROLC: carry into LSB, MSB into carry
RORC: carry into MSB, LSB into carry

concepts.text: Program control instructions change the flow of execution instead of the data: branch and jump (conditional on the status bits C, S, Z, V or unconditional), skip, call and return for subroutines using the stack, and compare and test, which perform a subtraction or an AND only to set the flags. Interrupts are a hardware-initiated form of program control that saves the return address and status, then transfers to a service routine.
Going Deeper: Field Sizing, Expanding Opcodes and Flags

Every field of an instruction must be wide enough for the largest value it has to name. An opcode that distinguishes N operations needs ⌈log2 N⌉ bits, a register field for R registers needs ⌈log2 R⌉ bits, a mode field for M addressing modes needs ⌈log2 M⌉ bits, and a direct address into a word-addressable memory of 2^n words needs n bits. The instruction length is the sum of its fields; when the length is fixed (say one 32-bit word) the fields compete, so whatever is left after the others decides the number of opcodes or the range of an immediate or displacement. A k-bit two's-complement field covers −2^(k−1) to 2^(k−1) − 1.

concepts.latex: L = \lceil \log_2 N_{op} \rceil + \lceil \log_2 M \rceil + r\lceil \log_2 R \rceil + a\,n
concepts.plainText: Length = ceil(log2 N_op) + ceil(log2 M) + r × ceil(log2 R) + a × n, for r register fields and a address fields of n bits

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: one-word 32-bit instruction, fields opcode | mode | reg | address
Memory 128K x 32, word-addressable: 128K = 2^17  -> address field 17 bits
40 registers: 2^5 = 32 < 40 <= 64 = 2^6         -> register field  6 bits
5 addressing modes: 4 < 5 <= 8                    -> mode field      3 bits
Opcode = 32 - 17 - 6 - 3                          -> opcode field    6 bits
Operations available = 2^6 = 64
Format: | opcode 6 | mode 3 | reg 6 | address 17 |

Expanding opcodes exploit the fact that an instruction with fewer address fields has spare bits. The designer leaves some patterns of the short opcode unused; each unused pattern, followed by the bits of an address field that the next format no longer needs, opens a whole block of longer opcodes. If a k-bit opcode field has U patterns in use and the next format releases an a-bit address field, 2^k − U patterns remain and each expands into 2^a new opcodes. Giving the commonest instructions the short opcodes also brings the average opcode length down, much like a variable-length code.

concepts.plainText: Opcodes available at the next level = (2^k − U) × 2^a

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: 16-bit instructions with 6-bit address fields
Two-address : opcode = 16 - 2 x 6 = 4 bits -> 16 patterns; 12 used, 4 free
One-address : 4 free x 2^6 = 256 opcodes;  250 used, 6 free
Zero-address: 6 free x 2^6 = 384 opcodes available
Check       : 12 x 2^12 + 250 x 2^6 + 384 x 1
            = 49152 + 16000 + 384 = 65536 = 2^16 bit patterns

Worked example 3: two-word LOAD at 300-301, address field 250 in word 301
PC = 302 after fetch, R1 = 1200, XR = 40, M[250] = 700 (word-addressable)
Direct            EA = 250
Immediate         operand = 250 itself (read with word 301, no extra access)
Indirect          EA = M[250] = 700 (two data accesses)
Relative          EA = PC + 250 = 302 + 250 = 552
Indexed           EA = XR + 250 = 40 + 250 = 290
Register          operand = R1 = 1200 (no EA)
Register indirect EA = R1 = 1200
Autoincrement     EA = 1200, then R1 = 1201
Autodecrement     R1 = 1199 first, then EA = 1199

The ALU sets the status bits after every data manipulation instruction. For an n-bit result, C is the carry out of the most significant position, S is the most significant bit of the result, Z is 1 when every result bit is 0, and V is 1 when a signed result has overflowed, which happens exactly when two operands of the same sign produce a result of the other sign. A compare instruction forms A − B as A + B' + 1, sets the flags and throws the difference away; with this convention C = 1 means no borrow, that is A ≥ B for unsigned numbers. Unsigned branch conditions therefore test C and Z, while signed conditions test S ⊕ V and Z, because S alone gives the wrong answer whenever overflow occurs.

Worked example 4: 8-bit flags
ADD 0111 1010 (+122) + 0100 0110 (+70)
    carry into bit 7 = 1, carry out of bit 7 = 0
    result 1100 0000 -> S = 1, Z = 0, C = 0, V = 1 xor 0 = 1
    (+192 is outside -128..+127, so the signed result is wrong)
CMP A = 0011 0000 (48), B = 0101 0000 (80)
    A + B' + 1 = 0011 0000 + 1010 1111 + 1 = 1110 0000, carry out 0
    C = 0 (A < B unsigned); S = 1, V = 0, S xor V = 1 (A < B signed)

Common slips: adding the relative offset to the address of the branch instead of the updated PC; incrementing an autoincrement register by 1 instead of by the operand size (4 for a 32-bit word in byte-addressable memory); counting an immediate operand as a memory access; sizing an opcode with ⌊log2 N⌋ instead of ⌈log2 N⌉; multiplying by the opcode width instead of the released address-field width in expanding-opcode problems; and testing S alone for a signed less-than. The C-flag test in the table assumes C = 1 means no borrow; some processors, such as x86, store the borrow instead.

formulas.plainText: Direct EA = A; indirect EA = M[A] (two memory accesses in total)
Relative EA = PC + A, with PC already pointing to the next instruction

formulas.latex: EA_{indexed} = XR + A,\quad EA_{base} = BR + A
formulas.plainText: Indexed EA = XR + A; base-register EA = BR + A
Arithmetic shift right = floor(x/2); arithmetic shift left = 2x (sign preserved)

notes.text: Effective-address MCQs give an instruction address, an address field and PC, XR or memory contents. Remember: relative uses the incremented PC; indirect reads memory once to get EA and again to get the operand; immediate has no EA at all.
Two-address and three-address formats count address fields, not operands. ADD R1, R2 is two-address even though it uses two operands and a result, because the result overwrites R1.
The one-address program above needs a temporary location T because a single accumulator cannot hold both partial sums; the stack machine avoids T because the stack keeps the intermediate value.

concepts.text: CISC: Complex Instruction Set Computers

Early computers had tiny memories and were programmed in assembly, so designers kept adding powerful instructions that did more work per word of program: one instruction might load two operands from memory, multiply them and store the result. The result is a complex instruction set with hundreds of opcodes, many instruction lengths and many addressing modes. Such instructions need several clock cycles and are most easily implemented with a microprogrammed control unit. The Intel x86 family, the DEC VAX and IBM System/370 are the classic examples.
Characteristics of CISC:
items: Large instruction set (often 200 or more) with variable-length instruction words (x86: 1 to 15 bytes).
Many addressing modes (5 to 20) and instructions that operate directly memory-to-memory, so a single instruction may access memory several times.
Instructions take a variable number of cycles; average CPI is high (typically 2 to 6 without micro-op tricks).
Microprogrammed control unit, which makes complex instructions manageable but adds control-memory delay.
Relatively few general-purpose registers, because register space was spent on decode logic and microcode; compilers historically produced short programs.

concepts.text: RISC: Reduced Instruction Set Computers

Studies in the late 1970s (IBM 801, Berkeley RISC, Stanford MIPS) showed that compilers used only a small fraction of a CISC instruction set, and that simple instructions dominated execution. RISC removes the rarely used instructions and modes, makes every instruction one word long and one cycle long, and lets only load and store touch memory. The freed chip area goes into registers and a hardwired control unit, and the uniform instruction shape makes pipelining straightforward. ARM, MIPS, SPARC, PowerPC and RISC-V are RISC designs.
Characteristics of RISC:
items: Few instructions (typically under 100 to 150) with a fixed-length format (32 bits), so decoding is simple and fast.
Few addressing modes (usually register, immediate and register plus displacement).
Load/store architecture: arithmetic works only on registers; only LOAD and STORE reference memory.
Hardwired control unit and one instruction completed per clock cycle (CPI close to 1) using an instruction pipeline.
Large register file (32 or more) and often overlapped register windows; heavy reliance on an optimising compiler.

concepts.text: Side by Side

Overlapped register windows (Berkeley RISC) attack the cost of procedure calls. The register file is divided into windows, one per active procedure; each procedure sees a fixed set of global registers plus its own window, and adjacent windows overlap so that parameters passed to a callee sit in the registers shared between the two windows without any memory traffic. A call simply moves the window pointer, and a return moves it back. With G global registers, L local registers per window, C common (overlapped) registers between neighbours and W windows, a procedure sees G + L + 2C registers and the file holds (L + C)W + G registers in total. Berkeley RISC I used G = 10, L = 10, C = 6, W = 8: 32 registers visible, 138 in total.

concepts.latex: N_{reg} = (L + C)W + G,\quad \text{window size} = L + 2C + G
concepts.plainText: Total registers = (L + C)W + G; registers visible per procedure = L + 2C + G

concepts.text: Examples and the Performance Argument

x86 (Intel and AMD) is the surviving CISC line: variable-length instructions, rich modes, a long history of backward compatibility. ARM (phones, embedded, Apple M-series), MIPS (routers, older consoles), SPARC and the open RISC-V standard are RISC lines. Embedded designs favour RISC because fixed-length, single-cycle instructions give predictable timing and low power; desktop and server software stayed on x86 largely because of the installed base of binaries.

concepts.plainText: CPU time = instruction count × cycles per instruction × clock period

concepts.text: The performance argument is the classic CPU time equation. CISC lowers the instruction count IC but raises CPI; RISC raises IC (more, simpler instructions) but brings CPI to about 1 and permits a shorter clock period because each stage does less. Experience showed that the RISC side wins: a 30 to 50 percent increase in instruction count is more than paid for by a two- to three-fold reduction in CPI and a faster clock. Compare two implementations by computing IC × CPI × T for each rather than by counting instructions alone.

Modern processors have converged. Since the Pentium Pro, x86 chips decode each CISC instruction into one or more fixed-length micro-operations (micro-ops) that a RISC-like pipelined, superscalar core executes; frequently used simple instructions are hardwired and only rare complex ones fall back to microcode. Meanwhile RISC families have added multiply-accumulate, SIMD and compressed 16-bit instruction encodings (ARM Thumb, RISC-V C). The instruction-set argument today is mostly about code density, decoder power and licensing rather than raw speed.
Going Deeper: CPI, MIPS and Register Windows

The CPU time equation comes from counting clock cycles: a program needs a certain number of cycles, each lasting T = 1/f, and the number of cycles equals the instructions executed (IC) times the average cycles per instruction (CPI). When instructions fall into classes with different cycle counts, CPI is the average of the class CPIs weighted by the fraction of executed (dynamic) instructions in each class, not by how often they appear in the listing. Roughly, IC depends on the instruction set and the compiler, CPI on the organisation and the instruction set, and the clock period on circuit technology and organisation. RISC and CISC push these factors in opposite directions, so only their product decides which is faster.

concepts.plainText: CPI = Σ f_i × CPI_i (f_i = fraction of instructions in class i); CPU time = IC × CPI / f

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: weighted CPI, time and MIPS
Mix: ALU 50% (1 cycle), load 20% (2), store 10% (2), branch 20% (3)
CPI  = 0.5x1 + 0.2x2 + 0.1x2 + 0.2x3 = 0.5 + 0.4 + 0.2 + 0.6 = 1.7
IC   = 2 x 10^6 instructions, f = 400 MHz (T = 2.5 ns)
Time = 2 x 10^6 x 1.7 x 2.5 ns = 8.5 ms
MIPS = f / (CPI x 10^6) = 400 / 1.7 = 235.3

MIPS (million instructions per second) equals IC / (T_CPU × 10^6), or f / (CPI × 10^6), and MFLOPS counts only floating-point operations: FP operations / (T_CPU × 10^6). Both are rates of doing something, not measures of getting the job done. A RISC machine executes more, simpler instructions for the same work, so its MIPS figure flatters it; on one machine a code sequence with many cheap instructions can raise MIPS while taking longer; and MFLOPS treats a divide like an add. Execution time for the same program is the only fair comparison.

concepts.plainText: MIPS = IC / (CPU time × 10^6) = f / (CPI × 10^6)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: a higher MIPS rating but a slower program
Classes A, B, C take 1, 2 and 4 cycles; clock 500 MHz
Code 1: 4M A + 2M B + 1M C -> cycles = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12M, IC = 7M
        time = 12M / 500 MHz = 24 ms, MIPS = 7 / 0.024 = 291.7
Code 2: 8M A + 1M B + 1M C -> cycles = 8 + 2 + 4 = 14M, IC = 10M
        time = 14M / 500 MHz = 28 ms, MIPS = 10 / 0.028 = 357.1
Code 2 has the higher MIPS rating yet takes 28 / 24 = 1.17 times as long.

In the circular-buffer organisation of overlapped windows, a current-window pointer (CWP) selects the running procedure's window; a call advances CWP by one window, so the caller's outgoing registers become the callee's incoming registers, and a return moves CWP back. Because the windows form a ring, the outgoing registers of the newest window would overlap the incoming registers of the oldest one, so an N-window file holds at most N − 1 procedure activations. A call that would go deeper raises a window-overflow trap that saves the oldest window's incoming and local registers to memory, and a return into a saved procedure raises a window-underflow trap that reloads them. Call depth in real programs usually moves within a narrow band, so these traps are rare.

Worked example 3: a SPARC-style file with 8 windows
Each window: 8 in, 8 local, 8 out; 8 global registers
Map to the formula: G = 8, L = 8, C = 8 (outs of one window = ins of the next)
Visible per procedure = G + L + 2C = 8 + 8 + 16 = 32 registers
Total in the file     = (L + C) x W + G = 16 x 8 + 8 = 136 registers
Activations held      = W - 1 = 7 before a window-overflow trap
Saved per trap        = L + C = 16 registers = 64 bytes (32-bit registers)

rows: Gates, flip-flops and decoders forming a sequential circuit
A control memory of microinstructions plus a sequencer
Faster; no control-memory read per step
Slower; every step reads a microinstruction
Easy to add as longer microroutines
RISC, and the simple instructions of modern x86
Classic CISC such as the VAX and most IBM System/360 models

concepts.text: Why the RISC recipe suits a pipeline:
items: Fixed length and alignment: the next instruction's address is known during fetch, and one fetch per cycle never straddles two words.
Fixed field positions: register numbers sit in the same bits of every format, so the register file can be read while the opcode is still being decoded.
Load/store only: an arithmetic instruction never waits for memory, and each instruction makes at most one data access, so a single memory stage suffices.
Uniform simple steps: every instruction flows through the same stages instead of variable-length microroutines that stall a CISC pipeline.
Compiler help: the compiler reorders code to fill load-delay and branch-delay slots, so the hardware needs fewer interlocks.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: judging machines by instruction count or by MIPS instead of by execution time; taking the plain mean of class CPIs instead of the frequency-weighted mean; mixing up CPI and IPC (IPC = 1 / CPI); mixing MHz with ns or ms without converting; and using (L + 2C)W + G for the total register count, which counts every overlap twice. Remember also that a window-overflow trap saves only the incoming and local registers of one window.

formulas.plainText: CPU time = IC × CPI × T_clk = IC × CPI / f_clk
Speedup = (IC_CISC × CPI_CISC) / (IC_RISC × CPI_RISC) at equal clock
Total registers with W overlapped windows = (L + C)W + G
Registers visible to one procedure = L + 2C + G

notes.text: Attach one keyword to each side and the comparison table writes itself: CISC = variable length, many modes, microprogrammed, memory-to-memory, few registers; RISC = fixed length, few modes, hardwired, load/store, many registers, CPI about 1.

RISC does not mean a smaller or slower program. The program is longer in instructions but usually faster because CPI is near 1 and the clock is faster; judge with IC × CPI × T_clk, never with instruction count alone.
Berkeley RISC I figures worth remembering: 138 registers, 10 global, 8 windows, 32 registers visible per procedure; window size = 10 + 2 × 6 + 10 = 32.

concepts.text: Parallel Processing

Parallel processing is any technique that lets a computer perform several operations at the same time to raise throughput, the amount of work completed per unit time. It can be applied at many levels: inside the ALU (bit-parallel adders), between functional units (separate integer, floating-point and shift units working concurrently), between instructions (pipelining and superscalar issue), between data elements (vector and array processors) and between whole processors (multiprocessors and multicomputers). The higher the level, the more hardware is replicated and the more the software must be organised to exploit it.
Levels of parallelism named by the syllabus source:
items: Instruction-level parallelism (ILP): several instructions of one thread in flight at once, via pipelining, superscalar issue and out-of-order execution.
Data-level parallelism (DLP): one instruction applied to many data items, as in SIMD vector units and GPUs.
Thread-level parallelism (TLP): independent threads run on separate cores or hardware threads of an MIMD machine.
Task-level parallelism: whole jobs or processes distributed across processors, typically MIMD multiprocessors or clusters.

rows: One instruction stream, one data stream
One instruction stream, many data streams
Array processors, vector units, GPUs, SSE/NEON
Many instruction streams, one data stream
Largely theoretical; sometimes cited: systolic arrays, fault-tolerant redundant pipelines
Many instruction streams, many data streams

concepts.text: Pipelining

Pipelining decomposes a task into a sequence of sub-operations, each handled by a dedicated segment (stage) separated from the next by a register, so that different tasks occupy different segments at the same time, like cars on an assembly line. A space-time diagram plots segments on the vertical axis against clock cycles on the horizontal axis: in cycle 1 task T1 is in segment 1; in cycle 2 T1 moves to segment 2 while T2 enters segment 1; after k cycles the pipeline is full and one task finishes every cycle. With k segments and n tasks the first task takes k cycles and the remaining n − 1 tasks take one cycle each, so the whole batch takes k + n − 1 cycles.

concepts.plainText: Speedup S = n·t_n / ((k + n − 1)·t_p); as n grows S → k when t_n = k·t_p

concepts.text: Pipeline performance measures (t_p = clock period of the pipeline, t_n = time for one task without pipelining):
items: Speedup S = n t_n / ((k + n − 1) t_p). If each segment takes the same time and t_n = k t_p, this becomes S = nk/(k + n − 1), whose limit for large n is k.
Efficiency E = S/k = n/(k + n − 1), the fraction of the maximum speedup achieved; it approaches 1 as n grows and equals 1/k for a single task.
Throughput H = n/((k + n − 1) t_p) tasks per unit time; ideally 1/t_p, one task per clock.
The clock period t_p is fixed by the slowest segment plus register delay, so unbalanced stages waste time in the faster ones.

concepts.text: Worked example: a 4-segment pipeline processes 100 tasks. Cycles needed = k + n − 1 = 4 + 99 = 103, against 100 × 4 = 400 for the non-pipelined machine. Speedup S = 400/103 ≈ 3.88, efficiency E = 3.88/4 ≈ 0.97, and throughput is 100 tasks in 103 clocks. With only 4 tasks the speedup would be 16/7 ≈ 2.29, which shows why the pipeline is only worth its cost when many tasks flow through it.
Arithmetic and Instruction Pipelines
An arithmetic pipeline splits a long calculation into stages; the standard example is floating-point addition X = A × 2^a plus Y = B × 2^b:
items: Stage 1: compare the exponents a and b by subtraction.
Stage 2: align the mantissas by shifting the smaller-exponent mantissa right by the exponent difference.
Stage 3: add or subtract the aligned mantissas.
Stage 4: normalise the result (shift and adjust the exponent) and round.
Each stage holds its result in a register, so a new pair of operands can enter every clock; vector supercomputers run their add and multiply units this way.

concepts.text: An instruction pipeline overlaps the phases of the instruction cycle; a typical 5-stage RISC pipeline is:
items: IF (fetch): read the instruction at PC from the instruction cache and increment PC.
ID (decode and operand fetch): decode the opcode, read source registers, compute the effective address.
EX (execute): perform the ALU operation or the address arithmetic for a load/store or branch.
MEM (memory): access the data cache for load and store instructions.
WB (write-back): write the result into the destination register.

Mano's four-segment version is FI (fetch instruction), DA (decode and compute address), FO (fetch operand), EX (execute), with a memory conflict between FI and FO removed by separate instruction and data caches.

concepts.text: Pipeline Hazards and Remedies

rows: Two instructions need the same hardware in the same cycle, e.g. one memory for instruction and data
Duplicate resources (Harvard caches, extra ports); stall one instruction
Instruction reads a register before an earlier instruction has written it
Operand forwarding (bypass), hardware interlock stalls, compiler instruction reordering or NOP insertion
Later instruction writes a register that an earlier one still reads (WAR) or writes (WAW); arise with out-of-order execution
Branch changes PC after later instructions have already been fetched
Delayed branch, branch prediction, branch target buffer, prefetching both paths, loop buffer

concepts.text: The remedies trade hardware for lost cycles. Forwarding routes an ALU result straight from the EX/MEM register to the next instruction's ALU input, removing most RAW stalls; a load followed immediately by a use still costs one stall. A delayed branch lets the compiler fill the slot after a branch with a useful instruction that executes whether or not the branch is taken. Branch prediction guesses the outcome (static: backward taken, forward not taken; dynamic: history bits in a branch target buffer) and flushes the pipeline only on a misprediction. Stalls, also called bubbles or interlocks, are the fallback whenever no trick applies.

Vector processing extends pipelining to whole arrays: one vector instruction such as C(1:100) = A(1:100) + B(1:100) streams 100 element pairs through a pipelined adder, replacing a loop of scalar instructions and its overhead, and is implemented with vector registers and multiple memory modules (interleaving) to sustain one operand per clock. An array processor instead uses many identical processing elements under one control unit (SIMD): the attached array processor is a back-end accelerator for a host computer, while the SIMD array processor has each element with its own local memory executing the same broadcast instruction on different data, the ancestor of today's GPUs.
Going Deeper: Pipeline Timing, Stalls and Speedup Limits

Where k + n − 1 comes from: the first task needs k clocks to pass through all k stages (the fill time), and after that the full pipeline delivers one result per clock, so the other n − 1 tasks add n − 1 clocks. The clock cannot be shorter than the slowest stage plus the delay d of the latch (pipeline register) that separates the stages, so τ = max(τ_i) + d. A non-pipelined unit has no latches and needs only the sum of the stage delays per task, so with unequal stages the speedup for very long batches tends to Σ τ_i / τ, which is below k. Pipelining also lengthens the latency of one task to k τ ≥ Σ τ_i; it is the throughput that improves.

concepts.plainText: Clock τ = max(τ_i) + d; batch time T_k = (k + n − 1)·τ; limiting speedup S∞ = (Σ τ_i) / (max τ_i + d)

concepts.text:
Stages 45, 60, 75, 50 ns; latch d = 5 ns; n = 1000 tasks
Clock          τ = max(45, 60, 75, 50) + 5 = 80 ns
Pipelined      T = (4 + 1000 − 1) × 80 = 80 240 ns ≈ 80.24 µs
Non-pipelined  1000 × (45 + 60 + 75 + 50) = 1000 × 230 = 230 000 ns
Speedup        S = 230 000 / 80 240 ≈ 2.87  (limit 230/80 = 2.875, not k = 4)
Efficiency     E = S/k = 2.87/4 ≈ 0.72  (imbalance and latches waste 28%)
Latency        one task: 4 × 80 = 320 ns, against 230 ns unpipelined

Hazards are paid for in stall cycles. With an ideal CPI of 1, each stall adds directly to the average, so CPI_eff = 1 + Σ f_j c_j, where f_j is the fraction of instructions that suffer c_j stall cycles, and for balanced stages the speedup over the unpipelined machine becomes k / CPI_eff. A branch resolved at the end of stage s has s − 1 wrong-path instructions behind it: with predict-not-taken only taken branches pay this penalty, while a pipeline that stalls fetch until every branch resolves pays it on all of them.

5-stage pipeline, ideal CPI = 1, full forwarding, predict-not-taken
Loads     25% of instructions; 40% of them are followed at once by a user
          → 1 load-use stall each: 0.25 × 0.40 × 1 = 0.10 cycles/instr
Branches  20% of instructions; 65% taken; taken penalty 2 cycles
          → 0.20 × 0.65 × 2 = 0.26 cycles/instr
CPI_eff = 1 + 0.10 + 0.26 = 1.36
Speedup over the unpipelined datapath (5 clocks/instr, same clock)
          = 5 / 1.36 ≈ 3.68

Cycle          1    2    3    4    5    6    7    8
LW  R1,0(R2)   IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB
ADD R3,R1,R4        IF   ID   ID   EX   MEM  WB
OR  R7,R8,R9             IF   IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB
Cycle 4: ADD is held in ID, OR is held in IF and a bubble enters EX.
Cycle 5: LW's data in the MEM/WB register is forwarded to ADD's EX.
Total 8 cycles instead of the ideal 5 + 3 − 1 = 7.

A vector instruction on n elements streams through a k-stage pipelined unit in about k + n − 1 clocks, so vector machines hide the fill time by working on long vectors and by chaining the output of one pipelined unit into the next. Memory must keep up: if a module needs m clocks per access, at least m modules are interleaved, with consecutive addresses in consecutive modules, so that one word can be delivered every clock although no single module is any faster. Matrix work shows why this matters: multiplying two n × n matrices takes n^2 inner products of length n, that is n^3 multiply-add operations, 27 for n = 3 and a million for n = 100.

Amdahl's law applies the same reasoning to parallel processors. If a fraction f of the original run time can be spread perfectly over p processors and the remaining 1 − f is serial, the new time is (1 − f) + f/p of the old one. The serial part sets a hard ceiling of 1/(1 − f): a program that is 10% serial can never run more than 10 times faster, and 16 processors give only 1/(0.1 + 0.9/16) = 6.4. Replacing p by the speedup of any enhanced part gives the general form used for vector units and other accelerators.

concepts.plainText: S(p) = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/p); S_max = 1/(1 − f) as p → ∞, where f is the parallelisable fraction of the original time

concepts.text: Common slips in pipeline problems: taking the average stage delay instead of the slowest one for the clock, forgetting the latch delay (or adding it to the non-pipelined time), counting nk or k + n cycles instead of k + n − 1, and quoting a speedup above k, or above Σ τ_i / τ when the stages are unequal. In CPI problems, multiply the branch penalty by the fraction of instructions that actually pay it, for example only taken branches under predict-not-taken.

formulas.plainText: Speedup of a k-stage pipeline on n tasks, S = nk/(k + n − 1)
Maximum speedup as n → ∞ equals the number of stages k
Efficiency E = S/k = n/(k + n − 1)
Throughput H = n / ((k + n − 1) t_p) tasks per unit time
Cycles: k + n − 1 pipelined versus nk non-pipelined

notes.text: For any speedup MCQ compute cycles first: pipelined = k + n − 1, unpipelined = nk (or n t_n / t_p when the times differ), then divide. 4 stages, 100 tasks → 400/103 ≈ 3.88; 5 stages, 200 tasks → 1000/204 ≈ 4.90.
Speedup never exceeds k, and only approaches it for large n. If an option is greater than the number of stages it is wrong, and for a handful of tasks the speedup is far below k.
RAW is the only true data dependency; WAR and WAW are name dependencies that appear only when instructions can complete out of order, and register renaming removes them.
Flynn's MISD class has no widely accepted commercial example; if asked which class is 'rarely or never implemented', the answer is MISD.

concepts.text: The Memory Hierarchy

No single memory technology is at the same time fast, large and cheap: faster memory costs more per bit and therefore comes in smaller sizes. A computer therefore uses a hierarchy of levels. Moving down the pyramid from registers to tape, the access time increases, the cost per bit decreases, the capacity increases and the frequency with which the processor accesses that level decreases. The design goal is to give the processor the average speed of the top levels at close to the cost per bit of the bottom levels, which works because programs obey the principle of locality of reference.
Locality of reference, the property that makes the hierarchy work:
items: Temporal locality: a location referenced now is likely to be referenced again soon (loop bodies, counters, stack variables). Keeping the item in a faster level after first use pays off.
Spatial locality: locations near a referenced address are likely to be referenced soon (sequential instructions, array elements). Fetching a whole block or line at once exploits this.
Sequential locality is the special case of spatial locality where the next reference is the next address, typical of instruction fetch.
Because of locality the hit ratio h of an upper level is high (often above 0.9), so the average access time is close to that of the fast level even though most data live in the slow one.

concepts.text: Internal Memory: RAM

rows: Required periodically (about every 64 ms) as the charge leaks
Cache memory, register files, small embedded RAM

concepts.text: A DRAM chip arranges its cells in a square array of rows and columns. To halve the number of address pins the address is multiplexed: the row half is latched by the RAS (row address strobe) signal and the column half by CAS (column address strobe), so a 16M × 1 chip needs only 12 address pins for its 24-bit address. Reading a cell discharges its capacitor, so the sense amplifiers immediately rewrite the whole row; refresh is done by reading every row in turn within the retention period (for example 4096 rows in 64 ms), during which the chip is unavailable. A DRAM is therefore slower in cycle time than in access time, and needs a memory controller to generate RAS, CAS and refresh cycles.

Synchronous DRAM (SDRAM) ties the memory to the system clock: the processor issues the address and control signals, and after a known number of clock cycles (the CAS latency) the data appear, so the processor can do other work instead of waiting; burst mode then streams successive words one per clock without further addresses. Double data rate (DDR) SDRAM transfers data on both the rising and falling clock edges, doubling the bandwidth at the same clock; DDR2, DDR3, DDR4 and DDR5 raise the prefetch width and transfer rate while lowering the supply voltage. Memory modules (DIMMs) place several chips side by side to provide a 64-bit wide data path.
Internal Memory: ROM and Error Correction

rows: User once, with a programmer that blows fuses
Ultraviolet light through a quartz window, whole chip, minutes
Electrically, one block (sector) at a time
SSDs, USB drives, BIOS/UEFI, microcontroller program memory

concepts.text: Error detection and correction in memory:
items: Parity: one extra bit per word makes the number of 1s even (even parity) or odd (odd parity). It detects any single-bit error but cannot locate it and misses double-bit errors.

Hamming single-error-correcting (SEC) code: k check bits are added to m data bits such that 2^k ≥ m + k + 1. Each check bit is the parity of a chosen subset of positions; the check bits sit at positions 1, 2, 4, 8, … of the code word.

On a read the check bits are recomputed and XOR-ed with the stored ones. The result, the syndrome, is 0 if there is no error, otherwise it equals the position of the flipped bit, which is then inverted.
Check bits needed: 8 data bits → 4, 16 → 5, 32 → 6, 64 → 7. Adding one more overall parity bit gives SEC-DED (single error correcting, double error detecting), the scheme used in ECC memory modules.

concepts.plainText: Hamming SEC: k check bits for m data bits need 2^k ≥ m + k + 1

concepts.text: External Memory

A magnetic disk drive has one or more platters coated on both surfaces, each surface read by its own head on a common movable arm. Data lie on concentric tracks; each track is divided into sectors of typically 512 bytes or 4 KB, the smallest unit transferred. The set of tracks at the same radius on all surfaces is a cylinder, and a location is given by cylinder, head and sector. Reading a sector costs three delays: seek time, to move the head to the right track (a few ms); rotational latency, waiting for the sector to rotate under the head (on average half a revolution, 4.17 ms at 7200 rpm); and transfer time, proportional to the number of bytes and the rotation speed. Disks are block devices with direct (random) access, unlike tape, which is sequential.

concepts.plainText: T_access = T_seek + 1/(2r) + b/(rN), r = revolutions per second, b = bytes transferred, N = bytes per track

rows: 2; highest throughput, any disk failure loses all data
2; fast reads, tolerates one failure per mirrored pair
Block-level striping with parity distributed over all disks
3; tolerates one failure, small writes pay a read-modify-write parity penalty

concepts.text: Other external storage technologies:
items: Solid-state drive (SSD): NAND flash with a controller; no moving parts, so no seek or rotational delay (access in tens of μs), shock resistant and low power. Flash blocks must be erased before rewriting and wear out after roughly 10^4 to 10^5 program/erase cycles, so the controller does wear levelling and garbage collection.

Optical disc: data stored as pits and lands read by a laser along a single spiral track; CD about 700 MB, DVD 4.7 GB per layer, Blu-ray 25 GB per layer; CD-ROM uses constant linear velocity (rotation speed changes with radius). Variants: read-only (pressed), recordable (-R, write once), rewritable (-RW).

Magnetic tape: sequential access on a long ribbon, serpentine recording of many parallel tracks; very high capacity per cartridge (LTO) and the lowest cost per bit, but access times of seconds to minutes, so it is used for backup and archive.
Access-time model for a non-random-access device: T_N = T_A + n/R, where T_A is the average time to reach the start, n the number of bits and R the transfer rate in bits per second.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Storage Timing, RAID and Virtual Memory

A memory hierarchy is judged by two averages. If level 1 holds S1 bits at a cost of C1 per bit and level 2 holds S2 bits at C2 per bit, the average cost per bit of the system is weighted by size, so a small expensive level hardly changes it when S1 is much smaller than S2. The access efficiency T1/Ts compares the access time of the fast level with the average access time the processor actually sees; it approaches 1 only when level 1 satisfies almost every reference, because a reference that goes to disk is many thousands of times slower. Together the two numbers state the goal of the hierarchy: speed close to T1 at a cost close to C2.

concepts.latex: C_s = \frac{C_1 S_1 + C_2 S_2}{S_1 + S_2},\quad E = \frac{T_1}{T_s}
concepts.plainText: Average cost per bit C_s = (C1 × S1 + C2 × S2) / (S1 + S2); access efficiency E = T1 / Ts, where Ts is the average access time seen by the processor

concepts.text: Disk capacity is the product of recording surfaces, tracks per surface, sectors per track and bytes per sector; a double-sided platter contributes two surfaces, and the number of cylinders equals the number of tracks per surface. Older drives use constant angular velocity (CAV) with the same number of sectors on every track, so the longer outer tracks are recorded at a lower bit density; modern drives use multiple-zone recording and put more sectors on the outer zones. Because one whole track passes under the head in every revolution, the sustained transfer rate equals the bytes per track multiplied by the revolutions per second (rpm / 60). A file stored on adjacent tracks pays the seek only once, while scattered sectors pay a seek and a rotational latency each, which is why disk layout matters so much.

Worked example 1: sequential versus random reading
Disk: average seek 8 ms, 6000 rpm, 250 sectors of 512 B per track
Revolution = 60 / 6000 s = 10 ms, average latency = 5 ms
One sector passes the head in 10 / 250 = 0.04 ms
File of 1000 sectors on 4 adjacent full tracks:
  track 1:     8 + 5 + 10 = 23 ms
  tracks 2-4:  3 x (5 + 10) = 45 ms   (track-to-track seek ignored)
  total      = 68 ms
Same 1000 sectors scattered at random:
  per sector:  8 + 5 + 0.04 = 13.04 ms
  total      = 1000 x 13.04 ms = 13.04 s (about 192 times slower)

rows: Usable capacity (n disks of size C)
Mirroring: every block written to two disks
Bit striping with Hamming-code check disks
(n − m)C, m check disks growing with log2 of the data disks
Byte or bit striping, one dedicated parity disk
Block striping, one dedicated parity disk
Block striping, parity rotated over all disks
Block striping, two independent check blocks P and Q

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: RAID 5 parity (one byte per block, hex)
Stripe: D0 = B2, D1 = 6C, D2 = 1F
Parity P = D0 xor D1 xor D2 = B2 xor 6C xor 1F = DE xor 1F = C1
Disk holding D1 fails, rebuild it from the survivors:
  D1 = P xor D0 xor D2 = C1 xor B2 xor 1F = 73 xor 1F = 6C
Small write, D2 changes from 1F to 20 (read-modify-write):
  read old D2 and old P                    2 reads
  P' = P xor D2old xor D2new = C1 xor 1F xor 20 = FE
  write new D2 and new P'                  2 writes
  total = 4 disk accesses for one small write
Check: B2 xor 6C xor 20 = FE
Details of semiconductor and optical storage that calculations rely on:
items: DRAM refresh overhead: with R rows, a retention period T_ref and a time t_r per row refresh, the fraction of time lost is R × t_r / T_ref. Burst refresh does all rows back to back; distributed refresh issues one row refresh every T_ref / R, for example 64 ms / 4096 rows = 15.6 µs.

NOR flash connects cells in parallel, giving random byte reads and execute-in-place for firmware; NAND flash connects cells in series strings, giving higher density with page reads and writes and block erase, the medium of SSDs and memory cards.

A flash cell storing n bits must distinguish 2^n charge levels: SLC 1 bit (2 levels), MLC 2 bits (4), TLC 3 bits (8), QLC 4 bits (16). More bits per cell lower the cost per bit but also the endurance and the write speed.

An SSD cannot overwrite a page in place: it writes the new data to an erased page, marks the old page invalid and later garbage-collects whole blocks; wear levelling spreads the program/erase cycles evenly over all blocks.

Optical discs record along one spiral track at constant linear velocity (CLV), so the drive spins faster near the centre. The laser wavelength limits the pit size: CD 780 nm (about 700 MB), DVD 650 nm (4.7 GB per layer), Blu-ray 405 nm (25 GB per layer).

concepts.text: Virtual memory adds one more level below main memory, which then acts as a cache for pages kept on disk or SSD. A virtual address is split into a virtual page number and an offset; the page table, indexed by the page number, supplies the physical frame number, and the offset is copied unchanged, so physical address = frame × page size + offset. If the entry is marked not present, a page fault traps to the operating system, which loads the page (replacing another one if memory is full) and restarts the instruction. Every translation would otherwise cost an extra memory access to read the page table, so recent translations are cached in a translation lookaside buffer (TLB).

concepts.plainText: EAT = (1 − p) × t_m + p × t_fault, where p = page-fault rate, t_m = memory access time and t_fault = page-fault service time

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: paging arithmetic
32-bit virtual address, 8 KB pages, 4-byte page-table entries
  offset = log2 8192 = 13 bits, page number = 32 - 13 = 19 bits
  page table = 2^19 entries x 4 B = 2 MB per process
Translate VA 0000 5A3C (hex); the table maps page 2 to frame 7
  page = 5A3C >> 13 = 2, offset = 5A3C - 4000 = 1A3C
  PA = 7 x 2000 + 1A3C = E000 + 1A3C = 0000 FA3C (hex)
Page faults: t_m = 60 ns, t_fault = 5 ms, p = 2 x 10^-6
  EAT = (1 - p) x 60 + p x 5,000,000 = 59.99988 + 10 = about 70 ns
TLB: lookup 5 ns, hit ratio 0.95, one-level page table
  EAT = 0.95 x (5 + 60) + 0.05 x (5 + 60 + 60) = 61.75 + 6.25 = 68 ns

Common slips in storage calculations: using rpm as revolutions per second (divide by 60 first); taking a full revolution instead of half of one as the average rotational latency; forgetting that a double-sided platter has two surfaces; mixing bits with bytes or 10^9 with 2^30; quoting the RAID 1 capacity as the sum of both disks; charging the average seek to every track of a file stored on adjacent tracks; and writing 8 ms as 8,000 ns in page-fault problems (it is 8,000,000 ns).

formulas.plainText: Two-level hierarchy: T_avg = h × T_1 + (1 − h) × T_2, where h is the hit ratio of the fast level
Average rotational latency = half a revolution = 30 / rpm seconds (4.17 ms at 7200 rpm)
Disk access time = seek + average rotational latency + transfer time b/(rN)
Hamming SEC code: k check bits for m data bits need 2^k ≥ m + k + 1
Memory capacity = 2^n words × w bits per word, n = address lines

notes.text: Going down the hierarchy (registers → cache → main memory → disk → tape) four things change together: access time up, capacity up, cost per bit down, access frequency down. MCQs often ask which of these is the odd one out.

Both SRAM and DRAM are volatile. The difference is refresh: DRAM stores charge on a capacitor and must be refreshed every few milliseconds; SRAM stores the bit in a flip-flop and needs no refresh but uses about six transistors per cell, which is why it is used only for cache.
RAID 0 gives speed but no redundancy; RAID 1 gives redundancy by mirroring at 50% overhead; RAID 5 spreads parity so that n disks give (n − 1) disks of usable space and survive one failure.
Rotational latency questions: average latency is half a revolution. 7200 rpm = 120 rev/s → 8.33 ms per revolution → 4.17 ms average; 5400 rpm → 5.56 ms; 10000 rpm → 3 ms.

concepts.text: Why Cache Works

A cache is a small, fast SRAM placed between the processor and main memory that holds copies of the main-memory blocks most recently used. Main memory is viewed as 2^n / K blocks of K words; the cache has m lines, each holding one block plus a tag that identifies which block it is and a valid bit. On every reference the processor first looks in the cache: a hit delivers the word immediately; a miss makes the cache fetch the whole block containing the word from main memory into a line (exploiting spatial locality) and then deliver the word. Because of temporal and spatial locality most references hit, so the processor sees nearly cache speed with main-memory capacity. The cache is transparent: programs need no changes.

concepts.plainText: t_avg = h × t_c + (1 − h) × t_m, h = hit ratio, t_c = cache access time, t_m = main-memory access time

concepts.text: Worked example: t_c = 10 ns, t_m = 100 ns, h = 0.9. Then t_avg = 0.9 × 10 + 0.1 × 100 = 9 + 10 = 19 ns, and the speed-up over memory alone is 100 / 19 ≈ 5.3. If the question states that main memory is accessed only after the cache lookup fails (look-through with no overlap), the miss cost is t_c + t_m and t_avg = 10 + 0.1 × 100 = 20 ns. The hit ratio h is hits divided by total references; the miss ratio is 1 − h, and the miss penalty is the extra time a miss costs.
Cache size is the first design element and is a trade-off:
items: A larger cache raises the hit ratio, but with diminishing returns once the working set of the program fits.
A larger cache is slower (bigger tag comparison and addressing logic), costs more and takes chip area; the cost per bit should stay close to that of main memory overall.
Typical sizes: L1 16–64 KB per core, L2 256 KB to a few MB, L3 several MB to tens of MB shared by all cores.

Cache performance is also limited by compulsory misses (first touch), capacity misses (working set larger than cache) and conflict misses (blocks competing for the same line), which the mapping function influences.

concepts.text: Mapping Functions

The mapping function decides which cache line a main-memory block may occupy, and it fixes how the memory address is split into fields. Running example for all three mappings: a byte-addressable main memory of 64 KB (16-bit address), a cache of 2 KB and a block (line) size of 16 bytes. The cache therefore has 2048 / 16 = 128 lines, main memory has 4096 blocks, and the lowest 4 address bits (the word or byte-offset field) select a byte within a block in every mapping.
Direct mapping: block j goes to line i = j mod m (m = number of lines):
items: Address fields: tag | line | word. Line field = log2(128) = 7 bits, word = 4 bits, tag = 16 − 7 − 4 = 5 bits. Each line can hold any of 2^5 = 32 different blocks, distinguished by the tag stored with it.
Access: use the line bits to select one line, compare its stored tag with the tag bits of the address, and check the valid bit. Only one comparator is needed, so it is simple, fast and cheap.

Weakness: two frequently used blocks that map to the same line keep evicting each other (thrashing, conflict misses) even when the rest of the cache is empty. No replacement algorithm is needed because there is no choice.
Example: block 0, block 128 and block 256 all map to line 0; block 5 maps to line 5 with tag 0, block 133 maps to line 5 with tag 1.

concepts.text: Fully associative mapping: a block can be loaded into any line:
items: Address fields: tag | word. Tag = 16 − 4 = 12 bits, which is the full block number; there is no line field.

Access: the tag of the address must be compared with the tags of all 128 lines simultaneously, which needs one comparator per line or a content-addressable (associative) memory. This is expensive and limits the size.
Strength: no conflict misses; a block is evicted only when the cache is full, so a replacement algorithm is essential.
Used where the cache is small, for example translation lookaside buffers and some L1 caches.

concepts.text: Set-associative mapping: the cache is divided into v sets of k lines each (k-way), and block j goes to set i = j mod v:
items: Address fields: tag | set | word. In the example a 2-way cache has 128 / 2 = 64 sets, so set = 6 bits and tag = 16 − 6 − 4 = 6 bits; a 4-way cache has 32 sets, set = 5 bits and tag = 7 bits.
Access: the set bits select one set, then the k tags of that set are compared in parallel, so only k comparators are needed.

k = 1 is direct mapping and k = m is fully associative; 2-way to 8-way is the usual compromise, giving most of the hit-ratio benefit of full associativity at modest cost. Replacement is needed within a set.
Increasing k from 1 to 2 gives the largest hit-ratio gain; beyond 8-way the improvement is small.

concepts.plainText: tag bits = address bits − set (or line) bits − word bits; sets = lines / k, lines = cache size / block size

rows: the k lines of one set

concepts.text: Replacement Algorithms and Write Policies
When a new block must be loaded into a full set (associative or set-associative caches; direct mapping has no choice) a hardware replacement algorithm picks the victim:
items: LRU (least recently used): replace the block that has gone unreferenced for the longest time; best approximation of the optimal policy and the most used. A 2-way set needs only one USE bit per pair; larger sets keep age counters or use approximations such as pseudo-LRU.
FIFO (first-in first-out): replace the block that has been in the set longest, regardless of use; implemented with a round-robin pointer; may evict a heavily used block.
LFU (least frequently used): replace the block with the fewest references; needs a counter per line and unfairly penalises a block just loaded.
Random: pick any line; simplest hardware and in simulation only slightly worse than LRU.

concepts.text: Write policy decides how a write to a cached block reaches main memory:
items: Write-through: every write updates both the cache and main memory, so memory is always current (safe for I/O modules and other processors that read memory directly) but memory traffic is high. A write buffer between cache and memory lets the processor continue while the memory write completes.

Write-back: a write updates only the cache and sets the line's dirty (update) bit; the block is written to main memory only when it is evicted and its dirty bit is set. Traffic is much lower, but memory can be stale, so I/O and multiprocessor accesses must go through the cache or the cache must be flushed.

Write miss handling: write-allocate loads the block into the cache and then writes (natural with write-back); no-write-allocate (write-around) writes directly to memory without loading the block (natural with write-through).
Typical combination: write-through with a write buffer for L1, write-back for L2/L3.

concepts.text: Line Size, Number of Caches and Coherence
The remaining elements of cache design:
items: Line (block) size: larger lines bring in more neighbouring words and raise the hit ratio at first (spatial locality), but with a fixed cache size fewer lines fit, useful data get replaced sooner and each miss takes longer to service; the hit ratio rises then falls, with 32–128 bytes being typical.

Number of caches, levels: a multilevel hierarchy places a small, very fast L1 on the core, a larger L2 on the chip and an L3 shared by all cores; each level is checked in turn and the average access time nests as t_avg = h1·t1 + (1 − h1)[h2·t2 + (1 − h2)·t_m].

Number of caches, unified vs split: a unified cache holds instructions and data together and balances itself automatically, giving a higher hit ratio for a given size; a split (Harvard-style) cache has separate instruction and data caches so that instruction fetch and data access in a pipeline never contend for the same cache. Modern processors use a split L1 and unified L2/L3.
Cache and virtual memory: a cache can be addressed by physical or virtual addresses; a physically addressed cache needs the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) lookup first.

concepts.text: Cache coherence is the problem of keeping multiple copies of the same block consistent. It arises in a multiprocessor where each processor has its own cache, and with DMA devices that write main memory directly. With write-back caches a processor can hold a modified copy that other processors and main memory do not see; even with write-through, another cache may still hold an old copy. Solutions include bus watching (snooping) with write-through, in which every cache monitors the bus and invalidates its copy when it sees a write to that block; hardware directory protocols that record which caches hold each block; snoopy protocols such as MESI that mark each line Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid; and marking shared data as non-cacheable. This topic is expanded in the multiprocessor section of 4.3.
Going Deeper: Address Decoding, Traces and Cache Cost

Every mapping problem reduces to the same three steps. First find the block number, which is the address divided by the block size (drop the word field). Then find the index: block mod number of lines for direct mapping, or block mod number of sets for set-associative mapping; the remaining high-order part, block div number of sets, is the tag. When the address is given in hexadecimal it is quicker to write out the bits and cut them into fields from the right: word bits first, then index bits, and the rest is the tag.

Worked example 1: splitting an address
32-bit byte address, 64 KB cache, 32-byte blocks (1 KB = 1024 B)
lines = 65536 / 32 = 2048, word field = log2 32 = 5 bits
Direct mapped: line = log2 2048 = 11 bits, tag = 32 - 11 - 5 = 16 bits
4-way:  sets = 2048 / 4 = 512, set = 9 bits, tag = 32 - 9 - 5 = 18 bits
Address 7F3A5B64 (hex), block = address >> 5 = 03F9D2DB
  direct: line = block mod 2048 = 2DB (731), tag = 7F3A, word = 04
  4-way:  set = block mod 512 = 0DB (219), tag = 1FCE9, word = 04
Storage of the direct-mapped version if write-back (valid + dirty bit):
  2048 x (256 data + 16 tag + 2 status) = 561,152 bits = 68.5 KB

The capacity quoted for a cache, such as 64 KB, counts only the data. Every line also stores its tag, a valid bit, a dirty bit if the cache is write-back and, in set-associative caches, replacement state such as LRU bits. Each doubling of associativity lengthens every tag by one bit, so a fully associative cache has the largest tag store. Multiply the bits per line by the number of lines, and divide by 8 when the answer is wanted in bytes.

concepts.plainText: Total cache bits = m × (8K + t + v + d): m lines, K bytes per block, t tag bits, v valid bits and d dirty bits per line (add replacement bits if the question includes them)

Worked example 2: LRU versus FIFO in a 2-way cache
2 sets of 2 lines, set = block mod 2, cache initially empty
Contents of the set used, least recent (LRU) or oldest (FIFO) first
block set  LRU    result        FIFO   result

  6    0   [2 6]  miss          [2 6]  miss
  2    0   [6 2]  hit           [2 6]  hit
  4    0   [2 4]  miss, 6 out   [6 4]  miss, 2 out
  5    1   [5]    miss          [5]    miss
  2    0   [4 2]  hit           [4 2]  miss, 6 out
  4    0   [2 4]  hit           [4 2]  hit
  1    1   [5 1]  miss          [5 1]  miss
  0    0   [4 0]  miss, 2 out   [2 0]  miss, 4 out
