LRU: 4 hits, 6 misses        FIFO: 2 hits, 8 misses

rows: Working set larger than the whole cache
Too many active blocks map to the same line or set
Another processor's write invalidated the copy

concepts.text: Architecture texts usually write the average access time as AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, which is the hierarchical (look-through) model: the cache is always probed and a miss adds the penalty. The penalty itself is the time to fetch a block, the memory latency plus the block size divided by the bus bandwidth, so larger blocks raise it. For a processor, memory stalls add to the base CPI: stall cycles per instruction = memory references per instruction × miss rate × miss penalty. With two levels, the L1 miss penalty is the AMAT of L2, and the product of the L1 miss rate and the L2 local miss rate is the global miss rate that reaches main memory.

concepts.plainText: AMAT = t1 + m1 × (t2 + m2 × t_mem), where t1, t2 are the L1 and L2 hit times, m1 the L1 miss rate and m2 the L2 local miss rate

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: two-level cache and CPI
L1: hit time 1 cycle, miss rate 5%
L2: hit time 12 cycles, local miss rate 30%; memory 120 cycles
L1 miss penalty = 12 + 0.30 x 120 = 48 cycles
AMAT = 1 + 0.05 x 48 = 3.4 cycles   (without L2: 1 + 0.05 x 120 = 7)
Global miss rate = 0.05 x 0.30 = 1.5% of references reach memory
Base CPI 1.0, 1.3 memory references per instruction:
  stall cycles per instruction = 1.3 x 0.05 x 48 = 3.12
  CPI = 1.0 + 3.12 = 4.12
Mistakes that cost marks in cache problems:
items: Mixing the two access-time models: the simultaneous form h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m and the look-through form t_c + (1 − h)·t_m differ by (1 − h)·t_c, so always state which one is used.
Using log2 of the cache size in bytes instead of log2 of the number of lines (or sets) as the index field.
Taking the block size in bits instead of bytes, or assuming byte addressing when the memory is word-addressable.
Forgetting that the tag grows by one bit each time the associativity doubles, and that a fully associative cache has no index field at all.
Counting only the data bits when the total cache size is asked; tags, valid, dirty and LRU bits are storage too.
In traces, mapping the address instead of the block number: divide by the block size first, then take the block number mod the number of sets.

concepts.text: For hit/miss traces draw one column per set and keep its blocks in order, least recently used (LRU) or oldest (FIFO) on the left. On a hit, LRU moves the block to the right end while FIFO changes nothing; on a miss in a full set, both remove the leftmost block and append the new one on the right.

formulas.plainText: Average access time t_avg = h × t_c + (1 − h) × t_m
Look-through form when memory is accessed only after a cache miss: t_avg = t_c + (1 − h) × t_m
Lines m = cache size C / block size K; sets v = m / k for a k-way cache
Tag bits = address bits − set bits (log2 v) − word bits (log2 K); use v = m for direct mapping
Speed-up from the cache = main-memory access time / average access time

notes.text: Bit-split recipe: word bits = log2(block size); direct: line bits = log2(lines); set-associative: set bits = log2(lines / k); fully associative: no index bits; tag = remaining bits. Doubling associativity removes one index bit and adds one tag bit.

Two formulas for average access time appear in books. Use t_avg = h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m unless the question says memory is accessed only after the cache lookup fails, in which case the miss costs t_c + t_m.

Direct mapping needs no replacement algorithm and a single comparator; fully associative mapping needs a comparator per line (associative memory) and a replacement algorithm; set-associative needs k comparators and replacement within the set.

Write-back reduces bus traffic and uses a dirty bit; write-through keeps memory always up to date, which matters for DMA and multiprocessors. Write-allocate pairs naturally with write-back, no-write-allocate with write-through.

concepts.text: Write Ability and Storage Permanence

Embedded-system designers (Vahid & Givargis) classify memories on two axes instead of the crude RAM-versus-ROM split. Write ability is the manner and speed in which a memory can be written: at one end sit memories that only the manufacturer can set, at the other memories the processor writes at full speed. Storage permanence is how long a memory holds its bits after they are written: from bits that last essentially forever to bits that leak away in milliseconds. Traditional ROM is the high-permanence, low-write-ability corner and traditional RAM is the opposite corner, but most real devices lie in between.
Write-ability spectrum, from lowest to highest:
items: Mask-programmed ROM: bits are fixed by a metal-layer mask during fabrication; not writable at all, cheapest per bit in volume.
OTP ROM / PROM: written once by blowing fuses with an external programmer.
EPROM: written by a programmer using high voltage, erased as a whole chip by ultraviolet light through a quartz window (minutes).
EEPROM: written electrically in-system, byte by byte, but each write takes microseconds to milliseconds and the chip must not be read during a write.
Flash: written electrically in-system in pages, erased in large blocks; faster bulk writes and higher density than EEPROM.
NVRAM: battery-backed SRAM, or SRAM paired with an EEPROM that saves its contents on power loss; written at processor speed.
SRAM and DRAM: written at processor speed with no practical limit on the number of writes.

concepts.text: Storage-permanence spectrum, from highest to lowest:
items: Mask ROM and OTP: hold data essentially forever with no power (nonvolatile, no erase cycles).
EPROM, EEPROM and flash: nonvolatile, but the stored charge leaks over years (about 10-year retention) and cells wear out after 10^3 to 10^6 program/erase cycles.
NVRAM: keeps data as long as its battery lasts or the backup EEPROM is intact.
SRAM: holds data only while powered (volatile) but needs no refresh.
DRAM: holds data for milliseconds only; needs refresh every few milliseconds even with power applied.
Nonvolatile memories are those on the high-permanence side of the line (they keep their bits without power); volatile ones lose them.

concepts.text: An in-system programmable memory can be written by the processor it is connected to without removing the chip from the board: EEPROM, flash, NVRAM and RAM qualify, while mask ROM, OTP and EPROM need an external programmer. In-system programmability makes field firmware updates, boot loaders, calibration tables and event logs possible. Flash has two practical constraints: a block must be erased (all bits set to 1) before any of its bytes can be rewritten, and writes are far slower than reads. Embedded systems therefore execute code directly from flash (execute-in-place) and keep changing data in SRAM, copying it to flash only occasionally.
Composing Memory

A system often needs a memory that is wider, deeper or both than any single available chip. Memory composition builds the required memory from several identical smaller chips. Three cases arise: increasing the width of each word, increasing the number of words, and increasing both. Every memory chip provides address inputs, bidirectional (tri-state) data lines and control inputs such as chip select (CS), output enable (OE) and read/write (R/W); composition is a matter of wiring these correctly.
Increasing the width (more bits per word):
items: Connect the chips in parallel: all chips receive the same address lines and the same CS, OE and R/W signals, so they are always accessed together.
Each chip supplies a slice of the data word: chip 0 drives data bits 0–7, chip 1 drives bits 8–15, and so on.
Number of chips = wanted width / chip width; the number of address lines does not change. Example: two 1K × 8 chips give a 1K × 16 memory.
Byte-enable signals can be added so that a single byte of the wide word can be written without disturbing the other chips.

concepts.text: Increasing the number of words (more depth):
items: Each chip holds a different range of addresses. The low-order address lines go to every chip in parallel; the high-order lines go to a decoder whose outputs drive the chip-select of exactly one chip.
The data lines of all chips are tied together; because outputs are tri-state, only the selected chip drives the bus.

Number of chips = wanted words / chip words; decoder size = log2(number of chips) inputs. Example: four 1K × 8 chips give 4K × 8 using address lines A0–A9 for every chip and a 2-to-4 decoder on A10–A11.
Total address lines = log2(total words); a 4K memory needs 12.

concepts.text: Increasing both width and depth:
items: Arrange the chips as a matrix: each row is one address range and the chips within a row are connected in parallel to supply the full word width.
The decoder on the high-order address bits selects one row; the low-order bits go to all chips; each column of chips drives its own slice of the data bus.
Chips needed = (words wanted / words per chip) × (width wanted / width per chip).

concepts.plainText: Chips = (total words × total bits per word) / (chip words × chip bits per word)

rows: Address lines of the composed memory
Selects one of the 4 rows via chip select
Each supplies 8 of the 16 data bits; both get the same CS

concepts.text: Memory Maps, Address Decoding and Timing

A memory map assigns a range of addresses to every memory chip and memory-mapped peripheral in the processor's address space; address decoding is the logic that activates the right chip select for each range. Full (absolute) decoding uses all address lines, so every location has exactly one address; partial decoding ignores some high-order lines, saving gates but making each device appear at several mirrored addresses (fold-back). A 3-to-8 decoder such as the 74LS138 is the classic building block: in a 64 KB space, an 8 KB ROM at 0000H–1FFFH is selected when A15 A14 A13 = 000, and an 8 KB RAM at 2000H–3FFFH when they are 001. The decoder can also carry the IO/M signal so that memory-mapped and isolated I/O ranges do not overlap.
Memory timing parameters:
items: Access time: for random-access memory, the time from presenting the address (or the read command) until valid data are available; for disk or tape, the time to position the head at the start.
Cycle time: the minimum time between two successive independent accesses; for DRAM it exceeds the access time because of precharge and the possibility of refresh; for SRAM the two are almost equal.
Transfer rate: for RAM, 1 / cycle time words per second; for a non-random device T_N = T_A + n / R, where n is the number of bits and R the rate in bits per second.

Wait states: if a memory's access time is longer than the processor allows in one bus cycle, the processor inserts idle clock cycles; wait states = ceil((t_access − t_allowed) / T_clk). Write cycles also need address setup and data hold times to be met.

concepts.plainText: Time to read n bits from a sequential device = average access time T_A + n / R

concepts.text: Embedded systems use the same hierarchy idea as general computers but with different priorities: cost, board space, power and predictable timing matter more than raw capacity. A typical microcontroller keeps its program in on-chip flash executed in place, its variables in on-chip SRAM, and its constants and calibration data in EEPROM or a flash data block; larger systems add external SDRAM for buffers and an SD card or serial flash for files. Caches appear only in higher-end embedded processors, because a cache miss makes execution time unpredictable; real-time designs therefore lock critical lines in the cache or use tightly coupled scratchpad memory that is addressed directly and always takes the same time. When external DRAM is used, a memory controller must generate the refresh cycles.
Going Deeper: Chip Pins, Composition and Decoding

A memory chip described as W × B holds W words of B bits, so it needs log2 W address pins, B data pins (usually bidirectional), a few control pins such as chip select (CS), output enable (OE) and write enable (WE), and power pins. The same number of bits can be organised in different ways: a 16-Kbit part may be 16K × 1 or 2K × 8, trading address pins for data pins. The 2K × 8 static RAM is a handy reference: 11 address pins, 8 data pins, 3 control pins and 2 power pins fit a 24-pin package. DRAMs halve the address pins by sending the row half and the column half of the address one after the other on the same pins.

concepts.plainText: Pins = log2(words) + data bits + control pins + power pins; for 2K × 8: 11 + 8 + 3 + 2 = 24

concepts.text: Why the composition rules work: one word of the composed memory is read in a single access, so all its bits must come from chips that are selected together, which is what a row of chips is. Different rows must hold different addresses, so a row is chosen by the address bits that the chips themselves do not use, decoded to one-of-R. Hence rows = total words ÷ words per chip, columns = word width ÷ chip width, the decoder has log2(rows) inputs, and the lowest log2(words per chip) address bits go to every chip.

Worked example 1: 16K x 16 memory from 4K x 4 chips (K = 1024)
rows    = 16K / 4K = 4          columns = 16 / 4 = 4
chips   = 4 x 4 = 16
address = log2(16384) = 14 lines, A13-A0 (word addresses)
to every chip : A11-A0 (log2 4096 = 12 lines)
decoder       : A13 A12 -> 2-to-4; output Yi = CS of all 4 chips in row i
data          : column j drives D(4j+3)-D(4j), j = 0..3
row 0: 0000H-0FFFH   row 1: 1000H-1FFFH
row 2: 2000H-2FFFH   row 3: 3000H-3FFFH

In a larger address space the high-order lines that the memory does not need must still be dealt with. Full decoding feeds every one of them into the chip-select logic, so each location has exactly one address. Partial decoding leaves m of them out; because the chip cannot tell their values apart, each location answers to 2^m addresses and the whole chip appears 2^m times (mirror images or fold-back). That is harmless as long as the images of different chips never overlap and software uses only one of them, but it blocks later expansion into the mirrored space. Linear select is the extreme case: one address line drives each chip select directly and no decoder is used at all.

concepts.plainText: Images = 2^(bus address lines − lines used inside the chip − lines used for chip select)

inputs  C B A = A13 A12 A11     enables G1 = 1, /G2A = A15, /G2B = A14
enabled only when A15 = A14 = 0  -> decoded window 0000H-3FFFH
Y0: 0000H-07FFH   Y1: 0800H-0FFFH   Y2: 1000H-17FFH   Y3: 1800H-1FFFH
Y4: 2000H-27FFH   Y5: 2800H-2FFFH   Y6: 3000H-37FFH   Y7: 3800H-3FFFH

if /G2B is tied to 0 instead of A14: 2^1 = 2 images (Y0 also at 4000H-47FFH)

rows: Decoder plus gating on every unused high-order line
Decoder on only some of the high-order lines
Mirror images use up space and hinder expansion
None: one address line per chip select
Few chips, wasted space, bus contention if two select lines are active

concepts.text: Write ability also has a time cost. An EEPROM byte write starts an internal erase-and-program cycle of several milliseconds, but many parts accept a whole page per cycle: at 10 ms per cycle, 96 bytes take 0.96 s byte by byte but only 3 × 10 ms = 30 ms in 32-byte pages. Flash must erase a whole block before it can be reprogrammed and each block survives only about 10^4 to 10^5 erase cycles, so flash file systems buffer small changes in RAM and spread erasures over all blocks (wear levelling). DRAM is the opposite extreme: fast, unlimited writes, but bits that must be refreshed every few milliseconds.
Common mistakes in composition and address-map questions:
items: Counting address lines from bits instead of words: a 64-Kbit chip organised as 8K × 8 has 13 address lines, not 16.
Adding a decoder for width expansion: chips placed side by side share one chip select and the same address lines.
Off-by-one range ends: the last address is start + size − 1, so an 8 KB block starting at 6000H ends at 7FFFH, not 8000H.
Mixing K = 1000 and K = 1024: memory sizes use K = 1024, so a span of 1000H addresses is 4096 bytes = 4 KB.
Confusing decoder inputs with outputs: selecting one of 64 rows needs a 6-to-64 decoder, i.e. 6 address inputs.
Forgetting byte lanes: in a byte-addressable memory with a 32-bit data bus, A1–A0 pick the byte, so the chip address lines start at A2.

concepts.text: For any address-map question, write the address in binary: the bits used inside the chip are x's, the decoded bits are fixed 0s and 1s, and each ignored bit doubles the number of images. The first address has all x's = 0 and the last has all x's = 1.

formulas.plainText: Chips needed = (total words × bits per word) / (chip words × chip bits per word)
Address lines = log2(words); decoder input lines = log2(rows of chips)
Time to transfer n bits from a device with access time T_A and rate R
Wait states = ceiling((t_access − t_allowed) / T_clk), zero if negative

notes.text: Composition rule of thumb: parallel chips with shared address lines increase the width; a decoder on the high-order address bits selecting chip selects increases the number of words. Rows × columns of chips = (words ratio) × (width ratio).

When counting address lines for a composed memory, use the total number of words (4K → 12 lines), then split them: low bits to every chip, high bits to the decoder. Do not add the widths; extra width never needs extra address lines.

On Vahid's two axes, write ability rises from mask ROM through OTP, EPROM, EEPROM, flash and NVRAM to SRAM/DRAM, while storage permanence falls in the same order; nonvolatile memories are simply those that keep data without power.
Access time is the delay to get one word; cycle time is the minimum spacing between accesses and is longer for DRAM. A memory slower than the bus cycle forces the processor to insert wait states.

concepts.text: Three Modes of Data Transfer

Data between an I/O device and memory can be moved in three ways: under program control (programmed I/O), on demand of the device (interrupt-driven I/O), or by dedicated hardware that takes over the bus (direct memory access, DMA). The modes differ in how much CPU time each transfer consumes and in how much extra hardware is required. A fourth arrangement, the I/O processor, moves the whole I/O program out of the CPU.
Programmed I/O (Polling)
In programmed I/O every word passes through the CPU under the control of an I/O routine. For input the flow is:
items: 1. CPU issues a read command to the interface and the device begins to produce a word.
2. CPU reads the status register and tests the flag bit; if the flag is 0 it loops back and reads the status again (busy waiting).
3. When the flag is 1 the CPU reads the data register into the accumulator, which clears the flag.
4. CPU stores the word in memory, updates the address and count, and repeats until the block is complete.

Cost: the CPU spends its time in the polling loop. If a device delivers one byte every 100 µs and a poll takes 1 µs, the CPU wastes 99% of that period doing nothing useful; with several devices the loop must poll all of them in turn.

concepts.text: Interrupt-Driven I/O

Instead of polling, the CPU issues the I/O command and continues with other work. When the interface has data (flag = 1) it raises an interrupt request line. At the end of the current instruction cycle the CPU checks the request: if interrupts are enabled (IEN = 1) it saves the return address (program counter) and status on the stack, disables further interrupts, branches to the interrupt service routine (ISR), transfers the word, re-enables interrupts and returns. Only the transfer itself and the save/restore overhead consume CPU time.
How the CPU finds the service routine and decides between simultaneous requests:
items: Non-vectored interrupt: the branch address is fixed (e.g. location 0 in Mano's basic computer); the ISR must then poll the devices to find who interrupted.
Vectored interrupt: the interrupting device supplies a vector address (VAD) on the data bus during the interrupt acknowledge cycle, so the CPU jumps straight to that device's routine.

Daisy-chain (serial) priority: devices are connected in a chain on the interrupt acknowledge line. The acknowledge passes from device to device (PI in, PO out); the first device in the chain that has a pending request blocks it and puts its VAD on the bus. Priority is fixed by position: the device nearest the CPU is highest.

Parallel priority: each device sets one bit of an interrupt register; a mask register (set by software) can disable individual bits; a priority encoder converts the highest active bit into the VAD. Priorities can be changed by software, unlike the daisy chain.
Priority in software: a single interrupt line and an ISR that polls devices in priority order; cheapest hardware, slowest response.

concepts.text: Direct Memory Access (DMA)

For high-speed devices such as disks, even interrupt-driven transfer is too slow because every word still goes through the CPU registers. DMA lets the interface transfer data directly between the device and memory over the system bus while the CPU is idle or executing other instructions. The CPU hands over control of its address, data and control buses to a DMA controller: the CPU asserts bus grant (HLDA, hold acknowledge) in response to bus request (HOLD), tri-states its bus drivers and waits, or keeps executing from its internal cache and registers.
A DMA controller contains three registers the CPU initialises through ordinary programmed I/O, plus bus-control logic:
items: Address register: the starting memory address of the block; it is placed on the address bus and incremented after each word.
Word count register: the number of words to transfer; decremented after each word, and a zero count ends the transfer and raises an interrupt to the CPU.
Control register: transfer direction (read or write), mode (burst, cycle stealing) and a start bit.

Bus interface: bus request (BR/HOLD) and bus grant (BG/HLDA) lines to the CPU, DMA request and DMA acknowledge lines to the device, and drivers for the address bus and RD/WR lines when it is bus master.

The CPU sees the controller as an I/O port: DMA select (DS) plus register select (RS) choose the controller and the register; RD and WR are inputs while the CPU is master and outputs while the DMA is master.

concepts.text: DMA transfer sequence, step by step:
items: 1. The CPU program writes the start address, word count and control word (direction, mode, start) into the DMA controller and then continues with other work.
2. The device signals DMA request when it has a word (input) or needs a word (output).
3. The controller asserts bus request; the CPU completes its current bus cycle, releases the buses and answers with bus grant.
4. The controller puts the address on the address bus, drives RD or WR, and the word moves directly between the device and memory; it then increments the address and decrements the count.
5. In cycle-stealing mode the controller releases the bus after one word and repeats steps 2 to 4; in burst mode it keeps the bus until the count reaches zero.
6. When the word count is zero the controller releases the bus and sends an interrupt to the CPU, whose ISR checks status and starts the next block if needed.

CPU is halted for the duration of the block
Fast devices that cannot be stopped mid-block: magnetic disk, tape
One word per bus grant, interleaved with CPU cycles
CPU slowed slightly; it loses one bus cycle per word
Medium-speed devices; most common general mode
Only in bus cycles the CPU is not using
Slowest transfer rate; used when CPU performance must be untouched
Only at start and end of a block
Fastest; limited by bus and memory speed
DMA controller with address, count and control registers

concepts.text: Worked Example: DMA vs Programmed I/O

A disk delivers a 4 KB block (1024 words of 32 bits) and one memory cycle takes 100 ns. Under programmed I/O suppose each word costs the CPU 20 clock cycles (poll status, read data, store, update pointers) at 100 MHz, i.e. 200 ns of CPU time per word: the CPU is busy for 1024 × 200 ns = 204.8 µs for the block. Under DMA in burst mode the block moves in 1024 × 100 ns = 102.4 µs of bus time and the CPU spends only the set-up and completion interrupt, say 500 + 500 cycles = 10 µs. In cycle-stealing mode the same block steals 1024 bus cycles; if the disk supplies a word every 2 µs, the CPU loses 100 ns of every 2 µs, a 5% slowdown, while the transfer proceeds in the background.

concepts.plainText: T_DMA = N × t_cycle = 1024 × 100 ns = 102.4 µs

concepts.text: I/O Processor (Channel)

An I/O processor (IOP), called a channel in IBM systems, is a small processor with its own instruction set that executes I/O programs (channel programs) stored in main memory. The CPU only tells the IOP where the channel program is (via a shared memory location and an interprocessor command); the IOP then handles polling, device control, DMA-style transfers, code conversion and error checking for many devices, and interrupts the CPU when the whole job is done. A selector channel serves one high-speed device at a time; a multiplexer channel interleaves many slow devices. The IOP is the most independent transfer method and the most expensive.
Going Deeper: Transfer Costs, Priority Hardware and DMA Timing

The CPU cost of every transfer mode fits one equation: the fraction of processor time used equals the number of CPU-handled events per second multiplied by the cycles each event costs, divided by the clock frequency. For programmed I/O an event is one poll, and the device must be polled at least as often as it produces data or words are lost. For interrupt-driven I/O an event is one interrupt per word, so no time is wasted while the device is idle, but the save, service and restore overhead is paid for every word. For DMA an event is a whole block, costing only the controller set-up and the completion interrupt, which is why it wins for fast block devices.

concepts.plainText: Fraction of CPU time = events per second × CPU cycles per event / clock frequency (event = one poll, one interrupt or one DMA block)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: one disk, three transfer modes
CPU 200 MHz; disk sends 4-byte words at 2 MB/s (1 MB = 10^6 B)
Words per second = 2,000,000 / 4 = 500,000
Polling at the word rate, 150 cycles per poll:
  500,000 x 150 = 75 x 10^6 cycles/s  -> 37.5 % of the CPU
Interrupt per word, 250 cycles (save + ISR + restore):
  500,000 x 250 = 125 x 10^6 cycles/s -> 62.5 % of the CPU
DMA with 4 KB blocks (4096 B), 1500 set-up + 800 completion cycles:
  2,000,000 / 4096 = 488.28 blocks/s
  488.28 x 2300 = 1.12 x 10^6 cycles/s -> 0.56 % of the CPU
For this fast device interrupts cost even more than polling.

The DMA modes differ in how often the bus changes master. Every change costs a bus request/bus grant handshake, so burst mode pays it once per block while cycle stealing pays it once per word; burst therefore finishes a block sooner, but the CPU cannot use the bus until the burst ends. In cycle stealing the CPU loses one bus cycle per word, so its slowdown is the stolen cycle time divided by the interval between device words. Transparent DMA uses only bus cycles the CPU leaves idle, so its top rate is the idle fraction times the bus cycle rate. When a controller buffers a block and then bursts it, the CPU is shut out for burst time divided by buffer-fill time, which equals device rate divided by burst rate.

Worked example 2: burst versus cycle stealing for one block
Clock 50 MHz (20 ns); block of 512 words
Acquire bus (BR -> BG) = 2 clocks, release = 1 clock, 1 word = 2 clocks
Burst:          2 + 512 x 2 + 1   = 1027 clocks = 20.54 µs
Cycle stealing: 512 x (2 + 2 + 1) = 2560 clocks = 51.2 µs of bus use,
                spread over the time the device needs to supply 512 words
Buffered burst: device fills 2 KB at 128 KB/s -> one block per 15.625 ms
  burst of 1024 16-bit words x 50 ns = 51.2 µs
  CPU shut out 51.2 µs / 15,625 µs = 0.33 % of the time
When the CPU responds to an interrupt and when to a DMA request:
items: An interrupt request is recognised only at the end of the current instruction's execute phase, so the worst-case latency is the rest of the longest instruction plus the interrupt (acknowledge) cycle plus the context saving done before the first useful ISR instruction.

A DMA request can be granted at any DMA breakpoint, that is after any bus cycle, even in the middle of an instruction. The CPU saves no registers, because it only pauses and its program state is not disturbed.

Mano's basic computer performs the interrupt cycle as RT0: AR ← 0, TR ← PC; RT1: M[AR] ← TR, PC ← 0; RT2: PC ← PC + 1, IEN ← 0, R ← 0, SC ← 0. The return address goes to location 0 and a branch to the ISR is kept in location 1.

IEN is cleared by hardware so that a second interrupt cannot overwrite the saved return address before the ISR has dealt with it; the ISR re-enables interrupts (ION) just before it returns, or earlier if nesting is allowed.

Interrupt sources (Mano): external (I/O devices, timers, power failure), internal or traps (overflow, divide by zero, invalid opcode, stack overflow, protection violation) and software interrupts (a supervisor-call instruction that switches to supervisor mode for an OS service). A non-maskable interrupt (NMI) cannot be disabled by the program and is kept for events such as power failure.

rows: No acknowledge reached it; passes 0 down the chain
Request waits; a device nearer the CPU is being served
No request here; acknowledge passed to the next device
This device wins and places its VAD on the data bus

concepts.text: In the parallel priority scheme each interrupt register bit is ANDed with its mask bit and the results drive a priority encoder. With four inputs and I0 the highest, the encoder gives x = I0'I1' and y = I0'I1 + I0'I2', plus IST = I0 + I1 + I2 + I3 to tell the CPU that a valid request exists. The code xy is inserted into a fixed vector pattern: placing it in bits 3 and 2 of an 8-bit vector with all other bits 0 gives vectors 0, 4, 8 and 12, leaving four words per device for a jump to its routine. Changing mask bits under program control changes which devices may interrupt, with no rewiring.
How DMA modules and I/O processors are connected and commanded (Stallings, Mano):
items: Single-bus, detached DMA: the DMA module, the I/O modules and memory share the one system bus, so each word crosses the bus twice (I/O module to DMA, DMA to memory) and costs two bus cycles.
Single-bus, integrated DMA and I/O: the DMA logic is part of the I/O module or reaches the devices by its own path, so each word uses the system bus only once.
Separate I/O bus: all devices attach to an I/O bus behind the DMA module, which then needs a single system-bus interface and again uses one system-bus cycle per word.

CPU and IOP (Mano): the CPU tests the I/O path, then issues start I/O with the address of the IOP program in memory and goes on with other work. The IOP fetches its commands from memory (IBM channel command words hold a command code, data address, flags and byte count), moves the data by cycle stealing, stores a status word in memory and interrupts the CPU when the whole job is done.

concepts.text: Common slips: mixing bits and bytes (a 32-bit bus moves 4 bytes per transfer, so 4 KB is 1024 transfers, not 4096); mixing 1 KB = 1024 B for block sizes with 1 MB/s = 10^6 B/s for rates when the question fixes only one convention; forgetting the completion interrupt in DMA overhead; confusing the CPU time consumed with the bus time a transfer takes; and assuming an interrupt can be accepted in the middle of an instruction.

For percentage-of-CPU-time questions write F = events per second × cycles per event ÷ clock rate and first decide what one event is: a poll, one interrupt per word or one DMA block. For the percentage of time the CPU is blocked, use stolen cycle ÷ word interval in cycle stealing and device rate ÷ burst rate for a buffered burst.

formulas.plainText: DMA block time = number of words × memory cycle time
CPU time in programmed I/O = N × (cycles per word / clock frequency)
CPU slowdown fraction = stolen cycle time / time between words
Interrupt-driven CPU time = N × (save + service + restore time)

notes.text: Order by CPU involvement: programmed I/O (most, busy-waits) > interrupt-driven (per word, no waiting) > DMA (only start and end of block) > IOP (only start and end of an entire I/O program).

HOLD/BR is the request from the DMA controller to the CPU; HLDA/BG is the grant from the CPU. The DMA controller never generates the interrupt at the start of a transfer; it interrupts only when the word count reaches zero.

In a daisy chain the device nearest the CPU has the highest priority and priorities cannot be changed by software; the parallel scheme with a mask register can. Transparent DMA is the slowest mode but causes zero CPU slowdown; burst is the fastest but stalls the CPU.

For time questions: DMA block time = words × memory cycle time; cycle-stealing slowdown = stolen cycle time ÷ interval between device words. Convert KB to words using the bus width first (4 KB = 1024 words on a 32-bit bus).

concepts.text: What a Multiprocessor Is

A multiprocessor is a computer system with two or more CPUs that share main memory and I/O equipment under a single integrated operating system. In Flynn's classification it is an MIMD machine: each processor executes its own instruction stream on its own data. A system in which each processor has private memory and communicates only by messages is a multicomputer; a multiprocessor with several processors on one chip is a multicore. Multiprocessors are the standard way to get more performance than one processor can deliver.
Characteristics and benefits of multiprocessors:
items: Improved throughput: several independent jobs run in parallel, and one job can be split into cooperating tasks (parallel processing at the job or program level).
Improved reliability and fault tolerance: if one processor fails the others continue at reduced performance (graceful degradation).
Shared resources: memory, I/O channels and the operating system are shared, which is cheaper than separate complete computers.
Cost: interconnection hardware, coherence logic and the parallel operating system add cost and complexity, and speed-up is limited by the sequential part of the work (Amdahl's law).

rows: One common global memory accessible to all processors; each may also have a local cache
Each processor has its own private memory; no global memory
Message passing over a network, slower
Bus, multiport memory, crossbar, multistage network
Message-transfer system (links, switches), e.g. hypercube, mesh
Limited by memory contention; tens of processors
Scales to thousands of nodes (clusters, supercomputers)
Tasks that share much data and interact often

concepts.text: Shared-memory machines are classified by access latency. In UMA (uniform memory access, the symmetric multiprocessor or SMP) every processor reaches any memory word in the same time through a common bus or switch. In NUMA (non-uniform memory access) each processor has its own nearby memory and can also reach remote memory over the interconnect, but more slowly; the memories together form one address space. In COMA (cache-only memory architecture) every local memory acts as a large cache and data migrates to whichever processor uses it.
Interconnection Structures

The interconnection structure is the hardware that connects processors to memory modules and I/O. It determines how many transfers can happen at once, how the cost grows with the number of units, and whether the network can block. Mano lists five physical forms: time-shared common bus, multiport memory, crossbar switch, multistage switching network and hypercube.
Time-shared common bus and multiport memory:
items: Time-shared common bus: all processors, memory modules and I/O share one bus. Only one processor can transfer at a time, so the bus becomes the bottleneck as processors are added; cheapest and simplest. A system bus needs arbitration logic to choose the next bus master (serial, parallel or dynamic; see the synchronization subtopic).
Dual-bus variant: each processor has a local bus with local memory and cache, and only accesses the system bus for shared memory; this reduces contention.

Multiport memory: each memory module has one port per processor, with separate address, data and control lines to each. Conflicts are resolved by fixed priorities assigned to the ports. Every processor can access a different module simultaneously; very high transfer rate, but expensive wiring and control logic, so practical only for a small number of processors.

concepts.text: Crossbar switch and multistage switching networks:
items: Crossbar: a grid of switch points between N processors (rows) and M memory modules (columns). Each crosspoint contains multiplexing and arbitration logic, so any processor can connect to any free module and all N×M combinations are possible at once. Non-blocking, but hardware grows as N×M (an 8×8 crossbar needs 64 crosspoints).
2×2 interchange switch: the building block of multistage networks; two inputs, two outputs, four states — straight through, cross, upper broadcast, lower broadcast — selected by one control bit.

Omega network: an N×N network built from log₂N stages of N/2 interchange switches, with a perfect-shuffle wiring between stages. For 8×8: log₂8 = 3 stages of 4 switches = 12 switches instead of 64 crosspoints. Routing is by destination bits: at stage i the switch sends the request to its upper output if bit i of the destination is 0 and to its lower output if it is 1.
Multistage networks are cheaper than a crossbar but blocking: two requests to different destinations may need the same switch or link and must be serialised.

concepts.latex: \text{Omega } N\times N:\ \log_2 N \text{ stages},\ \tfrac{N}{2}\log_2 N \text{ switches}
concepts.plainText: Omega N×N: log2 N stages, (N/2) log2 N 2×2 switches; 8×8 → 3 stages, 12 switches

concepts.text: Hypercube (binary n-cube) interconnection, a loosely coupled point-to-point structure:
items: An n-cube has 2^n processors (nodes), each with its own memory and I/O. Node addresses are n-bit binary numbers; two nodes are directly linked if their addresses differ in exactly one bit.

Each node has n links, the total number of links is n × 2^(n−1), and the longest route (diameter) between any two nodes is n hops. A 3-cube has 8 nodes, 3 links per node, 12 links and diameter 3; a 4-cube has 16 nodes, 4 links per node, 32 links, diameter 4.

Routing: XOR the source and destination addresses; the number of 1s in the result is the distance, and the message is forwarded along the dimension of each 1 bit in turn (e.g. 010 → 111: XOR = 101, route 010 → 011 → 111 or 010 → 110 → 111).
Used in the Intel iPSC and nCUBE machines; scales well because the diameter grows only as log₂ of the node count.

concepts.latex: n\text{-cube: } 2^{n} \text{ nodes},\ n \text{ links/node},\ n\,2^{n-1} \text{ links},\ \text{diameter } n
concepts.plainText: n-cube: 2^n nodes, n links per node, n·2^(n−1) links in total, diameter n

rows: Up to one per memory module
Conflicts inside the network; delay of log₂N stages
Node degree grows with n; no shared memory

concepts.text: Cache Coherence

When each processor of a shared-memory system has a private cache, the same memory block may be copied into several caches. If one processor writes to its copy, the others hold stale data; the inconsistency is the cache coherence problem. It arises with write-back caches (memory itself is stale), with write-through caches (other caches are stale) and with I/O or DMA writing memory behind the caches. The common solution on a bus is a snoopy write-invalidate protocol such as MESI: every cache controller watches (snoops) the bus, and a write to a shared line first invalidates all other copies so that only one cache holds a Modified line; each line is tagged Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid. Directory-based protocols replace snooping for larger NUMA systems (details in the next subtopic).
Amdahl's Law: The Limit of Speed-up

If a fraction f of a program's execution time can be parallelised perfectly over N processors and the remaining (1 − f) must run sequentially, the time on N processors is (1 − f) + f/N of the original, so the speed-up is S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/N). As N grows without limit the speed-up saturates at 1/(1 − f): the serial part sets a ceiling no number of processors can beat. Example: f = 0.9 and N = 10 gives S = 1 / (0.1 + 0.09) = 5.26, not 10; with infinite processors the ceiling is 1/0.1 = 10. Efficiency E = S/N = 0.526 tells how well the ten processors are used.

concepts.plainText: S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/N); maximum speed-up as N → ∞ is 1/(1 − f)

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Counting Switches, Links, Paths and Bus Load

An N×N omega network (N = 2^n) needs n = log₂N stages because each stage of 2×2 switches settles one bit of the destination address, and each stage has N/2 switches because every switch serves two lines. Before each stage the lines are wired as a perfect shuffle, which moves line a(n−1)…a1a0 to line a(n−2)…a0a(n−1), a one-bit left rotation of the line number, like riffling a deck of cards. After n shuffles and n switch decisions every source bit has been replaced by a destination bit, so each source reaches each destination by exactly one path. With two useful settings per switch (straight or exchange) the network has 2^((N/2)log₂N) = N^(N/2) settings in total, so an 8×8 omega network realises only 2^12 = 4096 of the 8! = 40,320 permutations, which is why some request patterns block.

concepts.plainText: Omega settings = 2^((N/2)·log2 N) = N^(N/2); for 8×8 that is 2^12 = 4096 realisable permutations out of 8! = 40,320

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: routing and blocking in an 8 x 8 omega network
Rule: stage i uses destination bit i counted from the MSB; 0 = upper, 1 = lower
Line after stage i = last 3 bits of (source shifted left i places,
                     with the first i destination bits shifted in)
Request A: source 010 -> destination 110
  stage 1: line 101 (bit 1, lower)
  stage 2: line 011 (bit 1, lower)
  stage 3: line 110 (bit 0, upper) = destination
Request B: source 110 -> destination 100
  stage 1: line 101 (bit 1, lower) -> the same output line as A
A and B collide at stage 1, so one must wait: the network is blocking.
Cost: 3 stages x 4 switches = 12 switches (48 crosspoints) vs 64 in a crossbar

In an n-cube with N = 2^n nodes each node has n neighbours, one per address bit, and because every link joins two nodes the link count is n·2^n ÷ 2 = n·2^(n−1) = (N log₂N)/2. The distance between two nodes is the Hamming distance of their addresses, so exactly C(n, k) nodes lie k hops from any node and the farthest node, the bitwise complement, is n hops away. Cutting the cube across one dimension leaves two (n−1)-cubes joined by 2^(n−1) = N/2 links; this bisection width measures how much traffic can cross the middle of the machine. The usual deterministic routing, e-cube routing, corrects the differing bits in a fixed order (lowest dimension first), giving a unique shortest path that is also deadlock-free.

Worked example 2: a 4-cube (16 nodes)
Links = 4 x 2^3 = 32; bisection width = 2^3 = 8; diameter = 4
Route 0101 -> 1110: 0101 XOR 1110 = 1011, so the distance is 3 hops
e-cube order (bit 0 first): 0101 -> 0100 -> 0110 -> 1110
Nodes at distance 0..4 from 0000: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 (= C(4,k), total 16)
Average distance to the other 15 nodes = (4 + 12 + 12 + 4) / 15 = 2.13

A time-shared bus saturates when the processors together demand more than all of its time. If each processor makes r memory references per second, a fraction m of them miss in its private cache and each miss holds the bus for t_bus, one processor keeps the bus busy for the fraction r·m·t_bus, and the bus can carry at most 1/(r·m·t_bus) processors, rounded down. With 50 million references per second, a 5% miss ratio and 50 ns of bus time per miss, each processor uses 12.5% of the bus, so 8 processors saturate it. Private caches that cut m are therefore essential in bus-based SMPs, and larger systems move to crossbars, multistage networks or NUMA.

concepts.plainText: Bus utilisation U = N × r × m × t_bus must not exceed 1, so N_max = floor(1 / (r × m × t_bus))
