Then P1 writes 15 (option b: write-back, no protocol)
Then P1 writes 15 (option c: write-back with write-invalidate snooping)

concepts.text: SMP, NUMA, multiport memory and speed-up in numbers:
items: SMP (Stallings): two or more similar processors of comparable capability share main memory and I/O over a bus or other interconnect with about the same access time, all can perform the same functions, and one integrated operating system controls them. A master–slave arrangement in which only one processor runs the OS is not symmetric.

NUMA average access time = p_local × t_local + (1 − p_local) × t_remote; with 90% local references at 80 ns and 10% remote at 500 ns it is 72 + 50 = 122 ns, so the OS tries to place a process's pages in its own node's memory. CC-NUMA adds hardware cache coherence, usually with a directory.

Multiport memory with P processors and M modules needs P ports on every module and P × M processor–module paths, with fixed port priorities resolving conflicts; this is why it suits only small systems.

Amdahl's law rearranged gives the parallel fraction needed for a target speed-up S on N processors: f = (1 − 1/S) / (1 − 1/N). For S = 6 on N = 8, f = (5/6) / (7/8) = 0.952, so less than 5% of the work may stay serial.
Sources of cache incoherence (Hwang): sharing of writable data, process migration from one processor to another, and I/O or DMA that writes memory behind the caches.

concepts.text: Common slips: counting crossbar crosspoints as N + M instead of N × M; forgetting that one 2×2 switch contains four crosspoints; writing hypercube links as n·2^n, which counts every link twice; giving the node count 2^n as the diameter; treating the NUMA remote time as an extra delay on top of the local time; and rounding the bus limit 1/(r·m·t_bus) up instead of down.

formulas.plainText: Amdahl speed-up S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/N), f = parallel fraction, N = processors
Efficiency E = S / N
Hypercube: nodes = 2^n, links = n·2^(n−1), diameter = n

formulas.latex: \text{Crossbar } N\times M:\ N M \text{ crosspoints};\ \text{Omega } N\times N:\ \tfrac{N}{2}\log_2 N \text{ switches}
formulas.plainText: Crossbar N×M: N·M crosspoints; Omega N×N: (N/2)·log2 N switches in log2 N stages

notes.text: Numbers to memorise: 8×8 crossbar = 64 crosspoints; 8×8 omega = 3 stages × 4 switches = 12 switches; 3-cube = 8 nodes, 3 links each, diameter 3; 4-cube = 16 nodes, diameter 4. Amdahl ceiling = 1/(1 − f).

Tightly coupled = shared memory (communication through memory); loosely coupled = private memories (communication by message passing). Do not equate loosely coupled with NUMA: NUMA still has one shared address space, it is just non-uniform in latency.

A crossbar is non-blocking but grows as N×M; a multistage network is cheaper (N/2·log₂N switches) but blocking. The time-shared bus is the cheapest and the least scalable because only one transfer can use it at a time.

concepts.text: How Processors Communicate

In a shared-memory (tightly coupled) multiprocessor the common memory is the communication medium. A processor that wants to send information writes it into a shared memory area that the operating system reserves for this purpose; the receiver reads it. Each processor may be assigned a mailbox, a memory area holding messages addressed to it, and the sender simply deposits the message there. The receiver must learn that a message has arrived: it can periodically inspect its mailbox (polling of memory), or the sender can raise an interprocessor interrupt, a signal that one processor sends over the bus to a specific other processor to notify it of an event or of a pending message.
Communication mechanisms, from tightly to loosely coupled:
items: Shared variables in common memory: fastest; the operating system allocates the area and processors use ordinary load/store instructions. Needs synchronization to avoid corrupting shared data.
Mailbox: a dedicated memory area per processor plus a status flag; the sender writes the message and sets the flag, the receiver clears it after reading.

Interprocessor interrupt: a processor writes to an interrupt register of the target processor (or uses a dedicated line), forcing it to run a handler; used to deliver urgent events and to start the operating system's scheduler on another CPU.

Message passing (loosely coupled): each node has private memory; information is packaged into packets and sent over communication channels (point-to-point links, a switching network or a LAN). The sending node does not wait; the packet is routed through intermediate nodes to its destination.
Shared I/O and shared operating system data: the OS also keeps a process table and other structures in shared memory that all processors must access consistently.

concepts.text: Why Synchronization Is Needed

Processors that share data must coordinate their accesses in time, which is called synchronization. A critical section is a program segment that accesses a shared resource and must be completed by one processor before any other processor may begin a section that touches the same resource. If two processors execute read-modify-write sequences on the same variable at the same time, the result depends on the exact timing (a race condition) and can be wrong: two processors each incrementing a shared counter can leave it incremented once. The property that only one processor at a time executes a critical section is mutual exclusion.
Mutual exclusion with a semaphore:
items: A binary semaphore is a variable in shared memory that indicates whether a resource is in use: 1 = busy (a processor is in the critical section), 0 = free.
Before entering a critical section a processor tests the semaphore; if it is 0 it sets it to 1 and enters; if it is 1 it waits and retries. On leaving it resets the semaphore to 0.
The test and the set must be a single indivisible operation. If processor A reads 0 and, before it writes 1, processor B also reads 0, both enter the critical section and mutual exclusion is broken.
Counting semaphores extend this to resources with several instances; higher-level constructs (locks, mutexes, monitors) are built on the same primitive.

concepts.text: Hardware support is the test-and-set instruction (TSL SEM in Mano's treatment). In one indivisible read-modify-write memory cycle it copies the current value of the semaphore into a processor flag and writes 1 into the semaphore: SEM → F, 1 → SEM. To make the cycle indivisible the processor asserts a bus lock signal that prevents any other processor from taking the bus between the read and the write. After TSL the processor examines F: F = 0 means the semaphore was free and is now taken, so it proceeds; F = 1 means it was already busy, so the processor loops and tries again (a spin lock or busy wait). Other atomic primitives serve the same purpose: swap (exchange), fetch-and-add, compare-and-swap.

concepts.latex: \text{TSL SEM}:\ SEM \rightarrow F,\ 1 \rightarrow SEM\ (\text{one locked bus cycle})
concepts.plainText: TSL SEM: copy SEM to flag F, then set SEM = 1, in one indivisible bus-locked cycle

concepts.text: Other synchronization mechanisms:
items: Barrier: a point that every participating processor must reach before any may continue; implemented with a shared counter that each arrival increments atomically and a flag released when the count equals the number of processors. Used between phases of a parallel algorithm.
Event flags and condition variables: a processor waits until another sets a flag, avoiding continuous polling when combined with interrupts.

Deadlock: two or more processors wait forever for resources held by each other. It requires four conditions at once — mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait — and is handled by prevention (break one condition, e.g. acquire locks in a fixed order), avoidance, or detection and recovery.

concepts.text: Interprocessor Arbitration

Processors, memory and I/O of a tightly coupled system share a system bus (Mano's example has 86 lines: 16 data, 24 address, control and arbitration lines). When several processors request the bus at the same time, arbitration logic decides which becomes the bus master; the others wait. Arbitration is either static (priorities fixed by hardware) or dynamic (priorities change during execution to be fair).

rows: Bus-grant line passes through the arbiters PI → PO; the first requesting unit blocks it and takes the bus when the bus-busy line is free
Fixed by position; nearest the arbiter is highest
Simplest; few lines; slow for long chains; cannot be changed
Each unit has a request line into a priority encoder; a decoder returns the grant on the selected line
Faster than daisy chain; one line per unit
The bus is allotted to each processor for a fixed interval in round-robin order
The arbiter puts a processor number on poll lines; the addressed processor takes the bus if it has a request; the sequence can be programmed
Highest priority to the unit that has not used the bus for the longest time
Requests queued in order of arrival; the earliest is served first
Like the daisy chain but the highest priority moves to the unit after the one that last held the bus
Fair version of the daisy chain

concepts.text: Cache Coherence Solutions
Ways of keeping private caches consistent in a shared-memory system:
items: No private caches for shared data: a single shared cache, or shared writable data marked non-cacheable so that all such accesses go to main memory; simple but slow.
Write-through with software control: the compiler or OS marks which data are shared and read-only (cacheable) versus shared and writable (non-cacheable) or flushes caches at critical points.

Snoopy (bus-watching) protocols: each cache controller monitors the shared bus for writes to lines it holds. Write-invalidate (MESI: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) invalidates other copies before a write so one cache owns the line; write-update (write-broadcast) instead sends the new data to every cache holding the line. Suits bus-based UMA systems.

Directory-based protocols: a directory in memory (or distributed with each memory module) records which caches hold each line; a write consults the directory and sends invalidations only to those caches, avoiding bus broadcasts. Used in scalable NUMA systems with point-to-point interconnects.
Synchronization primitives interact with coherence: the bus lock during test-and-set guarantees that the semaphore read and write are seen by all processors as one atomic action.

rows: On a write to a shared line
In every cache; all watch the bus
Other copies invalidated; writer gets Modified state
In every cache; all watch the bus
New value broadcast to all caches holding the line
Data written and then read by many processors
Central or distributed directory in memory
Directory sends invalidations only to listed sharers
Large NUMA systems with switched interconnects

concepts.text: Putting it together: a tightly coupled multiprocessor needs three layers of coordination. Arbitration decides who may use the bus in the next cycle; cache coherence guarantees that every processor sees the same value for a memory word; synchronization (semaphores built on test-and-set, barriers) guarantees that critical sections of the software run one at a time. MCQs on this subtopic mostly ask for the indivisibility of test-and-set, the meaning of the semaphore values, the name of an arbitration algorithm from its description, and snoopy versus directory coherence.
Going Deeper: MESI, Lock Traffic and Bus Contention

MESI is the write-invalidate snooping protocol used with write-back caches in many bus-based multiprocessors; every cache line carries one of four states. Modified (M) means the line is valid only in this cache and has been written, so main memory is stale and this cache must supply or write back the data before anyone else uses it. Exclusive (E) means only this cache holds the line and it equals memory; Shared (S) means other caches may also hold it and all copies equal memory; Invalid (I) means the line holds nothing usable. The E state is what MESI adds to a three-state MSI protocol: a processor that reads private data and later writes it moves E to M silently, with no bus transaction.

rows: Another cache wants to write (snooped RWITM or invalidate)
Read or write hit; stays M, no bus traffic
Supplies the line and writes it back to memory; goes to S
Writes the line back to memory; goes to I
Read hit stays E; write hit goes to M with no bus traffic
Read hit stays S; write hit sends an invalidate and goes to M
Read miss: BusRd, loads E if no other cache has the line, else S. Write miss: RWITM, loads M

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: MESI trace, three write-back caches, X starts in memory only
Step Access       Bus action                          P1 P2 P3
1    P1 reads X   BusRd, no other copy                E  I  I
2    P2 reads X   BusRd, P1 E -> S                    S  S  I
3    P1 writes X  Invalidate, P2 S -> I               M  I  I
4    P3 reads X   BusRd, P1 writes X back, M -> S     S  I  S
5    P2 writes X  RWITM, P1 and P3 S -> I             I  M  I
6    P2 reads X   Hit, no bus action                  I  M  I
Bus transactions = 3 BusRd + 1 invalidate + 1 RWITM = 5
Write-backs = 1 (step 4); memory is stale again after step 5

Write-update protocols such as Dragon and Firefly keep every copy valid by broadcasting each written word, so a consumer that reads right after a write hits in its own cache; but a processor that writes the same line many times sends one broadcast per write even when nobody reads in between. Write-invalidate pays one invalidation for the first write and then writes locally, while every other processor that later reads the line takes a miss. Because runs of writes to the same line without intervening reads by others are common, most commercial processors use write-invalidate (MESI and variants such as MOESI and MESIF). False sharing is its pathological case: two processors write different words that happen to lie in one line, so the line ping-pongs between their caches although no data is really shared, and padding the variables into separate lines cures it.
Spin locks and atomic primitives on a snooping bus:
items: Plain test-and-set spinning: every retry is an atomic read-modify-write that needs the line in the Modified state, so each attempt is a bus transaction; k waiters retrying every t seconds cause k/t transactions per second while the lock stays busy, slowing even the lock holder's own memory traffic.

Test-and-test-and-set: a waiter first reads the lock with an ordinary load; after one read miss it spins on its Shared cached copy with no bus traffic and issues test-and-set only when it sees 0. The release write invalidates all copies and causes one short burst of misses.
Exponential backoff: after a failed attempt a waiter delays for a growing random time before retrying, trading a little latency for much less contention.
Compare-and-swap CAS(addr, expected, new): writes new only if M[addr] equals expected and always returns the old value, so a failed CAS leaves memory unchanged and tells the caller what it found.
Fetch-and-add FAA(addr, k): returns the old value and adds k indivisibly; n processors each doing FAA(c, 1) receive n different values, the basis of ticket locks and barrier counters.

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: how many processors can one shared bus carry?
Each processor: 10^8 memory references/s, hit ratio 0.97 in its private cache
Every miss holds the bus for 40 ns (address plus block transfer)
Bus requests per processor = 10^8 x (1 - 0.97) = 3 x 10^6 per second
Bus share per processor    = 3 x 10^6 x 40 ns = 0.12 (12 % of bus time)
Saturation: N x 0.12 <= 1  ->  N <= 8.33, so at most 8 processors
With 6 processors U = 6 x 0.12 = 0.72; waiting time rises steeply as U -> 1

concepts.plainText: Bus utilisation U = N × r × t_b must stay ≤ 1, so N_max = floor(1 / (r × t_b)); r = bus transactions per second per processor, t_b = bus time per transaction

concepts.text: A directory protocol replaces broadcasting with bookkeeping. In a full-map directory every memory block has an entry with one presence bit per processor and a dirty bit, plus a state such as Uncached, Shared or Exclusive; on a write the home node sends invalidations only to the processors whose bits are set and records the writer as the owner. Because the entry grows with N, large machines use limited-pointer directories that store a few processor numbers of log2 N bits each, or chain the sharers in a linked list kept in the caches, as the SCI standard does.

concepts.plainText: Full-map directory: N presence bits + 1 dirty bit per memory block of B bytes; storage overhead = (N + 1)/(8B)

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: size of a full-map directory
Memory 1 GiB = 2^30 bytes, block B = 64 bytes, N = 32 processors
Blocks          = 2^30 / 2^6 = 2^24 = 16,777,216
Bits per entry  = 32 presence bits + 1 dirty bit = 33
Directory size  = 33 x 2^24 bits = 33 x 2^21 bytes = 66 MiB
Overhead        = 33 / (64 x 8) = 6.4 % of main memory
Limited pointers (4 x log2 32 + 1 = 21 bits) would need 42 MiB

Common slips in these problems: an E line changes to M on a local write without any bus transaction, but an S line must first broadcast an invalidate; a read miss loads E only when no other cache holds the line; a snooped read of an M line forces a write-back and leaves both copies Shared. When sizing a directory, remember the dirty bit and convert bits to bytes.

formulas.plainText: Test-and-set: SEM → F, then 1 → SEM, indivisibly
Links to connect N nodes fully = N(N − 1)/2
Time-slice arbitration: each of N processors gets T_round / N of the bus per round
Speed-up with synchronization overhead: S = T1 / (T1/N + T_sync)

notes.text: Test-and-set must be indivisible (one read-modify-write cycle with the bus locked). In Mano's convention semaphore = 1 means the resource is busy and 0 means free; after TSL, flag F = 0 means you got the resource.

Do not mix up the two daisy chains: the interrupt daisy chain passes interrupt acknowledge, the arbitration daisy chain passes bus grant. Both give the unit nearest the source the highest fixed priority; only the rotating daisy chain makes it fair.
Snoopy protocols need a broadcast medium (a bus) so every cache can listen; directory protocols work over point-to-point networks and therefore scale to large NUMA machines.

Dynamic arbitration keywords: fixed interval in turn = time slice; arbiter addresses each unit = polling; longest idle wins = LRU; earliest request wins = FIFO; priority moves to the unit after the last master = rotating daisy chain.

concepts.text: Combinational Logic Review

A single-purpose processor is a digital circuit designed to execute exactly one program: hard-wired logic with no instruction fetch, giving maximum performance and low power at the cost of zero flexibility. Because it is built directly from logic, its design starts with the basics. Transistors form gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR), and a combinational circuit is one whose outputs depend only on the current inputs. The standard design flow is: state the problem, build a truth table, write the output equations, minimise them with a Karnaugh map or Boolean algebra, and draw the gate-level circuit. Ready-made combinational components used in datapaths are the n-bit adder, comparator, multiplexer, decoder, shifter and ALU.
Sequential Logic and Finite-State Machines

A sequential circuit has outputs that depend on the current inputs and on the stored state; its building blocks are flip-flops, registers, counters and shift registers, all driven by a clock. Its behaviour is captured by a finite-state machine (FSM) defined by a set of states, a set of inputs, a set of outputs, a next-state function, an output function and an initial state. In a Moore machine the outputs depend only on the current state; in a Mealy machine they depend on the state and the current inputs, so a Mealy FSM often needs fewer states but its outputs can change in the middle of a clock period.
Sequential design flow (RT-level):
items: Draw the state diagram: states as circles, transitions labelled with input conditions and outputs.
Build the state table listing present state, inputs, next state and outputs.
Encode the states: n flip-flops give up to 2^n states, so the minimum register width is the ceiling of log2 of the state count.
Derive the next-state and output logic as combinational circuits using truth tables and K-maps.
Implement as a state register plus the combinational block; the clock period must exceed the longest register-to-register delay.

concepts.plainText: n_FF = ceil(log2 N_states);  f_max = 1 / t_critical

concepts.text: Custom Single-Purpose Processor: Datapath + Controller

Any processor, custom or general-purpose, consists of a datapath and a controller. The datapath stores and manipulates data: registers hold variables, functional units (adders, subtractors, comparators, ALUs) perform operations, and multiplexers and buses route values between them. The controller is an FSM that, in each clock cycle, reads status signals from the datapath (for example x is less than y) and sets control signals (register load enables, mux selects, ALU function) so the datapath performs the right step. In a custom single-purpose processor both blocks are built for one program, so there is no instruction register, no program memory and no decode logic.
Register-transfer level design flow from a program to a custom processor:
items: Write the desired behaviour as a program (usually in C-like pseudocode).
Convert the program to an FSMD, a finite-state machine with datapath: an FSM whose transitions may carry complex conditions and whose states carry arithmetic actions on declared variables.
Create the datapath: allocate a register for each variable, a functional unit for each arithmetic operation, and connect them with multiplexers according to the data flow.
Create the controller FSM by replacing each FSMD action with the control signals that make the datapath perform it, and each condition with a datapath status signal.
Optimise the result, then describe it in VHDL or Verilog and synthesise it.

concepts.text: Worked GCD example. The program above becomes an FSMD with roughly eight states: state 1 waits while go_i is 0; state 2 loads x from x_i; state 3 loads y from y_i; state 4 tests x != y and exits to the output state if false; state 5 tests x < y; state 6 performs y = y - x; state 7 performs x = x - y; both return to state 4; state 8 writes d_o = x and returns to state 1. The datapath needs registers x, y and d, two subtractors (or one shared), a not-equal comparator, a less-than comparator, and 2-to-1 multiplexers in front of x and y to choose between the external input and the subtractor output. The controller is the same eight-state FSM with actions replaced by control signals x_sel, y_sel, x_ld, y_ld, d_ld and conditions replaced by status signals x_neq_y and x_lt_y.
Optimizing the Custom Single-Purpose Processor
Optimising the original program (the largest gains come first):
items: Analyse the algorithm: repeated subtraction for GCD needs up to max(x, y) iterations, while the Euclidean form using a modulo operation (x = x mod y, then swap) needs only about log(max) iterations, trading a costlier operation per step for far fewer steps.
Remove redundant operations and variables, reuse computed values and choose data widths no larger than needed.
Bear in mind the hardware cost of each operation: a modulo or divide needs a large slow unit, a subtract is small, a shift is almost free.

concepts.text: Optimising the FSMD:
items: Merge states: two consecutive states with no data dependency (x = x_i and y = y_i) can be done in one state; a state whose only purpose is to test a condition can be merged with the next; constant assignments can be folded.
Separate states: an operation too slow for one cycle (a multiply) is split into several states so the clock can stay fast.
Schedule: reorder independent operations to shorten the number of cycles along the critical loop.

concepts.text: Optimising the datapath and the FSM:
items: Functional-unit sharing (allocation and binding): the two subtractors of the GCD datapath become one subtractor with multiplexers on its inputs, because y - x and x - y are never computed in the same state.
Register sharing: variables whose lifetimes do not overlap can share a register; unused multiplexers are removed.

State encoding: binary encoding uses the fewest flip-flops, one-hot uses one flip-flop per state but simpler, faster next-state logic, Gray encoding reduces switching; encoding tools search for the smallest logic.
State minimisation: merge states that are equivalent (same outputs and same next states for every input) using an implication table or partitioning.

rows: Better algorithm, fewer operations, cheaper operations
Functional-unit sharing, register sharing, mux removal, pipelining, parallel units
Pipelining, parallelism, hardware sharing, clock gating of idle registers

concepts.text: Going Deeper: From Program to Optimised GCD Processor

Vahid's conversion of a program into an FSMD is mechanical, with one template for each kind of statement. An assignment becomes one state that holds that action. A loop becomes a condition state whose true branch enters the body and whose false branch leads to a join state, and the last state of the body returns to the condition state. An if-else becomes a condition state with one path per branch, all paths ending in a join state. Applying the templates literally produces many states that do no work, which is exactly what FSMD optimisation later removes.

Worked example 1: GCD program -> FSMD with Vahid's templates
1    : while(1) test (always true)        -> 2
2    : go_i = 0 -> 2 ;  go_i = 1         -> 2-J
2-J  : join                               -> 3
3    : x = x_i                            -> 4
4    : y = y_i                            -> 5
5    : x != y -> 6 ;  x = y              -> 5-J
6    : x < y  -> 7 ;  x >= y             -> 8
7    : y = y - x -> 6-J      8 : x = x - y -> 6-J
6-J  : join -> 5             5-J : join -> 9
9    : d_o = x -> 1-J        1-J : join -> 1
Total 13 states: binary needs ceil(log2 13) = 4 flip-flops, one-hot needs 13

Optimising this FSMD removes every state that does no useful work. State 1 tests the constant 1, so it goes, and states 2 and 2-J merge into one wait state. States 3 and 4 merge because x = x_i and y = y_i do not depend on each other, and the tests x != y and x < y merge into a single three-way decision in state 5. The join states 5-J, 6-J and 1-J disappear because their transitions can be taken directly from the states before them (5-J's exit from the decision state, 6-J's return from states 7 and 8, and 1-J's return from state 9), leaving six states: wait, load, decide, y = y - x, x = x - y and output. Each loop iteration now costs 2 clock cycles instead of 4.

Worked example 2: clock cycles for x_i = 27, y_i = 12 (one state = one cycle)
(27,12) -> (15,12) -> (3,12) -> (3,9) -> (3,6) -> (3,3)    s = 5 subtractions
Unoptimised, from state 3 up to state 9 inclusive:
  states 3,4 = 2  +  s x (5, 6, 7 or 8, 6-J) = 4s  +  final 5, 5-J, 9 = 3
  cycles = 4s + 5 = 25
Optimised, from the merged load state up to the output state:
  load = 1  +  s x (5, 7 or 8) = 2s  +  final 5, 9 = 2
  cycles = 2s + 3 = 13          saving = 12 cycles (48%)

The controller is a state register plus combinational logic. Its inputs are the n_s present-state bits and the n_i status and external inputs, and its outputs are the n_s next-state bits and the n_o control signals. Written as a truth table it therefore has 2^(n_s + n_i) rows, which is also the number of words if the logic is stored in a ROM. For the unoptimised GCD controller, with 4 state bits, inputs go_i, x_neq_y and x_lt_y and outputs x_sel, y_sel, x_ld, y_ld and d_ld, that is 128 words of 9 bits; real designs minimise the table with don't-cares instead of storing it whole.

concepts.plainText: ROM bits = 2^(n_s + n_i) x (n_s + n_o); select lines of a k-input multiplexer = ceil(log2 k)

rows: Deeper next-state and output logic; several bits can toggle per transition
Simple, fast logic: each output is an OR of state bits
Most flip-flops; 8179 of the 8192 codes are unused
Only one bit changes between consecutive states, lowering switching power
Helps only when transitions follow the code sequence

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: should the two GCD subtractors be shared?
Area (gate equivalents): SUB = 40, 8-bit 2-to-1 MUX = 24
  unshared: 2 x SUB = 80          shared: SUB + 2 x MUX = 40 + 48 = 88
Delay: unshared T = tcq + tsub + tmux + tsu = 1 + 6 + 1 + 0.5 = 8.5 ns
       shared   T = 8.5 + 1 (input mux)                   = 9.5 ns
Verdict: sharing a small 8-bit subtractor costs area AND speed here;
         sharing pays off for large units such as multipliers or dividers.
Common mistakes when designing and optimising custom processors:
items: Counting one-hot flip-flops as ceil(log2 N): one-hot needs N flip-flops, binary needs ceil(log2 N).
Merging dependent assignments: in x = a + b; y = x + 1 the second statement needs the new x, but a merged state would read the old one.
Sharing one functional unit between two operations in the same state, which both need it in the same clock cycle.
Adding the delays of separate register-to-register paths: the clock period is set by the single longest path, not by their sum.
Forgetting the extra states, and therefore extra cycles, when a slow operation is separated into several states.
Treating the FSMD as the controller: the controller FSM exists only after the datapath has been built.

concepts.text: For state-count questions apply the templates literally: one state per assignment, a condition state plus a join state for each loop and each if-else. Then count flip-flops as ceil(log2 N) for binary and N for one-hot. For GCD cycle counts, first trace the operand pairs to find the number of subtractions s, then use 4s + 5 (unoptimised) or 2s + 3 (optimised).

formulas.plainText: Minimum state-register bits = ceil(log2 of number of states)
Clock period >= clock-to-Q delay + longest combinational delay + setup time
Execution time = number of controller cycles x clock period

notes.text: Moore: outputs depend on state only, so outputs are on the state circles. Mealy: outputs depend on state and inputs, so outputs are written on the transition arrows. A Mealy machine can usually do the job with fewer states.

An FSMD is not the finished controller. The controller FSM is obtained only after the datapath is built, by replacing each FSMD action with control signals and each condition with a status signal from the datapath.

Sharing a functional unit saves area but adds multiplexers and may lengthen the critical path; adding parallel units or pipelining does the reverse. Every optimisation trades one design metric against another.

concepts.text: Basic Architecture

A general-purpose processor is a programmable digital system built for a wide variety of applications rather than one task: the manufacturer sells the same chip to many customers, spreading its NRE cost, and each customer supplies a program. For the embedded designer this gives low NRE, high flexibility, short time-to-market and low unit cost at small volumes, at the price of higher power and lower performance than a custom design because the general datapath carries hardware the program may never use. Internally every general-purpose processor consists of a datapath, a control unit and memory connected by buses.
Datapath: the part that manipulates data:
items: Arithmetic logic unit (ALU) performing add, subtract, AND, OR, shift and compare, and producing status flags (zero, carry, overflow, sign).
Registers: a small number of fast storage locations (general-purpose registers and the accumulator) holding operands and results.
Internal buses that move data between registers, the ALU and the memory interface; the bit width N (8, 16, 32 or 64) of the datapath usually fixes the word size of registers, buses and ALU.

concepts.text: Control unit and memory:
items: Program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction; instruction register (IR) holds the instruction just fetched.
Controller: an FSM (hardwired) or a microprogram that decodes the IR and sequences the datapath, memory and PC through each instruction.

Memory holds both the program (instructions) and the data. Princeton (von Neumann) architecture uses one memory and one bus for both; Harvard architecture uses separate instruction and data memories so a fetch and a data access can overlap, common in microcontrollers and DSPs.

Cache: small fast SRAM near the processor that keeps recently used instructions and data; most processors have separate instruction and data caches, forming a hierarchy of registers, cache, main memory and secondary storage.

concepts.text: Operation
Instruction execution: the processor repeats the instruction cycle for each instruction:
items: Fetch: read the instruction at the PC address into the IR and increment the PC.
Decode: the controller determines the operation and the operands required.
Fetch operands: read operands from registers or memory into the ALU inputs.
Execute: the ALU or other datapath unit performs the operation.
Store results: write the result back to a register or memory; branch instructions instead update the PC.

concepts.text: Pipelining overlaps these stages like an assembly line: while one instruction executes, the next is decoded and a third is fetched, so a k-stage pipeline can approach k times the throughput of a non-pipelined processor once full, though branches and data dependencies (hazards) cause stalls. Superscalar processors go further by fetching and issuing several instructions per cycle to multiple ALUs with dynamic hardware scheduling. VLIW (very long instruction word) processors also execute several operations per cycle, but the compiler packs them statically into one wide instruction, which keeps the hardware simple and is popular in DSPs.

concepts.plainText: Pipeline speedup S = n k / (k + n - 1) for n instructions on k stages

concepts.text: Programmer's View
What the programmer sees (the instruction-set architecture):
items: Instruction set grouped as data transfer (MOV, LOAD, STORE, PUSH, POP), arithmetic and logic (ADD, SUB, MUL, AND, OR, XOR, shift, compare) and control flow (JMP, conditional branch, CALL, RET, interrupt return).
Program memory space and data memory space: with an n-bit address the processor can reach 2^n locations; program code, constants, stack and heap are laid out inside these spaces.
Registers visible to software: general-purpose registers, the PC, stack pointer (SP) and status or flag register; special-function registers configure peripherals in microcontrollers.
Programs may be written in assembly language, one mnemonic per machine instruction, or in a structured language such as C that a compiler translates into many instructions.

rows: Inside the instruction itself as a constant
In the register named by the instruction
In memory at the address held in a register
In memory at the address given in the instruction
The instruction gives a memory address that holds the operand's address

concepts.text: I/O from the programmer's side is either memory-mapped, where peripheral registers occupy addresses in the normal memory space and ordinary load and store instructions access them, or standard (port-mapped), where special IN and OUT instructions address a separate I/O space. Interrupts let a peripheral suspend the current program: the processor finishes the current instruction, saves the PC, jumps to the interrupt service routine at the address given in the vector table, and returns with an interrupt-return instruction; the programmer writes the ISR and enables the interrupt through control registers. An operating system, when present, adds process scheduling, memory management, device drivers and system calls; many small embedded systems run without one and use a simple polling loop or a lightweight RTOS.
Development Environment

Embedded software is written and compiled on a development processor (the host PC) but executed on the target processor, so the tools are cross-tools. The design flow is: write assembly or C source files; the assembler or compiler translates each into an object file; the linker combines object files and libraries into a single executable image with resolved addresses; the image is tested on an instruction-set simulator, a development board or through an in-circuit emulator under a debugger; finally the image is programmed into the target's Flash or ROM. Integrated development environments bundle all of these with an editor and project manager.

rows: Translates assembly mnemonics into machine code object files, resolving labels and symbols
Translates a high-level language such as C into assembly or machine code, with optimisation for size or speed
Combines object files and libraries, assigns final addresses and produces the executable image (HEX/ELF)
Lets the programmer set breakpoints, single-step, and inspect registers and memory of a running program
Software on the host that models the target processor cycle by cycle so code can run before hardware exists
Hardware that replaces or attaches to the target processor and gives real-time, full-speed debugging in the real system
Ready-made board with the target processor, memory and I/O for early hardware testing and prototyping

concepts.text: Application-specific versus general-purpose, and how to select a processor:
items: Application-specific processors (ASIPs, custom hardware) win on performance, power and unit cost at high volume; general-purpose processors win on NRE, flexibility, tool availability and time-to-market.

Selection metrics: clock frequency and MIPS or benchmark scores (Dhrystone, EEMBC), datapath width, on-chip memory and peripherals, power and voltage range, package size, unit cost and volume pricing, quality of compilers, debuggers and vendor support.
A raw MIPS number is not comparable across architectures because instructions do different amounts of work; use benchmarks that resemble the actual application.
Match the processor to the task: a general-purpose 32-bit core for control-heavy software, a DSP for signal processing, a microcontroller for cheap I/O-centric control.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Inside a General-Purpose Processor

Vahid and Givargis build a general-purpose processor as if it were a single-purpose processor whose one job is to execute instructions. Its controller is an FSMD with a Fetch state (IR ← M[PC], PC ← PC + 1), a Decode state that branches on the opcode, and one or more execute states for each instruction, all returning to Fetch; the control unit holds the PC and IR, while the datapath holds a register file and an ALU connected to memory. Because each state lasts one clock cycle, an instruction takes as many cycles as the states it visits, and the clock period must cover the slowest register-to-register path in any state, which is usually the memory access.

rows: If Rn = 0 then PC ← PC + rel

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: total = 10 + 9 + ... + 1 on the simple instruction set
0       MOV R0, #0     ; total = 0
1       MOV R1, #10    ; i = 10
2       MOV R2, #1     ; constant 1
3       MOV R3, #0     ; constant 0
4 Loop: JZ  R1, Next   ; leave when i = 0
5       ADD R0, R1     ; total += i
6       SUB R1, R2     ; i--
7       JZ  R3, Loop   ; always jumps, since R3 = 0
Executed: 4 MOV + 11 x JZ R1 + 10 x (ADD, SUB, JZ R3) = 45 instructions
At 3 cycles each (Fetch, Decode, one execute state) = 135 cycles
At 50 MHz: 135 x 20 ns = 2.7 µs, and R0 = 55

An issue width w sets the best-case CPI at 1/w, but real code rarely reaches it: an instruction cannot issue in the same cycle as one it depends on, so superscalar hardware checks register dependences every cycle, and an in-order core issues only the older instruction of a dependent pair. A VLIW processor moves that work to the compiler, which fills each long word with independent operations and pads the empty slots with NOPs; the hardware is simpler and uses less power, but the code grows and binaries are tied to one machine's slot count and latencies. Branches hurt every pipeline: without prediction, a taken branch resolved at the end of stage s discards the s − 1 instructions fetched behind it.

concepts.plainText: Cycles for N independent instructions on a w-issue, k-stage pipeline = (k − 1) + ceil(N / w); w = 1 gives the scalar pipeline

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: 40 independent instructions, 5 stages (k = 5)
Non-pipelined, 1 cycle per stage : 40 x 5          = 200 cycles
Scalar pipeline                  : (5 - 1) + 40    = 44 cycles
2-issue superscalar              : (5 - 1) + 40/2  = 24 cycles
One taken branch resolved in stage 4 (scalar): 44 + 3 = 47 cycles
VLIW, 4 slots x 32 bits, 14 operations packed into 5 words:
  slots = 20, NOPs = 20 - 14 = 6 (30 %)
  code  = 5 x 16 bytes = 80 bytes, against 14 x 4 = 56 bytes on a scalar RISC

To the programmer memory is an array of bytes, but three details decide whether code is correct and fast. Byte order: a little-endian processor (x86, most ARM systems) stores the least significant byte of a word at the lowest address and a big-endian one the most significant byte, which matters whenever words are read through byte pointers or sent over a link. Alignment: compilers pad structures so that each field sits at a multiple of its own size, so a peripheral register's offset in a struct overlay is counted in bytes, including padding. Locality: the cache is invisible to the instruction set, yet a loop that walks a row-major array column by column can need a new cache block on every access, while the row-by-row loop misses only once per block.

A typical assembler makes two passes: pass 1 steps a location counter through the source, adding each instruction's size and entering every label's address in a symbol table, and pass 2 emits the machine code, now able to fill in forward references. Object files are relocatable, so the linker places each section at its final address (rounding up for alignment), adds that base to every relocatable reference and writes an image such as ELF or Intel HEX, whose records end in a checksum that the device programmer verifies. An ISS gives full controllability and observability but runs slowly and without the real environment, whereas an in-circuit emulator or on-chip debug logic reached over JTAG or SWD runs the real chip at full speed; software breakpoints patch a break instruction into writable memory, so code in ROM needs hardware breakpoint comparators.

Worked example 3: choosing a processor (all candidates share one ISA)
Workload: 0.9 M instructions every 10 ms, processor load at most 75 %
Required rate = 0.9 M / 10 ms = 90 MIPS; 90 / 0.75 = 120 MIPS
X: 300 MHz, CPI 2.0 -> 150 MIPS  meets, $4.20
Y: 200 MHz, CPI 1.5 -> 133 MIPS  meets, $3.10
Z: 250 MHz, CPI 2.5 -> 100 MIPS  fails despite its clock
Choose Y, the cheapest candidate that meets the requirement
Across different ISAs use benchmarks instead of native MIPS:
DMIPS = Dhrystones per second / 1757, e.g. 1,405,600 / 1757 = 800 DMIPS

Common slips: a loop that runs n times executes its exit test n + 1 times; the k − 1 fill cycles are added once, not divided by the issue width; NOP slots of a VLIW word still occupy program memory; a memory-mapped register's address is base plus its byte offset including padding, not base plus its field number; an n-bit program counter that addresses instruction words reaches 2^n words, i.e. 2^n times the word size in bytes; and native MIPS figures compare fairly only between processors with the same instruction set.

An instruction-set simulator runs on the host and models the target in software; an in-circuit emulator is hardware plugged into the real target system. Do not swap the two when asked which one runs at full speed on real I/O.

Harvard architecture is standard in microcontrollers such as the 8051 and AVR and in DSPs; Princeton (von Neumann) is standard in PCs and in the 8085 and 8086. Many modern processors are Princeton at the main memory but Harvard at the cache level (separate instruction and data caches).

concepts.text: Where ASIPs Sit

An application-specific instruction-set processor (ASIP) is a programmable processor whose instruction set, datapath and peripherals are tailored to one class of applications, for example signal processing, control, graphics or packet handling. Programs are still written and loaded as software, but custom instructions (such as a single-cycle multiply-accumulate) and special functional units let the application run faster and with less power than on a general-purpose processor, while the design remains far more flexible than a custom single-purpose processor. The price is higher NRE than buying a general-purpose chip, because the ASIP and its compiler, assembler and simulator must be developed; digital signal processors, microcontrollers and graphics processing units are the common examples.
Microcontrollers
A microcontroller (MCU) is an ASIP for embedded control: a whole computer on one chip.
items: On-chip resources: CPU, program Flash, SRAM, sometimes EEPROM, plus peripherals such as timers and counters, PWM generators, ADC and DAC, UART, SPI and I2C interfaces, GPIO ports, a watchdog timer and an interrupt controller.
Instruction set tuned for control: bit set, clear and test instructions on single I/O pins, direct access to special-function registers, short branch offsets.
Low cost (from a fraction of a dollar), low power with sleep and idle modes, small packages, wide supply-voltage range and no external memory chips.
Programmed in C or assembly, often without any operating system; the reset vector starts a main loop or a small RTOS.

rows: 4 KB ROM, 128 B RAM, 4 x 8-bit ports, 2 timers, UART, 5 interrupt sources
32 KB Flash, 2 KB SRAM, 1 KB EEPROM, 16 MHz, 10-bit ADC, PWM; the Arduino Uno chip
Nested vectored interrupt controller, low-power modes, M4 adds DSP instructions and optional FPU; used in STM32, nRF, LPC
Few instructions, on-chip Flash, ADC, timers, cheap and popular for small products

concepts.text: Digital Signal Processors

A digital signal processor (DSP) is an ASIP for algorithms that operate on streams of samples: FIR and IIR filtering, FFT, correlation, audio and video codecs, modems and motor control. These algorithms are dominated by the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation applied over long loops, so DSPs provide a hardware MAC unit that multiplies and adds in a single cycle with a wide accumulator to avoid overflow. They use a Harvard or modified Harvard architecture with several buses so that an instruction and two data operands can be fetched in one cycle, address generators with circular (modulo) addressing for delay-line buffers and bit-reversed addressing for FFT, zero-overhead hardware loops, saturating arithmetic and often VLIW or SIMD execution of several MACs per cycle.

concepts.plainText: FIR filter: y[n] = sum over k of h[k] x[n-k], one MAC per tap

concepts.text: Fixed-point versus floating-point DSPs:
items: Fixed-point (16- or 24-bit): smaller, cheaper and lower power; the programmer must scale data to avoid overflow and manage precision (e.g. Q15 format holds values in the range -1 to just under +1 with a resolution of 2^-15). Examples: TI TMS320C5000 and C2000, ADI Blackfin.
Floating-point (32-bit): wide dynamic range, easier programming and porting of algorithms, higher cost and power. Examples: TI TMS320C67x, ADI SHARC.
Many modern chips mix a general-purpose core with a DSP core or DSP instructions (ARM Cortex-M4/M7, application processors with SIMD extensions).

concepts.text: Less-General ASIPs and Implementation Choices

Beyond MCUs and DSPs there are ASIPs built for narrower domains. Network processors (Intel IXP, Cavium Octeon, Marvell) handle packet classification, forwarding, checksum and CRC computation and queue management with many small multithreaded processing engines and table-lookup hardware, at wire speed. Graphics processing units run thousands of threads in SIMD fashion for pixel and matrix work, media processors accelerate video codecs, and crypto engines implement AES and RSA. Configurable processor cores such as Tensilica Xtensa or ARC let a designer add custom instructions and generate a matching compiler automatically, which lowers the NRE that normally limits ASIP use.

rows: High per device, flat with volume
None; a change needs a new mask set
Low volume, prototypes, designs that will change

concepts.text: Choosing between an MCU, a DSP and a general-purpose processor for a task:
items: Control-oriented work with many I/O pins, timers and interrupts, modest computation and tight cost or power: microcontroller.
Repetitive arithmetic on sampled data such as filtering, FFT, audio, modem or motor-current loops: DSP (or an MCU with DSP extensions if the load is light).
Large, changing software with an operating system, networking stacks, file systems and user interfaces: general-purpose 32/64-bit processor, often with an MCU or DSP alongside.
Extreme performance or power at very high volume with a fixed function: custom single-purpose hardware in an ASIC, prototyped on an FPGA.

concepts.text: IC technology is independent of processor type: any of the three processor types can be implemented in full-custom VLSI (every transistor and wire placed by hand for the best performance, size and power at the highest NRE), in semi-custom ASIC technology (gate arrays with prefabricated transistors and custom metal layers, or standard cells assembled from a library), or in a programmable logic device (PLA and PAL for small logic, FPGA for large designs) that needs no fabrication at all. An ASIP is usually bought as a fabricated chip, but a soft-core ASIP such as a configurable RISC or MicroBlaze/NIOS can also be synthesised into an FPGA next to custom hardware.
Going Deeper: Inside MCUs and DSPs

An ASIP designer starts by profiling the target applications, finds the few operations that dominate run time and turns each into a single instruction backed by its own hardware. On a general-purpose RISC one FIR tap costs about seven instructions: two loads, a multiply, an add, two pointer updates and a loop test and branch. A DSP performs the same tap with one MAC instruction whose two operand fetches and pointer updates happen in parallel in the same cycle, so both time and energy per result fall because far fewer instructions are fetched and decoded. The price is that code outside the chosen domain gains nothing, and the compiler, assembler and debugger must all understand the special instructions.

Modified Harvard with two or more data buses
Von Neumann view; split L1 instruction and data caches

concepts.text: A Q15 number stores the fraction x as the 16-bit integer round(x × 2^15), so its range is −1 to 1 − 2^−15. Multiplying two Q15 integers gives a Q30 product in 32 bits with two sign bits; shifting it right by 15 returns a Q15 result, while DSP hardware in fractional mode shifts left by one to form Q31 and keeps the upper half. Addition needs no shift but can leave the range, so DSPs saturate, clamping to 7FFFH or 8000H instead of wrapping round to the wrong sign. The only product that overflows is −1 × −1 = +1, and a 40-bit accumulator holding 32-bit products has 8 guard bits, so sums of up to 2^8 times full scale fit before the final rounding and saturation.

DSP address generators update pointers in parallel with the arithmetic. With circular (modulo) addressing the pointer follows p ← base + ((p − base + step) mod L), so the samples of a filter delay line of length L never have to be shifted; bit-reversed addressing reverses the log2 N index bits so that radix-2 FFT results can be read out in natural order. A zero-overhead loop keeps a loop counter and the loop start and end addresses in hardware registers: when the program counter reaches the end address the sequencer jumps back and decrements the counter without executing any instruction. With a one-cycle MAC body and a three-cycle software decrement, test and branch, a 64-tap loop drops from 256 to 64 cycles.

Selecting a processor, and when to add a co-processor:
items: Start from the workload: control and I/O with modest arithmetic points to an MCU, continuous arithmetic on sampled data to a DSP (compared in MMACS), and large, changing software with an OS to a general-purpose processor.

Then check the peripheral mix, memory size, active and sleep power, unit cost, tool chain and RTOS support, and long-term availability; for battery products compare energy per task, E = P × t, not power alone.

A co-processor is a separate execution unit that the host CPU drives through special instructions or memory-mapped command registers, such as the 8087 floating-point unit beside the 8086, an AES engine or a GPU; the host keeps control of the program.
A co-processor speeds up only the fraction f of run time that it handles, so the overall gain follows Amdahl's law below.

concepts.plainText: Overall speedup S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/k), where f is the accelerated fraction of run time and k is the co-processor's speedup on that fraction

notes.text: Key DSP features to recall: single-cycle hardware MAC, Harvard architecture with multiple buses, circular and bit-reversed addressing, zero-overhead loops and saturating arithmetic. Key MCU features: everything on one chip, bit-level I/O instructions, low cost and low power.

ASIP and ASIC are different things. An ASIP is a programmable processor with a domain-specific instruction set; an ASIC is an IC technology (a chip fabricated for one customer) in which any processor type, or pure custom logic, can be built.

In embedded-system terminology a GPU or a network processor is still an ASIP, because it runs software but its instruction set is tuned to one class of computation. Only hard-wired logic with no instruction stream counts as a single-purpose processor.

concepts.text: Multiprogramming, Multitasking and Multiprocessing

rows: Several programs in memory; CPU switches when one waits for I/O
CPU rapidly switched among tasks so they appear concurrent
Tasks run truly in parallel on two or more processors/cores
Several threads of one process scheduled concurrently

concepts.text: In cooperative (non-pre-emptive) multitasking a task keeps the CPU until it voluntarily yields or blocks, so one misbehaving task can starve all others and response time depends on the longest task. In pre-emptive multitasking the kernel can take the CPU away at a tick or when a higher-priority task becomes ready, giving bounded response for high-priority work. Most RTOSes use priority-based pre-emptive scheduling, often with round robin among equal-priority tasks.
Scheduler, dispatcher and scheduling criteria:
items: Scheduler: decides which ready task runs next according to the policy.
Dispatcher: performs the context switch and jumps to the chosen task; its delay is dispatch latency.
Maximise CPU utilisation and throughput (tasks completed per unit time).
Minimise turnaround time, waiting time and response time.
Real-time criterion: meet every deadline (predictability over average performance).

concepts.text: Scheduling Algorithms

rows: Simple; convoy effect behind long jobs
Minimum average waiting time; may starve long jobs
Fixed time quantum in circular order
Fair; quantum too small raises switch overhead
Fixed priority: shorter period = higher priority

concepts.text: FCFS worked example: bursts P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3 ms arriving in that order give waiting times 0, 24 and 27 ms, an average of 17 ms. If the short jobs arrive first (P2, P3, P1) the waits become 0, 3 and 6 ms, average 3 ms; this gap is the convoy effect. SJF always picks the order that minimises average waiting time, e.g. bursts 6, 8, 7, 3 run as 3, 6, 7, 8 giving waits 0, 3, 9, 16 and an average of 7 ms.

Round robin worked example with quantum q = 4 ms on the same bursts 24, 3, 3: P1 runs 0 to 4, P2 4 to 7, P3 7 to 10, then P1 finishes 10 to 30. Waiting times are P1 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7 ms, average about 5.67 ms. A very large quantum turns RR into FCFS; a very small one wastes CPU on context switches.
Rate-Monotonic and Earliest Deadline First

concepts.plainText: U = sum(C_i/T_i) <= n(2^(1/n) - 1); tends to ln 2 = 0.693 as n grows

concepts.text: RMS check for three periodic tasks (C, T) = (1, 4), (2, 6) and (1, 10) ms: U = 0.25 + 0.333 + 0.10 = 0.683. The Liu and Layland bound for n = 3 is 3(2^(1/3) - 1) = 0.780. Since 0.683 <= 0.780 the set is guaranteed schedulable under RMS, with priorities T = 4 highest and T = 10 lowest. If U lies between the bound and 1 the test is inconclusive and response-time analysis is needed.

concepts.plainText: EDF: schedulable if U = sum(C_i/T_i) <= 1 (deadline = period)

concepts.text: Priority Inversion

Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority task H blocks on a resource (mutex) held by a low-priority task L, and a medium-priority task M, which does not need the resource, pre-empts L. H is then effectively delayed by M for an unbounded time. A famous case is the 1997 Mars Pathfinder resets, fixed by enabling priority inheritance on a mutex.
Remedies for priority inversion:
items: Priority inheritance: L temporarily inherits H's priority while holding the resource, so M cannot pre-empt it.
Priority ceiling protocol: each resource has a ceiling equal to the highest priority of any task using it; a task locking it runs at the ceiling, which also prevents deadlock between such resources.
Keep critical sections short and avoid sharing resources across widely different priorities.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Scheduling Calculations and Schedulability

Every scheduling calculation starts from a Gantt chart and then uses four measures per task: completion time CT, turnaround time TAT = CT - arrival time, waiting time WT = TAT - CPU burst, and response time = first start - arrival time. State the tie-break rule (usually earlier arrival, then lower index) and, for round robin, where a new arrival joins the queue; the usual textbook convention is that a task arriving at the same instant a quantum expires is queued ahead of the pre-empted task. A pre-emptive policy is re-evaluated at every arrival and completion, a non-pre-emptive one only when the running task finishes or blocks.

Worked example 1: SRTF (pre-emptive SJF), no I/O, times in ms
Task  Arrival  Burst
P1    0        8
P2    1        4
P3    2        9
P4    3        5
Gantt: | P1 0-1 | P2 1-5 | P4 5-10 | P1 10-17 | P3 17-26 |
t = 1: P2 (4) is shorter than P1's remaining 7, so P1 is pre-empted
WT = CT - AT - burst: P1 17-0-8 = 9    P2 5-1-4 = 0
                      P3 26-2-9 = 15   P4 10-3-5 = 2
Average WT = 26/4 = 6.5 ms (non-pre-emptive SJF gives 7.75 ms)

concepts.plainText: R_i = C_i + B_i + sum over higher-priority tasks j of ceil(R_i / T_j) x C_j; iterate from R_i = C_i + B_i

concepts.text: The Liu and Layland bound comes from the critical instant: a task's worst response occurs when it is released together with every higher-priority task, and n(2^(1/n) - 1) is the least upper bound: every set at or below it is schedulable, while just above it some unlucky choice of periods and execution times misses a deadline. The bound is sufficient but not necessary; for example, task sets with harmonic periods (each period divides the next) stay RM-schedulable right up to U = 1. Response-time analysis (RTA) is exact for fixed priorities with D <= T: start with R = C + B, recompute the interference from higher-priority tasks until the value stops changing, and the task is schedulable if that R <= D. B is the blocking caused by lower-priority tasks holding shared resources.

concepts.text: How long priority inversion lasts depends on the locking protocol. With no protocol, a high-priority task H that is blocked on a mutex also waits for every medium-priority task that pre-empts the holder, so its blocking has no fixed limit. Basic priority inheritance limits H's blocking to at most one critical section of each lower-priority task that shares a resource with it, but blocking can still chain through several holders and deadlock is still possible. The priority ceiling protocol, and its simpler immediate-ceiling form used in OSEK/AUTOSAR kernels, limits blocking to a single critical section and makes deadlock through nested locks impossible.
Deadlines, laxity and jitter:
items: Relative deadline D is measured from a job's release; the absolute deadline is d = release time + D, so job k of a task released first at t = 0 has d = (k - 1)T + D.
Laxity (slack) at time t is d - t - remaining execution; least-laxity-first runs the job with the smallest laxity, and a negative laxity means the deadline can no longer be met.
Release jitter is the variation in when a job actually becomes ready, for example up to one tick when periodic tasks are released by a 1 ms system tick.
Response (output) jitter is the spread of response times, R_max - R_min; control loops keep it small by sampling and actuating at the start of a high-priority task or inside a timer ISR.

concepts.plainText: Laxity = absolute deadline d - current time t - remaining execution time c_rem

concepts.text: Common slips: measuring waiting time from t = 0 instead of from arrival; letting a newly arrived job cut in under a non-pre-emptive policy; using ln 2 = 0.693 instead of the bound for the actual n; calling a set unschedulable just because U exceeds the RM bound, when that test is only sufficient; and applying U <= 1 to EDF when deadlines are shorter than periods, where a processor-demand test is needed instead.

For RM questions work in this order: compute U, compare it with n(2^(1/n) - 1) for the actual n, and if U lies between the bound and 1, run response-time analysis for each task from the highest priority down. For EDF with deadlines equal to periods, the single check U <= 1 decides the answer.

formulas.plainText: RMS bound: U <= n(2^(1/n) - 1)
As n grows the RMS bound tends to ln 2 = 0.693
EDF schedulability: U <= 1
Average waiting time = sum of waiting times / n

notes.text: Memorise RMS bounds: n = 1 gives 1.0, n = 2 gives 0.828, n = 3 gives 0.780, n = 4 gives 0.757, and the limit is 0.693.
The RMS bound is sufficient, not necessary: a task set with U above n(2^(1/n) - 1) but at most 1 may still be schedulable. U > 1 is never schedulable on one processor.
RMS is static (priorities fixed at design time from periods); EDF is dynamic (priorities change with each job's absolute deadline) and can use up to 100% of the CPU.

concepts.text: Race Conditions and Critical Sections

A race condition occurs when two or more tasks (or a task and an ISR) access shared data concurrently and the result depends on the timing of their execution. For example count++ compiles to load, add and store; if a task is pre-empted between load and store and another task also increments count, one update is lost. The code that touches shared data is a critical section and must execute with mutual exclusion.
Ways to protect a critical section in an embedded system:
items: Atomic operations: a single uninterruptible instruction (test-and-set, compare-and-swap, load-linked/store-conditional).
Disabling interrupts: simplest on a single core; keep it very short because it increases interrupt latency.
Scheduler lock: disables pre-emption but still allows ISRs to run.
Semaphores and mutexes: block the waiting task instead of busy-waiting.
A correct solution must give mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.

concepts.text: Semaphores and Mutexes

A semaphore (Dijkstra) is an integer counter with two atomic operations: P/wait/take decrements it and blocks the caller if no unit is available, and V/signal/give increments it and wakes a waiting task. A binary semaphore takes only 0 or 1 and is used for signalling events or simple locking. A counting semaphore is initialised to the number of identical resources (e.g. 5 buffers) and tracks how many remain.

rows: Only the locking task may unlock
Any task or ISR may give

concepts.text: Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions at once:
items: Mutual exclusion: a resource can be held by only one task.
Hold and wait: a task holds one resource while waiting for another.
No pre-emption: resources cannot be forcibly taken away.
Circular wait: a cycle of tasks each waiting for the next one's resource.
Prevention breaks one condition, e.g. always acquire locks in a fixed global order to prevent circular wait; use timeouts on takes.
