concepts.text: Device Drivers

A device driver is software that hides a peripheral's register-level details behind a standard interface (open, read, write, ioctl, close). Drivers are layered: the application calls an RTOS or OS API, which calls the device-independent driver layer, which calls the hardware-specific low-level driver or Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) that finally touches memory-mapped or port-mapped registers. Drivers also initialise the device, manage buffers and handle its interrupts.

rows: CPU repeatedly reads a status register
Device raises an interrupt when ready

concepts.text:
#define UART0_BASE  0x4000C000u
#define UART0_DR    (*(volatile uint32_t *)(UART0_BASE + 0x00))
#define UART0_FR    (*(volatile uint32_t *)(UART0_BASE + 0x18))
#define TXFF        (1u << 5)          /* transmit FIFO full */

void uart_putc(char c) {
    while (UART0_FR & TXFF) { }       /* poll status */
    UART0_DR = (uint32_t)c;           /* write data  */
}
ISR design, deferred work and reentrancy:
items: Keep ISRs short: acknowledge the device, move data to a buffer, then signal a task (semaphore/queue) to do the rest (deferred work, top half vs bottom half).
ISRs must never block, so they cannot take a mutex or wait on a queue.
volatile tells the compiler a register or ISR-shared variable can change outside program flow, so every access is really performed.
A reentrant function can be safely interrupted and called again: it uses only local variables/parameters or protects shared data, and calls only reentrant functions.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Semaphore Traces, Deadlock Handling and Driver Design

Textbooks keep semaphore values in two ways. In the RTOS convention the count never goes below zero: a take on a zero count puts the caller in a waiting queue, and a give with tasks waiting hands the unit straight to one of them without changing the count. In the Silberschatz blocking implementation, wait always decrements, so a value of -k means k tasks are waiting, and signal always increments and wakes one task if the result is still 0 or less. Both describe the same behaviour, so always state the convention when you write a trace.

Worked example 1: counting semaphore S = 2, four tasks, FIFO wake-up
Step       RTOS count  Silberschatz S  Waiting  Holding
A wait     1           1               -        A
B wait     0           0               -        A B
C wait     0           -1              C        A B
D wait     0           -2              C D      A B
A signal   0           -1              D        B C
B signal   0           0               -        C D
C signal   1           1               -        D
D signal   2           2               -        -

The order of the two waits in the producer matters. Waiting on empty before taking the lock means a producer that finds the buffer full sleeps without holding the lock, so the consumer can still get in and free a slot; reversing the order lets the producer sleep inside the critical section and deadlocks both tasks. The consumer mirrors the producer with wait(full), lock, remove at out, unlock and post(empty), and between operations empty + full = N.

concepts.plainText: count = (head - tail + N) mod N, head = next write slot, tail = next read slot; capacity N - 1 when one slot is kept empty

rows: Design so that one Coffman condition can never hold
Fixed global lock order, or request everything at once; may waste resources
Grant a request only if the system stays in a safe state
Banker's algorithm; needs every task's maximum claim in advance
Let deadlock happen, find a cycle in the wait-for graph, then abort or roll back a task
Periodic graph check; recovery loses work
Assume deadlock is rare and restart if it happens
Desktop OSes; a watchdog reset in embedded products

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: Banker's algorithm, one resource type, 10 units
Task  Allocated  Max  Need
A     3          7    4
B     2          4    2
C     2          6    4
Available = 10 - 7 = 3
B: need 2 <= 3 -> finishes, available 3 + 2 = 5
A: need 4 <= 5 -> finishes, available 8; C: need 4 <= 8 -> finishes
Safe sequence B, A, C, so the state is safe
Request: A asks for 2 more -> available 1; needs A 2, B 2, C 4
No task can finish with 1 unit -> unsafe, so A must wait
Rules for ISRs and deferred work:
items: Acknowledge or clear the interrupt source early; otherwise a level-triggered request fires again as soon as the ISR returns.
Do only the urgent part (read the data register, time-stamp, move bytes to a buffer) and defer the rest to a task or bottom half.
Use only non-blocking from-ISR kernel calls to give semaphores, post to queues or set event bits, and request a context switch on exit if a higher-priority task was woken.
Protect data shared with a task by briefly masking that interrupt inside the task, because the ISR cannot wait for a lock.
Keep interrupt-disabled sections short: the longest one adds directly to the worst-case latency of every interrupt.

concepts.text: A typical interrupt-driven UART driver keeps a receive ring buffer and a transmit ring buffer. The receive ISR moves each byte from the data register into the RX buffer and gives a semaphore, so read() blocks only when the buffer is empty. write() copies bytes into the TX buffer and enables the transmit-empty interrupt, whose ISR sends one byte per interrupt and disables itself when the buffer runs dry. A polled driver instead checks the status register in a loop or periodic task; it is simpler and more deterministic, but an event can wait up to one full polling period before it is noticed.

Classic synchronisation bugs: taking the lock before the counting semaphore in a producer; giving a mutex from an ISR or from a task that does not own it; using a binary semaphore where several events can arrive before the task runs, so events are lost; leaving the transmit-empty interrupt enabled with nothing to send; and returning from an error path without releasing a lock.

For any semaphore trace, draw a table with one row per operation and columns for the value, the waiting queue and the holders, and say which convention you use. Check the answer with S = S0 - waits + signals: it always gives the final value in the negative-count convention, and in both conventions when no task is left waiting.

formulas.plainText: Semaphore value S = initial S0 - number of waits + number of signals (no task left blocked)
Fraction of CPU used by polling = time per poll x polls per second

notes.text: Mutex = ownership plus priority inheritance for locking; semaphore = signalling or counting, and it may be given from an ISR.
Forgetting volatile on a memory-mapped register or an ISR-shared flag lets the optimiser cache the value in a register, so a polling loop may never see the hardware change.
Deadlock is impossible if any one of the four Coffman conditions is broken; a fixed global lock order is the most common practical fix.

concepts.text: Control System Vocabulary
Basic terms used in every control loop:
items: Plant (process): the physical system being controlled, e.g. a room, motor or tank.
Controller: computes the control action from the error or the reference input.
Actuator: converts the controller output into physical action (heater, motor driver, valve).
Sensor (transducer): measures the output, e.g. thermistor, encoder, pressure sensor.
Setpoint (reference r): the desired value of the output.
Error e = r - y: difference between setpoint and measured output y.
Disturbance: an unwanted external input that changes the output (open window, load torque).

concepts.text: Open-Loop vs Closed-Loop

rows: None; output does not affect the control action
Output measured and compared with setpoint
Can oscillate or become unstable if badly tuned
Timer toaster, washing machine timer, traffic light on fixed timing
Thermostat, cruise control, servo motor, PID loops

concepts.text: Open-loop block diagram in words: reference input goes into the controller, then the actuator, then the plant, giving the output; nothing flows back. Closed-loop block diagram: the reference enters a summing junction, which subtracts the fed-back sensor signal to form the error; the error drives the controller G_c and plant G_p to give the output, and the sensor H feeds the output back to the summing junction. With negative feedback the loop continually acts to drive the error toward zero.

concepts.plainText: Closed-loop gain T = G / (1 + GH) for negative feedback

concepts.text: Performance Measures
Step-response and loop quality measures:
items: Stability: a bounded input gives a bounded output; the response settles instead of growing or oscillating forever.
Steady-state error: the error left after transients die out; for a unity-feedback type-0 system with a step input e_ss = 1/(1 + K_p).
Overshoot: how far the output goes beyond the setpoint, usually as a percentage.
Rise time: time to go from 10% to 90% of the final value.
Settling time: time to stay within a band (2% or 5%) of the final value.
Negative feedback reduces sensitivity to plant changes by the factor 1 + GH, at the cost of lower gain.

concepts.text: On-off (bang-bang) control is the simplest closed-loop controller: the actuator is fully on when the error is positive and fully off when it is negative. A household thermostat or refrigerator uses it with hysteresis (a dead band such as +/-0.5 °C) so the relay does not chatter around the setpoint. The output therefore oscillates in a small band rather than settling exactly.
P, PI and PID Control

concepts.latex: u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\,d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}
concepts.plainText: u(t) = Kp*e(t) + Ki*integral of e dt + Kd*de/dt

rows: Zero steady-state error with fair speed

concepts.text: Digital Control Loop
A microcontroller implements the loop once every sampling period T:
items: Sample the sensor through an ADC at a fixed rate driven by a timer interrupt or periodic RTOS task.
Compute error and the discrete control law, e.g. u[k] = Kp e[k] + Ki T sum(e) + Kd (e[k] - e[k-1])/T.
Output through a DAC or PWM to the actuator driver.
Choose T well below the plant's time constants (often 10 to 20 times faster); jitter in T degrades control, which is why control tasks get high RMS priority.
Clamp the output and stop integrating when saturated to avoid integral windup.

concepts.text: Worked thermostat example: setpoint 22 °C, measured temperature 19 °C, so e = 22 - 19 = 3 °C. With a proportional controller Kp = 10 % per °C the heater is driven at u = 10 x 3 = 30% power. As the room warms to 21 °C the error falls to 1 °C and power to 10%; a pure P controller leaves a small steady-state error because some error is needed to keep the heater on, and adding an integral term removes it.
Going Deeper: Feedback Analysis and Digital PID

The closed-loop gain follows from two equations read off the block diagram. The summing junction gives E = R − HC and the forward path gives C = G·E, so C = G(R − HC), which rearranges to C(1 + GH) = G·R and C/R = G/(1 + GH). With positive feedback the junction adds the fed-back signal, giving G/(1 − GH), which grows without limit as GH approaches 1. The product GH is the loop gain, and a disturbance D entering at the plant output is reduced by the same factor, appearing at the output as D/(1 + GH).

concepts.plainText: Sensitivity of the closed-loop gain T to the forward gain G: S = (dT/T)/(dG/G) = 1/(1 + GH)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: G = 200, H = 0.05  ->  loop gain GH = 10
T = 200 / (1 + 10)                          = 18.18
G falls 20 % to 160:  GH = 8,  T = 160 / 9  = 17.78
Change in T = (17.78 - 18.18) / 18.18       = -2.2 %  (open loop: -20 %)
Small-change estimate: S = 1/(1 + GH) = 0.091, 0.091 x 20 % = 1.8 %
Output disturbance of 30 rpm -> 30 / (1 + 10) = 2.7 rpm remains

With a proportional gain Kp driving a plant of DC gain Kplant in a unity-feedback loop, the loop gain is K = Kp·Kplant, the output settles at K/(1 + K) of the setpoint and the steady-state error is 1/(1 + K) of the step. The error cannot reach zero because the plant needs a non-zero drive and a P controller produces drive only from error; raising Kp shrinks the offset but increases overshoot and eventually threatens stability. Closing the loop around a first-order plant K/(τs + 1) also speeds it up: the closed-loop transfer function K/(τs + 1 + K) has time constant τ/(1 + K), and the 2% settling time is about four time constants. For example, τ = 15 s and K = 4 give a closed-loop time constant of 3 s, a settling time near 12 s and a final value of 0.8 of the setpoint.

rows: Overshoot rises; settling time changes little

concepts.text: Practical details used when tuning and implementing controllers:
items: Ziegler–Nichols ultimate-gain method: with I and D off, raise Kp until the loop oscillates steadily at gain Ku with period Pu, then set Kp = 0.6 Ku, Ti = Pu/2 and Td = Pu/8 for PID (P only: Kp = 0.5 Ku; PI: Kp = 0.45 Ku, Ti = Pu/1.2).
The standard and parallel PID forms are linked by Ki = Kp/Ti and Kd = Kp·Td, so a longer integral time Ti means weaker integral action.

On-off control with switching points L and H: heating time = (H − L)/heating rate and cooling time = (H − L)/cooling rate; a narrower band gives a smaller swing but more frequent switching and relay wear.
Integral windup: while the actuator is saturated the integral keeps growing and later causes a large overshoot, so the integral is clamped or integration is stopped during saturation.
Derivative kick: a setpoint step makes de/dt very large for one sample, so many controllers differentiate the measurement instead of the error and low-pass filter the D term to limit noise.

concepts.latex: \Delta u_k = K_p(e_k - e_{k-1}) + K_i T e_k + \frac{K_d}{T}(e_k - 2e_{k-1} + e_{k-2})
concepts.plainText: Velocity (incremental) PID: Δu[k] = Kp(e[k] − e[k−1]) + Ki·T·e[k] + (Kd/T)(e[k] − 2e[k−1] + e[k−2]), then u[k] = u[k−1] + Δu[k]

concepts.text: A continuous closed-loop system is stable when every root of its characteristic equation 1 + G(s)H(s) = 0, i.e. every closed-loop pole, has a negative real part and so lies in the left half of the s-plane. For G = K/(s(s + 6)) with unity feedback the equation is s² + 6s + K = 0: K = 5 gives real poles at −1 and −5, while K above 9 gives a complex pair with an oscillatory, overshooting response. A sampled loop is stable when its poles lie inside the unit circle; the plant y[k+1] = a·y[k] + b·u[k] under u[k] = Kp(r − y[k]) has the single pole a − b·Kp, so it is stable only while |a − b·Kp| < 1. Extra loop delay, such as a long sampling period or slow computation, adds phase lag and lowers the gain at which oscillation starts.

Common mistakes: using G/(1 + GH) for a positive-feedback loop; writing the step error of a P loop as 1/K instead of 1/(1 + K); forgetting the sampling period in the discrete integral (Ki·T·Σe) and derivative ((e[k] − e[k−1])/T) terms; quoting the integral time Ti or derivative time Td as if they were the gains Ki and Kd; and letting the integrator wind up while the actuator is saturated.

formulas.plainText: Closed-loop gain T = G / (1 + GH)

formulas.latex: u(t) = K_p e + K_i \int e\,dt + K_d \frac{de}{dt}
formulas.plainText: PID law u = Kp*e + Ki*integral(e dt) + Kd*de/dt
Steady-state error to a unit step, type-0 unity feedback: e_ss = 1/(1 + K_pos)

formulas.latex: u[k] = K_p e[k] + K_i T \sum_{j=0}^{k} e[j] + K_d \frac{e[k] - e[k-1]}{T}
formulas.plainText: Discrete PID: u[k] = Kp e[k] + Ki T sum e[j] + Kd (e[k] - e[k-1])/T

notes.text: Link each PID term to its job: P for speed, I for zero steady-state error, D for damping and reduced overshoot.
If GH is much greater than 1, T = G/(1 + GH) is approximately 1/H: the closed-loop gain depends mainly on the feedback sensor, not on the plant.
Feedback can destabilise a system: too much gain or too much loop delay causes oscillation, which is why closed-loop systems must be tuned and checked for stability.

concepts.text: Numbers Are Just Bit Patterns

A std_logic_vector is only a collection of bits with no numeric meaning. The standard package ieee.numeric_std adds two array types, unsigned (plain binary) and signed (2's complement), with arithmetic and comparison operators defined on them. The same bit pattern 1111 is 15 as unsigned and -1 as signed. The older std_logic_arith and std_logic_unsigned packages are vendor (Synopsys) packages, not IEEE standards, and should not be mixed with numeric_std.

rows: resize(x, m): zero-extends unsigned, sign-extends signed

concepts.text: Wraparound and Unsigned Overflow

In numeric_std, adding two n-bit unsigned values returns an n-bit result (the width of the larger operand), so any carry out of the MSB is silently discarded and the result wraps modulo 2^n. Unsigned overflow therefore means a carry out of the most significant bit. To capture it, extend the operands to n+1 bits with resize(a, n+1) or '0' & a before adding; the extra MSB of the sum is the carry.

concepts.plainText: S = (A + B) mod 2^n; Cout = 1 when A + B >= 2^n

concepts.text: Signed (2's Complement) Overflow

An n-bit signed value covers -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1, e.g. -128 to +127 for 8 bits. Overflow can occur only when both operands have the same sign and the result has the opposite sign; adding numbers of different signs can never overflow. Equivalently, overflow V is the XOR of the carry into the sign bit and the carry out of it. The carry out on its own means nothing for signed arithmetic.
Related representation issues:
items: Saturation vs wraparound: wraparound (default hardware behaviour) turns 127 + 1 into -128; saturating logic clamps to the maximum or minimum instead, preferred in DSP and audio.
Negation: -x = (not x) + 1; negating the most negative value (-128 in 8 bits) overflows back to -128.
Sign extension: resize on signed copies the MSB into the new bits (1010 becomes 11111010); on unsigned it fills with zeros.
integer vs unsigned: integer is at least 32-bit and has no wraparound; exceeding a declared range is a simulation error, whereas unsigned wraps silently.
Multiplication: an n-bit by m-bit product needs n + m bits, which numeric_std '*' returns automatically.

concepts.text: Fixed-point numbers store fractions in ordinary signed or unsigned vectors with an implied binary point. In Qm.f format there are m integer bits and f fraction bits, so the value is the integer reading divided by 2^f and the resolution is 2^-f. Adding requires aligned binary points; multiplying Qa.b by Qc.d gives a Q(a+c).(b+d) result that is usually truncated or rounded back. VHDL-2008 adds the ufixed and sfixed types in fixed_pkg for this purpose.
Worked Example: 4-bit 7 + 9

0111 + 1001 = 1 0000, with a carry generated at every bit position. Read as unsigned, 7 + 9 = 16 exceeds 15, so C_out = 1 and the 4-bit sum wraps to 0000; the add4 entity above would output sum = 0000, cout = '1'. Read as signed, 1001 is -7, so the operation is 7 + (-7) = 0: the operands have different signs, the carry into the MSB is 1 and the carry out is 1, so V = 1 XOR 1 = 0 and the result 0000 is correct.
Going Deeper: Widths, Overflow and Fixed Point

numeric_std never widens a sum on its own. For + and − the shorter operand is first extended (zero-extended for unsigned, sign-extended for signed) to the length of the longer one, and the result has that same length. An integer operand is converted to the vector's width with to_unsigned or to_signed, and a value that does not fit is truncated with a 'vector truncated' warning. Multiplication is the operator that grows: its result is as wide as both operands together, so a product can never overflow.

rows: Wraps modulo 2^8; the carry or borrow is lost
Sum of the widths; never overflows
a mod b, a rem b
One spare bit keeps the carry

concepts.latex: L(a \pm b) = \max(L_a, L_b), \quad L(a \times b) = L_a + L_b
concepts.plainText: len(a ± b) = max(La, Lb); len(a × b) = La + Lb

concepts.text: One spare bit is always enough to detect overflow. The sum of two n-bit signed numbers lies between −2^n and 2^n − 2, which fits in n + 1 bits, so sign-extending both operands to n + 1 bits makes the sum exact. The n-bit result is correct exactly when the top two bits of that exact sum are equal; if they differ, the n-bit result has overflowed. For unsigned operands the spare bit is simply the carry, and for a − b it is the borrow.

Worked example 1: 8-bit signed 100 + 50
a = +100  -> resize to 9 bits : 0 0110 0100
b =  +50  -> resize to 9 bits : 0 0011 0010
t = a + b (exact)              : 0 1001 0110 = +150
t(8) = 0, t(7) = 1  -> top two bits differ: overflow
wrapped 8-bit sum t(7 downto 0) = 1001 0110 = -106
sign-bit rule: a(7) = b(7) = 0 but s(7) = 1 -> V = 1
saturating output              : 0111 1111 = +127

-- a, b, y : signed(7 downto 0);  t : signed(8 downto 0)
t   <= resize(a, 9) + resize(b, 9);   -- exact sum, cannot overflow
ovf <= t(8) xor t(7);                  -- top two bits differ
y   <= "01111111" when t(8) = '0' and t(7) = '1' else   -- clamp at +127
       "10000000" when t(8) = '1' and t(7) = '0' else   -- clamp at -128
       t(7 downto 0);
-- simulated: (100, 50) -> y = 127, ovf = '1';  (-100, -50) -> y = -128, ovf = '1'
--            (100, -50) -> y = 50, ovf = '0';  (-128, -1) -> y = -128, ovf = '1'

Fixed-point multiplication needs one more bookkeeping step. If a and b are n-bit signed vectors with f fraction bits each, their 2n-bit product has 2f fraction bits. To return to n bits with f fraction bits, drop the lowest f bits and keep the next n, which is the slice p(n + f − 1 downto f). The bits above that slice must all equal its sign bit; otherwise the true result is out of range and should be saturated.

Worked example 2: 8-bit signed, 4 fraction bits (value = N / 16)
a = 0010 1000 ->  40 / 16 =  2.5
b = 1110 1100 -> -20 / 16 = -1.25
p = a * b (16 bits, 8 fraction bits) = -800 -> -800 / 256 = -3.125
p = 1111 1100 1110 0000
keep p(11 downto 4) = 1100 1110 = -50 -> -50 / 16 = -3.125
p(15 downto 11) = 11111 (all equal to the sign) -> no overflow
wrong slice p(7 downto 0) = 1110 0000 = -32 -> -2.0
Simulation behaviour that often surprises:
items: to_integer on a vector containing 'U', 'X', 'Z', 'W' or '-' returns 0 with a metavalue warning, while +, − and * return a vector of all 'X'.
A counter with no reset and no initial value starts at "UUUU", and cnt + 1 keeps it at "XXXX" for the whole run.
to_unsigned(300, 8) and to_signed(200, 8) keep only the low 8 bits (44 and −56) and print 'vector truncated'; to_unsigned(−1, 8) is a bound-check error because its argument is of subtype natural.
Assigning a result to a target of a different length is a run-time bound-check failure, never a silent truncation.
An integer subtype such as range 0 to 15 stops the simulation when it reaches 16, whereas unsigned(3 downto 0) wraps to 0 like the hardware.
Shrinking with resize keeps the low bits of an unsigned value, but for a signed value it keeps the sign bit plus the low bits.

concepts.text: Size first, then operate: widen the operands before + or − when you need the carry or the overflow flag, remember that * returns the sum of the widths, and use resize or a slice to fit a target, because a width mismatch on assignment stops the simulation instead of truncating.

formulas.plainText: V = Cout XOR (carry into MSB)
S = (A + B) mod 2^n (wraparound)

notes.text: numeric_std '+' does not widen its result: unsigned(3 downto 0) + unsigned(3 downto 0) is 4 bits, so the carry is lost unless you resize the operands to n+1 bits first.
Signed overflow rule: same-sign operands and a result of the opposite sign. Unsigned overflow: carry out of the MSB. Different-sign signed addition never overflows.
Use ieee.numeric_std for arithmetic; do not combine it with the non-standard std_logic_arith or std_logic_unsigned packages in the same unit.

concepts.text: Concurrent Statements for Combinational Logic

Statements written directly in an architecture body are concurrent: they all run in parallel and their order in the file does not matter. Each concurrent assignment behaves like a small process that re-evaluates whenever a signal on its right-hand side changes, which is exactly how combinational gates behave. Combinational logic such as AND/OR networks, multiplexers, decoders, adders and comparators is usually written this way.
Concurrent statement forms and typical circuits:
items: Simple assignment: y <= (a and b) or c; full adder: s <= a xor b xor cin; cout <= (a and b) or (cin and (a xor b));
Conditional assignment (when-else): has priority, like a chain of 2:1 muxes; used for priority encoders and decoders.
Selected assignment (with-select): one choice per value, like a true multiplexer; all choices must be covered, usually with others.
Comparator: gt <= '1' when a > b else '0'; with a, b of type unsigned.
for-generate replicates hardware (e.g. n full adders); if-generate includes hardware conditionally from a generic.

concepts.text:
-- 4-to-1 multiplexer (selected assignment)
with sel select
  y <= d0 when "00",
       d1 when "01",
       d2 when "10",
       d3 when others;
-- 2-to-4 decoder with enable (conditional assignment)
dec <= "0001" when en = '1' and a = "00" else
       "0010" when en = '1' and a = "01" else
       "0100" when en = '1' and a = "10" else
       "1000" when en = '1' else
       "0000";

Combinational logic can also be written as a process, but its sensitivity list must contain every signal read inside it (VHDL-2008 allows process (all)), and every output must be assigned on every path through the code. If some path leaves an output unassigned, the output must remember its old value, and synthesis infers a latch, which is almost never intended. Assign default values at the top of the process or cover every if/case branch.
Sequential Logic with Clocked Processes

Sequential logic is written as a process triggered by the clock. Inside, if rising_edge(clk) (or the older clk'event and clk = '1') marks the active edge, and every signal assigned under it becomes a flip-flop. A synchronous reset is tested inside the clock-edge branch, so only clk is in the sensitivity list; an asynchronous reset appears in the sensitivity list and is tested before the clock edge.

rows: At the next active clock edge
Filters reset glitches; needs a running clock
Works without a clock; release must be synchronised

concepts.text: Other common sequential blocks:
items: Register: a vector of D flip-flops, e.g. if en = '1' then r <= d; end if; inside the clocked branch.
Shift register: sr <= sr(2 downto 0) & din; shifts left by one bit each clock using concatenation.
Mod-N counter: reset the count to zero when it reaches N - 1 instead of letting it wrap at 2^n.
Clock divider: the MSB of an n-bit free-running counter toggles at f_clk / 2^n.

concepts.text: Finite State Machines

An FSM is coded with an enumerated state type, a clocked process holding the state register, and a case statement for next-state logic. In a Moore machine outputs depend only on the current state, so they change one clock after the input and are glitch-free. In a Mealy machine outputs depend on the state and the current inputs, so they react in the same cycle and often need fewer states. Synthesis chooses binary, Gray or one-hot state encoding.

concepts.plainText: flip-flops = ceil(log2 N) for binary encoding, N for one-hot

concepts.text: Going Deeper: From VHDL Code to Gates and Flip-Flops

Synthesis reads a process by asking, for every signal, when it is assigned. A signal assigned under if rising_edge(clk) becomes a flip-flop, one per bit, and all right-hand sides in that branch use the values from before the edge. In a combinational process, a signal that some path leaves unassigned must keep its value, so a latch is built. Within one run of a process the last assignment to a signal wins, which makes a default assignment at the top a simple way to cover every path.

rows: y <= a when s = '1' else b;
Choices are exclusive and must cover every value, usually with others
case in process (all), every output assigned
A path without an assignment gives a latch
rst must be in the sensitivity list
if en = '1' inside the clock branch
Not a latch: the flip-flop holds the value
Shifts left one place per edge

concepts.text:
Simulated trace (x changes just after each edge; cycle k lies between edges k and k+1)
cycle        :  1    2    3     4     5     6
x            :  1    0    1     0     1     1
Moore state  :  S0   S1   S10   S101  S10   S101
z_moore      :  0    0    0     1     0     1
z_mealy      :  0    0    1     0     1     0

The trace shows the defining difference between the two machines. The Mealy detector needs only the states none, 1 and 10, and raises z as soon as the final 1 is on its input, in cycles 3 and 5. The Moore detector needs a fourth state, 101 seen, and its output appears only after the edge that enters that state, one cycle later in cycles 4 and 6. Because the Moore output comes from the state register it is not disturbed by input changes, whereas input glitches pass straight through to a Mealy output.

rows: One clock after the input is sampled
In the same cycle as the input
z <= '1' when st = M10 and x = '1' else '0';

concepts.plainText: f_tick = f_clk / N; bits = ceil(log2 N) for a counter that counts 0 to N - 1

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: 1 kHz tick from a 50 MHz clock
N       = f_clk / f_tick = 50,000,000 / 1,000 = 50,000 states (count 0 .. 49,999)
bits    = ceil(log2 50,000) = 16   (2^15 = 32,768 < 50,000 <= 65,536 = 2^16)
tick    = '1' for one clock when cnt = N - 1 = 49,999
check   : 50 MHz / 50,000 = 1 kHz, pulse width 1 / 50 MHz = 20 ns
mistake : comparing with N gives N + 1 states -> 50e6 / 50,001 = 999.98 Hz
simulated with N = 6 and a 10 ns clock: tick every 60 ns; compare-with-N version every 70 ns
Mistakes that make the hardware differ from what was intended:
items: An output left unassigned on some path of a combinational process: a latch is inferred.
Reset tested before rising_edge(clk) but missing from the sensitivity list: simulation resets only at the next clock event, while the hardware resets at once.
A synchronous reset pulse shorter than a clock period can fall between two edges and be missed completely.
Comparing a counter with N instead of N − 1: the counter has N + 1 states.
Signals where variables were intended, or the reverse, in a clocked process: the number of register stages changes.
An else branch after if rising_edge(clk): no flip-flop can implement it, so synthesis rejects it or builds no register.

concepts.text: To trace a clocked process, read every right-hand side with the values from before the edge, let the last assignment to each signal win, and update all signals together at the end; only variables change immediately.

concepts.text: Pipelining a Datapath in VHDL

A long combinational path limits the clock frequency. Pipelining inserts registers between smaller combinational blocks so that each block works on a different data item in the same clock cycle. The clock period is then set by the slowest stage plus register overhead instead of the whole path. Latency grows to k clock cycles for k stages, but once the pipeline is full one result emerges every cycle, so throughput rises.

concepts.plainText: f_max = 1 / (t_clk-to-q + t_comb,max + t_setup)

concepts.text: Points illustrated by the multiply-add pipeline:
items: Every signal assigned under rising_edge(clk) is a register, so prod, c_d and v1 form the stage-1/stage-2 boundary.
Operands that skip a stage (c) must be delayed by the same number of registers, otherwise data from different items mix.
A valid bit travels with the data so downstream logic knows which outputs are real, especially while the pipeline fills or drains.
Latency is 2 clocks, but a new a, b, c set can be accepted every clock.
Retiming lets synthesis tools move registers across logic to balance stage delays.

concepts.text: Timing closure is about the critical path, the longest register-to-register delay. Data must be stable for the setup time before the clock edge and for the hold time after it. For example, an unpipelined 12 ns path with 1 ns of register overhead allows 1/13 ns, about 77 MHz; splitting it into two 6 ns stages gives 7 ns per stage and about 143 MHz, at the cost of one extra cycle of latency.
IC Technology Options
Ways to implement a digital design in silicon:
items: Full-custom: every transistor and wire is hand-designed; best speed, area and power but highest cost and design time (used for CPUs, memory cells).
Semi-custom standard cell: the design is built from a library of pre-characterised gates and flip-flops, then placed and routed; all masks are custom.
Semi-custom gate array: prefabricated wafers of uncommitted transistors; only the metal interconnect layers are customised, so turnaround is faster.
Programmable logic devices (PLDs): fabricated generically and configured by the user in the field (PLA, PAL, CPLD, FPGA).

items: LUT (look-up table): a k-input LUT is a 2^k-bit memory that can implement any k-input Boolean function.
CLB / logic element: several LUTs, flip-flops, multiplexers and fast carry chains grouped together.
Programmable interconnect: switch matrices and routing channels that connect CLBs.
IOBs (I/O blocks): configurable pins supporting different voltage standards, tri-state and registers.
Block RAM (BRAM) for on-chip memory, DSP slices (hardware multiply-accumulate), PLL/clock managers.
Configuration memory, usually SRAM loaded from external flash at power-up, which makes the FPGA reconfigurable.

concepts.text: Almost all digital ICs use CMOS, whose complementary nMOS and pMOS pairs draw very little static current. Moore's law observes that the number of transistors on a chip doubles about every two years, driven by shrinking process nodes from micrometres to 180 nm, 90 nm, 28 nm and today's 7, 5 and 3 nm classes. Dynamic power grows with switching activity, capacitance, the square of supply voltage and frequency, which is why lowering voltage is so effective.

concepts.text: Worked Example: 5-Stage Pipeline, 1000 Items

Take k = 5 stages of 10 ns each and n = 1000 items. Without pipelining each item needs 5 x 10 = 50 ns, so 1000 items take 50,000 ns. Pipelined, the first result appears after 5 cycles and one follows every cycle, so the total is (k + n - 1) x 10 = 1004 x 10 = 10,040 ns. Speedup = 50,000 / 10,040 = 4.98, close to the ideal 5; efficiency = n / (k + n - 1) = 99.6%, and throughput approaches 1 item per 10 ns (100 million items per second).
Going Deeper: Pipelined Datapaths and IC Technology

Data launched by one register at a clock edge must settle at the next register one setup time before the following edge, so every stage needs t_cq + t_logic + t_su ≤ T and the whole pipeline runs at the pace of its slowest stage; this is why stages should be balanced. If the capturing register's clock arrives δ later than the launching one (positive skew), the setup requirement relaxes by δ, but the hold check t_cq + t_logic,min ≥ t_hold + δ becomes harder. The clock period does not appear in the hold check, so a hold violation cannot be cured by slowing the clock. Latency is the number of register stages L times T, while the throughput is one result per clock once the pipeline is full.

A typical FPGA or ASIC implementation flow, in order:
items: RTL design in VHDL, checked by functional (behavioural) simulation against a testbench.
Synthesis: the RTL is translated and optimised into a gate-level netlist; technology mapping fits it onto library cells, or onto LUTs, flip-flops, DSP slices and block RAM in an FPGA.
Place and route: every cell gets a physical site and the nets are routed, so the real wire delays become known.
Static timing analysis: arrival and required times are computed on every path without test vectors; slack = required time − arrival time must be ≥ 0 for both setup and hold.
Optional timing simulation with back-annotated delays; then an FPGA bitstream is generated, or for an ASIC the final layout is sent for mask making (tape-out).

concepts.text: Worked example 3: an FPGA version needs $5,000 of one-time tools and boards and costs $18 per chip, while an ASIC needs $150,000 of design and verification plus a $250,000 mask set and then costs $3 per chip. N_BE = (400,000 − 5,000) / (18 − 3) = 26,333.3 units, so the FPGA is cheaper up to 26,333 units and the ASIC from 26,334 units upward; at 50,000 units the totals are $905,000 for the FPGA against $550,000 for the ASIC. One mask respin adds another $250,000 to the ASIC NRE and moves break-even to 43,000 units. The ASIC unit cost itself comes from wafer cost / (dies per wafer × yield) plus packaging and test.
LUT mapping and CMOS facts behind many calculations:
items: A k-input LUT is a 2^k × 1 memory addressed by its inputs; bit n of its INIT value is the output for input value n, so it can realise any of the 2^(2^k) functions of k inputs with the same delay.
A LUT has one output, so a function with m output bits needs at least m LUTs even when it has few inputs.
Wide AND, OR or XOR trees: each k-LUT merges k signals into one, so n inputs need ⌈(n − 1)/(k − 1)⌉ LUTs; a 12-input AND needs ⌈11/3⌉ = 4 four-input LUTs in 2 levels.
A 2^s-to-1 multiplexer has 2^s + s inputs, so a 4-to-1 multiplexer (6 inputs) is the largest that fits in one 6-input LUT.
Static CMOS pairs a pMOS pull-up network with an nMOS pull-down network that are never both on in steady state, so only leakage flows when idle; an n-input NAND or NOR uses 2n transistors.
In a NAND the series transistors are nMOS and in a NOR they are pMOS; because pMOS has lower carrier mobility, NAND gates are faster for the same size and are preferred.

concepts.text: What the CPU Contains

The central processing unit executes the instructions of a program. It fetches each instruction from memory, decodes it, and carries out the operation on data held in registers or memory. Three functional parts are always present: an arithmetic logic unit that performs the data processing, a register set that holds operands, addresses and status, and a control unit that generates the timing and control signals which steer everything. They talk to each other over an internal bus and to memory and I/O over the external system bus.
The four building blocks of a CPU and what each does:
items: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): combinational circuit that performs add, subtract, AND, OR, XOR, complement, shift and compare on operands supplied from the registers.
Register set: a small, very fast storage array inside the processor; holds the next-instruction address, the current instruction, operands, intermediate results and the status flags.
Control unit: decodes the opcode in the instruction register and, using a timing generator, issues the sequence of control signals that move data between registers, the ALU and memory.
Internal (CPU) bus: the common path over which register contents are routed to the ALU and back; a bus with 2^k sources needs k select lines.

concepts.text: Register Set

rows: Holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched; incremented after each fetch, overwritten by a branch.
Holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.
Holds the address placed on the address bus for a memory read or write.
Holds the word just read from memory or the word about to be written.
Default operand and result register in single-accumulator machines; the ALU output normally lands here.
Hold operands, results, addresses, loop counters; used by register-to-register instructions.
Individual bits set by the ALU: carry C, zero Z, sign S, overflow V, plus interrupt enable and mode bits.

concepts.text: Arithmetic and Logic Unit

The ALU is a combinational circuit with two n-bit data inputs, a function-select input from the control unit, and an n-bit output plus status bits. The arithmetic section is built from an n-bit parallel adder; adding a control line M that complements the second operand and injects a carry-in of 1 turns the same adder into a subtractor (A − B = A + B' + 1 in 2's complement). The logic section computes AND, OR, XOR and NOT bit by bit, and a shifter provides logical, arithmetic and circular shifts. After every operation the flags are updated: Z if the result is all zeros, S from the most significant bit, C from the final carry-out, and V when the carries into and out of the sign position differ.
A one-bit adder/subtractor cell, repeated n times, is the core of the arithmetic section:
items: Full adder: sum S = A XOR B XOR Cin; carry-out Cout = AB + Cin(A XOR B). Chaining n cells with ripple carry gives an n-bit adder.
Subtractor: feed B through an XOR gate with the mode line M. With M = 0 the cell adds; with M = 1 it adds the complement of B and, with the initial carry set to 1, computes A − B.
Overflow in signed arithmetic is detected as V = Cn XOR Cn−1, the XOR of the carry into and out of the sign bit.
Multiplication and division are usually done by repeated add-and-shift sequences under control-unit supervision rather than by a single ALU function.

concepts.latex: S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in},\quad C_{out} = AB + C_{in}(A \oplus B)
concepts.plainText: Full adder: S = A XOR B XOR Cin; Cout = AB + Cin(A XOR B)

concepts.text: Instruction Cycle and Register Transfer Language

Every instruction passes through the same cycle: fetch (read the instruction word at the address in PC into IR and advance PC), decode (the control unit examines the opcode and mode bits, and computes the effective address if the operand is in memory), execute (perform the micro-operations the instruction requires), and finally an interrupt check (if interrupts are enabled and one is pending, save PC and jump to the service routine). Register transfer language (RTL) describes each step as a micro-operation, an elementary transfer that happens in one clock pulse, written as destination ← source with an optional control condition in front of a colon.
The fetch and decode phases of Mano's basic computer written in RTL (T0, T1, T2 are timing signals):
items: T0: AR ← PC. The address of the next instruction is moved to the address register.
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1. The instruction word is read into IR while PC is incremented in the same clock pulse.
T2: D0…D7 ← Decode IR(12–14), AR ← IR(0–11), I ← IR(15). The opcode is decoded, the address field goes to AR and the mode bit to flip-flop I.
D7'IT3: AR ← M[AR]. If the instruction is memory-reference and indirect (I = 1), one more read fetches the effective address.
Four classes of micro-operation appear in RTL: register transfer (R1 ← R2), arithmetic (R1 ← R1 + R2), logic (R1 ← R1 XOR R2) and shift (R1 ← shl R1).

concepts.text: Computer Configuration: Mano's Basic Computer
Morris Mano's basic computer is the standard reference configuration for the syllabus:
items: Memory: 4096 words of 16 bits (4096 × 16), so an address is 12 bits and one word holds an instruction or a data item.

Instruction format: bit 15 is the mode bit I (0 direct, 1 indirect), bits 12–14 are the opcode, bits 0–11 are the address. Opcodes 000–110 are memory-reference (AND, ADD, LDA, STA, BUN, BSA, ISZ); opcode 111 with I = 0 is register-reference and with I = 1 is input-output.
Registers: AR 12 bits, PC 12 bits, DR 16, AC 16, IR 16, TR 16 (temporary), OUTR 8 and INPR 8 for the output and input devices.
Flip-flops: I (indirect), S (start/stop), E (carry out of AC), R (interrupt), IEN (interrupt enable), FGI and FGO (input and output flags).
Common bus: one 16-bit bus with three select lines S2 S1 S0 chooses among 8 sources (000 none, 001 AR, 010 PC, 011 DR, 100 AC, 101 IR, 110 TR, 111 memory); each register has an LD, INR and CLR input.

concepts.text: Timing and control signals come from a 4-bit sequence counter SC whose output drives a 4 × 16 decoder producing timing signals T0 to T15; a 3 × 8 decoder on IR(12–14) produces the opcode signals D0 to D7. A control function is a Boolean product of these, for example the BUN instruction executes as D4T4: PC ← AR, SC ← 0, and the last micro-operation of every instruction clears SC so that the next fetch starts at T0. The control unit's design problem is to generate every LD, INR, CLR, bus-select and memory read/write signal as a Boolean function of the D, T, I and flag variables. There are two ways to realise those Boolean functions. A hardwired control unit implements them directly with gates, decoders and flip-flops, so a change in the instruction set means rewiring the circuit; it is fast and is the choice for RISC processors. A microprogrammed control unit stores the control signals for each step as words in a control memory, and a sequencer reads them out one after another; it is slower but flexible and is the traditional CISC approach. The next subtopic develops the microprogrammed design in detail.

rows: Faster; signals are one gate delay away
Slower; one control-memory read per micro-step
Hard to modify; any change reworks the circuit
High for complex machines; hard to debug

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Datapath, Hardwired Control and Stacks

A common bus for k registers of n bits can be built in two ways. With multiplexers, bit i of every register goes to multiplexer i, so the bus needs n multiplexers of size k × 1 that share ceil(log2 k) select lines. With three-state buffers, every register bit gets its own buffer (k × n buffers) and a log2 k × k decoder enables exactly one register at a time, because two drivers on one bus line would conflict. Either way only one source can use the bus in a clock, but paths that bypass the bus still work in parallel: in Mano's basic computer AC ← DR (through the adder and logic circuit) can happen in the same clock as DR ← AC (over the bus), and the INR and CLR inputs change a register without using the bus at all.

concepts.latex: N_{mux} = n,\ \text{size} = k \times 1,\ s = \lceil \log_{2} k \rceil,\ N_{buf} = k\,n
concepts.plainText: Bus for k registers of n bits: n multiplexers of size k × 1 with s = ceil(log2 k) select lines, or k × n three-state buffers plus a log2 k × k decoder

rows: D = A + B + 1, add with carry
D = A + B', subtract with borrow
D = A + B' + 1 = A − B, subtract

concepts.text: Mano's arithmetic circuit computes D = A + Y + Cin (table above); logic micro-operations manipulate bits and shifts move them sideways:
items: Selective set A ← A ∨ B sets the bits of A where B has 1s; selective complement A ← A ⊕ B inverts them; selective clear A ← A ∧ B' clears them.

Mask A ← A ∧ B keeps the bits of A only where B has 1s; insert first masks the target bits to 0 and then ORs in the new pattern; the clear (compare) operation A ← A ⊕ B gives all 0s exactly when A and B are equal.
Example with A = 1001 0110 and B = 0000 1111: selective set gives 1001 1111, selective complement 1001 1001, selective clear 1001 0000 and mask 0000 0110.

Logical shifts insert 0 and circular shifts feed the bit that falls out back into the other end. Arithmetic shift right copies the sign bit (a signed divide by 2); arithmetic shift left multiplies by 2 and overflows when R(n−1) and R(n−2) differ before the shift, Vs = R(n−1) ⊕ R(n−2).

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: clock cycles in Mano's basic computer, 100 ns clock (10 MHz)
Every instruction: T0-T2 fetch and decode, T3 indirect check
LDA X (I = 1) : D2T4 DR <- M[AR]; D2T5 AC <- DR, SC <- 0      T0..T5 = 6
ADD Y (I = 0) : D1T4 DR <- M[AR]; D1T5 AC <- AC + DR           T0..T5 = 6
ISZ C         : D6T4 read; D6T5 DR <- DR + 1; D6T6 write, skip  T0..T6 = 7
BUN L         : D4T4 PC <- AR, SC <- 0                         T0..T4 = 5
CMA (reg-ref) : D7 I' T3 B9: AC <- AC'                          T0..T3 = 4
Total = 6 + 6 + 7 + 5 + 4 = 28 cycles
Time  = 28 x 100 ns = 2.8 µs
I = 1 costs no extra cycle: every memory-reference instruction spends T3 anyway

Designing a hardwired control unit is careful bookkeeping. List every micro-operation that changes a register, note the control function (decoder output D, timing signal T, mode bit I, flags) under which it occurs, and OR those functions to drive that register's LD, INR or CLR input. For Mano's PC, PC ← AR occurs in BUN (D4T4) and BSA (D5T5), so LD(PC) = D4T4 + D5T5, while PC ← 0 in the interrupt cycle gives CLR(PC) = RT1. The timing signals come from a binary counter plus decoder (log2 k flip-flops for k signals), a ring counter (k flip-flops, no decoder) or a Johnson counter (k/2 flip-flops, each state decoded by a 2-input AND gate), and only as many signals are needed as the longest instruction uses.
Mano's interrupt cycle replaces the next fetch when flip-flop R is 1:
items: R is set by T0'T1'T2'(IEN)(FGI + FGO): R ← 1, that is outside the fetch and decode steps, with interrupts enabled and a device flag raised.
RT0: AR ← 0, TR ← PC. The return address is parked in TR while AR is cleared.
RT1: M[AR] ← TR, PC ← 0. The return address is stored in memory word 0.
RT2: PC ← PC + 1, IEN ← 0, R ← 0, SC ← 0. The next fetch comes from word 1, which holds a BUN to the service routine; IEN stays 0 until the routine executes ION.
The service routine ends with an indirect BUN 0, which jumps back through the address saved in word 0.

concepts.text: A stack is either a set of fast registers or a region of main memory, addressed by the stack pointer SP. Mano's 64-word register stack has a 6-bit SP and flags FULL and EMTY: PUSH is SP ← SP + 1, M[SP] ← DR (FULL ← 1 if SP has wrapped to 0, EMTY ← 0), and POP is DR ← M[SP], SP ← SP − 1 (EMTY ← 1 if SP = 0, FULL ← 0). Because SP is incremented before the write, the first item goes into word 1 and the 64th wraps into word 0. A memory stack usually grows toward lower addresses (PUSH: SP ← SP − 1, M[SP] ← DR; POP: DR ← M[SP], SP ← SP + 1), and limit registers compared with SP catch overflow and underflow. Stack machines evaluate expressions in reverse Polish notation, so zero-address instructions find their operands on the top of the stack.

Worked example 2: evaluate (4 + 6) x (7 - 2) on a stack
Postfix: 4 6 + 7 2 - x
Token  Action                       Stack (top at right)
4      PUSH 4                       4
6      PUSH 6                       4 6
+      POP 6, POP 4, PUSH 10        10
7      PUSH 7                       10 7
2      PUSH 2                       10 7 2
-      POP 2, POP 7, PUSH 7 - 2     10 5
x      POP 5, POP 10, PUSH 50       50
Result 50; maximum depth 3 (after PUSH 2)
For - and /, the item popped first is the RIGHT operand

rows: Temporary registers Y and Z at the ALU
Two bus (one source bus into the ALU, one result bus)
Three bus (sources A and B, result bus C)
1: R1 on A, R2 on B, sum on C into R3
Register file with 2 read ports and 1 write port

concepts.text: Common slips: the number of bus multiplexers equals the word length, not the number of registers; an arithmetic shift right copies the sign bit while a logical shift inserts 0; in postfix evaluation the item popped first is the right operand of − and /; whether SP changes before or after the write depends on whether it points to the top item or to the next free word; and in Mano's timing an indirect memory-reference instruction takes no more clock cycles than a direct one.

formulas.latex: S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in},\quad C_{out} = AB + C_{in}(A \oplus B)
formulas.plainText: Full adder: S = A XOR B XOR Cin; Cout = AB + Cin(A XOR B)
Signed overflow V = carry out of sign bit XOR carry into sign bit
Address bits = log2(number of words); 4096 words need 12 bits
Select lines on a common bus = ceil(log2(number of sources)); 8 sources need 3

notes.text: Memorise the numbers of Mano's basic computer: 16-bit word, 4096 × 16 memory, 12-bit address, 3-bit opcode plus 1 mode bit, 8 registers (AR PC DR AC IR TR OUTR INPR), 3 bus select lines. MCQs often ask for one of these figures directly.

MAR and MBR (AR and DR in Mano's notation) sit between the CPU and memory: MAR carries an address out, MBR carries data in or out. Do not confuse MBR with the accumulator, which is an ALU operand register.
In RTL, all micro-operations listed on one line with a common control function happen in the same clock pulse, e.g. T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1 reads memory and increments PC simultaneously.

concepts.text: Integer Representations

An n-bit register can hold an unsigned integer from 0 to 2^n − 1, or a signed integer if the most significant bit is used as a sign (0 = positive, 1 = negative). Three signed conventions exist. In sign-magnitude the remaining n − 1 bits hold the magnitude. In 1's complement a negative number is the bitwise inverse of the positive one. In 2's complement a negative number is the inverse plus 1, which is the same as 2^n − |x|. Practically every processor uses 2's complement because it has a single zero, subtraction is done with the same adder as addition, and the carry out of the sign position is simply discarded.
Addition, Subtraction and Overflow

A parallel (ripple-carry) adder is a chain of n full adders, the carry of each stage feeding the next; its delay grows with n, so wide ALUs use carry-lookahead logic that computes all carries from generate (G = AB) and propagate (P = A ⊕ B) signals in a fixed number of gate levels. An adder-subtractor adds one XOR gate per bit on the B input and a mode control M: with M = 0 the XORs pass B unchanged and the input carry is 0, so the circuit computes A + B; with M = 1 every B bit is complemented and the input carry is 1, so the circuit computes A + B' + 1 = A − B in 2's complement. Comparison (A − B) uses the same hardware and only the flags are kept.
Overflow in signed (2's complement) arithmetic:
items: Overflow can occur only when two numbers of the same sign are added (or numbers of opposite sign are subtracted); the result then shows the wrong sign. Adding numbers of opposite sign can never overflow.
Hardware test: V = C_n ⊕ C_(n−1), the XOR of the carry out of the sign bit and the carry into the sign bit. V = 1 means the result is invalid.
Worked example, 4 bits: 0111 (+7) + 0001 (+1) = 1000 (−8). C4 = 0 and C3 = 1, so V = 1: overflow. Also 1000 (−8) + 1111 (−1) = 0111 (+7) with C4 = 1, C3 = 0: overflow.

Unsigned overflow is different: it is signalled by the carry out C_n alone. The ALU sets both the carry flag and the overflow flag; the program picks the one that matches how it interprets the operands.
In 1's complement arithmetic the carry out is not discarded but added back into the LSB (end-around carry), one reason 1's complement lost out to 2's complement.

concepts.plainText: V = C_n XOR C_(n−1) (carry out of sign bit XOR carry into sign bit)

concepts.text: Multiplication and Division

Unsigned multiplication is done by shift-and-add. The multiplicand is in register B, the multiplier in Q, an accumulator A is cleared and a counter is set to n. Each step examines the least significant bit of Q: if it is 1, B is added to A; then the pair (A, Q) is shifted right one place and the counter is decremented. After n steps the 2n-bit product sits in A:Q. Sign-magnitude numbers are multiplied by multiplying magnitudes and XOR-ing the sign bits. Booth's algorithm multiplies 2's complement numbers directly, without sign correction, by treating a run of 1s in the multiplier from bit j to bit k as 2^(k+1) − 2^j, so it only adds or subtracts at the ends of runs and can be faster when the multiplier has long runs of identical bits.
Booth's algorithm (multiplicand M, multiplier in Q, accumulator A = 0, an extra bit Q−1 = 0, counter = n):
items: Look at the pair Q0 Q−1. If it is 1 0, do A ← A − M. If it is 0 1, do A ← A + M. If it is 0 0 or 1 1, do nothing.
Arithmetic-shift right the triple (A, Q, Q−1) one place: the sign bit of A is copied, the old Q0 moves into Q−1.
Decrement the counter; repeat until it reaches 0. The signed 2n-bit product is in A:Q; Q−1 is discarded.
Number of add/subtract operations equals the number of 0→1 and 1→0 transitions in the multiplier, not the number of 1s.

concepts.text: Division of unsigned or magnitude numbers uses shift-and-subtract. In restoring division the dividend pair (A, Q) is shifted left, the divisor M is subtracted from A, and the new quotient bit Q0 is set to 1 if the result is non-negative; if it is negative Q0 is set to 0 and M is added back (restored). After n steps Q holds the quotient and A the remainder. Non-restoring division avoids the restore: if A is negative, the next step shifts and adds M instead of subtracting, and a single correction (add M if A is still negative) is made at the end, so it needs one add or subtract per bit instead of up to two. Before starting, the hardware checks for divide-by-zero and for divide overflow, which occurs when the high half of the dividend is greater than or equal to the divisor, so the quotient would not fit in n bits.
Floating-Point Representation (IEEE 754)
IEEE 754 single precision packs a real number into 32 bits as sign, biased exponent and fraction:
items: Fields: 1 sign bit S, 8 exponent bits E with bias 127 (stored E = true exponent + 127), 23 fraction bits F. A normalised number has an implied leading 1, so the significand is 1.F and the effective precision is 24 bits. Double precision uses 1/11/52 with bias 1023.

Special encodings: E = 0 and F = 0 is ±0; E = 0 and F ≠ 0 is a denormalised (subnormal) number with no hidden 1; E = 255 and F = 0 is ±infinity; E = 255 and F ≠ 0 is NaN. Normalised exponents therefore run from 1 to 254, true exponents −126 to +127.
Range: roughly ±1.18 × 10^−38 to ±3.4 × 10^38 for single precision; about 7 significant decimal digits (15–16 for double).

Worked encoding of −6.5: 6.5 = 110.1 in binary = 1.101 × 2^2. S = 1; E = 2 + 127 = 129 = 1000 0001; F = 101 followed by twenty 0s. The word is 1 10000001 10100000000000000000000 = C0D0 0000 in hexadecimal.
Decoding: value = (−1)^S × 1.F × 2^(E − 127). A bigger bias-coded exponent field means a bigger number, so floating-point values of the same sign can be compared like sign-magnitude integers.

concepts.plainText: x = (−1)^S × 1.F × 2^(E − 127) for a normalised IEEE 754 single-precision number

concepts.text: Floating-point arithmetic is done on the sign, exponent and mantissa parts separately:
items: Addition/subtraction: check for zero operands; align the exponents by shifting the mantissa of the smaller number right by the exponent difference; add or subtract the mantissas; normalise the result (shift and adjust the exponent); round to the available bits; check exponent overflow or underflow.

Multiplication: add the exponents and subtract one bias; multiply the mantissas; sign = S1 ⊕ S2; normalise and round. Division: subtract the exponents and add the bias; divide the mantissas; sign = S1 ⊕ S2; normalise and round.
Guard, round and sticky bits are kept beyond the mantissa during the operation so that rounding (default: round to nearest, ties to even) is accurate.
Alignment can lose all the bits of a much smaller operand, so floating-point addition is not associative: (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c).

concepts.text: Logical and Shift Micro-operations

rows: Mask: clears the bits of A where B has 0s, keeps the rest
Selective-set / insert: sets the bits of A where B has 1s
Selective-complement; A ⊕ B = 0 tests two words for equality
Bitwise inversion (1's complement); selective-clear is A ← A ∧ B'
Vacated bit filled with 0; used on unsigned data and bit fields
ashr copies the sign bit (divide by 2); ashl multiplies by 2 and overflows if the sign changes
The bit shifted out re-enters at the other end; rotate-through-carry includes the C flag

concepts.text: BCD (binary-coded decimal) arithmetic stores each decimal digit in 4 bits (0000 to 1001), so the codes 1010 to 1111 are invalid. Two BCD digits are added with an ordinary 4-bit binary adder; if the binary sum is greater than 9 or the adder produces a carry, 0110 (6) is added to skip the six unused codes and generate the decimal carry. For example 8 + 5: 1000 + 0101 = 1101 (13, invalid), add 0110 → 1 0011, which reads as carry 1 and digit 3. A decimal adder is therefore a binary adder plus this correction logic, and a k-digit BCD adder cascades k of them. BCD subtraction is done by adding the 9's or 10's complement of the subtrahend. BCD is used where exact decimal results matter (calculators, financial software, display drivers) at the cost of speed and storage.
Going Deeper: Arithmetic Algorithms Step by Step

Mano's sign-magnitude adder-subtractor keeps the magnitudes in registers A and B, their signs in As and Bs, the end carry in flip-flop E and an overflow flag AVF. Subtraction is first turned into addition by complementing Bs, after which only two cases remain. If the signs are equal, the magnitudes are added and the end carry is copied into AVF as the overflow indication. If the signs differ, A + B' + 1 is formed: E = 1 means A ≥ B and the result is already correct, while E = 0 means A < B, so A is replaced by its 2's complement and As is complemented. When the magnitudes cancel (A = B), As is cleared so that the result is +0, never −0.

rows: A ← A + B' + 1, then A ← A' + 1

concepts.plainText: Q·M = Σ (q_(i−1) − q_i)·2^i·M over i = 0 … n−1, with q_(−1) = 0: pair Q0 Q−1 = 10 gives −M, 01 gives +M, 00 and 11 give nothing

concepts.text: The recoded digit q_(i−1) − q_i is −1 at the right-hand end of a run of 1s, +1 just past its left-hand end and 0 inside a run of 1s or of 0s. Summed over all positions, these digits reproduce the 2's complement weight −2^(n−1) of the sign bit automatically, so Booth's algorithm needs no sign correction, provided the partial product is kept signed by an arithmetic right shift. The worst case is an alternating multiplier such as 0101 0101, which needs an operation in every cycle; bit-pair (radix-4) recoding looks at two bits at a time, uses the digits −2 to +2 and halves the number of partial products. The table multiplies M = 0111 (+7) by Q = 1101 (−3).

Restoring division of 1011 (11) by 0011 (3), tabulated below, keeps the dividend in Q, the divisor in M = 00011 and a 5-bit partial remainder A that starts at 00000, the extra bit showing the sign of A − M. Each cycle shifts A and Q left as one register, subtracts M, and keeps the difference only if it is not negative (q0 = 1); otherwise q0 = 0 and M is added back. Non-restoring division skips the add-back: when A is negative, the next cycle shifts and adds M, because 2(A + M) − M = 2A + M, and after n cycles one correction A ← A + M is made if A is still negative. Both methods leave the quotient in Q and the remainder in A.

Add X = 9.75 = 1.00111 × 2^3 (E = 130) and Y = 0.5625 = 1.001 × 2^−1 (E = 126)

2. Align:  shift Y's significand right 4 places: 1.001 → 0.0001001 (× 2^3)
3. Add significands:  1.0011100 + 0.0001001 = 1.0100101
4. Normalise:  already in 1.F form, exponent stays 3
5. Round and check range:  fits in 23 fraction bits, no overflow or underflow
Result 1.0100101 × 2^3 = 1010.0101 (binary) = 10.3125 = 4125 0000 (hex)

concepts.plainText: Floating-point multiply (single precision): S = S1 XOR S2; stored exponent E = E1 + E2 − 127 (one bias removed); significand M = M1 × M2, then normalise (if 2 ≤ M < 4 shift right once and add 1 to E) and round

concepts.text: Common slips: using a logical instead of an arithmetic right shift in Booth's algorithm; forgetting that the restoring divider's A register needs an extra bit for the sign; reading the carry flag as signed overflow; forgetting the hidden 1 when decoding IEEE 754, or storing it in F when encoding; adding both biases, or neither, when multiplying floating-point numbers; and applying the BCD +6 correction only when the 4-bit sum exceeds 9 while ignoring the case where the adder itself produced a carry (8 + 9 = 1 0001). One special case: with an n-bit A register, Booth's algorithm gives wrong products when the multiplicand is −2^(n−1) (1000 in 4 bits), because −M does not fit in n bits; one extra bit in A and M removes the problem.

formulas.plainText: Range of an n-bit 2's complement integer: −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1
Signed overflow flag: V = C_n XOR C_(n−1)
2's complement of x: invert all bits and add 1, equal to 2^n − x
IEEE 754 single precision: x = (−1)^S × 1.F × 2^(E − 127)

notes.text: For the 2's complement of a number: copy the bits from the right up to and including the first 1, then invert the rest. 0101 1000 → 1010 1000. This is faster and less error-prone than invert-and-add-1 in the exam.

Carry and overflow are different flags. In 2's complement addition ignore the carry out and check V = C_n ⊕ C_(n−1); a carry out of 1 does not by itself mean the signed result is wrong, and a carry out of 0 does not mean it is right.
Booth's algorithm needs the extra Q−1 bit and an arithmetic (sign-preserving) right shift; the plain shift-and-add multiplier uses a logical shift and works only for unsigned or magnitude values.
IEEE 754 numbers to remember: single 1/8/23 with bias 127, double 1/11/52 with bias 1023, hidden leading 1 in normalised numbers, all-1s exponent means infinity or NaN.

concepts.text: Peripheral Devices

Peripheral devices (peripherals) are the input, output, storage and communication devices attached to a computer but external to the CPU and main memory. Every peripheral is electromechanical or electronic hardware that speaks its own language: a keyboard produces key codes at a few bytes per second, a disk streams megabytes per second, a network card exchanges packets. The CPU never talks to a peripheral directly; each device is attached through an I/O module (interface) that translates between the device and the system bus.

rows: 100 KB/s (laser printer) to hundreds of MB/s (display)
Hard disk, SSD, optical drive, magnetic tape
Ethernet card, modem, Wi-Fi, USB host

concepts.text: Why an I/O device cannot simply be wired to the system bus (the three mismatches an interface must resolve):
items: Speed mismatch: peripherals are orders of magnitude slower than the CPU and memory and are not synchronised to the CPU clock, so transfers must be buffered and paced.
Format mismatch: devices use their own data codes and word lengths (serial bit streams, 7-bit ASCII, analog signals) which must be converted to the CPU word format.
Electrical and mechanical mismatch: devices use different voltage levels, connectors and signalling (electromechanical or electromagnetic), so signal conversion and isolation are needed.
Diversity: different devices need different control sequences; the interface hides these so the CPU sees a uniform set of ports.

concepts.text: I/O Modules and Their Functions
An I/O module (I/O interface unit, controller) sits between the system bus and one or more devices and performs five functions:
items: Control and timing: coordinates the flow of traffic between the device and the internal resources, e.g. requests the bus, waits for the device to be ready, completes the transfer.
Processor communication: decodes commands (READ, WRITE, SEEK, SCAN), exchanges data, reports status (READY, BUSY, ERROR) and recognises its own address on the bus.
Device communication: sends commands, status information and data to and from the attached device in the device's own signalling.
Data buffering: temporarily holds data so that a slow device can be served without tying up the fast bus, and a fast device (disk) can burst data without overrunning memory.
Error detection: detects mechanical faults (paper jam, bad sector) and transmission errors, usually with a parity bit, and reports them in the status register.

concepts.text: There are three ways to organise the buses for I/O. Some large computers use a separate I/O bus driven by an I/O processor, so that the memory bus is free for CPU-memory traffic. Most small systems share one common bus between memory and I/O but use separate control lines (memory read/write versus I/O read/write) — this is isolated I/O. Alternatively the same bus and the same control lines serve both memory and I/O, and the address itself decides which one responds — this is memory-mapped I/O.

rows: Separate for memory and I/O ports; both may use the full range
One shared space; ports occupy some memory addresses
Any memory instruction (LOAD, STORE, MOV, ADD) can access a port
Extra I/O read and I/O write lines (or IO/M signal)
Same memory read and write lines
Simpler; address decoder alone selects memory or port
Reduces addressable memory by the ports used

concepts.text: The I/O Interface Unit: Registers and Ports
A typical interface unit (Mano's example connects one device through four addressable registers) contains:
items: Data register (port A, port B): holds the data word being transferred; for an output device the CPU writes it, for an input device the CPU reads it. A bidirectional data bus buffer connects it to the system bus.
Status register: bits set by the interface report device conditions, e.g. bit F = data available (flag), bit E = error, and a busy bit. The CPU reads it to decide whether to transfer.
Control register: bits written by the CPU select the mode of operation (transfer direction, interrupt enable, baud rate, parity).

Selection logic: a chip select (CS) input decoded from the high address bits picks this interface, and register select lines (RS1 RS0) pick one of the four registers; I/O read and I/O write lines time the transfer.
Port addressing: with an 8-bit port address a CPU can address 2^8 = 256 input and 256 output ports; each port number is what appears in IN port and OUT port instructions.

concepts.plainText: Number of ports = 2^k for a k-bit port address, e.g. 2^8 = 256

concepts.text: Asynchronous Data Transfer: Strobe and Handshake

When two units are driven by the same clock (synchronous transfer) data is exchanged at known clock edges. The CPU and an interface, or an interface and its device, usually run on independent clocks, so the transfer is asynchronous and each unit must tell the other when data is valid. Two schemes are used: strobe control with a single control line, and handshaking with two control lines.

rows: Source places data on the bus, then pulses strobe; destination latches data on the pulse
Source cannot know whether data was accepted
Destination pulses strobe to request; source places data for the strobe duration
Destination cannot know whether source had data
Source: data + data valid = 1; destination reads, data accepted = 1; source drops valid; destination drops accepted
Destination raises request; source places data and raises valid; destination reads and drops request; source drops valid
Same; used when the receiver sets the pace

concepts.text: A handshake is a closed loop: each step is acknowledged before the next begins, so the transfer works at the speed of the slower unit and a missing response is detectable with a timeout. Strobe is open loop and relies on a fixed pulse width. In MCQs, "two-wire" or "acknowledged" transfer means handshake; "single control pulse" means strobe.
Serial and Parallel Interfaces
Interfaces also differ in how many bits move at once:
items: Parallel interface: one line per bit of the word (8, 16 or 32 lines plus control); fast over short distances; used for printers (Centronics), disk controllers, internal buses.
Serial interface: one line carries the bits one after another; cheaper, longer distances, fewer pins; used for terminals, modems, UART/RS-232, USB, SATA, Ethernet.
Synchronous serial: sender and receiver share or recover a common clock and send long blocks with only a small header; efficient for high speed.

Asynchronous serial: each character is framed independently; the line idles at 1, a start bit (0) marks the beginning, then 5 to 8 data bits (LSB first), an optional parity bit and 1, 1.5 or 2 stop bits (1). The receiver resynchronises on every start bit.

Baud rate is the number of signal changes per second; for a binary line it equals bits per second. Characters per second = baud ÷ bits per frame, e.g. 9600 baud with 1 + 8 + 1 = 10 bits gives 960 char/s.

USB: a serial, host-controlled, hot-pluggable, tree-topology bus (up to 127 devices per host) that carries data and power on 4 wires. PCI/PCIe: the standard internal expansion interconnect; PCI is a 32/64-bit parallel bus, PCIe uses point-to-point serial lanes.

concepts.plainText: characters per second = baud / bits per frame = 9600 / 10 = 960

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Interface Registers, Serial Frames and Bus Arbitration

On a common I/O bus every interface watches the address lines; the one whose decoder recognises its address becomes active and obeys the function code on the control lines, while the others ignore the cycle. The register-select bits come from the lowest address lines, so an interface with four registers occupies four consecutive port addresses. What the processor can ask an interface to do falls into four kinds of I/O command, which the interface carries out with its data, status and control registers.
Mano's four types of I/O command:
items: Control command: activates the peripheral and tells it what to do, for example rewind a tape or start the motor; its meaning depends on the device.
Status command: tests conditions in the interface and the peripheral (ready, busy, error, parity) and returns them through the status register.
Data output command: moves a word from the data bus into the interface's output data register, from which the device takes it.
Data input command: the interface places the word received from the device, held in its input data register, on the data bus for the CPU.

concepts.text: A UART transmitter has a holding register that the CPU writes and a shift register that adds the start bit, shifts the data out least significant bit first, and appends the optional parity bit and the stop bit or bits. The receiver waits for the 1-to-0 edge of a start bit, checks half a bit later that the line is still 0 (so a noise spike is not taken for a start bit), and then samples every following bit at its centre using a clock of 16 times the baud rate. Three error flags result: a parity error (parity bit wrong), a framing error (stop bit found to be 0) and an overrun error (a new character completed before the previous one was read).

Worked example 1: send 'C' (43H) as 8 data bits, even parity, 1 stop bit, 9600 baud
43H = 0100 0011 -> LSB first: 1 1 0 0 0 0 1 0   (three 1s)
even parity bit = 1  (makes the count of 1s even: 3 + 1 = 4)
line: idle 1 | start 0 | 1 1 0 0 0 0 1 0 | parity 1 | stop 1 | idle 1 ...
frame  = 1 + 8 + 1 + 1 = 11 bits
T_bit  = 1 / 9600 s = 104.17 us
T_char = 11 x 104.17 us = 1.146 ms  -> 9600 / 11 = 872.7 characters/s

concepts.plainText: Bit time = 1 / baud; useful data rate = baud × d / (1 + d + p + s) on a two-level line

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: UART clock divisor and clock tolerance (8N1 frame)
crystal 1.8432 MHz, sampling clock = 16 x baud
divisor = 1 843 200 / (16 x 9600) = 12   -> 153.6 kHz sampling clock
start edge -> wait 8 ticks (centre of start bit) -> then sample every 16 ticks
data bit 0 sampled 1.5 bit times after the edge
stop bit sampled 1 + 8 + 0.5 = 9.5 bit times after the edge
allowed drift at that point < 0.5 bit
max total bit-period mismatch = 0.5 / 9.5 = 5.3 %   (tick quantisation ignored)

concepts.text: Keyboards, displays and printers as seen from the interface:
items: Keyboard: the keys form a row × column matrix, so r + c lines serve up to r × c keys; the controller drives one row at a time, reads the columns, debounces for 10–20 ms and sends a scan code to the host.

Rollover: two-key or n-key rollover lets a new key be recognised while an earlier one is still held; a matrix without diodes can show a ghost key when three keys at the corners of a rectangle are pressed.
Display: a raster frame buffer needs W × H × bits-per-pixel / 8 bytes and is read once per refresh; a multiplexed 7-segment display shares the segment lines and adds one enable line per digit.

Printer: impact printers (dot-matrix, daisy-wheel, line) strike an inked ribbon, non-impact printers (laser, inkjet, thermal) do not; the Centronics port hands over bytes with STROBE, BUSY and ACK, and the printer's buffer absorbs the speed mismatch.
