concepts.text: Baud is signal changes (symbols) per second, not bits or bytes per second: the two are equal only on a two-level line. Character rates always divide by the full frame (start + data + parity + stop), and rate answers must keep µs and ms, bits and bytes, and MB = 10^6 versus MiB = 2^20 apart.

formulas.plainText: Number of I/O ports = 2^k for a k-bit port address
Frame bits = 1 start + d data + p parity + s stop
Characters per second = baud rate / bits per frame
Efficiency = data bits / frame bits, e.g. 8/11 ≈ 73%

notes.text: Isolated I/O = separate address space + IN/OUT instructions + separate I/O control lines (8085 IO/M). Memory-mapped I/O = one address space, no special instructions, ports eat memory addresses. The 8085/8086 use isolated I/O; most RISC machines use memory-mapped.

Strobe uses ONE control line and gives no acknowledgement; handshake uses TWO (data valid + data accepted, or data request + data valid). Do not describe the strobe method as "self-checking": only handshaking can detect a missing response.

The status register is read by the CPU and written by the interface; the control register is written by the CPU and read by the interface. Polling means repeatedly reading the status register's flag bit.

concepts.text: What an Embedded System Is

An embedded system is a microprocessor-based computing system designed to perform a specific, dedicated task, usually as part of a larger product and often under strict real-time, size, cost and power constraints. Vahid and Givargis define it loosely as any computing system other than a desktop computer: the processor inside a washing machine, a car engine controller, a pacemaker or a router is embedded, while the user never sees a general-purpose computer. Billions of such systems are manufactured every year, far more than desktop machines.
Three characteristics shared by almost all embedded systems:
items: Single-functioned: the system executes one program, or a small fixed set of programs, repeatedly for the life of the product (a pager always runs the pager program), unlike a PC that runs whatever the user installs.
Tightly constrained: design metrics such as cost, size, performance and power have hard limits. A remote control must be cheap, fit in the hand, respond instantly and run for a year on batteries.

Reactive and real-time: the system continually responds to changes in its environment (sensor inputs, network packets) and must compute results within fixed deadlines; a late result from a car brake controller is as bad as a wrong one.

concepts.text: Typical building blocks of an embedded system:
items: Core processor: a microcontroller (AVR/Arduino, ARM Cortex-M, PIC, 8051), a DSP or a system-on-chip; sometimes custom hardware in an ASIC or FPGA.
Memory: Flash or ROM for the fixed program, RAM (SRAM) for variables and buffers, sometimes EEPROM for calibration data.
I/O interfaces: GPIO pins, ADC and DAC for analog signals, PWM outputs for motors and LEDs, timers and watchdog.
Communication modules: UART, SPI, I2C on the board; CAN, USB, Ethernet, Wi-Fi or Bluetooth to the outside world.
Sensors and actuators, a power supply or battery management, and firmware that may run bare-metal or on a real-time operating system.

rows: Digital cameras, smart TVs, washing machines, microwave ovens, game controllers
Engine control unit, anti-lock braking, airbag controller, infotainment
Pacemakers, infusion pumps, patient monitors, glucose meters
Programmable logic controllers, robot arms, motor drives, smart meters
Routers, switches, mobile phone basebands, modems
Printers, scanners, thermostats, security cameras, elevators

concepts.text: Design Metrics and Their Trade-offs
Common design metrics (a measurable feature of an implementation):
items: NRE (non-recurring engineering) cost: the one-time cost of designing the system; paid once regardless of how many units are made.
Unit cost: the money spent to manufacture each copy, excluding NRE.
Size: physical space, measured in bytes for software and in gates or transistors for hardware.
Performance: execution time or throughput; latency (time from start to finish of a task) and throughput (tasks per unit time) can differ.
Power: energy consumed per unit time, which decides battery life, heat and cooling.
Flexibility: how cheaply the functionality can be changed without large NRE cost.
Time-to-prototype: time to build a working version; time-to-market: time until the product can be sold.
Maintainability, correctness (does it do what was specified) and safety (does it never cause harm).

concepts.text: These metrics compete: shrinking size may raise power, adding custom hardware improves performance and power but increases NRE cost and destroys flexibility, and a faster clock raises power. Improving one metric usually worsens another, so the designer must understand both hardware and software and pick the implementation that best balances the metrics for the intended production volume. Because NRE is spread over every unit sold, a high-NRE custom design is only economical at high volume.

Time-to-market matters because product revenue follows a rough triangle: sales rise after launch, peak in the middle of the market window and fall to zero after 2W months. A product launched D months late enters a smaller triangle and, by the simplified revenue model, loses the fraction D(3W minus D) / (2W squared) of total revenue. With a one-year window (W = 26 weeks) a delay of only 4 weeks costs about 22 percent of revenue, so a late but perfect product can earn less than an earlier, adequate one.

concepts.plainText: Percentage revenue loss = D(3W - D) / (2 W^2), D = delay, 2W = market window

concepts.text: Classification of Embedded Systems
Classification by function and operating context:
items: Stand-alone: works independently, takes inputs from sensors or keys and drives outputs directly; digital camera, microwave oven, MP3 player.

Real-time: must produce results within a deadline. Hard real-time means a missed deadline is a system failure (airbag, flight control, pacemaker); soft real-time tolerates occasional misses with degraded quality (video streaming, DVD player).
Networked: connected to a LAN, WAN or the Internet and often acting as a client or server; home security system, IoT sensor node, network printer.
Mobile: portable and battery powered with tight size, weight and energy limits; mobile phones, smart watches, handheld GPS units.

concepts.text: Classification by complexity and by processor type:
items: Small-scale: a single 8-bit or 16-bit microcontroller, little memory, programmed in C or assembly, no operating system (toys, simple appliances).
Medium-scale: one or more 16/32-bit microcontrollers or DSPs, more memory, an RTOS and complex software tools (routers, printers).
Sophisticated: 32/64-bit processors, systems-on-chip, FPGA or ASIC co-processors and an embedded Linux or RTOS with heavy hardware-software co-design (mobile phones, automotive ECUs).
By processor type the three choices are general-purpose, single-purpose and application-specific instruction-set processors, compared in the table below.

rows: Medium to high; needs compiler and tools

concepts.text: Three technologies the embedded designer chooses among (Moore's law, transistor counts doubling every 18 months, keeps pushing all three):
items: Processor technology: general-purpose (software), single-purpose (hardware) or ASIP; the architecture used to implement the desired functionality.

IC technology: how the processor is mapped onto silicon: full-custom VLSI, semi-custom ASIC (gate array or standard cell) or programmable logic device (PLD, FPGA); higher NRE buys lower unit cost, size and power.

Design technology: the tools that convert the concept into an implementation: compilation and synthesis, libraries and IP cores, test and verification; better tools shrink NRE cost and time-to-market.

rows: One dedicated function fixed at design time
Microcontroller, DSP or SoC chosen for the task; limited memory
Powerful CPU, large RAM and disk, expandable
Cost, size, power and real-time deadlines dominate

None, a small RTOS or embedded Linux, stored in Flash
Full OS (Windows, Linux) loaded from disk

Developed and run on the same machine

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Cost Models, Market Windows and Technology Choices

The simplified time-to-market model draws revenue against time as a triangle. An on-time product's revenue rises linearly from launch at time 0 to a peak at W and falls back to zero at 2W, so with a rise of one unit per unit time its area is (1/2)(2W)(W) = W². A product launched D late climbs at the same rate, must peak at the same time W because the market does not wait for it, and still dies at 2W, so its triangle has base 2W − D and height W − D. The fraction of revenue lost is the difference of the two areas divided by W², which simplifies to D(3W − D)/(2W²).

concepts.plainText: Loss fraction = [W^2 − (1/2)(2W − D)(W − D)] / W^2 = D(3W − D) / (2W^2); 2W = market window, D = delay

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: revenue lost by a late launch
Market window 2W = 20 months (W = 10); on-time revenue $8.0 million
Delay D = 3 months
Loss = D(3W - D) / (2W^2) = 3 x (30 - 3) / (2 x 100) = 81 / 200 = 0.405
Revenue lost = 0.405 x $8.0 million = $3.24 million (naive 3/20 = 15 % is far too low)
Largest delay for a loss of at most 20 %:  D(30 - D) <= 0.20 x 200 = 40
D^2 - 30D + 40 >= 0  ->  D <= (30 - sqrt(900 - 160)) / 2 = (30 - 27.20) / 2
D <= 1.40 months: about six weeks late already costs a fifth of the revenue

Total cost = NRE + unit cost × N and per-product cost = NRE/N + unit cost, where N is the production volume. For two technologies where NRE1 is lower than NRE2 but unit cost u1 is higher than u2, the total costs are equal at the break-even volume N_be = (NRE2 − NRE1)/(u1 − u2); below N_be the low-NRE choice is cheaper and above it the low-unit-cost choice wins. As N grows the per-product cost falls towards the unit cost, which is why full-custom or standard-cell silicon pays off only for high-volume products, while FPGAs and off-the-shelf processors suit small runs.

concepts.plainText: Break-even volume N_be = (NRE2 − NRE1) / (u1 − u2), where u1 and u2 are the unit costs and NRE1 < NRE2

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: choosing among three technologies
Option             NRE        Unit cost
A  FPGA            $5,000     $40
B  gate array      $45,000    $15
C  standard cell   $250,000   $5
A = B at (45,000 - 5,000) / (40 - 15)    = 1,600 units
B = C at (250,000 - 45,000) / (15 - 5)   = 20,500 units
Cheapest: A below 1,600 units, B from 1,600 to 20,500, C above 20,500
At N = 10,000: A $405,000 ($40.50 each), B $195,000 ($19.50), C $300,000 ($30.00)

concepts.text: Design technology and designer productivity:
items: Compilation and synthesis automate the move down the abstraction levels: behavioural (high-level) synthesis turns a sequential program into a datapath and controller, RT synthesis turns FSMs and register transfers into gates and flip-flops, logic synthesis optimises the gate network, and a compiler turns C into machine code.
Libraries and IP cores bring in pre-designed, pre-verified blocks such as a UART, a USB controller or a whole processor core, so they need not be designed again.
Test and verification (simulation, co-simulation of hardware and software, formal checks, FPGA prototypes) catch errors at each level and avoid costly iterations late in the flow.

Productivity gap: IC capacity has grown about 58 % per year while designer productivity grew about 21 % per year (SEMATECH figures quoted by Vahid), so the transistors available outrun what teams can design.
Mythical man-month: adding designers adds communication overhead; beyond some team size each extra person lowers total output and the project finishes later.

Hard (failure), firm (late result useless but harmless), soft (quality degrades)
Airbag; a sensor reading discarded when late; video player
Event-triggered (interrupts on input changes) or time-triggered (fixed timer ticks)
Keypad controller; engine ECU sampling every 5 ms

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: latency, throughput and power
Camera: one image takes 0.4 s end to end -> latency 0.4 s, throughput 2.5 images/s
Two equal pipelined stages of 0.2 s: throughput 5 images/s, latency still 0.4 s
Dynamic power P = aCV^2f; supply lowered from 5.0 V to 3.3 V, same C and f
P_new / P_old = (3.3 / 5.0)^2 = 0.4356  ->  56.4 % less dynamic power
Also halving f: P ratio = 0.4356 x 0.5 = 0.218, but the task takes twice as long
Energy per task = P x t is proportional to V^2 only: 0.4356 of the original either way

Common slips: W is half the market window, not the whole window; the loss formula gives a fraction, so multiply by 100 for a percentage and by the on-time revenue for money. Per-product cost includes NRE/N while unit cost does not, and pipelining raises throughput but does not shorten the latency of a single task.

formulas.plainText: Cost per unit = unit cost + NRE / N units
Revenue loss fraction = D(3W - D) / (2 W^2)
Dynamic power = activity factor x switched capacitance x V^2 x frequency
Moore's law: transistors per chip double about every 18 months

notes.text: Remember the three defining characteristics as one phrase: single-functioned, tightly constrained, reactive and real-time. NRE is the one-time design cost; unit cost is per copy. MCQs often swap these two definitions.

Hard versus soft real-time is about the consequence of a missed deadline, not about speed. A pacemaker running at a few hertz is hard real-time; a video player at 60 frames per second is soft real-time.

The three processor types differ only in how much of the datapath and controller is fixed: general-purpose has a general datapath and a program memory, single-purpose has a custom datapath and controller with no program memory, and an ASIP sits in between.

concepts.text: What an Operating System Does

An operating system (OS) is the software layer that manages hardware resources (CPU time, memory, I/O devices, files) and provides services to application programs. It hides hardware details behind system calls, shares the CPU among many activities, protects programs from each other and handles interrupts. In an embedded system the OS is often a small real-time kernel linked with the application into one firmware image.
Kernel space vs user space:
items: Kernel space: privileged (supervisor) mode; the kernel can execute every instruction and access all memory and device registers.
User space: unprivileged mode; applications reach hardware only through system calls, which trap into the kernel.
Monolithic kernels (e.g. Linux) put drivers and services in kernel space; microkernels (e.g. QNX) keep only scheduling, IPC and basic memory management in the kernel.
Many small RTOSes (FreeRTOS, uC/OS on MCUs without an MMU) run tasks and kernel in one address space, trading protection for speed and simplicity.

concepts.text: RTOS vs General-Purpose OS

rows: Bounded, small interrupt and dispatch latency
Variable, may be long under load

concepts.text: Classes of real-time systems (by the cost of a missed deadline):
items: Hard real-time: missing a deadline is a system failure (airbag deployment, pacemaker, flight control).
Firm real-time: a late result is useless and discarded, but occasional misses are tolerated (video frame decoding).
Soft real-time: late results still have reduced value; quality degrades gracefully (audio streaming, online games).
Real-time means correct AND on time: determinism matters more than raw speed.

concepts.text: Tasks, Processes and the PCB

A program is passive code on disk or flash; a process is a program in execution with its own address space, stack, registers and resources. In an RTOS the schedulable unit is usually called a task, which behaves like a thread. The kernel keeps a Process (or Task) Control Block (PCB/TCB) for each one, holding the process ID, state, priority, saved program counter and registers, stack pointer, memory limits, open files/resources and accounting information.

rows: Can run, waiting for the CPU
Pre-empted to Ready; waits to Blocked; exits to Terminated
Waiting for an event, I/O, delay or semaphore
Shared with other threads of the process
A crash can bring down the whole process

concepts.text: Context Switch and Interrupt Timing

A context switch saves the state (registers, PC, stack pointer, status word) of the running task in its TCB and restores the state of the next task chosen by the scheduler. It is pure overhead: no useful work is done during the switch, so an RTOS keeps it short and bounded. Interrupt latency is the time from an interrupt request to the first instruction of its ISR; it grows when interrupts are disabled for long periods inside the kernel or drivers.

concepts.plainText: Interrupt response time = interrupt latency + ISR execution time

concepts.text: Kernel objects an RTOS typically provides:
items: Tasks/threads with fixed priorities and their TCBs and stacks.
Semaphores (binary and counting) and mutexes for synchronisation.
Message queues, mailboxes, pipes and event flags for communication.
Software timers, delays and tick counter (system tick, e.g. 1 ms).
Memory pools with fixed-size blocks for deterministic allocation.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Kernels, Task States and Switching Cost

An embedded OS differs from a desktop OS less in its ideas than in its priorities. It is configured when the firmware is built, so only the kernel objects the application uses are linked in, and the image runs from Flash with a few kilobytes of RAM. Tasks, stacks and queues are often created statically at start-up; there is usually no disk, no demand paging and no MMU, and every kernel service is written so that its worst-case execution time is known. A GPOS instead optimises average throughput and fairness, and paging, dynamic memory allocation and long non-pre-emptible kernel paths make its worst case large and hard to bound.

rows: Scheduler, memory manager, drivers, file systems, network stack
Only scheduling, IPC, basic memory management and interrupt dispatch
One system call; services call each other directly
Message to a user-space server and a reply, with extra mode and context switches
Slower per request because of IPC
Confined to its server process, which can be restarted

concepts.text: Determinism means that every kernel service and every path from an event to its response has a known upper bound; it does not mean that the average is fast. Between an external event and the first instruction of the task that handles it, four delays add up: interrupt latency (hardware recognition plus any time interrupts are disabled), ISR execution, the scheduler's decision and the context switch, the last two together being the scheduling or dispatch latency. The variation of these delays from one occurrence to the next is called jitter. RTOS kernels keep the scheduler O(1), for example with one bit per priority level in a ready bitmap whose highest set bit is found by a count-leading-zeros instruction, so dispatch time does not grow with the number of tasks.

concepts.plainText: Event-to-task latency = interrupt latency + ISR execution time + scheduler time + context-switch time

rows: Scheduler dispatches the highest-priority ready task
Kernel decision after a tick, ISR or API call
Pre-empted by a higher-priority task, or its time slice ends
taskYIELD() or a tick with equal-priority tasks ready
Waits for a delay, semaphore, queue or event
The awaited event occurs or the timeout expires

concepts.text: What the kernel keeps for each task, and where:
items: TCB: task ID or name, state, current and base priority, saved stack pointer (or saved registers), stack base and size, links into the ready or waiting lists, the event or timeout being waited for, and statistics such as run time.

Context: program counter, stack pointer, status register and general-purpose registers, plus FPU registers if the task uses floating point; many small kernels push it onto the task's own stack and keep only the stack pointer in the TCB.
Not in the TCB: the task's code, which stays in Flash or the process image, and its local variables, which live on its stack.
A GPOS process control block adds the memory map (page-table pointer), open-file table, signal handlers and parent/child links; a thread control block holds only the per-thread part.

concepts.text:
Context-switch time on an 80 MHz CPU (12.5 ns per cycle)
save 16 registers + restore 16 registers = 32 transfers
32 transfers x 1 cycle              = 32 cycles
exception entry/exit + scheduler    = 48 cycles
t_cs = (32 + 48) x 12.5 ns          = 1.0 µs
RAM for 6 tasks: TCB 80 B, stack 512 B (1 KB = 1024 B)
6 x (80 + 512) = 3552 B = 3.47 KB
each stack must also leave room for one saved frame: 16 x 4 B = 64 B

Round robin: q = 10 ms, t_cs = 0.2 ms
overhead = t_cs / (q + t_cs) = 0.2 / 10.2 = 1.96 %
smallest q for overhead <= 5 %: q >= t_cs (1 - 0.05) / 0.05 = 3.8 ms
RTOS load: 1 kHz tick at 4 µs, 300 switches/s at 5 µs
per second: 1000 x 4 µs + 300 x 5 µs = 4.0 ms + 1.5 ms = 5.5 ms
overhead = 5.5 ms / 1000 ms = 0.55 %
32-bit tick counter at 1 kHz wraps after 2^32 ms = 49.7 days

Threads can be provided by a user-space library or by the kernel itself. In the many-to-one model the kernel sees one thread per process, so switching is cheap, but a blocking system call stops every thread and two threads can never run on two cores at once; the one-to-one model of Linux and Windows maps each thread to a kernel thread and removes both limits at the cost of a kernel call per thread operation, and the many-to-many model multiplexes user threads over a pool of kernel threads. In an RTOS every task is effectively a kernel-level thread, and all tasks share one address space. Multithreading brings responsiveness (one thread waits for I/O while another runs), cheap data sharing, lower creation and switching cost than processes, and parallel speed-up on multicore chips.
Common mistakes and special cases:
items: Blocked never goes straight to Running, and Ready never goes to Blocked: a task must be running to ask to wait.
Round-robin overhead is t_cs / (q + t_cs), not t_cs / q; the two differ noticeably when the slice is short.
With n tasks in round robin, a task waits (n − 1) slices plus n switches before it runs again, because the switch back to it counts too.
A delay of n ticks blocks for between n − 1 and n tick periods, because the call happens part-way through a tick.
A thread switch inside one process is cheaper than a process switch because the address space, page tables and TLB stay the same, but the registers must still be saved.
Firm real-time: a late result is worthless but occasional misses are tolerated; soft real-time: a late result still has some value.

concepts.text: For overhead questions, draw the time line slice, switch, slice, switch, and count every switch, including the one back to the task you are following. Convert cycles to time with t = cycles / f_clk, and add per-second costs (rate × duration) before dividing by one second.

formulas.plainText: Response time = interrupt latency + ISR execution time
Context-switch overhead = t_cs / (q + t_cs), q = time slice
Waiting time = turnaround time - CPU burst time

notes.text: Remember the three items a thread owns privately: program counter, register set and stack. Everything else (code, data, heap, open files) is shared with sibling threads.
Real-time does not mean fast. An RTOS is judged by worst-case, bounded response time; a GPOS may be faster on average yet still unsuitable for hard deadlines.
Running to Ready happens on pre-emption or time-slice expiry; Running to Blocked happens when the task waits for I/O, a delay or a semaphore; Blocked never goes directly to Running.

concepts.text: Why a Hardware Description Language

VHDL stands for VHSIC Hardware Description Language, where VHSIC is Very High Speed Integrated Circuit, a US Department of Defense programme of the 1980s. It is standardised as IEEE 1076 (revisions 1987, 1993, 2002, 2008). Unlike a software language, VHDL describes hardware that operates concurrently, and the same description is used both to simulate a design and to synthesise it into gates for an FPGA or ASIC. Verilog (IEEE 1364, now SystemVerilog IEEE 1800) is the other major HDL, with a terser C-like syntax.
Typical HDL design flow:
items: Specification: define function, interfaces and timing targets.
HDL coding (RTL): write entities and architectures in VHDL.
Functional simulation: a testbench applies stimulus and checks outputs, no timing yet.
Synthesis: the tool maps RTL to a gate-level netlist of the target library or FPGA primitives.
Implementation: place and route (FPGA) or floorplan, placement and routing (ASIC), followed by static timing analysis.
Timing simulation and sign-off, then programming the FPGA bitstream or ASIC fabrication.

concepts.text: Design Units: Library, Entity, Architecture

A VHDL file usually begins with library ieee; and use clauses such as use ieee.std_logic_1164.all; to make standard types visible. The entity declares the external interface: its name, ports and optional generics. The architecture body describes what happens inside, and one entity may have several architectures. A package collects shared types, constants, functions and components, and a configuration binds an entity to a chosen architecture (or component instances to specific entities).

rows: Can only be read inside the architecture

Used for tri-state buses; driven with 'Z' when released

concepts.text: The three architecture (modelling) styles:
items: Behavioural: describes what the circuit does using processes with if, case and loops, e.g. a process that compares two inputs.
Dataflow: describes how data flows using concurrent signal assignments and Boolean equations, e.g. s <= a xor b.
Structural: builds the design by instantiating and wiring components with port map, like a schematic netlist.
Real designs mix styles: a top level is often structural, while leaf blocks are dataflow or behavioural.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: VHDL Semantics, Types and Attributes

A VHDL simulator works in cycles: each triggered process runs until it reaches a wait statement (or the end of a process with a sensitivity list), and only then are the scheduled signal values updated, one delta cycle later at the same simulation time. Every signal read during one run of a process therefore sees the old value, and when the same signal is assigned twice in one run the last assignment wins. Variables change at once, and a process's variables keep their values from one activation of the process to the next (variables declared in a subprogram are re-created on every call). At time zero every object without an explicit initial value starts at the leftmost value of its type, T'left: 'U' for std_logic, the first literal of an enumeration, 0 for natural and integer'left for integer.
Type rules that often trip up beginners:
items: VHDL is strongly typed: std_logic_vector, unsigned and signed are distinct types, so an unsigned result must be converted back with std_logic_vector(...), and a vector becomes a number only through to_integer(unsigned(...)).

A subtype such as natural, positive or integer range 0 to 255 is compatible with its base type, and a value outside its range is a run-time bound-check error, never a silent wrap-around; a type declared with type t is range ... is a new type that needs an explicit conversion.
Array assignments must match in length: VHDL never pads or truncates automatically, so a 7-element value assigned to an 8-element target is an error.
Aggregates build composite values by position or by name, e.g. (7 => '1', others => '0') for a 7 downto 0 vector sets only its leftmost bit, and others fills whatever remains.
Bit-string literals: X"3C" is 00111100 and O"17" is 001111; VHDL-2008 allows a width prefix, and without a signed specifier the value is zero-extended on the left.
Record fields are selected with a dot (p.r, p.g) and array elements with parentheses, so mem(3)(7) is bit 7 of word 3 of an array of vectors.

concepts.text: Operator rules worth memorising:
items: and, or, xor, nand, nor and xnor have equal precedence, so mixing them needs parentheses: a and b or c does not compile while a and b and c does, and nand or nor cannot be chained at all.
not binds more tightly than the binary logical operators, so not a and b means (not a) and b.
Integer / truncates toward zero, rem takes the sign of the left operand and mod takes the sign of the right operand: 7 rem (−3) = 1 but 7 mod (−3) = −2.
Unary minus has lower precedence than *, /, mod and rem, so −7 mod 3 is read as −(7 mod 3) = −1; write (−7) mod 3 when a negative operand is meant.

The predefined relational operators on std_logic_vector compare element by element from the left, like strings, and vectors of different lengths are never equal; convert to unsigned or signed for a numeric comparison.
& concatenates elements and arrays, so for a 4-bit a, a(2 downto 0) & '0' shifts left by one place and a(0) & a(3 downto 1) rotates right.

concepts.text: Rules for concurrent statements and processes:
items: Concurrent statements (signal assignments, when-else, with-select, processes and instances) run whenever their inputs change, so their order in the architecture does not matter; if, case and loop are sequential and belong inside a process or subprogram.

In when-else the first true condition wins, giving a priority structure; with-select and case must cover every value of the selector, and since std_logic has nine values a 2-element std_logic_vector has 9² = 81 values, so when others is needed.

A process has either a sensitivity list or wait statements, never both; an incomplete sensitivity list makes simulation differ from the synthesised logic, and VHDL-2008 process (all) avoids the problem.
y <= a after 5 ns uses inertial delay, which swallows pulses shorter than 5 ns, while transport delay passes every pulse; synthesis ignores after clauses.
clk'event and clk = '1' is also true for a change from 'U' or 'X' to '1', whereas rising_edge(clk) additionally requires the previous value to be '0' or 'L'.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: reading a signal in the same process run that assigns it and expecting the new value; leaving inputs out of a combinational process's sensitivity list; using the non-standard std_logic_arith or std_logic_unsigned packages instead of numeric_std; comparing std_logic_vector values with < or > and expecting a numeric result; driving one std_logic signal from two processes, which resolves to 'X' when they disagree; and forgetting when others in a case or with-select on a std_logic_vector.

formulas.plainText: length of (h downto l) = h - l + 1
unsigned(n-1 downto 0) holds 0 to 2^n - 1
integer range 0 to M needs ceil(log2(M+1)) bits

notes.text: Entity = interface (ports), architecture = implementation. MCQs often test the nine std_logic values, especially 'Z' (high impedance), 'X' (unknown) and 'U' (uninitialised).
Signals use <= and update only after the process suspends; variables use := and update immediately. Reading a signal just after assigning it in the same process returns the old value.
VHDL is not case sensitive, comments start with --, and every statement ends with a semicolon.

concepts.text: Connecting Devices by Layer

Connecting devices are classified by the highest OSI layer they understand. Physical-layer devices (repeaters, hubs) only see bits, data-link devices (bridges, switches) read frame MAC addresses, network-layer devices (routers) read IP addresses, and gateways can work up to the application layer. The higher the layer, the more intelligent the forwarding decision and the more traffic the device can isolate.
Physical-layer devices regenerate and repeat bits without examining addresses:
items: Repeater: receives a weakened or corrupted signal and regenerates the original bit pattern before retransmitting it, extending the physical length of a LAN segment. It regenerates rather than amplifies, so noise is not amplified.

Hub: a multiport repeater. A frame arriving on one port is broadcast out of every other port, so all attached stations share the bandwidth and form a single collision domain, which causes congestion as the network grows.
Hubs operate half-duplex and cannot filter traffic; a passive hub simply joins wires, while an active hub also regenerates the signal.

concepts.text: Bridges

A bridge operates at the physical and data link layers and connects two (or a few) LAN segments. It keeps a table of MAC addresses and ports: a frame whose destination is on the same segment it arrived from is filtered (dropped), otherwise it is forwarded only to the correct segment, and frames with an unknown destination are flooded. A transparent (learning) bridge builds its table automatically by recording the source MAC address and incoming port of every frame, so stations are unaware of it. Because redundant bridges create loops in which broadcasts circulate forever, bridges run the Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1D), which blocks redundant ports to form a loop-free tree.
Switches

A layer-2 switch is essentially a fast multiport bridge implemented in hardware. It learns MAC addresses into a MAC address (CAM) table and delivers each frame only to the port of the destination, so every port is a separate collision domain and full-duplex links remove collisions entirely. All ports still belong to one broadcast domain: broadcasts and unknown unicasts are flooded to every port.
Switching methods and extensions to know:
items: Store-and-forward: receives the entire frame and checks the CRC before forwarding; higher latency but drops corrupt frames.
Cut-through: starts forwarding as soon as the destination MAC (first 6 bytes after the preamble) is read; lowest latency but forwards errored frames.
Fragment-free: reads the first 64 bytes before forwarding, filtering most collision fragments (runts).
VLAN (IEEE 802.1Q): logically divides one switch into several broadcast domains, each behaving like a separate LAN.
Layer-3 switch: a switch that also routes between VLANs or subnets using IP addresses at hardware speed.

concepts.text: Routers and Other Devices

A router works at layers 1 to 3 and connects different networks (for example a LAN to a WAN or to the Internet). It forwards packets using the destination IP address and a routing table built statically by an administrator or dynamically by routing protocols such as RIP, OSPF and BGP. Every router interface belongs to a different network, so a router separates both collision domains and broadcast domains; it does not forward broadcasts by default. Routers also choose best paths, decrement TTL and can filter traffic with access control lists.
Other devices commonly found in a network:
items: Gateway: operates up to the application layer and translates between networks that use different protocol stacks or formats (e.g. an e-mail or VoIP gateway); in TCP/IP the term 'default gateway' simply means the router a host uses to leave its subnet.
Modem (modulator-demodulator): converts digital data to analog signals for telephone or cable lines and back, e.g. DSL and cable modems.
Wireless access point (AP): a layer-2 device that bridges 802.11 wireless stations onto a wired Ethernet LAN.
NIC (network interface card): gives a host its physical connection and its unique 48-bit MAC address; it works at layers 1 and 2.
Brouter: a combined bridge and router that routes routable protocols and bridges the rest.

rows: 1 collision domain per port, 1 broadcast domain
1 collision domain per port, 1 broadcast domain (per VLAN)
1 collision and 1 broadcast domain per interface

concepts.text: Worked Example: Counting Domains

A router R has two interfaces in use. Interface 1 connects to switch S; S also connects three PCs directly and one hub H1 that has four PCs. Interface 2 connects to hub H2 with six PCs. Collision domains: each used switch port is one domain, so S gives 5 (link to R, three PCs, the H1 segment with its four PCs); H2 and its link to R form 1 more, so the total is 6. Broadcast domains: only the router splits them, so there are 2, one per router interface.

concepts.plainText: Broadcast domains = number of router interfaces in use (without VLANs)

concepts.text: Going Deeper: How Devices Learn, Filter and Forward
A quick picture of each device, with an everyday analogy:
items: Hub (layer 1), the least intelligent device: whatever arrives on one port is repeated out of all the others, like shouting in a room where everyone hears. All ports share one collision domain, so every added station adds congestion, and a hub is never faster than a switch.

Bridge (layer 2): joins two LAN segments and passes a frame across only when the destination MAC address is on the other side, like a doorkeeper between two rooms who carries a note through only if the addressee is in the other room. Each side becomes its own collision domain.

Switch (layer 2), a 'smart hub' or multiport bridge: sends each unicast frame only to the port of its destination MAC address, like whispering directly to one person, and lets every port run full-duplex at full speed.
Router (layer 3): joins different networks and forwards packets by destination IP address, making a path decision for each packet, like a post office sorting mail for different cities.
Memory line: hub = repeat to all; switch = direct delivery by MAC; router = between networks by IP.
A home 'Wi-Fi router' is several devices in one box: a router with NAT, a small Ethernet switch, a wireless access point and a DHCP server, and often a DSL, cable or fibre modem too.

concepts.text: A learning switch or bridge runs the same procedure for every frame. It first records the frame's source MAC address against the arrival port, with a timestamp. It then looks up the destination: a broadcast or an unknown unicast is flooded out of every port except the arrival port, a destination learned on the arrival port is filtered (dropped), and any other known destination is forwarded out of just its own port. Entries that are not refreshed within the ageing time (300 s by default in IEEE 802.1D) are deleted, so a station that moves is relearned at its new port.

rows: Flood to all ports except the arrival port (within the VLAN)
Unicast not yet in the MAC table
Flood to all ports except the arrival port
Unicast learned on the arrival port
Filter: discard, the segment already delivered it
Forward out of that one port only
Any frame failing the FCS check (store-and-forward)

concepts.text:
Worked trace 1: 4-port switch, empty table; A on port 1, B on 2, C on 3, D on 4
Frame        Learns   Destination known?   Action
1  A -> B    A = 1    no                   flood to 2, 3, 4
2  B -> A    B = 2    yes (port 1)         forward to 1
3  C -> A    C = 3    yes (port 1)         forward to 1
4  A -> D    (A)      no                   flood to 2, 3, 4
5  D -> all  D = 4    broadcast            flood to 1, 2, 3
6  A -> D    (A)      yes (port 4)         forward to 4
Final table: A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4; 3 of the 6 frames were flooded

A router treats each packet quite differently. It removes the layer-2 frame, checks the IPv4 header and looks up the destination IP address in its routing table using the longest-prefix match. It then decrements TTL (discarding the packet and sending ICMP Time Exceeded if TTL reaches 0), recomputes the header checksum, uses ARP to find the next hop's MAC address and sends the packet in a brand-new frame. Limited broadcasts (255.255.255.255) are never forwarded, which is why every router interface bounds a broadcast domain.

concepts.plainText: Store-and-forward over N links (N - 1 switches): d = N x L/R; cut-through: d is about L/R + (N - 1) x h/R, where h bits are read before forwarding starts (propagation, queueing and processing ignored)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: 1,000-byte frame, 2 switches (3 links), 1 Gbps links
L/R = 8,000 bits / 10^9 bit/s                 = 8 µs per link
Store-and-forward: each switch waits for the whole frame
  d = 3 x 8 µs                                = 24 µs
Cut-through: forward after the 6-byte destination MAC
  h/R = 48 bits / 10^9 bit/s                   = 0.048 µs per switch
  d = 8 + 2 x 0.048                            = 8.096 µs
Propagation, queueing, processing and preamble ignored

Worked example 3: counting domains with VLANs
24-port switch: VLAN 10 = ports 1-8, VLAN 20 = 9-16, VLAN 30 = 17-22
Ports 1-7: one PC each; port 8: a hub with 5 PCs
Ports 9-16 and 17-22: one PC each; port 23: trunk to a router
Port 24: unused
Collision domains = used ports = 7 + 1 (hub segment) + 8 + 6 + 1 = 23
Broadcast domains = VLANs = 3 (the router routes between them)
Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1D) in brief:
items: Every switch has a bridge ID made of a priority (default 32768) followed by its MAC address. The lowest bridge ID wins the root-bridge election, so priority is compared first and the MAC address only breaks ties.
Each non-root switch chooses one root port, its port with the lowest total path cost to the root; each LAN segment gets one designated port; all remaining ports are blocked.
Port costs fall with link speed (802.1D-1998 values: 100 for 10 Mbps, 19 for 100 Mbps, 4 for 1 Gbps), so faster paths are preferred.
Classic STP moves a port through blocking, listening, learning and forwarding, taking 30 to 50 s; Rapid STP (802.1w) converges in a few seconds or less.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: bridges and switches do not split broadcast domains (only routers or VLANs do); a layer-2 switch forwards by MAC address, never by IP; a repeater regenerates the bit pattern instead of amplifying the analog signal and its noise; a hub is not faster than a switch, because its ports share one half-duplex collision domain; and a basic bridge does not translate between protocols.

For domain counting, give one collision domain to every link or segment that ends at a switch, bridge or router port (a hub and everything on it is one segment), and one broadcast domain to every router interface or VLAN in use.

formulas.plainText: Collision domains on a switch = number of ports in use
Broadcast domains = router interfaces in use (without VLANs)
A hub with n ports forms a single collision domain

notes.text: Quick rule: a hub gives 1 collision and 1 broadcast domain; an n-port switch gives n collision domains and 1 broadcast domain; a router gives one collision and one broadcast domain per interface.
Bridges and switches do not stop broadcasts; they flood broadcast and unknown-destination frames to all ports. Only routers (or VLANs on a switch) break up broadcast domains.
A switch is often called a multiport bridge and a hub a multiport repeater; MCQs often test this pairing along with the layer of each device.

concepts.text: Guided vs Unguided Media

Transmission media sit below the physical layer and carry signals between devices. Guided (wired) media confine the signal to a physical path: twisted-pair and coaxial cable carry electrical signals, and optical fibre carries light. Unguided (wireless) media broadcast electromagnetic waves through air or space without a physical conductor: radio waves, microwaves and infrared. Choice depends on bandwidth, distance, cost, noise immunity, security and ease of installation.
Copper cables in practice:
items: Twisted pair: two insulated copper wires twisted together so that interference and crosstalk induced in the two wires cancel; terminated with RJ-45 connectors and limited to about 100 m per Ethernet segment.
UTP (unshielded twisted pair) is cheap and flexible and dominates LANs; STP (shielded twisted pair) adds a metal foil or braid for better noise immunity at higher cost and stiffness.

Coaxial cable: a central copper conductor, insulator, braided outer conductor (shield) and jacket; higher bandwidth and better shielding than twisted pair. RG-59/RG-6 carry cable TV, RG-58 was thin Ethernet (10Base2, 185 m) and RG-8 thick Ethernet (10Base5, 500 m), using BNC connectors.

rows: 1 Gbps (10 Gbps up to about 55 m)

concepts.text: Optical Fibre

Optical fibre guides light through a thin glass or plastic core surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index. When light strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle, it undergoes total internal reflection and stays inside the core, travelling long distances with very little loss. A light source (LED or laser) at the transmitter and a photodiode at the receiver convert between electrical and optical signals.
Fibre modes, advantages and drawbacks:
items: Multimode: wider core (50 or 62.5 micrometres), many light paths, LED source; modal dispersion limits it to short distances (hundreds of metres to about 2 km). Step-index has a sharp core boundary; graded-index gradually lowers the index to reduce dispersion.
Single-mode: very narrow core (about 8-10 micrometres), one path, laser source; lowest dispersion, used for long-haul links of tens to hundreds of kilometres.
Advantages: very high bandwidth, low attenuation, immunity to electromagnetic interference, light weight, and difficult to tap (better security).
Disadvantages: higher installation cost, needs skilled splicing, fragile, and light travels in one direction so a duplex link needs two fibres.

concepts.text: Unguided (Wireless) Media
Wireless media are grouped by frequency band:
items: Radio waves (about 3 kHz to 1 GHz): omnidirectional, travel long distances and penetrate walls; used for AM/FM radio, TV and paging, but prone to interference.
Microwaves (1 to 300 GHz): unidirectional, need line of sight between dish or horn antennas and relay towers roughly every 50 km; used for cellular, terrestrial links, Wi-Fi and satellite.
Infrared (300 GHz to 400 THz): very short range, line of sight, cannot penetrate walls, so it does not interfere between rooms; used in remote controls and IrDA.
Satellite: a microwave relay in orbit; a geostationary satellite at about 35,786 km covers a third of the Earth, but the up-and-down path adds roughly 240-270 ms of propagation delay.

rows: Line of sight / a few metres

concepts.text: Impairments, Bandwidth and Data Rate

Signals are degraded by three impairments. Attenuation is loss of energy with distance, measured in decibels and compensated by amplifiers or repeaters. Distortion is change of signal shape because different frequency components travel at different speeds. Noise is unwanted energy: thermal (random electron motion), induced (from motors and appliances), crosstalk (from adjacent wires) and impulse (spikes from lightning or power lines). Bandwidth in hertz is the range of frequencies a channel passes; together with the number of signal levels and the signal-to-noise ratio it limits the data rate in bits per second.

concepts.plainText: Nyquist bit rate = 2 x B x log2(L), B = bandwidth in Hz, L = number of signal levels
Shannon capacity = B x log2(1 + SNR), SNR as a ratio, not in dB

concepts.text: Transmission delay is the time to push all bits of a frame onto the link, L/R, and depends on frame length and bandwidth; propagation delay is the time for one bit to travel the link, d/v, and depends on distance and signal speed (about 2 x 10^8 m/s in copper or fibre). Example: a 2,500-byte (20,000-bit) frame on a 10 Mbps link that is 1,000 km long has transmission delay 20,000 / 10^7 = 2 ms and propagation delay 10^6 / (2 x 10^8) = 5 ms, so the last bit arrives 7 ms after sending begins (ignoring queuing and processing).

Line coding converts a digital bit sequence into a digital signal. NRZ-L represents 1 and 0 by two fixed voltage levels, and NRZ-I represents a 1 by inverting the level; both are bandwidth-efficient but lose synchronisation on long runs of identical bits and have a DC component. Manchester coding (used in 10 Mbps Ethernet) places a transition in the middle of every bit, a low-to-high for one value and high-to-low for the other, giving self-clocking and no DC component at the cost of twice the bandwidth; differential Manchester (Token Ring) always transitions mid-bit and encodes 0 by an extra transition at the bit start.
Going Deeper: Media Choices, Fibre Optics and Channel Limits
Guided (wired) media at a glance, from cheapest to most capable:
items: Twisted pair: two insulated copper wires twisted together; the cheapest and easiest to install, used for telephone lines and Ethernet (Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a), but limited to short runs of about 100 m per Ethernet segment.

Coaxial cable: a central conductor, insulation, a braided shield and an outer jacket; better shielded and higher in bandwidth than twisted pair, used for cable TV and cable broadband and for the old 10Base2/10Base5 Ethernet; medium distances.

Optical fibre: carries light instead of electric current; the highest bandwidth and lowest attenuation, immune to electromagnetic interference, and used for Internet backbones, fibre-to-the-home and data-centre links over long distances, but the most costly to install and splice.

Correction to a common note: fibre is not 'faster' in propagation. Light in glass travels at about 2 x 10^8 m/s, roughly the speed of signals in copper; fibre's advantage is bandwidth (bits per second) and low loss, not a shorter delay, and it still suffers attenuation and dispersion even though it picks up no electrical interference.

concepts.text: Unguided (wireless) media, and where everyday systems fit:
items: Radio waves (about 3 kHz to 1 GHz in Forouzan's split): omnidirectional, long range and able to pass through walls; used for AM/FM radio, TV and paging.

Wi-Fi (2.4, 5 and 6 GHz), Bluetooth (2.4 GHz) and mobile networks are called radio systems in everyday speech; by the same split most of their carriers lie in the microwave range, but they use omnidirectional antennas and still pass through walls, with more loss at higher frequencies.
Microwaves (1 to 300 GHz) with dish or horn antennas: highly directional and need line of sight; used for point-to-point terrestrial links and satellite communication.
Infrared (300 GHz to 400 THz): very short range and blocked by walls, so neighbouring rooms do not interfere; used in TV remotes and the old IrDA links between phones and laptops.
Satellites: the lower the orbit, the shorter the delay, but the more satellites are needed to cover the Earth and the faster each one moves across the sky.

rows: Ground-satellite-ground delay (minimum: stations directly below, 3 x 10^8 m/s)

concepts.text: Light passing from a denser medium (index n1) into a less dense one (n2 < n1) bends away from the normal, following Snell's law n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2. At the critical angle the refracted ray just grazes the boundary (θ2 = 90°), and at any larger angle of incidence all the light is reflected back into the core; this is total internal reflection. The numerical aperture (NA) measures the cone of light a fibre accepts: a larger index difference gives a larger NA, which eases coupling but increases modal dispersion in multimode fibre.

concepts.plainText: Critical angle θc = arcsin(n2 / n1); numerical aperture NA = sqrt(n1^2 - n2^2), where n1 is the core index and n2 the cladding index

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: critical angle and NA of a fibre
Core n1 = 1.48, cladding n2 = 1.46
n2 / n1 = 1.46 / 1.48 = 0.98649
θc = arcsin(0.98649) = 80.6°  (rays hitting the wall above 80.6° stay in)
NA = sqrt(1.48^2 - 1.46^2) = sqrt(2.1904 - 2.1316) = sqrt(0.0588) = 0.242
Acceptance half-angle in air = arcsin(0.242) = 14.0°

Decibels turn the multiplication of gains and losses into addition: a loss of 3 dB halves the power, 10 dB divides it by 10 and 20 dB by 100. Cable loss is quoted in dB per km (about 0.2 to 0.35 dB/km for single-mode fibre, far more for copper at high frequencies), so the total loss is the rate times the length plus connector and splice losses. Absolute power is often given in dBm, decibels relative to 1 mW: 0 dBm = 1 mW, 10 dBm = 10 mW and -30 dBm = 1 µW.

Worked example 2: a power budget in dB
Transmitter power              = 10 dBm (10 mW)
5 km of cable at 3 dB/km       = -15 dB
Amplifier                      = +10 dB
Two connectors at 0.5 dB each  = -1 dB
Output = 10 - 15 + 10 - 1      = 4 dBm
In milliwatts: 10^(4/10) mW    = 2.51 mW

Worked example 3: Shannon limit first, then Nyquist levels
B = 2 MHz, SNR = 24 dB -> S/N = 10^(24/10) = 251.2
C = B log2(1 + S/N) = 2 x 10^6 x log2(252.2) = 2 x 10^6 x 7.98 = 15.96 Mbps
Choose a safer rate below the limit, e.g. 12 Mbps
Nyquist: 12 x 10^6 = 2 x 2 x 10^6 x log2 L -> log2 L = 3 -> L = 8 levels
More levels cannot push the rate above 15.96 Mbps on this channel

Worked example 4: bandwidth-delay product and bit length
Fibre link 4,000 km, v = 2 x 10^8 m/s, R = 1 Gbps
Tp  = 4 x 10^6 m / 2 x 10^8 m/s        = 20 ms
BDP = R x Tp = 10^9 x 0.02            = 2 x 10^7 bits (2.5 MB) in flight
Over a full round trip: 2 x BDP        = 4 x 10^7 bits
Length of one bit = v / R = 2 x 10^8 / 10^9 = 0.2 m
A 1,500-byte frame (12,000 bits) fills only 2.4 km of the 4,000 km

Common mistakes: convert dB to a ratio before using Shannon (S/N = 10^(dB/10)); keep bandwidth in Hz and data rate in bit/s apart; use 1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s and multiply bytes by 8; do not double a one-way propagation delay unless a round trip is asked for; and remember that adding signal levels (Nyquist) helps only up to the Shannon limit, never beyond it.

formulas.plainText: SNR in dB = 10 log10(S/N); e.g. 30 dB means S/N = 1000
Transmission delay = frame length in bits / bandwidth in bits per second
Propagation delay = distance / propagation speed (about 2 x 10^8 m/s in cable)

notes.text: Convert dB to a ratio before using Shannon: S/N = 10^(dB/10). For B = 3,000 Hz and 30 dB (S/N = 1000), C = 3000 x log2(1001), about 3000 x 9.97, or roughly 30 kbps.

Nyquist gives the maximum rate for a noiseless channel with L levels, while Shannon gives the absolute capacity of a noisy channel. When both apply, Shannon is the upper limit and Nyquist tells you how many levels are needed to approach it.
Do not confuse the two delays: a faster link reduces transmission delay but not propagation delay, which depends only on distance and the medium.

concepts.text: Flow Control vs Error Control

Flow control is a set of procedures that tells the sender how much data it may send before it must wait for an acknowledgement, so that the receiver's buffer is not overrun. Error control combines error detection with retransmission of lost or damaged frames; at the data link layer this is done by Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ). In practice both are implemented together in the same protocol using sequence numbers, acknowledgements (ACK/NAK) and timers.
Stop-and-Wait

The sender transmits one frame and waits for its ACK before sending the next. It is simple but wastes the link whenever the propagation delay is large compared with the frame transmission time. Define a = t_prop / t_frame, where t_frame = frame length / bandwidth. One cycle lasts t_frame + 2 t_prop, of which only t_frame carries data.

concepts.plainText: U = 1 / (1 + 2a), a = t_prop / t_frame

concepts.text: Worked example: 1000-bit frames on a 1 Mbps link with 20 ms one-way propagation delay. t_frame = 1000 / 10^6 = 1 ms, so a = 20 and U = 1 / 41 ≈ 2.4%. A sliding window of W = 7 frames raises utilisation to 7 / 41 ≈ 17%, and a window of 41 or more frames keeps the link fully busy.
Sliding Window and ARQ Protocols

In sliding-window protocols the sender may have up to W unacknowledged frames outstanding. Frames carry m-bit sequence numbers that wrap around modulo 2^m. As ACKs arrive the window slides forward. Utilisation becomes W / (1 + 2a) when W < 1 + 2a, and 1 otherwise.
The three ARQ schemes:
items: Stop-and-wait ARQ: window of 1; frames and ACKs numbered 0 and 1 (1-bit sequence number) so duplicates can be recognised; the sender retransmits when its timer expires.
Go-Back-N ARQ: sender window up to 2^m − 1, receiver window 1; the receiver discards out-of-order frames, and on a timeout or NAK the sender resends the lost frame and every frame after it.

Selective Repeat ARQ: sender and receiver windows up to 2^(m−1) each; the receiver buffers out-of-order frames and only the damaged or lost frame is resent, saving bandwidth at the cost of buffering and complexity.

rows: Lost frame and all after it

concepts.text: Piggybacking: in bidirectional communication the acknowledgement for received frames is carried in the header of an outgoing data frame instead of a separate ACK frame, which improves efficiency. HDLC's N(R) field in I-frames is a piggybacked ACK.
HDLC (High-Level Data Link Control)

HDLC is an ISO bit-oriented protocol for point-to-point and multipoint links, implementing sliding-window ARQ. A frame has the fields Flag (01111110), Address, Control, Information, FCS (CRC-16 or CRC-32) and a closing Flag, with bit stuffing for transparency. Stations are primary, secondary or combined.

rows: Carries user data plus N(S) send and N(R) piggybacked ACK numbers
Flow/error control only: RR, RNR, REJ, SREJ
Link management: SABM, SNRM, UA, DISC, FRMR
Unbalanced: secondary may send only when polled by the primary
Balanced: two combined stations, either may start transmission

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Windows, Link Efficiency and HDLC

The basic problem of flow control is that a fast sender can overwhelm a slow receiver, and the two basic answers are stop-and-wait (send one frame, wait for its ACK, then send the next) and sliding window (send several frames before waiting). Why the sliding window wins is easiest to see by picturing the link as a pipe: it takes t_frame to push a frame in, and another 2 t_prop before the first ACK can come back. Stop-and-wait keeps the pipe busy for only 1 of every 1 + 2a frame times, while a window of 1 + 2a frames fills it completely. That number is the bandwidth × round-trip-delay product divided by the frame length, plus one.

concepts.latex: W_{full} = 1 + 2a = 1 + \frac{2\, t_{prop}\, B}{L},\quad S = U \cdot B
concepts.plainText: Window for 100% use: W_full = 1 + 2a = 1 + 2 t_prop B / L; throughput S = U × B

concepts.text:
Link: 10 Mbps, 2000 km of fibre (2 x 10^8 m/s), 1000-byte frames
t_frame = 8000 bits / 10^7 bit/s    = 0.8 ms
t_prop  = 2 x 10^6 m / 2 x 10^8 m/s = 10 ms  (one way)
a = t_prop / t_frame = 12.5,   1 + 2a = 26
Stop-and-wait: U = 1/26 = 3.85%  -> S = 0.0385 x 10 Mbps = 385 kbps
Window W = 7 : U = 7/26 = 26.9%  -> S = 2.69 Mbps
Full use needs W >= 26 frames outstanding:
  Go-Back-N        2^m - 1 >= 26 -> m = 5 bits (window up to 31)
  Selective Repeat 2^(m-1) >= 26 -> m = 6 bits (window up to 32)

3-bit numbers; S sends frames 0 1 2 3; frame 1 is lost; ACKs are not lost
Go-Back-N (receiver window 1, cumulative ACK = next frame expected)
  R: 0 ok -> ACK 1; 2 and 3 out of order -> discarded, ACK 1 repeated
  S: timer of frame 1 expires (or a NAK arrives) -> resends 1, 2, 3
Selective Repeat (receiver window 4, frames acknowledged individually)
  R: 0 ok -> delivered; 2 and 3 buffered and acknowledged; NAK 1 sent
  S: resends only frame 1; R then delivers 1, 2, 3 in order

Why the window limits? Take m = 2, so the numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3
Go-Back-N, W = 4: S sends 0 1 2 3, all arrive, all four ACKs are lost
  R now expects the NEXT frame 0; S times out and resends the OLD 0
  R accepts the old frame as new -> duplicate delivered
  With W = 3, R expects 3 and rejects the old 0: W <= 2^m - 1
Selective Repeat, W = 3: S sends 0 1 2, all arrive, all ACKs are lost
  R's window has moved to {3, 0, 1}; the resent old 0 falls inside it
  and is accepted as new -> duplicate delivered
  With W = 2, R's window is {2, 3} and the old 0 is rejected: W <= 2^(m-1)
Acknowledgements, timers and piggybacking in practice:
items: ACK n normally means 'every frame before n has arrived; send n next'. Go-Back-N and HDLC's N(R) use this cumulative form, so one ACK can confirm several frames.
A NAK (HDLC REJ or SREJ) lets the sender resend before its timer runs out. The timeout itself must exceed t_frame + 2 t_prop plus the ACK's transmission and processing time.
Go-Back-N needs only one timer, for the oldest outstanding frame; Selective Repeat keeps a timer for every outstanding frame.
Piggybacking puts the ACK in the header of a data frame going the other way. The receiver keeps a short ACK timer, and if no data frame is ready when it expires, it sends a separate ACK.
Sequence numbers wrap around modulo 2^m: with m = 3 the ninth frame is numbered 0 again.

rows: N(S) and N(R) (3 bits each) and the P/F bit
2-bit code (RR, REJ, RNR, SREJ), P/F and N(R); no N(S)
5 modifier bits (SABM, SNRM, DISC, UA, FRMR, …) and P/F
16-bit control field for I- and S-frames (U-frames keep 8 bits)
7-bit N(S) and N(R), so windows up to 127

concepts.text: HDLC supervisory frames, stations and modes:
items: RR (Receive Ready) acknowledges frames up to N(R) − 1 and invites more; RNR (Receive Not Ready) acknowledges them but tells the sender to pause, which is flow control.
REJ asks for frame N(R) and every frame after it (Go-Back-N); SREJ asks for frame N(R) only (Selective Repeat).
The P/F bit is Poll in a command (the primary asks for a response) and Final in a response (the last frame of the reply).

Stations: a primary sends commands, a secondary sends responses and a combined station does both. NRM (unbalanced) lets a secondary send only when polled, ABM (balanced) lets either combined station start, and ARM lets a secondary start without a poll but is rarely used.

concepts.text: Common mistakes in flow-control problems:
items: Using the round-trip time in a: a uses the one-way propagation delay, and the 2 in 1 + 2a already covers the return trip.
Mixing bits and bytes in t_frame = L / B, or treating 1 Mbps as 2^20 bit/s instead of 10^6 bit/s.
Forgetting the cap: when W ≥ 1 + 2a the utilisation is 100%, not W / (1 + 2a).
Using 2^m as the window: Go-Back-N allows 2^m − 1 and Selective Repeat 2^(m−1).
In Go-Back-N the sender resends the lost frame and every frame sent after it, not the frames before it that were already acknowledged.

concepts.text: Solve every efficiency problem in the same order: t_frame = L / B, t_prop = d / v, a = t_prop / t_frame, then U = W / (1 + 2a) capped at 100% (W = 1 for stop-and-wait), and finally throughput = U × B. Write the units at each step and check whether a question states a one-way delay or a round-trip time.

formulas.plainText: stop-and-wait U = 1/(1 + 2a), a = t_prop / t_frame
sliding window U = min(1, W / (1 + 2a))
Go-Back-N W <= 2^m - 1; Selective Repeat W <= 2^(m-1)

notes.text: For window-size MCQs, first find m (the number of sequence-number bits). Go-Back-N allows 2^m − 1 outstanding frames, Selective Repeat only half the sequence space, 2^(m−1).
Do not confuse the ratio a: it is propagation delay divided by transmission time. Use one-way propagation delay in a and remember the factor 2 accounts for the round trip.
PPP and LAPB, LAPD and LLC are all derived from HDLC; PPP keeps the HDLC-like frame but normally runs without numbered sequence control.

concepts.text: The Multiple Access Problem

When many stations share one broadcast channel, the MAC sublayer needs a rule for who transmits next; otherwise simultaneous transmissions collide and are lost. Multiple access protocols fall into three families: random access (contention), controlled access, and channelisation.
Random Access: ALOHA

In pure ALOHA a station sends whenever it has a frame; if no ACK comes back it waits a random time and resends. A frame is vulnerable to collision for 2 × T_fr (one frame time before and after it starts). Slotted ALOHA divides time into slots of one frame time and allows transmission only at slot boundaries, halving the vulnerable time to T_fr. With G the average number of frames offered per frame time, throughput S is:

concepts.latex: S_{pure} = G e^{-2G},\quad S_{slotted} = G e^{-G}
concepts.plainText: pure ALOHA S = G e^(-2G); slotted ALOHA S = G e^(-G)

concepts.text: CSMA and Persistence Methods
Carrier Sense Multiple Access: listen before talking. What a station does when it senses the channel:
items: 1-persistent: if idle, send immediately; if busy, keep sensing and send as soon as it becomes idle. Highest collision chance (classic Ethernet).
Non-persistent: if busy, wait a random time before sensing again. Fewer collisions but more idle time and delay.
p-persistent: used with slotted channels; when idle, send with probability p or defer to the next slot with probability 1 − p. Balances delay and collisions.
Collisions can still occur because of propagation delay: a station may sense idle before another station's signal has reached it.

concepts.text: CSMA/CD (Collision Detection)
Operation in classic (shared, half-duplex) Ethernet:
items: Sense the carrier; wait until the medium is idle (plus the inter-frame gap).
Transmit while monitoring the medium; if the signal on the wire differs from what is sent, a collision has occurred.
On collision stop sending the frame and transmit a 32-bit jam signal so every station notices.
Binary exponential backoff: after the n-th collision choose K at random from 0 to 2^min(n,10) − 1 and wait K slot times (slot = 512 bit times = 51.2 µs at 10 Mbps).
Abort and report failure after 16 unsuccessful attempts.

concepts.text: For collision detection to work, a station must still be transmitting when news of a collision from the far end arrives, i.e. the frame transmission time must be at least the round-trip propagation time. Worked example: classic 10 Mbps Ethernet allows a worst-case round trip of 51.2 µs, so L_min = 51.2 × 10^-6 × 10^7 = 512 bits = 64 bytes, which is why Ethernet frames are padded to 64 bytes.

concepts.plainText: L_min = 2 x t_prop x B, t_prop = distance / signal speed

concepts.text: CSMA/CA, Controlled Access and Channelisation

Wireless stations cannot listen while transmitting and cannot hear every other station, so 802.11 avoids collisions rather than detecting them. A station senses the channel, waits an inter-frame space (SIFS < PIFS < DIFS, shorter means higher priority) plus a random contention window, then sends. Optionally it first exchanges RTS/CTS; other stations set their Network Allocation Vector (NAV) and stay quiet. The receiver confirms every correct frame with an ACK. Controlled access methods avoid collisions entirely: reservation (stations book slots in a reservation frame), polling (a primary polls or selects secondaries) and token passing (only the holder of the token may send).

rows: Time slots on a shared frequency
Orthogonal codes; all users share time and frequency

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Multiple Access

Access control, the last of the five data link functions (framing, error detection, error correction, flow control and access control), decides who may use a shared medium at any moment. CSMA/CD follows the rules of a polite conversation: listen first (carrier sense), speak only when the line is quiet, keep listening while speaking, stop at once if someone else starts (collision detection), send a short jam signal so everyone knows, then wait a random backoff time and try again. A radio cannot follow the same rules, because its own signal drowns out any distant one while it is transmitting and it may not even hear every other station. Wi-Fi therefore uses CSMA/CA, which tries to avoid collisions before sending and learns about the ones that still happen from a missing ACK.

The ALOHA formulas assume that transmission attempts, new frames and retransmissions together, arrive as a Poisson process with an average of G attempts per frame time T_fr. A pure ALOHA frame survives only if no other attempt starts inside its 2 × T_fr vulnerable window, which happens with probability e^(−2G), while a slotted ALOHA frame only needs its own slot to itself, probability e^(−G). Multiplying by G gives the throughput S, and setting dS/dG = 0 puts the peaks at G = 0.5 for pure and G = 1 for slotted ALOHA. With a finite number N of stations that each send in a slot with probability p, a slot succeeds when exactly one station sends; the best choice p = 1/N gives a success rate that falls towards 1/e as N grows.

Worked example 1: ALOHA throughput
Channel 50 kbps, frame 500 bits -> T_fr = 500 / 50 000 = 10 ms
Capacity = 1 / T_fr = 100 frames/s; offered 50 frames/s -> G = 0.5
Pure ALOHA:    S = G e^(-2G) = 0.5 e^(-1)   = 0.184 -> 18.4 frames/s succeed
Slotted ALOHA: S = G e^(-G)  = 0.5 e^(-0.5) = 0.303 -> 30.3 frames/s succeed
Offered 100 frames/s (G = 1):
Pure ALOHA:    S = 1 x e^(-2) = 0.135 -> 13.5 frames/s (past its peak)
Slotted ALOHA: S = 1 x e^(-1) = 0.368 -> 36.8 frames/s (exactly its peak)

The ratio a = t_prop / t_trans compares how long a station stays unaware of another transmission with the length of a frame. Carrier sensing only helps if news of a transmission spreads quickly relative to the frame time, so every CSMA variant works best when a is small, that is with short cables and long frames. Raising the bit rate while keeping the frame and cable unchanged shrinks t_trans and raises a, which is why half-duplex Gigabit Ethernet had to stretch its slot to 512 bytes (carrier extension) and why 10 Gbps Ethernet dropped CSMA/CD altogether.

concepts.plainText: Slotted ALOHA with N stations each sending with probability p: success probability per slot S_N = N p (1 − p)^(N − 1), largest at p = 1/N. CSMA/CD: a = t_prop / t_trans and efficiency η ≈ 1 / (1 + 5a) (Kurose–Ross approximation), which tends to 1 as a tends to 0.

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: CSMA/CD distance and efficiency (v = 2 x 10^8 m/s)
Rule: T_fr >= 2 x t_prop, so d_max = v x T_fr / 2; minimum frame 64 bytes = 512 bits
100 Mbps: T_fr = 512 / 10^8 = 5.12 us  -> d_max = 2e8 x 5.12e-6 / 2 = 512 m
1 Gbps:   T_fr = 512 / 10^9 = 0.512 us -> d_max = 51.2 m (too short to be useful)
1 Gbps, 512-byte slot (4096 bits): T_fr = 4.096 us -> d_max = 409.6 m
Efficiency at 100 Mbps, 500 m cable, 1500-byte frames:
  t_prop = 500 / 2e8 = 2.5 us; t_trans = 12 000 / 10^8 = 120 us; a = 0.0208
  eta = 1 / (1 + 5 x 0.0208) = 0.906 -> about 90.6 %
Real limits are shorter (about 205 m at 100 Mbps) because repeaters add delay

Worked trace: binary exponential backoff for two stations A and B (10 Mbps, slot 51.2 us)
After collision 1: K from {0, 1}         P(same K, collide again) = 2/4  = 1/2
After collision 2: K from {0, 1, 2, 3}   P(same K, collide again) = 4/16 = 1/4
After collision 3: K from {0 .. 7}       P(same K, collide again) = 1/8
  longest wait after collision 3 = 7 x 51.2 us = 358.4 us
After collision n (n <= 10): K from {0 .. 2^n - 1}; collisions 10 to 15 keep {0 .. 1023}
After the 16th collision the frame is dropped and an error is reported upward
CSMA/CA as used by the 802.11 distributed coordination function (DCF):
items: Physical carrier sense: a station senses the medium; if it has been idle for DIFS the countdown may proceed, otherwise the station waits.

Random backoff: the station picks a number of slots between 0 and the contention window CW; the counter drops by one for every idle slot and is frozen while the medium is busy, resuming after the next DIFS.
When the counter reaches zero the whole frame is sent; the sender cannot detect a collision during the transmission.
The receiver checks the CRC and returns an ACK after SIFS; a missing ACK means a collision or error, so the sender doubles CW (up to CWmax) and retries.
Virtual carrier sense: every frame carries a Duration field, and stations that hear it load their NAV timer and treat the medium as busy until it expires.
Collisions are reduced, not eliminated: two stations whose counters reach zero in the same slot still collide.

concepts.text:
Worked trace: CDMA with Walsh codes, N = 4
A = +1 +1 +1 +1   B = +1 -1 +1 -1   C = +1 +1 -1 -1
Data: bit 1 -> +code, bit 0 -> -code, silent -> 0
A sends 0:   -1 -1 -1 -1
B sends 1:   +1 -1 +1 -1
C sends 1:   +1 +1 -1 -1
Channel sum: +1 -1 -1 -3
Decode B: (+1)(+1) + (-1)(-1) + (-1)(+1) + (-3)(-1) = 4 -> 4 / 4 = +1 -> bit 1
Decode A: (+1)(+1) + (-1)(+1) + (-1)(+1) + (-3)(+1) = -4 -> -4 / 4 = -1 -> bit 0
Orthogonality: different codes give inner product 0, a code with itself gives N
W(2N) = [W(N) W(N); W(N) -W(N)], so the number of codes N is a power of 2

rows: Each interval starts with a reservation frame of N minislots, one per station; a station marks its minislot to book a data slot
Minislot overhead grows with the number of stations
A primary polls secondaries to collect data (poll, then data or NAK) and selects a secondary before sending to it (SEL, ACK, data)
Polling overhead; the primary is a single point of failure
A token circulates round a logical ring; only its holder sends, for at most the token holding time
A lost or duplicated token needs a monitor station; a station waits for the token even on an idle network
Stations send when they wish and recover from collisions by backoff
No delay bound; throughput falls under heavy load

concepts.text: Common mistakes: using the one-way delay where CSMA/CD needs the round trip (T_fr ≥ 2 × t_prop); mixing bits and bytes (512 bits = 64 bytes); quoting 36.8 % for pure ALOHA (it is 18.4 %); treating G as successful frames when it counts all attempts including retransmissions; assuming CSMA/CA prevents every collision; and applying CSMA/CD to full-duplex switched links, where there is no contention at all.

formulas.plainText: pure ALOHA S = G e^(-2G), max 0.184 at G = 0.5
slotted ALOHA S = G e^(-G), max 0.368 at G = 1
CSMA/CD minimum frame size L_min = 2 x t_prop x B

notes.text: Memorise the ALOHA pair: pure 18.4% at G = 0.5, slotted 36.8% at G = 1. Slotted doubles the throughput because the vulnerable time halves.
CSMA/CD is used only on shared half-duplex Ethernet. Modern switched full-duplex Ethernet has no collisions, and Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA because a radio cannot reliably detect collisions while sending.

In minimum-frame-size problems convert distance to propagation delay with the given signal speed (often 2 × 10^8 m/s), double it for the round trip and multiply by the bit rate; divide by 8 for bytes.

concepts.text: The IEEE 802 Family
Ethernet (IEEE 802.3)

Ethernet is the dominant wired LAN. Classic Ethernet was a shared bus using 1-persistent CSMA/CD and Manchester encoding at 10 Mbps; modern Ethernet uses switches and full-duplex links, so collisions no longer occur, but the frame format is unchanged. Every frame carries 48-bit source and destination MAC addresses and a CRC-32 trailer.

rows: 10101011, marks the start of the frame
EtherType (e.g. 0x0800 IPv4) or length of data (≤ 1500)
Payload, padded up to 46 bytes if shorter
CRC-32 over addresses, type and data

concepts.text: Frame size is counted from the destination address to the CRC: minimum 6 + 6 + 2 + 46 + 4 = 64 bytes and maximum 6 + 6 + 2 + 1500 + 4 = 1518 bytes. The 64-byte minimum comes from the CSMA/CD round-trip rule; the preamble and SFD are not counted. After each frame there is an inter-frame gap of 96 bit times.
Reading Ethernet media names (speed + BASE for baseband + medium):
items: 10BASE5 (thick coax, 500 m) and 10BASE2 (thin coax, about 185 m): 10 Mbps bus.
10BASE-T: 10 Mbps over twisted pair (Cat 3) to a hub/switch, 100 m.
100BASE-TX (Fast Ethernet): 100 Mbps over two pairs of Cat 5 UTP; 100BASE-FX over fibre.
1000BASE-T (Gigabit): 1 Gbps over four pairs of Cat 5e; 1000BASE-SX/LX over multimode/single-mode fibre.
10GBASE-T and faster use full duplex only, so CSMA/CD is not used.

concepts.text: Token Bus (802.4) and Token Ring (802.5)

Token bus arranges stations on a physical bus (usually broadband coaxial cable) but passes a token in a logical ring by descending address. Only the token holder may transmit, so the maximum waiting time is bounded, which suited factory automation (the MAP protocol). Token ring connects stations in a physical ring (star-wired through MAUs in practice) at 4 or 16 Mbps using differential Manchester coding. A 3-byte token (start delimiter, access control, end delimiter) circulates; a station seizes it, sends its frame, and the frame returns to the sender, which removes it and releases the token. The access control byte has 3 priority bits and 3 reservation bits, and an active monitor station regenerates lost tokens and removes orphan frames.
Wireless LANs (IEEE 802.11)

An 802.11 Basic Service Set (BSS) is a group of stations; an ad hoc (independent) BSS has no access point, while an infrastructure BSS has an access point (AP) connecting it to a wired distribution system. Several BSSs joined by a distribution system form an Extended Service Set (ESS), which lets users roam between APs. Access uses CSMA/CA (DCF) with optional RTS/CTS, and every unicast frame is acknowledged.
Problems specific to wireless LANs:
items: Hidden terminal: A and C both reach B but not each other, so carrier sensing fails and their frames collide at B. RTS/CTS solves it because C hears B's CTS and defers.
Exposed terminal: B refrains from sending to A because it hears C sending to D, although the two transmissions would not interfere.
Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15.1): short-range 2.4 GHz personal area network; a master and up to 7 active slaves form a piconet, using frequency hopping.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Ethernet, Token LANs and Wi-Fi

Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) is the most common wired LAN: every frame carries MAC addresses, speeds have grown from 10 Mbps through 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps to 10 Gbps and beyond, and CSMA/CD is used on the old shared, half-duplex segments. In token ring (IEEE 802.5) the stations form a ring and a token travels round it; only the token holder may transmit, so there are no collisions at all (not merely fewer), but in a simple ring one broken link or station stops the whole network, which is why real rings were star-wired through MAUs that bypass a failed station. Token bus (IEEE 802.4) combines the two ideas: the cabling is a bus like Ethernet, but access follows a token passed round a logical ring in descending order of station address, so the waiting time is bounded. Each token bus station knows its successor, and new stations join through periodic solicit-successor frames sent by the token holder.

rows: Thick / thin coaxial bus, 500 m / 185 m
2 pairs of Cat 3 UTP to a hub or switch, 100 m
Multimode fibre, 2 km in full duplex
4 pairs of Cat 5e UTP, 100 m, 250 Mbps per pair
Multimode fibre up to 550 m / single-mode fibre 5 km
Multimode 300 m / single-mode 10 km / Cat 6a 100 m; full duplex only

concepts.text: Manchester coding puts a transition in the middle of every bit, so the receiver recovers the clock from the signal itself and the line carries no DC component. The price is bandwidth: every bit needs two signal elements, so 10 Mbps Ethernet signals at 20 Mbaud. Fast Ethernet therefore switched to 4B/5B block coding, which sends every 4 data bits as a 5-bit code word chosen so that no more than three 0s ever occur in a row, an overhead of 25 % instead of 100 %. Differential Manchester, used by 802.5 token ring, also has a mid-bit transition in every bit but encodes a 0 as a transition at the start of the bit and a 1 as no transition there, so it does not depend on the polarity of the wires.

Worked trace: Manchester, IEEE 802.3 convention (1 = low->high, 0 = high->low)
Bits:         1     0     1     1     0
Half-bits:   L H   H L   L H   L H   H L
Mid-bit transitions: 5, one in every bit (this is the clock)
Bit-boundary transitions: only between two equal bits (the 1-1 pair here): 1
Total = 6 transitions; 10 signal elements for 5 bits, so baud = 2 x bit rate
The opposite polarity convention (used in some textbooks) gives the same counts
