concepts.plainText: Wire time of one Ethernet frame T_wire = 8 × (L + 20) / R, where L is the frame size in bytes from destination address to FCS (64 to 1518) and 20 bytes = 8 preamble/SFD + 12 inter-frame gap; payload efficiency η = P / (P + 38) for a payload of P = 46 to 1500 bytes (38 = 8 + 14 header + 4 FCS + 12 gap).

concepts.text:
Worked example: Ethernet overhead and frame rate at 1 Gbps (1 Gbps = 10^9 bit/s)
Per frame on the wire: preamble + SFD 8 + header 14 + data + FCS 4 + inter-frame gap 12 bytes
Minimum frame: 8 + 64 + 12 = 84 bytes = 672 bits -> 672 ns
  frame rate = 10^9 / 672 = 1 488 095 frames/s; payload efficiency = 46 / 84 = 54.8 %
Maximum frame: 8 + 1518 + 12 = 1538 bytes = 12 304 bits -> 12.304 us
  frame rate = 10^9 / 12 304 = 81 274 frames/s; payload efficiency = 1500 / 1538 = 97.5 %
Useful IP data rate with full frames = 0.975 x 1000 Mbps = 975 Mbps

In 802.5 a free token is 3 bytes (start delimiter, access control, end delimiter); a station that wants to send flips the token bit in the access control byte, turning the token into the start of a data frame, and may keep it for the token holding time, 10 ms by default. The frame travels all the way round and the sender removes it (source stripping), reading the A and C bits of the frame status byte to learn whether the destination recognised its address and copied the frame. With early token release, used on 16 Mbps rings, the sender issues a new token straight after its frame instead of waiting for the frame to return. Ring latency is the propagation time round the ring plus about one bit of delay in each station, and the active monitor adds a 24-bit latency buffer so that a whole token always fits on a short ring.

rows: 0 / 0: station to station in one BSS

concepts.text:
Worked trace: A sends to B; C is hidden from A but in range of B (802.11 DCF with RTS/CTS)
Medium idle for DIFS and A's backoff reaches 0
A -> B  RTS  Duration = 3 SIFS + CTS + DATA + ACK     C cannot hear it
        SIFS
B -> A  CTS  Duration = 2 SIFS + DATA + ACK           C hears it, sets NAV and stays silent
        SIFS
A -> B  DATA                                         stations near A deferred on the RTS
        SIFS
B -> A  ACK                                          NAVs expire; contention restarts after DIFS
More on 802.11 and Bluetooth:
items: DCF (distributed coordination function) is the mandatory CSMA/CA mode; PCF (point coordination function) is an optional contention-free mode in which the AP polls stations, taking priority by waiting only PIFS; a beacon opens each contention-free period, which is followed by an ordinary contention period.
Exposed station problem: B hears C sending to D and defers, although its own frame to A would not disturb D's reception; RTS/CTS does not cure it, because B still hears C's traffic.
802.11 frame types: management (beacon, probe, authentication, association), control (RTS, CTS, ACK) and data.

Speeds such as 300+ Mbps for 802.11n and 1+ Gbps for 802.11ac are typical figures for two or three spatial streams; the standards' maxima are 600 Mbps and about 6.9 Gbps. 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7) adds 320 MHz channels and multi-link operation.

Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15.1) uses the 2.4 GHz band with frequency hopping over 79 channels of 1 MHz at 1600 hops/s; a piconet has one master (central) and up to 7 active slaves plus up to 255 parked ones, and piconets linked through a shared device form a scatternet. Bluetooth Low Energy uses 40 channels of 2 MHz.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: including the 8-byte preamble and SFD in the 64 to 1518-byte frame size, yet forgetting them and the 12-byte inter-frame gap when working out wire time or frame rate; confusing Manchester's baud rate (twice the bit rate) with its bit rate; saying token ring has fewer collisions (it has none); and mixing up 802.4 (token bus: physical bus, logical ring) with 802.5 (token ring: physical ring).

formulas.plainText: Ethernet frame 64 bytes min, 1518 bytes max (DA+SA+Type+Data+CRC)
10 Mbps Ethernet slot time = 512 bits / 10 Mbps = 51.2 us

notes.text: Map numbers to names: 802.3 Ethernet, 802.4 token bus, 802.5 token ring, 802.11 Wi-Fi, 802.15 Bluetooth. Ethernet data field 46–1500 bytes, frame 64–1518 bytes.
Do not include the 8-byte preamble and SFD when stating Ethernet minimum or maximum frame size; they belong to the physical layer.
The 1500-byte Ethernet payload limit is the MTU seen by IP; larger IP datagrams must be fragmented or the path MTU reduced.

concepts.text: LAN (MAC) Addressing

Every network interface has a 48-bit (6-byte) MAC address, written as 12 hexadecimal digits such as 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. The first 24 bits are the Organisationally Unique Identifier (OUI) assigned by IEEE to the manufacturer, and the last 24 bits are assigned by the vendor. MAC addresses are flat (not hierarchical) and identify a node on the local link only; IP addresses handle end-to-end delivery.
Kinds of MAC destination address:
items: Unicast: least significant bit of the first byte is 0; delivered to one interface.
Multicast: least significant bit of the first byte is 1 (e.g. 01:00:5E:xx:xx:xx for IPv4 multicast); delivered to a group.
Broadcast: all 48 bits are 1, FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF; received by every station on the LAN.
The second-least significant bit of the first byte distinguishes universally administered (0) from locally administered (1) addresses.

concepts.text: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)

Before a host can send an IP packet on a LAN it needs the MAC address of the next hop (the destination host or the default gateway). ARP resolves this mapping dynamically. The sender broadcasts an ARP request (destination MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, EtherType 0x0806) asking who owns the target IP; only the owner replies with a unicast ARP reply containing its MAC address. Both sides store the mapping in an ARP cache with a timeout (typically a few minutes), so later packets need no new request.
ARP variants and related protocols:
items: Proxy ARP: a router answers ARP requests on behalf of hosts on another network, so hosts without proper routes can still reach them.
Gratuitous ARP: a host announces its own IP-to-MAC mapping to detect duplicate IPs or update caches after failover.
RARP: the reverse, MAC to IP, used by diskless hosts at boot; replaced by BOOTP and DHCP. InARP: finds the IP address for a known Frame Relay DLCI.
Security: ARP has no authentication, so ARP spoofing/poisoning enables man-in-the-middle attacks; dynamic ARP inspection on switches counters it.

concepts.text: PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol)

PPP is a byte-oriented data link protocol for direct links such as dial-up, DSL (PPPoE) and serial router links. Its HDLC-like frame is Flag 0x7E, Address 0xFF, Control 0x03, Protocol (2 bytes), Payload (default up to 1500 bytes) and FCS (2 or 4 bytes), with byte stuffing using escape 0x7D. PPP adds link negotiation, authentication and support for multiple network protocols, but no numbered flow control.
PPP components and phases:
items: LCP (Link Control Protocol, 0xC021): establishes, configures (MRU, authentication type, compression) and tests the link.
NCP (Network Control Protocols): one per network protocol; IPCP (0x8021) negotiates IP addresses for IPv4.
Phases: Dead, Establish (LCP), Authenticate (optional), Network (NCP), Open (data transfer), Terminate, back to Dead.
Authentication: PAP or CHAP, compared below.

rows: Two-way: user name and password sent, ACK/NAK
Never sent; response is an MD5 hash of challenge and secret
Random challenge each time, repeated periodically

concepts.text: Wide Area Protocols

X.25 is an older ITU packet-switching standard with error and flow control at every hop, suited to noisy analogue lines but slow. Frame Relay removed hop-by-hop error correction for speed; virtual circuits are identified by a 10-bit DLCI, and the Committed Information Rate (CIR) is the rate the carrier guarantees, with excess frames marked discard-eligible. ATM switches fixed 53-byte cells (5-byte header, 48-byte payload) over virtual paths and circuits (VPI/VCI), giving predictable delay for voice and video. MPLS forwards packets by short labels (a 32-bit shim header with a 20-bit label) placed between the layer 2 and layer 3 headers, often called layer 2.5, and is the basis of most modern carrier VPNs and traffic engineering.

rows: Sliding-window ARQ; basis of PPP, LAPB
Error control at every node; slow
Label switching between L2 and L3

concepts.text: Going Deeper: MAC Addressing, ARP, PPP and WAN Links

ARP exists because the two layers speak different languages: the network layer addresses packets with logical IP addresses, while the data link layer can deliver a frame only to a physical MAC address, so every link needs a translation. It works in three steps: the sender broadcasts “Who has 192.168.1.5?”, the owner of that address answers “I do, my MAC is …”, and the sender keeps the answer in its ARP cache for later packets. RARP did the reverse, MAC to IP, for diskless machines at boot, but it is obsolete and was replaced by BOOTP and then DHCP. PPP connects exactly two devices over a direct link, such as a dial-up modem connection, a DSL line (as PPPoE) or a serial link between routers, and adds authentication and error detection: a frame whose FCS fails is simply discarded, because PPP does not retransmit.

rows: The address being resolved; total 28 bytes

concepts.text:
Worked trace: A (192.168.1.10, MAC 00:1A:2B:00:00:0A) sends to B (192.168.1.5) on the same /24
1. A's ARP cache has no entry for 192.168.1.5
2. A -> all: Ethernet dst FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, type 0x0806, ARP operation 1
             'who has 192.168.1.5? tell 192.168.1.10 at 00:1A:2B:00:00:0A'
3. Every host reads it; only B answers, and B also caches A's mapping from the request
4. B -> A:   Ethernet dst 00:1A:2B:00:00:0A, type 0x0806, ARP operation 2
             '192.168.1.5 is at 00:1A:2B:00:00:05'
5. A caches 192.168.1.5 -> 00:1A:2B:00:00:05 and sends the IP packet (type 0x0800)
Off-subnet destination such as 8.8.8.8: A ARPs for its default gateway's IP instead;
the frame goes to the gateway's MAC while the IP header still says 8.8.8.8

The first byte of a MAC address carries two flag bits. Its least significant bit, the I/G bit, is 0 for an individual (unicast) address and 1 for a group (multicast) address, and it is the very first bit on an Ethernet wire because each byte is sent least significant bit first. The next bit, U/L, is 0 for a universally administered address built on an IEEE-assigned OUI and 1 for a locally administered one, such as the random addresses phones use for Wi-Fi privacy or the 02:42:… addresses Docker gives containers. IPv4 multicast groups map onto MAC addresses by placing the low 23 bits of the group address after the prefix 01:00:5E, so 2^5 = 32 groups share each multicast MAC and the receiving host must still check the destination IP address.

Worked example 1: IPv4 multicast group 224.0.0.251 (mDNS) -> Ethernet MAC
224.0.0.251 = 1110 0000 . 0000 0000 . 0000 0000 . 1111 1011
Low 23 bits = 000 0000 . 0000 0000 . 1111 1011 -> 00:00:FB
MAC = 01:00:5E, then a 0 bit, then those 23 bits = 01:00:5E:00:00:FB
224.128.0.251 and 225.0.0.251 map to the same MAC (32 groups in all)
Worked example 2: MAC 02:42:AC:11:00:02
First byte 0x02 = 0000 0010 -> I/G bit 0 = unicast, U/L bit 1 = locally administered

concepts.plainText: ATM with AAL5: a packet of L bytes plus the 8-byte AAL5 trailer is padded to a multiple of 48 bytes, so it needs N = ceil((L + 8) / 48) cells of 53 bytes, and the efficiency is L / (53 × N).

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: IP packets over ATM with AAL5 (8-byte trailer, pad to a multiple of 48)
1000-byte packet: (1000 + 8) / 48 = 21 -> 21 cells, no padding needed
  bytes on the line = 21 x 53 = 1113 -> efficiency 1000 / 1113 = 89.8 %
40-byte TCP ACK:  (40 + 8) / 48 = 1 -> 1 cell of 53 bytes -> efficiency 75.5 %
41-byte packet:   (41 + 8) / 48 = 1.02 -> 2 cells = 106 bytes -> efficiency 38.7 %
Compare the raw cell efficiency 48 / 53 = 90.6 %: the trailer and padding cost extra
PPP in more detail:
items: Byte stuffing (RFC 1662): a data byte 0x7E is sent as 0x7D 0x5E and a byte 0x7D as 0x7D 0x5D (the escape byte, then the original byte XOR 0x20); control characters below 0x20 are escaped too unless LCP negotiates this away with the ACCM option.
LCP options include the MRU (default 1500 bytes), the authentication protocol, a magic number that detects looped-back links, and compression of the address/control and protocol fields.
IPCP, the NCP for IPv4, lets the ISP assign the client's IP address and DNS servers; IPV6CP only negotiates a 64-bit interface identifier, and the IPv6 address itself then comes from SLAAC or DHCPv6.

PPPoE (RFC 2516) carries PPP over Ethernet for DSL: a discovery stage (PADI, PADO, PADR, PADS) finds the access concentrator and a session ID, and the 6-byte PPPoE header plus the 2-byte PPP protocol field cut the MTU from 1500 to 1492 bytes.
Multilink PPP bundles several physical links into one logical link and spreads fragments across them.

concepts.text:
Worked trace: CHAP authentication (RFC 1994) after LCP has agreed on CHAP with MD5
Authenticator -> peer: Challenge (identifier 7, random challenge value C)
Peer -> authenticator: Response  (identifier 7, MD5(7 || shared secret || C), name)
Authenticator computes the same hash from its own copy of the secret and compares
Authenticator -> peer: Success (or Failure, and the link is terminated)
Repeated at random intervals with a new challenge, so an old response cannot be replayed
PAP for comparison: peer -> authenticator: user name + password in clear text; ACK or NAK

HDLC is the parent of a family of WAN link protocols: LAPB for X.25, LAPD for the ISDN D channel, LAPF for Frame Relay and the HDLC-like framing of PPP. Frame Relay traffic contracts use the committed information rate (CIR), the committed burst Bc = CIR × Tc allowed in each measurement interval Tc, and an excess burst Be: data up to Bc is forwarded normally, data between Bc and Bc + Be is forwarded but marked discard eligible (DE = 1) so that a congested switch drops it first, and anything beyond Bc + Be is discarded at once, while the FECN and BECN bits warn the end systems of congestion. X.25 works in three layers (X.21 physical, LAPB link and the packet layer protocol) and checks errors at every hop, which is exactly the work Frame Relay removed. An MPLS shim header is 32 bits: a 20-bit label, 3 traffic-class bits, a bottom-of-stack bit S and an 8-bit TTL, and label switch routers push, swap or pop labels as packets cross the network.

Common mistakes: ARP requests are broadcast but replies are unicast; ARP works only within one link, so a host never ARPs for a remote destination, only for its gateway; RARP (MAC to IP) is obsolete and replaced by DHCP; the ATM header is 5 bytes and the payload 48, not the other way round; a Frame Relay DLCI has only local significance, so the two ends of one virtual circuit may use different numbers; and PAP sends the password in clear text.

formulas.plainText: 48-bit MAC: 2^48 addresses; 2^24 per OUI
ATM cell 5 + 48 = 53 bytes; payload efficiency 48/53 = 90.6%

notes.text: ARP request = broadcast, ARP reply = unicast. RARP goes the other way (MAC to IP). For PPP, remember LCP sets up the link, NCP (IPCP) sets up the network protocol, and CHAP is safer than PAP.
A MAC address is only meaningful on the local link: routers rewrite source and destination MAC addresses at every hop, while the IP addresses stay the same end to end (without NAT).
The ATM cell size of 53 bytes was a compromise between 32 and 64 bytes of payload proposed by different countries; the small cell keeps voice packetisation delay low.

concepts.text: Routing Basics

Routing is the network-wide process of computing paths and building routing tables; forwarding is the per-packet local action of looking up the destination in the forwarding table and sending the packet out of the correct interface. A routing algorithm treats the network as a graph whose nodes are routers and whose edges carry a cost (hops, delay, bandwidth-based cost). The optimality principle states that if router J lies on the optimal path from I to K, then the optimal path from J to K follows the same route; the set of optimal routes to one destination therefore forms a sink tree.
Static vs dynamic routing and the properties a good algorithm needs:
items: Static (non-adaptive) routing: routes are computed in advance and entered manually by the administrator; simple and secure but does not react to failures or load.
Dynamic (adaptive) routing: routers exchange information and recompute routes automatically when topology or traffic changes (RIP, OSPF, BGP).
Desirable properties: correctness, simplicity, robustness (survive failures), stability (converge and stay converged), fairness and optimality.
Algorithms are also classed as global (link state, full topology known) or decentralised (distance vector, only neighbour information).

concepts.text: Flooding

In flooding every incoming packet is sent out on every outgoing line except the one it arrived on. It needs no routing table and always finds the shortest path (some copy travels it), which makes it very robust and useful for broadcasting and for distributing link-state packets, but it generates huge numbers of duplicates. Duplicates are limited with a hop counter in the header, initialised to the path length (or network diameter) and decremented at each hop, with the packet discarded at zero; or with sequence numbers so a router forwards each packet only once. Selective flooding sends the packet only on lines that go approximately in the right direction.
Shortest Path Routing (Dijkstra)

Dijkstra's algorithm finds the least-cost path from a source to every other node when all link costs are non-negative. Each node carries a tentative distance; at each step the tentative node with the smallest distance is made permanent and its neighbours are relaxed. Worked example with source A and links A–B 2, A–C 5, B–C 1, B–D 4, C–D 1, C–E 6, D–E 2: the table below shows each iteration, with distances listed for B, C, D, E.

rows: Tree A–B–C–D–E; next hop for all is B

concepts.text: Distance Vector Routing

In distance vector routing (distributed Bellman-Ford) each router keeps a vector of its best known distance and next hop to every destination and periodically sends this whole vector to its directly connected neighbours only. On receiving a neighbour's vector, a router adds the cost of the link to that neighbour and keeps any shorter route. Routers never see the full topology; they route 'by rumour'. RIP is the classic distance vector protocol and uses hop count as its metric.

concepts.plainText: D_x(y) = min over neighbours v of { c(x,v) + D_v(y) }

concepts.text: Distance vector reacts fast to good news but slowly to bad news (count-to-infinity) and uses these fixes:
items: Count-to-infinity: in a line A–B–C, if C fails, B hears A advertise 'C at 2' and sets C at 3; A then sets 4, and so on until the metric reaches infinity (16 in RIP).
Split horizon: a router never advertises a route back out of the interface through which it learned that route.
Poison reverse: the route is advertised back to that neighbour, but with an infinite metric, so the neighbour is told explicitly not to use it.
Route poisoning, triggered updates and hold-down timers speed up the spread of bad news; none removes loops of three or more routers completely.

concepts.text: Link State and Hierarchical Routing
Link state routing (used by OSPF and IS-IS) works in five steps at every router:
items: Discover neighbours and learn their addresses, using HELLO packets.
Measure the cost (delay or bandwidth-based) to each neighbour.
Build a link state packet (LSP) containing its identity, sequence number, age and the list of neighbours with costs.
Flood the LSP reliably to all routers; sequence numbers and age discard old or duplicate copies.
With every router holding the same full topology database, run Dijkstra locally to compute the shortest path tree and forwarding table.

concepts.text: As networks grow, routing tables and routing traffic grow too. Hierarchical routing divides routers into regions (areas, domains): each router knows full details of routes inside its own region but only one entry per remote region. For example, 720 routers arranged as 24 regions of 30 routers need about 30 + 23 = 53 table entries per router instead of 720. The cost is that some paths are slightly longer than optimal. OSPF areas and the Internet's split into autonomous systems are real examples.

rows: Only the router's own link states (LSP)
When a link changes, plus refresh
Fast; loop-free after flooding, more CPU and memory

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Routing Algorithms

In brief: a distance vector router knows only its distance to each destination and shares it with its neighbours, while a link state router learns the whole topology by flooding and runs Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm, which finds the minimum-cost path from one node to every other node. Flooding sends each packet to every neighbour except the one it came from; it is simple and always finds a path but wastes bandwidth on duplicates. Hop count is the metric of RIP, the classic distance vector protocol, not a rule of distance vector itself: the algorithm works with any additive cost such as delay or a bandwidth-based cost. Link state converges quickly and accurately because every router computes from the same complete map; the price is extra memory and processing.

rows: Only the routes the administrator typed in
No routing traffic; simple and predictable
No reaction to failures; manual upkeep
Nothing: no routing table is needed
Very robust; finds a path whenever one exists
More memory, CPU and flooding traffic
Own region in detail; each other region as one entry

concepts.text: Dijkstra's algorithm keeps two sets of nodes: permanent ones, whose least cost is final, and tentative ones. At each step it makes permanent the tentative node with the smallest total distance from the source, not the node behind the cheapest single link, and then relaxes that node's neighbours. A tentative label can drop several times before it becomes permanent, and the predecessor stored with each final label gives the shortest-path tree. The next hop to a destination is found by walking the predecessors back to the node adjacent to the source.

Worked example: Dijkstra from A
Links: A-B 1, A-C 4, B-C 5, B-D 2, C-E 1, D-E 6, D-F 3, E-F 2
Label = cost + predecessor; * = made permanent in this step
Step  Permanent   B     C     D     E     F
0     A           1A    4A    inf   inf   inf
1     +B (1)      1A*   4A    3B    inf   inf
2     +D (3)      .     4A    3B*   9D    6D
3     +C (4)      .     4A*   .     5C    6D
4     +E (5)      .     .     .     5C*   6D
5     +F (6)      .     .     .     .     6D*
Next hops from A: B, D and F via B; C and E via C

Worked example: distance vector update at router X
Links: X-A 2, X-B 5, X-C 1. Latest vectors received:
            to W   to Y   to Z
from A        6      3      9
from B        2      4      1
from C        8      3      7
W: min(2+6, 5+2, 1+8) = min(8, 7, 9)  = 7 via B
Y: min(2+3, 5+4, 1+3) = min(5, 9, 4)  = 4 via C
Z: min(2+9, 5+1, 1+7) = min(11, 6, 8) = 6 via B
New vector at X: W 7 (B), Y 4 (C), Z 6 (B); X's old values are not used

Line A-B-C-D-E, unit costs; columns = distance to A held by B, C, D, E
Bad news: link A-B fails (synchronous exchanges, no split horizon)
               B   C   D   E
Before         1   2   3   4
Exchange 1     3   2   3   4   B believes C's stale 2 and sets 3
Exchange 2     3   4   3   4
Exchange 3     5   4   5   4
Exchange 4     5   6   5   6   rises by 2 every 2 exchanges, up to infinity
Good news: when A comes back, a router k hops away learns of it in k exchanges
How link state flooding stays reliable and consistent:
items: Each LSP carries a sequence number that its originator increases for every new LSP; receivers remember the highest number seen from each source.
An arriving LSP with a higher number is stored and forwarded on every line except the one it came in on; a duplicate or lower-numbered LSP is discarded as obsolete.
An age field counts down as time passes and at each hop; an LSP whose age reaches zero is removed, which clears out information from crashed routers or corrupted sequence numbers.
LSPs are acknowledged hop by hop and held briefly before forwarding, so a newer copy that arrives meanwhile replaces the older one.
Once flooding finishes every router holds the same database and computes a consistent shortest-path tree; a router floods again only when one of its links changes, plus a slow periodic refresh.

concepts.plainText: T = d + d(d − 1) + … + d(d − 1)^(h − 1) transmissions when every router has d lines, copies live h hops and duplicates are not suppressed

concepts.text: More levels save even more table space. In a three-level hierarchy a router keeps one entry per router in its own region, one per other region in its own cluster and one per other cluster, so 720 routers arranged as 8 clusters of 9 regions of 10 routers need 10 + 8 + 7 = 25 entries, against 30 + 23 = 53 with two levels (24 regions of 30 routers) and 720 with none. Kamoun and Kleinrock showed that for N routers the best number of levels is about ln N, needing about e ln N entries per router. The price is longer paths: traffic for a remote region always enters it by the route chosen for the region as a whole, which may not be the best route to every router inside it.
Common mistakes in routing calculations:
items: Picking the next permanent node by the cheapest single link instead of the smallest total distance from the source.
Forgetting to lower a tentative label when a newly permanent node offers a cheaper path; in the Dijkstra trace above E falls from 9 to 5.

In a distance vector update, using a neighbour's advertised cost without adding the cost of the link to that neighbour, or mixing in the router's own old values: the new table comes only from the neighbours' latest vectors plus the link costs.
Confusing the destination with the next hop: a forwarding table stores only the first router on the path, found by walking the predecessors back towards the source.
Believing split horizon cures count-to-infinity: it stops two-router loops only, and a loop through three or more routers can still count up.

concepts.text: For Dijkstra questions draw one column per node and one row per step, write every label as cost plus predecessor (such as 3B), and circle the smallest tentative label in each row. The last row gives the least costs, and following the predecessors gives the paths and the next hops.

formulas.plainText: Dijkstra relaxation: D(v) = min{ D(v), D(w) + c(w,v) }
Bellman-Ford: D_x(y) = min over v { c(x,v) + D_v(y) }
Dijkstra with a simple array: O(N^2) for N nodes

notes.text: Pair them: distance vector = Bellman-Ford = neighbours only = whole table = RIP = count-to-infinity; link state = Dijkstra = flooding of LSPs to all = OSPF. Path vector (BGP) is the inter-AS cousin of distance vector.

Dijkstra needs non-negative link costs. Bellman-Ford tolerates negative weights in graph theory, but routing metrics are always positive, so the difference that matters in networking is centralised vs distributed computation.
Flooding is not only a toy algorithm: link state protocols use controlled flooding to distribute LSPs because it reaches every router even when parts of the network have failed.

concepts.text: Autonomous Systems, IGP and EGP

The Internet is too large for one routing protocol, so it is divided into autonomous systems (AS): groups of networks and routers under a single administrative authority, each identified by an AS number (originally 16-bit, now 32-bit). Routing inside an AS uses an interior gateway protocol (IGP) such as RIP or OSPF, chosen freely by the AS administrator and optimised for performance. Routing between ASes uses an exterior gateway protocol (EGP); today that is BGP-4, optimised for policy and scale rather than shortest paths.
RIP (Routing Information Protocol)
RIP is a simple distance vector IGP for small networks:
items: Metric is hop count; the maximum valid path is 15 hops and 16 means infinity (unreachable), which limits the network diameter.
Each router sends its full routing table to neighbours every 30 seconds; a route is marked invalid after 180 s without updates.
RIP messages are carried in UDP on port 520.
RIPv1 is classful (no subnet mask in updates), broadcasts updates and has no authentication.
RIPv2 is classless (carries the mask, supports VLSM/CIDR), multicasts updates to 224.0.0.9 and supports authentication; RIPng is the IPv6 version.
Uses split horizon, poison reverse, triggered updates and hold-down timers against count-to-infinity.

concepts.text: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)
OSPF is an open-standard link state IGP for large enterprise networks:
items: Runs directly over IP with protocol number 89 (not over TCP or UDP).
Metric is cost, by default reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth (10^8 / BW, so 100 Mbps = 1, 10 Mbps = 10).
Divides an AS into areas; all areas attach to the backbone area 0 through area border routers, limiting LSA flooding to an area.
Routers exchange link state advertisements (LSAs) in five packet types: Hello, Database Description, Link State Request, Link State Update and Link State Acknowledgement.
On broadcast networks a designated router (DR) and backup DR (BDR) are elected to reduce adjacencies; multicast addresses 224.0.0.5 (all OSPF routers) and 224.0.0.6 (DR/BDR).
Supports VLSM, equal-cost multipath, authentication and fast convergence; runs Dijkstra (SPF) on the area database.

concepts.text: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)
BGP-4 is the path vector EGP that glues the Internet's autonomous systems together:
items: Path vector: each advertised route carries the full list of ASes it traverses (AS_PATH); a router rejects any route whose AS_PATH already contains its own AS number, which prevents loops.
Runs over TCP port 179 for reliable delivery; messages are OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE and NOTIFICATION.
eBGP runs between routers in different ASes; iBGP distributes externally learned routes among routers of the same AS.
Route selection is policy-based using path attributes: AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, LOCAL_PREF, MED (multi-exit discriminator) and ORIGIN.
Updates are incremental (only changes are sent), not periodic full tables.

concepts.text: Worked Metric Comparison

Router X can reach network N by path P1 (2 hops over 10 Mbps links) or path P2 (3 hops over 100 Mbps links). RIP counts hops only, so it chooses P1 (2 < 3) even though it is slower. OSPF computes cost = 10^8 / bandwidth: each 10 Mbps link costs 10 and each 100 Mbps link costs 1, so P1 costs 20 and P2 costs 3, and OSPF chooses the faster P2. This is why hop-count metrics can pick poor paths in networks with mixed link speeds.

concepts.plainText: OSPF cost = 10^8 / bandwidth in bps

concepts.text: Delivery Modes and Multicast Routing
Four ways a network-layer packet can be delivered:
items: Unicast: one sender to one receiver (one-to-one); ordinary routing with RIP, OSPF, BGP.
Multicast: one sender to a group of interested receivers (one-to-many); IPv4 class D 224.0.0.0–239.255.255.255.
Broadcast: one sender to all hosts on a network (one-to-all); routers do not forward limited broadcasts.
Anycast: one sender to the nearest one of a group of servers sharing an address (one-to-nearest), e.g. DNS root servers.

concepts.text: Multicast routing builds distribution trees so that each packet crosses each link at most once:
items: IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) runs between hosts and their local router so the router learns which groups have members on each interface.
Source-based trees build one shortest-path tree per source and group; group-shared trees use one tree rooted at a core or rendezvous point for all sources.
Reverse path forwarding (RPF): a router accepts a multicast packet only if it arrives on the interface it would use to send unicast traffic back to the source, which kills loops and duplicates.
DVMRP: distance vector multicast routing using flood-and-prune with RPF; MOSPF adds group membership LSAs to OSPF.

PIM dense mode (PIM-DM) floods and prunes, suited to groups with members everywhere; PIM sparse mode (PIM-SM) uses a rendezvous point and explicit joins, suited to widely scattered members. PIM works with any unicast routing protocol.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: RIP, OSPF, BGP and Multicast Routing

The three unicast routing protocols in one line each: RIP is a simple distance vector protocol for small networks that counts hops (at most 15) and sends its table every 30 seconds, but it converges slowly. OSPF is a link state protocol with no hop-count limit; it converges fast and scales to large networks, at the price of more configuration, memory and CPU than RIP. BGP is the path vector protocol used between autonomous systems such as ISPs and is the routing protocol of the Internet backbone; it chooses routes by policy, not just by distance. In practice RIP or OSPF runs inside an organisation, and BGP is added where a network connects to several ISPs or is itself an ISP.

rows: 30 s, with a random offset of up to 5 s
The router sends its whole table to every neighbour
The route is marked unreachable: metric set to 16
The route, still advertised with metric 16 meanwhile, is deleted
At once, at most one every 1–5 s
Changed routes are sent without waiting for the 30 s timer

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: RIP update processing at router R (each hop adds 1)
R's table before:  Net1 2 via A | Net2 5 via B | Net3 3 via C
Update from B:     Net1 1 | Net2 7 | Net3 1 | Net4 14
Add one hop:       Net1 2 | Net2 8 | Net3 2 | Net4 15
Net1: 2 via B is not better than 2 via A -> keep 2 via A
Net2: B is the current next hop -> accept 8 via B although it is worse
Net3: 2 via B is better than 3 via C -> replace with 2 via B
Net4: new and 15 < 16 -> add 15 via B (one hop more would be unreachable)
R's table after:   Net1 2 via A | Net2 8 via B | Net3 2 via B | Net4 15 via B
OSPF router roles and the main LSA (link state advertisement) types:
items: Internal router: all interfaces in one area. Backbone router: at least one interface in area 0.
Area border router (ABR): joins an area to area 0 and summarises routes between them. Autonomous system boundary router (ASBR): brings in routes from outside OSPF, such as BGP or static routes.
Type 1 router LSA: every router describes its own links; flooded only inside its area.
Type 2 network LSA: the designated router describes a multi-access network and the routers attached to it.
Type 3 summary LSA: an ABR advertises one area's networks into another; type 4 tells other areas how to reach an ASBR.
Type 5 AS-external LSA: an ASBR advertises external routes to the whole OSPF domain except stub areas; type 7 carries them inside a not-so-stubby area (NSSA).
Hello packets every 10 s (dead interval 40 s) on broadcast links find and keep neighbours; two routers become neighbours only if area ID, hello/dead timers and authentication match.

concepts.text: On a shared segment with n routers, an adjacency between every pair would need n(n − 1)/2 adjacencies and would flood the same LSAs many times. OSPF therefore elects a designated router (DR) and a backup designated router (BDR): the highest interface priority wins (default 1, and 0 means never eligible), and a tie is broken by the highest router ID. Every other router (a DROther) forms full adjacencies only with the DR and BDR, sends its updates to 224.0.0.6, and the DR floods them to everyone on 224.0.0.5. The election is not pre-emptive, so a higher-priority router that joins later does not take over until the DR fails.

concepts.plainText: Adjacencies on a segment of n routers: full mesh n(n − 1)/2; with DR and BDR 2(n − 2) + 1 = 2n − 3 (for n = 6: 15 against 9)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: OSPF cost = reference / bandwidth, fraction dropped, minimum 1
Path P1: two 1 Gbps links        Path P2: one 100 Mbps link
Reference 10^8 (100 Mbps, the old default):
  1 Gbps -> 0.1 -> raised to 1;  100 Mbps -> 1
  P1 = 1 + 1 = 2,  P2 = 1        -> OSPF picks P2, the slower path
Reference 10^10 (10 Gbps):
  1 Gbps -> 10;  100 Mbps -> 100
  P1 = 10 + 10 = 20,  P2 = 100   -> OSPF picks P1
Rule: configure the same reference, at least the fastest link speed, on every router

Worked example 3: BGP routes to 203.0.113.0/24, originated by AS 300
Router in AS 100 hears:   via AS 200: AS_PATH 200 300
                          via AS 400: AS_PATH 400 500 300
No local policy: equal LOCAL_PREF, shorter AS_PATH wins -> via AS 200
Import policy sets LOCAL_PREF 200 on routes from AS 400 (others 100):
  LOCAL_PREF is compared before AS_PATH length -> via AS 400
To its eBGP peers AS 100 advertises AS_PATH 100 400 500 300 (own AS prepended)
To its iBGP peers inside AS 100 the AS_PATH stays 400 500 300
A router in AS 500 that hears 100 400 500 300 finds 500 in it and drops it (loop)
Multicast details beyond the basic page:
items: IGMP (IP protocol 2, TTL 1) works only on the local network: the router sends General Queries (every 125 s by default) and hosts answer with Membership Reports; IGMPv2 added Leave Group, and IGMPv3 lets a host name the sources it wants (source-specific multicast).

Reverse path forwarding grows into reverse path broadcasting (only the parent router of each network forwards onto it) and reverse path multicasting (routers with no members downstream send prune messages, and graft messages rejoin the tree).
Dense-mode protocols (DVMRP, PIM-DM) flood first and prune later; sparse-mode protocols (PIM-SM, CBT) send nothing until a receiver explicitly joins through the rendezvous point or core.
PIM-SM starts on a shared tree (*, G) rooted at the rendezvous point and can switch to a source tree (S, G) once traffic flows.

224.0.0.0/24 is link-local and never forwarded (224.0.0.1 all hosts, 224.0.0.2 all routers); 232.0.0.0/8 is for source-specific multicast and 239.0.0.0/8 is administratively scoped, like private addresses.
On Ethernet the low 23 bits of the group address are copied into 01-00-5E-00-00-00, so 32 IPv4 groups share each multicast MAC address and hosts must still filter by IP address.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: RIP's 15 hops is a metric limit (16 means unreachable), not the IP TTL. OSPF runs directly over IP as protocol 89, not over TCP or UDP, while BGP needs TCP port 179. Administrative distance only chooses between different sources offering the same prefix: the longest matching prefix always wins first, and metrics of different protocols are never compared. IGMP is not a multicast routing protocol; it only tells the local router which groups have members, and PIM, DVMRP or MOSPF build the trees.

formulas.plainText: OSPF cost = 10^8 / bandwidth
Path cost = sum of link costs along the path

notes.text: Transport of routing protocols is a favourite detail: RIP uses UDP 520, OSPF sits directly on IP as protocol 89, BGP uses TCP 179. OSPF backbone is always area 0.
RIP's 16 = infinity limit is a design choice that bounds count-to-infinity: the larger infinity is, the longer bad news takes to spread, so RIP trades network diameter for convergence time.
Do not call BGP a distance vector or link state protocol. It is a path vector protocol: it advertises whole AS paths and chooses routes by policy, not by the smallest metric.

concepts.text: IP: Connectionless Datagram Delivery

The Internet Protocol (IP) is the network-layer protocol of the TCP/IP suite. It is connectionless and unreliable (best effort): each datagram is routed independently, and datagrams may be lost, duplicated, delayed or delivered out of order without IP noticing. Reliability, if needed, is added by TCP above it, while ICMP reports errors. An IPv4 datagram has a header of 20 to 60 bytes followed by data; the total datagram size can be up to 65,535 bytes.
IPv4 Datagram Header

rows: Header length in 4-byte words (5 to 15, i.e. 20 to 60 bytes)
Service class for QoS and congestion notification
Header plus data in bytes, maximum 65,535
Same value in all fragments of one datagram
Position of this fragment's data, in 8-byte units
Decremented by each router; datagram discarded at 0
Upper-layer protocol: ICMP 1, IGMP 2, TCP 6, UDP 17, OSPF 89
Covers the header only; recomputed at every hop
IPv4 address of the final receiver

concepts.plainText: Header length in bytes = HLEN × 4

concepts.text: Fragmentation and Reassembly

Each link has a maximum transfer unit (MTU), 1500 bytes for Ethernet. A router that must send a datagram larger than the next link's MTU splits it into fragments, each with its own IP header copied from the original, unless DF is set, in which case it drops the datagram and returns an ICMP error. All fragments share the identification value; MF = 1 on all but the last; the offset gives each fragment's data position in 8-byte units, so every fragment except the last carries a multiple of 8 data bytes. Reassembly happens only at the destination host.

concepts.plainText: Offset field = position of first data byte / 8

concepts.text: Working through the fragmentation example and related header fields:
items: The 4000-byte datagram has a 20-byte header, so 3980 data bytes must be carried.
Maximum data per fragment = 1500 − 20 = 1480 bytes, already a multiple of 8, giving 1480 + 1480 + 1020 bytes.
TTL prevents datagrams looping forever: common starting values are 64 or 128, and a router sends ICMP Time Exceeded when TTL reaches 0.
The protocol field tells the receiver which module gets the payload: 1 ICMP, 2 IGMP, 6 TCP, 17 UDP, 41 IPv6-in-IPv4, 89 OSPF.

concepts.text: ARP, RARP, BOOTP and DHCP
Address resolution maps between logical (IP) and physical (MAC) addresses:
items: ARP maps a known IP address to a MAC address: the sender broadcasts an ARP request ('who has 192.168.1.1?') and the owner replies by unicast; results are cached in the ARP table. EtherType 0x0806.
Proxy ARP lets a router answer on behalf of hosts on another network; gratuitous ARP announces one's own mapping and detects duplicate addresses.
RARP does the reverse, MAC to IP, for diskless machines at boot; it needs a RARP server on every physical network and returns only an IP address.
BOOTP (UDP 67 server, 68 client) replaced RARP: it runs above IP, can cross routers via relay agents and also supplies mask, gateway and boot file, but uses static tables.
DHCP extends BOOTP with dynamic, leased allocation from a pool (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) and is the standard method today.

concepts.text: ICMP: Error Reporting and Diagnostics

rows: Network, host, port unreachable; fragmentation needed but DF set
Router tells host a better next-hop router

concepts.text: ICMP messages are carried inside IP datagrams (protocol 1) and drive two everyday tools:
items: ping sends ICMP Echo Request (type 8) and waits for Echo Reply (type 0), reporting reachability, round-trip time and packet loss.

traceroute (tracert on Windows) sends probes with TTL = 1, 2, 3, …; each router where TTL expires returns Time Exceeded (type 11), revealing the path hop by hop. The destination answers with Port Unreachable (UDP probes, Unix) or Echo Reply (ICMP probes, Windows).
ICMP never reports errors about ICMP error messages, about fragments other than the first, or about broadcast/multicast datagrams, to avoid message storms.
An ICMP error carries the original IP header plus the first 8 bytes of its data so the sender can identify the affected connection.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: IP, ICMP, RARP and DHCP

In four words IP is connectionless, unreliable, best-effort and routed: nothing is set up before sending, delivery is not guaranteed, nothing is retransmitted, and every datagram is routed on its own by its destination address. ICMP is IP's companion for error reporting and diagnostics; the ping command uses its Echo Request and Echo Reply to test connectivity, and traceroute uses Time Exceeded messages to find the path. ARP turns a known IP address into a MAC address, while RARP did the reverse (MAC to IP) and has been replaced by DHCP.

Worked example 1: 2400-byte datagram (20-byte header, 2380 data bytes), next link MTU 1000
Data per fragment = 1000 - 20 = 980 -> round down to a multiple of 8 -> 976
Frag  Data bytes    Offset field      MF  Total length
1     0-975         0/8    = 0        1   996
2     976-1951      976/8  = 122      1   996
3     1952-2379     1952/8 = 244      0   448
A later link has MTU 500, so fragment 2 is split again (480 data bytes per piece):
2a    976-1455      976/8  = 122      1   500
2b    1456-1935     1456/8 = 182      1   500
2c    1936-1951     1936/8 = 242      1   36
Offsets stay relative to the original datagram, and 2c keeps MF = 1
because fragment 3 still follows; only the true end of the data has MF = 0

concepts.plainText: Data per fragment d = 8 × floor((MTU − H) / 8); number of fragments N = ceil(D / d), where H is the header length and D the original data length

concepts.text: The field sizes fit together: the 13-bit offset counts 8-byte blocks, so it can reach 2^13 × 8 = 65,536 bytes, just enough for the largest datagram of 65,535 bytes allowed by the 16-bit Total Length. Every router must recompute the header checksum because it decrements the TTL, which is also why the checksum covers only the header; checking the whole payload at every hop would be slow and is left to TCP, UDP and the link layer. Fragments are reassembled only at the destination because they may travel by different routes. If any one fragment is lost, the reassembly timer expires and the whole datagram is discarded, so fragmentation multiplies the effect of packet loss.

Worked example 2: IPv4 header checksum (a ping from 192.168.1.10 to 8.8.8.8)
Header words: 4500 0054 1A2B 4000 4001 [0000] C0A8 010A 0808 0808
Sum = 4500 + 0054 + 1A2B + 4000 + 4001 + C0A8 + 010A + 0808 + 0808 = 1B142
Fold the carry back in: B142 + 1 = B143
Checksum = one's complement of B143 = 4EBC, so the header carries 40 01 4E BC
Receiver: sum of all ten words including 4EBC = B143 + 4EBC = FFFF -> no error found
Next router: TTL 64 -> 63 turns word 4001 into 3F01, so it recomputes the checksum: 4FBC

Worked trace: traceroute (Unix: UDP probes to port 33434 and up, 3 per TTL), target 4 hops away
TTL 1 -> R1 decrements it to 0, drops the probe, returns Time Exceeded (11/0) -> line 1: R1
TTL 2 -> R2 returns Time Exceeded -> line 2: R2
TTL 3 -> R3 returns Time Exceeded -> line 3: R3
TTL 4 -> target: no process on that UDP port -> Port Unreachable (3/3) -> trace ends
Each line shows three round-trip times; '* * *' means no answer before the timeout
Windows tracert sends ICMP Echo Requests instead and stops at the Echo Reply (type 0)
ping: Echo Request (8/0) carries an identifier and sequence number; the reply echoes them
A reply arriving with TTL 57 from a host that starts at 64 has crossed 64 - 57 = 7 routers
DHCP step by step (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge, remembered as DORA):
items: Discover: the client, still without an address, broadcasts from 0.0.0.0, UDP port 68, to 255.255.255.255, UDP port 67.
Offer: each server that can help offers an address with mask, default gateway, DNS servers and a lease time.
Request: the client broadcasts which offer it accepts, which also tells the other servers that their offers were declined.
Acknowledge: the chosen server confirms the lease. A client that finds the address already in use (for example by an ARP probe) sends DHCPDECLINE, and a server can refuse a request with DHCPNAK.

Renewal: at T1 (50 % of the lease by default) the client unicasts a Request to its own server; if that fails, at T2 (87.5 %) it broadcasts to any server (rebinding). DHCPRELEASE returns the address early.

A relay agent on the router turns the client's broadcast into a unicast to a server on another subnet and writes its own interface address into the giaddr field, so the server picks the right address pool.

rows: No: a server is needed on every network
IP address, mask, default gateway, DNS server, boot file
All of BOOTP's plus a lease time and many more options
Dynamic leases from a pool, or fixed reservations

concepts.text: Fragmentation checklist: subtract the header from the MTU and round the data down to a multiple of 8; offset field = data bytes before this fragment / 8; Total Length = data + header; every fragment keeps the original Identification; MF = 1 on every fragment except the one holding the last byte of the original data. To find the original size from the last fragment, compute offset × 8 + (Total Length − header) and add one header.

Common mistakes: the fragment offset is in 8-byte units and HLEN in 4-byte words, but Total Length is in bytes and includes the header. The header checksum covers the header only; TCP and UDP checksums cover the data. TTL is decremented by one per router, so it acts as a hop limit rather than a time. A failed ping does not prove a host is down, because many hosts and firewalls block ICMP Echo. ICMP travels inside IP (protocol 1) but is still a network-layer protocol.

formulas.plainText: Header length = HLEN × 4 bytes
Fragment offset = byte position / 8
Fragments = ceil((L − H) / (floor((MTU − H)/8) × 8))

notes.text: Fragmentation questions: subtract the header from the MTU, round data down to a multiple of 8, then divide byte positions by 8 for the offset field. 4000-byte datagram over MTU 1500 gives offsets 0, 185, 370.

The IPv4 header checksum covers only the header, not the data, and must be recomputed at every router because TTL changes. HLEN and fragment offset are both scaled fields: multiply HLEN by 4 and the offset by 8.
ICMP is a network-layer protocol even though it is carried inside IP datagrams, just as ARP is usually drawn at the boundary of the data link and network layers.

concepts.text: Why IPv6

IPv6 was designed mainly because the 32-bit IPv4 address space was running out, despite CIDR and NAT. It uses 128-bit addresses, giving 2^128 (about 3.4 × 10^38, or 340 undecillion) addresses, enough to give every device a globally unique address with no need for NAT. It also brings a simplified fixed 40-byte header for faster router processing, optional features moved into extension headers, stateless address autoconfiguration, built-in support for IPsec, better QoS through the flow label, and no fragmentation by routers.
Address Notation and Types
An IPv6 address is written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, and can be shortened:
items: Rule 1: leading zeros in any group may be dropped → 2001:db8:0:0:0:ff00:42:8329.
Rule 2: one run of consecutive all-zero groups may be replaced by :: → 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329.
The :: may appear only once in an address; otherwise the number of missing groups would be ambiguous.
Prefixes use CIDR notation, e.g. 2001:db8:abcd::/48; a LAN subnet is normally /64, leaving a 64-bit interface identifier.

rows: Valid on one link only; used by neighbour discovery
Delivered to the nearest member of a group

concepts.text: IPv6 Base Header (40 bytes)

rows: Identifies packets of one flow for special handling
Bytes after the 40-byte base header, including extension headers
Type of the following extension header or upper-layer protocol (6 TCP, 17 UDP, 58 ICMPv6)
Decremented at each hop, like IPv4 TTL

concepts.plainText: Total packet length = 40 + payload length

concepts.text: Extension Headers

rows: Options every router must examine (e.g. jumbograms, router alert)
Options for the destination (or for listed routers when before routing)
List of intermediate nodes to visit (source routing)
Fragmentation by the source: identification, offset, M flag

concepts.text: Extension headers form a daisy chain: each Next Header field names the header that follows, and the last one names the upper-layer protocol. The recommended order is hop-by-hop options (must come first, immediately after the base header), destination options, routing, fragment, AH, ESP, destination options for the final destination, then the upper-layer header. Only the hop-by-hop header is processed by every router, so ordinary routers look at just the fixed 40-byte header. IPv6 routers never fragment: the source uses path MTU discovery and the fragment header, and every link must support at least 1280 bytes.

rows: None (left to link and transport layers)
Neighbour discovery (ICMPv6); IPsec built into the design

concepts.text: Transition from IPv4 to IPv6
Because the whole Internet cannot switch on one day, three families of transition mechanisms are used:
items: Dual stack: hosts and routers run IPv4 and IPv6 side by side and use DNS answers (A vs AAAA records) to pick the version for each destination; the preferred long-term approach.

Tunnelling: IPv6 packets are encapsulated in IPv4 packets (IP protocol 41) to cross an IPv4-only region. Configured tunnels are set manually; automatic ones include 6to4 (prefix 2002::/16 embedding the site's IPv4 address), Teredo (through NAT over UDP) and ISATAP.

Header translation: used when one side speaks only IPv6 and the other only IPv4. NAT64 translates headers at the boundary, usually with DNS64 synthesising addresses in 64:ff9b::/96; SIIT is the stateless variant.
IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses (::ffff:a.b.c.d) let dual-stack software represent IPv4 peers in IPv6 form.

concepts.text: ICMPv6, Neighbour Discovery and Multicasting
ICMPv6 (next header 58) merges the roles of ICMP, ARP and IGMP:
items: Error messages: 1 destination unreachable, 2 packet too big (used by path MTU discovery), 3 time exceeded, 4 parameter problem; informational 128/129 echo request/reply.
Neighbour discovery replaces ARP: neighbour solicitation (135) and advertisement (136) resolve link-layer addresses using solicited-node multicast addresses (ff02::1:ffXX:XXXX), not broadcast.
Router solicitation (133) and router advertisement (134) announce prefixes for stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC); redirect is type 137; duplicate address detection checks uniqueness.
IPv6 multicast addresses start with ff and carry flags and a 4-bit scope (ff02 link-local, ff05 site-local, ff0e global); ff02::1 is all nodes and ff02::2 all routers.
Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) replaces IGMP: MLDv1 corresponds to IGMPv2 and MLDv2 to IGMPv3 (source-specific). Multicast routing still uses PIM.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: IPv6 Addressing, Headers and Transition

IPv4 offers only 2^32, about 4.3 billion, addresses, and the Internet grew far faster than its designers expected, so the free pool ran out despite CIDR and NAT. IPv6 has 2^128, about 3.4 × 10^38 or 340 undecillion, addresses, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits (16 bits per group), for example 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334, which shortens to 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334. Its other improvements are a simpler fixed header that routers process faster, end-to-end addressing without NAT, better multicast support and automatic address configuration. Three families of methods let the two versions coexist: dual stack (run both), tunnelling (IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets) and translation (convert between the two).

IPsec in IPv6 is often described as 'mandatory', but that is out of date. AH and ESP are defined as IPv6 extension headers and early node requirements (RFC 4294, 2006) made IPsec support mandatory, but RFC 6434 (2011) and RFC 8504 (2019) only recommend it, and actually using IPsec has always been optional, exactly as in IPv4.

Worked example 1: shortening and expanding IPv6 addresses
Full form:                2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334
1. Drop leading zeros:    2001:db8:85a3:0:0:8a2e:370:7334
2. Longest zero run -> :: 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334
Expanding: 6 groups are written, so :: stands for 8 - 6 = 2 groups of 0000
Tie between two runs: 2001:db8:0:0:ab:0:0:5 -> compress the first -> 2001:db8::ab:0:0:5
A single zero group is not replaced by ::  -> 2001:db8:0:1:1:1:1:1 stays as written
Canonical form (RFC 5952): lowercase hex, no leading zeros, :: once on the longest run

concepts.plainText: A /p1 prefix holds 2^(p2 − p1) subnets of length /p2, and a /p prefix holds 2^(128 − p) addresses (no network or broadcast address is subtracted in IPv6)

Worked example 2: MAC 00:0C:29:AB:CD:EF on a LAN with prefix 2001:db8:1:1::/64
Split the MAC and insert FFFE:        000C29 | FFFE | ABCDEF

Interface ID:           020c:29ff:feab:cdef

Tunnels: 6in4 and 6to4 use IPv4 protocol 41; Teredo uses UDP port 3544 and 2001::/32
