For a^(n²): p² < |xy²z| ≤ p² + p < (p + 1)², so the length is not a perfect square
De Morgan: L1 ∩ L2 = complement(complement(L1) ∪ complement(L2))

notes.text: Choose the string so that the condition |xy| ≤ p forces y into one uniform block (for example, only a's in a^p b^p). Then a single value of i, usually 0 or 2, breaks the language for every possible split.
Closure properties give a quick non-regularity proof: if L ∩ a*b* = {a^n b^n} and a*b* is regular, then L cannot be regular, since regular languages are closed under intersection.
Regular languages are closed under finite union but not under infinite union: every language, including {a^n b^n}, is an infinite union of singleton (regular) languages.

concepts.text: Ambiguous Grammars

A CFG is ambiguous if at least one string in L(G) has two or more distinct parse trees. Equivalently, the string has two different leftmost derivations, or two different rightmost derivations. Ambiguity is a property of the grammar, not of the string alone, and it matters because a compiler assigns meaning by the parse tree. The classic example is E → E + E | E * E | id, which gives id + id * id two trees.

Grammar: E -> E + E | E * E | id     String: id + id * id

Tree 1 (+ at root, means id + (id * id)):
E => E + E => id + E => id + E * E => id + id * E => id + id * id

Tree 2 (* at root, means (id + id) * id):
E => E * E => E + E * E => id + E * E => id + id * E => id + id * id

Two different leftmost derivations -> the grammar is ambiguous.
Removing ambiguity from expression grammars:
items: Precedence: introduce one variable per precedence level, lowest precedence nearest the root: E for +, T for *, F for atoms.
Left associativity: use left recursion, E → E + T | T and T → T * F | F, so a + b + c groups as (a + b) + c.
Right associativity (e.g. exponent): use right recursion, P → F ^ P | F.
Dangling else: split statements into matched and unmatched forms so each else pairs with the nearest unmatched if.
There is no general algorithm: deciding whether an arbitrary CFG is ambiguous is undecidable.

concepts.text: A context-free language is inherently ambiguous if every grammar that generates it is ambiguous; the standard example is {aⁱbʲcᵏ | i = j or j = k}, where strings aⁿbⁿcⁿ always have two parse trees.
Simplifying a CFG
Before converting to a normal form, clean the grammar in this safe order:
items: Remove ε-productions: find nullable variables (A ⇒* ε), then for each production add versions with every combination of nullable symbols omitted, and delete A → ε (keep S → ε only if ε ∈ L).
Remove unit productions A → B: for each unit pair (A, B) with A ⇒* B, copy all non-unit bodies of B to A.
Remove useless symbols: first delete non-generating variables (those deriving no terminal string), then delete symbols unreachable from S.
Doing these steps in this order guarantees that none reintroduces a problem removed earlier.

concepts.text: Chomsky Normal Form (CNF)

concepts.latex: A \rightarrow BC \ \mid\ a \quad (A, B, C \in V,\ a \in T;\ S \rightarrow \varepsilon \text{ only if } \varepsilon \in L)
concepts.plainText: A → BC | a, with B and C variables and a a terminal; S → ε allowed only when ε is in the language

concepts.text: Converting any CFG to CNF:
items: Step 1: add a new start symbol S0 → S so S never appears on a right side.
Step 2: remove ε-productions, then unit productions, then useless symbols.
Step 3: in every body of length ≥ 2, replace each terminal a by a new variable Ca with Ca → a.
Step 4: break bodies longer than 2 into a chain: A → B1B2B3 becomes A → B1X and X → B2B3.
Every CFL without ε has a CNF grammar; the parse tree of a CNF grammar is a binary tree.

concepts.text:
Convert S -> aSb | ab to CNF
Step 3 (terminals): A -> a, B -> b;  S -> ASB | AB
Step 4 (split):     S -> AX, X -> SB
CNF:  S -> AX | AB,  X -> SB,  A -> a,  B -> b

Check aabb (n = 4, so 2n - 1 = 7 steps):
S => AX => aX => aSB => aABB => aaBB => aabB => aabb

concepts.latex: \text{steps to derive } w \text{ in CNF} = 2n - 1,\quad n = |w| \ge 1
concepts.plainText: In CNF a string of length n needs exactly 2n − 1 steps: n − 1 uses of A → BC and n uses of A → a

concepts.text: Greibach Normal Form (GNF) and BNF

In Greibach Normal Form every production has the shape A → aα, a single terminal followed by zero or more variables (α ∈ V*). Each step therefore emits exactly one terminal, so a string of length n is derived in exactly n steps, and the grammar has no left recursion. GNF maps directly onto a PDA that reads one input symbol per move, which is why it is used in the CFG-to-PDA proof. Conversion requires removing left recursion (A → Aα | β becomes A → β | βA′, A′ → α | αA′) and substituting until each body starts with a terminal.

Backus-Naur Form (BNF), introduced by John Backus and Peter Naur for ALGOL 60, is the standard notation for writing CFGs that define programming-language syntax. Non-terminals are written in angle brackets, ::= means 'is defined as', | separates alternatives, and terminals appear literally, e.g. <expr> ::= <expr> + <term> | <term>. Extended BNF (EBNF) adds { } for repetition, [ ] for optional parts and ( ) for grouping, so it needs fewer recursive rules.

rows: Building a PDA, no left recursion

formulas.plainText: CNF: A → BC | a
CNF derivation length = 2n − 1 for a string of length n
GNF: A → aα with α a string of variables; n steps for a string of length n

notes.text: For numeric MCQs: a string of length n needs 2n − 1 derivation steps in CNF and exactly n steps in GNF. For n = 5 that is 9 steps in CNF and 5 in GNF.

Ambiguity belongs to a grammar and can often be removed by rewriting it; inherent ambiguity belongs to a language and can never be removed. Showing one string with two parse trees proves a grammar ambiguous, but no algorithm decides ambiguity in general.
Simplify in the order ε-productions, unit productions, useless symbols. Removing useless symbols first can leave new useless symbols after the other steps.

concepts.text: What a Pushdown Automaton Is

A pushdown automaton (PDA) is a finite automaton with ε-moves plus an unbounded stack used as last-in first-out memory. On each move it looks at the current state, the next input symbol (or reads nothing, an ε-move) and the symbol on top of the stack; it then changes state and replaces the top symbol by a string of stack symbols (popping, keeping or pushing). The stack lets it count and match nested structure such as aⁿbⁿ, which a finite automaton cannot. PDAs recognise exactly the context-free languages.

concepts.plainText: M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F)

concepts.text: The seven components of a PDA:
items: Q: finite set of states; q0 ∈ Q is the start state.
Σ: input alphabet; Γ: stack alphabet (may include input symbols).
δ: transition function Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × Γ → finite subsets of Q × Γ*.
Z0 ∈ Γ: initial stack symbol, marking the bottom of the stack.
F ⊆ Q: set of final (accepting) states.
(p, γ) ∈ δ(q, a, X) means: in state q, reading a with X on top, go to p and replace X by γ (γ = ε pops, γ = X leaves it, γ = YX pushes Y).

concepts.text: An instantaneous description (ID) is a triple (q, w, γ): the current state, the unread input, and the stack contents with the top written leftmost. If (p, β) ∈ δ(q, a, X) then (q, aw, Xγ) ⊢ (p, w, βγ), and ⊢* denotes zero or more moves. Acceptance is defined in terms of the IDs reachable from (q0, w, Z0).
Acceptance: Final State vs Empty Stack

rows: (q0, w, Z0) ⊢* (p, ε, γ) with p ∈ F, any stack γ
(q0, w, Z0) ⊢* (p, ε, ε) for any state p
For NPDAs each mode can be converted to the other

concepts.text: Worked PDA for aⁿbⁿ (n ≥ 1)

Q = {q0, q1, q2}, Σ = {a, b}, Γ = {a, Z0}, F = {q2}

d(q0, a, Z0) = {(q0, aZ0)}   push first a
d(q0, a, a)  = {(q0, aa)}    push each further a
d(q0, b, a)  = {(q1, e)}     first b pops one a
d(q1, b, a)  = {(q1, e)}     each b pops one a
d(q1, e, Z0) = {(q2, Z0)}    all a's matched -> accept
(d = delta, e = epsilon)

Trace for aabb (accepted):
(q0, aabb, Z0) |- (q0, abb, aZ0) |- (q0, bb, aaZ0)
  |- (q1, b, aZ0) |- (q1, e, Z0) |- (q2, e, Z0)   q2 in F

Trace for aab (rejected):
(q0, aab, Z0) |- (q0, ab, aZ0) |- (q0, b, aaZ0) |- (q1, e, aZ0)
  no move on (q1, e, a) -> halt in non-final state
Deterministic vs Nondeterministic PDA
Unlike finite automata, determinism reduces the power of a PDA:
items: DPDA: in every configuration at most one move is possible, and an ε-move on (q, X) is not allowed alongside an input move on (q, a, X).
DPDAs accept the deterministic CFLs (DCFLs), a proper subset of the CFLs; LR(k) parsers are DPDAs.
{wcwᴿ} is a DCFL: the centre marker c tells the machine when to switch from pushing to popping.
Even palindromes {wwᴿ} need an NPDA, which must guess the middle of the input nondeterministically.
Every DCFL has an unambiguous grammar, and DCFLs are closed under complement (general CFLs are not).

concepts.text: CFG ↔ PDA Equivalence
CFG → PDA (single-state PDA accepting by empty stack, simulating leftmost derivations):
items: Step 1: use one state q; stack alphabet Γ = V ∪ T; the initial stack symbol is the start symbol S.
Step 2: for each variable A, add δ(q, ε, A) ∋ (q, β) for every production A → β (expand the top variable).
Step 3: for each terminal a, add δ(q, a, a) = {(q, ε)} (match input against the top terminal and pop it).
Step 4: accept by empty stack; the stack always holds the unmatched tail of a leftmost sentential form.

PDA → CFG (outline): convert to an empty-stack PDA, create variables [pXq] meaning 'from state p the PDA can pop X and end in state q', write productions from each transition, and add S → [q0 Z0 p] for every state p.

formulas.plainText: PDA M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F)
δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × Γ → finite subsets of Q × Γ*

formulas.latex: L(M) = \{\, w \mid (q_0, w, Z_0) \vdash^* (p, \varepsilon, \gamma),\ p \in F \,\}

notes.text: For aⁿbⁿ the pattern is always: push one symbol per a, pop one per b, and accept when the bottom marker Z0 reappears exactly as the input ends. Reading aaabbb, the stack reaches its maximum height of 4 (three a's plus Z0).
DFA and NFA are equal in power, but DPDA is strictly weaker than NPDA. Do not assume every CFL has a deterministic PDA; even palindromes {wwᴿ} do not.
A PDA with two stacks can simulate a Turing machine, so adding a second stack jumps from type 2 straight to type 0 power.

concepts.text: Pumping Lemma for Context-Free Languages

For every context-free language L there is a constant p (the pumping length) such that every string s ∈ L with |s| ≥ p can be split as s = uvwxy satisfying three conditions: |vwx| ≤ p, |vx| ≥ 1, and uvⁱwxⁱy ∈ L for every i ≥ 0. Unlike the regular pumping lemma, two pieces v and x are pumped together, in step. Some books write the split as uvxyz with |vxy| ≤ p and |vy| > 0; the meaning is identical. The lemma gives a necessary condition, so it is used to prove that a language is not context-free.

concepts.latex: s = uvwxy,\ |vwx| \le p,\ |vx| \ge 1,\ uv^i w x^i y \in L\ \ \forall i \ge 0
concepts.plainText: s = uvwxy, |vwx| ≤ p, |vx| ≥ 1, and uvⁱwxⁱy ∈ L for all i ≥ 0

concepts.text: Why it holds (proof idea using a CNF grammar with k variables, p = 2^k):
items: A CNF parse tree is binary, so a yield of length ≥ 2^k forces a root-to-leaf path with more than k variables.
By the pigeonhole principle some variable A repeats on that path.
The upper A derives vwx and the lower A derives w, so A ⇒* vAx and A ⇒* w.
Repeating the A ⇒* vAx part i times gives uvⁱwxⁱy; choosing the lowest repetition keeps |vwx| ≤ p, and CNF having no unit or ε rules gives |vx| ≥ 1.

concepts.text: Proving aⁿbⁿcⁿ Is Not Context-Free

1. Assume L = {a^n b^n c^n | n >= 0} is a CFL with pumping length p.
2. Choose s = a^p b^p c^p, so |s| = 3p >= p.
3. Consider any split s = uvwxy with |vwx| <= p and |vx| >= 1.
4. |vwx| <= p, so vwx cannot touch both the a's and the c's
   (the p b's lie between them).
5. Case 1: v and x each hold one kind of symbol -> pumping i = 2
   raises at most two of the three counts, the third stays p.
6. Case 2: v or x mixes two symbols -> uv^2wx^2y has them out of
   order (e.g. ...abab...).
7. Either way uv^2wx^2y is not in L: contradiction, so L is not a CFL.
Other standard non-context-free languages:
items: {ww | w ∈ {a, b}*}: copying needs queue-like memory; choose s = aᵖbᵖaᵖbᵖ.
{aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 0} and {aⁿbⁿcⁿdⁿ}: three or more counts that must agree.
{a^(n²) | n ≥ 0} and {a^q | q prime}: lengths grow too irregularly for linear pumping.
{aⁱbʲcᵏ | i < j < k}: two independent comparisons must hold at once.

concepts.text: Ogden's lemma is a stronger version in which any p or more positions of s are marked, and vx must contain at least one marked position (vwx at most p marked positions); it proves some languages non-context-free where the basic lemma fails, e.g. {aⁱbʲcᵏdˡ | i = 0 or j = k = l}.
Closure Properties

Otherwise intersection would follow by De Morgan

In CNF, look for a cycle among useful variables

concepts.text: The Cocke-Younger-Kasami (CYK) algorithm tests membership using a grammar in CNF and dynamic programming. A triangular table has a cell for every substring, n(n + 1)/2 cells for a string of length n; cells for length-1 substrings get every A with A → a, and longer substrings get every A with A → BC where B derives a prefix and C the remaining suffix. The string is accepted if S appears in the cell for the whole string. With three nested loops over start, length and split point, the running time is O(n³·|G|).

concepts.latex: V_{i,j} = \{ A \mid A \rightarrow BC,\ B \in V_{i,k},\ C \in V_{i+k,\,j-k} \}
concepts.plainText: V(i, j) = { A | A → BC, B in V(i, k), C in V(i + k, j − k) } for 1 ≤ k < j; accept if S ∈ V(1, n)

concepts.text: Related facts that MCQs often combine:
items: Every regular language is context-free; a CFL intersected with a regular language is context-free.
CFL minus a regular language is context-free (L − R = L ∩ complement of R).
The complement of a particular CFL may or may not be context-free; the class is simply not closed.
DCFLs are closed under complement and intersection with regular sets, but not under union or intersection.
CFLs are closed under substitution, inverse homomorphism and reversal as well as the operations in the table.

formulas.latex: s = uvwxy,\ |vwx| \le p,\ |vx| \ge 1,\ uv^i w x^i y \in L
formulas.plainText: s = uvwxy with |vwx| ≤ p, |vx| ≥ 1 and uvⁱwxⁱy ∈ L for all i ≥ 0

formulas.latex: \{a^n b^n c^m\} \cap \{a^m b^n c^n\} = \{a^n b^n c^n\}
formulas.plainText: {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} ∩ {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}: two CFLs whose intersection is not a CFL
CYK table has n(n + 1)/2 cells and runs in O(n³) time

notes.text: For aⁿbⁿcⁿ pick s = aᵖbᵖcᵖ. The key observation is that the window vwx has length at most p, so it can touch at most two of the three blocks; pumping with i = 2 (or i = 0) then unbalances the counts.
The pumping lemma can only prove that a language is NOT context-free. A language that satisfies the pumping conditions is not thereby proven to be context-free.

To prove non-closure under complement, argue by contradiction: if CFLs were closed under complement, De Morgan's law with closure under union would make them closed under intersection, which is false.

concepts.text: Recursive vs Recursively Enumerable Languages

Used as a language recognizer, a TM M accepts L(M). If some TM accepts L, L is recursively enumerable (RE), also called Turing-recognisable; such a machine may loop forever on strings outside L. If some TM accepts L and halts on every input, L is recursive, also called decidable, and the machine is a decider. Every recursive language is RE, but not the reverse: the halting language and the universal language are RE but not recursive.

concepts.plainText: L recursive ⟺ L ∈ RE and complement(L) ∈ RE

concepts.text: TM as a Computing Function

A TM computes a function f if, started with an encoding of the argument on the tape, it halts with an encoding of f(argument) on the tape. Numbers are usually written in unary (n as 1ⁿ) with 0 as a separator. A function computed by a TM that halts on every argument is total recursive; if it may loop on some arguments it is partial recursive. Unary addition 1ᵐ01ⁿ → 1^(m+n) needs only three states: move right over the 1s, change the separator 0 into 1, run to the right end, and erase the last 1.
Other arithmetic TMs in outline:
items: Proper subtraction m ∸ n on 1ᵐ01ⁿ: repeatedly replace the leftmost 1 of the first block and the leftmost 1 of the second block with blanks; stop when either block runs out, then clean up so the remaining 1s give max(m − n, 0).
Multiplication m × n on 1ᵐ01ⁿ: for each 1 of the first block, mark it and copy the whole second block to the end of the tape; finally erase the inputs, leaving 1^(mn).
Composite functions are built by running such machines as subroutines one after another.

concepts.plainText: m ∸ n = max(m − n, 0)

concepts.text: TM as an Enumerator

An enumerator is a TM with an output tape (or printer) that starts with a blank input and prints strings of a language, possibly forever and possibly with repeats. The language it enumerates is the set of all strings it ever prints. A language is RE exactly when some enumerator enumerates it, which is why RE languages are called recursively enumerable.
Why enumerators and recognisers are equivalent:
items: Enumerator to recogniser: on input w, run the enumerator and accept whenever it prints w (loops if w is never printed).

Recogniser to enumerator: for i = 1, 2, 3, ..., run M for i steps on each of the first i strings s1..si of Σ* in shortlex order and print those accepted. Dovetailing avoids getting stuck on a looping input.
A language is recursive if and only if some enumerator prints it in shortlex (length, then lexicographic) order.

concepts.text: Closure Properties

A language whose complement is RE is called co-RE. Recursive = RE ∩ co-RE: if both L and its complement have recognisers, run them in parallel on w; exactly one must accept, so the combination always halts. Since HALT_TM is RE but not recursive, its complement is not RE, and so it is co-RE but not RE.

formulas.plainText: Recursive = RE ∩ co-RE
m ∸ n = max(m − n, 0)

notes.text: The quickest test for which class a closure property belongs to is complement: recursive languages are closed under it, RE languages are not. If both L and its complement are RE, L must be recursive.
Recognisable and decidable are not synonyms. A recogniser only has to accept strings in L; it may loop on the rest. Only a decider is required to halt on every input.
Recursive languages are closed under inverse homomorphism but not under homomorphism; RE languages are closed under both. Every context-free and context-sensitive language is recursive.

concepts.text: Variants of the Turing Machine

The TM model is robust: adding tapes, tracks, a two-way infinite tape or nondeterminism does not enlarge the class of languages accepted. Each variant can be simulated by the standard single-tape deterministic TM, and vice versa. The variants differ only in convenience and speed, which matters for complexity theory but not for computability.
Tape-shape variants:
items: Two-way infinite tape: the tape extends without bound in both directions. Simulated by a one-way tape with two tracks, one holding the right half and one holding the left half reversed, plus a marker at the fold.
Multi-track TM: one tape and one head, but each cell holds a k-tuple of symbols, one per track. It is a standard TM whose tape alphabet is the set of all tuples.
A track is often used to hold a marker (for example * under the head position of another tape) while the other track keeps the data.

concepts.text: Multi-tape TM

A k-tape TM has k tapes, each with its own independent head. The input starts on tape 1 and the others are blank. In one move the machine reads all k scanned symbols, then writes on each tape and moves each head independently (L, R or S). A single-tape TM simulates it with 2k tracks: k tracks hold the tape contents and k tracks mark the head positions. Each simulated step needs a sweep over the used portion of the tape, so t(n) steps become O(t(n)²) steps.

concepts.plainText: δ: Q × Γ^k → Q × Γ^k × {L, R, S}^k

concepts.text: Non-deterministic TM

In a non-deterministic TM (NTM), δ(q, a) is a finite set of possible moves, so a computation is a tree of branches. The NTM accepts w if at least one branch reaches an accepting state. A deterministic TM simulates it by breadth-first search of the computation tree, using a queue of IDs on a work tape (depth-first search could follow an infinite branch forever). If every branch has length at most t(n) and each node has at most b children, the simulation takes about bᵗ⁽ⁿ⁾ steps, an exponential slowdown, but the language accepted is the same.

rows: Cost of simulation on a standard TM

concepts.text: Encoding TMs and the Universal TM

Any TM can be written as a binary string ⟨M⟩. In the Hopcroft–Motwani–Ullman scheme, number the states q1, q2, ... (q1 start, q2 the single final state), tape symbols X1 = 0, X2 = 1, X3 = B, and directions D1 = L, D2 = R. The transition δ(qi, Xj) = (qk, Xl, Dm) is coded as 0ⁱ 1 0ʲ 1 0ᵏ 1 0ˡ 1 0ᵐ, and codes of successive transitions are separated by 11. Because every TM has such a code, TMs are countable, while languages over {0, 1} are uncountable, so some languages are not RE at all.

A universal Turing machine U takes ⟨M, w⟩ (the code of a TM followed by an input) and simulates M on w: it accepts if M accepts w and loops if M loops. A convenient U has three tapes: one for ⟨M⟩, one for M's simulated tape and one for M's current state. U is the theoretical model of a stored-program computer, and its language L_u = { ⟨M, w⟩ : M accepts w } is RE but not recursive.
Linear Bounded Automata

A linear bounded automaton (LBA) is a non-deterministic TM whose head may never leave the cells holding the input, which are bracketed by end markers. LBAs accept exactly the context-sensitive (type 1) languages, such as { aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1 }, which no PDA can accept. Membership for an LBA is decidable because it has only finitely many IDs for a given input length, so every context-sensitive language is recursive.

formulas.latex: \mathrm{TIME}_{1\text{-tape}} = O(t(n)^2) \text{ for a } t(n)\text{-time } k\text{-tape TM}
formulas.plainText: k-tape TM in t(n) steps → single-tape TM in O(t(n)²) steps
NTM in t(n) steps → DTM in 2^O(t(n)) steps
δ(qi, Xj) = (qk, Xl, Dm) coded as 0^i 1 0^j 1 0^k 1 0^l 1 0^m

notes.text: Remember the pair of slowdowns: multi-tape to single-tape is quadratic, nondeterministic to deterministic is exponential. Neither changes which languages can be accepted.
Nondeterminism adds power to PDAs (NPDA > DPDA) but not to finite automata or Turing machines. Do not carry the PDA result over to TMs.
The universal TM is a recogniser, not a decider: when the simulated machine loops, U loops too. This is the root of the undecidability of L_u and the halting problem.

concepts.text: The Church–Turing Thesis

The Church–Turing thesis states that every function that is effectively computable by an algorithm (a finite, mechanical step-by-step procedure) can be computed by a Turing machine. It is a thesis, not a theorem: effective computability is an informal notion, so it cannot be proved, but every proposed model (lambda calculus, recursive functions, Post systems, RAM machines, modern programming languages) has turned out equivalent to the TM. In practice it lets us say that a problem with no TM solution has no algorithm at all.
Undecidability

A problem is decidable if some TM halts on every instance with the correct yes/no answer. The halting problem HALT_TM = { ⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w } is the classic undecidable problem, proved by diagonalisation: assuming a decider H exists, one builds a machine D that does the opposite of what H predicts about D run on its own description.

Assume decider H(<M>, w) answers 'halts' or 'loops'.
Build D(<M>):
    if H(<M>, <M>) = 'halts' then loop forever
    else halt
Run D on <D>:
    D halts  => H said D loops   (contradiction)
    D loops  => H said D halts   (contradiction)
So H cannot exist: HALT_TM is undecidable (but RE).
Other standard undecidable problems:
items: Post correspondence problem (PCP): given pairs of strings (x1, y1) ... (xk, yk), is there an index sequence i1...im with x_i1...x_im = y_i1...y_im? Undecidable, and used to prove CFG problems undecidable.
Rice's theorem: every non-trivial property of the language recognised by a TM is undecidable (for example, is L(M) empty, finite or regular?).
Whether a CFG is ambiguous, whether two CFGs generate the same language, and whether a CFG generates Σ* are all undecidable.

concepts.text: Reducibility

A mapping (many-one) reduction from A to B, written A ≤m B, is a computable function f such that w ∈ A exactly when f(w) ∈ B. It turns any solver for B into a solver for A. So if A ≤ B and B is decidable, A is decidable; equivalently, if A is undecidable, B is undecidable. To prove a new problem B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable problem (such as HALT_TM or L_u) to B, never the other way round.

concepts.latex: A \le_m B \iff \exists \text{ computable } f : w \in A \Leftrightarrow f(w) \in B
concepts.plainText: A ≤m B ⟺ there is a computable f with w ∈ A ⟺ f(w) ∈ B

concepts.text: Time and Space Complexity

The time complexity of a deterministic TM that halts on all inputs is the function t(n) giving the maximum number of moves on any input of length n; space complexity s(n) is the maximum number of tape cells scanned. Complexity is stated in big-O form, and the model matters: a language decided in O(n) on a two-tape TM (such as 0ⁿ1ⁿ, by copying the 0s to tape 2) takes O(n²) with the simple single-tape method. Polynomial time is the same class on all reasonable deterministic models, which is why P is robust. PSPACE is the class of problems decidable in polynomial space, and P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME.

rows: Decidable by a DTM in polynomial time O(nᵏ)
Decidable by an NTM in polynomial time; a certificate is verifiable in polynomial time
Every problem in P, SAT, graph isomorphism
In NP, and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time
SAT, 3-SAT, clique, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, TSP decision
Every NP problem reduces to it; need not be in NP

concepts.text: NP-completeness, key facts:
items: Cook–Levin theorem (1971): SAT, satisfiability of a Boolean formula, is NP-complete; it was the first problem shown to be so.
A polynomial-time reduction A ≤p B maps instances of A to instances of B in polynomial time. If A is NP-complete, A ≤p B and B ∈ NP, then B is NP-complete.
Standard chain: SAT ≤p 3-SAT ≤p clique ≤p vertex cover; 3-SAT ≤p Hamiltonian cycle ≤p TSP.
P vs NP: P ⊆ NP is known; whether P = NP is open. If any NP-complete problem is in P, then P = NP.

concepts.plainText: P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME

concepts.text: Intractability
A problem is intractable when it is decidable but has no known polynomial-time algorithm (for NP-complete problems, none exists unless P = NP). Ways of coping:
items: Approximation algorithms with a guaranteed ratio, such as a 2-approximation for vertex cover.
Heuristics and metaheuristics (greedy, local search, genetic algorithms, simulated annealing) that work well in practice.
Exact algorithms that are exponential but pruned: backtracking, branch and bound, dynamic programming on small or special inputs.
Restricting the input to special cases solvable in P, such as 2-SAT or problems on trees.

formulas.latex: A \le B,\; B \text{ decidable} \Rightarrow A \text{ decidable}
formulas.plainText: A ≤ B and B decidable ⇒ A decidable
P = union over k ≥ 1 of TIME(n^k)

formulas.latex: B \in \mathrm{NP},\; A \text{ NP-complete},\; A \le_p B \Rightarrow B \text{ NP-complete}
formulas.plainText: B ∈ NP, A NP-complete, A ≤p B ⇒ B NP-complete

notes.text: Direction of reduction is a favourite trap: to show B is hard, reduce a known hard problem A to B (A ≤ B). Reducing B to a hard problem proves nothing about B.

NP does not mean non-polynomial. It means non-deterministic polynomial time, and every problem in P is also in NP. NP-hard problems need not be in NP at all; the halting problem is NP-hard but undecidable.
Decidability and complexity are separate questions. Undecidable problems have no algorithm at all; intractable problems have algorithms, but only impractically slow ones.

concepts.text: The Cathode-Ray Tube

In a CRT an electron gun (heated cathode and control grid) emits a beam of electrons, which focusing and accelerating anodes direct at the phosphor-coated screen. Deflection plates (electrostatic) or deflection coils (magnetic) steer the beam horizontally and vertically. Where the beam strikes, the phosphor glows; the control grid voltage sets the beam intensity and hence the brightness of the spot.
Why the picture must be refreshed:
items: Persistence: the time for light emitted by the phosphor to decay to one-tenth of its original intensity. Low-persistence phosphors need frequent refreshing but suit animation; high-persistence phosphors suit static, complex pictures.
Refresh rate: the number of times per second the picture is redrawn. Below roughly 50 to 60 Hz the eye sees flicker; raster monitors typically use 60 to 80 Hz or more.
Resolution: the maximum number of points that can be displayed without overlap, usually quoted as horizontal pixels x vertical pixels (e.g. 1920 x 1080).

concepts.text: Raster-Scan Displays

In a raster-scan display the beam sweeps the whole screen one horizontal scan line at a time from top to bottom, turning the intensity on and off to form a pattern of pixels. The intensity or colour of every pixel is held in a memory area called the frame buffer (refresh buffer). Because the picture is a grid of pixels, raster displays can show shaded, filled and realistic images, but sloping lines show jagged steps (aliasing).
Retrace and interlacing:
items: Horizontal retrace: at the end of each scan line the beam returns to the left edge of the next line with the beam turned off.
Vertical retrace: after the last scan line the beam returns to the top-left corner to start the next frame.

Interlacing: odd-numbered lines are drawn in one pass (field) and even-numbered lines in the next, so the whole screen is covered twice per frame. A 30 frame/s picture then refreshes at 60 fields/s, reducing flicker at lower bandwidth.

concepts.plainText: Frame buffer size = H x V x n bits (n = bits per pixel)

concepts.text: Colour depth, lookup tables and aspect ratio:
items: With n bits per pixel (n bit planes) a pixel can take 2^n distinct values: 1 bit gives black and white (bitmap), 8 bits give 256 colours, 24 bits give 16,777,216 colours.
Colour lookup table: pixel values index a table of full-colour entries, e.g. 8-bit pixels select 256 simultaneous colours from a palette of 2^24 held as 24-bit table entries.
Aspect ratio: the ratio of horizontal to vertical size of the display (e.g. 4:3, 16:9), or of the number of vertical points to horizontal points needed to draw equal-length lines.

concepts.text: Random-Scan (Vector) Displays

A random-scan or vector display directs the beam only to the parts of the screen where the picture is drawn, tracing each line directly from one endpoint to the other like a pen plotter. The picture is stored as a set of line-drawing commands called the display file (display list or refresh display file). The display processor cycles through these commands 30 to 60 times per second; lines are smooth with no staircase effect, but filled areas and realistic shading are not possible.

rows: Fixed pattern, every line of the screen
Only along the lines to be drawn
Pixel intensities in a frame buffer
Line commands in a display file
Grows with the number of lines

concepts.text: Colour CRTs and Flat-Panel Displays
Two ways a CRT produces colour:
items: Beam penetration: two phosphor layers (red outside, green inside); the beam speed decides how far electrons penetrate. Only four colours (red, green, orange, yellow) are possible; cheap and used with random-scan systems.

Shadow mask: three electron guns (red, green, blue) and a screen of RGB phosphor dot triads; a metal shadow mask with one hole per triad ensures each beam hits only its own colour. It gives a wide range of colours and is used in raster-scan colour monitors.

concepts.text: Flat-panel technologies:
items: LCD: liquid crystal between polarisers twists light to pass or block it; it is non-emissive and needs a backlight. TN panels are fast and cheap but have narrow viewing angles; IPS panels give better colour and wide viewing angles.

Passive-matrix LCD: pixels are addressed at the crossings of row and column conductors, which is cheap but slow with lower contrast. Active-matrix LCD: a thin-film transistor (TFT) at each pixel holds its state, giving faster response and better contrast.
LED display: either an LCD with an LED backlight, or a direct-view panel of light-emitting diodes (large outdoor screens).
OLED: organic layers emit light at each pixel, so no backlight is needed, blacks are true black, contrast is very high and panels can be thin or flexible.
Plasma: cells of neon-based gas between electrode grids glow when ionised; emissive and bright, used for large screens, but heavy and power-hungry.

rows: Cost, burn-in, ageing of blue pixels

formulas.plainText: Frame buffer (bytes) = H x V x n / 8
Number of colours = 2^n for n bits per pixel
Horizontal scan rate = number of scan lines x refresh rate (ignoring retrace)

notes.text: For frame-buffer questions multiply resolution by bits per pixel, divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1024 for KB and again for MB: 1024 x 768 x 24 / 8 = 2,359,296 bytes = 2.25 MB.
Raster = frame buffer of pixels, aliasing, fixed scan pattern; vector = display file of line commands, smooth lines, no filled areas. Swapping these is the classic MCQ trap.
Beam penetration gives only four colours and pairs with random-scan displays; the shadow mask with three guns is the method used in colour raster monitors.

concepts.text: Raster-Scan System Architecture

A simple raster system connects the CPU, system memory, a video controller and I/O devices to the system bus. The frame buffer may be a fixed area of system memory or separate video memory; the video controller has direct access to it so it can refresh the screen without involving the CPU. The CPU runs the application and writes pixel values, while the video controller continuously reads them out to the monitor.
How the video controller refreshes the screen:
items: Two registers hold the current pixel's x and y; starting at the top-left, the controller fetches the pixel value from the frame buffer and uses it to set the beam intensity.
x is incremented along the scan line; at the end of the line x is reset and y moves to the next line; after the last line both are reset for the next frame.
To keep up, several pixels are fetched in one memory access and held in a shift register.
Extra features: colour lookup tables, double buffering (draw into one buffer while the other is displayed, then swap) for smooth animation, and zooming or panning.

concepts.text: More capable systems add a display processor (graphics controller or display coprocessor) with its own display-processor memory. Its main job is scan conversion: digitising a picture definition from the application into pixel values in the frame buffer, e.g. drawing lines, circles, filled polygons and characters. It also performs raster operations such as bit-block transfers (BitBLT), pattern filling, antialiasing and, in many designs, clipping and transformations, freeing the CPU from graphics work.

concepts.plainText: Pixel rate = H x V x refresh rate (pixels per second, ignoring retrace)

concepts.text: Random-Scan System Architecture

In a random-scan system the application program and graphics package translate drawing commands into a display file stored in system memory. The display processor, sometimes called the display processing unit or graphics controller, fetches and executes these commands one by one, driving the deflection system so the beam traces each line. It cycles through the whole display file once per refresh, typically 30 to 60 times per second.

A modern graphics processing unit (GPU) is the descendant of the display processor: a massively parallel processor with thousands of simple cores and its own high-bandwidth video memory. It runs the whole rendering pipeline in hardware, executing programmable vertex and fragment shaders, rasterisation, texturing, depth testing and blending, and is also used for general-purpose parallel computing such as machine learning.
Input Devices

Ball rotated by hand in a fixed housing
Pointing where desk space is limited
Stick tilted from a centre position
Stylus or puck position sensed on a grid
Photocell detects the CRT beam passing under its tip

concepts.text: Output Devices
Printers are divided by whether they strike the paper:
items: Impact printers press formed characters or pins against an inked ribbon onto paper: dot-matrix, daisy-wheel and line printers. They are noisy but can print multi-part forms.

Non-impact printers form the image without striking the paper: laser printers (a laser charges a drum that picks up toner), inkjet printers (fine ink droplets), thermal and dye-sublimation printers. They are quieter and give higher quality.

concepts.text: Other hard-copy and immersive output devices:
items: Pen plotters: flatbed or drum (roller) plotters move pens along the paper to draw vector lines, used for large engineering drawings; raster plotters use electrostatic or inkjet methods.
3D printers: build a solid object layer by layer (additive manufacturing) from a 3D model, e.g. fused deposition modelling, stereolithography or selective laser sintering.
VR headsets: a head-mounted display shows a separate image to each eye for stereoscopic depth and tracks head movement so the view updates as the user turns.

formulas.plainText: Time per pixel = 1 / (H x V x refresh rate)
Video bandwidth = H x V x refresh rate x n/8 bytes per second

notes.text: Remember the six logical input classes by what they return: locator (a point), stroke (many points), string (text), valuator (a number), choice (an option), pick (an object).

The video controller only reads the frame buffer to refresh the screen; the display processor writes into it by scan-converting primitives. In random-scan systems the display processor instead executes the display file directly.
A light pen works by detecting the CRT electron beam, so it does not work on LCD panels; a touch screen, not a light pen, is the modern way to point directly at the display.

concepts.text: Reflection

A reflection produces the mirror image of an object about an axis (a line) or a point. It is equivalent to a 180° rotation out of the plane about the reflection axis, so sizes and angles are preserved but the orientation (clockwise order of vertices) is reversed. Each reflection is its own inverse: applying it twice returns the original object. The standard reflections have simple matrices made of 0s and ±1s.

concepts.plainText: Reflection about y = x: [0 1 0; 1 0 0; 0 0 1]

concepts.text: Shear

A shear distorts an object so that it appears as if its layers had slid over one another. An x-direction shear shifts x in proportion to y: x' = x + sh_x·y, y' = y. A y-direction shear shifts y in proportion to x: y' = y + sh_y·x, x' = x. Worked example: an x-shear with sh_x = 2 maps the unit square (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1) to (0,0), (1,0), (3,1), (2,1), a parallelogram with the same area.

Shear can also be taken relative to a reference line: x' = x + sh_x(y − y_ref) shears in x relative to the line y = y_ref, and y' = y + sh_y(x − x_ref) shears in y relative to x = x_ref. Points on the reference line do not move.
Composite Transformations

A composite transformation is a sequence of basic transformations combined into one matrix by multiplication. With column vectors, P' = M3·M2·M1·P means M1 is applied first, so the product is read right-to-left. Matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative, so the order matters: rotating then translating gives a different result from translating then rotating. Transformations of the same kind (two translations, two rotations about the same point, two scalings) do commute with each other.
Rotation About an Arbitrary Pivot

To rotate about a pivot (x_r, y_r): (1) translate so the pivot moves to the origin, T(−x_r, −y_r); (2) rotate by θ, R(θ); (3) translate back, T(x_r, y_r). Worked example: rotate P(5, 2) by 90° about (2, 2). Step 1 gives (3, 0), step 2 gives (0, 3), step 3 gives (2, 5). The same three-step idea gives scaling about a fixed point: T(x_f, y_f)·S(s_x, s_y)·T(−x_f, −y_f).

concepts.plainText: R_pivot = T(xr, yr) · R(θ) · T(−xr, −yr)

concepts.text: Reflection about an arbitrary line y = mx + c (θ = tan⁻¹ m):
items: Translate by (0, −c) so the line passes through the origin.
Rotate by −θ so the line lies along the x-axis.
Reflect about the x-axis.
Rotate back by +θ.
Translate back by (0, c). Composite: M = T(0, c)·R(θ)·M_x·R(−θ)·T(0, −c).

concepts.text: Why composite matrices are efficient and other facts:
items: Multiply the matrices once, then apply one 3 × 3 matrix per vertex instead of several.
Any 2D affine composite has the form x' = a·x + b·y + c, y' = d·x + e·y + f (six numbers).
Two reflections about lines through the origin at angle α to each other equal a rotation by 2α.
Rotation and uniform scaling commute; rotation and differential scaling generally do not.

formulas.plainText: x-shear: x' = x + shx·y; y-shear: y' = y + shy·x
M = T(xr, yr) · R(θ) · T(−xr, −yr)
x' = xr + (x − xr) cos θ − (y − yr) sin θ
y' = yr + (x − xr) sin θ + (y − yr) cos θ

notes.text: For pivot problems do the three steps numerically: subtract the pivot, rotate, add the pivot back. It is faster and less error-prone than multiplying out the full matrix.
Write composites right-to-left for column vectors: the first transformation applied is the rightmost matrix. Reversing the order generally gives a different (wrong) result.
Reflection reverses the orientation of a figure (its determinant is −1), while shear keeps area unchanged (determinant 1) but does not preserve angles.

concepts.text: Window and Viewport

A scene is described in world coordinates, a device-independent Cartesian system chosen by the application (metres, kilometres, anything). A window is the rectangular area of the world selected for display: it defines what is seen. A viewport is the rectangular area of the display device where the window's contents are shown: it defines where it is seen. Mapping the window onto the viewport is called the viewing (window-to-viewport, or world-to-screen) transformation.
The 2D Viewing Pipeline
Coordinate systems a 2D picture passes through, and the transformation between each pair:
items: Modelling coordinates (MC): each object defined in its own local frame; the modelling transformation places it in the scene.
World coordinates (WC): the whole scene; the viewing transformation sets up a viewing frame (origin and view-up vector), which allows a rotated window.
Viewing coordinates (VC): the window is defined here; the window is mapped to a normalised viewport.
Normalised device coordinates (NDC): device-independent range 0 to 1 (or −1 to 1) in each axis.
Device coordinates (DC): pixel coordinates of a specific monitor or plotter, reached by the workstation transformation.

concepts.text: Clipping is performed against the window (or against the normalised viewport) so that only the visible part of the scene is converted to device coordinates. Because NDC are device-independent, the same picture can be sent to several output devices, each with its own workstation transformation from NDC to its pixel grid.
Window-to-Viewport Mapping

The mapping keeps relative position: a point that is a given fraction of the way across the window appears the same fraction of the way across the viewport. Setting (x_v − xv_min)/(xv_max − xv_min) = (x_w − xw_min)/(xw_max − xw_min) and solving gives x_v = xv_min + (x_w − xw_min)·s_x, with an analogous equation for y. The scale factors s_x and s_y are the ratios of viewport size to window size.

concepts.plainText: xv = xvmin + (xw − xwmin)·sx, sx = (xvmax − xvmin)/(xwmax − xwmin)
yv = yvmin + (yw − ywmin)·sy, sy = (yvmax − yvmin)/(ywmax − ywmin)

concepts.text:
Window   (10,10) to (50,50)   -> 40 x 40
Viewport (100,100) to (300,200) -> 200 x 100
sx = 200/40 = 5        sy = 100/40 = 2.5
World point (30, 20):
  xv = 100 + (30 - 10) * 5   = 200
  yv = 100 + (20 - 10) * 2.5 = 125
Viewport point = (200, 125)
sx != sy -> picture is stretched horizontally

As a composite matrix the mapping is T(xv_min, yv_min)·S(s_x, s_y)·T(−xw_min, −yw_min): move the window corner to the origin, scale to viewport size, then move to the viewport corner. If the window and viewport have different aspect ratios then s_x ≠ s_y and objects are distorted (circles become ellipses). Choosing s_x = s_y, i.e. equal aspect ratios, preserves the shapes.

rows: Less of the scene shown, objects magnified
More of the scene shown, objects smaller
Scene appears to slide across the viewport
Same scene drawn at a new screen place or size

concepts.text: Practical points about device coordinates:
items: Many raster devices put the origin at the top-left with y increasing downwards, so y_screen = H − y (H = screen height) may be needed.
Several viewports can be open at once, each showing a different window of the same world.
Normalised coordinates let an application be written once and displayed on devices of any resolution.

formulas.plainText: sy = (yvmax − yvmin)/(ywmax − ywmin)
xv = xvmin + (xw − xwmin)·sx
Mwv = T(xvmin, yvmin) · S(sx, sy) · T(−xwmin, −ywmin)

notes.text: Remember: window = what is seen (world coordinates), viewport = where it is seen (device coordinates). Shrinking the window zooms in; moving the window pans.
If the window and viewport aspect ratios differ, s_x ≠ s_y and the picture is distorted. Match the aspect ratios when shapes must be preserved.
The step from normalised device coordinates to actual pixel coordinates of a particular output device is called the workstation transformation.

concepts.text: Clipping and Point Clipping

Clipping is the procedure that identifies the parts of a picture lying inside a specified region (the clip window) and discards the rest, so that only visible primitives are scan-converted. A point (x, y) is kept if xw_min ≤ x ≤ xw_max and yw_min ≤ y ≤ yw_max. Lines are harder because a segment may be fully inside, fully outside, or cross one or more window edges, so efficient algorithms try to accept or reject whole segments with cheap tests before computing any intersections.
Cohen–Sutherland Region Codes

The window edges extended to infinity divide the plane into nine regions. Each endpoint is given a 4-bit region code in the order T B R L (bit 4 to bit 1): Top = 1 if y > yw_max, Bottom = 1 if y < yw_min, Right = 1 if x > xw_max, Left = 1 if x < xw_min. The window itself has code 0000.
Cohen–Sutherland procedure for a segment P1P2:
items: Compute the region codes of both endpoints.
Trivial accept: both codes are 0000, so the whole line is inside.
Trivial reject: the bitwise AND of the codes is not 0000, so both ends lie outside the same edge.
Otherwise pick an endpoint that is outside, find where the line meets the boundary indicated by one of its set bits, replace that endpoint with the intersection and recompute its code.
Repeat until the segment is trivially accepted or rejected.

concepts.plainText: Vertical edge x = xb: y = y1 + m(xb − x1); horizontal edge y = yb: x = x1 + (yb − y1)/m

concepts.text: Liang–Barsky Parametric Clipping

Liang–Barsky writes the segment parametrically: x = x1 + t·Δx, y = y1 + t·Δy for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, where Δx = x2 − x1 and Δy = y2 − y1. A point is inside when xw_min ≤ x ≤ xw_max and yw_min ≤ y ≤ yw_max, which rearranges into four inequalities of the form t·p_k ≤ q_k, one per window edge. Each gives a candidate parameter r_k = q_k/p_k.
Rules for finding the visible part:
items: If p_k = 0 the line is parallel to that edge; if also q_k < 0 it lies outside and is rejected.
If p_k < 0 the line enters across that edge: t_entry = max(0, all q_k/p_k with p_k < 0).
If p_k > 0 the line leaves across that edge: t_exit = min(1, all q_k/p_k with p_k > 0).
If t_entry > t_exit the line is completely outside; otherwise the clipped endpoints are at t_entry and t_exit.

rows: Region codes and repeated edge intersection
Parametric line and inequalities t·p_k ≤ q_k
May compute several, some later discarded
Computes only the final two endpoints
Many lines trivially accepted or rejected

concepts.text: Polygon clipping cannot simply clip each edge as a line, because the result must be a closed polygon. The Sutherland–Hodgman algorithm clips the whole vertex list against one window edge at a time (left, right, bottom, top). For each edge from vertex S to vertex P: inside to inside outputs P; inside to outside outputs the intersection; outside to inside outputs the intersection and P; outside to outside outputs nothing. It works for convex clip windows but can leave extra connecting edges for concave polygons, which Weiler–Atherton handles.

formulas.plainText: x = x1 + t·Δx, y = y1 + t·Δy, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1
t·pk ≤ qk, rk = qk/pk
t_entry = max(0, rk for pk < 0), t_exit = min(1, rk for pk > 0)

notes.text: To find a region code quickly, test each bit separately in the order T B R L: y above top, y below bottom, x right of right edge, x left of left edge. A point can have at most two bits set.
A bitwise AND of 0000 does not mean the line is visible. Both ends may be outside different edges and the line may still miss the window; further intersection steps decide.
In Liang–Barsky, p_k < 0 means the line goes from outside to inside that boundary (entering) and p_k > 0 means inside to outside (leaving).

concepts.text: Reflection About the Principal Planes

A 3D reflection mirrors an object through a plane (or, less often, a line or a point). Reflection about a principal coordinate plane simply negates the coordinate perpendicular to that plane, so its matrix is the identity with one −1 on the diagonal. A reflection converts a right-handed description of an object into a left-handed one, which is why it cannot be produced by any sequence of pure rotations. Reflection about an arbitrary plane is built as a composite: move the plane onto a principal plane, reflect, and move it back.

concepts.plainText: Reflection about xy-plane: diag(1, 1, −1, 1)

concepts.text: Shear in 3D

A shear slides points parallel to a plane by an amount proportional to their distance from it. Shear relative to the z-axis changes x and y in proportion to z while leaving z unchanged: x' = x + a·z, y' = y + b·z, z' = z. Similar shears exist relative to the x- and y-axes. In general each off-diagonal position of the upper-left 3 × 3 block can hold a shear parameter, giving six directional shear parameters (x by y, x by z, y by x, y by z, z by x, z by y). Example: with a = 1, b = 2 the point (1, 1, 2) becomes (1 + 2, 1 + 4, 2) = (3, 5, 2).

concepts.plainText: z-axis shear: x' = x + a·z, y' = y + b·z, z' = z

concepts.text: Composite Transformations

A composite transformation is a sequence of basic transformations multiplied into one 4 × 4 matrix. With column vectors, M = M_n ··· M_2 · M_1 applies M_1 first, so matrices are written right to left in the order they act. Matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative: translating then rotating is generally different from rotating then translating. Two successive translations, two rotations about the same axis, or two scalings do commute and simply add (translations, angles) or multiply (scale factors).
Why composite matrices are efficient:
items: The sequence is multiplied once (a few 4 × 4 products) and the single result is applied to every vertex.
Applying a 4 × 4 affine matrix to a point costs about 9 multiplications and 9 additions (the last row is fixed), whatever the number of steps in the sequence.
For a model with thousands of vertices this is far cheaper than applying each basic transformation to every vertex in turn.
Graphics hardware and APIs such as OpenGL keep a current transformation (matrix stack) for exactly this reason.

concepts.text: Rotation About an Arbitrary Axis

Let the axis pass through P1(x1, y1, z1) and P2, with unit direction vector u = (a, b, c) and d = √(b² + c²). The idea is to move the axis onto the z-axis, perform the easy rotation R_z(θ), and then undo the alignment. The full composite is R(θ) = T⁻¹ · R_x⁻¹(α) · R_y⁻¹(β) · R_z(θ) · R_y(β) · R_x(α) · T, where T = T(−x1, −y1, −z1). If the axis is already parallel to a coordinate axis, only translate–rotate–translate back is needed.

Rotation by θ about axis P1→P2, u = (a, b, c) unit, d = sqrt(b² + c²)
1. T(−P1): translate so the axis passes through the origin
2. Rx(α): rotate about x into the xz-plane, cos α = c/d, sin α = b/d
3. Ry(β): rotate about y onto the z-axis, cos β = d, sin β = −a
4. Rz(θ): perform the required rotation
5. Ry⁻¹(β): undo step 3
6. Rx⁻¹(α): undo step 2
7. T(+P1): undo step 1 (inverses applied in reverse order)
Worked composite: scale by 2 about the fixed point (2, 2, 2), applied to P(3, 4, 5):
items: Composite M = T(2, 2, 2)·S(2, 2, 2)·T(−2, −2, −2) has diagonal (2, 2, 2, 1) and fourth column (−2, −2, −2, 1); M·P gives (4, 6, 8) in one multiplication.

formulas.latex: M = M_n\cdots M_2\, M_1,\qquad P' = M\cdot P
formulas.plainText: M = Mn ··· M2 · M1 (M1 applied first); P' = M·P
R(θ) = T⁻¹·Rx⁻¹(α)·Ry⁻¹(β)·Rz(θ)·Ry(β)·Rx(α)·T
d = √(b² + c²), cos α = c/d, sin α = b/d

notes.text: For reflection about a coordinate plane, negate the coordinate that is NOT in the plane's name: xy-plane flips z, yz-plane flips x, xz-plane flips y.
Order matters: with column vectors the rightmost matrix acts first. When undoing an alignment sequence, apply the inverses in the reverse order.
A reflection has determinant −1 and reverses handedness; rotations have determinant +1. This is why no combination of rotations can produce a mirror image.

concepts.text: The Synthetic Camera

3D viewing is modelled on taking a photograph. We choose where to stand (camera position), which way to point the camera (viewing direction), which way is up, and the lens and film size (projection and window). The scene is then projected onto a 2D view plane and mapped to the screen. Unlike 2D viewing, 3D viewing needs a projection step to collapse depth, and clipping takes place against a 3D view volume rather than a rectangle.
Stages of the Pipeline

Modelling coordinates (MC)
   | modelling transformation
World coordinates (WC)
   | viewing transformation
Viewing / camera coordinates (VC)
   | projection transformation
Projection coordinates
   | normalisation (map view volume to a unit cube)
Normalised coordinates -> clipping, visible-surface removal
   | viewport (workstation) transformation
Device / screen coordinates (DC)
What happens at each coordinate stage:
items: Modelling coordinates: each object is defined in its own local frame, convenient for building it.
World coordinates: modelling transformations place all objects into one common scene.
Viewing coordinates: the scene is re-expressed relative to the camera, with the viewer looking along the −z_v (or n) axis.
Projection and normalisation: 3D points are projected towards the view plane and the view volume is mapped to a normalised cube, which simplifies clipping.
Device coordinates: the normalised window is mapped to the viewport in pixels on the output device.

concepts.text: Camera Parameters and the u, v, n Frame

rows: Becomes the origin of viewing coordinates
Direction perpendicular to the view plane
Which way is up for the camera
Fixes the v (y_v) axis after being made perpendicular to N
Position of the view plane along n

concepts.text: From N and V a right-handed orthonormal frame is built. The unit vector n is N normalised. The u axis must be perpendicular to both V and n, so u = (V × n)/|V × n|. Finally v = n × u, which is the component of V perpendicular to n and is already a unit vector. V does not have to be exactly perpendicular to N; the cross products correct it, but V must not be parallel to N.

concepts.latex: n=\frac{N}{|N|},\quad u=\frac{V\times n}{|V\times n|},\quad v=n\times u
concepts.plainText: n = N/|N|, u = (V × n)/|V × n|, v = n × u

concepts.text: World-to-Viewing Transformation

Converting world coordinates to viewing coordinates is the same as moving the camera frame onto the world axes. First translate the view reference point to the world origin with T(−x0, −y0, −z0). Then rotate so that u, v and n line up with the x, y and z axes; the rotation matrix simply has u, v and n as its first three rows. The complete viewing matrix is M_WC,VC = R · T. Alternatively, the alignment can be done with a sequence of rotations about x, y and z, as in the arbitrary-axis rotation.

concepts.plainText: M = R · T(−x0, −y0, −z0), where the rows of R are u, v and n

concepts.text: View Volume and 3D Clipping
The view volume is the region of space that can appear in the picture:
items: It is bounded by the four sides through the edges of the window on the view plane, plus a near (front) and a far (back) clipping plane parallel to the view plane — six planes in all.
Parallel projection: the sides are parallel, so the view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped (a slanted one for oblique projection).
Perspective projection: the sides meet at the centre of projection, so the view volume is a frustum (a truncated pyramid).
Near and far planes remove objects too close to or too far from the camera and bound the depth range used for visible-surface tests.

3D clipping extends 2D methods: Cohen–Sutherland uses 6-bit region codes (one bit per plane), and Liang–Barsky and Sutherland–Hodgman generalise to six boundary planes; clipping is usually done in the normalised unit cube.

formulas.plainText: P_VC = R · T(−P0) · P_WC
R = [ux uy uz 0; vx vy vz 0; nx ny nz 0; 0 0 0 1]

formulas.latex: \text{clip region code} = 6 \text{ bits (left, right, bottom, top, near, far)}
formulas.plainText: 3D Cohen–Sutherland region code = 6 bits: left, right, bottom, top, near, far

notes.text: Remember the shapes: parallel projection gives a parallelepiped view volume, perspective projection gives a frustum. Both are bounded by six planes, including near and far.
The world-to-viewing transformation is always 'translate the VRP to the origin, then rotate'. Doing the rotation first would rotate the camera position as well and give the wrong result.
The view-up vector V must not be parallel to the view-plane normal N; otherwise V × n is zero and the u axis cannot be defined.

concepts.text: What a Projection Does

A projection maps 3D points onto a 2D view (projection) plane along straight lines called projectors. If all projectors are parallel, the projection is parallel; if they all converge at a single centre of projection (COP), it is perspective. Parallel projection keeps parallel lines parallel and preserves relative proportions, so it suits engineering drawings. Perspective projection looks realistic because distant objects appear smaller, but it does not preserve true dimensions.

rows: Projectors perpendicular to the plane; plane parallel to a principal face
Projectors perpendicular; plane tilted to show several faces
Projectors at an angle to the plane
Projectors meet at the COP; classified by vanishing points

concepts.text: Orthographic Projection

In orthographic projection onto the xy-plane (z = 0) the projectors are parallel to the z-axis, so a point simply drops its z-coordinate: x_p = x, y_p = y. Multiview drawings show the front, top and side elevations, each with true lengths and angles for faces parallel to the plane. Axonometric views tilt the object so that three faces are visible: isometric foreshortens all three axes equally, with the projected axes 120° apart; dimetric foreshortens two axes equally; trimetric foreshortens all three differently.

concepts.plainText: Orthographic onto z = 0: x_p = x, y_p = y (z dropped)

concepts.text: Oblique Projection

In oblique projection the projectors hit the view plane at an angle α other than 90°. A point (x, y, z) projects to a position shifted from (x, y) by a length L·z in a chosen direction φ on the plane, where L = 1/tan α. Faces parallel to the view plane keep their true shape, while depth lines are drawn at angle φ (commonly 30° or 45°) and scaled by L.

concepts.plainText: x_p = x + L·z·cos φ, y_p = y + L·z·sin φ, L = 1/tan α

concepts.text: The two standard oblique projections:
items: Cavalier: α = 45°, so tan α = 1 and L = 1. Depth lines are drawn at full length, which makes objects look too deep.
Cabinet: α ≈ 63.4°, so tan α = 2 and L = 1/2. Depth lines are halved, giving a more realistic look.
Example (cabinet, φ = 45°): the point (2, 3, 4) gives x_p = 2 + 0.5·4·0.707 ≈ 3.41 and y_p ≈ 4.41.

concepts.text: Perspective Projection

With the centre of projection at the origin and the view plane at z = d, similar triangles give x_p = x·d/z and y_p = y·d/z. Division by z makes far objects smaller (foreshortening). In homogeneous form the perspective matrix puts 1/d in the last row so that w = z/d, and the division by w performs the perspective divide. Example: with d = 5, the point (4, 6, 10) projects to (4·5/10, 6·5/10) = (2, 3); moving it back to z = 20 gives (1, 1.5). In Hearn & Baker's general form, with the projection reference point at z_prp and the view plane at z_vp, x_p = x·(z_prp − z_vp)/(z_prp − z).

concepts.plainText: x_p = x·d/z, y_p = y·d/z, homogeneous w = z/d

concepts.text: Vanishing points and foreshortening:
items: Parallel lines that are not parallel to the view plane converge in the image at a vanishing point.
The principal vanishing points belong to lines parallel to the x, y or z axes; their number is the number of principal axes that cut the view plane.

One-point perspective: only one axis cuts the plane (a road or corridor seen head-on). Two-point: two axes cut it (a building seen from a corner). Three-point: all three cut it (looking up at a tall building).
Foreshortening: the projected size of an object is inversely proportional to its distance from the COP.

rows: Meet at vanishing points (unless parallel to the plane)

formulas.plainText: Perspective matrix: identity rows 1–3, last row (0, 0, 1/d, 0)
x_p = x(z_prp − z_vp)/(z_prp − z), same for y
Cavalier α = 45°, L = 1; cabinet α ≈ 63.4°, L = 1/2

notes.text: Link angle to depth factor through L = 1/tan α: tan 45° = 1 gives cavalier (full depth), tan 63.4° = 2 gives cabinet (half depth).
Orthographic is a kind of parallel projection, not a separate family. Axonometric views (isometric, dimetric, trimetric) are orthographic too, even though they show three faces.
The number of principal vanishing points (1, 2 or 3) depends on how many principal axes intersect the view plane, not on how many objects are in the scene.

concepts.text: How to use this sheet

Theory of computation questions test the language hierarchy, closure properties and the exact form of each automaton, lemma and normal form. Graphics questions test transformation matrices, clipping codes and projection types. This page puts all of them on one screen, in syllabus order, so you can rehearse them before a test.
1. Language hierarchy
2. Finite automata and regular languages

concepts.text: Finite-automaton facts:
items: DFA, NFA and ε-NFA recognise exactly the regular languages; NFAs are only more convenient, not more powerful.
Minimization merges indistinguishable states (partition / table-filling); the minimal DFA is unique up to renaming.
Regular expressions ↔ finite automata: Thompson's construction (RE → ε-NFA) and state elimination or Arden's theorem R = Q + RP ⇒ R = QP* (FA → RE).

PDA = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, Z0, F); acceptance by final state and by empty stack are equivalent for NPDAs; DPDAs are weaker (they cannot accept even-length palindromes).
CFG ↔ PDA: every CFL has an NPDA and every NPDA's language is context-free.

concepts.text: Computability facts:
items: Recursive (decidable) languages have a TM that always halts; recursively enumerable ones have a TM that halts on every member but may loop otherwise.
Multi-track, multi-tape, two-way-infinite and non-deterministic TMs all recognise the same languages as a standard TM (only speed differs).
A universal TM takes an encoded machine ⟨M⟩ and input w and simulates M on w.
Church–Turing thesis: every effectively computable function is Turing-computable.
Undecidable: halting problem, Post correspondence problem, CFG ambiguity and equivalence; Rice's theorem covers every non-trivial property of RE languages.
