concepts.text: Worked query on Student(sid, name, dept), Enroll(sid, cid) and Course(cid, title): names of CS students enrolled in DB101 are π name (σ dept='CS' ∧ cid='DB101' (Student ⋈ Enroll)). Students enrolled in every course are Enroll ÷ π cid (Course): with Enroll = {(s1,c1), (s1,c2), (s2,c1)} and courses {c1, c2}, the result is {s1}. The equivalent SQL expresses division with a double NOT EXISTS.

SELECT s.name FROM Student s JOIN Enroll e ON s.sid = e.sid
WHERE s.dept = 'CS' AND e.cid = 'DB101';

-- division: students enrolled in all courses
SELECT s.sid FROM Student s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT c.cid FROM Course c
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT * FROM Enroll e WHERE e.sid = s.sid AND e.cid = c.cid));
Query Processing Steps
A SQL query passes through these stages before results are returned:
items: Parsing and translation: check syntax, verify relation and attribute names against the catalog, and translate the query into an internal relational-algebra expression (parse tree).
Query decomposition: normalise the WHERE predicate (conjunctive normal form), analyse it for semantic errors, eliminate redundancy and rewrite it into an algebra tree.
Optimization: generate equivalent expressions and evaluation plans, estimate their costs from catalog statistics and pick the cheapest plan.
Evaluation: the query-execution engine runs the chosen plan using algorithms for each operation and returns the answer.

concepts.text: Cost Estimation and Operation Algorithms

Disk access dominates query cost, so cost is measured as the number of block transfers b and disk seeks S, weighted by the time per transfer tT and per seek tS. Statistics in the catalog, such as the number of tuples n_r, blocks b_r and distinct values V(A, r), let the optimizer estimate the sizes of intermediate results. CPU cost is usually ignored in textbook estimates.

concepts.plainText: Cost = b x tT + S x tS (block transfers and seeks)

rows: File sorted on the selection attribute
Any join condition; r is the outer relation
Scans inner once per outer block
c = cost of an index lookup on s

concepts.text: An expression tree can be evaluated by materialisation, where each operation's result is written to a temporary relation on disk and read by the parent, or by pipelining, where tuples are passed to the parent operation as soon as they are produced. Pipelining saves the cost of writing and re-reading temporaries but is impossible for blocking operations such as sorting. Pipelines can be demand-driven (the parent pulls tuples) or producer-driven (the child pushes tuples).
Equivalence rules and heuristics used by the optimizer:
items: Cascade of selections: σ θ1∧θ2 (E) = σ θ1 (σ θ2 (E)); selections are commutative.
Push selections down: perform σ as early as possible, below joins, to shrink intermediate results.
Push and combine projections: π L1 (π L2 (E)) = π L1 (E); project out unneeded attributes early.
Join commutativity and associativity: E1 ⋈ E2 = E2 ⋈ E1 and (E1 ⋈ E2) ⋈ E3 = E1 ⋈ (E2 ⋈ E3), used to choose a good join order.
Replace a σ over a × by a join, and perform the most restrictive selections and joins first.

concepts.text: Cost-based optimization enumerates alternative plans produced by the equivalence rules, with different join orders and algorithms, estimates each plan's cost using catalog statistics, and picks the cheapest. Dynamic programming over subsets of relations (as in System R, often restricted to left-deep join trees) keeps this search feasible. Practical optimizers combine heuristics to prune the search with cost estimates to choose among the remaining plans.

Block nested-loop join worst case = b_r x b_s + b_r block transfers

Projection in relational algebra removes duplicates (set semantics), but SQL SELECT keeps duplicates unless DISTINCT is written.
Division answers 'for all' queries such as 'students who took every course'; in SQL it is written with a double NOT EXISTS or with GROUP BY and COUNT comparison.

concepts.text: Shared and Exclusive Locks

A lock is a variable attached to a data item that controls how transactions may access it. A shared lock (S, lock-S) lets the holder read the item only, and many transactions may hold S locks on the same item together. An exclusive lock (X, lock-X) lets the holder read and write the item, and no other transaction may hold any lock on it at the same time. A transaction requests the lock from the concurrency-control manager and waits if the request is incompatible with locks already granted.
Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
Under 2PL each transaction issues lock and unlock requests in two phases:
items: Growing phase: the transaction may acquire locks but may not release any.
Shrinking phase: the transaction may release locks but may not acquire any new one.
Lock point: the moment the transaction obtains its final lock; ordering transactions by lock point gives an equivalent serial order.
Guarantee: every schedule allowed by 2PL is conflict serializable.
Limitations: basic 2PL does not prevent deadlock and does not prevent cascading rollback.

rows: Hold all exclusive (X) locks until commit or abort
Strict, cascadeless schedules; no cascading rollback
Hold all locks (S and X) until commit or abort
Transactions serialize in commit order; simplest to reason about
Acquire every needed lock before starting
Deadlock-free, but needs the lock set in advance

concepts.text:
T1 under strict 2PL (transfer 50 from A to B):
  lock-X(A)
  read(A); A := A - 50; write(A)
  lock-X(B)             <- lock point (last lock acquired)
  read(B); B := B + 50; write(B)
  commit
  unlock(A); unlock(B)  <- shrinking phase after commit

Lock conversion lets a transaction change the mode of a lock it already holds. An upgrade converts S to X and is allowed only in the growing phase; a downgrade converts X to S and is allowed only in the shrinking phase. Conversion improves concurrency because a transaction can read an item under a shared lock and take the exclusive lock only when it actually needs to write.

Timestamp ordering is a lock-free alternative: each transaction gets a unique timestamp TS(Ti) when it starts, and each item keeps its largest read timestamp R-TS(X) and write timestamp W-TS(X). An operation that would violate timestamp order (for example Ti writing X when TS(Ti) < R-TS(X)) causes Ti to be rolled back and restarted with a new timestamp. The protocol guarantees conflict serializability and is deadlock-free because no transaction ever waits, though it may cause starvation and cascading rollbacks; Thomas' write rule ignores obsolete writes.
Deadlock in Databases

A deadlock exists when every transaction in a set waits for a lock held by another transaction in the same set, so none can proceed. For example, T1 holds X(A) and requests X(B) while T2 holds X(B) and requests X(A). It requires the four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Deadlock is handled by prevention (never let it happen), or by detection and recovery (let it happen, find it, break it).

Wait-for graph (edge Ti -> Tj: Ti waits for a lock held by Tj)
  T1 waits for T2 (item B)   T1 -> T2
  T2 waits for T3 (item C)   T2 -> T3
  T3 waits for T1 (item A)   T3 -> T1
  T4 waits for T2 (item B)   T4 -> T2
Cycle T1 -> T2 -> T3 -> T1  => T1, T2, T3 are deadlocked.
T4 is not in the cycle: it is blocked, but not deadlocked.
Roll back one cycle member (e.g. T3) to break the deadlock.

concepts.plainText: Deadlock exists if and only if the wait-for graph has a cycle

rows: Scheme (Ti requests an item held by Tj)
Ti dies (rolls back, restarts with same timestamp)

concepts.text: Other prevention approaches deny one Coffman condition:
items: Lock all items at once before starting (conservative 2PL) removes hold and wait.
Impose a total order on data items and lock them only in that order (resource ordering) removes circular wait.
Preemption through wait-die or wound-wait; restarted transactions keep their original timestamp, so they eventually become the oldest and cannot starve.

concepts.text: Detection, recovery, timeouts and starvation:
items: Detection: the system maintains the wait-for graph and periodically searches it for cycles; a cycle means deadlock.
Victim selection: roll back the transaction with the least cost, judged by work done so far, locks held, work remaining and how many transactions would be involved.
Rollback: total rollback aborts and restarts the victim; partial rollback undoes it only as far as needed to release the required lock.
Timeout: a transaction that waits longer than a set interval is assumed deadlocked and rolled back; simple, but it may abort transactions that were not deadlocked.
Starvation: the same transaction repeatedly chosen as victim, or repeatedly overtaken in lock queues; avoided by counting rollbacks in the cost factor and granting locks in FIFO order.

formulas.plainText: Wait-die: if TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) then Ti waits, else Ti is rolled back

formulas.latex: \text{Wound-wait: } TS(T_i) < TS(T_j) \Rightarrow T_j \text{ rolled back, else } T_i \text{ waits}
formulas.plainText: Wound-wait: if TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) then Tj is rolled back, else Ti waits
Deadlock exists if and only if the wait-for graph has a cycle

notes.text: In both wait-die and wound-wait the older transaction is never rolled back. Remember: wait-die, the older one waits; wound-wait, the older one wounds.
Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability but NOT freedom from deadlock or cascading rollback. Strict 2PL removes cascading rollback; only conservative 2PL removes deadlock.
A transaction blocked behind a deadlocked set (like T4 in the example) is not itself part of the deadlock; only the transactions on the cycle are.

concepts.text: Failure Classification

rows: Logical error (bad input, constraint violation) or system error (deadlock victim)
Power failure, OS or DBMS bug, hardware fault
Main memory (buffers) contents; disk intact (fail-stop assumption)
Redo committed, undo uncommitted transactions from the log
Head crash, media corruption during transfer
Part or all of the disk
Restore from backup/archive copy, then redo from the archived log

concepts.text: Storage types, by how well they survive failures:
items: Volatile storage: main memory and cache; fast, but contents are lost in a system crash.
Non-volatile storage: magnetic disk, SSD, tape; survives crashes but can still fail (disk failure).

Stable storage: an abstraction of storage that never loses data, approximated by keeping multiple copies on independent non-volatile media (for example RAID or remote replicas) and writing them one after another. The log must be kept on stable storage.

concepts.text: Recovery and Atomicity

A transaction may modify several data items, and a crash can happen after some of those modifications have reached disk but not others. To keep atomicity, the DBMS first writes information describing the modifications to stable storage, without modifying the database itself. After a crash this information lets the system undo the effects of transactions that did not commit and redo the effects of those that did, preserving both atomicity and durability. The most widely used structure for this is the log.
Log records (the log is a sequential file of records):
items: <Ti start>: transaction Ti has started.
<Ti, X, V1, V2>: Ti wrote item X, changing it from old value V1 to new value V2. The old value is used for undo, the new value for redo.
<Ti commit>: Ti has committed; once this record is on stable storage the transaction is durable.
<Ti abort>: Ti has aborted and its rollback is complete.

concepts.text: Write-ahead logging (WAL) requires that a log record for an update reach stable storage before the corresponding data page is written to disk, and that all log records of a transaction, including <Ti commit>, be forced out before the transaction is declared committed. This guarantees that whenever a modified page is on disk, the old value needed to undo it can be found in the log.
Deferred vs Immediate Modification

rows: Only after the transaction partially commits
While the transaction is still active
Redo only; no undo is ever needed

concepts.text:
Immediate-modification log at the moment of a crash:
  <T0 start>
  <T0, A, 1000, 950>
  <T0, B, 2000, 2050>
  <T0 commit>
  <T1 start>
  <T1, C, 700, 600>
  --- crash ---
Recovery: T0 has start and commit  -> redo(T0): A = 950, B = 2050
          T1 has start, no commit  -> undo(T1): C = 700, log <T1 abort>
Undo scans backward; redo scans forward. Both are idempotent.

concepts.plainText: Redo Ti if the log contains both <Ti start> and <Ti commit>

concepts.text: Checkpoints

Without checkpoints the recovery manager would have to scan the whole log and would redo many transactions whose updates already reached disk. A checkpoint writes all log records in memory to stable storage, flushes all modified buffer blocks to disk, and then writes a <checkpoint L> record listing the transactions L active at that moment. At recovery the system scans back only to the last checkpoint: transactions that committed before it need no action, transactions that committed after it are redone, and transactions in L or started after it with no commit are undone.
Other recovery techniques:
items: Shadow paging: the database keeps two page tables, a current table updated by the transaction and a shadow table that is never changed during it. Modified pages are written to new locations; commit simply makes the current table the new shadow by atomically updating a single on-disk pointer. No undo or redo log is needed, but it causes data fragmentation, needs garbage collection and handles concurrency poorly.
ARIES: the industrial log-based algorithm using log sequence numbers (LSNs), WAL and three passes (analysis, redo, undo) that repeats history and supports fuzzy checkpoints.

formulas.plainText: Redo Ti if the log contains both <Ti start> and <Ti commit>

formulas.plainText: Recovery scans only from the last checkpoint (and transactions in its list L) to the end of the log

notes.text: Undo uses the OLD value and proceeds backward through the log; redo uses the NEW value and proceeds forward. Deferred modification never needs undo.
A system crash destroys volatile storage only; data on disk is assumed intact (fail-stop). Disk failure is the case that needs an archival backup.
A transaction that committed before the last checkpoint needs neither redo nor undo, because the checkpoint already flushed its updates to disk.

concepts.text: Process, Program and the PCB

A program is a passive file of instructions on disk; a process is a program in execution, an active entity with its own program counter, registers and memory image (text, data, heap and stack). One program can give rise to several processes. The OS describes each process by a Process Control Block (PCB), also called a task control block, which it keeps in the kernel and saves and restores on every context switch.
Fields held in a Process Control Block:
items: Process identifier (PID), parent PID and process state.
Program counter and CPU registers (saved on a context switch).
CPU-scheduling information: priority, pointers to scheduling queues.
Memory-management information: base/limit registers, page or segment tables.
Accounting information (CPU time used, time limits) and I/O status (open files, allocated devices).

concepts.text: Five-state model and transitions:
items: New -> Ready: admitted by the long-term scheduler.
Ready -> Running: dispatched by the short-term scheduler.
Running -> Ready: pre-empted (time quantum expired or a higher-priority process arrived).
Running -> Waiting (blocked): requests I/O or waits for an event; Waiting -> Ready when the event completes.
Running -> Terminated: exit. A suspended (swapped-out) ready or blocked state is added in the seven-state model by the medium-term scheduler.

concepts.text: Process control covers creation, termination and switching. In UNIX a parent calls fork(), which creates a child that is a near-copy of the parent; fork returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent. The child typically calls exec() to replace its memory image with a new program, and the parent calls wait() to collect the child's exit status. A process terminates by exit() or by being killed; a finished child not yet waited for is a zombie, and a child whose parent died first is an orphan adopted by init/systemd. A context switch saves the running process's state in its PCB and loads another's; it is pure overhead.
Threads

A thread is a lightweight unit of CPU execution within a process. Threads of one process share its code, data, heap and open files, but each thread has its own thread ID, program counter, register set and stack. User-level threads are managed by a library without kernel knowledge (fast switching, but one blocking call blocks the whole process); kernel-level threads are scheduled by the kernel and can run in parallel on multiple CPUs. Multithreading models: many-to-one (many user threads on one kernel thread, no parallelism), one-to-one (each user thread gets a kernel thread, as in Linux and Windows) and many-to-many (m user threads multiplexed on n kernel threads).

rows: Shares address space of its process
Faulty thread can crash the whole process

concepts.text: Schedulers and scheduling criteria:
items: Long-term (job) scheduler: chooses which jobs enter memory; controls the degree of multiprogramming.
Medium-term scheduler: swaps processes out and in to reduce load or improve the process mix.
Short-term (CPU) scheduler: picks the next ready process very frequently; the dispatcher then performs the context switch.
Maximise CPU utilisation and throughput; minimise turnaround, waiting and response time.
Non-pre-emptive: a process keeps the CPU until it blocks or ends (FCFS, SJF). Pre-emptive: the OS can take the CPU away (SRTF, RR, pre-emptive priority).

concepts.text: Principles of Concurrency

Concurrency means several processes or threads make progress in overlapping time, either interleaved on one CPU or truly in parallel on many. When they share data, the result can depend on the exact interleaving, which the programmer cannot control. Concurrency therefore needs mechanisms for mutual exclusion, synchronisation (ordering events) and communication, while avoiding deadlock and starvation.

A race condition occurs when two or more processes access shared data concurrently and the outcome depends on the order of execution. Example: counter = 5; a producer executes counter++ and a consumer counter--. Each is really three machine steps (load into a register, modify, store). If the producer loads 5, the consumer loads 5, the producer stores 6 and the consumer stores 4, the final value is 4 instead of 5. The fix is to make each update a critical section executed under mutual exclusion.
A solution to the critical-section problem must satisfy three requirements:
items: Mutual exclusion: at most one process executes in its critical section at a time.
Progress: if no process is in the critical section, only processes wanting to enter take part in the decision, and the choice cannot be postponed indefinitely.
Bounded waiting: there is a limit on how many times other processes may enter before a waiting process is admitted (no starvation).
Structure of every process: entry section, critical section, exit section, remainder section.

concepts.text: Peterson's algorithm is a classic software solution for two processes using a shared boolean array flag[2] and an integer turn. A process announces interest by setting its flag, then politely gives the turn to the other, and waits only while the other is interested and it is the other's turn. It satisfies all three requirements, although on modern CPUs it needs memory barriers because of instruction reordering.
Hardware support for mutual exclusion:
items: Disabling interrupts: prevents pre-emption on a uniprocessor, but is unsafe to give to user programs and does not work on multiprocessors.
Test-and-set: atomically returns the old value of a lock word and sets it to true; while (test_and_set(&lock)); builds a spinlock.
Compare-and-swap (and exchange): atomically replaces a value only if it equals an expected value; the basis of lock-free structures.
These simple spinlocks satisfy mutual exclusion but not necessarily bounded waiting.

concepts.text: Semaphores

A semaphore (Dijkstra) is an integer variable accessed only through two atomic operations: wait, also P or down, and signal, also V or up. A counting semaphore can range over any integer and controls access to a pool of identical resources; a binary semaphore takes only 0 and 1. The busy-waiting (spinlock) version loops while S <= 0; the blocking version decrements S and, if the result is negative, puts the caller on the semaphore's queue, so a negative value -k means k processes are blocked.

rows: Only the thread that locked it may unlock
Mutual exclusion on a critical section
Resource counting and signalling between processes

concepts.text: Message passing and monitors:
items: Message passing uses send(destination, msg) and receive(source, msg); it works across machines and needs no shared memory.
Direct communication names the partner process; indirect communication sends to a mailbox or port that several processes may share.
Synchronous (blocking) send/receive gives a rendezvous; asynchronous (non-blocking) send uses a buffer so the sender continues.
A monitor is a high-level language construct grouping shared data and the procedures that operate on it; only one process can be active inside at a time, so mutual exclusion is automatic.
Condition variables inside a monitor: x.wait() suspends the caller and releases the monitor; x.signal() resumes exactly one waiting process and does nothing if none is waiting (unlike a semaphore V).

concepts.text: Deadlock is a state in which each process of a set waits for an event that only another process in the set can cause. It can arise only if all four Coffman conditions hold together: mutual exclusion (non-sharable resources), hold and wait, no pre-emption, and circular wait. Deadlock is handled by prevention (break one condition), avoidance (Banker's algorithm), detection and recovery, or ignoring it (the ostrich approach). Starvation differs: a process waits indefinitely while others continue to progress.

concepts.plainText: Final semaphore value = initial - number of wait(P) + number of signal(V)

formulas.plainText: Final value = initial - P operations + V operations
If S < 0 then |S| processes are blocked on the semaphore

notes.text: Semaphore numericals: start with the initial value, subtract one for every P (wait) and add one for every V (signal). A negative final value tells how many processes are blocked.
Swapping the order of two wait() calls, or forgetting a signal(), easily causes deadlock; semaphores are powerful but error-prone, which motivated monitors.
Strict alternation using only a turn variable guarantees mutual exclusion but violates progress; Peterson's algorithm adds the flag array to fix this.

concepts.text: Bounded-Buffer (Producer-Consumer) Problem

A producer puts items into a shared buffer of n slots and a consumer removes them. The producer must wait when the buffer is full, the consumer must wait when it is empty, and both must not manipulate the buffer at the same time. The standard solution uses three semaphores: empty = n counts free slots, full = 0 counts filled slots, and mutex = 1 protects the buffer.

If the producer calls wait(&mutex) before wait(&empty) and the buffer is full, it sleeps holding the mutex, the consumer can never enter, and the system deadlocks. Always wait on the counting semaphore first.
Readers-Writers Problem

Many readers may read a shared database simultaneously, but a writer needs exclusive access. The first readers-writers (readers-preference) solution uses semaphore rw_mutex = 1 for writers, semaphore mutex = 1 protecting an integer read_count = 0. The first reader to arrive locks rw_mutex and the last reader to leave releases it, so while any reader is active writers wait. Writers can therefore starve; the second (writers-preference) solution makes readers wait whenever a writer is waiting, which can starve readers instead. Reader-writer locks in modern systems implement this pattern.
Dining Philosophers and Sleeping Barber

Five philosophers sit round a table with one chopstick between each pair; a philosopher needs both neighbouring chopsticks to eat. Representing each chopstick as a semaphore initialised to 1 and having everyone pick up the left then the right can deadlock if all five pick up their left chopstick at once. Fixes: allow at most four philosophers at the table at a time, make pick-up asymmetric (odd philosophers take left first, even take right first), pick up both chopsticks only if both are free inside a critical section, or use a monitor with states THINKING, HUNGRY, EATING where a philosopher eats only when neither neighbour is eating. The monitor solution is deadlock-free but can still starve a philosopher.

In the sleeping barber problem, a barber sleeps when there are no customers; an arriving customer wakes the barber, sits in one of n waiting chairs if the barber is busy, or leaves if all chairs are full. It is solved with semaphores customers = 0, barbers = 0, mutex = 1 and a counter of waiting customers, and models client-server queueing with a bounded waiting room.

rows: Deadlock when all take left chopstick; starvation
Lost wake-ups and races on the waiting count

concepts.text: Banker's Algorithm (Deadlock Avoidance)

The Banker's algorithm grants a request only if the resulting state is safe, meaning there exists a sequence in which every process can obtain its maximum need and finish. Safety check: set Work = Available and Finish[i] = false; repeatedly find a process with Finish[i] = false and Need_i <= Work, then set Work = Work + Allocation_i and Finish[i] = true. If all processes finish, the state is safe and the order found is a safe sequence.

Worked safety check: Work = (3, 3, 2). P1's need (1, 2, 2) fits, so P1 finishes and Work = (3, 3, 2) + (2, 0, 0) = (5, 3, 2). P0's need (7, 3, 3) does not fit, but P2's need (3, 0, 0) does, so Work = (5, 3, 2) + (3, 0, 2) = (8, 3, 4). Now P0's need (7, 3, 3) fits and Work becomes (8, 4, 4). All finish, so the state is safe with safe sequence <P1, P2, P0>.

concepts.plainText: Need = Max - Allocation (per process, per resource type)

formulas.plainText: Need = Max - Allocation
If Need_i <= Work, process i can finish and Work = Work + Allocation_i
Minimum resources for no deadlock: R >= n(k - 1) + 1

notes.text: For the producer-consumer MCQ remember the initial values empty = n, full = 0, mutex = 1, and that wait on empty/full must come before wait on mutex.
An unsafe state is not necessarily a deadlock; it only means deadlock is possible. A safe state guarantees deadlock can be avoided.
If n processes each need at most k units of one resource type, R = n(k - 1) + 1 units guarantee freedom from deadlock: even when every process holds k - 1 units, one spare unit lets someone finish.

concepts.text: Virtual Memory and Demand Paging

Virtual memory separates the logical memory seen by a program from physical memory, so a program can be larger than RAM and only the parts in use need to be resident. It is usually implemented by demand paging: a page is brought into memory only when it is referenced (a lazy swapper, or pager). Each page-table entry has a valid-invalid bit; a reference to a page marked invalid (not in memory) traps to the OS as a page fault. Benefits are a higher degree of multiprogramming, less I/O at load time and faster process start.
Steps in handling a page fault:
items: The reference finds the valid-invalid bit set to invalid, and the hardware traps to the OS.
The OS checks an internal table: if the reference is illegal the process is terminated; if legal but not resident, it continues.
A free frame is found (or a victim page is chosen by the replacement algorithm and written out if dirty).
A disk read schedules the page into the frame; the CPU may run another process meanwhile.
When I/O completes, the page table is updated (frame number, valid bit set).
The faulting instruction is restarted as if the page had always been in memory.

concepts.text: Performance: Effective Access Time

If p is the page-fault rate (0 ≤ p ≤ 1), ma the memory access time and t_fault the page-fault service time, then EAT = (1 − p) × ma + p × t_fault. Worked example: ma = 200 ns, t_fault = 8 ms = 8,000,000 ns and p = 0.001 give EAT = 0.999 × 200 + 0.001 × 8,000,000 = 199.8 + 8000 ≈ 8200 ns, about 8.2 µs, a slowdown of 40 times. To keep degradation below 10 percent (EAT < 220 ns), p must be below about 1 fault in 400,000 accesses.

A translation look-aside buffer (TLB) is a small, fast associative cache of recent page-table entries. On a TLB hit the frame is known after the TLB lookup; on a miss the page table in memory must be read first, costing an extra memory access. Example: TLB lookup 20 ns, memory 100 ns, hit ratio 80 percent: EAT = 0.8 × (20 + 100) + 0.2 × (20 + 200) = 96 + 44 = 140 ns.

concepts.plainText: EAT = h(t + m) + (1 − h)(t + 2m), h = TLB hit ratio, t = TLB time, m = memory time

concepts.text: Page-table size = number of pages × entry size. Example: a 32-bit virtual address with 4 KB (2^12) pages gives 2^20 pages; with 4-byte entries the table is 2^20 × 4 B = 4 MB per process, too large to keep contiguous. Multilevel (hierarchical) page tables page the page table itself: a two-level scheme splits the 20-bit page number into a 10-bit outer index and a 10-bit inner index, so only the inner tables actually in use need to exist. Hashed and inverted page tables (one entry per physical frame) are alternatives for 64-bit spaces.
Page Replacement Algorithms
When no frame is free a victim page must be chosen:
items: FIFO: replace the page that has been in memory longest; simple, but can remove heavily used pages and suffers Belady's anomaly.
Optimal (OPT, MIN): replace the page that will not be used for the longest time in future; lowest possible fault rate, not implementable, used as a benchmark.
LRU: replace the page not used for the longest time in the past; good approximation of OPT, implemented with counters (timestamps) or a stack; a stack algorithm, so no Belady's anomaly.
Clock (second chance): frames in a circular list with a reference bit; the hand clears bits set to 1 and replaces the first page whose bit is 0; a cheap approximation of LRU.
A dirty (modify) bit lets the OS skip writing back pages that were not changed.

rows: Bit set on load and on hit; hand advances after replacement

concepts.text: The table uses the reference string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1 with 3 frames initially empty (the first three references are compulsory faults in every algorithm). Clock results depend on the exact convention for setting bits and moving the hand, so exam questions nearly always use FIFO, OPT or LRU.

Belady's anomaly: for some reference strings FIFO produces more faults when given more frames. With 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, FIFO gives 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 faults with 4 frames. OPT and LRU are stack algorithms (the pages held with n frames are always a subset of those held with n + 1 frames), so they never show the anomaly.
Thrashing, Working Set and Frame Allocation

Thrashing is a state where processes spend more time paging than executing: each has too few frames for its active pages, so faults are constant, CPU utilisation drops, and a naive scheduler raises the degree of multiprogramming, making it worse. The working-set model defines WS(t, Δ) as the set of pages referenced in the last Δ references; if the sum of working-set sizes D exceeds the available frames m, the OS suspends a process. Page-fault-frequency control is an alternative: give a process more frames if its fault rate is above an upper bound and take frames away below a lower bound.
Frame allocation among processes:
items: Equal allocation: m frames shared equally among n processes, m/n each.
Proportional allocation: a_i = (s_i / S) × m, where s_i is the size of process i and S the total size. Example: 62 frames, processes of 10 and 127 pages get about 4 and 57 frames.
Priority allocation uses priority instead of (or with) size.
Global replacement picks a victim from all frames; local replacement only from the faulting process's own frames.

formulas.plainText: EAT = (1 − p) × ma + p × t_fault
Page table size = (virtual space / page size) × entry size

formulas.latex: a_i = \frac{s_i}{S} \times m,\quad \text{thrashing if } D = \sum WSS_i > m
formulas.plainText: a_i = (s_i / S) × m; thrashing if D = sum of WSS_i > m

notes.text: In EAT problems convert everything to the same unit first: 8 ms = 8,000,000 ns. Forgetting this is the most common arithmetic slip.
Some books ignore the TLB lookup time and write EAT = h × m + (1 − h) × 2m. Read the question: if a TLB time is given, add it to both the hit and miss paths.
OPT always gives the fewest faults for a given number of frames; use it to check your FIFO and LRU answers (they can never be lower).

concepts.text: The File Concept

A file is a named collection of related information recorded on secondary storage; to the user it is the smallest unit of logical storage. The OS maps files onto physical devices and hides the details. Files may be text, source, object or executable, and the type is often indicated by an extension (.c, .exe, .txt) or, in UNIX, by a magic number at the start of the file.
Typical file attributes and operations:
items: Attributes: name, identifier (unique number, e.g. inode number), type, location (pointer to blocks), size, protection (read, write, execute permissions), owner, and timestamps (creation, last modification, last access).
Operations: create, open, read, write, reposition (seek), close, delete and truncate; append and rename are built on these.
An open-file table tracks open files; per-process entries hold the file pointer, while the system-wide entry holds the open count, disk location and access rights.

rows: In order, one after another; read next / write next with an automatic pointer
Any block by number n in any order
An index maps keys to block pointers; search index then access block

concepts.text: Directory Structures

rows: A master directory with one user directory per user
Isolates users; same name allowed per user
No sharing of a file between directories
Tree plus shared links (hard or symbolic)
Dangling links, aliasing; cycles are forbidden

concepts.text: A general graph directory allows cycles, which complicates traversal and deletion (garbage collection is needed), so most systems prevent cycles by disallowing hard links to directories.
Absolute and relative paths:
items: Absolute path starts from the root: /home/ram/notes/os.txt (UNIX) or C:\Users\Ram\notes\os.txt (Windows).
Relative path starts from the current working directory: if the current directory is /home/ram, then notes/os.txt names the same file.
. means the current directory and .. the parent: from /home/ram/notes, ../photos/a.jpg refers to /home/ram/photos/a.jpg.
The path is resolved component by component, each directory lookup giving the inode of the next component.

concepts.text: File-System Implementation
A file system is built in layers, from top to bottom:
items: Application programs issue system calls such as open and read.
Logical file system: manages metadata, directories and file control blocks (inodes), plus protection.
File-organisation module: maps logical block numbers to physical blocks and manages free space.
Basic file system: issues generic block read/write commands and manages buffers and caches.
I/O control: device drivers and interrupt handlers talk to the disk controller.
Devices: the disk itself.

rows: Code to boot the OS from this volume; empty if the volume is not bootable
Block size, total blocks and inodes, free-block and free-inode counts and pointers
One inode per file: type, permissions, owner, size, times, link count and block pointers
File contents and directory contents (name-to-inode-number entries)

concepts.text: A classic UNIX inode holds 12 direct block pointers plus one single-indirect, one double-indirect and one triple-indirect pointer. With 4 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers an index block holds 1024 pointers, so the maximum file size is (12 + 1024 + 1024² + 1024³) × 4 KB = 48 KB + 4 MB + 4 GB + 4 TB, about 4 TB. Small files are reached through direct pointers with no extra disk access, while large files pay one to three extra index-block reads.

concepts.latex: Max = (D + P + P^2 + P^3) \times B,\quad P = B / \text{ptr size}
concepts.plainText: Max size = (D + P + P² + P³) × B, where P = block size / pointer size

concepts.text: Directory implementation and mounting:
items: Linear list of (file name, inode pointer) entries: simple, but finding a file needs a linear search; a sorted list or B-tree speeds lookup.
Hash table: the file name is hashed to an entry, giving near constant-time lookup; collisions must be handled and a fixed table size may need resizing.

Mounting attaches a file system on a device to a mount point (an empty directory) in the existing tree, e.g. mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/usb; after that its files appear under /mnt/usb, and umount detaches it.

formulas.plainText: Pointers per index block P = block size / pointer size
UNIX inode max file size = (12 + P + P² + P³) × block size

notes.text: For inode questions, first compute pointers per block (block size / pointer size), then add the contribution of each pointer level only if the question includes it.
A directory in UNIX is itself a file whose data blocks hold (name, inode number) pairs; the file name is not stored in the inode.
A hard link is another directory entry for the same inode and cannot cross file systems; a symbolic link is a separate small file holding a path and can dangle if the target is deleted.

concepts.text: Allocation Methods and Fragmentation

rows: Fast sequential and direct access; only start and length stored
Hard to grow files; must know size in advance
Files grow easily; any free block usable
Sequential access only, pointer space overhead, one bad pointer loses the rest
No external; small internal in last block
Chain kept in a table (cacheable), so random access is faster
FAT must be cached or each access needs extra seeks
Index block overhead, wasteful for tiny files
No external; internal in last block

concepts.text: Allocation policy decides the kind of fragmentation. Contiguous allocation behaves like variable memory partitioning: holes appear as files are deleted, and first fit or best fit is used to choose a run of free blocks. Linked and indexed allocation use any free block, so external fragmentation disappears, but a file's blocks can become scattered across the disk, which increases seek time; this is sometimes called file fragmentation and is what defragmentation tools repair. Block size is a trade-off: larger blocks improve transfer rate but waste more space in each file's last block.
Free-Space Management
Ways to track free disk blocks:
items: Bit vector (bitmap): one bit per block (1 free, 0 allocated in the Silberschatz convention); finding the first free block is easy with word-level instructions, but the map must fit in memory. A 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks has 2^28 blocks, needing 2^28 bits = 32 MB.
Linked list: free blocks linked together, head pointer kept in memory; no space wasted, but traversal needs many disk reads.
Grouping: the first free block stores the addresses of n free blocks, the last of which holds the next n addresses; many free blocks found quickly.
Counting: store (first free block, count of contiguous free blocks) pairs; compact when free space occurs in runs, as with contiguous allocation or extents.

concepts.text: Disk Structure and Block Mapping

A magnetic disk has several platters, each with two surfaces read by one head per surface on a common arm. Each surface is divided into concentric tracks, each track into sectors (traditionally 512 bytes, now often 4 KB). The set of tracks at the same arm position across all surfaces is a cylinder. The OS sees the disk as a one-dimensional array of logical blocks, which the controller maps onto cylinder, head and sector, filling a whole track, then the rest of the cylinder, before moving the arm outward to the next cylinder, so consecutive blocks need minimal arm movement.

concepts.plainText: LBA = (C × heads + h) × sectors per track + (s − 1)

concepts.text: Inverse mapping: C = LBA div (H × S), h = (LBA div S) mod H, s = (LBA mod S) + 1, where H is heads per cylinder and S sectors per track. Example with H = 16 and S = 63: LBA 5000 gives C = 5000 div 1008 = 4, h = (5000 div 63) mod 16 = 79 mod 16 = 15, and s = (5000 mod 63) + 1 = 23 + 1 = 24. Modern drives do the mapping internally and may remap bad sectors, so the OS only approximates physical layout.
Disk Access Time

Access time = seek time (move the arm to the cylinder) + rotational latency (wait for the sector to come under the head) + transfer time. Average rotational latency is half a revolution. Worked example: a 7200 rpm disk turns 120 times per second, so one revolution takes 8.33 ms and the average latency is 4.17 ms. With an average seek of 5 ms and a 4 KB transfer at 100 MB/s (about 0.04 ms), the average access time is 5 + 4.17 + 0.04 ≈ 9.2 ms, dominated by the mechanical parts.

concepts.plainText: T_access = seek + 1 / (2 × rps) + bytes / transfer rate

concepts.text: Disk Scheduling

The table uses the request queue 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 with the head at cylinder 53, cylinders 0–199, and the head moving towards higher numbers for SCAN-family algorithms. FCFS is fair but slow; SSTF picks the nearest request, reducing movement but risking starvation of far requests; SCAN (elevator) sweeps end to end; C-SCAN services in one direction only, giving more uniform waits; LOOK and C-LOOK turn around at the last request instead of the disk edge.
Improving file-system performance:
items: Buffer cache / page cache: keep recently used blocks in memory; a unified buffer cache avoids double caching of memory-mapped files.
Read-ahead and free-behind: prefetch the next blocks of a sequential file and free the pages just read.
Write-back (delayed write) caching batches writes, while synchronous writes are used for metadata that must be safe.
Journaling (log-structured metadata updates, e.g. ext4, NTFS) makes crash recovery fast by replaying or discarding logged transactions instead of a full consistency check (fsck).
Defragmentation and placing related inodes and data in the same cylinder group reduce seek time; SSDs need TRIM rather than defragmentation.

formulas.plainText: Bit-vector size = disk size / block size bits
Average rotational latency = 0.5 × 60 / RPM seconds

formulas.latex: C = \lfloor LBA/HS \rfloor,\; h = \lfloor LBA/S \rfloor \bmod H,\; s = LBA \bmod S + 1
formulas.plainText: C = LBA div (H×S), h = (LBA div S) mod H, s = LBA mod S + 1

notes.text: In disk-scheduling problems note the initial direction and whether the C-SCAN return sweep is counted; the answer choices usually include both versions.
SSTF is not optimal and can starve requests far from the head; do not confuse it with SJF's optimality for CPU scheduling.
Only the average rotational latency uses half a revolution; the maximum latency is one full revolution (8.33 ms at 7200 rpm).

concepts.text: Role of a System Administrator

A system administrator keeps multi-user computers and servers reliable, secure and available. The job covers installing and configuring the OS and software, managing user accounts and access rights, protecting data through backups, monitoring performance and logs, and planning capacity. Good administration follows written procedures and documents every change so that another administrator can repeat or reverse it.

rows: Create, modify, lock and delete accounts; groups; password policy; quotas
Full, incremental and differential backups; off-site copies; test restores
Apply OS and application patches; package management (apt, dnf); change control
CPU, memory, disk and network usage; log review; alerts (top, df, free, journalctl)
Least privilege, firewalls, SSH keys, disabling unused services, audit
Partitioning, mounting file systems, RAID/LVM, free-space and quota control

concepts.text: User Account Management on Linux

sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G developers ram   # create user with home dir
sudo passwd ram                                  # set or change password
sudo usermod -aG docker ram                      # append to extra group
sudo usermod -L ram                              # lock the account
sudo groupadd developers                         # create a group
sudo userdel -r ram                              # delete user and home dir
sudo chown ram:developers report.txt             # change owner and group
chmod 754 script.sh                              # rwxr-xr--
chmod u+x,g-w file.txt                           # symbolic form

UNIX permissions have three classes (user/owner, group, others), each with read (r = 4), write (w = 2) and execute (x = 1). An octal digit is the sum for one class: 7 = rwx, 6 = rw-, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--, 0 = ---. So chmod 754 gives the owner rwx, the group r-x and others r--, and chmod 644 (rw-r--r--) is typical for ordinary files. On a directory, x means permission to enter (traverse) it and r to list its names. The umask removes bits from the default: with umask 022 new files get 644 and new directories 755.

concepts.plainText: Octal digit = 4r + 2w + 1x, each of r, w, x is 0 or 1

rows: 7 fields, world-readable; x means password is in /etc/shadow; UID 0 is root
9 fields, readable only by root; salted password hash and ageing data
Group names, IDs and supplementary members

concepts.text: sudo lets an authorised user run a single command with root (or another user's) privileges after authenticating with their own password; the rules live in /etc/sudoers, edited with visudo, and every use is logged. It supports the principle of least privilege: each user and service gets only the rights needed for its job, and the administrator works as an ordinary user, elevating only when necessary, instead of logging in as root.

On Windows, accounts are managed through Settings, the Computer Management console (Local Users and Groups) or commands such as net user and net localgroup, and in organisations centrally through Active Directory with Group Policy. Permissions are NTFS access control lists, and User Account Control (UAC) plays the role of sudo by requiring elevation for administrative actions.
Start-up (Boot) Sequence
From power-on to login on a Linux PC:
items: Firmware (BIOS or UEFI) runs the power-on self-test (POST), initialises hardware and selects a boot device.
BIOS loads the boot loader from the MBR (first 512-byte sector); UEFI loads an EFI application from the EFI system partition.
The boot loader (GRUB 2) shows a menu, loads the kernel image and the initial RAM disk (initramfs) and passes kernel parameters.
The kernel initialises CPU, memory and drivers, mounts the root file system (read-only first) and starts the first user process, PID 1.
PID 1 (systemd, or SysV init on older systems) starts services in dependency order until the default target or run level is reached, then presents a login prompt or graphical login.

concepts.text: Shutdown Procedures

sudo shutdown -h now            # halt / power off immediately
sudo shutdown -h +10 'Maintenance'  # warn users, halt in 10 min
sudo shutdown -r now            # reboot now (same as: reboot)
sudo shutdown -c                # cancel a scheduled shutdown
sync                            # flush buffered data to disk
sudo systemctl poweroff         # systemd equivalent
sudo systemctl isolate multi-user.target  # switch target

A graceful shutdown warns logged-in users, blocks new logins, sends SIGTERM to processes so they can save state (followed by SIGKILL for those that do not exit), stops services in reverse dependency order, flushes buffers with sync and unmounts file systems before power-off. A forced shutdown (power cut, holding the power button, or halt -f) skips these steps and can lose cached data or leave file systems inconsistent, requiring fsck or journal recovery at the next boot. System logs (/var/log, journalctl) record boot, service and security events for troubleshooting, and cron (crontab -e, entries of the form minute hour day month weekday command) schedules routine jobs such as backups and log rotation.

formulas.plainText: Mode digits: owner, group, others; each digit = 4r + 2w + x
Default perms = base AND NOT umask (umask 022: files 666 → 644, dirs 777 → 755)

notes.text: Decode octal permissions digit by digit: 7 = rwx, 6 = rw-, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--. For example 640 means rw-r----- (owner read/write, group read, others nothing).
usermod -G without -a replaces all of a user's supplementary groups; use usermod -aG to add a group while keeping the existing ones.
Passwords were moved from the world-readable /etc/passwd to root-only /etc/shadow so that hashes cannot be copied and attacked offline by ordinary users.

concepts.text: How to use this sheet

This chapter spans three subjects — data structures and algorithms, databases, and operating systems — and each is tested through a small set of complexities, definitions and formulas. The tables below collect them in syllabus order. Use them for last-minute revision; every entry is explained with worked examples in its subtopic.
1. Data structures

concepts.latex: f(n) = O(g(n)) \iff \exists\, c, n_0:\ f(n) \le c\,g(n)\ \forall n \ge n_0
concepts.plainText: Big-O: f is bounded above by c·g for all n ≥ n₀ (Ω bounds below, Θ both)

rows: linear search, one pass over a list
merge sort, heap sort, average quick sort
bubble, selection, insertion sort; nested loops
insert at head O(1), search O(n)
search O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed

concepts.text: Data Type, Data Structure and ADT

A data type is the kind of value a variable can hold together with the operations allowed on it, such as int, float or char in C. A data structure is a particular way of organising data in memory so that it can be used efficiently, such as an array, linked list or tree. An abstract data type (ADT) is a logical description or blueprint: it states what data is stored and which operations are provided, but says nothing about how they are implemented. The Stack ADT, for example, is defined by push, pop, peek and isEmpty and can be implemented with either an array or a linked list.
Three levels of looking at data:
items: Data type: the set of values plus built-in operations (int supports +, -, *, /, %).
Abstract data type: the specification (interface) of a user-defined type, independent of language and storage details; it separates what from how.
Data structure: the concrete implementation of an ADT in memory, chosen for the time and space trade-off it gives.
Primitive data structures are handled directly by machine instructions (int, float, char, pointer); non-primitive ones are built from primitives (arrays, lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs).

concepts.text: Time and Space Analysis

Time complexity measures how the number of basic operations of an algorithm grows with the input size n; space complexity measures the extra memory it needs (fixed part for code and simple variables plus a variable part for dynamic data and the recursion stack). We count operations rather than seconds so that the measure is independent of the machine and compiler. Asymptotic analysis keeps only the fastest-growing term and ignores constant factors, because for large n that term dominates.

concepts.latex: f(n)=O(g(n)) \iff \exists\, c>0, n_0:\ f(n)\le c\,g(n)\ \forall n\ge n_0
concepts.plainText: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff there exist c > 0 and n0 such that f(n) <= c·g(n) for all n >= n0

concepts.text: The three asymptotic notations:
items: Big-O (O): asymptotic upper bound; f grows no faster than g. Most often quoted for the worst case.
Big-Omega (Ω): asymptotic lower bound; f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0. Often quoted for the best case.
Big-Theta (Θ): tight bound; c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for n ≥ n0, i.e. f is both O(g) and Ω(g).
Example: f(n) = 3n² + 5n + 2 is O(n²) (take c = 4, n0 = 6), Ω(n²) (c = 3) and therefore Θ(n²).

concepts.text: The best case is the input on which the algorithm does the least work (for linear search, the key is the first element: 1 comparison). The worst case is the input needing the most work (key absent: n comparisons). The average case is the expected work over all inputs under an assumed distribution (for a successful linear search about (n + 1)/2 comparisons). The worst case is the most useful guarantee, which is why complexities are usually quoted as worst-case Big-O.
Analysing Loops

Consecutive statements add (keep the larger term) and nested loops multiply. A triangular nest such as for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 0; j < i; j++) runs 0 + 1 + ... + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2 times, which is still O(n²). A loop whose control variable is multiplied or divided by a constant k runs about log_k n times.

Recursive algorithms are analysed with recurrences. Merge sort gives T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, which solves to Θ(n log n); binary search gives T(n) = T(n/2) + 1, which solves to Θ(log n). The master theorem handles T(n) = aT(n/b) + Θ(n^d) with a ≥ 1 and b > 1: if d < log_b a the answer is Θ(n^(log_b a)), if d = log_b a it is Θ(n^d log n), and if d > log_b a it is Θ(n^d).

concepts.plainText: T(n) = a·T(n/b) + Θ(n^d): compare d with log_b a

formulas.plainText: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) iff f(n) >= c·g(n) for all n >= n0

formulas.latex: c_1 g(n)\le f(n)\le c_2 g(n)\ \forall n\ge n_0 \iff f=\Theta(g)
formulas.plainText: f = Θ(g) iff c1·g(n) <= f(n) <= c2·g(n) for all n >= n0
1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < 2ⁿ < n! (growth order)
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n gives Θ(n log n)

notes.text: Do not equate Θ with the average case or Ω with the best case. The notations are bounds on a function; best, average and worst case are different functions. You can state a Θ bound for the worst case (insertion sort's worst case is Θ(n²)) or an O bound for the best case.

For loop-counting MCQs, write out the values the loop variable takes. Doubling or halving means log n iterations; a nested loop whose inner bound depends on the outer variable is usually a triangular sum n(n − 1)/2, still O(n²).
An ADT answers 'what operations', a data structure answers 'how stored'. The same ADT (a queue) can be built from an array, a circular array or a linked list, each with different costs.

concepts.text: Sorting Terminology

Sorting arranges records in ascending or descending order of a key so that later searching, merging and reporting become efficient. In internal sorting all the records fit in main memory (RAM) at once, e.g. insertion, selection, bubble, quick and heap sort. In external sorting the file is too large for memory, so the data stays on disk and is processed in chunks; external merge sort is the standard method. For internal sorts the cost is counted in key comparisons and moves; for external sorts it is dominated by the number of disk passes.
Properties used to compare sorting algorithms:
items: Stable: records with equal keys keep their original relative order (insertion, bubble, merge, radix are stable; selection, quick, heap, shell are not).
In-place: needs only O(1) extra memory apart from the array (quick sort also uses an O(log n) recursion stack).
Adaptive: runs faster when the input is already partly sorted (insertion sort and bubble sort with a swap flag take O(n) on sorted input).
Comparison-based: orders items only by comparing keys; any such sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.
Exchange sorts (bubble sort, quick sort) work by swapping pairs of out-of-order elements.

concepts.text: Insertion and Selection Sort

Insertion sort keeps a sorted prefix a[0..i-1] and inserts the next element a[i] into its correct place by shifting larger elements one position right, exactly as one sorts playing cards in hand. It is stable, in-place and adaptive: on sorted input it makes only n - 1 comparisons (O(n)), while reverse-sorted input gives the worst case of n(n-1)/2 comparisons (O(n²)).

Array: 29 10 14 37 13
Insertion sort (sorted | unsorted)
  i=1: 10 29 | 14 37 13
  i=2: 10 14 29 | 37 13
  i=3: 10 14 29 37 | 13
  i=4: 10 13 14 29 37
Selection sort (minimum swapped to the front)
  pass 1: 10 | 29 14 37 13   (swap 29, 10)
  pass 2: 10 13 | 14 37 29   (swap 29, 13)
  pass 3: 10 13 14 | 37 29   (no swap)
  pass 4: 10 13 14 29 | 37   (swap 37, 29)

Selection sort finds the minimum of the unsorted part in each pass and swaps it to the front of that part. It always makes n(n-1)/2 comparisons whatever the input, so best, average and worst are all O(n²), but it performs at most n - 1 swaps, which is useful when writes are expensive. The long-distance swap can jump an element past an equal key, so selection sort is not stable.
Exchange Sorts: Bubble Sort and Quick Sort

Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are out of order, so after pass k the k largest keys have bubbled to the end. With a flag that stops the sort when a pass makes no swap, sorted input takes one pass of n - 1 comparisons (O(n)); otherwise it is O(n²). It is stable and in-place but usually the slowest simple sort in practice because of the many swaps.

Bubble sort on 29 10 14 37 13 (largest moves to the end each pass)
Pass 1: 29>10 swap, 29>14 swap, 29<37, 37>13 swap -> 10 14 29 13 37
Pass 2: 10<14, 14<29, 29>13 swap            -> 10 14 13 29 37
Pass 3: 10<14, 14>13 swap                   -> 10 13 14 29 37
Pass 4: 10<13, no swaps -> flag stops the sort

Quick sort (Hoare) is a divide-and-conquer exchange sort: partition places a chosen pivot in its final position with smaller keys to its left and larger keys to its right, then each side is sorted recursively. On 29 10 14 37 13 with the last element 13 as pivot, one Lomuto partition gives 10 13 14 37 29; the right part 14 37 29 with pivot 29 becomes 14 29 37, giving 10 13 14 29 37. Balanced partitions give O(n log n); if the pivot is always the smallest or largest key (e.g. first element of already sorted data) the recursion depth becomes n and the time O(n²). Median-of-three or a random pivot makes the worst case very unlikely.

rows: O(n log n) / O(n log n) / O(n²)

concepts.text: Efficiency and when to use which sort:
items: Small n (roughly under 20) or nearly sorted data: insertion sort; library quick sorts switch to it for small partitions.
Writes are costly (e.g. flash memory): selection sort, at most n - 1 swaps.
General large in-memory arrays: quick sort, fastest on average thanks to good cache behaviour.
Bubble sort is mainly of teaching value; its only advantage is detecting a sorted array in one pass.

formulas.plainText: Cmax = n(n-1)/2 comparisons (selection always; insertion and bubble worst case)
Quick sort best/average: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n = O(n log n)
Quick sort worst: T(n) = T(n-1) + n = O(n²)

notes.text: Memorise the complexity table as pairs: insertion and bubble are the only simple sorts with an O(n) best case, and selection is the one that is O(n²) even on sorted input.
Quick sort is in-place but not stable, and its O(n²) worst case occurs on already sorted input when the first or last element is taken as pivot.
Internal vs external depends on memory, not on the algorithm name alone: merge sort is used internally too, but its run-merging form is the classic external sort.

concepts.text: DBMS vs File-Processing System

A database is a collection of interrelated data, and a database management system (DBMS) is the software that stores, retrieves and protects it on behalf of many users and programs. Before DBMSs, organisations kept data in separate application-specific files, which led to duplication, inconsistency and programs tightly bound to file layouts. A DBMS centralises the data under one schema and provides a query language, concurrency control, recovery and security.

rows: Same data copied in many files; copies drift apart
New program needed for each new query
Constraints declared in the schema and enforced

concepts.text: Levels of Abstraction, ANSI-SPARC and Data Independence
The ANSI-SPARC three-schema architecture hides complexity through three levels, linked by mappings:
items: Physical (internal) level: how data is actually stored - files, record layouts, indexes, B+-trees, hashing and block placement.
Logical (conceptual) level: what data is stored and how it is related - the tables, attributes, types and constraints of the whole database, as seen by the DBA.
View (external) level: the part of the database each user group sees; many views can exist over one logical schema, and they also restrict access for security.
Mappings: external/conceptual mapping links each view to the logical schema; conceptual/internal mapping links the logical schema to storage structures.

concepts.text: Data independence is the ability to change a schema at one level without rewriting the level above it:
items: Physical data independence: change the internal schema (add an index, move files, change the file organisation) without changing the logical schema or application programs. It is easy to achieve and common.

Logical data independence: change the conceptual schema (add a column or table, split a table) without changing external views or programs. It is harder to achieve because programs depend closely on logical structure.

concepts.text: A schema is the overall design of the database - the relation names, attributes, types and constraints - and changes rarely. An instance (database state) is the actual data stored at a particular moment and changes with every insert, update or delete. In programming terms the schema is like a variable's type declaration and the instance is the variable's current value. Schemas exist at each level: physical schema, logical schema and several subschemas (views).

rows: Tree of records; each child has one parent (1:N)
Graph of records linked by sets; M:N allowed via owner-member links
Tables (relations) of tuples; links through key values
Entities, attributes and relationships drawn as a diagram
Conceptual design tool, mapped to tables later
Objects with identity, attributes, methods and inheritance
Self-describing tagged data with a flexible schema

concepts.text: The Entity-Relationship Model
Entities and entity sets:
items: Entity: a distinguishable real-world object (a particular student, a course). Entity set: all entities of the same type (STUDENT) sharing the same attributes.
Strong entity set: has a primary key of its own, drawn as a single rectangle.

Weak entity set: lacks enough attributes to form a primary key; it depends on an owner (identifying) strong entity set, is drawn as a double rectangle and must have total participation in its identifying relationship.
Identifying relationship: links the weak entity to its owner, drawn as a double diamond.
Partial key (discriminator): the attribute set that distinguishes weak entities of the same owner, drawn with a dashed underline; e.g. dependent_name for DEPENDENT owned by EMPLOYEE.

concepts.text: Types of attributes:
items: Simple (atomic) vs composite: roll_no cannot be divided; name can be split into first, middle and last.
Single-valued vs multivalued: date_of_birth has one value; phone_numbers may have several (double oval).
Stored vs derived: age can be derived from date_of_birth (dashed oval); total marks can be derived from subject marks.
Key attribute: uniquely identifies an entity, drawn underlined inside its oval.
Null values may appear when a value is not applicable or unknown.

concepts.text: A relationship is an association among entities, and a relationship set groups relationships of the same type; its degree is the number of participating entity sets (binary, ternary). Mapping cardinality for a binary relationship is 1:1, 1:N, N:1 or M:N, shown by labelling the lines or by arrows toward the 'one' side. Participation is total (every entity must take part, double line) or partial (single line). A relationship set may also carry descriptive attributes, such as grade on ENROLLS.

concepts.plainText: PK of weak entity = PK of owner + partial key of the weak entity

rows: Strong entity set / weak entity set

concepts.text: Worked design: a small university has STUDENT (roll_no, name, set of phones), COURSE (course_id, title, credits) and INSTRUCTOR (inst_id, name); students ENROLL in many courses and each course has many students (M:N, with attribute grade); each course is TAUGHT_BY exactly one instructor who may teach many courses (N:1); SECTION is a weak entity identified by COURSE with partial key sec_no. Mapping rules: each strong entity becomes a table, the multivalued attribute becomes its own table, the M:N relationship becomes a table whose key is the union of both keys, the N:1 relationship becomes a foreign key on the N side, and the weak entity takes its owner's key plus its partial key.

formulas.plainText: PK of weak entity = PK of owner + partial key
Key of an M:N relationship table = union of both entity keys

notes.text: Match level to change: adding an index or changing file organisation tests physical data independence; adding a column without breaking views tests logical data independence.
A double oval means multivalued and a dashed oval means derived; a double rectangle is a weak entity, not a multivalued one. MCQs often swap these symbols.
In E-R to relational mapping, a 1:N relationship needs no separate table (put the foreign key on the N side), while an M:N relationship always needs its own table.

concepts.text: What a Transaction Is

A transaction is a logical unit of database work: a sequence of read and write operations that must be executed as a whole, such as transferring money between two accounts. It begins with BEGIN (or implicitly with the first statement) and ends with COMMIT, which makes its changes permanent, or ROLLBACK (ABORT), which undoes them. The DBMS treats the transaction as indivisible even though it is made of many low-level steps.
A transaction moves through five states (state diagram in words):
items: Active: the initial state; the transaction is executing its reads and writes.
Partially committed: the final statement has executed, but the changes may still be only in main-memory buffers.
Committed: the commit record has reached stable storage; the changes are permanent. Path: active -> partially committed -> committed.
Failed: normal execution can no longer proceed (logic error, constraint violation, system failure). Reached from active or partially committed.

Aborted: the transaction has been rolled back and the database restored to its state before it started; the system may then restart it or kill it. Path: failed -> aborted. Committed and aborted are both terminated states.

concepts.text: Concurrent Executions and Anomalies

Running transactions concurrently improves throughput and resource utilisation, because while one transaction waits for disk I/O another can use the CPU. It also reduces average response time, since short transactions need not wait behind long ones. The price is that uncontrolled interleaving can produce anomalies, so the DBMS must restrict interleavings to those that are equivalent to some serial order.

rows: Two transactions read the same item and both write it; one write overwrites the other
T1 and T2 both read A = 100, T1 writes 150, T2 writes 80; T1's update is lost
A transaction reads a value written by another transaction that has not committed
T2 reads A written by T1, then T1 aborts; T2 used a value that never existed
A transaction reads the same item twice and gets different values
T1 reads A = 100, T2 updates A to 200 and commits, T1 reads A = 200
A repeated query with the same condition returns a different set of rows
T1 counts rows WHERE dept = 'IT', T2 inserts a new IT employee, T1 counts again

concepts.text: Schedules and Conflict Serializability

A schedule is the chronological order in which operations of several transactions are executed, preserving the order within each transaction. A serial schedule runs one transaction completely before the next starts and is always correct; a non-serial (interleaved) schedule is correct only if it is serializable, i.e. equivalent to some serial schedule. Two operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, access the same data item, and at least one of them is a write (read-write, write-read, write-write). A schedule is conflict serializable if it can be turned into a serial schedule by swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations.

concepts.plainText: Number of serial schedules of n transactions = n!

concepts.text:
Schedule S:  r1(A)  w1(A)  r2(A)  w2(A)  r2(B)  w2(B)  r1(B)  w1(B)
Conflicting pairs (earlier -> later):
  w1(A) ... r2(A)   gives edge T1 -> T2
  w1(A) ... w2(A)   gives edge T1 -> T2
  w2(B) ... r1(B)   gives edge T2 -> T1
  r2(B) ... w1(B)   gives edge T2 -> T1
Precedence graph: T1 -> T2 and T2 -> T1  => cycle
Result: S is NOT conflict serializable.
If r1(B) w1(B) came before r2(B), only T1 -> T2 exists:
acyclic, equivalent serial order T1, T2.
Precedence (serializability) graph test:
items: Draw one node per transaction.
For each conflicting pair where Ti's operation comes before Tj's, add a directed edge Ti -> Tj.
The schedule is conflict serializable if and only if the graph has no cycle; a topological sort of the graph gives an equivalent serial order.

concepts.text: View serializability is a weaker condition: a schedule is view equivalent to a serial schedule if every transaction reads the same initial values, reads each value from the same writer, and the same transaction performs the final write of each item. Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable, but not vice versa; the extra view-serializable schedules always contain blind writes (writes without a prior read). Testing view serializability is NP-complete, so practical systems enforce conflict serializability.
Recoverability of schedules (important when transactions abort):
items: Recoverable schedule: if Tj reads a value written by Ti, then Ti commits before Tj commits. Otherwise a committed Tj might depend on an aborted Ti, which cannot be fixed.
Cascading rollback: one abort forces several dependent transactions (that read its dirty data) to roll back too.
Cascadeless schedule: a transaction reads only values written by already-committed transactions, so no cascading rollback can occur. Every cascadeless schedule is recoverable.
Strict schedule: no transaction reads or overwrites an item until the last writer of that item has committed or aborted; produced by strict 2PL.

formulas.plainText: Number of serial schedules of n transactions = n!
Total schedules of k transactions with n1..nk operations = (n1 + ... + nk)! / (n1! n2! ... nk!)
Conflict serializable if and only if the precedence graph has no cycle

notes.text: To test a schedule, list only the conflicting pairs (same item, different transactions, at least one write) and draw edges in time order. Read-read pairs never create edges.
Conflict serializable is a subset of view serializable, which is a subset of all correct schedules. A view-serializable but not conflict-serializable schedule must contain a blind write.
Recoverable does not mean cascadeless. A schedule where Tj reads Ti's uncommitted write but commits after Ti is recoverable, yet aborting Ti still forces Tj to roll back.

concepts.text: What an Operating System Is

An operating system (OS) is the layer of system software that sits between the hardware and application programs. It acts as a resource manager, allocating CPU time, memory, storage and I/O devices fairly and efficiently among competing programs, and as an extended machine, hiding messy hardware details behind clean abstractions such as processes, files and sockets. The always-resident core of the OS is the kernel; everything else (shells, utilities, libraries) runs on top of it. Its goals are convenience for users, efficient use of hardware and the ability to evolve.
Evolution of Operating Systems

rows: Programmer loads program by hand, no OS
Huge setup time, CPU idle while scheduling machine
Resident monitor runs jobs in sequence from cards/tape
Several jobs in memory; CPU switches when one waits for I/O
Better CPU use, but no user interaction
CPU time sliced among interactive terminals (CTSS, MULTICS, UNIX)
Many machines cooperate, resources shared over a network
Deadline-driven control (VxWorks, QNX); battery-aware phones (Android, iOS)

concepts.text: Common types of operating system:
items: Batch OS: groups similar jobs, no interaction during execution; aims at throughput.
Multiprogramming / multitasking OS: keeps several processes in memory and switches between them; time-sharing is multitasking with a small time quantum for interactivity.
Multiprocessor (parallel) OS: symmetric (SMP, every CPU runs the kernel) or asymmetric (master-slave) on tightly coupled CPUs sharing memory.
Distributed OS: loosely coupled computers appear to users as one system; network OS instead lets users see and log in to separate machines.
Real-time OS: hard real-time must meet every deadline (airbag, pacemaker); soft real-time tolerates occasional misses (video streaming).
Embedded and mobile OS: small footprint, power management, often real-time features.

concepts.text: Major OS components (managers):
items: Process manager: creates and deletes processes, schedules the CPU, provides synchronisation and communication.
Memory manager: tracks which memory is in use, allocates and frees space, implements paging, segmentation and virtual memory.
File manager: files and directories, naming, protection, mapping onto secondary storage.
I/O (device) manager: device drivers, buffering, caching and spooling; disk scheduling.
Security and protection manager: authentication, access control, isolation of processes.
Networking manager: protocol stacks and sockets so processes on different machines can communicate.

concepts.text: Operating System Structures

rows: Whole OS is one large kernel binary in kernel mode
Fast calls; a bug can crash everything, hard to maintain
Layer n uses only services of layer n-1; hardware is layer 0
Easy to debug and verify; overhead, hard to define layers
Minimal kernel (IPC, basic scheduling, low-level memory); servers in user space
Core kernel plus loadable kernel modules
Flexible like microkernel, fast like monolithic
Mix of microkernel design with performance-critical services in kernel

concepts.text: Services an OS provides to users and programs:
items: User interface (CLI, GUI, batch), program execution, I/O operations and file-system manipulation.
Communication between processes (shared memory or message passing) and error detection.
For the system itself: resource allocation, accounting (usage statistics) and protection and security.

concepts.text: A system call is the programmatic interface through which a process requests a kernel service. Programs usually call a library wrapper (the C library or the Win32 API), which places a call number and parameters in registers, a memory block or the stack and executes a trap instruction. The kernel looks up the call number in the system-call table, runs the handler in kernel mode and returns the result to user mode.

Hardware provides dual-mode operation with a mode bit: user mode (1) runs applications, and kernel (supervisor, privileged) mode (0) runs the OS. Privileged instructions such as I/O, setting the timer or changing page tables can execute only in kernel mode; attempting them in user mode causes a trap. An interrupt is an asynchronous hardware signal (timer, disk completion, keyboard) while a trap or exception is a synchronous software-generated event (system call, divide by zero, page fault); both switch the CPU to kernel mode and transfer control through the interrupt vector to a handler, after which the saved state is restored.

concepts.plainText: CPU utilisation = 1 - p^n (n processes, each waiting for I/O a fraction p of time)

formulas.plainText: CPU utilisation = 1 - p^n
Worst wait for a time slice in time-sharing <= (n - 1) x q

notes.text: Microkernel = minimal kernel with services (file system, drivers) as user-space servers communicating by message passing; its selling point is reliability, its cost is IPC overhead. MCQs often contrast it with monolithic kernels.
Multiprogramming aims to keep the CPU busy (utilisation); time-sharing aims at short response time for interactive users; real-time aims at meeting deadlines.
A system call is not an ordinary function call: it crosses from user mode to kernel mode through a trap, which is why it costs more than a library call.

concepts.text: Logical and Physical Addresses

The CPU generates logical (virtual) addresses; the memory unit sees physical addresses. The set of all logical addresses a program can generate is its logical address space, and the matching set of real RAM locations is its physical address space. The Memory Management Unit (MMU) is the hardware that translates every logical address to a physical one at run time, so a user program never sees real physical addresses.

rows: Program must load at a known address; recompile to move it
Start address fixed once loaded; cannot move while running
Process can be moved (swapped, compacted) during execution; logical ≠ physical

concepts.text: Simple MMU with relocation (base) and limit registers:
items: Limit register holds the size of the process's logical space; every logical address must satisfy 0 ≤ address < limit, otherwise the hardware traps to the OS (addressing error).
Relocation register holds the smallest physical address of the process; physical = relocation + logical.
Example: relocation = 14000, limit = 3000. Logical 346 maps to 14346; logical 3200 exceeds the limit and causes a trap.
Only the OS in kernel mode may load these registers, which gives memory protection between processes.

concepts.text: Swapping and Contiguous Allocation

Swapping moves an entire process from main memory to a backing store (fast disk) and later back again, letting the total size of processes exceed physical memory. Its cost is dominated by transfer time, which is proportional to the amount of memory swapped. With execution-time binding a swapped-in process may land at a different address. In contiguous allocation each process occupies one single block of memory, either in fixed-size partitions (set up at boot) or variable partitions (carved to fit each process from free holes).
Placement strategies for choosing a hole in variable partitioning:
items: First fit: allocate the first hole large enough; fast, usually as good as best fit in storage use.
Best fit: allocate the smallest hole that is large enough; minimises leftover space but leaves many tiny, useless holes and must search the whole list unless it is sorted.
Worst fit: allocate the largest hole; leaves the largest leftover hole but in simulations is generally worse than first and best fit.
Next fit: like first fit, but continues searching from where the last search ended.

concepts.text: The worked example above uses free holes of 100, 500, 200, 300 and 600 KB (in that order) and processes of 212, 417, 112 and 426 KB arriving in that order. Only best fit places all four processes here, but this is a property of this input, not a general rule.
Fragmentation and its cure:
