items: Internal fragmentation: unused space inside an allocated block, because the block (fixed partition or page) is bigger than the request. Example: a 3.2 KB request in a 4 KB partition wastes 0.8 KB internally.
External fragmentation: enough total free memory exists but it is split into non-contiguous holes, so a request cannot be satisfied. Typical of variable partitioning and segmentation.
50-percent rule (first fit): for N allocated blocks about 0.5N blocks are lost to fragmentation, i.e. one-third of memory may be unusable.

Compaction shuffles processes to merge all free holes into one; it is possible only with execution-time (dynamic) relocation and is expensive. Paging and segmentation with paging are the non-contiguous alternatives.

concepts.text: Managing Free Memory

rows: Memory split into allocation units; one bit per unit (0 free, 1 used)
Fixed small size, but finding k consecutive free units needs a slow bit search
List of segments, each marked hole or process, with start and length
Fast merge of adjacent holes on release; list sorted by address; supports first/best/worst fit

concepts.text: Paging Basics

Paging divides logical memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size; any page can go into any free frame, so external fragmentation disappears (only internal fragmentation in the last page remains, on average half a page per process). A per-process page table maps page number p to frame number f. A logical address is split into p (high bits, index into the page table) and offset d (low bits, copied unchanged). Worked example: page size 1 KB = 1024 bytes, logical address 3085 gives p = 3085 div 1024 = 3 and d = 3085 mod 1024 = 13; if the page table maps page 3 to frame 7, the physical address is 7 × 1024 + 13 = 7181.

concepts.latex: p = \left\lfloor \frac{LA}{S} \right\rfloor,\; d = LA \bmod S,\; PA = f \cdot S + d
concepts.plainText: p = floor(LA / S), d = LA mod S, PA = f × S + d (S = page size, f = frame of page p)

concepts.text: Segmentation instead divides a program into variable-size logical units that match the programmer's view (code, data, stack, functions). A logical address is a pair (segment number s, offset d); the segment table holds a base and a limit for each segment, and d must be less than the limit or the hardware traps. Segmentation supports sharing and protection per logical unit but suffers external fragmentation; Intel x86 combines segmentation with paging.

formulas.latex: PA = R + LA,\quad \text{valid iff } 0 \le LA < L
formulas.plainText: PA = relocation + LA, valid only if 0 ≤ LA < limit

formulas.latex: p = m - n \text{ bits},\; d = n \text{ bits}
formulas.plainText: Logical space 2^m, page size 2^n → page number m − n bits, offset n bits
Bitmap bits = memory size / allocation unit

notes.text: For fit questions, update the hole sizes after each allocation: first fit and worst fit may reuse the leftover of an earlier hole (the 288 KB or 388 KB holes above).
Paging removes external fragmentation but not internal fragmentation; variable partitioning and segmentation have the opposite behaviour. Do not mix the two.
Bitmap sizing example: 32 MB of memory in 4 KB units = 8192 units, so the bitmap needs 8192 bits = 1 KB.

concepts.text: Software Process and Life-Cycle Models

A software process is a structured set of activities needed to develop a software system. Every process includes four fundamental activities: specification (what the system should do), design and implementation, validation (checking it does what the customer wants) and evolution (changing it as needs change). A process model (SDLC model) is an abstract description of how these activities are ordered and repeated. Plan-driven models fix the plan up front; agile models plan incrementally and embrace change.
Waterfall model (Royce, 1970): phases run strictly in sequence, each producing signed-off documents:
items: Requirements analysis and definition, then system and software design, then implementation and unit testing, then integration and system testing, then operation and maintenance.
Strengths: simple to manage, clear milestones and heavy documentation; suits stable, well-understood requirements and contract-based work.
Weaknesses: rigid; working software appears only late, so requirement errors are found late and are costly to fix.

concepts.text: V-Model (Verification and Validation)

The V-model is an extension of waterfall in which test planning starts during the matching development phase. Verification asks "are we building the product right?" (conformance to specification, via reviews and inspections); validation asks "are we building the right product?" (meeting real user needs, via testing). It still assumes stable requirements and does not produce early prototypes.
Incremental, Iterative and Spiral
Models that deliver or refine the system in repeated cycles:
items: Incremental: requirements are split into increments; each increment is designed, built and delivered, adding functionality to the previous one. Core features arrive first and customers get early value.
Iterative: a skeletal version of the whole system is built first and then refined through repeated cycles of design, build and review, each yielding a working release.

Spiral (Boehm, 1986): risk-driven; each loop passes through four quadrants: determine objectives and constraints, identify and resolve risks (often by prototyping), develop and test, and plan the next loop. Suited to large, high-risk projects.
Radius of the spiral represents cumulative cost; the angular position represents progress in the current loop.

concepts.text: Prototyping, RAD and Big Bang
Models for unclear requirements, tight deadlines or tiny projects:
items: Prototype model: a quick working model is built to clarify ambiguous requirements. Throwaway (rapid) prototypes are discarded after feedback; evolutionary prototypes are refined into the final system.

RAD (Rapid Application Development): very short time-boxed cycles (typically 60 to 90 days) using reusable components, code generators and JAD workshops; phases are requirements planning, user design, construction and cutover.
Big Bang: no formal planning or process; all resources go into coding and the product emerges at the end. Only for very small, academic or experimental work; highly risky and unpredictable.

concepts.text: Agile, Scrum and XP

The Agile Manifesto (2001) values individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan. Agile methods deliver working software in short increments, keep the customer involved and accept changing requirements even late in development.

rows: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers (no traditional project manager)
Sprint (1 month or less, typically 2 to 4 weeks), sprint planning, daily scrum (15 min), sprint review, sprint retrospective
Owns and orders the product backlog; maximises product value
Coaches the team, removes impediments, ensures Scrum is followed

concepts.text: Extreme Programming (XP, Kent Beck) practices:
items: Pair programming, test-first development (TDD), continuous integration and small, frequent releases.
Refactoring, simple design, collective code ownership and coding standards.
On-site customer, user stories for requirements, planning game and a sustainable pace (40-hour week).

concepts.plainText: Sprints needed = ceil(backlog story points / velocity)

rows: Large project with high technical risk
Early partial delivery of core features

formulas.plainText: Communication paths = n(n - 1) / 2
Velocity = story points completed per sprint
Risk exposure RE = probability x loss

notes.text: Keyword map: risk analysis = spiral; test phase paired with each development phase = V-model; unclear requirements = prototyping; no planning = big bang; sprints and backlog = Scrum; pair programming and TDD = XP; time-box of 60 to 90 days = RAD.

Incremental and iterative are not the same: incremental adds new pieces of functionality in each delivery, while iterative reworks and refines the whole system in each cycle. Many real methods (including Scrum) combine both.

Brooks' law, "adding manpower to a late software project makes it later", follows from ramp-up time and from communication paths growing as n(n - 1)/2 with team size n. Agile keeps teams small (commonly 10 or fewer) for this reason.

concepts.text: What CASE Means

Computer-Aided Software Engineering (CASE) is the use of software tools to support software process activities such as requirements engineering, design, programming, testing, project management and configuration management. CASE tools automate routine work, enforce methods and notations, keep documents consistent with each other and store all project information in a shared repository. The aim is higher productivity and better quality, not replacing engineering judgement.
Classification by Life-Cycle Phase

rows: DFD/ER/UML modelling, requirements managers, prototyping tools
Code generators, compilers, debuggers, test tools, reverse engineering
Upper and lower tools sharing one central repository

concepts.text: Tools classified by the activity they support (Sommerville's functional view):
items: Planning and estimation: PERT/CPM and Gantt tools, cost estimation tools.
Editing and diagramming: text editors, UML and data-flow diagram editors.
Requirements management and change management: traceability tools, issue trackers.
Configuration management: version control and build systems (for example Git and Make).
Prototyping: very high-level languages and user interface generators.
Language processing and program analysis: compilers, static analysers, cross-reference generators.
Testing and debugging: test data generators, file comparators, interactive debuggers.
Documentation and re-engineering: document generators, restructuring and cross-reference tools.

concepts.text: The CASE Repository

The heart of an integrated CASE environment is the repository (also called the data dictionary or encyclopedia). It stores every artefact of the project: requirements, models, data definitions, code, test cases and documents, together with the relationships between them. Because all tools read and write the same repository, a change made in one diagram can be propagated to related diagrams, generated code and documentation, and consistency checks can be run across the whole project.
Integration levels in an I-CASE environment:
items: Data integration: tools share data through the common repository.
Presentation (user-interface) integration: tools share a common look and interaction style.
Control integration: one tool can start or notify another (for example a build triggering tests).
Process integration: the environment embeds knowledge of the process and guides users through its steps.

concepts.text: Tools, Workbenches and Environments

rows: Supports one process phase with a set of tools
Analysis and design workbench, programming IDE
Supports all or most of the process with integrated workbenches

concepts.text: Forward, Reverse and Round-Trip Engineering
CASE tools can move between models and code in both directions:
items: Forward engineering: generate code skeletons or database schemas from design models.
Reverse engineering: analyse existing source code to recover design information such as class diagrams, call graphs and data models.
Re-engineering: reverse engineer a legacy system, restructure or migrate it, then forward engineer the improved version.
Round-trip engineering: keep model and code synchronised so that edits in either are reflected in the other.

concepts.text: Benefits, Limitations and Productivity

rows: Faster, cheaper development of routine parts
Tools may impose a method that does not fit the team
Easier maintenance and reuse via the repository
Cannot fix poor requirements or bad design decisions

concepts.plainText: Productivity = KLOC / person-months

formulas.plainText: Productivity P = KLOC / person-months
Productivity gain (%) = (P_CASE - P_manual) / P_manual x 100
ROI (%) = (benefit - cost) / cost x 100

notes.text: Upper CASE = front end (requirements, analysis, design); lower CASE = back end (coding, testing, maintenance); I-CASE = whole life cycle through a shared repository. A debugger or test generator is lower CASE; a DFD or UML editor is upper CASE.
Reverse engineering recovers design from code without changing the code; re-engineering goes further and produces an improved system. Forward engineering is the normal model-to-code direction.
CASE tools support a method; they do not supply one. Automating a chaotic process only produces chaos faster, which is why CASE adoption usually follows process improvement.

concepts.text: What a Requirement Is

A requirement is a description of a service the system must provide or a constraint on its operation. Requirements range from abstract, high-level statements for customers to detailed, precise specifications that can serve as part of a contract. Sommerville distinguishes them in two ways: by level of detail (user vs system requirements) and by kind (functional, non-functional and domain requirements).
Functional vs Non-Functional

rows: WHAT the system does: services, reactions to inputs, behaviour
HOW WELL it does it: qualities and constraints
Usually a specific feature or function
Often applies to the system as a whole
The system shall let a student download the admit card
Pages shall load within 2 seconds for 1,000 concurrent users
The whole system may be unusable

concepts.text: Non-functional requirements are often more critical than individual functional ones: an aircraft control system that is not certified as reliable cannot be used at all. They also drive the architecture, because performance, security and availability goals decide how components are distributed and replicated. A single NFR such as a security requirement may generate several related functional requirements, for example a login function and an audit log.
Classification of Non-Functional Requirements

rows: Policies and procedures of customer or developer
Environmental, operational, development (for example must use a given language or process)
Factors outside the system and its development
Regulatory, ethical, legislative (accounting, safety, privacy laws)

concepts.text: Domain requirements come from the application domain rather than a specific user:
items: They reflect fundamental rules of the domain, for example a banking rule for interest calculation or a train-protection deceleration formula.
They may be new functional requirements, constraints on existing ones or specific computations.
Problem: they are written in domain language that software engineers may misunderstand, and domain experts may omit them because they seem obvious.

concepts.text: User vs System Requirements

rows: Structured language, models, tables, formal notation
Abstract statements of services and constraints
Detailed, precise description of functions, services and constraints
Basis for design; may form part of the contract

concepts.text: Problems with natural-language requirements and how to reduce them:
items: Lack of clarity, requirements confusion (functional and non-functional mixed) and requirements amalgamation (several requirements in one sentence).
Use a standard format, use "shall" for mandatory and "should" for desirable requirements, and highlight key terms.
Avoid jargon and give the rationale for each requirement; use structured or form-based templates for system requirements.

concepts.text: Interface Specification and Measurable NFRs

Most systems must work with existing systems, so the requirements must include precise interface specifications. Sommerville lists three types: procedural interfaces (APIs offered by existing programs or subsystems), data structures passed from one subsystem to another, and representations of data such as bit ordering or encoding. Formal notations or programming-language interface definitions are effective because they are precise.

rows: Transactions per second, user or event response time
Training time, number of help frames
MTTF, probability of unavailability, rate of failure occurrence (ROCOF)
Time to restart after failure, probability of data corruption on failure
Percentage of target-dependent statements, number of target systems

concepts.plainText: Downtime per year = (1 - A) x 8760 hours

formulas.plainText: Downtime = (1 - A) x 8760 hours per year
Throughput = transactions / time
POFOD = failed demands / total demands

notes.text: Test for an FR: can you describe it as an input and a response ("the system shall calculate...")? Anything about speed, security, reliability, usability, portability, law or company policy is an NFR ("PURPS": performance, usability, reliability, portability, security).
Vague NFRs such as "the system shall be user-friendly" cannot be tested. Rewrite them with a measurable metric, for example "trained users shall make no more than 2 errors per hour".

Legislative and regulatory requirements (privacy law, tax law, safety standards) are external NFRs; rules about the development language or process are organisational NFRs; response time and memory limits are product NFRs.

concepts.text: The Requirements Engineering Process

Requirements engineering (RE) is the process of finding out, analysing, documenting and checking the services and constraints of a system. Its main activities are the feasibility study, requirements elicitation and analysis, requirements specification and requirements validation, with requirements management running alongside throughout the project. In practice these activities are interleaved and iterated, often drawn as a spiral in which each round adds more detail.

rows: Can it be built with available technology and skills?
Do the benefits justify the cost (cost-benefit analysis)?
Does it violate any law, licence or regulation?
Will the organisation and its users actually use it?
Can it be delivered within the required time?

concepts.text: Elicitation and Analysis
Sommerville's elicitation and analysis cycle:
items: Requirements discovery: interacting with stakeholders to collect their requirements, including domain requirements.
Classification and organisation: grouping related requirements into coherent clusters.
Prioritisation and negotiation: resolving conflicts between stakeholders and ranking requirements (for example MoSCoW: must, should, could, won't).
Specification: documenting the requirements as input to the next round.

rows: Structured or free-form questioning of stakeholders
Analyst watches real work in context
Tacit, social and actual work practices
Facilitated group workshops with users and developers
Users try a mock-up and give feedback

concepts.text: Elicitation is hard because stakeholders often do not know what they want, express requirements in their own terms, have conflicting needs, and are influenced by organisational politics. Requirements also change during analysis as the business environment changes. Combining several techniques, for example interviews plus observation plus prototyping, gives a more complete picture than any one alone.
The Software Requirements Specification (SRS)

The SRS is the official statement of what the developers must implement and often serves as a contract between customer and developer. It should say what the system does, not how it is designed. IEEE Std 830-1998 is the classic template; it has been superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, which keeps essentially the same content.

rows: Purpose, scope, definitions and abbreviations, references, overview
Product perspective, product functions, user characteristics, constraints, assumptions and dependencies
External interfaces, functional requirements, performance, logical database, design constraints, software system attributes

concepts.text: IEEE 830 qualities of a good SRS:
items: Correct (every requirement is one the software must meet) and unambiguous (only one interpretation).
Complete (all significant requirements, responses to all inputs, labelled figures and defined terms) and consistent (no conflicting requirements).
Ranked for importance and/or stability, and verifiable (a cost-effective finite process can check each requirement).
Modifiable (structured so changes are easy and not duplicated) and traceable (origin of each requirement is clear and it can be referenced forward).

concepts.plainText: Specificity Q1 = n_ui / n_r

concepts.text: Validation and Management
Requirements validation checks that the requirements define the system the customer really wants:
items: Checks: validity (right functions), consistency (no conflicts), completeness (all functions and constraints), realism (achievable within budget and technology) and verifiability (testable).
Techniques: requirements reviews (systematic manual analysis), prototyping (executable model shown to users) and test-case generation (a requirement that cannot be tested is flawed).
Errors found here are far cheaper to fix than errors found after delivery.

concepts.text: Requirements management controls change to requirements throughout the project:
items: Enduring requirements are stable and tied to the core domain; volatile requirements change (mutable, emergent, consequential, compatibility).

Traceability: backward traceability links a requirement to its source (stakeholder, document); forward traceability links it to design, code and tests. The Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) records these links.

Change management: problem analysis and change specification, change analysis and costing (impact analysis using traceability), then change implementation, usually approved by a change control board (CCB).

formulas.plainText: Specificity Q1 = n_ui / n_r
Completeness Q2 = n_u / (n_i x n_s)
Requirements volatility (%) = changed / total x 100
Trace coverage (%) = traced / total x 100

notes.text: Remember the SRS qualities as CUCVM-T plus ranked: correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, verifiable, modifiable, traceable, ranked for importance/stability. "The system shall be fast" fails verifiability because no test can decide it.
Validation checks are validity, consistency, completeness, realism and verifiability. Realism means the requirement can be implemented with the available budget, schedule and technology.
An SRS should state what the system must do, not how it will be built. Design decisions inside an SRS over-constrain the developers and make the document harder to change.

Pressman's metrics: Q1 = n_ui/n_r is specificity (lack of ambiguity), where n_ui is the number of requirements every reviewer interpreted identically and n_r the total; Q2 = n_u/(n_i x n_s) is completeness of functional requirements, where n_u is unique function requirements, n_i inputs and n_s states.

concepts.text: Architectural Design and Its Decisions

Architectural design identifies the subsystems that make up a system and the framework for their control and communication. It is the first stage of design and the link between requirements engineering and detailed design. An explicit architecture helps stakeholder communication, allows early analysis of whether non-functional requirements can be met, and supports large-scale reuse because similar systems often share an architecture.
Typical architectural design decisions the architect must make:
items: Is there a generic application architecture or reference architecture that can be used as a template?
How will the system be distributed across processors or hosts?
Which architectural style or styles fit the system?
What approach will structure the system (organisation) and how will it be decomposed into modules?
What control strategy will coordinate the components?
How will the architecture be evaluated and documented?

rows: Localise critical operations, minimise communication, use large-grain components
Layered structure with the most critical assets in the innermost layers
Put safety-critical features in one or a small number of subsystems
Include redundant components and fault-tolerance mechanisms

concepts.text: System Organisation Styles
Three classic ways of organising subsystems:
items: Repository model: all subsystems share data held in a central database or repository (IDEs, CASE toolsets, DBMS-centred systems). Efficient for sharing large amounts of data and centralises backup and security, but every subsystem must agree on one data model and the repository is a single point of failure that is hard to distribute.

Client–server model: a set of stand-alone servers provides services (printing, files, database) to clients over a network. Easy to distribute and to add servers, but no shared data model and management of many servers is harder.

Layered (abstract machine) model: the system is organised into layers, each providing services to the layer directly above it (OSI network model, operating systems). Supports incremental development and portability, but performance may suffer and clean separation is sometimes hard.

concepts.plainText: Point-to-point interfaces among n subsystems = n(n-1)/2; via a central repository = n

concepts.text: Modular Decomposition Styles

After organisation, each subsystem is decomposed into modules. In object-oriented decomposition the system is a set of loosely coupled objects with well-defined interfaces that call each other's services; it maps well onto real-world entities, but objects must know each other's interfaces explicitly. In function-oriented pipelining (data-flow model) functional transformations process inputs to produce outputs, with data flowing from one transformation to the next.
Pipe-and-filter (function-oriented pipeline) characteristics:
items: Each filter transforms its input stream and passes the result through a pipe to the next filter; filters do not share state.
Classic examples: a compiler (lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis, code generation), Unix shell pipelines, batch invoice processing.
Advantages: supports reuse of transformations, intuitive, easy to add new transformations, can be sequential or concurrent.
Disadvantages: requires a common data-transfer format, poor for interactive or event-based systems.

concepts.text: Control Styles

rows: Top-down subroutine calls; control passes down and returns up
One component starts, stops and coordinates concurrent processes
Event broadcast to all; handlers that registered interest respond
Interrupts routed via a vector to handlers

concepts.text: Reference Architectures and Other Styles
Reference models and common architectural patterns:
items: Reference architectures are idealised architectures for a domain, used to compare and evaluate designs rather than to implement directly, e.g. the OSI seven-layer model and the ECMA CASE (toaster) reference model.
MVC: Model holds data and business rules, View presents data to the user, Controller handles user input and updates the model; allows several views of the same data.
Microkernel: a minimal core with plug-in services (operating systems, IDEs with plug-ins).
Blackboard: independent knowledge sources cooperate by reading and writing a shared blackboard, guided by a controller (speech recognition, AI).
Broker: an intermediary locates services and forwards requests between distributed components.

formulas.plainText: Point-to-point interfaces among n subsystems = n(n-1)/2; via a central repository = n
Pipeline latency = sum of filter times; throughput = 1 / slowest filter time

notes.text: Centralised control means call–return or manager; event-based control means broadcast or interrupt-driven. If a question mentions fast response to external events in a real-time system, the answer is interrupt-driven.
A compiler is the textbook example of pipe-and-filter (function-oriented pipelining), and an IDE or CASE toolset around a shared database is the textbook example of the repository model.

Repository and client–server are about system organisation, object-oriented versus pipeline is about modular decomposition, and call–return versus event-based is about control. MCQs often mix these categories in the options.

concepts.text: Distributed Systems and Their Trade-offs

A distributed system is one in which processing is spread over several computers connected by a network. Nearly all large systems are now distributed. Their advantages are resource sharing, openness (use of standard protocols and heterogeneous hardware), concurrency, scalability and fault tolerance. Their disadvantages are greater complexity, harder security, more difficult management and unpredictable response times caused by network load.
Main distributed architecture types covered in the syllabus:
items: Multiprocessor architectures: the system is a set of processes that may run on separate processors.
Client–server architectures: the system is a set of services provided by servers to clients (two-tier, three-tier, multi-tier).
Distributed object architectures: no distinction between clients and servers; objects anywhere on the network provide and use services through an object request broker.
Inter-organisational distributed computing: peer-to-peer and service-oriented architectures that cross organisational boundaries.

concepts.text: Multiprocessor Architecture

The simplest distributed model: the system consists of multiple processes that may execute on different processors, with process allocation either predetermined or controlled by a dispatcher. It is common in large real-time systems such as traffic control, where separate processors handle sensor data, the traffic-flow model and the light-control actuators. Performance gains are limited by the part of the work that cannot run in parallel.

concepts.plainText: Amdahl speedup S(N) = 1 / ((1 - p) + p/N), p = parallel fraction, N = processors

concepts.text: Client–Server Architectures

An application is modelled as three logical layers: presentation (user interface), application processing (business logic) and data management. Client–server architectures differ in how these layers are mapped onto physical tiers of computers.

rows: Simple to manage; heavy server and network load
Uses client power; harder to deploy updates
Separate application server and database server
Scalable; each tier can be scaled or replaced independently
Several application, integration and data tiers
Used by large web and enterprise systems

concepts.text: Thin clients suit legacy migration and centrally managed systems such as a web browser front end. Fat clients suit cases where the client hardware is powerful and processing is known in advance, such as an ATM network where the ATM performs processing and the central server manages the account database. Three-tier architecture, as in internet banking with a web server, application server and database server, avoids the scalability and update problems of both two-tier forms.

concepts.plainText: Availability of tiers in series = A1 x A2 x ... x Ak; of m replicas = 1 - (1 - A)^m

concepts.text: Distributed Objects, CORBA and Middleware
Distributed object architecture and the software that makes it work:
items: Objects are distributed over the network and communicate through a software bus called an Object Request Broker (ORB), which locates the target object, marshals parameters and returns results.

Advantages: designers can delay decisions about where services are provided, very open and scalable, objects can be added or moved dynamically. Disadvantage: more complex to design than client–server.

CORBA (Common Object Request Broker Architecture) from the Object Management Group standardises ORBs; interfaces are written in a language-neutral IDL (Interface Definition Language) and compiled to stubs and skeletons.
Other distributed object technologies include Java RMI and Microsoft DCOM/.NET remoting.

Middleware is the general term for software that sits between the operating system/network and the application, managing communication and data exchange (ORBs, message-oriented middleware, transaction monitors, RPC).

concepts.text: Inter-organisational Distributed Computing
Architectures for systems that span organisations:
items: Peer-to-peer (P2P): decentralised systems in which every node can act as client and server (file sharing such as BitTorrent, blockchains). Can be fully decentralised or semi-centralised with a server that helps peers find each other.
Service-oriented architecture (SOA): applications are built by composing loosely coupled, platform-independent services, typically web services.
Web service standards: SOAP for message exchange, WSDL for describing a service interface, and UDDI for service discovery; RESTful services use HTTP operations on resources.
Services can be offered by different organisations and composed into business processes (e.g. with BPEL).

formulas.plainText: Availability in series = A1 x A2 x ... x Ak; of m replicas = 1 - (1 - A)^m
Amdahl speedup S(N) = 1 / ((1 - p) + p/N)
Links in a fully connected P2P network of n peers = n(n-1)/2; n clients to one server = n

notes.text: Thin client means the client does only presentation; fat client means the client also does application processing. Three-tier separates presentation, application logic and data onto different tiers.
In a distributed object architecture there is no distinction between clients and servers: every object can both provide and request services via the ORB. That is the key contrast with client–server.
Components in series multiply their availabilities, so adding tiers lowers overall availability unless tiers are replicated. Do not add or average availability figures.

concepts.text: Real-Time Systems

A real-time system is one whose correct functioning depends both on the results it produces and on the time at which they are produced. Most real-time systems are embedded systems that monitor and control hardware in their environment through sensors and actuators. Timing is a functional requirement, not just a performance goal.

rows: Airbag controller, pacemaker, flight control, ABS brakes
Degraded performance or quality, system continues
Video streaming, online games, ticket booking
Late result is useless but occasional misses are tolerated

concepts.text: Stimulus/response model of real-time systems:
items: A stimulus is an event detected by a sensor; the system must respond to it within a specified time.
Periodic stimuli occur at predictable intervals, e.g. reading a temperature sensor every 50 ms.
Aperiodic stimuli occur irregularly and are usually signalled by interrupts, e.g. a power-failure or emergency-stop signal.
Architecturally, sensor control processes collect data, data-processing processes compute responses, and actuator control processes drive the actuators.

concepts.text: Real-Time Design and Operating Systems

Real-time design identifies the stimuli and required responses, defines timing constraints, aggregates stimulus and response processing into concurrent processes, designs the algorithms, designs a scheduling system that meets the deadlines, and integrates everything under a real-time operating system (RTOS). State machine models are widely used to specify real-time behaviour.
Components of a real-time operating system (Sommerville):
items: Real-time clock: provides information to schedule processes periodically.
Interrupt handler: manages aperiodic requests for service.
Scheduler: chooses the next process to run, usually by priority.
Resource manager: allocates memory and processor resources to the scheduled process.
Dispatcher: starts execution of the chosen process.
Larger RTOSs add configuration management and fault management for dynamic reconfiguration.

concepts.plainText: Rate-monotonic bound: U = sum(Ci/Ti) <= n(2^(1/n) - 1); tends to 0.693 as n grows

concepts.text: Generic real-time architectural patterns:
items: Monitoring (observe and react) systems: poll sensors, display and log readings, and raise alarms when values go out of range, e.g. burglar or fire alarm.
Control (environmental control) systems: read sensors and drive actuators to keep the environment at a set point, e.g. heating or car cruise control.

Data acquisition (process pipeline) systems: collect sensor data for later processing; a producer process writes into a circular (ring) buffer and a consumer process reads from it, with mutual exclusion, e.g. reactor flux monitoring.

concepts.text: Component-Based Software Engineering (CBSE)

CBSE builds systems by composing loosely coupled, independent, reusable software components. A component (Councill and Heineman) is a software element that conforms to a component model and can be independently deployed and composed without modification according to a composition standard. Szyperski describes it as a unit of composition with contractually specified interfaces and explicit context dependencies only.
Component characteristics, interfaces and models:
items: Characteristics: standardised, independent, composable, deployable and documented.
Provides interface: the services the component offers to other components (drawn as a lollipop in UML).
Requires interface: the services the component needs from other components in order to work (drawn as a socket).
Component models define standards for interfaces, usage (naming, metadata) and deployment, e.g. Enterprise JavaBeans, CORBA Component Model, Microsoft COM/.NET.
Middleware supporting a component model supplies platform services (communication, exception management) and support services (transactions, security, persistence, concurrency).

rows: Keep requirements flexible so available components can be used
Search repositories, select and validate components
Negotiate requirements to match the components that exist
Design a framework into which components fit
Integrate components, writing glue code and adaptors where needed
Components are called one after another by glue code; outputs of A feed B
One component directly calls the services of another; A's requires interface is met by B's provides interface
Interfaces of two components are put together to form a new component offering both

concepts.text: Composition can hit interface incompatibilities: parameter incompatibility (different types or number of parameters), operation incompatibility (different operation names) and operation incompleteness (one component offers only part of what another requires). Adaptor components resolve these. The main benefits of CBSE are reuse, lower cost and faster delivery; the risks are component trustworthiness, certification, emergent properties and trade-offs between requirements and available components.

formulas.plainText: Rate-monotonic bound: U = sum(Ci/Ti) <= n(2^(1/n) - 1)
Reuse level = reused size / total size x 100%
Reliability of a sequential composition = R1 x R2 x ... x Rk

notes.text: Hard real-time: a missed deadline is a system failure. Soft real-time: a missed deadline only degrades service. Periodic stimuli are time-driven; aperiodic stimuli are usually interrupt-driven.

Provides interface = what the component offers; requires interface = what it needs from its environment. In hierarchical composition, one component's requires interface is satisfied by another's provides interface.

Rate-monotonic analysis is a sufficient test only: if U exceeds n(2^(1/n) - 1) the task set may still be schedulable, but it is no longer guaranteed. Earliest-deadline-first can schedule any task set with U up to 1.

concepts.text: Test Case Design: Two Views

A test case specifies preconditions, input values, the expected output and postconditions. White-box (structural, glass-box) testing designs tests from the internal logic of the code and measures coverage of statements, branches or paths. Black-box (functional, behavioural) testing designs tests from the specification only and finds incorrect or missing functions, interface errors, errors in data structures or external database access, performance errors, and initialisation and termination errors. Grey-box testing combines partial knowledge of internals with specification-based tests.

rows: Every statement executed at least once
Weakest; can miss the false side of an if
Every decision takes both true and false outcomes
Every atomic condition takes true and false
Does not by itself guarantee branch coverage
Each condition shown to independently change the decision outcome
Every feasible path from entry to exit
Strongest; infinite when loops are unbounded

concepts.text: Basis Path Testing and Cyclomatic Complexity

McCabe's basis path testing draws a flow graph of the module (nodes = statements or decisions, edges = flow of control) and derives a basis set of linearly independent paths; an independent path introduces at least one new edge. Cyclomatic complexity V(G) equals the number of independent paths, so it is the upper bound on the number of tests needed to execute every statement and every branch at least once. McCabe recommended keeping V(G) at 10 or less per module; higher values correlate with more defects and harder testing.

concepts.plainText: V(G) = E - N + 2P = (number of predicate nodes) + 1 = number of regions

concepts.text:
int f(int x, int y) {
  int s = 0;              // n1
  while (x > 0) {         // n2  decision 1
    if (x % 2 == 0)       // n3  decision 2
      s += y;             // n4
    else if (y > 10)      // n5  decision 3
      s -= 1;             // n6
    x--;                  // n7
  }
  return s;               // n8
}
Worked example for the function above (one connected component, P = 1):
items: Edges: n1-n2, n2-n3, n2-n8, n3-n4, n3-n5, n4-n7, n5-n6, n5-n7, n6-n7, n7-n2, so E = 10 and N = 8.
Check with predicate nodes: n2, n3 and n5 are decisions, so V(G) = 3 + 1 = 4; the planar graph also has 3 enclosed regions + 1 outer region = 4.
Test data: x = 0 for path 1; x = 2 for path 2; x = 1, y = 20 for path 3; x = 1, y = 5 for path 4.

concepts.text: Black-Box Techniques
Main black-box test design techniques:
items: Equivalence partitioning: divide the input domain into classes expected to be processed the same way; one test per class (valid and invalid).
Boundary value analysis (BVA): errors cluster at edges, so test at min, just above min, a nominal value, just below max and max; robustness testing also adds min-1 and max+1.
Decision table testing: list combinations of conditions and the resulting actions; each rule (column) becomes a test case. n binary conditions give up to 2^n rules.
State transition testing: model states, events and transitions; test every valid transition and selected invalid ones (e.g. an ATM card blocked after 3 wrong PINs).
Use case testing: derive tests from main and alternative flows of each use case.
Cause-effect graphing, pairwise (all-pairs) testing and experience-based error guessing complement these.

rows: Test values for age valid in 18 to 60

concepts.text: Test Automation
Test automation uses tools to execute tests, compare actual with expected results and report outcomes:
items: Test pyramid: many fast unit tests at the base, fewer service/API tests in the middle, few slow end-to-end UI tests at the top.

Framework styles: linear record-and-playback, modular, data-driven (test data held in external CSV/Excel/DB files), keyword-driven (actions described by keywords in tables), hybrid, and behaviour-driven (Given-When-Then scenarios).
Unit frameworks: JUnit, TestNG, NUnit, pytest, Google Test. UI: Selenium WebDriver, Cypress, Playwright, Appium for mobile.
API and performance: Postman, REST Assured, JMeter, LoadRunner, Gatling. BDD: Cucumber, SpecFlow. Coverage: JaCoCo, gcov.
Automate stable, repetitive, high-value tests (regression, smoke, data-heavy, performance); keep exploratory, usability and one-off tests manual.
Automated suites run in CI servers such as Jenkins or GitHub Actions on every commit.

concepts.text: Metrics for Testing
Common test metrics and what they indicate:
items: Statement, branch and path coverage percentages: how much of the code the tests exercise.
Defect density = defects / KLOC (or per function point): compares quality across modules and releases.
Defect removal efficiency (DRE) = defects found before release / total defects: filtering power of reviews and testing.
Defect leakage: defects that escape from one test level to the next or to customers.
Test execution rate and pass rate, test cases per requirement, defect age and defect arrival rate over time.
Cyclomatic complexity and Halstead measures to estimate how much testing a module needs.

concepts.plainText: DRE = E / (E + D), E = errors found before delivery, D = defects found after delivery

formulas.plainText: V(G) = edges - nodes + 2 x components = predicate nodes + 1 = regions
Branch coverage = branch outcomes executed / total branch outcomes x 100%
Defect density = number of defects / size in KLOC
DRE = E / (E + D)

notes.text: V(G) = decisions + 1 counts binary decisions. A compound condition such as if (a && b) is two predicate nodes in the flow graph, so it adds 2, not 1. A switch with k cases adds k - 1.

100% statement coverage does not guarantee 100% branch coverage (an if without an else can be fully covered by one true test). 100% branch coverage does guarantee 100% statement coverage. Path coverage subsumes both.
BVA test counts for n independent variables: standard BVA 4n + 1, robustness 6n + 1, worst-case 5^n and robust worst-case 7^n. MCQs often test these counts.

concepts.text: Software Productivity and Size Measures

Cost estimation predicts effort (person-months), schedule (calendar months) and cost; effort is the dominant cost in software. Productivity is output per unit of effort, and output is measured either by size (lines of code, usually counted in KLOC excluding comments and blank lines) or by functionality (function points, introduced by Albrecht in 1979, or object/application points). Estimates made at the start of a project can be out by a factor of four either way, and they become more accurate as the project proceeds (the cone of uncertainty).
LOC versus function points:
items: LOC: easy to count after coding and used directly by COCOMO, but depends on language and programming style and is hard to estimate early.
LOC penalises well-designed short programs, and high-level languages appear less productive per line.
Function points: language-independent and can be estimated from the requirements, but counting is subjective and needs trained counters.
Backfiring converts FP to LOC using language tables (roughly 128 LOC per FP for C, about 53 for Java, as published by Jones; figures vary).

concepts.text: Estimation Techniques
Techniques listed by Sommerville and Pressman:
items: Expert judgement and (wideband) Delphi: several experts estimate independently and iterate until they converge.
Estimation by analogy: compare with completed projects in the same application domain.
Parkinson's law: the work expands to fill the time available, so cost is set by resources, not by the product.
Pricing to win: the cost is whatever the customer can afford; the specification is then constrained.
Decomposition: top-down from the overall system, or bottom-up by estimating each work breakdown structure (WBS) task and summing.
Algorithmic cost modelling: effort = A x Size^B x M, calibrated on historical data (COCOMO, Putnam SLIM).
Agile: story points estimated by planning poker, with duration derived from team velocity.

concepts.plainText: Three-point (PERT) estimate S = (optimistic + 4 x most likely + pessimistic) / 6

concepts.text: Function Point Analysis

Unadjusted function points (UFP) are the sum of each component count multiplied by its weight. Fourteen general system characteristics (data communications, distributed processing, performance, reuse, online update and others) are each rated 0 (no influence) to 5 (essential), so their sum lies between 0 and 70 and the value adjustment factor VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 x sum lies between 0.65 and 1.35. Example: 20 average EI, 15 average EO, 10 average EQ, 6 average ILF and 4 average EIF give UFP = 80 + 75 + 40 + 60 + 28 = 283; with a sum of 42 the VAF is 1.07 and FP = 283 x 1.07 = 302.8, about 303.
Basic COCOMO (Boehm, 1981)

rows: Small, experienced team, familiar in-house problem
Medium size, mixed experience, e.g. a DBMS or compiler
Tight hardware, regulatory or real-time constraints

concepts.plainText: E = a x KLOC^b person-months, D = c x E^d months, average staff = E / D

concepts.text: Worked example, 32 KLOC organic project: 32^1.05 = 38.05, so E = 2.4 x 38.05 = 91.3 person-months. Then 91.3^0.38 = 5.56, so D = 2.5 x 5.56 = 13.9 months. Average staffing = 91.3 / 13.9 = 6.6, about 7 people, and productivity = 32,000 / 91.3 = about 350 LOC per person-month. Because b > 1, effort grows faster than size (diseconomy of scale), and because d < 1, doubling effort does not double the schedule.
Intermediate, detailed COCOMO and COCOMO II:
items: Intermediate COCOMO: E = a x KLOC^b x EAF, where the effort adjustment factor is the product of 15 cost drivers (product, hardware, personnel and project attributes) rated very low to extra high; a = 3.2, 3.0, 2.8 for organic, semi-detached, embedded with the same exponents.
Detailed COCOMO applies phase-sensitive cost drivers to each lifecycle phase.

COCOMO II (2000) has submodels used as the project matures: application composition (object/application points, prototypes), early design (function points, 7 effort multipliers), reuse, and post-architecture (17 effort multipliers).

COCOMO II effort: PM = 2.94 x Size^E x product of EMs, with exponent E = 0.91 + 0.01 x sum of five scale factors (precedentedness, development flexibility, architecture/risk resolution, team cohesion, process maturity).

concepts.text: Duration, Staffing, Brooks' Law and Putnam
Planning schedule and team size:
items: Average staffing = effort / duration; staff is not constant but follows the Norden-Rayleigh curve: builds up, peaks near delivery, then tails off.
Putnam's SLIM software equation relates size L, effort K and delivery time td: L = Ck x K^(1/3) x td^(4/3), so K is proportional to 1 / td^4 and small schedule compression costs a lot of effort.
Schedule cannot usefully be compressed below about 75% of the nominal time (the impossible region).
Brooks' law: adding manpower to a late software project makes it later, because newcomers need training and communication paths grow as n(n - 1)/2.
Example: a team of 4 has 6 paths, a team of 8 has 28 paths, so doubling the team more than quadruples the communication overhead.

formulas.plainText: FP = UFP x (0.65 + 0.01 x sum of 14 Fi), each Fi rated 0 to 5
Productivity = KLOC (or FP) delivered / person-months of effort
Communication paths C = n(n - 1) / 2 for a team of n people
Putnam software equation: L = Ck x K^(1/3) x td^(4/3)

notes.text: Memorise the basic COCOMO constants: a = 2.4, 3.0, 3.6 and b = 1.05, 1.12, 1.20 for organic, semi-detached, embedded; c = 2.5 in all modes with d = 0.38, 0.35, 0.32. VAF always lies between 0.65 and 1.35.
Effort E is in person-months, duration D is in calendar months, and D is computed from E, not from KLOC. Dividing effort by duration gives average staff, not productivity.

Brooks' law comes from The Mythical Man-Month (1975). Its reasons are ramp-up time for new members, task partitioning limits (some tasks cannot be split) and the n(n - 1)/2 growth of communication overhead.

concepts.text: Quality and Quality Management

Pressman defines software quality as conformance to explicitly stated functional and performance requirements, explicitly documented development standards, and implicit characteristics expected of all professionally developed software. Quality management has three parts: quality assurance (defining processes and standards that lead to quality), quality planning (choosing the standards for a particular project) and quality control (checking that the team follows them). The cost of quality is made up of prevention costs, appraisal costs, internal failure costs (defects found before delivery) and external failure costs (defects found by customers), and the latter are by far the most expensive.
SQA group activities and the SQA plan:
items: Prepare an SQA plan for the project, identifying evaluations, audits and reviews, standards, error reporting procedures and documents to be produced.
Participate in writing the project's software process description and review it for compliance with organisational policy.
Review software engineering activities and audit designated work products to verify compliance with the defined process.
Ensure deviations in software work and work products are documented and handled; record non-compliance and report it to senior management.

IEEE 730 SQA plan outline: purpose and scope, reference documents, management, documentation, standards, practices and metrics, reviews and audits, testing, problem reporting and corrective action, tools and methods, code/media/supplier control, records, training and risk management.

concepts.text: Reviews: FTRs, Inspections and Walkthroughs

A formal technical review (FTR) is an SQA activity in which software engineers examine a work product to uncover errors in function, logic or implementation, verify it meets its requirements, and check it follows standards. Guidelines: 3 to 5 people, advance preparation of no more than 2 hours each, meeting under 2 hours, review the product and not the producer, set and keep an agenda, limit debate, point out problems but do not try to solve them, use checklists, and take written notes. The review ends with a decision to accept, reject, or accept provisionally, recorded in a review summary report and an issues list.

rows: Defined roles, checklists, entry/exit criteria, defect metrics collected
Peers check technical content against specifications and standards
Author presents step by step; reviewers ask questions; also used for training
Second developer reviews code as it is written
Author or one colleague reads the work product alone

concepts.text: Fagan inspection roles and phases:
items: Roles: moderator (plans and leads the meeting), author (producer of the work product), reader (paraphrases the material), recorder or scribe (logs defects), and inspectors.
Phases: planning, overview, individual preparation, inspection meeting, rework by the author, and follow-up by the moderator to verify fixes.
Inspections typically find a large share of defects before testing and are cheaper per defect than testing.

concepts.text: Formal and Statistical Approaches to SQA
Beyond reviews and testing, SQA can be made more rigorous:
items: Formal approaches: specify programs mathematically (Z, B, VDM) and prove correctness using preconditions, postconditions and loop invariants (Hoare logic), or verify models by model checking.
Cleanroom software engineering: box-structure specification, correctness verification instead of developer unit testing, and statistical usage testing to certify reliability.

Statistical SQA: collect and categorise information about defects, trace each defect to its underlying cause (incomplete specification, misinterpreted customer communication, logic error, etc.), apply the Pareto principle to isolate the vital few causes behind about 80% of defects, then correct those causes.

Six Sigma (Motorola): a quality level of 3.4 defects per million opportunities; DMAIC (define, measure, analyse, improve, control) for existing processes and DMADV (define, measure, analyse, design, verify) for new ones.

concepts.plainText: DPMO = defects x 1,000,000 / (units x opportunities per unit); Six Sigma = 3.4 DPMO

concepts.text: A Framework for Software Metrics
Key terms and classifications (Pressman, IEEE):
items: Measure: a quantitative indication of an attribute (e.g. number of errors). Measurement: the act of determining a measure. Metric: a quantitative measure of the degree to which a system or process has an attribute. Indicator: a metric or combination that gives insight for decisions.
Direct measures (LOC, effort, defects, execution speed) versus indirect measures (functionality, quality, complexity, reliability, maintainability).

Product metrics (size, complexity, design quality), process metrics (defect removal efficiency, defect arrival rates across the organisation) and project metrics (effort, schedule, cost for tactical control).
Goal-Question-Metric (GQM, Basili): define a measurement goal, derive questions that characterise it, then choose metrics that answer the questions.

Good metrics are simple and computable, empirically and intuitively persuasive, consistent and objective, consistent in units and dimensions, programming-language independent, and give actionable feedback.

rows: Function points; Davis specificity Q1 = nui / nr
Size; lack of ambiguity (requirements all reviewers interpreted identically / total requirements)
Card and Glass: S(i) = fout^2, D(i) = v(i)/(fout + 1), C(i) = S + D
Structural, data and system complexity of each module
Henry-Kafura: length x (fan-in x fan-out)^2; cyclomatic complexity
CK suite: WMC, DIT, NOC, CBO, RFC, LCOM
Class complexity, inheritance depth, coupling and cohesion
Halstead: N = N1 + N2, V = N log2 n
Program length and volume from operators and operands

concepts.text: ISO Standards and CMMI
ISO standards relevant to software quality:
items: ISO 9000: fundamentals and vocabulary of quality management. ISO 9001: requirements for a quality management system (QMS); the only certifiable standard in the family; generic to any organisation, based on the process approach, the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle and risk-based thinking.
ISO/IEC 90003: guidelines for applying ISO 9001 to software development and maintenance.

ISO/IEC 9126 (superseded by ISO/IEC 25010): product quality model; 25010 has eight characteristics: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability.
ISO/IEC 12207: software life cycle processes; ISO/IEC 15504 (SPICE), now ISO/IEC 33000: process assessment.

rows: Ad hoc, chaotic; success depends on individual heroics
Projects are planned, tracked and controlled (requirements management, project planning, configuration management)
An organisation-wide standard process, tailored for each project
Processes controlled using statistical and quantitative objectives
Continuous process improvement through causal analysis and innovation

formulas.plainText: Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) = MTTF / MTBF

formulas.latex: N = N_1 + N_2,\quad V = N \log_2 n,\quad n = n_1 + n_2
formulas.plainText: Halstead length N = N1 + N2, volume V = N x log2(n), vocabulary n = n1 + n2
DPMO = defects x 10^6 / (units x opportunities per unit)

notes.text: CMMI staged levels in order: Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimizing ("I Must Do Quality Optimization"). Level 4 is about statistical control; level 5 is about continuous improvement.

ISO 9001 certifies an organisation's quality management system, not the quality of a particular software product. Product quality characteristics come from ISO/IEC 9126 and its successor ISO/IEC 25010.

CMMI also has a continuous representation in which individual process areas are rated by capability level rather than the whole organisation by maturity level. Formality ordering of reviews: inspection > technical review > walkthrough > desk check.

concepts.text: What Configuration Management Does

Software configuration management (SCM) is the set of policies, processes and tools for managing a changing software system; it is an umbrella activity applied throughout the life cycle because change can happen at any time. Sommerville divides it into four activities: change management, version management, system building and release management. Pressman lists five SCM tasks: identification of configuration objects, version control, change control, configuration auditing, and status reporting (configuration status accounting).
Configuration Management Planning
A configuration management plan (see IEEE 828) defines:
items: Which items are managed (the configuration items) and the scheme for identifying and naming them.
Who is responsible for CM procedures and for submitting controlled items to the CM team.
Policies for change control and version management, including who may approve changes.
The CM records to be kept and the reports (status accounting) to be produced.
The CM tools to use, how to use them, and the structure of the CM database or repository.
Schedule of configuration audits and baselines at project milestones.

concepts.text: Configuration Items and Baselines

A software configuration item (SCI) is any work product placed under configuration control: the SRS, design models, source code, test plans, test cases and data, user manuals, executables, and even the versions of compilers and tools used to build them. A baseline is a specification or product that has been formally reviewed and agreed upon, that thereafter serves as the basis for further development, and that can be changed only through formal change control procedures (IEEE). Typical baselines are functional (requirements), allocated, design and product baselines. Before an item is baselined, changes are informal; afterwards, every change needs an approved change request. A codeline is a sequence of versions of a component, and the mainline is the sequence of baselines forming the main development line.
Change Management
The change control process for a baselined item:
items: A user or developer submits a change request (CR) on a change request form.
The request is checked for validity; duplicate or misunderstood requests are closed.
Change analysis estimates the impact on other SCIs, the effort and the cost.
The change control board (CCB) decides to approve, reject or defer the change based on cost, benefit, risk, number of users affected and release plans.
If approved, an engineering change order (ECO) is issued; the SCIs are checked out, modified, reviewed (SQA audit) and tested.
The modified SCIs are checked in, a new baseline is established, the requester is notified and the CR is closed.
Every step is recorded in a change tracking tool, giving a full derivation history.

concepts.text: The CCB may be one person for a small project or a group of managers, customer representatives and technical staff for a large one; the key is that it is a recognised authority independent of the individual developer. Access control decides who may check out an object for change, and synchronisation control (locking) stops two people from overwriting each other's parallel changes. Configuration audits and formal technical reviews confirm that the change was made correctly and that the SCM procedures were followed.
Version Management

rows: One master repository on a server
Every clone holds the full history
Commit, branch and view history offline
Any clone can restore the repository

concepts.text: Branching, merging and semantic versioning:
items: Branches let work proceed in parallel: feature branches, release branches and hotfix branches (as in GitFlow), or short-lived branches merged daily into the trunk (trunk-based development).
Merging combines branches; when both changed the same lines a merge conflict must be resolved manually.
Storage: older tools store the latest version plus reverse deltas (RCS, SVN), while Git stores compressed snapshots of every committed file.
Tags label an exact set of versions, e.g. the source used for a release, so it can be rebuilt later.

Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: increment MAJOR for incompatible API changes (reset MINOR and PATCH to 0), MINOR for backward-compatible features (reset PATCH), PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes.
Pre-release and build labels follow the core number, e.g. 2.0.0-beta.1 or 1.4.2+build.57; version 0.y.z signals initial development with no stability promise.

concepts.text: System Building and Release Management
System building creates a complete executable system by compiling and linking components, libraries and configuration files:
items: Build tools and scripts: make, Ant, Maven, Gradle, MSBuild, CMake; they record dependencies and recompile only changed files (minimal recompilation using timestamps or checksums).
Continuous integration servers (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) build and test on every commit; daily builds are followed by smoke tests.
Builds should be reproducible: the same tagged sources, libraries and tool versions give the same executable.
Sommerville distinguishes the development system, the build server and the target (execution) environment.

concepts.text: Release management prepares software for external release and keeps track of released versions:
items: A release is a version of the system distributed to customers; major releases add significant new functionality, minor releases repair bugs and fix reported problems.
A release contains executable code plus configuration files, data files, an installation program, electronic and paper documentation, and packaging.

Release timing depends on technical quality, platform changes, Lehman's fifth law (a large release tends to be followed by a smaller corrective one), competition, marketing and customer change proposals.
The exact versions of all source files, libraries, tools and OS used must be recorded so any release can be re-created.

rows: Change request workflow, CCB decisions, traceability
Dependency analysis and automated compilation and linking
Automatic build, test and deployment on each commit
Combined version, change and build management

formulas.plainText: Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: 2.4.7 -> 2.4.8 (fix), 2.5.0 (feature), 3.0.0 (breaking)
Change failure rate = changes causing failure in production / total changes deployed x 100%

notes.text: When a semantic version field is incremented, every field to its right resets to 0: a new backward-compatible feature on 1.9.3 gives 1.10.0, and a breaking change on 1.10.0 gives 2.0.0.

Once an SCI is baselined it may not be changed informally; changes go through a change request, impact analysis and CCB approval. A version is any instance of an item; a release is a version actually distributed to customers.

Pressman's five SCM tasks (identification, version control, change control, configuration audit, status reporting) and Sommerville's four activities (change management, version management, system building, release management) describe the same discipline from two angles.

concepts.text: The Requirement Process

Requirements are the capabilities and conditions to which the system, and more broadly the project, must conform. In an iterative OO process such as the UP, requirements are not frozen up front: they are discovered and refined across iterations through elicitation, analysis, specification, validation and management of change. The main UP requirements artefacts are the use-case model (functional requirements as stories), the supplementary specification (non-functional requirements), the glossary (terms and data definitions), the vision (high-level goals) and business rules.
FURPS+ categorises the requirements to be captured:
items: Functional: features, capabilities, security.
Usability: human factors, help, documentation.
Reliability: frequency of failure, recoverability, predictability.
Performance: response times, throughput, accuracy, availability, resource usage.
Supportability: adaptability, maintainability, internationalisation, configurability.
The '+' covers implementation constraints, interface, operations, packaging and legal requirements.

concepts.text: Use Cases and Actors

A use case is a collection of related success and failure scenarios that describe an actor using the system to achieve a goal; a scenario (use case instance) is one specific sequence of actions and interactions. Use cases are text documents first; the use case diagram is only a context summary. The basic components of use case modelling are the actor, the use case and the system boundary. Good use cases pass the boss test, the elementary business process (EBP) test (one person, one place, one time, measurable business value) and the size test (usually several steps, not a single step).

rows: Has user goals fulfilled by using the system
Provides a service to the system
Has an interest in the behaviour but does not interact directly

concepts.text: Use Case Formats and Sections

rows: Terse one-paragraph summary, usually the main success scenario
All steps and variations with supporting sections
Important, high-risk use cases in elaboration

concepts.text: Sections of a fully dressed use case (Cockburn/Larman template):
items: Use case name (starts with a verb, e.g. Process Sale), scope (system under design), level (user-goal or subfunction), primary actor.
Stakeholders and interests: whose interests the behaviour must satisfy.
Preconditions: what must be true on start and is not tested in the use case; success guarantee (postconditions): what must be true on successful completion.
Main success scenario (basic flow, happy path): the typical unconditional path to the goal, written as numbered steps.
Extensions (alternate flows): all other success and failure branches, labelled against the step they branch from, e.g. 3a, *a.
Special requirements, technology and data variations, frequency of occurrence and open issues.

concepts.text:
Use Case UC1: Process Sale   Primary actor: Cashier
Main success scenario:
 1. Customer arrives at POS checkout with goods.
 2. Cashier starts a new sale.
 3. Cashier enters item identifier.
 4. System records sale line item and presents description, price, running total.
    Cashier repeats steps 3-4 until done.
 5. System presents total with taxes calculated.
 6. Customer pays and System handles payment.
Extensions:
 3a. Invalid identifier: System signals error and rejects entry.
Use Case Relationships and Diagrams

rows: Base use case always (mandatorily) uses shared behaviour of another
Dashed arrow from base to included use case
Extension adds optional behaviour at an extension point of the base, under a condition
Dashed arrow from extending use case to base
Child use case or actor specialises a parent
Solid line with hollow triangle towards parent
Actor participates in (communicates with) a use case
Solid line between actor and use case

concepts.text: A use case diagram shows the system boundary as a rectangle, use cases as ovals inside it and actors (stick figures, or boxes stereotyped «actor» for systems) outside it. Primary actors are conventionally placed on the left and supporting actors on the right. The diagram is a context overview; the real value of use case modelling lies in the written scenarios, which drive design, testing and the user manual.
Estimating from Use Cases: Use Case Points

concepts.plainText: UCP = (UUCW + UAW) x TCF x ECF

concepts.text: Karner's use case points weights:
items: Use case weight (UUCW): simple (≤ 3 transactions) = 5, average (4–7) = 10, complex (> 7) = 15.
Actor weight (UAW): simple (another system via API) = 1, average (system via protocol or text interface) = 2, complex (human via GUI) = 3.
Technical complexity factor TCF = 0.6 + 0.01 × TFactor (13 weighted technical factors).
Environmental factor ECF = 1.4 − 0.03 × EFactor (8 weighted team and environment factors).

formulas.plainText: UCP = (UUCW + UAW) x TCF x ECF
TCF = 0.6 + 0.01 x TFactor
ECF = 1.4 - 0.03 x EFactor

notes.text: «include» = mandatory, arrow from base to included; «extend» = optional and conditional, arrow from the extending use case back to the base. The arrow direction is a common MCQ trap.
Use cases are primarily text. A use case diagram without written scenarios captures almost none of the functional requirements.
Preconditions are assumed true and not checked within the use case; the success guarantee is what must hold after success. Do not swap them.

concepts.text: The Unified Modeling Language

The Unified Modeling Language (UML) is a standard visual language for specifying, constructing, visualising and documenting the artefacts of software systems. It was created by the Three Amigos, Grady Booch (Booch method), James Rumbaugh (OMT) and Ivar Jacobson (OOSE and use cases), and was adopted as a standard by the Object Management Group (OMG) in 1997. UML is a notation, not a process: it can be used with the UP, agile methods or any other process. It can be applied as a sketch, as a blueprint or as a programming language (model-driven development).

rows: Class, Object, Component, Deployment, Package, Composite structure, Profile
What the system is made of

concepts.plainText: 14 UML 2.5 diagrams = 7 structural + 7 behavioural

concepts.text: What each commonly tested diagram shows:
items: Class diagram: classes, attributes, operations and relationships; object diagram: a snapshot of instances and links at one moment.
Component diagram: modular replaceable parts and their interfaces; deployment diagram: physical nodes and the artefacts deployed on them; package diagram: grouping and dependencies.
Sequence diagram: interactions ordered in time along lifelines; communication (collaboration) diagram: the same messages numbered on a network of linked objects, emphasising relationships.
State machine diagram: states and event-triggered transitions of one object; activity diagram: flowchart-like workflow with actions, decisions, forks, joins and swimlanes.
Timing diagram: state changes against a time axis; interaction overview: an activity diagram whose nodes are interactions.

concepts.text: The Domain (Conceptual) Model

A domain model is a visual representation of conceptual classes or real-situation objects in a domain, drawn as a UML class diagram with no operations. It shows conceptual classes, associations between them and their attributes. It is the most important artefact of OO analysis: it builds a shared vocabulary and inspires the names of software classes in the design model, lowering the representational gap between how we think of the domain and how the code is structured. It is built iteratively, usually for the use cases chosen in the current iteration.
A domain model does NOT show:
items: Software artefacts such as windows, databases, controllers or DAO classes (unless the domain itself is software).
Responsibilities or methods: operations belong to design class diagrams.
Foreign-key style attributes: relationships are shown as associations, not as ID fields.

concepts.text: A conceptual class is an idea, thing or object in the domain. Larman describes it by its symbol (the words or image representing it), its intension (its definition) and its extension (the set of examples to which it applies). For example, Sale has the symbol 'Sale', the intension 'a purchase transaction event with a date and time' and an extension of all the sales that occur.
Identifying Conceptual Classes
Three strategies for finding conceptual classes:
items: Reuse or modify existing models: published domain and analysis patterns for common domains such as inventory, finance or health.

Use a category list: business transactions (Sale, Payment), transaction line items (SalesLineItem), products or services (Item), where transactions are recorded (Register, Ledger), roles of people (Cashier, Customer), places (Store), events, physical objects, descriptions of things (ProductDescription), catalogues, containers, other collaborating systems, records of finance and contracts.

Noun phrase identification (linguistic analysis): underline nouns and noun phrases in fully dressed use cases as candidates, then filter them, because natural language is ambiguous and some nouns are attributes or synonyms.

rows: Thought of as a number (Money data type)
Report of information already in Sale; include only if it has its own rules, e.g. returns
Synonyms: keep a single name in the glossary

concepts.text: Description Classes and Domain vs Design Model

A description class contains information that describes something else, such as ProductDescription (price, description, itemID) describing many physical Item instances. It is needed when deleting instances of the described things would lose information (if all items are sold, the price is still known), when there are groups of items or services that share the same description, and to reduce redundant or duplicated information. FlightDescription describing many Flight occurrences is another classic example.

rows: Visibility markers, typed attributes and navigability

formulas.plainText: 14 UML 2.5 diagrams = 7 structural + 7 behavioural
Conceptual class = symbol + intension + extension
A_max = n(n - 1)/2 possible binary associations among n conceptual classes

notes.text: Structural diagrams answer 'what is it made of' (class, object, component, deployment, package, composite structure, profile); everything else, including use case, is behavioural. Sequence, communication, timing and interaction overview are the interaction diagrams.
A domain model is not a picture of software objects and not a data model: no methods, no UI or database classes, and no foreign-key attributes.
When in doubt whether to include a candidate conceptual class, include it: in domain modelling it is better to over-specify with many fine-grained classes than to under-specify.

concepts.text: Adding Associations

An association is a relationship between classes (more precisely, between their instances) that indicates a meaningful and interesting connection. In a domain model, include associations for which knowledge of the relationship must be preserved for some duration (need-to-know associations) and those suggested by the common associations list, such as A is a transaction related to B, A is a line item of B, A is recorded in B, A is a member of B or A uses or manages B. Too many associations add visual noise, so avoid redundant or derivable ones.
Association notation and naming:
items: Drawn as a solid line between classes, named with a verb phrase in the ClassName-VerbPhrase-ClassName pattern, e.g. Sale Paid-by Payment, Register Records Sale.
An optional reading-direction arrow (small triangle) shows how to read the name; it says nothing about navigability.
Role names at each end describe the part an object plays, e.g. Person employee / employer Company.
Multiple associations between the same two classes are allowed, e.g. Flight Flies-to Airport and Flight Flies-from Airport.
A reflexive association links a class to itself, e.g. Employee manages Employee.

rows: A Team has 5..11 Players on the field list

concepts.latex: L_{min} = N \times lower,\quad L_{max} = N \times upper
concepts.plainText: L_min = N x lower bound, L_max = N x upper bound (links from N source objects)

rows: Weak whole-part (has-a); parts can exist independently and be shared
Strong whole-part; part belongs to one whole and is destroyed with it
is-a; subclass inherits from superclass (100% rule and is-a rule)
Solid line, hollow triangle at superclass
Dashed arrow to the used element

concepts.text: Adding Attributes

An attribute is a logical data value of an object, included when the requirements imply a need to remember the information, e.g. Sale needs dateTime. Attributes in a domain model should be simple data types such as Boolean, Date, Number, String, Time, or value-type data types such as Money, Address, Quantity or UPC. The key rule is: if we do not think of a concept as a number or text in the real world, it is probably a conceptual class, not an attribute; for example, a flight's destination is an Airport class, not a string.
