Derived attributes, computable from others, are prefixed with a slash, e.g. /total.

Do not use attributes to relate conceptual classes (e.g. a cashierID attribute on Register); show the relationship as an association. Foreign keys are a database design concern, not a domain modelling one.
System Sequence Diagrams and System Events

A system sequence diagram (SSD) shows, for one particular scenario of a use case, the events that external actors generate, their order and any inter-system events, treating the system as a black box. Each system event triggers a system operation, such as makeNewSale(), enterItem(itemID, quantity), endSale() and makePayment(amount) in Process Sale. SSDs are derived from use case text and give the system operations for which operation contracts are written and designs are created. Events should be named at the level of intent (enterItem) rather than the input mechanism (scan).

Cashier                     :System
   | makeNewSale()             |
   |-------------------------->|
   | loop [more items]         |
   | enterItem(itemID, qty)    |
   |-------------------------->|
   |<-- description, total ----|
   | endSale()                 |
   |-------------------------->|
   |<-- total with taxes ------|
   | makePayment(amount)       |
   |-------------------------->|
   |<-- change due, receipt ---|
Operation Contracts, State Machines and Activity Diagrams
An operation contract describes the effect of a system operation on domain objects, in sections:
items: Operation: name and parameters, e.g. enterItem(itemID: ItemID, quantity: integer); Cross references: related use cases.
Preconditions: noteworthy assumptions about the state of the system before the operation, e.g. there is an underway sale.

Postconditions: the state of domain objects after the operation, written declaratively in the past tense, in three categories: instance creation and deletion, attribute modification, and associations formed and broken.
Example: a SalesLineItem instance sli was created; sli was associated with the current Sale; sli.quantity became quantity; sli was associated with a ProductDescription based on itemID.

concepts.text: A UML state machine diagram shows the life cycle of one object or system: its states, the events that trigger transitions, guard conditions and actions, drawn as event [guard] / action on each transition, with a filled circle as the initial pseudo-state. It suits state-dependent objects such as a phone line, an order or a use case's legal sequence of system events. An activity diagram models workflows and business processes with actions, decisions and merges (diamonds), forks and joins (bars) for concurrency, and swimlanes (partitions) showing who performs each action.

formulas.latex: L_{min} = N \times lower,\quad L_{max} = N \times upper
formulas.plainText: L_min = N x lower bound, L_max = N x upper bound
Links in a many-to-many association between A and B <= |A| x |B|

notes.text: Operation contract postconditions describe changes to domain objects only: instances created or deleted, attributes modified, associations formed or broken. They never describe UI output or messages sent.
An SSD is drawn for one scenario, treats the system as a black box and shows only system events crossing the boundary; interactions between internal objects belong to design sequence diagrams.
Composition implies exclusive ownership and lifetime dependency (filled diamond); aggregation does not (hollow diamond). If a part can be shared or outlive the whole, it is not composition.

concepts.text: What Interaction Diagrams Show

Interaction diagrams model how a group of objects collaborate by exchanging messages to carry out one behaviour, typically one system operation or one use-case scenario. UML 2 has two main forms: the sequence diagram, which emphasises the time ordering of messages, and the communication diagram (called the collaboration diagram in UML 1.x), which emphasises the links between objects. Both are semantically equivalent for simple interactions and are the main tool for assigning responsibilities during design.
Sequence Diagram Elements
Basic notation of a UML sequence diagram:
items: Lifeline: a participant box at the top, written name : Class (e.g. s : Sale or :Register), with a vertical dashed line running down the page; time flows top to bottom.
Activation bar (execution specification): a thin rectangle on the lifeline showing the period during which the object is executing an operation.
Found message: the first message whose sender is not shown, drawn from a filled dot or the diagram edge.
Self message: an arrow looping back to the same lifeline, often with a nested activation bar.
Object creation: a message labelled create (or <<create>>) pointing at the participant box, which is drawn lower down where it comes into existence.
Object destruction: a large X at the end of the lifeline, usually after a <<destroy>> message.

rows: Sender waits until the receiver finishes
Returns control or a value to the caller
Dashed or solid line to the object box, <<create>>
Arrow to or from a filled dot

concepts.text: The full syntax of a message label is return = message(parameter : Type) : ReturnType, for example total = getTotal() : Money. Guards written in square brackets, such as [qty > 0], make a message conditional. A replicated message sent to each element of a collection is shown by iterating over a multiobject or by placing the message inside a loop fragment.
Combined Fragments

rows: Alternative: exactly one operand whose guard is true runs (if-else)
Optional: the single operand runs only if its guard is true (if without else)
Repeat the operand while the guard holds or for min..max times
Operands run in parallel, interleaving allowed
Send email and update stock concurrently
Exit enclosing fragment / atomic region / invalid trace

concepts.text:
:Register           :Sale              :Payment
    |  makePayment(cash) |                  |
    |------------------->|                  |
    |                    | create(cash)     |
    |                    |----------------->|
    |                    |<- - - - - - - - -|
    |<- - - - - - - - - -|                  |
 alt [cash >= total]  : issue change
     [else]           : reject payment
Communication (Collaboration) Diagrams

A communication diagram draws the participating objects as boxes anywhere on the page, joined by links (instances of associations or other visibility). Messages are written as arrows alongside the links, each with a sequence number that fixes the order because there is no time axis. Iteration is shown with an asterisk, e.g. 1*: [i = 1..n] li = next(), and conditions with a guard, e.g. 2 [isComplete]: print().
Sequence numbering rules in communication diagrams:
items: The first (found) message is often left unnumbered; messages it causes are numbered 1, 2, 3 in order.
Nested (Dewey decimal) numbering shows calls made while handling another message: 1 calls 1.1 and 1.2; 1.1 calls 1.1.1.
Mutually exclusive conditional paths use letters: 1a [test]: msg() and 1b [not test]: other().
Concurrent threads can be marked with letter suffixes on the thread, e.g. A1 and B1.

concepts.latex: \text{Nesting depth} = \text{number of dots in the sequence number} + 1
concepts.plainText: Nesting depth of message = number of dots in its sequence number + 1 (1.2.3 is depth 3)

concepts.text: Sequence vs Communication Diagram

rows: Grows to the right with each new object
Compact; objects can be placed anywhere
Easy to read call order, fragments, activations
Shows which objects must have visibility of each other
Harder to follow order in long interactions

concepts.latex: \text{Messages for a synchronous call shown with reply} = 2
concepts.plainText: A synchronous call drawn with its reply uses 2 arrows: the call and the dashed return

formulas.latex: \text{Nesting depth} = \text{number of dots in the sequence number} + 1
formulas.plainText: Nesting depth of message = number of dots in its sequence number + 1 (1.2.3 is depth 3)

formulas.latex: \text{Messages for a synchronous call shown with reply} = 2
formulas.plainText: A synchronous call drawn with its reply uses 2 arrows: the call and the dashed return
Maximum links among n objects in a communication diagram = n(n - 1) / 2

notes.text: Remember the fragment operators by programming analogues: alt = if-else, opt = if with no else, loop = while/for, par = concurrent threads, ref = function call to another diagram.
A filled arrowhead on a solid line is a synchronous call; an open arrowhead on a solid line is asynchronous; a dashed line with an open arrowhead is a reply. MCQs often swap these.
UML 1.x called it a collaboration diagram; UML 2 renamed it the communication diagram. The syllabus uses the older name, but both refer to the same link-and-numbered-message diagram.

concepts.text: Responsibility-Driven Design

Responsibility-driven design (RDD) views a software object as a member of a community that has responsibilities, meaning obligations or contracts it must fulfil, and that collaborates with others to meet them. Design becomes the act of deciding which class should take each responsibility, which is done while drawing interaction diagrams. A responsibility is not the same as a method: a large responsibility may be carried out by many methods across several classes.
Larman's two kinds of responsibility:
items: Doing responsibilities: doing something itself (creating an object, calculating a total), initiating action in other objects, and controlling or coordinating activities of other objects.
Knowing responsibilities: knowing about its own private encapsulated data, knowing about related objects, and knowing about things it can derive or calculate.
Example: a Sale is responsible for knowing its total (knowing) and for creating SalesLineItems (doing).

concepts.text: GRASP: General Responsibility Assignment Software Patterns

rows: Who should do a job needing some data?
The class that has the information needed
Who should create an instance of A?
B if B contains, aggregates, records, closely uses or has init data for A
Who first handles a system event from the UI?
A facade (whole system) or use-case controller object
How to reduce impact of change?
Assign responsibilities so dependencies stay low
How to keep objects focused and manageable?
Keep each class's responsibilities strongly related
How to handle behaviour that varies by type?
Give the varying behaviour to the types via polymorphic operations
Where to put a job no domain class fits?
Invent a convenience class, e.g. PersistentStorage

concepts.text: The remaining two GRASP patterns:
items: Indirection: assign the responsibility to an intermediate object that mediates between components so they are not directly coupled (e.g. an adapter to a tax calculator).
Protected Variations: identify points of predicted variation or instability and wrap them behind a stable interface, so changes do not ripple through the system.
Low Coupling and High Cohesion are evaluative patterns used to judge the other seven choices.

concepts.text: Gang of Four Design Patterns

Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides (the Gang of Four) catalogued 23 design patterns in 1994. A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem in a context, described by its name, problem, solution and consequences. The patterns are grouped by purpose into creational (object creation), structural (composition of classes and objects) and behavioural (algorithms and assignment of responsibility among interacting objects).

concepts.plainText: 23 GoF patterns = 5 creational + 7 structural + 11 behavioural

rows: Ensure a class has one instance with a global access point
Let subclasses decide the class to create / create families of related objects
Construct complex objects step by step / clone a prototype
Convert one interface into another / give one simple interface to a subsystem
Tree of part-whole objects / add duties dynamically / surrogate controlling access
Notify dependents of state change / interchangeable algorithms
Request as object / sequential access / algorithm skeleton with overridable steps

concepts.text: GoF and GRASP are related: Adapter and Facade are applications of Indirection and Protected Variations, Strategy relies on Polymorphism, and a Factory class is a Pure Fabrication that keeps creation logic out of domain classes. Patterns are also classified by scope: class patterns use inheritance and are fixed at compile time (Factory Method, class Adapter, Template Method), while object patterns use composition and can change at run time.

concepts.plainText: Possible coupling pairs among n classes <= n(n - 1) / 2

formulas.plainText: 23 GoF patterns = 5 creational + 7 structural + 11 behavioural
GRASP = 9 patterns: Expert, Creator, Controller, Low Coupling, High Cohesion, Polymorphism, Pure Fabrication, Indirection, Protected Variations
Possible coupling pairs among n classes <= n(n - 1) / 2

notes.text: Creational = how objects are made (Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype). Structural = how they are assembled (Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy). Everything else, such as Observer, Strategy, Command, Iterator, Template Method and State, is behavioural.

Controller in GRASP is not the UI window: it is a non-UI object in the domain layer that receives system events from the UI and delegates work. A bloated controller that does everything itself violates High Cohesion.
Decorator and Proxy both wrap an object with the same interface; Decorator adds behaviour, Proxy controls access (remote, virtual/lazy, protection). Adapter wraps to change the interface.

concepts.text: Why Visibility Matters

For object A to send a message to object B, B must be visible to A: A must hold some kind of reference or pointer to B. When interaction diagrams are drawn, every message arrow implies a visibility requirement, and the designer must decide how that reference is obtained. Larman identifies four ways that object B can be visible to object A.

rows: B is an attribute (field) of A
Relatively permanent, lasts as long as A and B exist
B is passed as a parameter to a method of A
B is a local variable in a method of A (created or returned by a call)
B is globally accessible, e.g. a Singleton or global variable
Relatively permanent while the program runs

concepts.text: Visibility in practice:
items: Attribute visibility is the most common in OO design and is what an association arrow in a DCD usually implies.
Parameter visibility is often converted to attribute visibility, e.g. a constructor parameter stored in a field.
Local visibility arises from assigning a returned object to a local variable, e.g. ProductDescription desc = catalog.getDescription(id).
Global visibility is the least desirable; the preferred way to achieve it is the Singleton pattern rather than a raw global variable.

concepts.text: Design Class Diagram vs Domain Model

rows: Method signatures with parameters and return types

concepts.text: DCD Notation
Elements drawn in a design class diagram:
items: Class box with three compartments: name, attributes, operations. Abstract classes and methods are shown in italics or with {abstract}.
Attribute syntax: visibility name : type [multiplicity] = default {property}, e.g. - total : Money.
Operation syntax: visibility name(parameter : Type, ...) : ReturnType, e.g. + makeLineItem(desc : ProductDescription, qty : Integer). Static members are underlined.
Visibility markers: + public, - private, # protected, ~ package.
Multiplicity on association ends: 1 exactly one, 0..1 zero or one, * or 0..* zero or more, 1..* one or more, m..n a range.

concepts.text: Navigability is shown by an open arrowhead on an association line pointing from the class that holds the reference to the class it references, e.g. Register to Sale, meaning Register has an attribute of type Sale. Navigability is derived from interaction diagrams: if A sends a message to B and needs lasting visibility, draw A to B. Associations without arrows in a DCD are ambiguous and are best avoided.
Other relationships in a DCD:
items: Dependency: dashed line with open arrowhead, for parameter, local or global visibility or other non-attribute use, optionally with a stereotype such as <<use>> or <<create>>.
Generalisation: solid line with a hollow triangle pointing to the superclass.
Interface realisation: dashed line with a hollow triangle to the interface, or the lollipop (ball) notation; a required interface uses the socket notation.
Interfaces are drawn as a class box with the <<interface>> stereotype and only operation signatures.

concepts.plainText: Weighted methods per class WMC = sum of complexities c_i of its n methods (c_i = 1 gives the method count)

concepts.latex: \text{Links in a 1..* to 1..* association} \le m \times n
concepts.plainText: Links between m objects of A and n objects of B in a many-to-many association <= m × n

formulas.plainText: Weighted methods per class WMC = sum of complexities c_i of its n methods (c_i = 1 gives the method count)

formulas.latex: \text{Links in a 1..* to 1..* association} \le m \times n
formulas.plainText: Links between m objects of A and n objects of B in a many-to-many association <= m × n
Visibility of B to A is one of: attribute, parameter, local, global

notes.text: Attribute and global visibility are relatively permanent; parameter and local visibility are temporary, lasting only for the scope of one method call.
Do not confuse UML visibility markers (+ - # ~, about access to a member) with Larman's visibility types (attribute, parameter, local, global, about how one object can reference another).
A navigable association arrow in a DCD normally means attribute visibility; parameter, local and global visibility are shown with dashed dependency arrows instead.

concepts.text: Creating Class Definitions from DCDs

A design class diagram lists each software class with its attributes, operation signatures, associations with navigability, and generalisation or realisation links. Writing the class definition is direct: declare the class, copy each simple attribute as an instance variable with its type and visibility, add reference attributes for navigable associations, and declare each operation as a method signature. Visibility markers map one-to-one: + public, - private, # protected, ~ package.
Kinds of attributes that appear in the generated class:
items: Simple attributes: primitive or data-type values shown in the attribute compartment (e.g. quantity : Integer becomes private int quantity).
Reference attributes: fields that refer to another complex object, implied by a navigable association rather than listed in the compartment (e.g. SalesLineItem has a reference to ProductDescription).
Role names: the name at the association end is used as the name of the reference attribute (e.g. 'description').
Derived attributes (/total) are usually implemented as methods (getTotal()) instead of stored fields.

concepts.text: Multiplicity and Collection Classes

A one-to-many association (multiplicity * or 1..*) at the target end is implemented with a collection object: the source class holds a List, Set or Map of target objects. The choice depends on access: List (ArrayList) for ordered, index-based sequences such as the line items of a Sale; Map (HashMap) for lookup by key such as a ProductCatalog keyed by itemID; Set when duplicates are forbidden. It is good practice to declare the attribute by its interface type (List, Map) and instantiate a concrete class (ArrayList, HashMap).
Creating Methods from Interaction Diagrams
Sequence or communication (collaboration) diagrams give the method bodies:
items: The message received by an object becomes a method of the receiver's class; its parameters become the method's parameters.
Each message that object then sends (in sequence-number order 1, 2, 2.1 ...) becomes a statement in that method body.
A create message (or «create») becomes a constructor call with new; its parameters define the constructor's parameters.
A message sent to a multiobject or collection (e.g. lineItems.add) maps to a call on the collection object.
Conditional or loop frames (alt, opt, loop) become if/else and for/while statements.

concepts.text:
Communication diagram for enterItem(id, qty) on Register:
  1: desc := getProductDescription(id)  -> ProductCatalog
  2: makeLineItem(desc, qty)             -> Sale
  2.1: create(desc, qty)                 -> SalesLineItem
  2.2: add(sli)                          -> lineItems : List
Updating Class Definitions, Inheritance and Interfaces

As each interaction diagram is coded, class definitions are updated: new methods discovered in later diagrams are added, parameters change, and helper attributes appear. Generalisation (hollow-triangle solid line) maps to extends in Java or public inheritance in C++; interface realisation (hollow-triangle dashed line) maps to implements in Java or to a class deriving from an abstract base with pure virtual functions in C++. Abstract classes in italics map to abstract classes, and polymorphic operations are overridden in subclasses.

concepts.plainText: WMC = sum of complexities c_i of the n methods of a class

formulas.plainText: WMC = c_1 + c_2 + ... + c_n (weighted methods per class)
DIT(root) = 0, DIT(child) = DIT(parent) + 1
multiplicity * => collection holding 0..n references

notes.text: Reference attributes are not written in the DCD attribute compartment; they are implied by navigable associations and named after the role name at the far end.
A create message in an interaction diagram maps to a constructor; the parameters of create(desc, qty) become the parameters of the SalesLineItem constructor.
Do not confuse the arrows: solid line with hollow triangle = generalisation (extends); dashed line with hollow triangle = realisation (implements); dashed open arrow = dependency.

concepts.text: Errors, Faults and Exceptions

An exception is an abnormal event during execution that disrupts the normal flow of a program, such as a missing file, a failed network call or an invalid argument. Exception handling separates error-handling code from normal logic: the code that detects a problem throws an exception object, and code higher up that knows how to recover catches it. In Java all throwable objects derive from Throwable, which has two branches: Error, for serious JVM or system problems (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) that applications normally should not catch, and Exception, for conditions a program can reasonably handle.

rows: Not caught; let the program terminate
Must catch or declare with throws
Fix the programming bug; validate inputs

concepts.text: try, catch, finally, throw and throws
The Java keywords (C++ has try, catch and throw but no finally):
items: try: encloses code that may throw an exception.
catch (Type e): handles an exception of that type or a subtype; several catch blocks are tried top to bottom, so more specific types must come before general ones.
finally: runs whether or not an exception occurred (even after return), used to release resources such as files, locks and connections.
throw: statement that raises an exception object, e.g. throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty < 0").
throws: clause in a method signature declaring the checked exceptions the method may pass to its caller.
try-with-resources (Java 7+) closes AutoCloseable resources automatically; C++ achieves the same with RAII destructors.

concepts.text: Custom Exceptions and Propagation

Applications define their own exception classes to express domain failures, for example InsufficientFundsException or ProductNotFoundException. Extending Exception makes a checked exception; extending RuntimeException makes an unchecked one. If a method does not catch an exception, it propagates up the call stack to the caller, then the caller's caller, until a matching catch is found; if none exists, the thread terminates and the stack trace is printed. Exception chaining (passing the original cause to the new exception's constructor) preserves the low-level detail when converting to a higher-level exception.
Exceptions in UML and Design
Design models record exceptions too, so that implementers know what to throw and catch:
items: In a class diagram an exception is modelled as a class, often with the stereotype «exception» or «signal»; operations may list the exceptions they raise.
In UML 2 an exception is a kind of signal; sequence diagrams can show it as an asynchronous message, and activity diagrams show exception handlers and interruptible regions.
Larman's operation contracts and use-case extensions (alternative flows such as 'invalid item ID') identify the exceptional conditions each system operation must handle.
Error handling is a cross-cutting design decision: decide where exceptions are caught (typically near the UI or controller layer) and how they are logged and reported.

concepts.text: Defensive Programming and Error-Handling Patterns
Good practice for robust code:
items: Validate inputs and preconditions at public method boundaries (guard clauses) and fail fast with a clear exception.
Use assertions to check internal invariants during development; do not use them for user-input validation.
Never swallow exceptions with an empty catch block; at least log and rethrow or translate.
Catch specific exceptions rather than Exception or Throwable, and release resources in finally or try-with-resources.
Patterns: convert low-level exceptions to higher-level ones (exception translation), centralised error logging, retry with limits, and Null Object or Optional instead of returning null.

concepts.plainText: Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) = MTTF / MTBF

formulas.plainText: Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR)
V(G) = number of decisions (if, loops, catch clauses) + 1
Throwable has two subclasses: Error and Exception; RuntimeException is a subclass of Exception

notes.text: Checked = compiler forces catch or throws (IOException, SQLException). Unchecked = RuntimeException and its subclasses plus Error (NullPointerException, ArithmeticException).
throw raises an exception inside a method body; throws declares exceptions in a method signature. Catch blocks must list subclasses before superclasses, otherwise Java reports unreachable code.
finally runs even if the try block executes return; it is skipped only if the JVM exits (System.exit) or the thread is killed.

concepts.text: How to use this sheet

Software engineering and OOAD questions test a compact set of orderings, model names, notation symbols and a handful of metrics. The tables below collect them in syllabus order, from process models to exception handling. Use this sheet for last-minute revision; each entry is explained with examples in its own subtopic.
1. Process models and requirements

rows: each dev phase paired with a test level
deliver or refine the system in slices

concepts.text: Requirements in one glance:
items: Functional requirements say what the system does; non-functional requirements constrain how well (performance, security, usability, reliability).
NFR classes (Sommerville): product, organisational and external requirements.
RE process: feasibility study → elicitation and analysis → specification (SRS) → validation, with requirements management throughout.
Good SRS (IEEE 830): correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked, verifiable, modifiable and traceable.
Verification: are we building the product right? Validation: are we building the right product?

concepts.text: 2. Design

rows: data, stamp, control, external, common, content
functional, sequential, communicational, procedural, temporal, logical, coincidental

concepts.text: Architecture and control styles:
items: Organisation styles: repository (shared data), client–server, layered, pipe-and-filter, MVC, broker, peer-to-peer.
Centralised control: call–return (top-down subroutines) or manager model (one process coordinates others).
Event-based control: broadcast (events sent to all subscribed components) or interrupt-driven (handlers for real-time events).
Client–server tiers: two-tier thin client (logic on server) vs fat client (logic on client); three-tier separates presentation, application and data.
CBSE: components expose provides and requires interfaces and are composed sequentially, hierarchically or additively.

concepts.text: 3. Testing, cost and quality

rows: at developer site vs at user site

concepts.plainText: Cyclomatic complexity: edges − nodes + 2 × components = decision points + 1
Basic COCOMO: effort in person-months, duration in months, average staff

concepts.text: Configuration management:
items: A baseline is a formally reviewed work product that changes only through change control.
Change requests are assessed by a change control board (CCB) for cost, impact and priority.
Version management tracks versions and branches; semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH bumps MAJOR for incompatible changes.
Release management packages executables, data, documentation and installation instructions for customers.

concepts.text: 4. Object-oriented analysis and design
Larman's OOAD path:
items: Use cases (brief, casual, fully dressed) → domain model (conceptual classes, associations, attributes) → system sequence diagrams and operation contracts.
Design: interaction diagrams assign responsibilities using GRASP; design class diagrams add methods, navigability and visibility.
GRASP: information expert, creator, controller, low coupling, high cohesion, polymorphism, pure fabrication, indirection, protected variations.
Visibility from A to B: attribute, parameter, local or global.
Implementation: map DCD attributes to fields, multiplicity * to collections, create messages to constructors; code least-coupled classes first.

rows: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype
Adapter, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Bridge, Flyweight
Observer, Strategy, Command, Iterator, Template Method, State

concepts.text: Exceptions:
items: try holds risky code, catch handles a matching exception, finally always runs, throw raises and throws declares.
Java checked exceptions (IOException) must be caught or declared; unchecked ones (RuntimeException subclasses) need not be.
An uncaught exception propagates up the call stack until a matching handler is found or the program ends.

formulas.plainText: Cyclomatic complexity
Basic COCOMO effort and duration
Function points with value adjustment factor
Defect removal efficiency
Communication paths among n people (Brooks' law)
Availability

notes.text: Numeric questions here are mostly: cyclomatic complexity from a flow graph, COCOMO effort and duration, function points, DRE, availability, communication paths and boundary-value test counts. Write the formula first, then substitute.

Easy swaps: aggregation (hollow) vs composition (filled) diamond; <<include>> (always runs) vs <<extend>> (conditional); verification vs validation; alpha (developer site) vs beta (user site); stub (replaces a called module) vs driver (calls the module under test).
Orderings are frequent MCQ material: coupling data → content, cohesion functional → coincidental, and CMMI Initial → Managed → Defined → Quantitatively Managed → Optimizing.

concepts.text: What Software Is

Software is the set of programs, data structures and documentation that together make a computer do useful work. Software engineering is the disciplined, quantifiable application of engineering principles to the development, operation and maintenance of software (IEEE definition). Because software is a logical rather than a physical product, it behaves very differently from hardware, and those differences explain why it needs its own engineering discipline.
Classic characteristics of software (Pressman):
items: Software is developed or engineered, not manufactured: the cost is in design and development, and making copies costs almost nothing.
Software does not wear out: it has no physical parts that degrade, but it deteriorates because every change can introduce new defects.
Most software is still custom-built, although component-based reuse (libraries, frameworks, services) is increasing.
Software is complex, intangible (cannot be seen or touched), malleable (easy to change, hence easy to damage) and conforms to arbitrary human rules rather than physical laws.

concepts.text: Failure Curves: Wear Out vs Deterioration

rows: Bathtub: infant mortality, flat useful life, wear-out
Idealised: high early failures then flat; actual curve has spikes
Side effects of changes made during maintenance
No spare parts; every defect is a design error to fix
Failure rate rises at end of life
Minimum failure rate slowly rises with each change

concepts.text: The Software Crisis

In the 1960s, growing hardware power allowed far larger programs than informal methods could handle. Projects ran over budget and schedule, delivered unreliable code that did not meet user needs, and were very hard to maintain. The 1968 NATO conference at Garmisch popularised the term software engineering as the response to this software crisis. Many of the same symptoms still appear today when process, requirements and quality are neglected.
McCall's Quality Factors (1977)

rows: How easy is it to change?
How easy is it to move or reuse?

concepts.text: The syllabus list "CRISP MURTI" defines ten attributes:
items: Correctness: the software satisfies its specification and the user's objectives.
Reliability: it performs its intended function without failure over time; Integrity: it resists unauthorised access or modification.
Efficiency: it uses minimum CPU time, memory and other resources; Usability: effort needed to learn, operate and interpret it.
Maintainability: effort to locate and fix defects; Portability: effort to move it to another platform.
Reusability: parts can be used in other applications; Interoperability: effort to couple it with other systems; Testability: effort to test that it performs its function.

concepts.text: ISO/IEC 9126 and ISO/IEC 25010

ISO/IEC 9126 (1991) defined six quality characteristics: functionality, reliability, usability, efficiency, maintainability and portability. It was replaced by ISO/IEC 25010:2011 (the SQuaRE series), whose product quality model has eight characteristics: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability. Security and compatibility became top-level characteristics, and 25010 also defines a separate quality-in-use model (effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction, freedom from risk, context coverage).

concepts.plainText: Availability A = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) = MTTF / MTBF

concepts.text: Legacy Software and Evolution
Legacy systems are older systems still critical to the business; they must evolve because:
items: Adaptive maintenance: the environment changes (new OS, hardware, database or regulations).
Perfective maintenance: users request new features or better performance.
Corrective maintenance: defects discovered in use must be fixed; Preventive maintenance: code is restructured to ease future change.
Maintenance usually consumes the majority of total lifetime cost, commonly quoted as 60 to 80 percent.

concepts.text: Lehman's laws of software evolution describe what happens to programs embedded in the real world (E-type systems). Continuing change says such a system must be continually adapted or it becomes progressively less useful. Increasing complexity says that as a system evolves its structure degrades unless work is done to reduce it. Other laws cover continuing growth of functionality and declining quality unless the system is rigorously maintained.

formulas.plainText: MTBF = MTTF + MTTR
Availability (%) = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) x 100
R(t) = e^(-lambda t), lambda = 1 / MTTF
Defect density = defects / KLOC

notes.text: "Software doesn't wear out, it deteriorates" is the favourite characteristic. The actual software failure curve rises in spikes because each maintenance change introduces new defects; hardware follows a bathtub curve.

McCall has 11 factors in 3 perspectives (operation 5, revision 3, transition 3). ISO 9126 has 6 characteristics; ISO/IEC 25010:2011 has 8. The 2023 revision of 25010 adds safety, so always check which edition a question names.

Reliability and availability are different: reliability is the probability of failure-free operation over time, while availability is the fraction of time the system is usable. A system that fails often but recovers instantly can have high availability and low reliability.

concepts.text: The Software Design Process

Software design is the activity that turns the requirements specification into a description of the structure of the software, the data it uses, the interfaces between its parts and, sometimes, the algorithms used. Design is iterative: the designer adds detail and corrects earlier decisions as understanding improves. The output is the blueprint from which the system is implemented and against which it is later maintained.
Sommerville's classic design activities, performed with feedback between them:
items: Architectural design: identify the subsystems that make up the system and their relationships.
Abstract specification: specify the services each subsystem offers and the constraints under which it operates.
Interface design: design the interface of each subsystem to other subsystems, unambiguously enough to be used without knowing its internals.
Component design: allocate services to components and design their interfaces.
Data structure design: design the data structures used in the implementation.
Algorithm design: design the algorithms that provide the services.

rows: Major structural elements and their relationships
How software talks to users, other systems and devices
Internal algorithms and data of each component
Allocation of software to computing nodes

concepts.text: Fundamental Design Concepts
Concepts that guide every good design:
items: Abstraction: concentrate on essential properties and suppress detail. Procedural abstraction names a sequence of instructions with a specific function (e.g. open door); data abstraction names a collection of data describing an object (e.g. door with its attributes).
Modularity: divide software into separately named and addressable components (modules) that are integrated to satisfy requirements; it makes a large program intellectually manageable.
Information hiding (Parnas, 1972): each module hides its design decisions (data structures, algorithms) from all others and exposes only what is needed through its interface, so changes stay local.

Stepwise refinement (Wirth, 1971): a top-down strategy in which a high-level statement of function is decomposed step by step into more detailed statements until programming-language statements are reached. Abstraction and refinement are complementary.
Functional independence: each module addresses one specific subset of requirements and has a simple interface; measured by cohesion and coupling.
Other Pressman concepts: separation of concerns, architecture, patterns, refactoring (restructuring without changing external behaviour), aspects and design classes.

concepts.text: Modularity has an optimum. As the number of modules grows, the cost of developing each module falls because each is smaller, but the cost of integrating the modules (interfaces) rises. Total cost is lowest in a middle region, so a design should be neither one huge monolith nor thousands of trivial fragments.
Structure Charts, Fan-in and Fan-out

In a structure chart (a tree of modules showing who calls whom), fan-out of a module is the number of modules it directly calls or controls, and fan-in is the number of modules that directly call it. High fan-in indicates good reuse of a utility module. Very high fan-out suggests a module doing too much coordination and is a sign that an intermediate level of control is missing. Depth is the number of levels of control and width is the overall span of the tree.

concepts.plainText: Henry-Kafura information flow complexity = length x (fan-in x fan-out)^2

concepts.text: Design heuristics for effective modularity (Pressman/Yourdon):
items: Evaluate the first iteration of the program structure to reduce coupling and improve cohesion, exploding or imploding modules as needed.
Attempt to minimise structures with high fan-out; strive for fan-in as depth increases (an oval or mosque-shaped structure rather than a pancake).
Keep the scope of effect of a module within its scope of control.
Evaluate module interfaces to reduce complexity and redundancy and improve consistency.
Define modules whose function is predictable, and avoid modules that are overly restrictive.
Strive for controlled-entry modules and avoid pathological connections (branches or references into the middle of another module).

concepts.text: Coupling and Cohesion

rows: A whole data structure is passed but only part is used
Passing an entire employee record to get the name
One module passes a flag that steers the other's logic
print(report, mode) where mode selects behaviour
Modules share an externally imposed format, protocol or device
Two modules both writing a fixed file format
Several functions updating a global variable
One module modifies or jumps into another's internals
Directly altering another module's local data
Elements of the module are grouped because
All contribute to one single well-defined task
Output of one element is the input of the next
They operate on the same input or output data
They follow a fixed order of execution
They run at the same time (e.g. initialisation, shutdown)
They are logically similar and one is selected by a flag

concepts.text: The golden rule is low coupling with high cohesion. Low coupling limits the ripple effect of a change and makes modules easier to understand, test and replace. High cohesion means a module does one thing well, which also tends to reduce coupling. Information hiding and encapsulation in object-oriented design are the main techniques for achieving both.

formulas.plainText: Coupling best to worst: Data > Stamp > Control > External > Common > Content
Cohesion best to worst: Functional > Sequential > Communicational > Procedural > Temporal > Logical > Coincidental
Henry-Kafura information flow complexity = length x (fan-in x fan-out)^2

notes.text: Memorise both ladders in order. Coupling runs Data, Stamp, Control, External, Common, Content (best to worst); cohesion runs Functional, Sequential, Communicational, Procedural, Temporal, Logical, Coincidental (best to worst). MCQs often give a scenario and ask which type it is.

Do not confuse temporal cohesion (grouped because executed at the same time, such as an init routine) with procedural cohesion (grouped because executed in a fixed sequence of steps). Similarly, logical cohesion uses a selector flag inside the module, while control coupling is about passing such a flag between modules.

Information hiding was proposed by David Parnas; stepwise refinement by Niklaus Wirth. Abstraction and refinement are complementary: abstraction suppresses detail, refinement reveals it level by level.

concepts.text: Why and Where Testing Fits

Testing is the process of executing a program with the intent of finding errors (Myers). As Dijkstra observed, testing can show the presence of defects but never their absence. Testing is one part of verification and validation (V&V). Verification asks "Are we building the product right?" and checks that each work product conforms to its specification, mostly through reviews, inspections and static analysis. Validation asks "Are we building the right product?" and checks that the finished software meets the customer's real needs, mostly through system and acceptance testing.
Widely quoted testing principles:
items: Exhaustive testing is impossible, so tests are chosen by risk and by systematic design techniques.
Early testing (shift-left): defects found in requirements and design are far cheaper to fix than defects found in operation.
Defect clustering: a small number of modules usually contain most of the defects (Pareto 80/20).
Pesticide paradox: repeating the same tests stops finding new bugs, so test suites must be reviewed and extended.
Testing is context dependent, and the absence of failures does not prove the system is useful (absence-of-errors fallacy).
Every test should be traceable to a customer requirement.

rows: A single function, method or class
A composite component through its interface
The system in the user's environment

concepts.text: Unit and Component Testing

Unit testing exercises one module in isolation. Pressman lists what it should examine: the module interface, local data structures, boundary conditions, all independent paths and all error-handling paths. Because a unit is not a standalone program, a driver (a main program that calls the unit and passes test data) and stubs (dummy subprograms that replace modules the unit calls) are written. Frameworks such as JUnit, NUnit and pytest, and mock objects, make this cheap and repeatable.
Component (interface) testing, as described by Sommerville, focuses on the interfaces between the objects in a composite component:
items: Interface types: parameter interfaces, shared-memory interfaces, procedural interfaces and message-passing interfaces.
Interface misuse: a caller passes parameters in the wrong order, of the wrong type or of the wrong number.
Interface misunderstanding: a caller makes wrong assumptions about the behaviour of the called component (e.g. calls binary search on an unsorted array).
Timing errors: producer and consumer run at different speeds in real-time or shared-memory systems and read out-of-date data.

Guidelines: test parameter values at the extremes of their ranges, pass null pointers, design tests that make the component fail, stress-test message passing, and vary the activation order of components sharing memory.

concepts.text: Integration Strategies

rows: All modules combined at once and tested as a whole
Simple to organise, but failures are very hard to localise
Start at the main control module and move down, depth-first or breadth-first
Early working skeleton and demo; low-level processing tested late
Start with atomic modules, combine them into clusters, move up
Low-level modules tested early; no complete program until the last module is added
Top-down for upper layers and bottom-up for lower layers, meeting at a target layer
Parallel testing of both ends; more scaffolding cost

concepts.text: Incremental strategies (top-down, bottom-up, sandwich) add one module or cluster at a time, so a new failure is almost certainly caused by the newly added piece. Each time a module is added, previously passed tests are rerun (regression testing). Many teams practise continuous integration, where every commit triggers an automated build and test run, and smoke testing, where each daily build is checked broadly for show-stopper errors before deeper testing begins.
System, Acceptance and Regression Testing
System testing checks the whole integrated system against the SRS, including non-functional requirements:
items: Functional testing: every specified function behaves as required.
Performance testing: response time and throughput; load testing at the expected peak, stress testing beyond the designed limits until the system breaks, volume testing with large data sets.
Security testing: the system resists improper penetration and protects data.
Recovery testing: the software is forced to fail and must recover correctly within a specified time.
Usability, compatibility, configuration and installation testing.
Release testing (Sommerville): a separate team tests a version intended for release, usually black-box, to convince the supplier it is good enough.

concepts.text: Acceptance testing decides whether the customer accepts the system:
items: User acceptance testing (UAT): end users confirm the system supports their business tasks.
Alpha testing: done by users or internal staff at the developer's site in a controlled environment, with developers watching and recording problems.
Beta testing: done by real users at their own sites without developers present; users report problems back to the developer.
Contract and regulatory acceptance testing: checks against contract acceptance criteria or legal and safety regulations.
Operational acceptance testing: backup, restore, maintenance and administration tasks work.

concepts.text: Regression testing reruns a subset of already passed tests after any change (bug fix, enhancement, new module) to make sure nothing that used to work has broken. Retesting (confirmation testing) reruns the specific test that failed to confirm the fix. Smoke testing is a broad, shallow check that a new build is stable enough to test at all, while sanity testing is a narrow, quick check of one changed area. Automated regression suites are the main reason teams invest in test automation.

concepts.plainText: DRE_i = E_i / (E_i + E_(i+1)), E_i = errors found in phase i, E_(i+1) = errors from phase i found later

formulas.plainText: Phase DRE = errors found in phase i / (errors found in phase i + errors from phase i found in phase i+1)
Requirements coverage = requirements with at least one test / total requirements x 100%

notes.text: Top-down integration needs stubs (lower modules are missing); bottom-up integration needs drivers (higher modules are missing); sandwich needs both; big bang needs neither. Alpha = developer's site with developers present; beta = customer's site without developers.

In the V-model each test level is planned against a development phase: unit testing against detailed design, integration testing against architectural design, system testing against the SRS, and acceptance testing against user requirements.

Do not swap the V&V definitions: verification = building the product right (conformance to specification, often static), validation = building the right product (meets user needs, dynamic). Regression testing is about re-checking old functionality after a change, not about testing the fix itself.

concepts.text: Objects and Classes

Object-oriented (OO) development models a system as a collection of cooperating objects rather than as a hierarchy of functions. An object is a concrete entity with state (the current values of its attributes), behaviour (the operations it can perform) and identity (what distinguishes it from every other object, even one with identical state). A class is the template or blueprint that describes the attributes and operations shared by a set of objects; each object is an instance of exactly one class. Objects collaborate by message passing: one object asks another to execute one of its operations, possibly passing arguments and receiving a result.

concepts.plainText: Object = State + Behaviour + Identity

concepts.text: The Four Pillars (APIE)
The four pillars of OOP, remembered as APIE:
items: Abstraction: hiding complexity by exposing only the essential features of an entity relevant to the problem, e.g. a Car class exposing start() and brake() but not fuel-injection timing.

Polymorphism: one interface, many forms. Compile-time (static) polymorphism is method overloading (same name, different parameter lists, resolved by the compiler); run-time (dynamic) polymorphism is method overriding (subclass redefines an inherited method, resolved by dynamic binding through a base-class reference).
Inheritance: a child (sub) class reuses and extends the attributes and operations of a parent (super) class, forming an is-a hierarchy; it supports reuse and generalisation-specialisation.
Encapsulation: bundling data and the methods that operate on it into one unit while restricting direct access to the data (private fields, public methods); it realises Parnas' information hiding.

concepts.text: Other core OO concepts that MCQs test:
items: Message passing: the only way objects interact; a message names the receiver, the operation and the arguments.
Abstract class: cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract (unimplemented) operations; an interface declares operations only and is realised by classes.
Multiple inheritance: a class with more than one parent (allowed in C++, avoided in Java which uses multiple interfaces instead); can cause the diamond problem.

Relationships between classes: association (general link), aggregation (weak has-a, hollow diamond, parts exist independently), composition (strong has-a, filled diamond, parts destroyed with the whole), generalisation (is-a).

concepts.text: Defining Models: Rumbaugh's OMT

A model is an abstraction of a system built to understand it before building it; it omits non-essential detail. Rumbaugh's Object Modeling Technique (OMT), one of the three methods merged into UML, describes a system with three complementary models. Each model captures one view, and together they describe what the system is, when things happen and how values are computed.

rows: Static structure: objects, classes, attributes, operations, relationships
Temporal and control aspects: events, states, sequences of operations
Data value transformations: what is computed from what

concepts.text: Object-Oriented Development Cycle and the Unified Process

The OO development cycle proceeds from object-oriented analysis (OOA: find and describe the concepts in the problem domain), through object-oriented design (OOD: define software objects and how they collaborate), to object-oriented programming (OOP: implement the design classes in an OO language), followed by testing. The Unified Process (UP, commercially RUP) organises this work as an iterative, incremental, use-case-driven, architecture-centric and risk-focused process. Each iteration is a short time-boxed mini-project (typically 2–6 weeks) that produces a tested, integrated, executable partial system.

rows: Vision, business case, scope, rough estimates; go/no-go decision
Refine vision, build and stabilise core architecture, resolve high risks, find most requirements
Iteratively implement remaining lower-risk, easier elements; prepare for deployment
Beta tests, deployment to users, training, fixes

concepts.text: UP disciplines (workflows) run across all phases with varying intensity:
items: Business modeling (domain model), Requirements (use-case model, supplementary specification), Analysis and design (design model), Implementation, Test and Deployment.
Supporting disciplines: configuration and change management, project management and environment.
Inception is not the requirements phase: in the UP most requirements are discovered during elaboration iterations.
Superimposing waterfall on UP (all requirements first, then all design) is a classic misunderstanding that MCQs often probe.

concepts.latex: WMC = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i,\qquad DIT(C) = \text{depth of } C \text{ from root}
concepts.plainText: WMC = sum of complexities c_i of the n methods of a class; DIT(C) = depth of class C in the inheritance tree (root = 0)

formulas.plainText: Object = State + Behaviour + Identity
WMC (weighted methods per class) = c_1 + c_2 + ... + c_n
