formulas.plainText: DIT(C) = number of edges from the root to C; NOC(C) = number of immediate subclasses of C

notes.text: Overloading = compile-time = static binding; overriding = run-time = dynamic binding and needs inheritance. Encapsulation is about bundling and access control; abstraction is about showing only essential features.
UP phase order is Inception, Elaboration, Construction, Transition (I-E-C-T). The architecture is baselined at the end of Elaboration, and each phase contains one or more iterations.
Do not confuse OMT's functional model (DFDs, value computations) with the dynamic model (state diagrams, control over time). The object model is the static one.

concepts.text: Moving from Analysis to Design

Object-oriented analysis (OOA) asks what the problem is: it identifies the concepts of the domain, the requirements and the behaviour the system must show at its boundary. Object-oriented design (OOD) asks how software objects will collaborate to meet those requirements: it assigns responsibilities to classes, decides message flows and fixes the attributes, methods and visibility of each class. In the Unified Process the two activities are iterative, so each iteration takes a few use cases from analysis through design to tested code rather than finishing all analysis first.

rows: How will software objects do it?
Use cases, domain model, SSDs, operation contracts
Interaction diagrams, design class diagrams, package/layer diagrams
Software classes with methods and types
Takes language, frameworks and platform into account

concepts.text: Describing Use Cases

A use case is a text story of an actor using the system to achieve a goal, such as Process Sale or Withdraw Cash. Larman distinguishes three levels of detail: brief (one paragraph for the main success scenario), casual (several informal paragraphs covering variations) and fully dressed (a structured template with every step and alternative). A use case diagram only summarises the names of use cases and actors; the real requirement lives in the text.
Sections of a fully dressed use case template:
items: Use case name, scope (system under design) and level (user-goal or subfunction).
Primary actor, plus stakeholders and their interests.
Preconditions (what must be true before) and success guarantee or postconditions (what is true after).
Main success scenario: numbered steps of the typical 'happy path'.
Extensions (alternate flows): numbered against the step they branch from, e.g. 3a, 7b.
Special requirements (non-functional), technology and data variations, frequency of occurrence, open issues.

concepts.text: Essential vs Real Use Cases

An essential use case is written in an abstract, technology-free style that records only the actor's intention and the system's responsibility, e.g. 'Cashier identifies item; System records item'. A real (concrete) use case describes the process in terms of a specific design and user interface, e.g. 'Cashier scans barcode with laser scanner; System shows price in window A'. Essential use cases belong to early requirements work because they keep design options open; real use cases appear later, when UI and hardware decisions have been taken.
Elaborating Use Cases into Design
Larman's path from a use case to design objects:
items: System sequence diagram (SSD): for one scenario, shows the external actor, the system as a single black-box lifeline and the system events (e.g. enterItem(itemID, qty), endSale(), makePayment(amount)).
System operations: each input system event becomes a system operation that the design must handle.
Operation contracts: for complex operations, state preconditions and postconditions in terms of domain objects (instance created/deleted, attribute modified, association formed/broken).
Interaction diagrams: design how objects inside the system collaborate to satisfy each system operation, applying GRASP.
Design class diagram: summarise the classes, attributes, methods and associations discovered in the interaction diagrams.

concepts.latex: \text{System operations} = \text{distinct input events on the SSDs}
concepts.plainText: System operations = distinct input system events drawn on the SSDs

concepts.text: Design Model Artefacts and Logical Architecture

The design model in the Unified Process contains interaction diagrams (sequence and communication), design class diagrams and package diagrams showing the logical architecture. Logical architecture is the large-scale organisation of software classes into packages, subsystems and layers, independent of how they are deployed to machines. A common layering is UI (presentation) at the top, then application or domain logic, then technical services such as persistence, logging and security.

rows: Windows, web pages, controllers of the view

concepts.text: Guidelines for layered design:
items: Model-view separation: domain objects must not know about UI objects; the UI calls the domain, not the reverse.
Strict layering lets a layer call only the one directly below; relaxed layering allows calls to any lower layer.
Upward notification, where needed, is done with the Observer pattern so that lower layers stay independent of upper ones.
A controller object in the domain layer receives system operations from the UI layer (GRASP Controller).

concepts.plainText: Operation contract = Operation + Cross references + Preconditions + Postconditions

formulas.latex: \text{System operations} = \text{distinct input events on the SSDs}
formulas.plainText: System operations = distinct input system events drawn on the SSDs
Operation contract = Operation + Cross references + Preconditions + Postconditions
Use case text -> SSD -> operation contracts -> interaction diagrams -> design class diagram

notes.text: If an MCQ describes a use case that mentions barcode scanners, screens or buttons, it is a real (concrete) use case; if it states only intentions and responsibilities, it is essential.
An SSD treats the whole system as one black-box lifeline and shows only events crossing the system boundary. Internal object messages belong to design-level sequence diagrams, not the SSD.

Operation contract postconditions describe state changes of domain objects (instances created or deleted, attributes modified, links formed or broken), not the actions or UI output that produced them.

concepts.text: From Design Artefacts to the Implementation Model

In object-oriented development the design model (interaction diagrams plus design class diagrams, DCDs) is the input to programming. Larman calls the output the implementation model: all the source code, database schema definitions, web pages, configuration and test code that realise the design. Mapping design to code is largely mechanical once the design is good, because each design construct has a direct language counterpart. The creative work of assigning responsibilities (GRASP) has already been done in the interaction diagrams; programming turns those decisions into class definitions and method bodies.

rows: Name and stereotype taken from the DCD
Type and visibility copied from the DCD
Signature from DCD, body from interaction diagram
Placed in the class at the navigable source end
Collection type chosen by access needs
Class must define every interface operation

concepts.text: Programming and Development Process
Implementation in an iterative (UP-style) project is not one big coding phase; each iteration repeats these activities:
items: Take the use-case scenarios chosen for the iteration and their interaction diagrams and DCDs.
Write unit tests and the classes they exercise, starting with the least-coupled classes.
Integrate and run all tests continuously, fixing failures immediately.
Refactor to remove duplication and improve structure while keeping every test passing.
Feed discoveries (missing methods, wrong responsibilities) back into the design model for the next iteration.

concepts.text: Design and code are expected to diverge a little: programmers discover details during coding that were not visible in diagrams. Larman therefore treats the design as a guide, not a rigid contract, and recommends updating diagrams (or regenerating them by reverse engineering in a CASE tool) rather than letting them rot. Round-trip engineering tools generate skeleton code from DCDs and regenerate DCDs from code.
Order of Implementation

Classes should be implemented, and unit-tested, from least-coupled to most-coupled. A class that depends on no other application class (for example Payment or ProductDescription in the POS case study) is written first, then the classes that use it, and finally the highly coupled coordinators such as Register or Store. This way every class can be compiled and tested against real, already-working collaborators instead of stubs.

Dependencies (A uses B):
  Register -> Sale, ProductCatalog
  Sale     -> SalesLineItem, Payment
  SalesLineItem -> ProductDescription
  ProductCatalog -> ProductDescription

Implementation order (least coupled first):
  1 Payment, ProductDescription
  2 SalesLineItem, ProductCatalog
  3 Sale
  4 Register, Store
Test-First (Test-Driven) Development
Test-driven development (TDD), promoted by Extreme Programming, writes the unit test before the code it tests:
items: Red: write a small automated test (e.g. JUnit) for the next bit of behaviour; it fails because the code does not exist yet.
Green: write the simplest code that makes the test pass.
Refactor: clean up the code and the test while the test suite stays green.
Benefits: tests actually get written, the programmer thinks about the interface first, instant regression safety and a clear signal of when a feature is done.

concepts.text: Refactoring

Refactoring (Fowler) is a disciplined method of restructuring existing code without changing its external behaviour, applied in small steps each followed by re-running the tests. Typical code smells that trigger it are duplicated code, long methods, large classes with many instance variables, long parameter lists and heavy use of literal constants. Common refactorings are Extract Method, Extract Constant, Rename, Move Method, Introduce Explaining Variable and Replace Constructor Call with Factory Method.

concepts.plainText: Statement coverage = statements executed by tests / total statements x 100%

formulas.plainText: Statement coverage = S_executed / S_total x 100%
V(G) = E - N + 2P = number of decisions + 1
TDD cycle: Red -> Green -> Refactor (repeat)

notes.text: Order of implementation: least-coupled classes first, most-coupled last. If an MCQ lists a dependency chain, the class that depends on nothing is coded and tested first.
Method signatures come from the DCD, but method bodies come from the interaction (sequence or communication) diagrams: each message a class sends becomes a statement in the body.
Refactoring must not change observable behaviour. Adding a feature or fixing a bug at the same time is not refactoring; the regression test suite is what proves behaviour was preserved.

concepts.text: Agents and Environments

An agent is anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon that environment through actuators. A human agent has eyes and ears as sensors and hands, legs and voice as actuators; a robot has cameras and range finders as sensors and motors as actuators; a software agent (softbot) receives keystrokes, files and network packets and acts by displaying output, writing files or sending packets. The agent repeatedly runs the cycle sensors → percepts → agent function → actions → actuators.
Key terms:
items: Percept: the agent's perceptual input at a given instant.
Percept sequence: the complete history of everything the agent has ever perceived; an agent's choice of action can depend on the whole percept sequence but not on anything it has not perceived.
Agent function: an abstract mathematical mapping from every possible percept sequence to an action; it describes the agent's behaviour externally.
Agent program: the concrete implementation of the agent function that runs on a physical system; it takes the current percept as input.
Architecture: the computing device with physical sensors and actuators on which the program runs (a PC, a robotic car, a phone).

concepts.plainText: Agent = Architecture + Program
Agent function f maps percept sequences P* to actions A

concepts.text: A table-driven agent implements the agent function literally by storing the action for every possible percept sequence in a lookup table. With |P| possible percepts and a lifetime of T percepts the table needs the sum of |P|^t for t = 1 to T entries, which becomes astronomically large (a chess table would need more entries than atoms in the universe). The design problem of AI is therefore to write small programs that produce rational behaviour without such a table.

function TABLE-DRIVEN-AGENT(percept) returns an action
  persistent: percepts, a sequence, initially empty
              table, indexed by percept sequences, fully specified
  append percept to the end of percepts
  action <- LOOKUP(percepts, table)
  return action
Rationality and Autonomy

A rational agent is one that does the right thing. For each possible percept sequence, a rational agent selects an action that is expected to maximise its performance measure, given the evidence provided by the percept sequence and whatever built-in knowledge it has. What is rational at any time depends on four things: the performance measure defining success, the agent's prior knowledge of the environment, the actions it can perform, and its percept sequence to date.
Rationality is not perfection:
items: Rationality is not omniscience: an omniscient agent knows the actual outcome of its actions; a rational agent maximises expected performance and can still suffer bad luck.
Information gathering (looking before crossing a road) and exploration are part of rational behaviour when the environment is not fully known.
Learning: a rational agent should learn as much as possible from what it perceives and modify its behaviour accordingly.
Autonomy: an agent is autonomous to the extent that its behaviour is determined by its own experience rather than only by the designer's built-in knowledge.

concepts.text: Properties commonly required of intelligent agents:
items: Autonomy: operates without direct human intervention and controls its own actions and internal state.
Reactivity: perceives the environment and responds in a timely way to changes in it.
Pro-activeness: exhibits goal-directed behaviour by taking the initiative rather than only reacting.
Social ability: interacts with other agents and humans through some agent-communication language; further properties often listed are learning (adaptivity), mobility and rationality.

concepts.text: PEAS Description of the Task Environment

Before designing an agent, its task environment is specified with PEAS: Performance measure (the criterion of success, defined on environment states, not on how the agent feels), Environment (what the agent operates in), Actuators (how it acts) and Sensors (how it perceives). A good performance measure rewards what one actually wants in the environment rather than how one thinks the agent should behave.

rows: Safe, fast, legal, comfortable trip; maximise profits
Percentage of parts placed in correct bins
Roads, other traffic, pedestrians, customers, weather
Steering, accelerator, brake, signal, horn, display
Display of questions, tests, diagnoses, treatments, referrals
Cameras, sonar, speedometer, GPS, odometer, accelerometer, engine sensors
Keyboard entry of symptoms, findings, patient's answers
Dirt sensor, bump sensor, location sensor

formulas.plainText: Agent = Architecture + Program
f: P* -> A (agent function)
Table entries = sum over t = 1..T of |P|^t

notes.text: In PEAS items, classify each phrase by role: what is measured is P, where the agent lives is E, what it outputs or moves is A, and what it reads or senses is S. 'Keyboard entry of symptoms' is a sensor for a diagnosis system; 'display of diagnoses' is an actuator.

Do not confuse the agent function (an abstract mapping over entire percept sequences) with the agent program (code that receives only the current percept and must remember history itself if it needs it).

Rational does not mean omniscient or successful: an agent that looked both ways and was then hit by a falling object still acted rationally, because it maximised expected performance on the information available.

concepts.text: Agent Programs from Simple to Complex

Russell and Norvig describe four basic kinds of agent program, in order of increasing generality: simple reflex agents, model-based reflex agents, goal-based agents and utility-based agents. Any of these can be turned into a learning agent that improves its performance over time. Each type keeps the agent cycle of perceiving and acting but differs in what it stores internally and how it chooses an action.
Simple Reflex Agent

A simple reflex agent selects actions on the basis of the current percept only, ignoring the rest of the percept history. It uses condition-action rules (if-then rules), for example 'if car-in-front-is-braking then initiate-braking'. It is simple and fast but works correctly only if the right decision can be made from the current percept, that is, only if the environment is fully observable. In partially observable environments it can fall into infinite loops, which randomising its actions can sometimes escape.

function SIMPLE-REFLEX-AGENT(percept) returns an action
  persistent: rules, a set of condition-action rules
  state  <- INTERPRET-INPUT(percept)
  rule   <- RULE-MATCH(state, rules)
  action <- rule.ACTION
  return action
Model-Based Reflex Agent

A model-based reflex agent handles partial observability by keeping an internal state that depends on the percept history and reflects unobserved aspects of the world. Updating this state needs a model of the world: knowledge of how the world evolves independently of the agent and of how the agent's own actions affect the world. It still chooses actions with condition-action rules, but matches them against its internal state rather than the raw percept.

function MODEL-BASED-REFLEX-AGENT(percept) returns an action
  persistent: state, model, rules, action (most recent, initially none)
  state  <- UPDATE-STATE(state, action, percept, model)
  rule   <- RULE-MATCH(state, rules)
  action <- rule.ACTION
  return action
Goal-Based and Utility-Based Agents

A goal-based agent has, in addition to a model, explicit goal information describing desirable situations. It considers the future, asking 'what will happen if I do action A?', and uses search and planning to find action sequences that achieve the goal. It is more flexible than a reflex agent because its knowledge is explicit and can be changed simply by changing the goal, but goals give only a binary distinction between happy and unhappy states.

A utility-based agent uses a utility function that maps a state (or sequence of states) to a real number describing the degree of happiness. It chooses the action that maximises expected utility, averaging over the possible outcomes weighted by their probabilities. Utility lets the agent trade off conflicting goals (speed against safety) and weigh the likelihood of success against the importance of goals when none can be achieved with certainty.

concepts.latex: EU(a) = \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, U(s'), \quad a^{*} = \arg\max_{a} EU(a)
concepts.plainText: EU(a) = sum over s' of P(s'|s,a) U(s'); choose a* = argmax EU(a)

rows: Search or planning towards an explicit goal
Tasks with clear goal states (route finding)

concepts.text: Learning Agents
A learning agent has four conceptual components:
items: Performance element: selects external actions; it is what the other four agent types consist of entirely.
Critic: observes the world and tells the learning element how well the agent is doing with respect to a fixed performance standard.
Learning element: responsible for making improvements, using feedback from the critic to modify the performance element.
Problem generator: suggests exploratory actions that lead to new and informative experiences, even if they are suboptimal in the short run.

concepts.text: Learning lets an agent start in an initially unknown environment and become more competent than its initial knowledge alone would allow. For a taxi, the performance element drives, the critic notices that other drivers honk after a sudden lane change, the learning element adds a rule against such changes, and the problem generator might propose testing the brakes on different road surfaces.

formulas.plainText: EU(a) = sum over s' of P(s'|s,a) U(s')
a* = argmax_a EU(a)
s_t = UPDATE(s_(t-1), a_(t-1), p_t, model)

notes.text: Keyword map for agent-type MCQs: 'current percept only / condition-action rules' = simple reflex; 'internal state / partially observable' = model-based; 'what will happen if / goal / planning' = goal-based; 'how happy / degree of desirability / trade-off' = utility-based; 'critic / problem generator' = learning agent.

A model-based reflex agent still decides by condition-action rules; having a model does not make it goal-based. Goal-based agents look ahead at the consequences of actions, which reflex agents never do.
The critic is needed because percepts alone give no indication of success; the performance standard is fixed outside the agent so that the agent cannot adjust the standard to suit its own behaviour.

concepts.text: Why Environment Properties Matter

The range of task environments is vast, but they can be categorised along a small number of dimensions. These properties largely determine the appropriate agent design: a fully observable, deterministic, static, discrete, single-agent environment is the easiest, while a partially observable, stochastic, sequential, dynamic, continuous, multi-agent environment such as taxi driving is the hardest case.
Observability and number of agents:
items: Fully observable: the sensors give access to the complete relevant state of the environment at each point in time, so the agent need not keep internal state (crossword, chess).

Partially observable (semi-observable): noisy or inaccurate sensors, or parts of the state are missing from the data (a vacuum agent with only a local dirt sensor, poker, taxi); unobservable if the agent has no sensors at all.
Single agent: only one agent acts (solving a crossword alone).

Multi-agent: other agents whose behaviour affects this agent's performance; competitive (chess, where one maximises while the other minimises) or cooperative (taxis avoiding collisions); communication and randomised behaviour can become rational.

concepts.text: Determinism, episodes and time:
items: Deterministic: the next state is completely determined by the current state and the agent's action; otherwise stochastic (outcomes quantified by probabilities) or nondeterministic (possible outcomes listed without probabilities).
Strategic: deterministic except for the actions of other agents (chess is often classed this way).

Episodic: experience is divided into atomic episodes; in each the agent perceives and performs one action, and the choice in one episode does not affect the next (defect detection on an assembly line, image classification).
Sequential: the current decision can affect all future decisions (chess, taxi driving), so the agent must think ahead.

concepts.text: Change, representation and knowledge:
items: Static: the environment does not change while the agent is deliberating (crossword).
Dynamic: the environment keeps changing while the agent deliberates; not deciding counts as deciding to do nothing (taxi driving).
Semi-dynamic: the environment itself does not change with time but the agent's performance score does (chess played with a clock).
Discrete vs continuous: applies to states, time, percepts and actions; chess has a finite number of distinct states and moves, whereas taxi speed, position and steering angle vary continuously.

Known vs unknown: refers to the agent's (or designer's) knowledge of the rules of the environment; in an unknown environment the agent must learn how it works. A known environment can be partially observable (solitaire) and an unknown one can be fully observable (a new video game).

concepts.plainText: Deterministic: s' = RESULT(s, a); Stochastic: probability P(s'|s, a) over next states

concepts.text: Classification of Example Environments

The classifications in these tables follow Russell and Norvig and depend on how the task is defined. Medical diagnosis is single-agent because the patient is modelled as part of the environment, not as an agent maximising its own performance; image analysis is semi-dynamic because the image does not change but slow analysis may be penalised; poker is stochastic because the deal of cards is random.
The Vacuum-Cleaner World

The two-square vacuum world is the standard small example. The agent can be in square A or B, and each square can be clean or dirty, so there are 2 × 2^2 = 8 world states. If the agent senses both its location and the dirt status of every square, the world is fully observable; with only a local dirt sensor it becomes partially observable. If sucking always cleans, it is deterministic; if dirt can reappear or suction sometimes fails, it becomes stochastic.

concepts.plainText: Number of states of an n-square vacuum world = n x 2^n (n = 2 gives 8)

formulas.plainText: Deterministic: s' = RESULT(s, a); Stochastic: P(s'|s, a)
Sum over s' of P(s'|s, a) = 1
|S| = n x 2^n

notes.text: Memorise the hardest case, taxi driving: partially observable, multi-agent, stochastic, sequential, dynamic, continuous. The easiest case is a crossword puzzle: fully observable, single agent, deterministic, sequential, static, discrete.

Semi-dynamic is not the same as dynamic: in chess with a clock the board does not change while a player thinks, only the score (time remaining) does. Also 'semi-observable' in the syllabus means partially observable.

Known versus unknown describes knowledge of the environment's rules (the transition model), while fully versus partially observable describes what the sensors reveal about the current state; the two dimensions are independent.

concepts.text: What a CSP Is

A constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) is a search problem whose states have a factored structure: a set of variables X = {X1, ..., Xn}, a domain Di of allowed values for each variable, and a set of constraints C that specify which combinations of values are allowed. A state is an assignment of values to some or all variables; an assignment is consistent if it violates no constraint and complete if every variable has a value. A solution is a complete, consistent assignment. Because the structure is explicit, general-purpose heuristics can prune huge parts of the space without problem-specific knowledge.
Kinds of domains and constraints:
items: Discrete finite domains (colours, digits 0 to 9), discrete infinite domains (integers, as in job-shop scheduling start times) and continuous domains (linear programming).
Unary constraint: restricts one variable, e.g. SA != green.
Binary constraint: relates two variables, e.g. WA != NT; a binary CSP can be drawn as a constraint graph.
Global (higher-order) constraint: involves many variables, e.g. Alldiff(F, T, U, W, R, O) in a cryptarithmetic puzzle.
Preference (soft) constraints express which solutions are better and turn the problem into constraint optimisation.

concepts.text: Standard Examples

rows: WA, NT, SA, Q, NSW, V, T
Adjacent regions differ, e.g. WA != NT, SA != Q
Letters F, T, U, W, R, O and carries C1, C2, C3
Alldiff on letters, column sums O + O = R + 10 C1 etc., leading digits non-zero
Q1 to Q8, one per column
No two queens share a row or diagonal
Alldiff in every row, column and 3x3 box

concepts.text: In the constraint graph each node is a variable and each edge joins two variables that share a constraint. For Australia, SA is adjacent to five regions (WA, NT, Q, NSW, V) while Tasmania has no edges and forms an independent sub-problem. Graph structure matters: a tree-structured CSP can be solved in O(n d^2) time, whereas a general CSP is NP-complete. In cryptarithmetic, the extra carry in the leftmost column forces the leading digit of the answer: in TWO + TWO = FOUR, F must be 1.

concepts.plainText: number of complete assignments = d^n (n variables, domain size d)

concepts.text: Backtracking Search

Backtracking search is depth-first search that assigns one variable per level and backtracks as soon as a variable has no legal value left. It exploits commutativity: the order in which values are assigned does not change the final assignment, so only one variable needs to be considered at each node, giving d^n leaves instead of n! d^n. Its efficiency depends on three choices: which variable to assign next, in what order to try its values, and what inference to perform after each assignment.

function BACKTRACK(assignment, csp):
  if assignment is complete: return assignment
  var <- SELECT-UNASSIGNED-VARIABLE(csp)       # MRV, then degree
  for value in ORDER-DOMAIN-VALUES(var)         # LCV
    if value is consistent with assignment:
      add {var = value} to assignment
      inferences <- INFERENCE(csp, var, value)  # forward checking / AC-3
      if inferences != failure:
        result <- BACKTRACK(assignment, csp)
        if result != failure: return result
      remove {var = value} and inferences
  return failure
Ordering heuristics:
items: Minimum remaining values (MRV, most-constrained variable, fail-first): choose the variable with the fewest legal values left, so failures are detected early.
Degree heuristic: break ties by choosing the variable involved in the most constraints with unassigned variables (SA in the Australia map, degree 5).
Least-constraining value (LCV): try first the value that rules out the fewest choices for neighbouring variables, leaving maximum flexibility.
Variable selection is fail-first, value selection is fail-last: we want to fail fast on hopeless variables but succeed with the chosen value.

concepts.text: Constraint Propagation: Forward Checking and Arc Consistency

Forward checking: whenever variable X is assigned, delete from the domain of every unassigned neighbour Y any value inconsistent with X. For example, WA = red removes red from NT and SA, leaving {green, blue}. If any domain becomes empty the branch is abandoned at once. Forward checking only looks one step ahead and does not check constraints between two unassigned neighbours, so it can miss that NT = blue and SA = blue are both forced.

Arc consistency is stronger. The directed arc X -> Y is consistent if for every value x in the domain of X there is some value y in the domain of Y that satisfies the constraint between them; values of X without support are deleted. AC-3 keeps a queue of arcs, revises each, and whenever the domain of X shrinks it re-enqueues all arcs Z -> X. Its worst-case time is O(c d^3) for c binary constraints. Example: with X, Y in {1, 2, 3} and X < Y, making X -> Y consistent removes 3 from X, and making Y -> X consistent removes 1 from Y.

concepts.latex: X \to Y \text{ consistent} \iff \forall x \in D_X\ \exists y \in D_Y : (x, y) \text{ satisfies } C_{XY}
concepts.plainText: arc X -> Y consistent iff for every x in D_X there exists y in D_Y with (x, y) satisfying C_XY

concepts.text: Other techniques worth knowing:
items: Node consistency: every value in a domain satisfies the variable's unary constraints.
Maintaining arc consistency (MAC): run AC-3 after each assignment, stronger than forward checking.
Conflict-directed backjumping: jump back to the variable that actually caused the failure instead of the most recent one.
Min-conflicts local search: start from a complete assignment and repeatedly change a conflicted variable to the value with fewest conflicts; solves million-queens problems in a few steps.

formulas.plainText: complete assignments = d^n

formulas.latex: X \to Y \text{ consistent} \iff \forall x \in D_X\ \exists y \in D_Y : C_{XY}(x, y)
formulas.plainText: X -> Y consistent iff every x in D_X has a supporting y in D_Y

formulas.latex: T_{\text{AC-3}} = O(c\, d^{3}),\quad T_{\text{tree CSP}} = O(n\, d^{2})
formulas.plainText: AC-3 time O(c d^3); tree-structured CSP solved in O(n d^2)

notes.text: Keep the three heuristics apart: MRV and degree choose the variable, LCV chooses the value. MRV is fail-first; LCV is the value least likely to cause failure.
Forward checking checks only arcs from unassigned neighbours to the just-assigned variable; arc consistency (AC-3) propagates further and can detect failures forward checking misses.
Arc consistency is directional: X -> Y being consistent does not imply Y -> X is consistent. AC-3 must check both directions of every constraint.

concepts.text: Uninformed (Blind) Search

Uninformed search strategies use only the information in the problem definition: they can generate successors and recognise a goal, but they have no estimate of how close a state is to the goal. They differ only in the order in which frontier nodes are expanded, which is fixed by the data structure used for the frontier. All are measured with b (branching factor), d (depth of the shallowest goal), m (maximum depth), l (depth limit) and C* (cost of the optimal solution).
Breadth-first and uniform-cost search:
items: Breadth-first search (BFS) expands the shallowest unexpanded node first using a FIFO queue, so all nodes at depth k are expanded before any at depth k + 1.
BFS is complete if b is finite and optimal when all step costs are equal; applying the goal test when a node is generated, its time and space are both O(b^d). Memory, not time, is its main weakness.
Uniform-cost search (UCS) expands the node with the lowest path cost g(n) using a priority queue; it is Dijkstra's algorithm on the state space.

UCS is complete if every step cost is at least some epsilon > 0 and is optimal for any non-negative costs; it applies the goal test when a node is selected for expansion. Time and space are O(b^(1 + floor(C*/epsilon))).

concepts.text: Depth-first family:
items: Depth-first search (DFS) expands the deepest node first using a LIFO stack (or recursion). It needs only O(bm) memory because it stores a single path plus the unexpanded siblings of its nodes.

DFS is not complete in infinite spaces or with loops (tree search), and is not optimal because it returns the first goal found, not the shallowest. Time is O(b^m), which can be far larger than O(b^d).
Depth-limited search (DLS) is DFS that treats nodes at depth l as having no successors; it avoids infinite descent but is incomplete if l < d and non-optimal if l > d. Time O(b^l), space O(bl).

Iterative deepening search (IDS) runs DLS with l = 0, 1, 2, ... until a goal is found. It is complete, optimal for unit step costs, uses O(bd) space and O(b^d) time; it is the preferred blind method when the space is large and d unknown.

concepts.text: Bidirectional search runs two simultaneous searches, one forward from the initial state and one backward from the goal, and stops when the two frontiers meet. Because each search only needs to reach depth d/2, the cost is about 2 b^(d/2), which is dramatically less than b^d. It requires that predecessors of a state can be computed (reversible actions) and that the goal is explicit; with BFS in both directions it is complete and optimal for unit costs, but it must store at least one frontier, so space is also O(b^(d/2)).

concepts.latex: T_{BFS} = O(b^{d}),\quad S_{DFS} = O(bm),\quad S_{IDS} = O(bd),\quad T_{bi} = O(b^{d/2})
concepts.plainText: BFS time O(b^d); DFS space O(bm); IDS space O(bd); bidirectional time O(b^(d/2))

concepts.text: Why Iterative Deepening Is Not Wasteful

IDS regenerates the upper levels on every iteration, but in a tree with constant branching most nodes lie on the bottom level, so the repetition costs little. Nodes at depth 1 are generated d times, at depth 2 d - 1 times, and nodes at depth d only once. For b = 10 and d = 5, IDS generates 50 + 400 + 3,000 + 20,000 + 100,000 = 123,450 nodes against 111,110 for BFS, only about 11 percent more while using linear memory.
Traced Example

Consider the tree with root A, children B and C, where B has children D and E, and C has children F and G; the goal is G. Tracing the frontier shows how the data structure alone changes the order of expansion. Children are generated left to right.

Tree: A -> B, C ; B -> D, E ; C -> F, G ; goal = G

BFS (queue)   expand order: A, B, C, D, E, F, G
  queue: [A] -> [B C] -> [C D E] -> [D E F G] -> ... -> G
DFS (stack)   expand order: A, B, D, E, C, F, G
  stack: [A] -> [B C] -> [D E C] -> [E C] -> [C] -> [F G]
IDS           l=0: A | l=1: A B C | l=2: A B D E C F G
UCS with costs S-A 1, S-B 5, A-G 10, B-G 3:
  pop S(0) -> A(1) -> B(5) -> G(8) via B ; G(11) via A never chosen
Choosing a blind strategy:
items: Unit costs, plenty of memory, shallow goal: BFS.
Varying step costs and an optimal answer is required: uniform-cost search.
Large or infinite space, unknown depth, little memory: iterative deepening.
Known single goal with reversible actions: bidirectional search.

formulas.plainText: BFS time = space = O(b^d)
DFS space O(bm); IDS space O(bd)
bidirectional O(b^(d/2)); UCS O(b^(1 + floor(C*/epsilon)))

notes.text: Data structures are a favourite MCQ: BFS uses a FIFO queue, DFS a LIFO stack, uniform-cost a priority queue ordered by g(n), A* a priority queue ordered by f(n).
BFS is optimal only when all step costs are equal. With unequal costs the shallowest goal need not be the cheapest; uniform-cost search is the optimal blind strategy then.
IDS combines the completeness and unit-cost optimality of BFS with the O(bd) memory of DFS, at the price of regenerating upper levels, which adds only about b/(b - 1) overhead.

concepts.text: Heuristics and Best-First Search

Informed (heuristic) search uses problem-specific knowledge in the form of a heuristic function h(n), the estimated cost of the cheapest path from node n to a goal, with h(goal) = 0. Best-first search is graph search that expands the frontier node with the lowest value of an evaluation function f(n), kept in a priority queue. The choice of f defines the algorithm: f(n) = h(n) gives greedy best-first search and f(n) = g(n) + h(n) gives A*.
Greedy best-first search, f(n) = h(n):
items: Expands the node that appears closest to the goal, e.g. straight-line distance to the destination in route finding.
Often fast, but not optimal because it ignores the cost already spent g(n).
Not complete in tree-search form (it can oscillate forever between two states); complete in finite spaces with graph search.
Worst-case time and space O(b^m), though a good heuristic reduces this greatly.

concepts.plainText: f(n) = g(n) + h(n): cost so far plus estimated cost to goal

concepts.text: A* search ranks nodes by f(n) = g(n) + h(n), the estimated cost of the cheapest solution through n. A heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates the true cost h*(n); with an admissible h, A* tree search is optimal. A heuristic is consistent (monotone) if for every node n and successor n' reached by action a, h(n) <= c(n, a, n') + h(n'), a form of the triangle inequality. Every consistent heuristic is admissible, and with consistency A* graph search is optimal because f values along any path never decrease, so the first time a node is expanded its cheapest path has been found.

concepts.plainText: admissible: h(n) <= h*(n); consistent: h(n) <= c(n, a, n') + h(n')

concepts.text: Properties and heuristic design:
items: A* is complete (finite b, step costs >= epsilon), optimal under the conditions above, and optimally efficient: no other optimal algorithm using the same h expands fewer nodes. Its drawback is memory, since it keeps all generated nodes.

8-puzzle heuristics: h1 = number of misplaced tiles, h2 = sum of Manhattan distances of tiles from their goal squares; both are admissible and h2 dominates h1 (h2 >= h1 everywhere), so A* with h2 expands fewer nodes.
Admissible heuristics come from relaxed problems (remove a rule, e.g. tiles may move anywhere gives h1) or from pattern databases.
If h = 0, A* becomes uniform-cost search; memory-bounded variants include IDA* and SMA*.

concepts.text: Worked A* Trace

Edges: S-A 1, S-B 4, A-B 2, A-G 12, B-G 5
h: S=7, A=6, B=4, G=0   (admissible and consistent)
step  expand     frontier after expansion (f = g + h)
 1    S (f=7)    A: 1+6=7,  B: 4+4=8
 2    A (f=7)    B: 3+4=7 (better path via A), G: 13+0=13
 3    B (f=7)    G: 8+0=8 (replaces G at 13)
 4    G (f=8)    goal -> path S-A-B-G, cost 8
Greedy (f=h): S -> B (h=4) -> G  => path S-B-G, cost 9 (not optimal)
Local Search: Hill Climbing

Local search keeps only a current state and moves to neighbouring states; the path does not matter, only the final configuration, as in 8-queens or VLSI layout. It uses constant memory and can work in very large or continuous spaces. Hill climbing (steepest ascent) repeatedly moves to the best neighbour and stops when no neighbour is better; it is greedy and neither complete nor optimal.

rows: A peak higher than its neighbours but lower than the global maximum; the search halts there
All neighbours have equal value, so there is no direction to move
Allow a limited number of sideways moves, big random jumps
A sequence of local maxima whose slope rises in a direction no single operator follows
Apply several operators at once, move in more than one dimension

concepts.text: Hill-climbing variants:
items: Simple (first-choice) hill climbing: take the first neighbour that improves on the current state; good when there are many successors.
Steepest-ascent hill climbing: examine all neighbours and take the best.
Stochastic hill climbing: choose randomly among uphill moves, with probability depending on steepness.
Random-restart hill climbing: repeat from random initial states; complete with probability approaching 1. Local beam search keeps k states, and genetic algorithms combine pairs of states.

concepts.text: Simulated Annealing

Simulated annealing, inspired by slowly cooling metal, picks a random neighbour. If it is better, the move is always made; if it is worse by an amount |ΔE|, the move is made with probability e^(ΔE/T), where ΔE = value(next) − value(current) is negative, so worse moves and lower temperatures make acceptance less likely. The temperature T starts high, allowing the search to escape local maxima, and is lowered by a cooling schedule such as T(k+1) = αT(k) with α around 0.8 to 0.99. If T decreases slowly enough, the algorithm finds a global optimum with probability approaching 1. For example, a move 2 worse at T = 5 is accepted with probability e^(−0.4) ≈ 0.67, but at T = 1 only e^(−2) ≈ 0.14.

concepts.latex: P(\text{accept worse move}) = e^{\Delta E / T} = e^{-|\Delta E| / T},\quad T_{k+1} = \alpha T_{k}
concepts.plainText: P(accept) = e^(dE/T) = e^(-|dE|/T); cooling T(k+1) = alpha T(k)

formulas.plainText: A*: f(n) = g(n) + h(n); greedy: f(n) = h(n)
admissible h(n) <= h*(n); consistent h(n) <= c(n,a,n') + h(n')
simulated annealing acceptance P = e^(dE/T) for a worse move (dE < 0)

notes.text: Admissible means never overestimates; consistent means obeys the triangle inequality. Consistency implies admissibility, not the other way round, and it is the condition needed for A* graph search to stay optimal without reopening nodes.

Watch the sign in the annealing formula. For maximisation with ΔE = new − current < 0 it is e^(ΔE/T); for cost minimisation with ΔE = new cost − old cost > 0 it is written e^(−ΔE/T). Both give a probability between 0 and 1.
In A* trace questions, apply the goal test when the goal is removed from the frontier, not when it is first generated; otherwise a suboptimal path (G at f = 13 in the worked trace) may be returned.

concepts.text: Games as Adversarial Search

Adversarial search deals with multi-agent environments in which agents' goals conflict. The classic setting is a two-player, turn-taking, deterministic, zero-sum game of perfect information such as chess, checkers, tic-tac-toe or Go: both players see the full state, and one player's gain is exactly the other's loss. The players are called MAX (moves first, wants a high utility) and MIN (wants a low utility). Unlike ordinary search, the agent cannot plan a fixed action sequence, because it must respond to whatever the opponent does; the answer is a strategy (contingent plan).
A game is formally defined by:
items: S0: the initial state (board set-up).
PLAYER(s): whose turn it is in state s; ACTIONS(s): the legal moves.
RESULT(s, a): the transition model giving the state after a move.
TERMINAL-TEST(s): true when the game is over; such states are terminal states.
UTILITY(s, p): the payoff of terminal state s for player p, e.g. +1, 0, −1 for win, draw, loss (chess), or 0 to 192 in backgammon.

concepts.text: The Minimax Algorithm

Minimax assumes both players play optimally. The minimax value of a node is the utility (for MAX) of being in that state: at a terminal it is the utility, at a MAX node it is the maximum of its children's values, and at a MIN node the minimum. Values are backed up from the leaves to the root by a complete depth-first traversal, and MAX chooses the move leading to the child with the highest value. Minimax is complete for finite trees and optimal against an optimal opponent; its time is O(b^m) and space O(bm). For chess, b ≈ 35 and m ≈ 100, so exact minimax is infeasible.

concepts.plainText: MINIMAX(s) = UTILITY(s) if terminal; max over actions if MAX to move; min over actions if MIN to move

concepts.text: Alpha-Beta Pruning

Alpha-beta pruning computes exactly the same minimax decision while skipping branches that cannot influence it. Alpha is the best (highest) value found so far for MAX along the path to the root, and beta is the best (lowest) value found so far for MIN. At a MIN node, once its value falls to alpha or below, MAX will never let play reach it, so the remaining children are pruned (alpha cut-off); at a MAX node, once its value reaches beta or above, the remaining children are pruned (beta cut-off). Alpha starts at minus infinity and beta at plus infinity.

Worked example (root MAX, three MIN children, leaves read left to right). B has leaves 3, 12, 8, so B = 3 and alpha at the root becomes 3. At C the first leaf is 2; since C can now be at most 2, which is below alpha = 3, the leaves 4 and 6 are pruned. At D the leaves 14, 5 and 2 must all be examined because each keeps D above 3 until the last one: D = 2. The root value is max(3, <=2, 2) = 3, and 2 of the 9 leaves were never evaluated.

MAX root = 3
       /           |            \
   MIN B=3     MIN C<=2       MIN D=2
   3 12 8      2  [4] [6]     14  5  2

B: alpha = 3 after leaves 3, 12, 8
C: leaf 2 <= alpha 3  -> prune 4 and 6
D: 14 -> 5 -> 2 (all needed); root = max(3, 2, 2) = 3

concepts.plainText: alpha-beta best case O(b^(m/2)) = O(sqrt(b)^m)

concepts.text: Improving move ordering in practice:
items: Try captures first, then threats, then forward moves, then backward moves.
Killer-move heuristic: try first the moves that caused cut-offs elsewhere at the same depth.
Iterative deepening supplies the best move from the previous, shallower search as the first move to try.
Transposition tables cache values of positions reached by different move orders.

concepts.text: Cutoffs and Evaluation Functions

Real games cannot be searched to the terminal states, so the search is stopped by a CUTOFF-TEST (usually a depth limit) and non-terminal leaves are scored by a heuristic evaluation function EVAL(s) estimating the expected utility. Evaluation functions are commonly weighted linear sums of features, such as material values in chess (pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9). Fixed-depth cutoffs suffer from the horizon effect, where an unavoidable loss is pushed just beyond the search depth; quiescence search extends the search in volatile positions (pending captures) until a quiet position is reached, and singular extensions deepen forcing moves.

formulas.plainText: minimax time O(b^m), space O(bm)
alpha-beta with perfect ordering O(b^(m/2))
EVAL(s) = sum of w_i f_i(s)

notes.text: Alpha-beta never changes the minimax value or the chosen move; it only reduces the number of nodes examined. With perfect move ordering it searches about twice as deep in the same time.
Alpha is updated only at MAX nodes and beta only at MIN nodes. Prune at a MIN node when its value <= alpha, and at a MAX node when its value >= beta.
The pruning pattern depends on the order in which children are visited. When tracing an alpha-beta question, always go strictly left to right unless the question says otherwise.

concepts.text: Syntax: Propositions and Well-Formed Formulas

Propositional logic (PL) is the simplest formal logic. Its atoms are propositions: declarative statements that are either true or false, written as symbols P, Q, R. 'Kathmandu is the capital of Nepal' is a proposition; 'Close the door' is not, because it has no truth value. Complex sentences are built from atoms using logical connectives.

rows: at least one of P, Q is false
both P and Q are false
P is true and Q is false
P if and only if Q
P and Q have different values

concepts.text: Rules that define a well-formed formula (WFF):
items: Every proposition symbol, and the constants True and False, is a WFF (an atomic sentence).
If A is a WFF then ¬A is a WFF.
If A and B are WFFs then (A ∧ B), (A ∨ B), (A → B) and (A ↔ B) are WFFs.
Nothing else is a WFF; so 'P ∧ ∨ Q' is not well formed.
Operator precedence, highest first: ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔; parentheses override it.

concepts.text: Semantics: Truth Tables and Classification

The semantics of PL assigns a truth value to every sentence under an interpretation (model), which is an assignment of true or false to each proposition symbol. With n symbols there are 2^n interpretations, and a truth table evaluates a sentence under all of them. Implication is true whenever its antecedent is false, which is why P → Q is equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q.

P  Q | ¬P  P∧Q  P∨Q  P→Q  P↔Q
T  T |  F   T    T    T    T
T  F |  F   F    T    F    F
F  T |  T   F    T    T    F
F  F |  T   F    F    T    T

rows: True in some and false in others
True in at least one interpretation (tautologies and contingencies)

concepts.text: A sentence is valid if and only if its negation is unsatisfiable, and KB entails α (KB ⊨ α) if and only if KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable. This relationship is the basis of proof by refutation: to show that a goal follows from a knowledge base, add the negated goal and derive a contradiction. An inference procedure is sound if it derives only entailed sentences and complete if it can derive every entailed sentence.
Standard logical equivalences used for rewriting:
items: Implication elimination: P → Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q.
Biconditional elimination: P ↔ Q ≡ (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P).
Contrapositive: P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P (the converse Q → P is NOT equivalent).
De Morgan: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q and ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q; double negation ¬¬P ≡ P.
Distribution: P ∨ (Q ∧ R) ≡ (P ∨ Q) ∧ (P ∨ R), and P ∧ (Q ∨ R) ≡ (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R).

concepts.latex: \dfrac{l_1 \vee \dots \vee l_k \vee P,\quad \neg P \vee m_1 \vee \dots \vee m_n}{l_1 \vee \dots \vee l_k \vee m_1 \vee \dots \vee m_n}
concepts.plainText: From (l1 v ... v lk v P) and (NOT P v m1 v ... v mn) infer (l1 v ... v lk v m1 v ... v mn)

concepts.text: CNF Conversion and Resolution Refutation
Converting a sentence to conjunctive normal form (a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals):
items: Eliminate ↔ using (A → B) ∧ (B → A).
Eliminate → using ¬A ∨ B.
Move ¬ inwards with De Morgan's laws and cancel double negations.
Distribute ∨ over ∧ so the result is an AND of ORs; each conjunct is one clause.
Example: P → (Q ∧ R) becomes ¬P ∨ (Q ∧ R), then (¬P ∨ Q) ∧ (¬P ∨ R).

concepts.text:
KB: P → Q,  Q → R,  P.   Goal: R
Clauses: 1) ¬P ∨ Q   2) ¬Q ∨ R   3) P   4) ¬R  (negated goal)
5) resolve 4 and 2  ->  ¬Q
6) resolve 5 and 1  ->  ¬P
7) resolve 6 and 3  ->  □ (empty clause)
Contradiction found, so KB ⊨ R

Resolution is sound, and resolution refutation is complete for propositional logic: if KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable, repeated resolution will eventually produce the empty clause □. If no new clauses can be generated and □ has not appeared, the goal is not entailed. Restricting clauses to Horn clauses (at most one positive literal) allows linear-time forward and backward chaining.

P ightarrow Q \equiv 
eg P \vee Q \equiv 
eg Q ightarrow 
eg P
formulas.plainText: P -> Q is equivalent to NOT P v Q and to NOT Q -> NOT P

formulas.latex:
eg(P \wedge Q) \equiv 
eg P \vee 
eg Q,\quad 
eg(P \vee Q) \equiv 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q
formulas.plainText: NOT(P AND Q) = NOT P OR NOT Q; NOT(P OR Q) = NOT P AND NOT Q
From P v Q and NOT Q v R infer P v R
KB entails alpha if and only if KB AND NOT alpha is unsatisfiable

notes.text: For 'which formula is a tautology' items, rewrite every → as ¬A ∨ B and look for a literal together with its negation in one disjunction; if that fails, test the single row that could make it false.
The converse (Q → P) and the inverse (¬P → ¬Q) are not equivalent to P → Q; only the contrapositive (¬Q → ¬P) is. Affirming the consequent (from P → Q and Q conclude P) is a fallacy.
Resolution needs clauses, so always convert to CNF first and add the negated goal before resolving; deriving □ proves the original goal.

concepts.text: Why First-Order Logic

Propositional logic treats 'Ram is a student' and 'Sita is a student' as unrelated symbols and cannot say 'every student studies' compactly. First-order predicate logic (FOPL) assumes the world contains objects, relations among them and functions, and adds variables and quantifiers so general statements can be written once. It is far more expressive than PL, at the cost that entailment in FOPL is only semi-decidable.
Syntax of FOPL:
items: Constants name specific objects: Ram, Kathmandu, 5.
Variables stand for objects: x, y, z.
Functions map objects to objects and form terms: Father(Ram), Plus(2, 3). A term is a constant, a variable or a function applied to terms.
Predicates map objects to truth values and form atomic sentences: Student(Ram), Loves(x, y), Greater(5, 3).
Connectives ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔ as in PL, plus equality (=).
Quantifiers: universal ∀x ('for all x') and existential ∃x ('there exists an x').

concepts.text: Semantics is given by a model consisting of a domain of objects and an interpretation that maps each constant to an object, each predicate to a relation and each function to a function on the domain. ∀x P(x) is true if P holds for every object in the domain, and ∃x P(x) is true if P holds for at least one. A variable is bound if it lies inside the scope of a quantifier that names it and free otherwise; a sentence has no free variables.
Quantifiers and Translation

rows: There is someone whom everyone loves

concepts.text: Rules to remember when translating:
items: ∀ normally pairs with →: ∀x (Student(x) ∧ Clever(x)) wrongly says everything is a clever student.
∃ normally pairs with ∧: ∃x (Student(x) → Clever(x)) is true merely if some non-student exists.
Quantifiers of the same type commute (∀x ∀y ≡ ∀y ∀x), but ∀x ∃y and ∃y ∀x mean different things.
Negation flips the quantifier: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x).

concepts.latex:
eg orall x\,P(x) \equiv \exists x\,
eg P(x),\qquad 
eg\exists x\,P(x) \equiv  orall x\,
eg P(x)
concepts.plainText: NOT forall x P(x) = exists x NOT P(x); NOT exists x P(x) = forall x NOT P(x)

concepts.text: FOPL adds quantifier rules to the propositional ones:
items: Universal instantiation (UI): from ∀x P(x) infer P(g) for any ground term g, e.g. ∀x (Man(x) → Mortal(x)) gives Man(Socrates) → Mortal(Socrates).
Existential instantiation (EI): from ∃x P(x) infer P(C) where C is a new constant not used anywhere else (a Skolem constant).
Existential generalisation: from P(Ram) infer ∃x P(x).
Generalised modus ponens (GMP): from p1', ..., pn' and (p1 ∧ ... ∧ pn → q), if a substitution θ makes each pi' equal to pi, infer SUBST(θ, q).
GMP example: King(John), Greedy(John) and ∀x (King(x) ∧ Greedy(x) → Evil(x)) give Evil(John) with θ = {x/John}.

concepts.text: Unification and the Most General Unifier

Unification is the process of finding a substitution θ that makes two atomic sentences identical: UNIFY(p, q) = θ such that SUBST(θ, p) = SUBST(θ, q). Predicate symbols and arities must match, a variable can be replaced by any term that does not contain that variable (the occurs check), and two different constants never unify. Among all unifiers, the most general unifier (MGU) makes the fewest commitments; every other unifier is an instance of it.

rows: fail (x cannot be John and Elizabeth); standardise apart first
fail (A and B are different constants)

concepts.text: Clausal Form and Resolution Refutation
Converting FOPL to clausal form:
items: Eliminate ↔ and → .
Move ¬ inwards, flipping quantifiers: ¬∀x P becomes ∃x ¬P.
Standardise variables apart so each quantifier uses a distinct variable.
Skolemise: replace each existential variable by a Skolem constant, or by a Skolem function of the universal variables whose scope it lies in; ∀x ∃y Loves(x, y) becomes ∀x Loves(x, F(x)).
Drop the remaining universal quantifiers (all variables are implicitly universal).
Distribute ∨ over ∧ and split the conjunction into separate clauses.

concepts.text:
Facts: ∀x (Dog(x) → Animal(x)), ∀y (Animal(y) → Mortal(y)), Dog(Fido)
Goal:  Mortal(Fido)
Clauses: 1) ¬Dog(x) ∨ Animal(x)   2) ¬Animal(y) ∨ Mortal(y)
         3) Dog(Fido)             4) ¬Mortal(Fido)   (negated goal)
5) 4 + 2, θ = {y/Fido}  ->  ¬Animal(Fido)
6) 5 + 1, θ = {x/Fido}  ->  ¬Dog(Fido)
7) 6 + 3               ->  □   so Mortal(Fido) is proved

First-order resolution combines unification with the propositional rule: two clauses containing literals l and ¬m resolve if l and m unify with MGU θ, and θ is applied to the resolvent. Resolution refutation is sound and refutation-complete for FOPL, but because FOPL is semi-decidable the procedure may run forever when the goal is not entailed. Strategies such as unit preference, set of support and input resolution reduce the search.

eg orall x\,P(x) \equiv \exists x\,
eg P(x),\qquad 
eg\exists x\,P(x) \equiv  orall x\,
eg P(x)
formulas.plainText: NOT forall x P(x) = exists x NOT P(x); NOT exists x P(x) = forall x NOT P(x)
UNIFY(p, q) = theta where SUBST(theta, p) = SUBST(theta, q)
GMP: from p1'..pn' and (p1 AND .. AND pn -> q) infer SUBST(theta, q) when theta unifies each pi' with pi
forall x exists y P(x, y) Skolemises to forall x P(x, F(x))

notes.text: Skolemisation: an existential with no universal to its left becomes a constant (∃x ∀y P(x, y) gives ∀y P(A, y)); an existential inside ∀x becomes a function of x (∀x ∃y P(x, y) gives ∀x P(x, F(x))).

Unification fails when the same variable would need two different constants, when two different constants or function symbols clash, or when a variable would be bound to a term containing itself (occurs check).
Always standardise variables apart before resolving two clauses: Knows(John, x) and Knows(x, Elizabeth) fail to unify only because they happen to share the name x.

concepts.text: Uncertainty and Probability Basics

Real agents rarely have complete, certain knowledge: sensors are noisy, rules have exceptions and some causes are hidden. Pure logic handles this badly because listing every exception is impractical (laziness), the domain may lack a complete theory (theoretical ignorance) and not every test can be run (practical ignorance). Probability theory summarises this uncertainty as degrees of belief between 0 and 1, and decision theory combines it with utilities.
Probability rules used throughout reasoning:
items: Axioms: 0 ≤ P(a) ≤ 1, P(true) = 1, P(false) = 0, and P(a ∨ b) = P(a) + P(b) − P(a ∧ b).
Prior (unconditional) probability P(a) is belief before evidence; posterior (conditional) probability P(a | b) is belief given evidence b.
Conditional probability: P(a | b) = P(a ∧ b) / P(b) for P(b) > 0; the product rule is P(a ∧ b) = P(a | b) P(b).
Total probability (marginalisation): P(b) = P(b | a) P(a) + P(b | ¬a) P(¬a).
Independence: a and b are independent if P(a ∧ b) = P(a) P(b), equivalently P(a | b) = P(a).

concepts.text: Bayes' Rule

concepts.plainText: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B)

concepts.text: Bayes' rule follows from writing the product rule both ways, P(A ∧ B) = P(A | B) P(B) = P(B | A) P(A). Its practical value is that causal knowledge P(effect | cause) is usually easier to obtain and more stable than diagnostic knowledge P(cause | effect). P(A) is the prior, P(B | A) the likelihood, P(B) the evidence (normalising constant) and P(A | B) the posterior.

Disease D: prevalence P(D) = 0.01
Test: sensitivity P(+|D) = 0.90, false-positive rate P(+|¬D) = 0.05
P(+) = 0.90 × 0.01 + 0.05 × 0.99 = 0.009 + 0.0495 = 0.0585
P(D|+) = 0.009 / 0.0585 ≈ 0.154
Only about 15% of positives are truly ill, because the disease is rare.
Bayesian Networks

A Bayesian network (belief network) is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in which each node is a random variable and each arrow X → Y means X has a direct influence on Y (X is a parent of Y). Each node carries a conditional probability table (CPT) giving P(node | parents) for every combination of parent values; a root node simply has its prior. The network is a compact encoding of the full joint distribution.

concepts.plainText: P(x1, ..., xn) = product over i of P(xi | Parents(Xi))

concepts.text: Compactness and conditional independence:
items: A Boolean node with k Boolean parents needs 2^k independent numbers, so the alarm network needs 1 + 1 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 10 numbers instead of 2^5 − 1 = 31 for the full joint table.
Local Markov property: each node is conditionally independent of its non-descendants given its parents (J is independent of B and E given A).
Chain A → B → C and common cause A ← B → C: A and C become independent once B is observed.
Common effect A → C ← B: A and B are independent until C (or a descendant of C) is observed; then they become dependent, which is called explaining away.
Build a network by adding variables in causal order (causes before effects) to keep it sparse.

concepts.text: Inference in a belief network computes the posterior distribution of query variables given observed evidence, summing out the hidden variables: P(X | e) = α Σ_y P(X, e, y), where α normalises the result. Each joint term is a product of CPT entries. Exact enumeration takes time exponential in the number of variables; variable elimination speeds it up by caching repeated sub-products, and approximate methods such as likelihood weighting and Gibbs sampling handle large networks.

Query P(B | j, m) in the alarm network (hidden: E, A)
P(b,j,m)  = P(b) Σe P(e) Σa P(a|b,e) P(j|a) P(m|a)   ≈ 0.000592
P(¬b,j,m) = P(¬b) Σe P(e) Σa P(a|¬b,e) P(j|a) P(m|a) ≈ 0.001492
α = 1 / (0.000592 + 0.001492)
P(b | j, m) ≈ 0.000592 / 0.002084 ≈ 0.284
Types of reasoning a belief network supports:
items: Diagnostic (effect to cause): P(Burglary | JohnCalls).
Causal or predictive (cause to effect): P(JohnCalls | Burglary).
Intercausal (explaining away): P(Burglary | Alarm, Earthquake) is lower than P(Burglary | Alarm).
Mixed: combinations of the above, such as P(Alarm | JohnCalls, ¬Earthquake).

formulas.latex: P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid \neg A)P(\neg A)}
formulas.plainText: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) / [P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|not A)P(not A)]
P(x1, ..., xn) = product over i of P(xi | Parents(Xi))
P(X | e) = alpha x sum over hidden y of P(X, e, y)
P(a|b) = P(a AND b) / P(b), for P(b) > 0

notes.text: For Bayes numericals, compute the denominator with total probability first: P(+) = P(+|D)P(D) + P(+|¬D)P(¬D). Then divide the true-positive term by it.
P(A | B) is not P(B | A): a 90% sensitive test does not mean a positive patient is 90% likely to be ill. With a low prior, the posterior can be small.
The arcs of a Bayesian network must form a DAG, and a node's CPT conditions only on its parents; the joint distribution is recovered by multiplying one CPT entry per node.

concepts.text: What Natural Language Processing Is

Natural language processing (NLP) is the branch of AI that enables computers to analyse, understand and produce human (natural) languages such as English or Nepali, in text or speech. It combines computational linguistics (rules about language structure) with statistical and machine-learning models trained on large corpora. NLP has two complementary halves: natural language understanding (NLU), which maps language to meaning, and natural language generation (NLG), which maps meaning to language; speech recognition and speech synthesis sit at the input and output ends.

rows: Smallest unit of sound that distinguishes meaning
Smallest meaningful unit of a word; free (stands alone) or bound (affix)
Dictionary of the words of a language with their parts of speech and meanings
Large structured collection of texts used for training and statistics
Formal rules describing how words combine into sentences
S → NP VP, NP → Det N
Assigning a syntactic structure (parse tree) to a sentence using a grammar
Tree for "The boy ate an apple"
A unit (word, number, punctuation) produced by splitting text

concepts.text: Levels of linguistic knowledge an NLP system uses:
items: Phonology: how sounds form words (needed for speech).
Morphology: how words are built from morphemes (walk, walks, walked).
Syntax: how words are arranged into grammatical sentences.
Semantics: the literal meaning of words and sentences.
Pragmatics: how context and speaker intention change meaning.
Discourse and world knowledge: links between sentences and general facts about the world.

concepts.text: Understanding versus Generation

rows: Text or speech → internal meaning representation
Internal data or meaning → text or speech
Resolving ambiguity: many readings for one sentence
Choosing: one meaning can be said many ways
Parsing, intent detection, information extraction, question understanding
Report writing, summaries, chatbot replies, weather forecasts from data
Generally considered easier because the system controls the input meaning

concepts.text: NLG is usually organised in stages. Content determination decides what information to say; document (text) planning orders and structures it; sentence planning aggregates facts into sentences, chooses words (lexicalisation) and referring expressions such as pronouns; and surface realisation produces grammatically correct final text with proper morphology and punctuation.
Steps of NLP
The classic five-step analysis pipeline (Rich and Knight):
items: Morphological and lexical analysis: split text into sentences and tokens (tokenisation), identify morphemes, stems and lemmas, and look up parts of speech in the lexicon.
Syntactic analysis (parsing): check word order against the grammar and build a parse tree; "Boy the school to goes" is rejected here.

Semantic analysis: assign literal meaning by mapping the structure to objects and relations; a meaningless sentence such as "hot ice cream" or "colourless green ideas sleep furiously" is flagged here.
Discourse integration: interpret a sentence using the sentences before it, e.g. resolving what "it" or "he" refers to.
Pragmatic analysis: reinterpret what was said as what was meant from context and intention; "Can you pass the salt?" is a request, not a question about ability.

concepts.text:
Grammar: S -> NP VP   NP -> Det N   VP -> V NP
Lexicon: Det: the, an   N: boy, apple   V: ate

Parse of "The boy ate an apple":
 S
 +-- NP
 |    +-- Det: The
 |    +-- N:   boy
 +-- VP
      +-- V:   ate
      +-- NP
           +-- Det: an
           +-- N:   apple
Ambiguity

rows: A word has several meanings or parts of speech
bank (river side or financial institution); book (noun or verb)
A sentence has more than one valid parse tree
"Old men and women" (are the women old?); "Visiting relatives can be boring"
The parse is clear but the meaning or scope is not
"Every student read a book" (one book or different books?)
It is unclear what a pronoun or phrase refers to
"The trophy did not fit in the case because it was too big"
The intended use depends on context
"Do you know the time?" (yes/no or a request for the time)

concepts.text: Applications of NLP:
items: Machine translation (English to Nepali, Google Translate) and speech recognition or voice assistants.
Chatbots, question answering and customer-support agents.
Sentiment analysis of reviews and social media; spam and email filtering.
Information extraction and named-entity recognition (people, places, dates); text summarisation.
Spelling and grammar checking, autocomplete and search engines.

concepts.text: Why NLP is hard (challenges):
items: Ambiguity at every level: lexical, syntactic, semantic, referential and pragmatic.
Context dependence and the need for common-sense world knowledge.
Idioms, metaphor, sarcasm and humour whose meaning is not literal.
Variation: informal text, spelling errors, dialects, code-mixing (Nepali written in Roman script mixed with English).
Low-resource and morphologically rich languages such as Nepali, with few annotated corpora.
Language keeps changing: new words, slang and names appear constantly.

formulas.plainText: P(w1...wn) ≈ product over i of P(w_i | w_(i-1))
F1 = 2PR/(P+R), P = TP/(TP+FP), R = TP/(TP+FN)

notes.text: Memorise the pipeline order as Morphological/Lexical → Syntactic → Semantic → Discourse → Pragmatic. Pronoun resolution across sentences belongs to discourse integration; working out the speaker's intention (a question used as a request) belongs to pragmatic analysis.
NLU goes from language to meaning and must resolve ambiguity; NLG goes from meaning to language and must choose among many ways of saying the same thing. Both together make up NLP.

Do not confuse syntactic and semantic ambiguity: if the sentence has two different parse trees ("I saw the man with the telescope") it is syntactic; if a single word has two meanings ("bank") it is lexical.

concepts.text: Machine Vision

Machine (computer) vision is the field of AI that enables a computer to acquire, process and interpret images or video so as to recognise objects and understand a scene. It is often described as the inverse of computer graphics: graphics turns a model into an image, vision recovers a description of the world from an image. The task is hard because projecting a 3D scene onto a 2D image loses depth, and lighting, viewpoint, occlusion and noise all change how the same object looks. In industry the term machine vision usually means camera-based inspection and guidance systems.

rows: A sensor captures the scene; sampling and quantisation give a digital image
CCD or CMOS camera, frame grabber, lighting
Improve the image: remove noise, enhance contrast, correct geometry
Median or Gaussian filters, histogram equalisation
Partition the image into regions or objects of interest
Thresholding, edge detection (Sobel, Canny), region growing
Compute measurable descriptors of each region
Area, perimeter, corners, texture, shape moments, colour histograms
Assign a label to each object from its features
Template matching, nearest neighbour, neural networks and CNNs
Assign meaning to the recognised objects and their relations
Knowledge-based scene analysis, reasoning about context

concepts.text: The stages are often grouped into levels. Low-level vision (acquisition and preprocessing) works on pixels and produces a cleaner image. Mid-level vision (segmentation and feature extraction) turns pixels into regions and descriptors. High-level vision (recognition and interpretation) turns descriptors into labels and a description of the scene, and uses AI reasoning and domain knowledge.

concepts.plainText: Edge strength G = sqrt(Gx^2 + Gy^2), direction theta = arctan(Gy/Gx)

concepts.text: Applications of machine vision:
items: Industrial inspection: detecting defects, measuring parts, reading labels and barcodes on production lines.
Optical character recognition and automatic number-plate recognition.
Face recognition and biometric access control; video surveillance.
Medical image analysis (X-ray, CT, MRI) and remote sensing from satellites.
Autonomous vehicles and robot guidance, e.g. bin picking and navigation.

concepts.text: Robotics

A robot is a machine that senses its environment, decides what to do and acts on the world, working in a sense-think-act loop. The Robot Institute of America defines an industrial robot as a reprogrammable, multifunctional manipulator designed to move material, parts, tools or specialised devices through variable programmed motions for the performance of a variety of tasks. The word robot comes from Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. (Czech robota, forced labour), and Isaac Asimov coined the word robotics. Robotics is embodied AI: it combines perception (vision, sensors), planning and reasoning, and control of motors and power supplies.

rows: Chain of rigid links connected by joints that positions the tool
Device at the wrist that interacts with the work
Gripper, suction cup, welding torch, spray gun
Convert energy into motion at the joints
Electric DC, servo and stepper motors; hydraulic and pneumatic cylinders
Camera, touch, force-torque, proximity, ultrasonic, LIDAR
The brain: runs the program and closes the feedback loop
Microcontroller or computer with control software
Batteries, mains supply, gears, belts, lead screws

concepts.text: Degrees of freedom (DOF) is the number of independent motions a robot can make; each revolute or prismatic joint normally adds one. To place an object at any position (x, y, z) with any orientation (roll, pitch, yaw) in 3D space a manipulator needs at least six DOF, three for position and three for orientation. A robot with more than six DOF is redundant, which lets it avoid obstacles; the human arm has about seven.
Other ways of classifying robots and their applications:
items: Fixed (industrial arms bolted to the floor) versus mobile (wheeled, tracked, legged robots, drones, underwater vehicles).
Autonomous versus teleoperated (remote-controlled, e.g. bomb disposal) versus collaborative robots (cobots) that work beside people.
Industrial robots: welding, painting, assembly, material handling and packaging.
Service and field robots: surgery (da Vinci system), space exploration (Mars rovers), agriculture, warehouses, domestic cleaning, humanoid robots.

concepts.text: Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics (science fiction, but often quoted in AI ethics):
items: First Law: a robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.
Second Law: a robot must obey orders given by human beings, except where such orders conflict with the First Law.
Third Law: a robot must protect its own existence as long as this does not conflict with the First or Second Law.
A later Zeroth Law places humanity as a whole above the individual: a robot may not harm humanity.
